In plain words first The idea in one line Hybrid memory runs three stores in parallel — vector for semantic similarity, KV for fast fact lookup, graph for entity-relationship reasoning — with a scoring layer that fuses them on retrieval. This is a widely used production pattern for external memory; Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) is one reference implementation. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Hybrid memory "Vector plus graph plus KV" Three stores written in parallel, fused on retrieval Fact extraction "Memory ingestion" LLM step that breaks text into (entity, relation, fact) tuples Fusion scoring "Relevance ranking" Weighted sum of relevance, importance, recency Scope "Memory namespace" user / session / agent — determines who sees what Mem0g "Memory graph" Typed edges with temporal validity for relationship queries Temporal invalidation "Soft delete" Mark contradicted edges invalid; never delete Embedding drift "Retrieval rot" Vector quality degrades as corpus grows; re-embed periodically From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Lesson 14.65 · Memory II: long-term, episodic and procedural memory Lesson 14.105 · Memory: trimming threads and the long-term store The problem In plain words first Memory questions come in different shapes. "What did we discuss about deadlines?" needs similarity search over past notes (a vector store finds text with similar meaning). "What is her phone number?" needs an exact lookup (a key-value store, like a dictionary). "Who else works on her project?" needs relationships (a graph store of who-is-connected-to-what). Mem0 keeps all three behind one add and one search , uses a language model to pull facts out of each message and decide whether each one is new, an update, or already known, and ranks results by a weighted mix of relevance, importance and recency. This lesson builds the three stores and the ranking in plain Python, then swaps in real embeddings and a real model for the write path, and checks what each change does. Each store is right for only one of three query classes: Semantic similarity — "what did we discuss about agent drift last week?" Vector wins; KV and graph miss. Fact lookup — "what is the user's phone number?" KV wins; vector is wasteful, graph is overkill. Relationship reasoning — "which customers share the same billing entity?" Graph wins; vector and KV cannot answer. Production agents issue all three in one session. A single-store memory is always wrong for two of them. Mem0's contribution is wiring all three behind a single add / search surface with a scoring function that fuses them. Idea 1 · Three stores in parallel Mem0 (arXiv:2504.19413, April 2025) on add(text, user_id, metadata) : Extract candidate facts from the text (an LLM-driven step). Write each fact to the vector store (embedding) for semantic search. Write each fact to the KV store keyed on (user_id, fact_type, entity) for lookup. Write each fact to the graph store (Mem0g) as typed edges for relationship queries. On search(query, user_id) : Vector store returns top-k by embedding cosine. KV store returns direct hits keyed on query-derived (user_id, type, entity). Graph store returns subgraph reachable from query entities. A scoring layer fuses the three. Idea 2 · Fusion scoring Copy Relevance — vector cosine, KV exact match, graph path weight. Importance — tagged at write time or learned (some facts matter more: names, IDs, policies). Recency — exponential decay over time since last write or read. Weights are tuned per product. Higher w_recency for chat agents; higher w_importance for compliance agents; higher w_relevance for retrieval agents. Idea 3 · Mem0g and temporal reasoning Mem0g adds a conflict detector. When a new fact contradicts an existing edge, the existing edge is marked invalid but not deleted. Temporal queries ("what was the user's city in March?") traverse the valid-at-time subgraph. This is the compliance-grade behavior Letta's invalidation pattern generalizes. Idea 4 · Benchmark numbers Mem0's April 2026 algorithm update reports, from its own evaluation: LoCoMo (long-form conversation memory): 92.5 LongMemEval (long-horizon episodic memory): 94.4 BEAM (1M-token memory benchmark): 64.1 (48.6 at 10M tokens) These are vendor-reported numbers. In the 2025 paper's own LOCOMO comparison, answering from the full conversation scored higher than Mem0 (72.9 against 66.9 on the LLM-judge metric) but used about 15 times as many tokens per question. Benchmarks alone don't justify choice — operational shape does — but the numbers show the fusion design is not a rounding error. Idea 5 · Scope taxonomy Mem0 splits memory by scope: User memory — persists across sessions, keyed on user_id . Session memory — persists within one thread. Agent memory — per-agent instance state. Every write picks one scope. Retrieval can query across scopes with per-scope weights. Mixing scopes without thought is how you get "the assistant told Alice about Bob's project" incidents. Idea 6 · Where this pattern goes wrong Embedding drift. Vector results that look right on the first hundred queries degrade as the corpus grows. Add periodic re-embedding of the top-N-used records. KV schema creep. (user_id, type, entity) looks simple until every team adds their own type . Audit the type set quarterly. Graph explosion. One noisy extractor adds 50 edges per message. Cap graph writes per add call; drop low-confidence edges. The same idea as a formula Fused score. Embeddings fix both paraphrases and the lesson's "where does ava live", but lose "what is ava building", because the small embedding model scores "ava lives in Berlin" closer to that question than the curriculum note. Better retrieval is not uniformly better on every query, which is why retrieval changes need an evaluation set rather than a few spot checks. Solution B1 · Invented facts in long-term memory Invented facts become "known" facts. Every later session retrieves them and the assistant tailors answers to a 25-year-old male software developer who may not exist: wrong recommendations, wrong tone, and, because one of the invented facts is a sensitive attribute (gender), a privacy problem if the memory is ever shown to the user or used for decisions. Noise such as "Thanks" also dilutes retrieval, and duplicates such as Berlin and Lisbon side by side make answers contradict each other. Checks for the write path: require each extracted fact to be supported by a span of the message (reject anything not grounded in the text); use a strict output schema and drop items that fail it; block sensitive categories unless the user explicitly asks you to remember them; require a minimum length and a subject; log the source message and session with every write; and evaluate the extractor on labelled conversations before deploying it, with a capable model if the small one fails, as it does here. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design You own the memory layer for three products on one platform: a consumer chat assistant, a compliance review agent and a research retrieval agent. The memory system runs a vector store, a key-value store and a graph store in parallel and fuses their results. How do you configure the fusion for each product, and which one scoping mistake would get you paged? Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The fused score is a weighted sum of relevance, importance and recency, and the weights are tuned per product: recency up for the chat assistant, importance up for the compliance agent, relevance up for the retrieval agent. Each store wins a query class the others miss, so the weights steer which class dominates without dropping a store. The paging mistake is a scope leak: every write picks the user, the session or the agent scope, and a retrieval that mixes scopes without per-scope weights tells one user about another user's project. Why three stores. Query class Example Winner Semantic similarity what did we discuss about drift last week vector Fact lookup the user's phone number key-value, keyed on user, fact type and entity Relationship reasoning which customers share a billing entity graph, as typed edges A single store is wrong for two of the three classes. A write extracts facts from the text and writes each one to all three stores; a search runs all three and fuses. The fusion. The score is w_relevance * relevance + w_importance * importance + w_recency * recency . Relevance is the cosine, the exact key match or the graph path weight. Importance is tagged at write time or learned. Recency decays with time since the last write or read. It is a weighted sum and not a hierarchy, because a hierarchy would make two of the three classes wait on the wrong store. Product Weight to raise Why Chat assistant recency the last few turns matter most Compliance agent importance names, ids and policies outrank chatter Retrieval agent relevance the question decides, not the clock Temporal truth for compliance. When a new fact contradicts a graph edge, the old edge is marked invalid and never deleted. A question about what was true in March traverses the edges valid at that time. The compliance agent depends on this. The scope rule. Each write picks one scope: user memory persists across sessions, session memory lives in one thread, agent memory is per instance. Retrieval can read across scopes with per-scope weights, but a search that mixes them without thought is how an assistant tells one user about another user's project. Maintenance that scales with the corpus. Vector results drift as the corpus grows; re-embed the most used records on a schedule. The key-value type set creeps as teams add types; audit it quarterly. A noisy extractor adds dozens of edges per message; cap graph writes per add and drop low-confidence edges. Plausible wrong answers. "One vector store is enough, embeddings capture everything." A fact lookup is wasteful on a vector store and a relationship query is impossible on one. "Set the weights once for the platform." Chat wants recency, compliance wants importance, retrieval wants relevance; one setting is wrong for two of the three. "Delete the old fact when a new one contradicts it." Mark it invalid and keep it, or the temporal query loses its history. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which query class does each store win? Expected: vector for semantic similarity, key-value for a fact lookup, graph for relationship reasoning. (level 4) Why a weighted sum and not vector first with fallbacks? Expected: each store wins a different class; a hierarchy makes two of three classes wait on the wrong store. (level 4) The compliance agent asks what was true in March. Which store answers, and how? Expected: the graph, by traversing the edges valid at that time; contradicted edges are marked invalid and kept. (level 4) Which failure grows with the corpus, and what is the maintenance? Expected: embedding drift in the vector store; re-embed the most used records periodically, audit the key-value type set quarterly, and cap graph writes per add. Where it is taught. In plain words first The idea in one line Voyager (Wang et al., TMLR 2024) treats executable code as a skill. Skills are named, retrievable, composable, and refined by environment feedback. This is the reference architecture for Claude Agent SDK skills, skillkit, and the 2026 skill-library pattern. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Skill "Reusable capability" Named chunk of code + description, retrievable by similarity Skill library "Agent memory of how-to" Persistent store of skills, searchable and composable Curriculum "Task proposer" Bottom-up goal generator driven by current capability gap Composition "Skill DAG" Skills invoking skills; topologically sorted on execution Iterative refinement "Self-correcting loop" Env feedback + errors + self-verification fold back into the next version Action-space-as-code "Programmatic actions" Emit functions, not primitive commands, for temporally extended behavior Dedup on write "Skill collapse" Near-duplicate descriptions collapse to one canonical skill From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Lesson 14.65 · Memory II: long-term, episodic and procedural memory The problem In plain words first An agent that solves every task from scratch keeps relearning the same things. Voyager , an agent that played Minecraft, kept what it learned as a skill library : every time it got something working, it saved the working code as a named function with a description. For a new task it looked up the most similar skills, called them from new code, and if the new code failed it read the error and rewrote it. Skills stack: "make an iron pickaxe" calls "mine ore" and "place a crafting table". Today's agent skills (folders of instructions and scripts that an agent loads when a task matches their description) are the same idea. This lesson builds a skill library in plain Python, then lets a real small model write, test, store and reuse skills. Agents that rebuild every capability from scratch in every session do three things wrong: Waste tokens. Every task re-elicits the same reasoning. Lose progress. A correction learned in session A doesn't transfer to session B. Fail on long-horizon composition. Complex tasks need capability hierarchies; one-shot prompts cannot express them. Voyager's answer: treat each reusable capability as a named chunk of code stored in a library, retrievable by similarity, composable with other skills, and refined by execution feedback. Idea 1 · Three components Voyager (arXiv:2305.16291) structures an agent around: Automatic curriculum. A curiosity-driven proposer picks the next task based on the agent's current skill set and environment state. Exploration is bottom-up. Skill library. Each skill is executable code. New skills are added when a task succeeds. Skills are retrieved by query-to-description similarity. Iterative prompting mechanism. On failure, the agent receives execution errors, environment feedback, and self-verification output, then refines the skill. The Minecraft evaluation (Wang et al., 2024): 3.3x more unique items, 8.5x faster stone tools, 6.4x faster iron tools, 2.3x longer map traversal versus baselines. The numbers are Minecraft-specific, but the pattern transfers. Idea 2 · Action space = code Most agents emit primitive commands. Voyager emits JavaScript functions. A skill is: Copy Composed from sub-skills. Stored keyed on description and embedding. Retrieved as a program, not a prompt. This is the 2026 Claude Agent SDK skill: a named, retrievable chunk of code plus instructions the agent loads on demand. Idea 3 · Skill retrieval New task "make a diamond pickaxe." Agent: Embeds the task description. Queries the skill library for top-k similar skills. Retrieves craftIronPickaxe , mineDiamond , placeCraftingTable etc. Composes the new skill from retrieved primitives + new logic. This is the pattern MCP resources (Phase 13) and Agent SDK skills implement: retrieval over a knowledge/code surface, scoped to the current task. Idea 4 · Iterative refinement Voyager's feedback loop: Agent writes a skill. Skill runs against the environment. One of three signals returns: success , error (with stack trace), self-verification failure . Agent rewrites the skill using the signal as context. Loop until success or max rounds. This is Self-Refine ( Lesson 14.5 ) applied to code generation with environment-grounded verification. CRITIC ( Lesson 14.5 ) is the same pattern with external tools as the verifier. Idea 5 · Curriculum and exploration Voyager's curriculum module proposes tasks like "build a shelter near the lake" based on what the agent has and what it has not yet done. The proposer uses the environment state + skill inventory to pick a task just above current capability — the exploration sweet spot. For production agents this translates to a "what's missing" operator: given the current skill library and a domain, what skills are we not yet covering? Teams typically implement this manually as curriculum review. Idea 6 · Where this pattern goes wrong Skill library rot. Same skill added 10 times with slightly different descriptions. Add deduplication on write; retrieval returns only one. Composed-skill drift. Parent skill depends on a child that was refined. Version skills; a parent pinned to v1 doesn't magically pick up v3. Retrieval quality. Vector retrieval over skill descriptions degrades as the library grows past a few hundred. Supplement with tag filters and hard constraints ("only skills with category=tooling "). Lesson 14.63 · Planning and reasoning patterns: ReAct, plan-and-execute, reflection and search The problem In plain words first Some plans must be right by construction: a deployment that applies a database migration before taking a backup is not "mostly fine". A Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planner guarantees this by working from explicit rules: operators are basic actions with preconditions (what must be true before) and effects (what becomes true after), and methods say how to break a big task into smaller ones. The planner only accepts a sequence in which every precondition holds. ChatHTN adds a language model only where the rules run out: if no method covers a task, the model suggests a breakdown, and the planner checks it against the rules before using it. AlphaEvolve is a different pairing: models propose changes to a program and an automatic scorer keeps the best. This lesson builds both in plain Python and puts a real small model in ChatHTN's seat. ReWOO ( Lesson 14.2 ), Plan-and-Execute, and ReAct cover most agent planning. Two cases they don't cover well: Plans with provable correctness. Scheduling, flight pathing, compliance workflows — the plan must be sound by construction. A fluent LLM plan that sometimes hallucinates a step is unacceptable. Optimizations with a machine-checkable fitness function. Matrix multiplication, scheduling heuristics, compiler passes — the goal is not "a correct plan" but "the best plan." HTN planning and AlphaEvolve solve the two different problems. Both use LLMs as amplifiers, not replacements. Idea 1 · Hierarchical Task Networks An HTN is: Tasks — compound (to be decomposed) and primitive (directly executable). Methods — ways to decompose a compound task into subtasks, with preconditions. Operators — primitive actions with preconditions and effects. State — a set of facts. Planning: given a goal task and an initial state, find a decomposition into primitive operators whose preconditions are satisfied in sequence. HTN is older than LLMs and still the reference for provably-correct plans. Idea 2 · ChatHTN (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2025) ChatHTN (arXiv:2505.11814) interleaves symbolic HTN with LLM queries: Try to decompose the current compound task with existing methods. If no method applies, ask the LLM: "how would you decompose task in state s ?" Translate the LLM response into candidate subtasks. Validate against the operator schema; reject invalid decompositions. Recurse. The paper's central claim: every plan produced is provably sound because LLM suggestions only enter as candidate decompositions, never as direct plan edits. The symbolic layer owns correctness; the LLM expands the method library. Online method learning (arXiv:2511.12901, November 2025) adds a learner that generalizes LLM-produced decompositions into reusable methods, reducing the number of LLM calls while solving at least as many problems. Idea 3 · AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) AlphaEvolve (arXiv:2506.13131, DeepMind, June 2025) is a different beast: evolutionary code search orchestrated by a Gemini 2.0 Flash/Pro ensemble. Loop: Start with a seed program + a programmatic evaluator (returns a fitness score). Ensemble of LLMs proposes mutations. Run mutations through the evaluator. Keep the best; mutate again. Published wins: First improvement over Strassen for 4x4 complex matrix multiplication in 56 years (48 scalar multiplications). 0.7% recovered Google compute via a Borg scheduling heuristic. 32% FlashAttention speedup on a frontier workload. The hard constraint: the fitness function must be machine-checkable. Evolutionary search over prose answers does not converge. Idea 4 · When to use which Problem class Use Why Scheduling with hard constraints HTN + ChatHTN Provable soundness Compiler optimization AlphaEvolve Machine-checkable fitness Multi-step task execution ReAct / ReWOO LLM in the loop, no formal guarantees Code improvement with tests AlphaEvolve Tests are the evaluator Policy-bound automation HTN Preconditions encode policy Idea 5 · Where this pattern goes wrong HTN without operators. Without precondition/effect schemas the soundness claim collapses. ChatHTN's "LLM suggests decomposition" requires the schema to reject invalid moves. AlphaEvolve without a real evaluator. "Ask the LLM if the code is better" is not a fitness function. The evaluator must be deterministic and fast. Over-engineering. Most agent tasks don't need either. Reach for ReAct or ReWOO first. Solutions Solution P1 · One accepted, none correct The lesson's planner accepts one suggestion ( open_editor , write_tests for ship_feature_with_migration ) and rejects the other two because a precondition fails during simulation. Solution B1 · A cached bad method The decomposition is stored in cached_methods even though it fails, because the lesson's code caches as soon as every step name is known. On every later call, plan() finds no matching method, finds the cached entry, expands it, fails the same precondition and returns None , without ever consulting the model again. A transient bad answer has become a permanent failure for that task, and the logs show "no plan" with no hint that the cache is the cause. Validate before caching: simulate the decomposition from the current state, check that it reaches the task's goal, and only then store it, ideally with the state conditions under which it worked (that is what makes it a method, with preconditions, rather than a fixed sequence). Give cache entries a way to be evicted when they fail. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.62 · Workflow patterns The problem In plain words first Not every job needs an "agent" that decides its own steps. Often a fixed recipe written in ordinary code works better: call the model, check the result, call it again with the next prompt. Anthropic's widely cited 2024 guide names five such recipes, or workflows . Chaining : one call's output feeds the next. Routing : classify the input, then send it to the right handler. Parallelization : run several calls at once and combine them, by splitting the work or by voting. Orchestrator-workers : one call decides which sub-tasks to hand out. Evaluator-optimizer : one call drafts, another grades, repeat. This lesson builds all five in plain Python, then tests the two most common, routing and voting, with real models on twenty support messages. Teams reach for multi-agent frameworks for problems that want a single function call. The cost is real: frameworks add layers that obscure prompts, hide control flow, and invite premature complexity. Schluntz and Zhang's Dec 2024 post is the most-cited industry pushback: start simple, add complexity only when it earns its cost. Idea 1 · Workflows vs agents Workflow. LLMs and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths. Engineers own the graph. Agent. LLMs dynamically direct their own tools and take their own steps. The model owns the graph. Both have their place. Workflows are cheaper, faster, and easier to debug. Agents unlock open-ended problems but make failure modes harder to reason about. Idea 2 · The augmented LLM Foundation for all five patterns: one LLM with three capabilities wired in — search (retrieval), tools (actions), memory (persistence). Any API call can use these. Idea 3 · The five patterns Prompt chaining. Output of call 1 is input to call 2. Use when a task has a clean linear decomposition. Optional programmatic gates between steps. Routing. A classifier LLM picks which downstream LLM or tool to invoke. Use when categorically different inputs need different handling (tier-1 support vs refund vs bug vs sales). Parallelization. Run N LLM calls concurrently, aggregate results. Two shapes: sectioning (different chunks) and voting (same prompt, N runs, majority/synthesis). Orchestrator-workers. An orchestrator LLM dynamically decides which workers (also LLMs) to run and synthesizes their output. Similar to agent loops but the orchestrator does not loop indefinitely. Evaluator-optimizer. One LLM proposes an answer, another LLM evaluates it. Iterate until the evaluator passes. This is Self-Refine ( Lesson 14.5 ) generalized. Idea 4 · Where workflows beat agents Predictable tasks. If you can enumerate the steps, you should. Cost-bound tasks. Workflows have bounded step counts; agents can spiral. Compliance-bound tasks. Auditors want to read the graph, not infer it from trajectories. Idea 5 · Where agents beat workflows Open-ended research. When the next step depends on what the last step returned. Variable-length tasks. Minutes to hours of work where step count is unknown. Novel domains. When you don't yet know the right workflow — exploration first, codify later. Idea 6 · The context-engineering companion "Effective context engineering for AI agents" (Anthropic 2025) formalizes the adjacent discipline: the 200k window is a budget, not a container. What to include, when to compact, when to let context grow. Lesson 11.5 (context engineering) covers it in detail. The same idea as a formula Routing is a classifier followed by a lookup: ​ ( x ) . Its accuracy bounds the whole workflow: a wrong label sends the message to a handler that cannot help, however good that handler is. Voting. If voters are independent and each is right with probability 1 ​ on a two-way choice, the majority is right with probability ​ = k > n /2 ∑ ​ ( k n ​ ) p k ( 1 − p ) n − k , which grows towards 1 with . Before you start Needs : Phase 14 · 01 (Agent Loop), Phase 14 · 12 (Workflow Patterns) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Agent is a state machine; nodes are functions; edges are transitions; state is checkpointed after each node. Resume from any failure at the last successful checkpoint. LangGraph is the 2026 reference for this model of low-level stateful orchestration. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means State graph "Agent as state machine" Typed state + nodes + edges + reducers Checkpointer "Persistence backend" Serializes state after every node; enables resume Reducer "State merger" Function that combines current state with a node's update Conditional edge "Branch" Edge chosen by a function of state Subgraph "Nested graph" A graph used as a node inside another graph Durable execution "Resume from failure" Restart at the last successful node with exact state Supervisor "Router LLM" Central dispatcher for specialist subagents Swarm "P2P agents" Agents hand off via shared tools; no central router From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Lesson 14.100 · Execution graphs from scratch Lesson 14.101 · LangGraph StateGraph: state, nodes, edges and reducers Lesson 14.102 · Routing, loops and the agent as a graph Lesson 14.103 · Persistence: checkpoints, threads, resume and time travel Lesson 14.104 · Human in the loop: interrupt and Command Lesson 14.115 · Inside the LangGraph runtime: supersteps, channels, checkpoints and durability The problem In plain words first A long agent run that crashes at step 38 should continue from step 38, not start again and repeat (and re-pay for) the first 37. LangGraph organises an agent as a graph : nodes are functions that each update a shared, typed state , and edges say which node runs next, possibly depending on the state. After each step it saves a checkpoint (a snapshot of the state) to a store such as SQLite or Postgres, under a thread id . Resuming is running the same thread again; pausing for a person to approve something is a node that waits; going back in time is starting from an earlier snapshot. This lesson builds a small graph runner in plain Python, then runs the same ticket graph in real LangGraph, kills the process mid-run, and resumes it from the database. Agents and workflows share a problem: when a 40-step run fails at step 38, you want to resume from step 38, not start over. Second-class state models leave operators hacking retries around a library that assumes fresh runs. LangGraph's design answer: state is a first-class typed object, mutations are explicit, and checkpoints persist after every node. Resuming is invoking the graph again with the same thread id. Idea 1 · The graph A graph is defined by: State type. A typed dict (or Pydantic model) that every node reads and mutates. Nodes. Pure functions (state) -> state_update . Updates are merged into state after return. Edges. Conditional or direct transitions between nodes. Entry and exit. START and END sentinel nodes mark the boundary. Example: an agent with classify , refund , bug , sales , done nodes — a routing workflow as a graph. Idea 2 · Durable execution After each node returns, the runtime serializes the state and writes it to a checkpointer (SQLite, Postgres, Redis, custom). On failure at step N, the runtime can resume(session_id) and pick up from step N+1 with exact state. The LangGraph docs explicitly highlight production users where this matters: Klarna, Uber, J.P. Morgan. The claim isn't the graph shape; it's that the graph shape plus checkpointing makes recovery cheap. Idea 3 · Streaming Every node can yield partial output. The graph streams per-node-delta events to the caller so UIs update as the graph runs. Idea 4 · Human-in-the-loop Inspect and modify state between nodes. Implementations: pause before a critical node, surface state to a human, accept modifications, resume. The checkpointer makes this easy because state is already serialized. Idea 5 · Memory Short-term (within a run — conversation history in state) and long-term (across runs — persistent via the checkpointer plus a separate long-term store). LangGraph integrates with external memory systems (Mem0, custom) via tools. Idea 6 · Three topologies Supervisor. Central router LLM dispatches to specialist subagents. create_supervisor() in langgraph-supervisor (though the LangChain team in 2026 recommends doing this through tool calls directly for more context control). Swarm / peer-to-peer. Agents hand off directly via a shared tool surface. No central router. Hierarchical. Supervisors managing sub-supervisors, implemented as nested subgraphs. Idea 7 · Where this pattern goes wrong Checkpoints too small. Only checkpointing conversation turns leaves tool state and memory writes unrecoverable. Full state must serialize. Non-deterministic nodes. Resume assumes node inputs produce the same state update. Random seeds, wall-clock, external APIs must be captured. Over-use of conditional edges. A graph with every edge conditional is a state machine that cannot be reasoned about. Prefer linear chains with occasional branches. The same idea as a formula A step. With state ​ , the node ​ chosen by the edges, and a reducer that merges its update: ​ = s t ​ ⊕ n t ​ ( s t ​ ) , n t + 1 ​ = edge ( n t ​ , s t + 1 ​ ) , and the checkpointer stores ​ = ( s t ​ , n t ​ ) for the thread. What a crash costs. If the process dies during step and the last durable checkpoint is ​ ( ), resuming re-runs steps . Durable writes after every step make : only the step that was interrupted runs again. That step runs at least once , so its side effects must be idempotent. Durability modes in LangGraph decide when ​ reaches the store: exit (only when the run ends), async (in the background while the next step runs; the default) or sync (before the next step starts). Worked example Counting re-runs in the crash below The graph runs classify, then bug; the process is killed inside bug (step 2). exit : nothing is written until the run ends, and this run never ended. The thread is empty: resuming fails with EmptyInputError , and the whole run must start again from the user's input. sync : the checkpoint after classify was committed before bug started, so and the resume re-runs only bug. Classify, which loads a model, runs once. async : the checkpoint after classify is being written while bug runs. If the crash wins the race, the last durable checkpoint is the input and classify runs again; if the write wins, only bug does. The trial count in the output shows how often the crash won. In every mode human_gate runs twice: once to raise the interrupt, once when the answer arrives. A node that pauses with interrupt() restarts from its beginning on resume, so code before the interrupt must be safe to repeat. Solutions Solution P1 · It depends on the durability mode With exit , nothing was saved, so there is nothing to resume: the run starts over from the input (or, as in the lab, the resume fails because no input is given). With sync , only bug runs again. With async , the default, it depends on timing: bug always, and classify too whenever the crash beat the background write of the checkpoint after classify. The interrupted node repeats in every mode. Solution B1 · A refund issued twice On resume the refund node runs again from the top, because its checkpoint was never written: it calls the payment API a second time and the customer is refunded twice. No durability mode prevents this; checkpoints are taken between steps, and the crash happened inside one. Make the side effect idempotent: send an idempotency key derived from the thread and ticket (for example refund-{thread_id} ) so the payment provider ignores the duplicate; or split the node so that one step records the intent in the state, a second step performs the call with the key, and a third records the result. For irreversible actions, put the human approval before the call, not after. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Actor "Agent" Private state + inbox + handler; no shared memory Message "Event" Typed payload; the only way actors interact Inbox "Mailbox" Per-actor queue of pending messages Runtime "Agent host" Event loop that routes messages and isolates failures Topic "Channel" Named publish-subscribe route between actors Fault isolation "Let it crash" One actor failing does not crash others RoundRobinGroupChat "Fixed-rotation team" Agents take turns in order SelectorGroupChat "Context-routed team" Selector picks who goes next Magentic-One "Reference team" Multi-agent squad for web + code + files From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Lesson 14.121 · Microsoft Agent Framework The problem In plain words first In most agent code one agent calls another like a function and waits; if the callee crashes, the caller crashes too. The actor model , used by AutoGen v0.4 and later, works differently. Each agent is an actor : it keeps its own state private, has an inbox , and reacts to one message at a time. Agents never call each other directly; they send messages, and a runtime delivers them. A crash in one actor's handler stays in that actor, many messages can be in flight at once, and moving an actor to another machine only changes how messages travel. This lesson builds a small actor runtime in plain Python, then runs the same reviewer as a real AutoGen actor and gives it a language-model twin. Most agent frameworks are synchronous: one agent produces, one agent consumes, in a call stack. Failures crash the stack. Concurrency is bolted on. Distribution requires rewriting. AutoGen v0.4's answer: the actor model. Each agent is an actor with a private inbox. Messages are the only interaction. The runtime decouples delivery from handling. Failures isolate to one actor. Concurrency is native. Distribution is just different transport. Idea 1 · Actors An actor has: A private state (never directly touched from outside). An inbox (message queue). A handler: receive(message) -> effects where effects can be "reply," "send to other actor," "spawn new actor," "update state," "stop self." Two actors cannot share memory. They can only send messages. Idea 2 · Three API layers AutoGen v0.4 splits its surface into three: Core. Low-level actor framework. AgentRuntime , Agent , Message , Topic . Async message exchange, event-driven. AgentChat. Task-driven high-level API (replacement for v0.2's ConversableAgent). AssistantAgent , UserProxyAgent , RoundRobinGroupChat , SelectorGroupChat . Extensions. Integrations — OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure, tools, memory. Idea 3 · Why decoupling matters In the v0.2 model, calling agent_a.chat(agent_b) synchronously blocks agent_a until agent_b returns. In v0.4, send(agent_b, msg) puts the message in agent_b's inbox and returns. The runtime delivers later. Three consequences: Fault isolation. Agent B crashing does not crash Agent A — the runtime catches the failure in B's handler and decides what to do (log, retry, dead-letter). Natural concurrency. Many messages in flight at once; actors process their inbox concurrently. Distribution-ready. Inbox + transport is the same abstraction whether the actor is in-process or on another host. Idea 4 · Topologies RoundRobinGroupChat. Agents take turns in a fixed rotation. SelectorGroupChat. A selector agent picks who goes next based on conversation context. Magentic-One. Reference multi-agent team for web browsing, code execution, file handling. Built on AgentChat. Idea 5 · Observability OpenTelemetry support is built in. Every message emits a span; tool calls carry gen_ai.* attributes per the 2026 OTel GenAI semantic conventions ( Lesson 14.23 ). Idea 6 · Status: maintenance mode Early 2026: AutoGen v0.7.x is stable for research and prototyping. Microsoft has shifted active development to the Microsoft Agent Framework, the production successor (public preview from 1 October 2025; version 1.0 shipped in April 2026). AutoGen patterns port forward cleanly — the actor model is the durable idea. The same idea as a formula An actor is a state and a handler . A message produces a new state and a set of outgoing messages: , { m 1 ​ , … , m k ​ }) = h ( σ , m ) . The runtime is the only thing that moves messages between inboxes. Two delivery styles. A direct send is a request with a reply, ​ ( σ B ​ , m ) , and an exception in ​ becomes an exception at the sender. A publish to a topic delivers to every subscriber with no reply; a failure stays with the subscriber that failed. Why many messages in flight helps. With independent requests that each wait on something slow (a model call, a network round trip) and a worker pool of size , the elapsed time drops from about to about , if the waiting really can overlap. Worked example What the reviewer's crash costs in each style Direct send of CrashMe : the reviewer raises; the runtime hands the RuntimeError back to the sender, which must catch it. Every other request is unaffected. Publish of Review , CrashMe , Review : the crash is logged by the runtime and dropped; the publisher sees nothing, and both reviews are handled. So "fault isolation" means different things: with send, the failure is isolated and reported ; with publish, it is isolated and silent unless you watch the logs or route failures to a dead-letter queue, as the lesson's runtime does. Concurrency here: ten model reviews of about 1.5 s each, sent at once, still take about 15 s, because two CPU cores run one model call at a time. Overlap needs a resource that can actually serve requests in parallel, such as a model server with batching. Solutions Solution P1 · Reported on send, silent on publish On a direct send, the caller gets the exception: await runtime.send_message(CrashMe(), ...) raises RuntimeError: simulated handler failure , and it must be caught. On publish, the publisher sees nothing; the runtime logs the failure, drops that message, and the reviews before and after it are still handled. Both are fault isolation; only the first tells you about the fault. Solution B1 · Silent failures They see nothing wrong. Every publish returns normally, the long snippets simply get no verdict, and any dashboard that counts "reviews requested" looks healthy. Unreviewed code then flows through as if it had been checked, which is worse than an outage because nobody knows. Make failures visible: catch exceptions in the handler and publish an explicit failure message (or a verdict of "not reviewed"), collect them in a dead-letter queue with the original message, alert on its size, and have downstream steps treat "no verdict" as "not approved". For this specific failure, check the input length before calling the model and split or reject long inputs explicitly. Before you start Needs : Phase 14 · 12 (Workflow Patterns), Phase 14 · 14 (Actor Model) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Four primitives: Agent, Task, Crew, Process. Two top-level shapes: Crews (autonomous, role-based collaboration) and Flows (event-driven, deterministic). CrewAI is the 2026 reference implementation, and its docs are blunt: "for any production-ready application, start with a Flow." Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Agent "Persona" Role + goal + backstory + tools Task "Unit of work" Description + expected output + assignee + optional structured output Crew "Agent team" Container for Agents + Tasks + Process Process "Execution strategy" Sequential / Hierarchical / Consensus (planned) Flow "Deterministic workflow" Event-driven, code-owned, testable Backstory "Persona prompt" Tone and judgment shaper for the Agent @tool "Function tool" Decorator that turns a function into a tool the Agent can call BaseTool "Class tool" Class-based tool with args schema, retries, async support Entity memory "Per-entity facts" Memory scoped to a customer / account / issue Long-term memory "Cross-run memory" Vector-backed memory that survives between kickoffs Contextual memory "Just-in-time retrieval" Memory pulled at the moment the Agent needs it Manager LLM "Router agent" Extra LLM in Hierarchical process that picks the next task expected_output "Task contract" String that tells the Agent (and audit) what shape to return From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.122 · CrewAI The problem In plain words first CrewAI describes a multi-agent system the way you would describe a small team. Each agent has a role, a goal and a backstory ("Researcher: you only report what the notes say"), and optionally tools. Each task says what to do, what a good result looks like, and which agent does it. A crew runs the tasks either in a fixed order ( sequential ) or with a manager deciding who goes next ( hierarchical ). CrewAI also has flows : ordinary Python steps that you wire together, which can call a crew where open-ended work helps. The trade is autonomy against control: crews decide more on their own, flows are predictable and testable. This lesson builds a miniature version of all of these in plain Python, then runs real CrewAI on a local small model and counts what each shape costs. Teams adopting multi-agent frameworks hit the same wall. "Autonomous collaboration" sounds great in a demo. Then a customer files a bug and you need deterministic replay. Or finance asks how much an LLM-routed crew costs per run. Or on-call needs to know which agent stalled at 3 AM. Free-form LLM-routed crews answer none of those cleanly. Pure DAGs answer them all but lose the exploratory shape a brainstorming agent needs. CrewAI's split is honest about the trade. Crews for collaborative, role-based, exploratory work. Flows for event-driven, code-owned, auditable production. Same framework, two shapes, pick per surface. Idea 1 · Four primitives CrewAI's surface is small. Memorize this and the rest is config. Agent. role + goal + backstory + tools + (optional) llm . The backstory is load-bearing. It shapes tone, judgment, when the agent stops. Tools are functions the agent can call (more below). Task. description + expected_output + agent + (optional) context + (optional) output_pydantic . A reusable unit of work. expected_output is the contract. context lists upstream tasks whose outputs are passed in. output_pydantic forces a structured shape. Crew. Container. Owns the list of agents , the list of tasks , the process , and optional memory + verbose + manager_llm settings. Process. Execution strategy. Sequential, Hierarchical, Consensus (planned). Picks the shape of the run. Agents do not see each other directly. Tasks reference agents. The Crew sequences tasks. The Process decides who picks the next task. That is the whole mental model. Checked against CrewAI 1.15 (November 2026), whose Process offers only sequential and hierarchical . Newer versions may rename or merge process types; check the CrewAI Processes docs before relying on a specific shape. Idea 2 · Sequential vs Hierarchical vs Consensus Sequential. Tasks run in declaration order. Output of task N is available as context to task N+1. Lowest cost. Most predictable. Use when the order is fixed. Hierarchical. A manager Agent (separate LLM call) routes between specialists. CrewAI spawns the manager either from your manager_llm config or a default. The manager picks the next task each round and can refuse or re-route. Use when you have four or more specialists and order genuinely depends on prior output. Consensus. Planned, not currently implemented in the public API. The docs reserve the name for a future voting-based process. Do not rely on it today. Hierarchical adds a per-round LLM call (the manager) on top of every specialist call. Token cost can triple on a five-step run. Pay for it only when you need the routing. Idea 3 · Crews vs Flows This is the framing the docs lead with in 2026. Crew. LLM-driven autonomy. The framework picks the shape at runtime. Good for: research, brainstorming, first drafts, anywhere the path is part of the answer. Hard to replay. Hard to test. Cheap to prototype. Flow. Event-driven graph you own. @start marks the entry. @listen(topic) marks a step that fires when another step emits that topic. Each step is plain Python (can call a Crew internally). Good for: production. Observable. Testable. Deterministic. The docs' 2026 production recommendation: start with a Flow. Fold Crews in as Crew.kickoff() calls from inside Flow steps when autonomy earns its cost. The Flow gives you the audit trail, the Crew gives you the exploration. Compose, do not pick. Idea 4 · Tool integration Three ways to give an Agent a tool. Pick the simplest one that fits. @tool decorator. Pure functions become tools. Signature is the schema; docstring is the description the LLM sees. Best for one-off helpers. ```python from crewai.tools import tool @tool("Search the web") def search(query: str) -> str: """Return top results for the query.""" return run_search(query) ``` BaseTool subclass. Class-based tool with explicit args schema, async support, retries. Use when the tool has state (a client, a cache) or needs structured args. ```python from crewai.tools import BaseTool from pydantic import BaseModel class SearchArgs(BaseModel): query: str limit: int = 10 class SearchTool(BaseTool): name = "web_search" description = "Search the web and return top results." args_schema = SearchArgs Copy ``` Built-in toolkits. CrewAI ships first-party adapters: SerperDevTool , FileReadTool , DirectoryReadTool , CodeInterpreterTool , RagTool , WebsiteSearchTool . Wired with one import. Structured outputs use Pydantic. Pass output_pydantic=MyModel on the Task. CrewAI validates the LLM response against the model and either coerces or retries. Pair this with a tight expected_output string. Free-text outputs are fine for drafts; structured outputs are what downstream Flows can consume. Idea 5 · Memory hooks CrewAI ships four memory types out of the box. They compose: a Crew can enable all four at once. Checked against CrewAI 1.15 (November 2026). Recent releases route everything through a unified Memory system that wraps these four stores. The conceptual model below still holds, but the public class surface may collapse to a single Memory entry-point in newer versions; check CrewAI memory docs for the current API. Short-term. Conversation buffer within a single run. Wiped at the end. Long-term. Persisted across runs. Stored in a vector DB (Chroma by default, swappable). Retrieved by similarity to the current task. Entity. Per-entity facts. "Customer X is on the enterprise plan." Keyed by entity, not by similarity. Survives across runs. Contextual. Assembly-time retrieval. Pulls relevant memory at the moment the Agent needs it, not preloaded. Enable on the Crew with memory=True or per-type config. Backed by an embeddings provider you configure (defaults to OpenAI, swappable to local). Memory is one of the places CrewAI earns its keep against thinner frameworks; pure LangGraph requires you to wire each of these yourself. Idea 6 · When role-based teams fit Three to six agents with named roles and a collaborative workflow. Drafting, reviewing, planning, brainstorming. Routing where the LLM's judgment about the next step is part of the value (Hierarchical). Anywhere the team is happier reading role + goal + backstory than reading a graph definition. Idea 7 · When they do not Deterministic DAGs with strict ordering. Use LangGraph ( Lesson 14.13 ). The graph shape is the right abstraction; CrewAI's role framing is friction. Sub-second latency budgets. Hierarchical adds round trips. Even Sequential serializes prompts that include backstories and prior outputs. Single-agent loops. Skip the framework; an agent loop (Lesson 1) plus a tool registry is shorter. Lesson 14.28 (Orchestration Patterns) compares the topologies side by side. The short version: CrewAI sits in the "collaborative role-based" corner. Idea 8 · Dependency shape Independent of LangChain. Python 3.10 to 3.13. Uses uv . Star count: see crewAIInc/crewAI (snapshot as of 2026-05). AWS Bedrock integration is documented; vendor benchmarks report a substantial speedup vs LangGraph on QA workloads, but the methodology (dataset, hardware, evaluation metric) is not published, so treat framework-vendor numbers as directional only. Idea 9 · Where this pattern goes wrong Prompt-bloat from backstories. A 2000-word backstory per agent and a five-agent crew burns the context budget before the first tool call. Keep backstories under 200 words. Reuse phrases across agents; do not repeat house style five times. Manager-LLM token tax. Hierarchical process adds a manager LLM call before every specialist call. On a five-task crew that is ten LLM calls instead of five, and the manager call carries the full task list plus prior outputs. Switch to Sequential unless routing depends on output. Brittle handoffs. Task N's expected_output is "an outline". Task N+1 reads it as context and tries to parse three sections. The LLM produced four. The downstream Agent ad-libs. Fix with output_pydantic on Task N so Task N+1 reads a typed object, not free text. Crew-as-prod. Free-form Crew shipped to production without a Flow wrapper. Output variability is high; replay is impossible; on-call cannot diff a bad run against a good one. Wrap with a Flow. The same idea as a formula Cost of a run. With model calls , each reading ​ prompt tokens and writing ​ : ∑ N ​ ( c in ​ p i ​ + c out ​ g i ​ ) . A team shape changes both (how many calls) and ​ (how much role text, tool descriptions and earlier output each call carries). Error compounding in a chain. If each of sequential steps keeps the facts it was given with probability , the final output keeps them with probability about . A step that checks the output in code resets this: it either passes the facts on or stops the run. Worked example The three runs below, by the numbers Sequential crew: 4 calls, prompt tokens. Hierarchical crew: the same 4 calls, prompt tokens, times as many, because every prompt now carries delegation tools and manager instructions. Wall time roughly doubles (about 35 s against 16 s). Flow: 2 calls, prompt tokens: retrieval is a function call, and the only model call is the writing step, made twice because the check failed the first draft. With per step for a 0.5B model, a three-step chain keeps the facts with probability = 0.125 ; the sequential crew's last step lost them entirely. Check your mental model ✗ "More agents means better results." ✓ Each extra step is another chance to lose information; with a weak model the chain degrades. ✗ "Hierarchical mode only adds a manager call." ✓ Here it added no calls at all but made every prompt about three times longer. ✗ "A Flow is just a crew without autonomy." ✓ It is code you own: retrieval, checks and retries are explicit, testable and cheap. ✗ "A crew's final answer reflects the research." ✓ Only if every step kept the facts; check the output against the sources. Solutions Solution P1 · No: the facts are lost after the first step No. The researcher calls the notes tool and reports the facts correctly, but the writer, given those facts in its context, writes about software modules, and the editor returns a fragment of the task instructions. Each step was another chance to drop what the previous one found, and with a 0.5B model every chance was taken. Nothing in the crew checks the output against the notes. Solution B1 · Fluent output, lost facts The writer ignores the researcher's facts and the editor sometimes returns instruction text; the final paragraphs can be fluent and unrelated to the sources. A reader who never sees the intermediate steps cannot tell a grounded paragraph from an invented one, and the crew reports success either way. Make it visible with traces and checks: log each agent's input and output (the server log above is the minimal version; LangSmith, Langfuse or CrewAI's tracing in production), compare the final text against the retrieved facts automatically (presence of key facts, or an entailment check), and fail the run when the comparison fails. Better still, move retrieval and checking into a flow and let the model only write. Lesson 14.117 · OpenAI Agents SDK I: agents, tools, sessions, approvals and guardrails Lesson 14.118 · OpenAI Agents SDK II: handoffs, run context, streaming, tests and tracing The problem In plain words first The OpenAI Agents SDK is a small Python library for building agents out of five pieces. An agent is a model plus instructions and tools. A handoff lets one agent pass the conversation to another (a triage agent sends a billing question to the billing agent); to the model it looks like one more tool, called something like transfer_to_billing_agent . A guardrail is a check on the incoming request or the outgoing answer that can stop the run. A session remembers earlier turns of a conversation. Tracing records every model call, tool call, handoff and guardrail as a span you can inspect. This lesson builds these pieces in plain Python, then runs the real SDK against a small local model and watches where handoffs and guardrails work and where they fail. Agents that cannot delegate cleanly end up stuffing everything into one prompt. Agents without guardrails ship PII, policy-violating output, or loop forever. OpenAI's SDK codifies the three primitives that make multi-agent work tractable. Idea 1 · Five primitives Agent. LLM + instructions + tools + handoffs. Handoff. Delegation to another agent. Represented to the model as a tool named transfer_to_<agent_name> . Guardrail. Validation on input (first agent only), output (last agent only), or tool invocation (per function tool). Session. Automatic conversation history across turns. Tracing. Built-in spans for LLM generations, tool calls, handoffs, guardrails. Idea 2 · Handoffs as tools The model sees transfer_to_billing_agent in its tool list. Calling it signals the runtime to: Copy the conversation context (or collapse it via nest_handoff_history beta). Initialize the target agent with its instructions. Continue the run with the target agent. This is the supervisor pattern ( Lesson 14.13 / Lesson 14.28 ) productized. Idea 3 · Guardrails Three flavors: Input guardrails. Run on the first agent's input. Reject unsafe or out-of-scope requests before any LLM call. Output guardrails. Run on the last agent's output. Catch PII leaks, policy violations, malformed responses. Tool guardrails. Run per-function-tool. Validate arguments, check permissions, audit execution. Mode: Parallel (default). Guardrail LLM runs alongside the main LLM. Lower tail latency. If tripped, the main LLM's work is discarded (token waste). Blocking ( run_in_parallel=False ). Guardrail LLM runs first. If tripped, no tokens wasted on the main call. Tripwires raise InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered / OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered . Idea 4 · Tracing On by default. Every LLM generation, tool call, handoff, and guardrail emits a span. OPENAI_AGENTS_DISABLE_TRACING=1 opts out. add_trace_processor(processor) fans spans to your own backend alongside OpenAI's. Idea 5 · Sessions Session stores conversation history in a backend (SQLite, Redis, custom). Runner.run(agent, input, session=session) auto-loads and appends. Idea 6 · Where this pattern goes wrong Handoff drift. Agent A hands off to Agent B which hands back to Agent A. Add a hop counter. Guardrail bypass. Tool guardrails only fire on function tools; built-in tools (file reader, web fetch) need separate policy. Over-tracing. Sensitive content in spans. Lesson 14.126 · The Claude Agent SDK: a harness as a library The problem In plain words first Calling a model's API gives you one reply. Everything that makes an agent useful (running tools, connecting to MCP servers, saving the conversation, letting a helper agent do part of the work, stopping dangerous actions) you have to build yourself. The Claude Agent SDK packages the harness that Claude Code uses as a library. It brings built-in tools (read and edit files, run shell commands, search, fetch web pages), subagents (helpers with their own fresh context that return only their result), a session store for conversations, and hooks : your own functions that run at fixed moments, for example just before a tool runs, and can block it. This lesson builds a miniature harness in plain Python, measures what subagents save and lose with a real small model, and exercises the real SDK's hook and tool interfaces. A raw LLM API gets you one round-trip. A production agent needs tool execution, MCP servers, lifecycle hooks, subagent spawning, session persistence, trace propagation. Claude Agent SDK ships this shape as a library — the same harness Claude Code uses, exposed for custom agents. Idea 1 · Client SDK vs Agent SDK Client SDK ( anthropic ). Raw Messages API. You own the loop, the tools, the state. Agent SDK ( claude-agent-sdk ). Built-in tool execution, MCP connections, hooks, subagent spawning, session store. The Claude Code loop as a library. Idea 2 · Built-in tools The SDK ships 10+ tools out of the box: file read/write, shell, grep, glob, web fetch, more. Custom tools register via the standard tool-schema interface. Idea 3 · Subagents Two purposes documented by Anthropic: Parallelization. Run independent work concurrently. "Find the test file for each of these 20 modules" is 20 parallel subagent tasks. Context isolation. Subagents use their own context window; only results return to the orchestrator. The orchestrator's budget is preserved. Python SDK recent additions: list_subagents() , get_subagent_messages() for reading subagent transcripts. Idea 4 · Session store Protocol parity with TypeScript: append(session_id, message) — add a turn. load(session_id) — restore conversation. list_sessions() — enumerate. delete(session_id) — with cascade to subagent sessions. list_subkeys(session_id) — list subagent keys. --session-mirror (CLI flag) mirrors the transcript to an external file as it streams, for debugging. Idea 5 · Hooks Lifecycle hooks you can register: PreToolUse , PostToolUse — gate or audit tool calls. SessionStart , SessionEnd — set up and tear down. UserPromptSubmit — act on user input before the model sees it. PreCompact — run before context compaction. Stop — cleanup on agent exit. Notification — side-channel alerts. Hooks are how pro-workflow (Phase 14 curriculum reference) and similar systems add cross-cutting behavior. Idea 6 · W3C trace context OTel spans active on the caller propagate into the CLI subprocess via W3C trace context headers. The whole multi-process trace shows up as one trace in your backend. Idea 7 · Claude Managed Agents The hosted alternative (beta header managed-agents-2026-04-01 ). Long-running async work, built-in prompt caching, built-in compaction. Trade control for managed infrastructure. Idea 8 · Where this pattern goes wrong Subagent over-spawn. Spawning 100 subagents for 100 tiny tasks. Overhead dominates. Batch instead. Hook creep. Every team adds hooks; startup time balloons. Review hooks quarterly. Session bloat. Sessions accumulate; size grows. Use list_sessions + expiry policy. The same idea as a formula What the orchestrator reads. With documents of tokens each and questions, an agent that reads everything for every question reads about ​ = q ( d L + c ) tokens, where is the question. With subagents that each return an -token summary, the subagents read ) once and the orchestrator reads only ​ = q ( d s + c ) , s ≪ L . What it can lose. The orchestrator can only answer what the summaries contain. If a summary keeps each relevant detail with probability , accuracy is bounded by about times what the full text allows; question-aware subagents raise at the cost of subagent calls. Worked example The three designs below, by tokens and answers Four documents of 530 to 720 tokens. One agent reading all of them for each of 4 questions: 9,770 prompt tokens, 2 of 4 right. Four summarising subagents and an orchestrator: 3,265 tokens in total, of which the orchestrator read only 722 ( of the single agent's reading). But 1 of 4 right: the summaries said "Four primitives: Agents, Tasks, Crews, and Tools", not "sequential versus hierarchical processes". Sixteen question-aware subagents (one per document and question, yes or no): 10,244 tokens, about the same as the single agent, but 3 of 4 right, and each call reads one document, so the calls can run in parallel and no single context holds more than about 650 tokens. Isolation is a choice about what the parent needs to see, not a free saving. Solutions Solution P1 · Subagents read less and answer worse The subagent design reads far fewer tokens (the orchestrator's own reading falls from 9,770 to 722 tokens) but answers fewer questions correctly, 1 of 4 against 2 of 4, because summaries written without the questions in mind drop the details the questions ask about. Making the subagents question-aware restores accuracy (3 of 4) at about the single agent's token cost, spread over small, parallel calls. Solution B1 · String matching is not a policy Ways around it: rm -r build/ or rm -fr build (different flags); find build -delete , python -c "import shutil; shutil.rmtree('build')" or git clean -fdx (different programs); a script written with the file-editing tool and then run (a different tool); and r''m -rf , variables or command substitution that only become rm when the shell runs them. A sturdier policy decides by effect and scope rather than spelling: run the agent in a sandbox or container where the protected paths are read-only; use the SDK's permission modes and allowed_tools to deny shell access unless needed; when shell is allowed, parse the command and allow a short list of known-safe programs instead of blocking a list of bad strings; restrict writes to a working directory with a PostToolUse check of what changed; and require human approval for anything outside it. Lesson 14.127 · Choosing among frameworks, their history, and no-code agent builders The problem In plain words first Not every team wants a framework with graphs, crews or actors. Agno (Python) and Mastra (TypeScript) offer something lighter: an agent object with a model, instructions and tools, and a way to call it, plus storage, memory and workflows when you need them. Agno advertises that creating an agent takes microseconds and a few kilobytes, so a web server can create a fresh agent for every request. Mastra builds on the Vercel AI SDK and fits TypeScript web stacks. The useful questions are practical: does it run against my model, does it call my tools, and does its overhead matter next to the model call? This lesson builds tiny versions of both, then runs the real Agno and Mastra against the same small local model and measures their overhead. LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI are framework-heavy. Teams that want "just the agent loop, fast, in my runtime" reach for Agno (Python) or Mastra (TypeScript). Both trade some of the framework-owned primitives for raw speed and a tighter fit to the surrounding stack. Idea 1 · Agno Python runtime, formerly Phi-data. "No graphs, chains, or convoluted patterns — just pure python." Performance targets from their docs: ~2μs agent instantiation, ~3.75 KiB memory per agent, ~23 model providers. Production path: stateless session-scoped FastAPI backend. Each request starts a fresh agent; session state lives in a DB. Native multimodal (text, image, audio, video, file) and agentic RAG. The speed targets matter when you have thousands of short-lived agents per second (chat fan-in, evaluation pipelines). They matter less when one agent runs for 10 minutes. Idea 2 · Mastra TypeScript, built on Vercel AI SDK. Three primitives: Agents , Tools (Zod-typed), Workflows . Unified Model Router — 3,300+ models across 94 providers (March 2026). Composite storage: memory, workflows, observability to different backends; ClickHouse recommended for observability at scale. Apache 2.0 with ee/ directories under source-available enterprise license. Server adapters for Express, Hono, Fastify, Koa; first-class Next.js and Astro integration. Ships Mastra Studio (localhost:4111) for debugging. 22k+ GitHub stars, 300k+ weekly npm downloads at 1.0 (Jan 2026). Idea 3 · Positioning Neither is trying to be LangGraph. They compete on: Language fit. Agno for Python-first teams; Mastra for TypeScript-first. Runtime ergonomics. Agno = near-zero overhead; Mastra = integrated with the Vercel ecosystem. Observability. Both integrate with Langfuse/Phoenix/Opik ( Lesson 14.24 ) but Mastra Studio is first-party. Idea 4 · When to pick each Agno — Python backend, many short-lived agents, strong perf requirements, FastAPI shop. Mastra — TypeScript backend, Next.js / Vercel deploy, unified multi-provider model routing, Zod-typed tools. LangGraph ( Lesson 14.13 ) — when durable state and explicit graph reasoning matter more than raw speed. OpenAI / Claude Agent SDK — when you want the provider's productized shape (Lessons 16–17). Ecosystem lock-in. Mastra's Vercel-flavored integration is a plus on Vercel, a minus elsewhere. Enterprise license confusion. Mastra's ee/ directories are source-available, not Apache 2.0. Lesson 14.144 · Evaluating agents end to end Lesson 10.47 · Evaluating models: benchmarks, metrics and hallucination The problem In plain words first A benchmark is a fixed set of tasks with an automatic way to score answers; a leaderboard ranks systems by that score. Agent benchmarks such as SWE-bench (fix real GitHub issues so that the project's tests pass) and GAIA (answer questions that need browsing, files and tools) are how the field compares agents. A score is only as trustworthy as three things: whether the tasks or answers leaked into the model's training data ( contamination ), whether the issue text gives the answer away ( leakage ), and whether the tests would catch a wrong fix ( test strength ). This lesson builds a SWE-bench-style scorer, then grades a real small model on four tiny bug fixes and shows how leakage and weak tests inflate the number. Leaderboards tell you which model wins on one benchmark. They do not tell you: Whether the benchmark is contaminated (solutions in training data, test leakage). Whether the benchmark measures what you care about (code vs browsing vs generalist). Whether the evaluator is robust (AST matching, state checks, human review). Know the three anchoring benchmarks and their failure modes before you quote a number. Idea 1 · SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., ICLR 2024 oral) 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 popular Python repos. Agent gets: the codebase at the pre-fix commit + natural-language issue description. Agent produces: a patch. Evaluator: apply patch, run the repo's test suite. The patch must flip FAIL_TO_PASS tests (previously failing, now passing) without breaking PASS_TO_PASS tests. SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024) hit 12.5% at release by emphasizing agent-computer interfaces (file editor commands, search syntax the model understands). Idea 2 · SWE-bench Verified OpenAI, Aug 2024. Human-curated 500-task subset. Removes ambiguous issues, unreliable tests, and tasks where the fix was unclear. For about two years it was the primary benchmark for "does your agent ship real patches?". In February 2026 OpenAI stopped reporting it: in an audit of 138 hard problems, 59.4% had flawed tests or descriptions, and every frontier model tested could reproduce some gold patches or problem text. OpenAI then recommended SWE-bench Pro, and in July 2026 retracted that as well, estimating that about 30% of Pro's tasks are broken. Idea 3 · Contamination Over 94% of SWE-bench issues predate most model cutoffs. SWE-bench+ found 32.67% of successful patches leaked solutions in the issue text (model saw the fix in the description), and 31.08% were suspicious due to weak test coverage. Verified is cleaner but not contamination-free. Practical implication: a model that scores 50% on SWE-bench may score 35% on SWE-bench+. Always report both if you claim SWE-bench performance. Idea 4 · GAIA (Mialon et al., Nov 2023) 466 questions; 300 retained for the private leaderboard at huggingface.co/gaia-benchmark. Design philosophy: "conceptually simple for humans (92%) but hard for AI (GPT-4 with plugins: 15%)." Tests reasoning, multi-modality, web, tool use. Three difficulty levels; Level 3 requires long tool chains across modalities. GAIA is what you run to measure "generalist capability." Do not confuse with code-specific benchmarks. Idea 5 · AgentBench (Liu et al., ICLR 2024) 8 environments: operating system (Bash), database, knowledge graph, a digital card game, lateral-thinking puzzles, household tasks (ALFWorld), web shopping (WebShop) and web browsing (Mind2Web). Multi-turn, ~4k-13k turns per split. Primary finding: long-term reasoning, decision-making, and instruction following are the blockers for OSS LLMs catching up to commercial. Idea 6 · What these do not measure Real-world operational cost (tokens, wall-clock). Safety behavior in adversarial conditions. Performance on your domain (use your own evals, Lesson 14.30 ). Tail failures (benchmarks average; production operators care about the worst 1%). Idea 7 · Where benchmarking goes wrong Single-number fixation. SWE-bench 50% tells you less than the P50/P75/P95 cost + step distribution. Contaminated claims. Reporting SWE-bench without mentioning Verified or SWE-bench+ is misleading. Benchmark-as-development-target. Optimizing for the benchmark diverges from production usefulness. The same idea as a formula SWE-bench's rule. The model is the same, the bugs are the same, and the tests are the same; the only difference is that the second issue text contains the answer. Noise: on 500 tasks at around 70%, the standard error is about 2 points, so a 2-point gap is within noise unless both systems were run several times. Same harness and settings: identical scaffold, attempts per task, time limits and tool access, or the comparison is between setups, not models. Flawed tasks: OpenAI's audit found many Verified tasks with tests that reject correct fixes or demand unstated behaviour, so check which tasks flipped and read the patches. Lesson 14.144 · Evaluating agents end to end Lesson 14.68 · Specialized agents: coding, browser and computer use, research, data and voice The problem In plain words first A web agent operates a website the way a person does: it reads the page, clicks, types, and repeats until the task is done. A computer-use agent does the same on a whole desktop, from screenshots. WebArena and OSWorld are the standard tests. Their key design choice is execution-based evaluation : a task counts as done only if the application's state changed correctly (the order exists, the setting is saved), not because the agent or the page says so. They also count steps, because an agent that takes three times as many clicks as a person is slow and more likely to break something on the way. This lesson runs a small model as a web agent on a real page in a browser and grades it both ways. Generalist agents can call tools. Can they drive a browser across 20 clicks to complete a shopping checkout? Can they configure a Linux box using only keyboard and mouse? These are the questions WebArena and OSWorld answer. Idea 1 · WebArena (Zhou et al., ICLR 2024) 812 long-horizon tasks across four self-hosted web apps: a shopping site, a forum, a GitLab-like dev tool, a business CMS. Plus utilities: map, calculator, scratchpad. Evaluation is execution-based via gym APIs — was the order placed, was the issue closed, was the CMS page updated? At release: best GPT-4 agent hit 14.41% success vs human 78.24%. The self-hosted framing matters — the benchmark is not flaky because the target apps are pinned and reproducible. Idea 2 · Extensions VisualWebArena — visually grounded tasks where success depends on interpreting images (screenshots as first-class observations). TheAgentCompany (Dec 2024) — adds terminal + coding; more like a real remote-work environment. Idea 3 · OSWorld (Xie et al., NeurIPS 2024) 369 real computer tasks across Ubuntu, Windows, macOS. Free-form keyboard and mouse control of real applications. 1920×1080 screenshots as the observation. At release: best model 12.24% vs human 72.36%. Idea 4 · Primary failure modes GUI grounding. Pixel → element mapping. Models struggle to localize UI elements reliably in 1920×1080. Operational knowledge. Which menu has the setting, which keyboard shortcut, which preference pane. Knowledge tail that humans build over years. Idea 5 · Follow-ups OSWorld-G — 564-sample grounding suite + Jedi training set. Decomposes grounding from planning so you can measure them separately. OSWorld-Human — manually curated gold action trajectories. Shows top agents use 1.4-2.7x more steps than necessary (the trajectory-efficiency gap). Idea 6 · Why this matters Claude computer use, OpenAI CUA, Gemini 2.5 Computer Use ( Lesson 14.21 ) all train on workloads shaped by WebArena and OSWorld. The benchmarks are the target; the production models are the shipped answer. Idea 7 · Where benchmarking goes wrong Screenshot-only evals. OSWorld is screenshot-driven; evaluating an agent that uses DOM or accessibility APIs on OSWorld misses the grounding challenge. Ignoring trajectory length. Scoring only success-rate misses the 1.4-2.7x step inefficiency OSWorld-Human surfaces. Stale self-hosted apps. WebArena's apps pin specific versions; update without re-curation breaks comparability. Solutions Solution P1 · None, by looping None. The model reads the buttons well enough to click plausible ones, but it does not track what it has already done: it adds the same item again and again, removes items the task said to keep, and never reaches Checkout or says DONE within 8 steps. The failure is long-horizon control, not perception. Solution B1 · Grading the message, not the state The evaluation grades the page, not the outcome. A message can say "thank you" when the order is wrong (wrong items, a duplicate order placed by a repeated click) and can say something else when the order is right, as when the agent's extra Checkout click replaced the confirmation with "Your cart is empty". A 92% pass rate on messages says little about orders. Change it to execution-based checks: after each run, query the order system for the orders the agent created and compare them exactly with the expected items, quantities and addresses; fail on missing, extra or duplicate orders. Record steps against a gold trajectory and flag runs far above it, since repeated clicks are what create duplicates. Keep a few message checks only as a secondary signal.
