Lesson 14.143 · Evaluation and testing in depth Lesson 14.144 · Evaluating agents end to end Lesson 14.147 · The LLMOps lifecycle and safe releases The problem In plain words first Eval-driven development treats an agent like any other software: you keep a suite of test cases ( evals ) next to the code, run it on every change, and block a change that makes the suite worse (a CI gate ). An eval case pairs an input with a way to check the output: an exact answer, a schema, a test run or a judge model. Two things make agent evals harder than unit tests: outputs vary between runs, so one run of a small suite can mislead; and a loop that refines outputs until a checker passes only fixes what that checker can see. This lesson runs a twenty-case suite on a real model, gates a prompt change, and wraps the weaker prompt in the lesson's evaluator-optimizer loop. Agents pass demos. They fail in production in ways demos cannot predict. Benchmarks answer "is this model broadly capable?" not "is this agent shipping the right patches for my product?" The answer: evaluation at three layers, running continuously, with every guardrail and learned rule mapped to an eval case. Online evals — production: - Session replays (Langfuse). - Guardrail-triggered alerts ( Lesson 14.16 , 21). - Per-step cost / latency tracking ( Lesson 14.23 OTel spans). a1431: Course home / Phase 14 · AI Agents: Design and Engineering Agent Workbench Engineering and Why Strong Models Still Fail Lesson 14.31 45 min Learn + Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Separate model capability from execution reliability. Name the seven workbench surfaces that decide whether an agent ships. Compare a prompt-only run against a workbench-guided run on a small repo task. Produce a failure-mode report that maps each missed surface to the symptom it caused. Before you start Needs : Phase 14 · 01 (Agent Loop), Phase 14 · 26 (Failure Modes) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A capable model is not enough. Reliable agents need a workbench: instructions, state, scope, feedback, verification, review, and handoff. Strip those away and even a frontier model produces work that is unsafe to ship. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Workbench "The setup" Engineered surfaces around the model that make work reliable Surface "A doc" or "a script" A named, machine-readable input the agent reads or writes every turn System of record "The notes" The file the agent treats as truth when chat history is gone Definition of done "Acceptance" An objective, file-backed checklist the agent cannot fake Workbench audit "Repo readiness check" A pass over the seven surfaces that flags missing pieces before work begins From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.67 · Long-running agents: harness and loop engineering Lesson 14.111 · Deep Agents: a harness on LangGraph The problem In plain words first A workbench (people also say harness ) is everything around the model while it works: the instructions it starts with, the files it may touch ( scope ), real output from the commands it runs ( feedback ), a check that must pass before "done" counts ( verification ), and notes that let the next session continue ( state and handoff ). The model decides; the workbench decides what the model sees and what it may claim. The usual failure without one is an agent that says it finished when nothing works. This lesson gives a small model the same bug-fix tasks with and without a workbench and counts real fixes and false "done"s. You drop a frontier model into a real repo and ask it to add input validation. It opens four files, writes plausible code, declares success, and stops. You run the tests. Two fail. A third file is touched that had nothing to do with validation. There is no record of what the agent assumed, what it tried first, or what is left to do. The model was not wrong about Python. It was wrong about the work. It had no idea what counted as done, where it was allowed to write, what tests were authoritative, or how the next session was supposed to pick up. This is not a model bug. It is a workbench bug. The surface around the agent is missing the parts that turn a one-shot generation into reliable, resumable engineering. The idea A workbench is the operating environment that wraps the model during a task. It has seven surfaces: Surface What it carries Failure when missing Instructions Startup rules, forbidden actions, definition of done Agent guesses what shipping means State Current task, touched files, blockers, next action Each session restarts from zero Scope Allowed files, forbidden files, acceptance criteria Edits leak into unrelated code Feedback Real command output captured into the loop Agent declares success on a 400 Verification Tests, lint, smoke run, scope check "Looks good" reaches main Review A second pass with a different role Builder marks own homework Handoff What changed, why, what is left Next session re-discovers everything The workbench is independent of the model. You can swap the model and keep the surfaces. You cannot swap the surfaces and keep reliability. The loop closes on the state file, not on chat history. Chat is volatile. The repo is the system of record. Idea 1 · Workbench versus prompt engineering Prompting tells the model what you want this turn. A workbench tells the model how to do work across turns and across sessions. Most agent failure stories are workbench failures wearing prompt-engineering clothes. Idea 2 · Workbench versus framework A framework gives you a runtime (LangGraph, AutoGen, Agents SDK). A workbench gives the agent a place to work inside that runtime. You need both. This mini-track is about the second one. Idea 3 · Reasoning from primitives, not from vendor taxonomies There is a lot of writing on "harness engineering" right now. Addy Osmani, OpenAI, Anthropic, LangChain, Martin Fowler, MongoDB, HumanLayer, Augment Code, Thoughtworks, the walkinglabs awesome list, and a steady drumbeat of Medium and Hacker News pieces are all carrying it. They disagree on the boundary of what a harness is, what is in scope, and which vocabulary to use. We do not need to pick a side. The seven surfaces are a UX layer; underneath every workbench is the same set of distributed-systems primitives that hold up any reliable backend. Strip the agent label off for a moment. An agent run is computation that crosses time, processes, and machines. To make that reliable you need the same primitives any production system needs. Primitive What it is What it carries for an agent Function Typed handler. Pure where possible. Owns its inputs and outputs. A tool call, a rule check, a verification step, a model invocation Worker Long-lived process that owns one or more functions and a lifecycle The builder, the reviewer, the verifier, an MCP server Trigger Event source that invokes a function Agent loop tick, HTTP request, queue message, cron, file change, hook Runtime The boundary that decides what runs where, with what timeouts and resources Claude Code's process, LangGraph's runtime, a worker container HTTP / RPC The wire between caller and worker Tool-call protocol, MCP request, model API Queue Durable buffer between trigger and worker; back-pressure, retry, idempotency The task board, the feedback log, the review inbox Session persistence State that survives crashes, restarts, model swaps agent_state.json , checkpoints, KV stores, the repo itself Authorization policy Who can call what function with which scope Allowed/forbidden files, approval boundaries, MCP capability lists Now map the seven workbench surfaces onto those primitives. Instructions — policy + function metadata. Rules are checks (functions). The router ( AGENTS.md ) is policy attached to the runtime's startup. State — session persistence. A keyed store the runtime reads at every step. File, KV, or DB; the persistence semantics matter, the storage backend does not. Scope — authorization policy per task. Allowed/forbidden globs are an ACL. Approvals required are a permission lattice. Feedback — invocation log written into a queue. Every shell call is a record, durable, replayable. Verification — a function. Deterministic over inputs. Triggered on task close. Fails closed. Review — a separate worker with read-only authz on builder artifacts and write-only authz on review reports. Handoff — a durable record emitted by a session-end trigger. The next session's startup trigger reads it. The agent loop itself is a worker that consumes events (user message, tool result, timer tick), calls functions (the model, then the tools the model picks), writes records (state, feedback), and emits triggers (verify, review, handoff). No mystery; the same shape as a job processor. Idea 4 · Patterns in circulation, translated to primitives Every popular harness pattern reduces to the eight primitives. Translation table. Vendor or community pattern What it actually is Ralph Loop (Claude Code, Codex, agentic_harness book) — re-inject original intent into a fresh context window when the agent tries to stop early A trigger that re-enqueues a task with a clean context; session persistence carries the goal forward Plan / Execute / Verify (PEV) Three workers, one per role, communicating via state and a queue between phases Harness-compute separation (OpenAI Agents SDK, April 2026) — split control plane from execution plane Restating control-plane / data-plane. Predates the agent label by decades Open Agent Passport (OAP, March 2026) — sign and audit every tool call against a declarative policy before execution An authorization policy enforced by a pre-action worker, with a signed audit queue Guides and Sensors (Birgitta Böckeler / Thoughtworks) — feedforward rules + feedback observability Authorization policy + verification functions + observability traces Progressive compaction, 5-stage (Claude Code reverse engineering, April 2026) A state-management worker that runs cron-like over session persistence to keep it within a budget Hooks / middleware (LangChain, Claude Code) — intercept model and tool calls Triggers + functions wrapped around the runtime's invocation path Skills as Markdown with progressive disclosure (Anthropic, Flue) A function registry where the function metadata is loaded into context just-in-time Sandbox agents (Codex, Sandcastle, Vercel Sandbox) The compute plane: a runtime with isolated filesystem, network, and lifecycle MCP servers Workers exposing functions over a stable RPC, with capability lists as authorization Every entry in that table is the agent community arriving at a primitive that already had a name in distributed systems and giving it a new one. Useful labels for marketing; not useful as engineering vocabulary. Idea 5 · What the receipts actually say The harness-over-model claim has numbers behind it now. Worth knowing, because they are also the only honest argument against "just wait for a smarter model." Terminal Bench 2.0 — same model (GPT-5.2-Codex), harness changes alone took LangChain's deepagents-cli from 52.8% (just outside the top 30) to 66.5% (top 5) (LangChain, Improving Deep Agents with harness engineering , February 2026). Vercel — deleted 80% of its agent's tools; success rate jumped from 80% to 100% (MongoDB). Harvey — legal agents more than doubled accuracy through harness optimization alone (MongoDB). 88% of enterprise AI agent projects fail to reach production. The failures cluster around runtime, not reasoning (preprints.org, Harness Engineering for Language Agents , March 2026). A 2025 benchmark study across three popular open-source frameworks reported ~50% task completion; long-context WebAgent collapsed from 40-50% to under 10% in long-context conditions, mostly from infinite loops and goal loss (covered widely in early 2026 writeups). The takeaway is not "harness wins forever." Models do absorb harness tricks over time. The takeaway is that today, the load-bearing engineering is around the model, not inside it, and the primitives that carry that load are the ones every production system has always needed. Idea 6 · Where vendor writeups stop short This is the part you do not need to be polite about. LangChain's Anatomy of an Agent Harness walks through the core harness components: prompts, tools, hooks, sandboxes, orchestration, memory, skills, subagents, and a runtime "dumb loop." It does not name queues, workers as a deployment unit, trigger semantics, session persistence as a separate concern, or authorization policy. It treats the harness as an object you configure, not as a system you deploy. Addy Osmani's Agent Harness Engineering lands the framing Agent = Model + Harness and the ratchet pattern, but stops short of saying what a harness is built out of. It reads as a stance, not a spec. Anthropic and OpenAI go deepest on the surfaces but stay inside their own runtimes. The "harness-compute separation" announcement in the April 2026 Agents SDK is the first vendor piece that explicitly endorses the control-plane / data-plane split. That is a primitive idea, not a new one. The agentic_harness book treats harness as a config object (Jaymin West's Agentic Engineering , chapter 6) and the strongest line in it is "the harness is the primary security boundary in an agentic system." That is just authorization policy, restated. Hacker News threads keep arriving at the same place. The April 2026 thread The agent harness belongs outside the sandbox argues the harness should sit "more like a hypervisor that sits outside everything and authorises access based on context and user." That is, again, authorization policy as a separate plane. You do not need to disagree with any of these pieces to notice the gap. They are writing UX descriptions of a system that already exists. We are writing the system. When the system is built right, the seven surfaces fall out of the primitives. When it is built wrong, no amount of AGENTS.md polish fixes the missing queue. So when you hear "harness engineering" elsewhere, translate to primitives. Prompts and rules are policy and functions. Scaffolding is the runtime. Guardrails are authorization + verification. Hooks are triggers. Memory is session persistence. The Ralph Loop is requeue. Subagents are workers. Sandboxes are compute planes. The vocabulary changes; the engineering does not. The workbench is the agent-facing UX; the harness, in the sense that survives the next vendor reframe, is functions, workers, triggers, runtimes, queues, persistence, and policy wired together correctly. Solutions Solution P1 · A false "done", then a blocked one Without a workbench it calls a made-up tool named after the function, then finish , claiming success with the bug untouched. With the workbench it runs the tests, then keeps calling finish ; the gate rejects every one because the tests still fail, so the run ends unfinished instead of falsely finished. Neither run fixes the bug. Solution B1 · Instructions are not a gate The instruction to run tests is a request the agent can ignore or misread; nothing checks it. The missing surface is a verification gate: code outside the model that, whenever the agent claims completion, runs the tests (and a scope check of the changed files) itself and refuses the completion if they fail, sending the output back. Add the gate on the finish path; mark tickets done only from the gate's verdict, never from the agent's summary; record false-completion attempts as a metric; and keep the agent's test runs as feedback, not as proof. Infinite loops and goal loss are not reasoning failures. They are a missing turn budget, a missing state file and a missing scope. What the harness is made of. The seven surfaces are a user-facing layer. Underneath them are the primitives every reliable production system already has: functions, workers, triggers, a runtime, a wire, queues, session persistence and an authorization policy. The agent loop is a worker that consumes events, calls functions, writes records and emits triggers. None of that is specific to this model generation, and none of it goes away when the model improves. What leadership gets right. Models do absorb harness tricks. A pattern that was a prompt trick two years ago is native now, and the thought-token scheme of the original loop became a reasoning channel. The honest claim is not that the harness wins forever. It is that today the load is around the model, and that the primitives you build to carry it are the ones you would need for any production system, model or not. The proposal to leadership. Build the surfaces as primitives, not as prompt text. Keep the state, the scope, the feedback, the gate and the handoff as files and checks that do not know which model is in the loop. When the next model arrives, swap it and keep the surfaces. The harness work is not a bet against the model. It is the part of the system you keep. Plausible wrong answers. "The model is the product, so the harness is overhead." The harness decided the rank on the benchmark while the model stayed the same. "A longer context window will fix the goal loss." The long-context result in the lesson went the other way, with completion falling under 10 percent as context grew. "Harness work is prompt engineering by another name." Prompting tells the model what you want this turn, and the harness carries the work across turns and sessions in files and checks. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. Reliable agents need a workbench with seven surfaces around the model: instructions, state, scope, feedback, verification, review and handoff. Each symptom in the run maps to one missing surface. The load today is carried by the engineering around the model. What a workbench is not. It is not prompt engineering, which tells the model what you want this turn. It is not the framework, which gives you a runtime. The workbench is the place the agent works in, across turns and across sessions, inside whatever runtime you chose. Plausible wrong answers. "The model hallucinated, so pick a model that hallucinates less." The model did not know what done meant or where it could write, and no model knows that without the surfaces. "Write a longer system prompt with all the rules." A prompt covers one turn, while the surfaces carry the work across turns and sessions. "The framework already does this." A framework gives the agent a runtime, and the workbench is what the agent reads and writes inside that runtime. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. The model cannot hold all of them in context, two teams once registered the same name and the second silently replaced the first, and the success rate has fallen as the catalog grew. Design the registry and the policy for what the model sees on each turn. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Make the registry the only source of truth for what exists, what shape the arguments take and which handler runs, and surface only ten to forty tools per turn. The registry holds a typed record per tool, rejects a second registration of a name unless the caller asks to override, and validates every call against a small schema subset with pointer-shaped errors. The exposure policy loads tool metadata into context only when the task needs it, and the fewer tools the model sees, the better it calls them. The record. Field Purpose name Unique, lower-case segments separated by dots description One line shown to the model schema A subset of JSON Schema with eight keywords handler The callable, opaque to the validator idempotent Lets the dispatcher decide whether a retry is safe timeout_ms Per-tool override of the dispatcher default The schema is data and the handler is code. Keep them apart so that validation never ends up inside handlers. Three registry rules. No silent overwrite. register raises on a known name unless override=True . The incident in the prompt is this rule missing. Validate before dispatch. A pure, recursive walk over the schema returns Ok or a list of errors with JSON pointer paths. No coercion, no handler call, no I/O, so the validator can run again over a replay log. The registry is shape, not safety. Timeouts and sandboxing live in the dispatcher. A validated call can still misbehave. The exposure policy. A catalog of two hundred tools and a context that fits forty is a routing problem. Surface a subset per turn based on the task, and load the rest just in time. The workbench lesson describes the pattern as skills that are revealed step by step: a function registry whose metadata enters context only when needed. The same lesson reports a team that deleted 80 percent of its agent's tools and saw the success rate go from 80 percent to 100 percent. More tools in view means more wrong choices, longer prompts and more schema to misread. Practical selection signals: the active scope contract, the task type on the board, the tools used in the last few turns, and an explicit request from the model for a named family. Log the exposed set per turn so that a failure can be traced to a missing tool rather than a wrong call. What grows next. Past about fifty tools, add $ref against a local definitions block so that shared argument shapes are written once, and additionalProperties: false so that an extra argument is an error rather than a silent drop. Both are small. Both are common. Plausible wrong answers. "Give the model the whole catalog and let it choose." The model cannot hold two hundred schemas, and success fell as the catalog grew, so the fix is fewer tools in view. "Put validation in each handler, close to the code it protects." Validation inside handlers drifts per team and turns the dispatcher into a guessing game that ends in a stack trace. "Allow re-registration so that teams can hot-fix a tool." A silent replace is the incident in the prompt, and a fix should pass an explicit override that shows up in review. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Two teams want the same tool name for different handlers. What do you do? Expected: refuse the collision, namespace by dotted segment, and let the exposure policy pick the family the task needs. (level 3) How do you prove the validator is still correct after a refactor? Expected: run it over a saved replay log of real calls, which works because it has no I/O, no clock and no globals. (level 4) What breaks if the exposure policy is itself a model call? Expected: a second nondeterministic step on every turn, so the selection should be rule-based from the contract and the board, with the model allowed only to request a named family. (level 4) The dispatcher retries a failed call. Which record field decides whether it may? Expected: idempotent , because a retry of a non-idempotent tool can repeat a side effect. Explain the mechanism A vendor deck lists its harness features: a loop that re-injects the original intent when the agent tries to stop early, a plan-execute-verify split, control-plane separation, signed tool-call passports, progressive compaction, hooks, skills with progressive disclosure, and sandboxed agents. Translate each one into the primitive it is, and say what the deck leaves out. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Every entry is a distributed-systems primitive with a new name. The re-inject loop is a trigger that re-enqueues the task with fresh context, plan-execute-verify is three workers with a queue between them, the passport is an authorization policy enforced by a pre-action worker, and compaction is a state-management worker over session persistence. Hooks are triggers around the invocation path, skills are a function registry whose metadata loads just in time, sandboxes are the compute plane, and the control-plane item is the control-plane and data-plane split that predates agents. The decks usually leave out queues, workers as the unit of deployment, trigger semantics, persistence as its own concern and authorization as a separate plane. The eight primitives. The lesson reads the circulating writeups and finds the same gap: they describe the harness as an object you configure, not as a system you deploy. They rarely name queues, workers as a deployment unit, trigger semantics, session persistence as a separate concern, or an authorization policy as its own plane. The strongest line in that literature, that the harness is the primary security boundary, is authorization policy restated. When the system is built from the primitives, the surfaces fall out of it. When it is built without them, no amount of instruction-file polish replaces the missing queue. Why the translation matters. Vocabulary changes every release cycle. The primitives do not. A team that translates each new pattern before adopting it can compare vendors on one table, spot a pattern that is two primitives wearing one name, and notice when a deck has no answer for persistence or authorization. Plausible wrong answers. "These patterns are new because agents are new." Each one has a name in distributed systems, and the agent label changes the vocabulary and not the engineering. a1432: Course home / Phase 14 · AI Agents: Design and Engineering A Minimal Agent Workbench Lesson 14.32 45 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Define the three files that form the minimum viable workbench. Explain why a short root router beats a long monolithic AGENTS.md . Build a state file the agent can read at every turn and write at the end. Build a task board that survives multi-session work without chat history. Before you start Needs : Phase 14 · 31 (Why Capable Models Still Fail) Type : Build. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The smallest useful workbench is three files: a root instructions router, a state file, and a task board. Everything else is layered on top. If a repo cannot carry these three, no model will save it. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Router AGENTS.md Short root file that points the agent at deeper docs and files State file "The notes" Machine-readable record of where the agent is, written every turn Task board "The backlog" JSON queue of work with status, owner, acceptance System of record "Source of truth" The file the workbench treats as authoritative when chat is gone From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.67 · Long-running agents: harness and loop engineering The problem In plain words first The smallest useful workbench is three files in the repo. AGENTS.md is a short router : it tells the agent where to look and how "done" is checked. agent_state.json is the system of record for where work stands: the active task, the files touched, the blockers, the next action. task_board.json is the queue of tasks with their status. Because progress lives in files, not in a chat, a new session can pick up exactly where a dead one stopped. This lesson runs a real model through five bug-fix tasks with exactly these files, then kills the session halfway and resumes it. Most teams reach for a workbench by writing a 3000-line AGENTS.md and calling it done. The model loads it, ignores the parts it cannot summarize, and still fails on the same surfaces it always failed on. You need the opposite. A tiny root file that routes the agent into deeper files only when relevant. Durable state the agent reads before acting and writes after. A task board that says what is in flight, what is blocked, and what is up next. Three files. Each one with a job. Each one machine-readable enough to evolve into a real system later. The idea Idea 1 · AGENTS.md is a router, not a manual A good AGENTS.md is short. It points the agent at: The state file (where you are). The task board (what is left). The deeper rules (under docs/agent-rules.md ). The verification command (how to know it works). Anything longer goes in deeper docs, loaded only when needed. Long manuals get ignored. Short routers get followed. Idea 2 · agent_state.json is the system of record State carries: the active task id, the touched files, the assumptions made, the blockers, and the next action. The agent reads it at every turn. The next session reads it instead of replaying chat. State lives in a file because chat history is unreliable. Sessions die. Conversations get trimmed. The file does not. Idea 3 · task_board.json is the queue The task board carries every task with status todo | in_progress | done | blocked . It is the queue the agent pulls from when state is empty, and the queue you read when you want to know whether the agent is on track. A task on the board has an id, a goal, an owner ( builder , reviewer , or human ), and acceptance criteria. The board is small on purpose: when it grows past a screen, you have a planning problem, not a board problem. Idea 4 · Three files is the floor, not the ceiling Later lessons add scope contracts, feedback runners, verification gates, reviewer checklists, and handoff packets. The three files here are what they all assume. The same idea as a formula Resume cost. If progress lives only in chat and a session dies after completing of tasks, the next session repeats up to all (it cannot tell what was done). If progress is written to a state file after every turn, the next session repeats at most the one turn that was in flight: ​ ≤ k tasks , rework state file ​ ≤ 1 turn . Narrowing the action. A free agent choosing among tools per turn has to get both the tool and its arguments right; a harness that fixes the sequence (read, propose a fix, test) leaves the model one job per turn. With per-decision accuracy , a task needing free decisions succeeds with about ; fixing the sequence removes all but the one that matters. Worked example Five tasks, nine turns The board starts with five todo tasks. Each turn: read agent_state.json , take the active task (or the next todo ), ask the model for the corrected function, write it, run the task's test. Pass: the task becomes done and the state's active task clears. Fail: the test's last error line is appended to blockers and goes back to the model; after three failures the task is blocked . Here: four tasks done, largest blocked after three attempts, nine turns in all. In lesson 14.31 the same model, free to call any tool, fixed none of these bugs. Kill the session after four turns: the files say T-001 done, T-002 blocked, three todo. The next session does five turns and reopens nothing. Check your mental model ✗ "The agent remembers where it was." ✓ Only the files remember; a new session starts from them. ✗ "AGENTS.md should hold every rule." ✓ Keep it a short router; long manuals get skimmed. ✗ "More tool freedom makes agents more capable." ✓ The same model fixed 4 of 5 bugs with one job per turn, and 0 of 5 with free tool choice. ✗ "Blocked is a failure of the workbench." ✓ Blocked with a recorded reason is the workbench working. Predict before you run The model from lesson 14.31, which fixed none of five one-line bugs when it chose its own tools, now gets one job per turn: "return the corrected function", with failing test output fed back for up to three attempts. How many of the five will it fix? (Solution P1.) See it drawn Three files and a real model Five buggy functions and their tests in a scratch folder, with agent_state.json and task_board.json written by the lesson's save_state and save_board . Each turn reads only those files, asks Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (greedy, CPU) for the corrected function, writes it and runs the test. About 1 minute. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Four of five fixed, by the same model that fixed none in lesson 14.31. is_even , reverse , to_fahrenheit and count_vowels pass their tests. The difference is the harness: instead of choosing among tools each turn (and never once choosing write_file ), the model gets one job, "return the corrected function", and the harness does the reading, writing and testing. The failure is recorded, not hidden. largest failed three attempts and is blocked with its error in the blockers list; the file still ends in return min(xs) . A person or a stronger model knows exactly where to start. The state file is small and current: no active task, the last touched file, and a next action. That is all the next session needs. See it drawn Kill the session, resume from the files This block continues from the one above. A fresh board; session 1 runs four turns and stops. Session 2 has nothing in memory except what it reads from the two files. About 1 minute. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Session 2 starts exactly where session 1 stopped. On disk it finds T-001 done, T-002 blocked (three attempts, last error AssertionError ) and three tasks still to do, so it asks the model only about reverse , to_fahrenheit (three attempts) and count_vowels . Nothing is redone. No task closed in session 1 is reopened, and the two sessions together take nine turns, as many as the uninterrupted run. If progress had lived in a chat, session 2 would have had to rediscover all of it. Codex / Cursor: workspace rules for the router, session memory for state, queued tasks in the chat sidebar for the board. Custom Python agent: the same files you just wrote. The names change. The shape does not. Production patterns in the wild The minimum workbench survives contact with real monorepos when three patterns are layered on top of it. They are independent; pick the ones your repo actually needs. Nested AGENTS.md with nearest-wins precedence. OpenAI ships 88 AGENTS.md files across its main repo, one per subcomponent. Codex, Cursor, Claude Code, and Copilot all walk from the working file toward the repo root and concatenate every AGENTS.md they find on the way. Sub-directory files extend the root file. Codex adds AGENTS.override.md to replace rather than extend; the override mechanism is Codex-specific and avoid it for cross-tool work. Augment Code's measurement is the line that matters: the best AGENTS.md files give a quality jump equivalent to upgrading from Haiku to Opus; the worst ones make output worse than no file at all. Anti-patterns to refuse, even when they look like coverage. Conflicting instructions silently drop the agent from interactive to greedy mode (ICLR 2026 AMBIG-SWE: 48.8% → 28% resolve rate); number priorities instead of stacking them flat. Unverifiable style rules ("follow the Google Python Style Guide") with no enforcement command let the agent invent compliance; pair every style rule with the exact lint command. Leading with style instead of commands buries the verification path; commands first, style last. Writing for humans instead of agents wastes context budget; terseness is a feature. Cross-tool symlinks. A single root file with symlinks ( ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md , ln -s AGENTS.md .github/copilot-instructions.md , ln -s AGENTS.md .cursorrules ) keeps every coding agent on the same source of truth. Nx's nx ai-setup automates this across Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini, Codex, and OpenCode from a single config. Break it on purpose Two agent sessions run in parallel on the same repo, both following this lesson's workbench. After an hour the board shows a task done that nobody fixed, and another task fixed twice with conflicting edits. What went wrong with the three files, and how would you fix it? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) AGENTS.md is a shared convention read by many coding agents (Codex, Cursor, Jules, Amp, and others); Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md and can import other files. Both are meant to be short and to point at deeper docs. State on disk is how long-running agent setups survive restarts: Anthropic's long-running-agent harness keeps a progress file and a feature list, and frameworks persist checkpoints (lesson 14.13). Task boards appear as TODO /plan files or as issue trackers the agent reads through tools. Structured steps over free tool choice is common in production: many teams fix the loop (plan, edit, test, review) and let the model fill one step at a time, especially with smaller models. On your laptop : these files and the loop are plain Python; any local model can sit in the propose step. Sources: AGENTS.md , Anthropic, Effective harnesses for long-running agents , Claude Code memory . Recap What to keep from this lesson Three files: a short router, a state file, a task board. Write state after every turn; resume from files, not chat. One job per turn makes a weak model useful. Record blockers with evidence and stop after a fixed budget. Concurrent sessions need locks or one owner per task. Practice and reference One-page references from the source repository that cover this lesson, with commands, defaults and fixes in one place. AH Cheat sheet · Engineering an Agent Harness Ship it outputs/skill-minimal-workbench.md generates the three-file workbench for any new repo: an AGENTS.md router tuned to the project, an agent_state.json with the right keys, and a task_board.json seeded with the current backlog. outputs/skill-minimal-workbench.md Copy Exercises Add a last_run timestamp to agent_state.json . Refuse to run if the file is older than 24 hours unless an operator confirms. Add a priority field to the task board and change the puller to always pick the highest priority todo . Migrate task_board.json to JSON Lines so each task is a line and diffs are clean in version control. Write a lint_workbench.py that fails if AGENTS.md is over 80 lines or references a file that does not exist. Decide which one of the three files would hurt the most to lose. Defend it. Solutions Solution P1 · Four of five Four. is_even , reverse , to_fahrenheit and count_vowels pass; largest fails three attempts and is marked blocked with its error. Same model as lesson 14.31: the gain comes from giving it one well-defined job per turn and doing the file handling and testing in the harness. Solution B1 · Two writers, no lock Both sessions read and wrote the same agent_state.json and task_board.json without coordination. Each picked a task by reading the board, so both could pick the same todo task (fixed twice, conflicting edits), and one session's save could overwrite the other's (a task marked done from a stale copy of the board, or state pointing at the wrong task). Fix: one state file per session (or per worker), with the board as the only shared file; claim a task atomically before working on it (a lock file, a compare-and-set on a status with an owner field, or a real queue or issue tracker that assigns work); write the board with optimistic concurrency (re-read, check the version, then write); and mark done only from a verification result that names the commit, so a stale writer cannot close a task it did not finish. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Weigh a trade-off A repo has a 3000-line instructions file for its coding agent. The agent follows about half of it. One engineer wants to cut it to a page. Another says that every line came from an incident and nothing can go. How do you settle it? Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Both are right about something, and the answer is a layered file set, not a shorter file. Keep a root router under about 50 lines that holds only pointers and the few hard rules. Move the rules into a rules file with one screen per category, and move the depth into topic documents that the agent loads only when a task touches them. Every rule stays, and the agent reaches any rule in at most two hops. Why the long file fails. The model loads the file, reads the first screen, runs out of attention budget, and acts on a fraction of what it was told. A long manual fails for the same reason a forty-page onboarding document fails. The reader skims it once and never returns to the part that mattered. Long manuals get ignored. Short routers get followed. The three tiers. Tier Lives in Read when Size Router the root instructions file Every session Under about 50 lines Rules docs/agent-rules.md Every session, at startup One screen per category Topic docs docs/<topic>.md Only when the task touches that topic As deep as needed The router points at the state file, the task board, the rules and the verification command. It links every topic document by path, not by description. Two tests that keep it honest. Reachability. The agent reaches any rule in at most two hops from the router. A pointer that no longer resolves is worse than a missing rule, so a broken link in the router is itself a startup violation. Freshness. The router is short enough that a reviewer reads it again on every pull request. That is the only thing that stops it from growing back into the manual. What to refuse while you trim. The lesson lists anti-patterns that look like coverage. Conflicting instructions silently drop the agent from asking to guessing; one measurement put the resolve rate at 48.8 percent with clear instructions and 28 percent with conflicting ones. A style rule with no lint command lets the agent invent compliance, so pair every style rule with its command. Lead with commands and end with style. Write for the agent, not for a human reader, because terseness saves context. Nested files. Large repos keep one router per subcomponent. Tools walk from the working file to the root and concatenate every router they find, so a subdirectory file extends the root file. One large repository in the lesson carries 88 of them. Measurements in the lesson place the best files at a quality jump equal to a model upgrade, and the worst files below no file at all. Plausible wrong answers. "Cut the file to one page and delete the rest." The rules came from incidents, and deleting them repeats the incidents, so move them to tiers instead. "Keep the long file, and tell the agent to read all of it." The model has an attention budget, and an instruction to read everything does not change how much it acts on. "Put the file in the system prompt so that it is always in context." Being in context is not the problem; acting on it is, and a short router with pointers gets followed where a long block does not. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) The team keeps a rule in the router because it is important. What is the test for whether it belongs there? Expected: the router holds pointers and the few hard rules that apply to every session, and anything that applies to one kind of task goes in a topic document. (level 2) How do you keep one source of truth when the team uses several coding agents? Expected: one root file and symlinks with the names each tool expects, so that every tool reads the same text. (level 3) What does a lint for the workbench check? Expected: the router is under the line budget, every path it references exists, and no two rules conflict. (level 3) Why does the lesson rank a dead link below a rule that was never written? Expected: the agent trusts the router, follows the pointer, finds nothing, and proceeds as if the rule did not exist, while a missing rule at least leaves no false promise. Where it is taught. The minimal workbench lesson makes the router one of three files, and the executable constraints lesson gives the tiers and the two tests. a1433: Course home / Phase 14 · AI Agents: Design and Engineering Executable Constraints as Agent Instructions Lesson 14.33 50 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Separate routing prose from operational rules. Express startup rules, forbidden actions, definition of done, uncertainty handling, and approval boundaries as machine-checkable constraints. Implement a rule checker that scores a run against the rule set. Make the rule set diff-friendly so review can see what changed. Before you start Needs : Phase 14 · 32 (Minimal Workbench) Type : Build. Time : about 50 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Instructions written as prose are wishes. Instructions written as constraints are tests. The workbench turns each rule into something an agent can check at runtime and a reviewer can verify after the fact. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Operational rule "A real instruction" A rule the workbench can check at runtime Aspirational rule "Be careful" A rule with no check; either delete or upgrade Definition of done "Acceptance" An objective, file-backed proof the task is complete Block severity "Hard rule" Violation halts the run; cannot be silenced without an operator Rule expiry "Stale rule sweep" A rule with no fails in N days is up for retirement From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.67 · Long-running agents: harness and loop engineering Lesson 14.97 · Middleware: approvals, limits, summaries and guardrails The problem In plain words first An agent's rules usually live as sentences in its instructions: "never edit the release script", "no new dependencies without approval". The model may follow them or not. An executable constraint pairs each rule with a check : code that inspects what the agent actually did (the files it changed, the imports it added, the tests it ran) and passes or fails. Rules then have a name, a category and a check, and a failing check can block the change or go back to the agent as feedback. This lesson asks a small model to write five functions with and without a "standard library only" rule, then enforces the same rule with the lesson's checker. A typical AGENTS.md reads like onboarding documentation. It tells the agent to "be careful" and "test thoroughly" and "ask if unsure." Three days later, the agent ships a change with no tests, writes to a forbidden directory, and never asks because it never knew where the line was. Instructions are powerful when they are operational and weak when they are aspirational. The fix is to write rules the workbench can interpret and the reviewer can score. The idea Rules belong in docs/agent-rules.md , away from the short root router. Each rule has a name, a category, and a check. Idea 1 · Five categories that cover most rules Category Question the rule answers Example Startup What must be true before work begins? "state file exists and is fresh" Forbidden What must never happen? "do not edit scripts/release.sh " Definition of done What proves the task is complete? "pytest exits 0 and acceptance line passes" Uncertainty What does the agent do when unsure? "open a question note instead of guessing" Approval What requires human approval? "any new dependency, any prod write" A rule that does not fit one of these five usually wants to be two rules. Force the split. Idea 2 · Rules are machine-readable Each rule has a slug, a category, a one-line description, and a check field that names a function in rule_checker.py . Adding a rule means adding a check; the checker grows with the workbench. Idea 3 · Rules are diff-friendly Rules live one per heading in a single markdown file. Renames are visible in diffs. New rules sit at the top of their category. Stale rules get deleted, not commented out, because the workbench is the source of truth, not the chat log of how the team felt last quarter. Idea 4 · Rules versus framework guardrails Framework guardrails (OpenAI Agents SDK guardrails, LangGraph interrupts) enforce rules at the runtime level. The rule set in this lesson is the human-readable, reviewable contract that those guardrails implement. You need both: the runtime catches violations during a turn, the rule set proves the runtime is doing the right thing. Idea 5 · Progressive disclosure: a map, not an encyclopedia The reason AGENTS.md keeps growing is that every incident adds a rule and no incident removes one. A year in, the file is two thousand lines, and the agent reads the first screen, runs out of attention budget, and acts on a fraction of what it was told. A giant instruction file fails for the same reason a forty-page onboarding doc fails: the reader skims it once and never returns to the part that mattered. The fix is not a shorter file. It is a layered one. The root router stays small enough to read every session and holds nothing but pointers. The depth lives in topic files the agent loads only when the task touches them. Give the agent a map, not the whole encyclopedia, and let it walk to the page it needs. Copy Tier Lives in Read when Size budget Router AGENTS.md Every session, always Under ~50 lines Rules docs/agent-rules.md Every session, on startup One screen per category Topic docs docs/<topic>.md Only when the task touches that topic As deep as needed Two tests keep the layering honest. The reachability test: an agent should reach any rule in at most two hops from the router, so the router must link every topic doc by path, not describe it in prose. The freshness test: the router is short enough that a reviewer rereads it on every PR, which is the only thing that stops it from silently growing back into the encyclopedia it replaced. A pointer that no longer resolves is a worse failure than a missing rule, so a broken link in the router is itself a startup-check violation. The same idea as a formula Prose versus check. For a deterministic check such as "every import is in sys.stdlib_module_names ", for the cases it covers, so the gate lets nothing through; the model's only decides how often work is blocked. Feedback loop. If a failed check is sent back and the model fixes it with probability per round, after rounds the remaining violations are ; with every round is wasted, and the gate is what protects you. With the rule stated in the system prompt, three of five import one anyway ( yaml , slugify , requests ). The sentence did not reduce violations. The lesson's RuleChecker with new_dependency_approved flags all three: for this rule. Feeding the failed check back once fixes none of the three, so for this model; the gate keeps all three out of the repo, which is the outcome that matters. Check your mental model ✗ "Stating a rule clearly enough makes the model follow it." ✓ Here the rule in the prompt changed nothing. ✗ "A check only helps if the agent can fix what it flags." ✓ Blocking the change is already the win; fixes are a bonus. ✗ "Every rule can be checked." ✓ Uncertainty and approval rules need traces and human input; name what you cannot check. ✗ "More rules in AGENTS.md mean a safer agent." ✓ Long rule lists get skimmed; checks do not get tired. Predict before you run Five functions where a library is the obvious shortcut (mean, parse a date, parse YAML, slugify, fetch a page title). The model writes each twice: without a rule, and with "standard library only; third-party packages need human approval, which you do not have" in its instructions. How many third-party imports will the rule remove? (Solution P1.) See it drawn A rule in prose Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (greedy, CPU) writes each module twice. Each result is parsed with Python's ast module and every top-level import is compared with sys.stdlib_module_names . About 2 minutes. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The rule did not help. Without it, two modules import a third-party package ( yaml for the config parser, requests for the page fetcher). With the rule in the system prompt, three do: the same two plus slugify . Only mean and the date parser stayed in the standard library both times. Three drafts without the rule do not even parse: the model ran past its token budget or mixed prose into the code. A check catches that too; a sentence in the prompt does not. The rule's wording was explicit, naming the policy, the reason and the lack of approval. A model that ignores it is not misreading; it is reaching for the most familiar solution. That is why rules need checks. See it drawn The same rule as a check This block continues from the one above. Find the causes and fix them in order. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. There are three independent causes, and any one of them is enough. The rule is three hops from the router, past the two-hop reachability limit, so the agent never loads it, and it is prose with no check, so nothing refuses the write even when the agent reads it. And the root file conflicts with the database document, and conflicting instructions silently move an agent from asking to guessing. Fix the reach first, make the rule an approval-category rule with a block-severity check, and remove the conflict. Cause one: reachability. The agent should reach any rule in at most two hops from the router. This rule needs three. The router must link every topic document by path, so docs/database.md belongs in the router, and the rule itself belongs in docs/agent-rules.md , which the agent reads at every startup. A pointer that does not resolve is a worse failure than a missing rule, so check that each path in the router exists, and make a broken link a startup violation. Cause two: an aspirational rule. "Do not change migrations without approval" is a wish until a check exists. Rewrite it as an approval-category rule with a slug, a one-line description, a check that compares the diff against migrations/** and looks for an approval record, and block severity. The runtime refuses on block. The checker reports it. An override needs a human signature in the audit log. Cause three: conflicting instructions. The root file requires the ORM everywhere. The database document requires raw SQL inside migration files. The agent cannot satisfy both, and the measured effect of conflicting instructions is a quiet shift from an interactive mode, where the agent asks, to a greedy mode, where it guesses. One measurement in the lesson put the resolve rate at 48.8 percent without the conflict and 28 percent with it. An agent in greedy mode does not ask for approval. Number the priorities instead of stacking them flat, or scope the ORM rule to application code and the SQL rule to migrations so that they no longer overlap. The order. Move the rule into the rules file and link the database document from the router. Now the agent reads it. Add the check and the severity. Now the runtime refuses. Resolve the conflict. Now the agent asks instead of guessing. Add a workbench lint that fails when the router is over its line budget or references a missing file, so the regression cannot return. Prove it. Run the checker over this week's two runs. The rule report must show the approval rule failing on both, with block severity. Then run the agent on a task that touches a migration and confirm that it opens an approval request before the write. Plausible wrong answers. "Add the rule to the system prompt in capital letters." Emphasis does not add a check, and the conflict in the router still pushes the agent toward guessing. "The model is ignoring instructions, so switch models." The rule was unreachable, uncheckable and contradicted, and a different model meets the same three problems. "Delete the ORM rule, since it caused the conflict." The ORM rule is correct for application code, so scope it rather than delete it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does a shorter root file help here? Lesson 14.60 · State, checkpoints, resume and human approval Lesson 14.67 · Long-running agents: harness and loop engineering The problem In plain words first Repo memory is the agent's state written into the repository: which task is active, which files it touched, what it assumed, what blocks it, what comes next. Two things keep that file trustworthy. A schema (JSON Schema) defines its shape, so a malformed write is refused instead of saved. An atomic write (write a temporary file, flush it to disk, then rename it over the old one) means a crash leaves either the old state or the new one, never half of each. Neither guarantees that the content is true. This lesson lets a small model write its own state updates and checks them both ways, then crashes a process in the middle of a write. The agent finishes a session. The chat closes. The next session opens and asks where to start. The model says "let me check the files," reads stale notes, and re-does work that was already complete. Or worse, it rewrites a finished file because no one told it the file was finished. The workbench fix is repo memory: state lives in JSON files in the repo, written under a schema, persisted atomically, diff-friendly in code review. Chat is a transient feed; the repo is the system of record. The idea Idea 1 · What belongs in repo memory Belongs Does not belong Active task id Raw chat transcripts Touched files this session Token-level reasoning traces Assumptions the agent made "The user seemed frustrated" Open blockers Sampled completions Next action Vendor-specific model ids The test is durability: would this be useful three months from now in a CI rerun? If yes, repo. If no, telemetry. Idea 2 · Schema-first state JSON Schema is the contract. Without it, every agent invents new fields, every reviewer learns a new shape, and every CI script has to special-case past versions. With it, a bad write is a refused write. The schema covers: Required keys. Allowed status values. Forbidden values (e.g. null for arrays). Pattern constraints (task ids match T-\d{3,} ). Version field for migrations. Idea 3 · Atomic writes State writes need to survive partial failures: write to a tempfile, fsync, rename over the target. The state file is the source of truth; a half-written one is worse than no file at all. Idea 4 · Migrations When the schema changes, ship a migration script next to the schema bump. The state file carries a schema_version field; the manager refuses to load a file from a version it cannot migrate. The same idea as a formula Three properties, three mechanisms. For a state update after an event : s ′ ∈ S ​ ​ true content: derived, not written by the model s ′ = f ( s , e ) ​ ​ no torn writes: atomic rename disk ∈ { s , s ′ } ​ ​ A schema checks the first only. If the model writes itself, the second can fail with a perfectly valid file. Atomicity is about the third: after a crash the file holds the old or the new state, never a mixture. Torn writes. A plain write of bytes interrupted after bytes leaves a prefix of the new state, almost never valid JSON. With write-to-temp then rename, the rename is a single filesystem operation on the same disk, so readers see either version. Worked example When valid is not true Start: T-007 active, app.py touched, next action "run the tests for T-007". Event: "the tests for T-007 passed and T-007 is done". The model writes active_task_id: "T-007" and next_action: "done" . The schema accepts it; the next session would still think T-007 is in progress. Event: "also edited test_app.py". The model replaces the list with ["test_app.py"] , dropping app.py . Valid, and now the reviewer will not look at app.py . Across six events: 6 of 6 valid, 2 of 6 right. The fix is to have the harness apply events to the state with code ( touched_files.append(...) , active_task_id = None ), and use the model only for free-text fields. A crash in the middle of the write leaves a truncated file that the next session loads as corrupt state, and the silent except hides it, so the agent resumes against garbage with no signal. The lesson's writer creates a temp file in the same directory, writes, syncs to disk and renames over the target, so the file on disk is either the old version or the new one. Around it belong a schema check that refuses a bad state before it is written, a version field with a migration path, and idempotency keys for tool calls that are not safe to repeat. The two bugs. The lesson points at a bug report from an open-source project in March 2026 with this exact shape: the state file was written with a plain text write and exceptions were caught and silenced. Partial writes left sessions resuming against corrupt state with no signal. The first bug is the non-atomic write. The second is the except clause that turns a loud failure into a quiet one. The atomic writer. Create a temp file with tempfile.mkstemp beside the target, inside its directory. Write the content. fsync so the bytes reach the disk. os.replace the temp file over the target, which is an atomic rename on POSIX and on Windows. A reader sees the old file or the new file, never a mix. Schema first. The state file carries a contract: required keys, an enum of allowed status values, forbidden values such as null for an array, a pattern for task ids, and a schema_version integer. The manager validates before it writes, so a bad write is a refused write, and it refuses to load a file at a version it cannot migrate. A migration script ships with every schema bump and runs idempotently on startup. Around the write. Idempotency keys. If a crash lands between a tool call and its checkpoint, recovery retries the call. Fine for a read; dangerous for an email or a database insert. Log a started record with the call id before execution and a completed record with the result after it. On retry, a call with a completed record is skipped and its stored result is used. A call with only a started record may or may not have run, so reconcile it first, for example by asking the target system whether that idempotency key was applied, before you repeat or skip it. Small state, separate artifacts. Transcripts, generated files and data sets live in their own files or in object storage; the state holds only the paths. Event log plus snapshot. Append every mutation to an event log and snapshot the state on a schedule; resume reads the snapshot and replays later events, which also lets you replay agent decisions when debugging. What belongs in the file. The active task id, the files touched this session, the assumptions made, open blockers and the next action. Not raw transcripts, reasoning traces, sampled completions or vendor model ids. The test is whether the entry would be useful three months from now in a CI rerun. Plausible wrong answers. "Catch the exception and keep going, the next write will fix it." The silent except is the second bug; it hides a truncated file that the next session loads. "Write to a temp file, then copy it over the target." A copy can be interrupted too; the atomic step is the rename. "Store the full transcript in the state so nothing is lost." Transcripts are telemetry, not durable state; keep the file small and keep artifacts in separate files with only their paths in state. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the temp file live in the same directory as the target? Expected: so the final step is a rename on the same filesystem and stays atomic; the lesson's recipe is a temp file beside the target, write, sync, replace. (level 4) An agent crashes after a tool call and before the checkpoint. What goes wrong on recovery, and what fixes it? Expected: the call is retried, which is dangerous for an email or an insert; log a started record with the call id before execution and a completed record with the result after it; reuse the result of a completed call, and reconcile a call that has only a started record before you repeat it. (level 4) Two agents write the same state file within 50 ms. What does the atomic rename save, and what does it not? Expected: it prevents a torn file, so each reader sees one complete version; it does not stop the second write from replacing the first, which needs coordination between the writers. (level 4) What belongs in the state file and what does not? Expected: the active task, touched files, assumptions, blockers and the next action; not transcripts, reasoning traces, completions or vendor model ids, and large artifacts only by path. Where it is taught. The lesson repo memory gives the atomic write recipe, the schema-first contract, idempotency keys and the event log pattern. Build a deterministic init script that probes runtime, dependencies, and repo health. Persist the probe result so the agent reads it instead of re-running checks. Fail loud, fast, and with one place to look when initialization fails. Before you start Needs : Phase 14 · 32 (Minimal Workbench), Phase 14 · 34 (Repo Memory) Type : Build. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Every session that starts cold pays a tax. The agent reads the same files, retries the same probes, and rediscovers the same paths. An init script pays the tax once and writes the answers into state. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Probe "A check" A deterministic function returning (name, status, detail) Init report "Setup output" JSON written next to state with the probe results Idempotent "Safe to re-run" Two runs in a row produce identical reports modulo timestamp Fail loud "Don't swallow" Halt and surface to the human; no silent fallback Setup tax "Bootstrap cost" The tokens the agent spends per session rediscovering the obvious From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Lesson 14.67 · Long-running agents: harness and loop engineering Lesson 14.133 · What production means: the stack and the readiness review The problem In plain words first An init script runs before an agent session starts and checks that the workbench can work at all: the right Python, the packages the tests need, the test command, required environment variables, a fresh state file, a known-good starting commit. Each check is a probe . If a probe fails, the script refuses to start the agent and says why, in one place. Without it, environment problems arrive later disguised as task failures, and the agent tries to "fix" code that was never the problem. This lesson starts a real session in an environment missing pytest , then runs the lesson's init probes first. Open a session. The agent guesses the Python version. Guesses the test command. Lists the repo root five times to find the entry point. Tries to import a package that is not installed. Asks the user where the config file lives. By the time it makes a real edit, ten thousand tokens have gone to setup work that should have been a single script. The fix is one initialization script that runs before the agent does anything else and writes a init_report.json the agent reads at startup. The idea Idea 1 · What the init script probes Probe Why it matters Runtime versions Wrong Python or Node version means silent wrong-version bugs Dependency availability A missing package later costs ten times the cost of catching it now Test command The agent must know how to verify; if the command is missing the workbench is broken Repo paths Hard-coded paths drift; resolve them once and pin Environment variables Missing OPENAI_API_KEY is a failure surface, not a runtime mystery State + board freshness Stale state from a crashed session is a footgun Last-known-good commit Anchor for the handoff diff at the end of the session Idea 2 · Fail loud, fail fast, fail in one place A probe failure means halt and surface to the human. No "the agent will figure it out." The whole point of init is to refuse to start when the workbench is broken. Idea 3 · Idempotent Run it twice in a row. The second run should be a no-op except for a fresh timestamp. Idempotency is what lets you wire the script into CI, hooks, or a pre-task slash command. Idea 4 · Init versus startup rules Rules (Phase 14 · 33) describe what must be true to act. Init is the script that establishes that those rules can be checked. Rules without init become "be careful." Init without rules becomes a polished failure. The same idea as a formula Cost of a late failure. With tasks, attempts each and cost per model call, an environment fault that makes every test fail wastes before anyone notices, and the blockers it records point at the code. An init probe costs milliseconds and stops at . Misattributed feedback. If a failure has cause (environment) but is reported as a test failure, the agent treats it as evidence about the code. Each retry changes the code in response to a signal unrelated to it, so a correct fix can be replaced by a wrong one. Worked example Fifteen calls for nothing Five tasks, three attempts each, acceptance command python -m pytest , which is not installed. Every test run fails with "No module named pytest". The harness records it as a blocker and sends it back; the model rewrites the function each time. After 15 model calls: 0 of 5 done, all blocked with the same environment error. Two files happen to be correct on disk; is_even , which this model fixes on the first try when its tests can run, ends wrong. With the lesson's probes run first and pytest declared as a dependency: init fails before any model call ( ). After the command is fixed, the same session uses 9 calls and finishes 4 of 5. Check your mental model ✗ "The agent will notice a broken environment." ✓ It read 'No module named pytest' fifteen times and kept editing code. ✗ "A failing test means the code is wrong." ✓ Only once the test command itself is known to work. ✗ "Init scripts are for CI, not for agents." ✓ Agents need them more: they cannot step outside the loop to look. ✗ "Warnings should stop the session too." ✓ Fail on what makes work impossible; warn on what needs a look. Predict before you run Five bug-fix tasks, three attempts each, but the acceptance command needs pytest , which is missing, and nothing checks for it. Every failure goes back to the model as feedback. How many tasks finish, how many model calls are spent, and what does the code look like at the end? (Solution P1.) Each probe returns (name, status, detail) . The script writes init_report.json with the full probe set and exits non-zero if any block-severity probe fails. Part 1 of 5 · Probe , _timed , probe_runtime Copy Part 2 of 5 · probe_dependencies , probe_test_command , probe_env , probe_state_freshness , probe_lkg_diff , _deps_fingerprint Copy Part 3 of 5 · lock_is_fresh , write_lock , run_probes Copy Part 4 of 5 · setup Copy Part 5 of 5 · run it (what python3 code/main.py does) Copy What you should see Copy Production patterns in the wild Three patterns separate a useful init script from a ceremony. Last-known-good commit anchoring. Probe the current commit against a LKG file written on the last successful merge. If the diff exceeds a budget (default 50 files), refuse to start and require a human to ratify the new baseline. This is what Cloudflare's AI Code Review uses to scope reviewer agents: every review session anchors against the same last-known-good and never compounds drift across sessions. Lock files with TTL. Write a prereqs.lock after the first successful probe pass. Subsequent runs trust the lock for N hours (24h default) and skip the expensive probes. The init script reads the lock first; if it is fresh and the dependency manifest hash matches, it short-circuits. This is the same pattern Docker uses for layer caches: idempotent probe + content hash = skip. No network, no LLM, no surprises in the hot path. Init probes are deterministic plumbing. A probe that calls an LLM to classify a failure or that hits an external service to check a license is not a probe; it is a workflow. If a probe takes longer than three seconds in a dry run, treat that as a workbench smell and either move it out of init or cache its result. Use it: the same idea with real libraries In production: Claude Code hooks. pre-task hook calls the init script and refuses to launch the agent if it fails. GitHub Actions. A setup-agent job runs the init script; the agent job depends on it. Docker entrypoint. The agent container runs the init script before exec-ing the agent runtime; logs surface on failure. The init script is portable because it makes no calls to a specific framework. Bash, Make, or a tasks file can all wrap it. Break it on purpose Your nightly agent run reports 40 tasks "blocked: connection refused" every few weeks, and on those mornings the repo also contains odd rewrites of database code. Using this lesson, what is happening and what should run before the agent starts? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Session-start hooks and setup scripts are how coding agents prepare environments: Claude Code SessionStart hooks, Codex and Jules environment setup scripts, dev containers and Nix shells that pin toolchains. Anthropic's long-running-agent harness starts each session with an initialiser step that sets up the environment and progress files and runs a basic test before new work. Practice : pin runtimes ( .python-version , lockfiles), fail fast on missing secrets, and run a smoke test of the test command itself before any task, so later failures can be trusted as code failures. On your laptop : the lesson's probes are standard-library Python and run in milliseconds; add one probe per thing your acceptance command needs. Sources: Claude Code hooks (SessionStart) , Anthropic, Effective harnesses for long-running agents , Dev Containers . Recap What to keep from this lesson Probe the environment before the first model call. Fail loud in one place; never let the agent "figure it out". Environment faults disguised as test failures make agents break good code. Declare what the acceptance command needs, and probe exactly that. Keep init idempotent so it can run on every session. Add a --fix flag that auto-installs missing dev dependencies but never modifies runtime dependencies without approval. Move probes from hardcoded functions to a YAML registry. Defend the trade-off. Add a timing budget per probe. A probe that runs longer than three seconds is a workbench smell. Solutions Solution P1 · None done, fifteen calls, worse code None finish. All 15 model calls are spent, every task is blocked with "No module named pytest", and the code is worse than it needs to be: two functions happen to be correct on disk but are marked blocked, and is_even , which the model fixes at once when tests can run, ends wrong after rewrites prompted by an error that had nothing to do with it. Solution B1 · Probe the database first On those nights the database the tests need is down or unreachable. Every test fails with "connection refused", the agent reads that as a failure of its code, rewrites database code to "fix" it, and the tasks end blocked with a misleading reason. Run an init script before the agent starts: probe that the database answers (connect and run a trivial query with a short timeout), that required environment variables and credentials are set, and that the test command passes on a known-good commit (a smoke test). If any probe fails, do not start the agent; alert a person with the probe's report. Add the same probe to the harness between tasks, and revert agent edits made during runs whose environment probe failed.
