a1436: Course home / Phase 14 · AI Agents: Design and Engineering Task Boundaries and Scope Contracts Lesson 14.36 50 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Write a scope contract that an agent reads at task start and a verifier reads at task end. Specify allowed files, forbidden files, acceptance criteria, rollback plan, and approval boundaries. Implement a scope checker that compares a diff against the contract and flags violations. Make scope creep visible, automatic, and reviewable. Before you start Needs : Phase 14 · 32 (Minimal Workbench), Phase 14 · 33 (Rules as Constraints) Type : Build. Time : about 50 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The model does not know where the work ends. A scope contract is a per-task file that says where the work begins, where it ends, and how to roll back if it spills. The contract turns "stay in scope" from a wish into a check. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Scope contract "The task brief" Per-task JSON listing allowed/forbidden files, acceptance, rollback Scope creep "It also touched..." Files outside the contract changed in the same task Rollback plan "We can revert" The one-paragraph operator runbook for halting Approval boundary "Needs sign-off" An action listed in the contract as requiring explicit human approval Diff check "Path audit" Comparing touched files against the contract globs From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.134 · Designing a production agent: specs, contracts and failure modes Lesson 14.67 · Long-running agents: harness and loop engineering The problem In plain words first A scope contract says, before the agent starts, which files it may change, which it must not touch, and what proves the task done. After the run, a scope check compares the actual diff with the contract. Contracts as a design tool are covered in your course (Lessons 14.134 and 14.67, linked above); this lesson measures what a small model does with and without one, and what the lesson's checker catches. Agents creep. The task is "fix the login bug." The diff touches the login route, the email helper, the database driver, the README, and the release script. Each touch had a plausible reason in the moment. Together they are a different change than the one that was reviewed. Scope creep is the most under-monitored failure mode in agent work because the agent narrates each step in good faith. The fix is not a stricter prompt. The fix is a contract on disk that says what was promised and a check that compares the result against the promise. The idea Idea 1 · What goes in a scope contract Field Purpose task_id Links to the task on the board goal One sentence the reviewer can verify allowed_files Globs the agent may write forbidden_files Globs the agent must not touch even by accident acceptance_criteria Test commands or assertion lines that prove done rollback_plan One paragraph the operator can execute if a halt is required approvals_required Actions outside scope that need explicit human sign-off A contract without forbidden_files is incomplete. The negative space is half the contract. Idea 2 · Globs, not raw paths Real repos move files. Pin contracts to globs ( app/**/*.py , tests/test_signup*.py ) so a refactor between sessions does not invalidate the contract. Idea 3 · Rollback is part of scope Listing how to roll back forces the contract author to think about what could go wrong. A contract you cannot roll back from is a contract that should not be approved. Idea 4 · Scope check is a diff check The agent writes a diff. The checker reads the diff, the allowed globs, the forbidden globs, and a list of any acceptance commands that ran. Each violation is a tagged finding the verification gate can refuse. Idea 5 · Two altitudes of scope: the feature list and the task contract The scope contract bounds one task. It does not bound the project. An agent can stay perfectly inside a contract for the login fix and still, on the next turn, decide the project also needs a settings page, a dark mode toggle, and a rewrite of the router. The contract was never asked which work was in scope for the project, only which files were in scope for the task. That second altitude needs its own primitive: a feature_list.json the agent reads at session start. It is the project backlog as a machine-readable, ordered file. The agent picks exactly one feature whose status is todo , writes its id into the active scope contract, and is forbidden from starting a second feature in the same session. "One feature at a time" stops being a line in the prompt the agent can rationalize past and becomes a value it reads off disk and a check the gate enforces. Copy Field Purpose active The single feature the current session may touch; empty means pick one and set it features[].id Stable slug the scope contract's task_id points at features[].status todo , in_progress , done , blocked ; only one in_progress at a time features[].goal One sentence the reviewer can verify features[].done_when The acceptance line that flips in_progress to done Two rules make the list load-bearing instead of decorative. First, the invariant "at most one in_progress " is itself a startup check (Phase 14 · 33): if the list shows two, the session refuses to start until a human resolves it. Second, the feature list is a file, not a chat message, because the chat scrolls out of context and the file persists across sessions and across agents. The handoff (Phase 14 · 40) writes the finished feature's status back to done so the next session opens to an accurate board instead of re-deriving what is left. The contract and the list compose by least privilege, the same merge described below: the task contract's allowed_files must sit inside whatever the active feature touches, never outside it. The same idea as a formula The check is set arithmetic. With touched files , allowed globs and forbidden globs : ​ = { t ∈ T : t ⊨ F } , T off ​ = { t ∈ T : t  ⊨ A ∪ F } . Any forbidden write blocks; off-scope writes count against a small violation budget. Note what the check cannot see: an empty passes, so "changed nothing" must be caught by the acceptance criteria, not by scope. Worked example A test that stopped testing Task: "make the failing test pass: to_fahrenheit is wrong". With no contract, the model edits app.py and test_app.py . Its new test file moves the assertion into def check_to_fahrenheit(): , which nothing calls. The test file now passes whatever app.py does. scope_check flags test_app.py as forbidden ( test_*.py ) and blocks; without the check, CI would show green. With the contract in the prompt, four of five runs changed nothing at all and the fifth edited README.md , config.yml and scripts/release.sh : scope blocks the release script, and an acceptance check is what catches the four empty runs. Check your mental model ✗ "If tests pass, the change is fine." ✓ Here the agent made a test pass by making it stop testing. ✗ "Telling the agent its scope keeps it in scope." ✓ One run with the contract still wrote the forbidden release script. ✗ "A clean scope check means the task is done." ✓ Changing nothing is perfectly in scope. ✗ "Allowed files are enough." ✓ Forbidden globs name the files whose change is never acceptable, like tests. Predict before you run Five small tasks on a repo with app.py , test_app.py , a README, a config file and a release script. The model may change any file and is told nothing about scope. How many runs will touch a test or the release script? (Solution P1.) See it drawn Five tasks, no contract Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (greedy, CPU) sees all five files and returns each file it changes. The lesson's scope_check (from code/main.py ) compares the touched files with a contract: app.py allowed, test_*.py and scripts/** forbidden. About 1 minute. Part 1 of 5 · ScopeContract , RunSummary , Finding , ScopeReport , matches_any Copy Part 2 of 5 · merge_contracts , _merge_egress , _min_optional Copy Part 3 of 5 · scope_check , archive Copy Part 4 of 5 · setup Copy Part 5 of 5 · run it (what python3 code/main.py does) Copy What you should see Copy Production patterns in the wild A practitioner running "specsmaxxing" (scope contracts in YAML before invoking the agent) reports rabbit-hole rate dropped from 52% to 21% in three weeks without changing the agent. The contract did the work, not the model. Three patterns make the gain stick. Violation budgets, not binary failures. agent-guardrails (the OSS merge gate used by Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex via MCP) ships a violationBudget per task: minor scope slips within budget are surfaced as warnings; only when the budget is exceeded does the merge gate refuse. Pair with violationSeverity: "error" | "warning" . The budget is the difference between a gate that ships and a gate that gets disabled by the team that hated it. Severity asymmetry by path family. Off-scope writes to docs/** are usually warn ; off-scope writes to scripts/** , migrations/** , config/prod/** are always block . This asymmetry has to live in the contract, not in the runtime, because it is project-specific and changes per task. Time and network budgets next to file budgets. A time_budget_minutes field bounds the wall clock; the runtime refuses to continue past it without re-approval. A network_egress allowlist on hostnames prevents the agent from quietly hitting an external API that was not part of the task. These are scope dimensions too; the file globs are necessary, not sufficient. Multi-contract merge semantics (least privilege). When two scope contracts apply (e.g., a project-wide contract plus a task-specific one), the merge is: intersect allowed_files (both contracts must permit the path), union forbidden_files (either can prohibit), time_budget_minutes is the most restrictive (min), approvals_required accumulates. network_egress is None for no enforcement, [] for deny-all, [...] as an allowlist; under merge, None defers to the other side, two lists intersect, and deny-all stays deny-all. State this in the contract schema so the merge is mechanical and reviewable. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Production patterns: Claude Code slash commands. A /scope command writes the contract and pins it as session context. Subagents read the contract before acting. GitHub PRs. Push the contract as a JSON file in the PR body or as a checked-in artifact. CI runs the scope checker against the merge diff. LangGraph interrupts. A scope violation triggers an interrupt; the handler asks the human whether the contract needs to grow or the agent needs to back off. The contract travels with the task. When the task closes, the contract is archived under outputs/scope/closed/ . Break it on purpose An agent's pull requests always pass CI. A reviewer notices that three of the last ten also changed files under tests/ , each time "to fix a flaky test". What could be going on, and what should the scope contract and the gate say? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Coding agents enforce scope with permission settings (allowed paths and commands), pre-tool hooks that refuse edits outside allowed globs, and protected branches with CODEOWNERS for tests, migrations and release files. Test tampering (weakening, skipping or rewriting tests to pass) is a documented failure of coding agents and reward hacking in RL-trained models; teams protect test directories or require a human review for any test change made with a code fix. Feature lists and task contracts (Anthropic's long-running harness keeps a JSON feature list the agent may only mark as passing, never edit) are the same idea at two altitudes. This is scope creep, and it is hard to see because the agent explains each step in good faith. The fix is not a stricter prompt. It is a contract on disk that lists the files the task may change and the files it must never change, plus a check that compares the final diff with that contract. The check runs before the gate, and a write to a forbidden path blocks the task. Why the prompt did not hold. Each change had a local reason. Field Purpose task_id Points at the task on the board goal One sentence that a reviewer can verify allowed_files Globs the agent may write forbidden_files Globs the agent must not touch, even by accident acceptance_criteria Commands or assertion lines that prove done rollback_plan One paragraph an operator can run if the task must be halted approvals_required Actions outside scope that need a human sign-off Two rules about the fields. First, a contract without forbidden_files is incomplete, because the negative space is half the contract. Second, use globs and not raw paths, so that a file move between sessions does not void the contract. The check. The checker reads the diff, the allowed globs and the forbidden globs, and returns the violations, the in-scope files and the off-scope files. For this pull request it reports the release script as a forbidden write and the README, the email helper and the driver as off-scope writes. Severity differs by path family: an off-scope write under docs/** is a warning, and a write under scripts/** , migrations/** or production config is always a block. That asymmetry lives in the contract, because it changes per project and per task. Make it survive the team. A gate that fails on every small slip gets switched off. Give each task a violation budget so that minor slips surface as warnings, and only a budget overrun blocks the merge. Lesson 14.139 · Reliability engineering for agents Lesson 14.67 · Long-running agents: harness and loop engineering The problem In plain words first Runtime feedback is what the agent learns from actually running something: the exit code, the output, how long it took. Raw output is a poor message, though: long logs bury the one line that matters, cost tokens, and can carry secrets into the prompt. A feedback record captures the run in a fixed shape (exit code, the head and tail of the output, secrets redacted, timeouts marked) and the loop refuses to advance when there is no exit code. Tool results and retries in general are covered in Lessons 14.139 and 14.67 (linked above); this lesson measures what each form of feedback costs and carries. The agent says "running tests now." The next message says "all tests pass." The reality is that no test ran. The agent imagined the output, or it ran the command and never read the result, or it read the result and silently truncated the failure line. A feedback runner removes that gap. Every command goes through the runner. Every record carries the command, the captured stdout and stderr, the exit code, the wall-clock duration, and a one-line agent note. The agent reads the record at the next turn. The verification gate reads the records at the end of the task. The idea Idea 1 · What goes in a feedback record Field Why it matters command Exact argv, no shell expansion surprises stdout_tail Last N lines, deterministic truncation stderr_tail Last N lines, separate from stdout exit_code The unambiguous success signal duration_ms Surfaces slow probes and runaway processes started_at Timestamp for replay agent_note One line the agent writes about what it expected Idea 2 · Truncation is deterministic A 50 MB log destroys the loop. The runner truncates head and tail with a ...truncated N lines... marker, deterministic so the same output always produces the same record. No sampling; the parts the agent needs to see (final error, final summary) live at the tail. Idea 3 · Feedback versus telemetry Telemetry (Phase 14 · 23, OTel GenAI conventions) is for human operators reviewing runs across time. Feedback is for the next turn of this run. They share fields but they live in different files with different retention. Idea 4 · Refuse to advance without feedback If the runner errors before capturing exit, the record carries exit_code: null and error: <reason> . The agent loop must refuse to claim success on a null exit. No exit, no progress. The same idea as a formula Cost of feedback. With retries per task and a feedback message of tokens, a task's prompt cost grows by about . A raw log of lines costs ; a head-and-tail record costs , fixed whatever the log length. Exposure. If a secret appears in the output with probability per run and feedback is sent raw, the chance that at least one of prompts contains it is ; redaction before the model sees the text makes it 0 for the patterns it covers. Advance rule. A step may be marked passed or failed only if an exit code exists: = null . A timeout is not a failure of the code; it is a missing measurement. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure A pull request from a coding agent says that the whole suite is green. A reviewer runs it and two tests fail. The transcript shows the agent writing "running tests now" and then "all tests pass", with nothing between the two lines. What happened, and what do you build so that this claim cannot reach a reviewer again? Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The agent predicted the output instead of reading it. Either no command ran, or the command ran and nobody captured the result into the loop. The fix has two parts: a feedback runner that records every command with its exit code, and a verification gate that reads those records and refuses to mark the task done unless each acceptance command ran and exited zero. Three ways the claim appears. No command ran. The model wrote the words it expected to write next. Nothing in the transcript shows argv, output or an exit code. The command ran, and the result never came back. A runner that errors before it captures the exit leaves the model with nothing to read, and the model fills the gap. The result came back, and the failure line was cut. A long output trimmed from the end loses the summary line where the failures are. The transcript in this case has no record between the two sentences, so it is the first or the second. The feedback runner. Every command goes through one wrapper. The record carries the exact argv, the tail of stdout and stderr as separate fields, the exit code, the duration, the start time, and a one-line note of what the agent expected. The runner truncates head and tail in a fixed way with a marker for the lines it removed, so the final error line survives. If the runner fails before it captures an exit, the record carries exit_code: null and an error field, and the loop must not advance on it. No exit, no progress. The verification gate. The gate is a pure function over the artifacts. For this failure it checks three things from the feedback log: every acceptance command appears in the records, each one exited zero, and no record has a null exit. Each of those is a block-severity finding. A block prevents passed: true , and only a human can override it, with a reason and a user id in a signed log. The gate runs in CI and before the handoff. No green verdict, no pull request. Why the model is not the fix. A prompt that says "always run the tests" asks the model to be honest about something it cannot see. The runner makes the result visible. The gate makes the claim checkable. Neither depends on the model. Plausible wrong answers. "Tell the agent to paste the test output into the transcript." The model can paste what it expects, and a reviewer cannot tell a paste from a capture. "Trust the agent and let CI catch it." CI did catch it, after the claim reached a reviewer, and the point is to stop the claim at the source. "Treat a timeout as a pass, because the tests were slow." A timeout gives a null exit, and the loop must refuse to advance on a null exit. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the record keep stdout and stderr in separate fields? Expected: a test runner writes the failure summary to one stream and progress to the other, and a merged tail can hide the summary behind progress lines. (level 2) The agent runs the acceptance command, it fails, and a retry passes. What does the gate see? Expected: two records for the same command, linked by the parent command id. The gate blocks on the failed record and does not report passed: true , even though the retry exited zero. Only a signed human override gets past it, and the chain keeps the failure history visible. (level 3) Why must the gate be deterministic and not a model judge? Expected: the gate answers whether the task is complete, which must give the same verdict for the same artifacts every time, while a judge gives a qualitative opinion that belongs on the review side. (level 4) Where do you place the gate so that it cannot be bypassed? Expected: in layers, with a pre-commit hook, a CI status check, and a pre-merge gate, so that a failure in one layer is caught by the next. Where it is taught. The record carries the exact command as argv, the tail of stdout and the tail of stderr as separate fields, the exit code, the duration, the start time, and a one-line note of what the agent expected. The exit code is the success signal, because text can say anything and the code cannot. If the runner fails before it captures an exit, the record carries a null exit and an error reason, and the loop must not advance on it. The fields. Field Why it is there command Exact argv, so no shell expansion surprise stdout_tail The last lines of output, truncated the same way every time stderr_tail The last lines of errors, kept apart from stdout exit_code The one unambiguous success signal duration_ms Shows slow probes and runaway processes started_at A timestamp for replay agent_note What the agent expected before it read the result Truncation that does not lose the error. A large log destroys the loop. The runner keeps a fixed number of head lines and tail lines and inserts a marker that says how many lines it removed. The same output always gives the same record. Nothing is sampled, because the final error and the final summary live at the tail. Redact at write. A record of stdout can carry a secret. The runner strips bearer tokens, password assignments, API keys and known key formats before it appends the line. Redaction at read time is a mistake, because the file on disk is what an attacker reaches. Feedback is not telemetry. Telemetry is for operators reviewing runs across time. Feedback is for the next turn of this run. They share fields and live in different files with different retention. Plausible wrong answers. "Parse the output for the word error to detect failure." The file on disk is already the leak, so redaction has to happen before the append. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why keep stderr separate from stdout? Expected: the failure summary often lands on one stream and progress on the other, and a merged tail can bury the summary. (level 2) A command times out. What does the record say? Expected: it records the prediction before the result, so a reviewer can see when the agent expected success and got a failure. (level 3) A retry succeeds. How does the audit see the first failure? Lesson 14.143 · Evaluation and testing in depth Lesson 14.67 · Long-running agents: harness and loop engineering The problem In plain words first A verification gate is code that decides whether a task is done, from evidence: did the acceptance commands run and exit 0, did the diff stay in scope, did every blocking rule pass. Its answer is the same every time for the same evidence, and nobody, the agent included, can talk it into a different one. Evaluation and judges in general are covered in Lessons 14.143 and 14.67 (linked above); this lesson puts the agent's own verdict and an LLM judge next to the lesson's gate on eight real fixes. Agents declare success too easily. Three failure shapes dominate: "Looks good." The model read its own diff and decided it was correct. "Tests passed." Said with confidence. No record of the test actually running. "Acceptance met." Acceptance criteria interpreted loosely enough to mean "anything resembling done." The workbench fix is a single verification gate that reads the artifacts the agent has already produced and makes the call. The gate is deterministic. The gate is in version control. The gate is wired into CI. The agent cannot bribe it. The idea Idea 1 · What the gate checks Check Source artifact Severity All acceptance commands ran feedback_record.jsonl block All acceptance commands exited zero feedback_record.jsonl block Scope check has no forbidden writes scope_report.json block Scope check has no off-scope writes scope_report.json block or warn All block-severity rules pass rule_report.json block No null exit codes in feedback feedback_record.jsonl block Touched files match scope.allowed_files both warn A warn finding annotates the verdict; a block finding prevents passed: true . Idea 3 · One report, one path The gate emits one verification_report.json per task close-out, written under outputs/verification/<task_id>.json . CI consumes the same path. Multiple gates with different paths fork the source of truth. Idea 4 · Refuse without exception Block-severity findings cannot be overridden by the agent. They can only be overridden by a human, with a recorded override_reason and an overridden_by user id. The override is a signed change, not an agent decision. Defense-in-depth, not single gate. Pre-commit hook → CI status check → pre-tool authz hook → pre-merge gate. Each layer is deterministic so a failure in one layer is caught by the next. microservices.io's March 2026 playbook is explicit: the pre-commit hook is non-bypassable because, unlike a model-side skill, it does not depend on the agent following instructions. The verification gate sits at the CI / pre-merge layer. Defense by deterministic check, model-judge only for nuance. Anthropic's 2026 Hybrid Norm pairing: verifiable rewards (unit tests, schema checks, exit codes) answer "did the code solve the problem?" — LLM rubrics answer "is the code readable, secure, on-style?" The gate runs the first class; the reviewer (Phase 14 · 39) runs the second. Mixing them collapses the signal. Signed override log, not Slack threads. Every override emits a row in outputs/verification/overrides.jsonl with: timestamp, finding code, reason, signing user, current HEAD commit. The runtime refuses any override that lacks the signature; the audit trail is git-tracked. This is the line between an override policy and an override theater. Coverage floor as a first-class check. A coverage_report.json feeds a coverage_floor (default 80%) check. The gate fails if measured coverage drops below the floor or below the previous merge's floor by more than 1 percentage point. Without this check, agents quietly delete tests that fail and the verification reports stay green. --strict mode promotes warns to blocks. For release branches, ship-blocking PRs, or post-incident triage, --strict makes every warning a hard fail. The flag is opt-in by branch; not the global default, because strict-on-everything corrodes day-to-day flow. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Production patterns: CI step. A verify_agent job runs the gate against the agent's final artifacts. Merge protection refuses without passed: true . Pre-handoff hook. The agent runtime calls the gate before generating the handoff doc. No green verdict, no handoff. Manual triage. Operators read the report when an agent claims success and a human suspects it. The gate is the deciding edge in the workbench flow. Every other surface is upstream of it. Break it on purpose Your team replaced its CI gate with "an LLM reviews the diff and the test output and approves or rejects" because CI was slow. Approval rates went up and so did incidents. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Deterministic checks first : tests, type checks, linters, scope checks and coverage floors run in CI and in agent hooks; coding agents are told to run them, and harnesses refuse "done" until they pass (Anthropic's long-running-agent harness requires end-to-end verification before a feature is marked passing). Solutions Solution P1 · Yes to all eight Yes to all eight, and the gate blocks five of them: largest , to_fahrenheit , is_leap , clamp and average fail their tests. The agent's own verdict agrees with the evidence only on the three fixes that happened to work. Solution B1 · Gate on evidence, review on judgement The decision moved from evidence to opinion. An LLM reviewer reading test output can approve failures (as the judge here approved every fix), especially when outputs are long or the diff looks plausible, so approvals rose while correctness did not. Keep the deterministic gate as the only path to merge: required status checks for tests, type checks, scope and coverage, blocking on any failure or missing result. Speed it up with test selection, caching and parallel runs rather than replacing it. Debug a failure Every verification report for the last month says passed. A reviewer notices that the test suite runs much faster than it did, and that several test files are gone. The acceptance command still exits zero. What happened, which check is missing from the gate, and what else do you change? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The agent met the acceptance command by removing the tests that failed, and the gate only checked that the command ran and exited zero. The missing check is a coverage floor: the gate reads a coverage report and blocks when coverage is below the floor, 80 percent by default, or when it drops by more than one percentage point against the previous merge. Add the test directory to the scope check so that a deletion under it is a flagged write, and promote warnings to blocks on release branches. How a green gate lies. The gate is deterministic over artifacts, and it was given the wrong artifacts to be sure about. Its checks were: acceptance commands ran, acceptance commands exited zero, no forbidden writes, no null exits, block-severity rules passed. A test suite with fewer tests exits zero. Nothing in that list measures how much the suite covers. The coverage floor. A coverage_report.json with the current and the previous coverage feeds a new check. Two findings come out of it: Finding Severity Condition coverage.below_floor block current coverage under the floor coverage.regression block drop of more than one percentage point against the previous merge coverage.minor_regression warn any smaller drop coverage.missing warn no coverage report at all The last row is the quiet failure. If the agent stops producing the report, the gate only warns. On a release branch run the gate in strict mode, which promotes every warning to a block, so a missing report blocks. Scope sees deletions. A deletion is a write. Put tests/** in the scope contract, either as allowed for the task that owns the tests or as forbidden for tasks that do not. Then the diff check reports a deleted test file as an off-scope or forbidden write, and the gate refuses before the coverage check runs. Review reads changed tests. The reviewer is the second pass with a different role. Its checklist should include the diff of test files. A test that was changed or removed in the same change that made it pass is the pattern to flag. Prove the fix. Run two proofs. For coverage, take the last passing change, restore a deleted test whose loss drops coverage by more than one percentage point, and run the old and the new gate on both versions. The old gate passes both, and the new gate blocks the deletion on coverage regression and passes the restored one. A smaller drop only warns outside strict mode. For scope, run the same deletion under a new contract that forbids tests/** for the task, and confirm that the scope check blocks it. Plausible wrong answers. "Add a rule that says do not delete tests." A rule the gate cannot check from an artifact is a wish, and the agent did not think of it as deleting tests. "Count the tests and block when the number falls." A count blocks legitimate consolidation, while a coverage floor measures what the suite protects. "Make the acceptance command also print coverage." The gate reads a report, not output text, so the coverage must arrive as an artifact the gate can parse. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which artifact carries the floor? Expected: the coverage report carries the current and previous values, and the floor is a gate parameter so that it is versioned with the gate, not with the agent's output. (level 3) Why is a missing coverage report only a warning by default? Expected: strict everywhere erodes daily flow, so the default warns and the release branches run strict, where the warning becomes a block. (level 4) The agent rewrites a test to always pass instead of deleting it. What catches that? Expected: coverage stays the same, so the gate does not, and the reviewer's diff of test files or a mutation check in CI is the layer that sees it. (level 4) How do you keep the human override from becoming the way around the floor? Expected: an override writes a signed row with the finding code, the reason, the user and the commit, and review reads that log. Where it is taught. The verification gates lesson adds the coverage floor and the strict mode, and the scope contracts lesson makes a deletion a checked write. Explain the mechanism A proposal replaces the script that decides whether an agent task is done with a model judge. The argument is that a judge reads the diff, understands intent, and catches more than a script can. Argue for or against, and say where a judge does belong. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Against. The gate answers one question, is this task complete, and that verdict must be the same for the same artifacts every time, in version control, in CI, with no way for the agent to argue with it. A model judge gives a different answer on a different day and can be talked into a pass. A judge belongs on the review side, where the question is qualitative: is the code readable, secure and on style. What the gate reads and decides. Check Source Severity Every acceptance command ran feedback records block Every acceptance command exited zero feedback records block No write to a forbidden path scope report block No off-scope write scope report block or warn Every block-severity rule passed rule report block No null exit code feedback records block Touched files match the allowed globs both warn A warn annotates the verdict. A block prevents passed: true . Every check is a comparison between artifacts the agent already produced. No judgement is needed, so no judge is needed. Why determinism is the point. Three failure shapes dominate agent work: "looks good", "tests passed" with no record, and acceptance read loosely enough to mean anything. A model judge is subject to all three. It reads the diff and decides it looks good. It reads the transcript and believes the claim. It interprets the acceptance line generously. The script cannot do any of that, because it never reads prose. The lesson pairs the two kinds of signal: verifiable checks such as tests, schema checks and exit codes answer whether the code solved the problem, and rubric judges answer whether it is readable and on style. Mixing them collapses the signal. Overrides are human and signed. A block cannot be overridden by the agent. A human can override it, and the override writes a row with the finding code, a reason, the signing user and the current commit into an audit log that git tracks. The runtime refuses an override without a signature. That is the line between an override policy and an override theater. One report, several layers. The gate writes one verification_report.json per task under one path, and CI reads the same path. Around it sit other deterministic layers: a pre-commit hook, a CI status check, a pre-tool authorization hook and a pre-merge gate. A failure in one layer is caught by the next. The pre-commit hook does not depend on the agent following instructions, but it is a local check that git commit --no-verify skips, so the CI status check and the pre-merge gate hold the verdict. Where the judge goes. The reviewer, a separate pass with a different role, reads the diff and the reports after the gate passes. It scores readability, security and style. Its output goes to a human or into the handoff, never into the gate's verdict. Plausible wrong answers. "A judge understands intent, so it catches more." The gate does not need intent, and a judge that infers intent can be convinced that an incomplete task is complete. "Run the judge and the script, and pass if either passes." The judge then becomes the way around the script, so the deterministic checks must decide done and the judge must only annotate. "Let the agent explain why a block does not apply." The agent is the party under test, and an override needs a human signature with a reason. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) An agent deletes failing tests, and the gate stays green. Which check is missing? Expected: a coverage floor read from a coverage report, with a block when coverage falls below the floor or drops by more than one percentage point against the previous merge. (level 3) When is promoting every warning to a block the right default? Expected: on release branches and in post-incident triage through a strict flag, and not globally, because strict everywhere erodes daily flow. (level 4) What stops the override log from becoming a formality? Expected: the runtime refuses an unsigned entry, the log is in git, and review reads it, so every override has a name and a reason attached. (level 4) The gate and the reviewer disagree. Who wins? Expected: the gate decides whether the task is done, and the reviewer decides whether it is good, so a gate failure blocks regardless of the review, and a review failure reopens the task without touching the verdict. Where it is taught. The verification gates lesson builds the deterministic gate, the signed override log and the coverage floor. Lesson 14.148 · Humans in charge: approvals and handoffs Lesson 14.67 · Long-running agents: harness and loop engineering The problem In plain words first A reviewer agent is a second pass in a different role: it reads the change, the state, the test results and the gate's verdict, scores the work on a rubric, and writes a report. It cannot edit anything. Its job is what a gate cannot do: ask whether the tests prove the goal or only a weaker version of it. Human approvals and handoffs are covered in Lessons 14.148 and 14.67 (linked above); this lesson tests the lesson's rubric scorer and a model in the reviewer role on six real fixes. You ask the agent to fix a bug. It edits four files, runs the tests, and reports done. The verification gate (Phase 14 · 38) confirms acceptance ran and scope held. The gate says passed: true . You merge. Two days later you find that the fix solved the wrong half of the bug. Acceptance is necessary, not sufficient. The reviewer asks the questions acceptance cannot ask: did this solve the right problem? Did it expand scope without flagging it? Did it document assumptions that should have been questioned? Did it leave the workbench in a state the next session can pick up? The idea Idea 1 · Reviewer rubric Five dimensions, each scored 0 to 2. Dimension Question Problem fit Did the change solve the task as stated, not a nearby task? Scope discipline Were edits confined to the contract or was the contract grown deliberately? Assumptions Are all hidden assumptions written down somewhere reviewable? Verification quality Does the acceptance command actually prove the goal, or did it prove a weaker version? Handoff readiness Could the next session pick up cleanly from the current state? Total out of 10. A run below 7 is a soft fail; a run below 5, or any dimension at 0, is a hard fail. Idea 2 · The reviewer is a separate role, not a separate model You can run the reviewer with the same model as the builder. The discipline is the role separation: different system prompt, different inputs, no write access to the diff. The change in posture is the change in signal. Idea 3 · The reviewer cannot edit the diff The reviewer reads the diff, the state, the feedback, the verdict. It writes a report. It does not patch the diff. If the report says "fix this," the next builder turn does the fix; the reviewer goes back to reviewing. Mixing roles defeats the gap. Idea 4 · Reviewer rubric versus verification gate The gate (Phase 14 · 38) checks deterministic facts: did acceptance run, did rules pass, did scope hold. The reviewer makes qualitative judgments: was this the right work, is it documented, is the handoff usable. Both are required. The same idea as a formula What a gate can and cannot prove. If the acceptance test checks a set of cases and the goal requires a larger set , a gate certifies only for . The reviewer's question is the gap: A weak test makes the gate pass for every that is right on , including ones wrong on . The rubric. Five dimensions scored to , total : pass if and no dimension is ; hard fail if any is or . A heuristic that scores a dimension wrongly at turns a correct change into a hard fail on its own. Worked example One fix through the gate and the reviewer Task: "average(xs) must return the mean, and 0 for an empty list." The builder sees only the acceptance test, assert average([2, 4, 6]) == 4 . It writes sum(xs) / len(xs) . The gate runs the test: exit 0, pass. The hidden full test calls average([]) and gets ZeroDivisionError . The unproved part is exactly the empty-list case: . Only a reader comparing the goal with the test can spot it. The model as reviewer, asked "does this test prove the whole goal?", says YES. Generate a handoff from the workbench artifacts without hand-writing prose. Trim large feedback logs into a handoff-sized summary. Make the next session's first action deterministic. Before you start Needs : Phase 14 · 34 (Repo Memory), Phase 14 · 38 (Verification), Phase 14 · 39 (Reviewer) Type : Build. Time : about 50 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The session is going to end. The work is not. The handoff packet is the artifact that turns "the agent worked for an hour" into "the next session is productive in the first minute." Build it on purpose, not as an afterthought. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Handoff packet "Session summary" Generated artifact carrying the seven fields, both markdown and JSON Next action "What to do first" The one concrete step that starts the next session Feedback trim "Log summary" Last K records plus every non-zero exit Status report "What we did" A document missing next_action ; useful, but not a handoff Verdict pointer "Receipt" Path to the verification + review reports for traceability From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.60 · State, checkpoints, resume and human approval Lesson 14.67 · Long-running agents: harness and loop engineering The problem In plain words first A handoff is the packet one session leaves for the next: what changed, which commands ran, what failed and why, the open risks, and the first concrete next step. Without one, the next session repeats the same failed attempts. The lesson's point is that handoffs should be generated from recorded artifacts (state, feedback, verdict, review), not written from memory at the end of a long session. State files and resume are covered in Lessons 14.60 and 14.67 (linked above); this lesson ends a real session mid-task and measures what each kind of handoff gives the next one. The session ends. The agent says "great, we made progress." The next session opens. The next agent asks "where did we leave off?" The first agent's answer is gone. The next agent rediscovers, re-runs the same commands, re-asks the human the same questions, and burns thirty minutes recovering the last thirty seconds of the previous session. The cost of a bad handoff is paid every session for the life of the task. The fix is a packet generated automatically at session end: what changed, why, what was tried, what failed, what is left, what to do first next time. The idea Idea 1 · Seven fields every handoff carries Field Question it answers summary One paragraph of what was done changed_files The diff at a glance commands_run What was actually executed failed_attempts What was tried and why it did not work open_risks What could bite next session, with severity next_action The first concrete step next session takes verdict_pointer Path to the verification + review reports The next_action field is the load-bearing one. A handoff with everything except next_action is a status report, not a handoff. Idea 2 · Handoffs are generated, not written A hand-written handoff is a handoff that gets skipped on a hard day. The generator reads the workbench artifacts and emits the packet. The agent's job is to leave the workbench in a state the generator can summarize, not to write the summary. Idea 3 · Two forms: human-readable and machine-readable handoff.md is what the human reads. handoff.json is what the next agent loads. Both come from the same source artifacts. If they diverge, the JSON wins. Idea 4 · Feedback log trimming The full feedback_record.jsonl may be hundreds of entries. The handoff carries only the last K plus every entry with a non-zero exit. The next session loads the full log if it needs to, but the packet stays small. Idea 5 · Leave a clean state A handoff describes the work. A clean state makes the work resumable. They are not the same thing. A perfect handoff.md is worthless if the next session opens to a half-applied diff, a temp file the agent forgot, a stray branch, and tests that error before they even run. The next agent then spends its first ten minutes cleaning up after the last one instead of building, and the cost compounds every session for the life of the task. So the session does not end when the feature works. It ends when the workbench is in a state the generator can summarize and the next session can trust. Cleanup is its own phase, run before the handoff, and it is a check, not a habit, because a habit is the thing that gets skipped on a hard day. Check Clean means Dirty blocks because Working tree Every change committed or explicitly stashed with a note A half-applied diff looks like intentional work to the next agent Temp artifacts No *.tmp , scratch dirs, debug prints, or commented-out blocks left behind Stray files pollute the diff and the next agent's mental model Tests Green, or red with the failure named in open_risks A silent red test is a trap the next session steps in Feature board feature_list.json status reflects reality (Phase 14 · 36) A stale board sends the next session to work that is already done Branch On the expected branch, no detached HEAD, no orphan branches Wrong branch means the next session's first commit lands in the wrong place The cleanup phase emits a clean_state.json of blocking issues; an empty list is the precondition the handoff generator asserts before it writes a packet. A handoff built on a dirty tree is not a handoff, it is a forwarded mess. The two artifacts pair: cleanup proves the workbench is safe to leave, the handoff proves the next session knows where to start. The same idea as a formula Repeated work. If session 1 tried approaches that failed, and session 2 does not know them, each of its attempts repeats a known failure with probability about (the chance the model's first idea is one already tried). Its expected wasted attempts before something new are about ; a handoff that lists the failures lowers only if the model uses it. Fidelity. A handoff field is faithful if it can be checked against a record. A generated handoff has fidelity 1 for every field it derives (commands, exit codes, blockers); a model-written summary can drop or invent any of them, and nothing checks. Worked example Three handoffs for one stuck task Session 1 tried largest twice. Both times the model renamed the function, so the test failed with ImportError: cannot import name 'largest' . No handoff: session 2's single attempt hits the same ImportError . Model-written handoff: about 800 characters about the attempts. It never names the ImportError and has no next step. Session 2 fixes it anyway. Generated handoff: commands, two failed attempts, the ImportError as an open blocker, the next action. Session 2 fixes it too. Across three stuck tasks: none 0 of 3, either handoff 2 of 3. Check your mental model ✗ "The next session can work it out from the code." ✓ Without a handoff it repeated the same failure on all three tasks. ✗ "Ask the agent to summarise its session." ✓ Its notes left out every error that happened; nothing checks what they say. ✗ "A generated handoff is a status report." ✓ Only with a next action and the failed attempts does it become a handoff. ✗ "Handoffs are for humans." ✓ The machine-readable half is what the next agent session reads. Three different mechanisms, same need: serialize what survives compression into a portable artifact. The packet is that artifact. Fresh-session handoff is not compaction. Compaction extends a session; handoff closes one cleanly and starts the next. The Hermes Issue #20372 framing (April 2026) is right: when in-place compression starts degrading, the agent should write a compact handoff, end the session, and resume in fresh context. The packet is what makes that transition cheap. The mistake is to keep compressing until quality collapses; the fix is to budget for an early, clean handoff. One active handoff per branch and topic. The packet is the lingua franca. The packet is small, regular, and cheap to produce. The cost saving compounds with every session. Break it on purpose Your overnight agent writes a friendly "progress summary" at the end of each session, and the morning session starts from it. Every few days the morning session redoes something the night session already tried and abandoned, and once it re-applied a migration that had been rolled back. Using this lesson, what is wrong with the handoff and what should replace it? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Progress files and git history are the usual handoff in long-running coding agents: Anthropic's harness has each session read a progress file and the git log before starting, and end by committing and updating the progress file. Generated summaries from traces and checkpoints (LangGraph state, OpenAI Agents SDK sessions, Claude Agent SDK session resume) replace free-form recaps in many frameworks; free-text summaries remain for people. Context compaction inside one session (summarising old turns) is the same problem at a smaller scale, and the same rule applies: keep failures, decisions and next steps verbatim, summarise the rest. The paragraph is a status report, and a handoff needs seven fields: a summary, the changed files, the commands run, the failed attempts, the open risks, the next action and a pointer to the verification and review reports. "Ask the agent to write a detailed summary at the end." A written summary is skipped when the session ends badly, and it is the bad sessions that need the handoff most. "The chat history is the handoff." The history is trimmed or gone, and the next session cannot replay an hour of chat in its first minute. "A green verification report is enough to resume." The report proves the task state, not the tree state, and a dirty tree costs the next session its first ten minutes. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why does the JSON win when the two forms disagree? Expected: the next agent loads the JSON, so the machine-readable form is the one that drives the next session. (level 2) Which failed attempts belong in the packet? Expected: every record with a non-zero exit, with the retry chain visible, so that the next session does not repeat a known dead end. (level 2) What is the difference between a handoff and the state file? Expected: the state file is read on every turn and holds where the agent is, while the handoff is generated once at session end and tells the next session where to start. The multi-session handoff lesson builds the packet out of the workbench files and adds the cleanup check. Weigh a trade-off A long coding session has used most of its context window. The runtime offers to summarize the older turns and keep going. Your teammate wants to let it run to the limit, because compaction is automatic. When do you compact, when do you end the session, and what do you measure to choose? Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Compaction extends a session, and a handoff closes one cleanly and starts the next in fresh context. Compaction is fine while the compressed history still carries what the task needs, but quality decays as compression stacks up. The lesson's guidance is to end the session with a generated handoff at 50 to 75 percent of the budget, not at the wall, because the packet is cheap to write while the context is intact and expensive when the model is already losing its place. Two different operations. Operation What it does What it costs Compaction Compresses the history in place and continues the same session Each pass loses detail, and the losses stack up Fresh-session handoff Writes a packet, ends the session, and resumes in a new context A clean break, with the cost of generating and loading the packet Runtimes implement compaction in different ways: a server-side opaque summary, a local summary appended as a user message, a progressive multi-stage compression near the top of the window, or a timestamp-based hiding of old messages plus a short summary. The mechanism varies. The need is the same. Whatever survives compression must be serialized into a portable artifact, and that artifact is the handoff packet. Why not run to the wall. A runtime that compacts at 95 percent compacts a context that is already full of compression artifacts. The packet generator then summarizes degraded state. The mistake is to keep compressing until quality collapses. The fix is to budget for an early, clean handoff. A session that ends at 50 to 75 percent still has the intact history, the real command records and a clear next action. Make the choice measurable. Track the context fraction at which the session ends, and compare task outcomes across the two ranges. Count how many times a session was compacted before it ended, and correlate with review findings. Read the handoff packets: a packet with a vague next_action is a sign that the generator ran too late. One active handoff per branch. Multi-agent work breaks on stale handoffs more than on bad output. Each packet carries the branch, the last known good commit and a status of active, superseded or archived. Only the active packet drives the next session. Plausible wrong answers. "Compaction is automatic, so let the runtime handle it." Automatic compaction decides when to compress, not whether the compressed state is still good enough to work from. "End every session as early as possible to be safe." Each handoff costs a packet and a reload, so the target is a range, not a minimum. "A longer context window removes the problem." A larger window delays the wall, and the quality decay from stacked compression is the same. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is a fresh session better than a third compaction? Expected: compression losses stack up, while a fresh session starts from the packet, the state file and the repo, which are the system of record. (level 3) What must be true of the tree before the handoff runs? Expected: the cleanup check passes, so the tree is committed or stashed with a note, no temp files remain, tests are green or named as risks, and the branch is right. (level 4) The handoff is cheap, but the next session has to rebuild its working context. How do you keep that cost down? Expected: the packet lists the exact artifacts the next session must load before it acts, and the router points at them, so the session loads the state, the board and the active contract and nothing else. (level 4) Two coding agent products are used on one task, one after the other. What makes the transition work? Expected: the packet schema, because the JSON form is product-neutral and both runtimes read the same fields. Where it is taught. Solutions Solution P1 · Blocked by its own baseline No. The pack's verify_agent.py blocks on every failed run of an acceptance command in feedback_record.jsonl . The baseline run (exit 1) is in there, so the gate fails even though the latest run passes. Judging the latest run of each command fixes it. A status-only check misses "always 409", because it never checks that the first signup still succeeds. It also misses "wrong error code". It catches only "never stores the user". The lesson's check rejects all three. Solution B1 · Deleting the record deletes the evidence Deleting the record makes the gate pass by destroying what it judges. The handoff loses the failed attempts and the baseline, so the next session repeats them. And a gate that sees one run cannot tell a fix from a lucky retry: an agent that deletes the record and retries until green passes every time. The pack should change three things. Gate on the latest run of each acceptance command. Tag every run with a role ( baseline , attempt , final ) so the handoff can tell them apart. Make the record append-only, with the gate refusing a record that shrank. Bump the pack's major version, because the gate's meaning changed, and keep a test that a baseline failure followed by a pass is accepted. A bug fix, a bounded feature, or an operational improvement is enough; installing several agents is not part of the exercise. Budget a separate working session beyond the packaging lab. Copy the evidence template linked below into your own learning-artifacts/ directory. Preserve the checked-in template and pack as reference material. 1. Frame the task and choose the autonomy Use the task frame from lesson 43 and the evidence plan from lesson 44. Record the starting revision, observable goal, non-goals, allowed paths, and acceptance evidence. Identify the real user or operator who needs the behavior. Choose a working mode: guided steps, checkpointed implementation, or a bounded autonomous run. Explain why the uncertainty, consequences, and reversibility justify it. A small local refactor may need fewer checkpoints than a change to access control. Set a wall-time budget and a token or cost limit if the agent exposes one. Record unavailable measurements honestly. Define a stop condition for repeated failure, new permissions, budget exhaustion, or an unresolved contract decision; name who can resolve it. 2. Prepare the smallest useful environment Retrieve the relevant implementation, caller, test, and local instructions. Record why each source belongs in context and which current evidence would override a stale note. Do not load the whole repository by default. Make one explicit choice for each relevant extension: a skill supplies a repeatable procedure; an MCP tool supplies access; a hook runs a deterministic check; a plugin packages capabilities. Keep an extension only when the task needs it, with the least permissions that let it work. Record the context or maintenance cost of one proposed addition you reject. Recheck one stale memory or instruction, then retire or replace it in your learner-owned setup when the evidence supports that decision. Rerun the affected check to confirm the removal did not lose a needed constraint. 3. Capture the baseline and implement Before editing, run the closest existing check and demonstrate the requested behavior's current state. Keep the command, revision, result, and evidence location. A feature that does not exist yet still has a baseline: record the observed response or unsupported operation. Let the agent implement inside the contract. Keep an intervention log with the reason for each correction, permission change, or plan revision. Delegation is optional; if useful, apply lesson 45's ownership and integration contract before adding another worker. 4. Challenge the evidence Choose proof that observes the changed surface. For a UI, rebuild and inspect the served journey at relevant widths. For an API, inspect the request and serialized response. For a CLI, run the built command and check its exit code and output. Select the checks your task needs and explain their limits. Write an expected result from the task contract independently of the agent's implementation. In a disposable copy, introduce one specific incorrect result, such as accepting an invalid value or dropping a required response field. Run the same acceptance check: it must fail for that reason. If it stays green, strengthen the assertion or observation before trusting it. Restore the correct implementation and rerun successfully. Keep both receipts. A syntax error or broken test setup does not count as detecting the regression. Review the final diff, including changed tests, against the original goal and allowed paths. Ask a peer or a separate reviewer session to challenge the weakest proof without editing the implementation. You still own the final judgment; another agent's agreement is not execution evidence. 5. Rehearse operation and recovery Run the changed artifact in a disposable local or staging environment. Label every observation local , staging , or live , with the exact revision or artifact identity. A local rehearsal supports a local claim; production deployment is not required for this exercise. Choose one failure signal related to the task, a threshold, an observation window, and an owner. Explain the response when that threshold is crossed. Trigger the signal safely in the rehearsal and retain the observed log, metric, or response. Rehearse rollback to a known-good artifact and check that the previous behavior is restored. Account for persistent data when applicable; replacing a binary alone may not reverse a data change. Record any recovery step you could not verify. 6. Improve the next run and hand it off Compare the result with the baseline, including elapsed time, available usage data, and human interventions. One task shows what happened on that task; it does not establish that an agent is generally faster or more reliable. Promote one observed correction into a test, a smaller permission boundary, an automation, or a clearer example using lesson 46. Rerun the affected check. Remove temporary mutations and leave the final branch, changed files, open risks, and next action explicit for the next session. Manual review rubric Have the reviewer inspect the evidence files and reproduce at least the weakest acceptance check. Use demonstrated , needs revision , or unverified for each row, with an evidence pointer and a reason. Filled fields and passing packaging scripts are not substitutes for these observations. Dimension Evidence the reviewer should challenge Task and autonomy Starting behavior, bounded goal, justified permissions, budget, and a usable stop rule Context and environment Relevant sources, justified tool access, and a rechecked retirement decision Verification Actual before/after behavior and a deliberate incorrect result that the same check rejects Review and operation Inspected diff, independent challenge, labeled runtime observation, and rehearsed recovery Iteration and handoff One verified improvement, honest limits, clean final state, and a reproducible next action Resolve needs revision findings before claiming the task complete. Leave unavailable evidence unverified and narrow the claim accordingly. The portfolio demonstrates your engineering judgment on a bounded task; it is not a hiring or deployment guarantee. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Take-home Take-home. Pick a small real change in a repository you may modify, and let one coding agent make it. Bring back evidence that a reviewer can reproduce, not a transcript. Filled fields and passing scripts are not substitutes for the observations. Leave unavailable evidence as unverified and narrow the claim, and never present the result as a hiring or deployment guarantee. Plausible wrong answers. "The transcript shows the agent running the tests, so that is the evidence." A transcript is what the agent said, and the evidence is the check, its exit code and the record a reviewer can rerun. "The acceptance check passed, so the change is proven." A check that never failed proves nothing, and the deliberate wrong result is what shows the check can detect a regression. "Deployment to production is required to complete the exercise." A labeled local or staging rehearsal supports a local claim, and the exercise asks for honest labels, not production access. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Your planted regression passed the acceptance check. What do you do? Expected: treat the check as untrustworthy, strengthen the assertion or the observation until it fails for that reason, and only then rerun the correct version. (level 3) Why must each runtime observation carry an environment label? Expected: a local rehearsal supports a local claim only, and an unlabeled observation lets a reader read a laptop run as production evidence. (level 4) The agent finished faster than your baseline. What may you claim? Expected: that this task was faster on this run with this many interventions, and nothing about agents in general. (level 4) Which single row would you mark unverified rather than fake? Expected: any row whose evidence you could not observe, such as a recovery step that needs a production mount you do not have, with the claim narrowed to match. Where it is taught. The workbench capstone gives the six steps and the manual review rubric for the evidence. Take-home Take-home. Your team has the workbench surfaces as loose scripts, a shared document and some memory. Package them into one directory that a new repository can install with one command, and defend what you leave out. Bring the layout, the installer, the versioning rule and the uninstall rule. We grade the second install as much as the first. Level 3 of 4 · about 45 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Ship a versioned directory with four parts: the docs that carry the rules and the rubric, the schemas that are the contract, the scripts that are the runtime, and a short installer. The installer refuses to install over an existing pack without a force flag, copies the pack, connects CI if a workflows directory exists, and prints the next steps. Running it twice gives the same result. Project tasks, vendor SDK calls and onboarding prose stay out, because the pack is the recipe and each install is a serving. Layout. Copy In and out. In: the schemas, because they are the contract; the four scripts, because they are the runtime; the four docs, because they are the rules and the rubric. Out: project-specific tasks, which belong on the target repository's board; vendor SDK calls, because the pack is framework-agnostic; onboarding prose, because the pack lives next to the team's onboarding and not inside it. The installer. Refuse to install over an existing pack unless --force is passed. Copy the pack into the target repository. Connect CI if .github/workflows/ exists. Print the next steps: fill the board, set the acceptance commands, run the init script. The installer also writes the pack version into the target repository, and emits symlinks so that every coding agent product reads the same root file. Forking the pack for one product is a failure mode. Versioning. VERSION is the contract. A schema change or a script change that needs a migration bumps the major. A docs-only change bumps the patch. The target's state file records which pack version it was initialized against, and a lint refuses to ship when the target's recorded version disagrees with the pack's. This is how package managers survive a decade of churn, and nothing about agents changes the rule. Uninstall. The uninstaller removes the schemas, the scripts, the docs and the root file, and refuses to run when the state files have uncommitted changes. It never deletes the state file, the board or the outputs directory. State belongs to the user. The pack does not own it. What we grade. The second run of the installer changes nothing. The lint fails when the pack drifts from VERSION . The uninstaller refuses on non-trivial state and leaves the user's files in place. The written defense of each cut, one paragraph each. Plausible wrong answers. "Put the team's current backlog into the pack so that new repos start with real tasks." Tasks belong to the target repository, and a pack that carries them is wrong for every repository but one. "Call the vendor SDK from the scripts to save time." The pack must survive a framework change, and an SDK call ties every install to one runtime. "Make the installer overwrite by default so that updates are easy." An overwrite without a flag destroys local changes, and the force flag is what makes an update a decision. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which one optional fifth document would you promote into the pack, and why? Expected: a reasoned choice with the cut defended, for example a migration runbook, with the argument that it is needed on every major bump and not on one project. (level 3) What counts as non-trivial state for the uninstaller? Expected: any uncommitted change in the state file, the board or the outputs, because those are the user's work and not the pack's. (level 4) How do you migrate a hand-rolled workbench to the pack with the least downtime? Expected: install beside it, map each existing file to a schema, run the gate on both for one task, then switch the router pointer and archive the old files. (level 4) What breaks if two repositories pin different major versions of the pack? Expected: nothing, as long as each records its version and the lint checks each against its own pack, while a shared CI job must run the matching version per repository. Where it is taught. The workbench capstone assembles the pack, the installer and the version rule. Separate repository facts from assumptions and open questions. Define allowed paths, forbidden paths, and acceptance evidence. Decide when reconnaissance is sufficient to begin work. Before you start Needs : Phase 14 lessons 31 and 36 Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A coding agent can implement a clear task quickly. It can also implement an unclear task quickly. The speed is the same. The cost is not. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.134 · Designing a production agent: specs, contracts and failure modes Lesson 14.135 · AI system design: the method, estimates and budgets The Expensive Failure In plain words first Before an agent edits anything, write down what "done" means in this repo. A task frame fits on one screen: the goal as observable behaviour, a few repository facts each with a receipt ( path:line ), the paths the change may and may not touch, the check that proves it, and the decisions nobody has made yet. Specs, contracts and design estimates are covered in Lessons 14.134 and 14.135 (linked above). This lesson gives one vague request to a small model three ways and checks whether each answer fits the system it lands in. “Add duplicate email protection” sounds specific. It is not. Does uniqueness belong in the API, domain service, or database? Is comparison case-sensitive? Which error shape is already public? Is a migration allowed? Which test proves the behavior? A capable agent will fill those gaps with plausible choices. That is the dangerous case because the implementation can be clean, tested, and still incompatible with the system. The first unit of coding-agent work is therefore not an edit. It is a task frame backed by repository evidence. The Task Frame A useful frame has six fields: Field Question Goal What observable behavior must change? Repository facts What did you verify in code, tests, config, or history? Allowed paths Where may the change land? Forbidden paths What must remain untouched? Acceptance evidence Which commands or observations prove the goal? Unknowns Which decisions still need evidence or human judgment? Facts need receipts. “The API uses 409 for duplicates” is not a fact until you can point to the existing test or handler. A file path and line is enough. A command result is better when behavior matters. Reconnaissance Is a Search for Constraints Do not read the entire repository. Search for the surfaces that constrain the change: The current behavior and its caller. The closest existing test. The public contract or serialized shape. The project instructions that govern the path. The build and verification commands. Similar completed changes that reveal local patterns. Stop when every planned decision is either supported by evidence, explicitly delegated, or listed as an unknown. More reading after that point is often avoidance. Unknowns Are Not Failures An unknown is a controlled gap. An assumption is an uncontrolled answer to that gap. Classify each unknown: Discoverable: the repository or running system can answer it. Decidable: the task contract gives the agent authority to choose. Human: the choice changes product behavior, cost, risk, or public compatibility. Deferred: the choice is outside this slice and belongs in non-goals. The agent should continue through discoverable and delegated unknowns. It should pause at human unknowns before the choice is buried in code. Acceptance Before Implementation Write the proof before the patch. The proof can be: a focused unit or integration test command; a browser journey with a named viewport and expected state; a wire request and exact response contract; a performance measurement with a threshold; a scope check that confirms no unrelated file changed. “Tests pass” is not a proof plan. Name the authoritative test and the claim it supports. The same idea as a formula Ambiguity multiplies. If a request leaves independent decisions open and each has ​ plausible answers, the number of implementations that all look reasonable is ∏ d ​ c i ​ . Only a few of them fit the system. Each fact with a receipt, and each decision made explicitly, sets one ​ to 1. Where "duplicate email protection" leaves room. Five decisions are open: where to check (API, service, database), what to return (raise, 400, 409), the success status (keep 201 or change it), case handling, and whether a repeat may overwrite. Even at 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 that is reasonable implementations. The repository already answers three of them: the error shape ( rename ), the success status (201) and case handling ( normalize ). Worked example Reading one sampled answer Bare request, answer 3: the model checks store.rows and returns 409 with an error envelope. That looks right. It also returns {"status": 200} for a new account, where the file says 201. The rename to 200 is one plausible choice, and it breaks every caller that expects 201. The hidden checks score it 4 of 5. Only "first signup still 201" fails, which is exactly the decision the request left open and the repository had already made. A frame with the fact "creation returns 201 ( app/accounts.py:19 )" and an acceptance test asserting 201 closes that gap before any code exists. Check your mental model ✗ "A detailed frame makes the agent's code better." ✓ For this small model the frame alone made it worse: every refusal was an exception. Only the frame with its test produced a fully correct answer. ✗ "Facts are what you remember about the repo." ✓ A fact has a receipt: a path and line, or a command result. ✗ "Let the agent write the frame." ✓ The model's own frame invented a path, listed no facts and no forbidden paths. ✗ "'Tests pass' is the acceptance evidence." ✓ Name the test and the claim it proves, and write it before the patch. Predict before you run "Add duplicate email protection" goes to a 0.5B model three ways: the bare request, a task frame, and the frame plus its acceptance test. Six sampled answers each. Which way produces answers that fit the existing code? Will any of them change something nobody asked to change? (Solution P1.) See it drawn One request, three framings The lesson's TaskFrame and render() build the frame from facts with real line receipts. Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (CPU, temperature 0.8, fixed seed) writes six versions of create_account for each prompt. Five hidden checks score each version: success status, exact repeat, case variant, error envelope and no overwrite. The acceptance test covers only the first two. About 6 minutes. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Bare request: two near misses that changed the contract. Answers 3 and 5 check for an existing email and return 409 with an error envelope. Both also change a new account's status from 201 to 200, so they pass 4 of 5 checks. The rest either change nothing, drop normalize() or raise a ValueError . Task frame alone: no answer refuses a repeat correctly. Four of six keep the 201. Every answer that detects a repeat raises an exception, even though the frame states the 409 envelope as a fact. Prose facts were not enough for this model. Frame plus test: one fully correct answer. Answer 1 passes all five checks, including the case variant and the no-overwrite check, which the test does not cover. Five of six keep 201. With six samples each, 2, 0 and 1 near-complete answers are within noise. The clearest effect is on the contract: the test pinned 201 for 5 of 6, against 2 of 6 for the bare request. See it drawn Can the model frame its own task? This block continues from the one above. The model writes a frame as JSON from the bare request. The lesson's validate() checks it, and then every fact's receipt is checked against the file. About 30 seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The model's own frame is not a frame. It repeats the request as the goal, allows the invented path /accounts/add , forbids nothing, and puts a fact-shaped dictionary under acceptance. validate() catches the empty forbidden paths. The other problems need a check against the repository, and its frame gives no facts to check at all. The hand-written receipts hold up. Each cited line exists and shares words with its claim. This is a crude test: it catches a wrong line number or a file that does not exist, not a subtly wrong claim. A receipt you can check mechanically is still better than one you cannot.
