Record two or three facts with exact evidence. Name the smallest allowed path set. Name negative space explicitly. Write the command or observation that closes the task. List the decisions you have not earned yet. The frame should fit on one screen. If it cannot, the task may contain multiple independently verifiable changes. Exercises Frame a real bug from one of your repositories without proposing a solution. Find one claim in the frame that is actually an assumption. Replace it with evidence. Add a human unknown whose answer would change the public contract. Split one broad allowed path into the smallest safe set. Add a scope receipt to the acceptance evidence. Solutions Solution P1 · The test helped most; the prose frame alone did not The frame with its acceptance test did best. It gave the only answer that passed all five checks, and it kept the 201 success status in 5 of 6 answers. The bare request gave two near misses that both changed 201 to 200, a change nobody asked for. The prose frame alone gave no correct refusal: every answer that caught a repeat raised an exception. With six samples per prompt these rates are noisy. The robust lesson is that the request left decisions open and the model filled them with plausible choices. An executable proof closed more of them than prose did. Solution B1 · The decisions were made in code, not in a frame Nobody framed the task. Two decisions the repository had already made, creation returns 201 and conflicts return 409 with an {code, message} envelope, were left open. The agent filled them with plausible choices. The test it wrote checked its own choices, so it passed. Before the first edit, a frame should record those two facts with receipts (the create_account return line and the existing conflict handler), allow only the service file and its test, forbid the HTTP layer and migrations, and list case handling as a decided or human unknown. Then write the acceptance test from the frame: first signup returns 201, a repeat returns 409 with email_taken , a case variant is refused, and the password is not overwritten. That test, written before the patch, would have failed the PR. What You Keep Keep outputs/task-frame.md . It is the input to the next lesson, where the frame becomes an evidence-backed execution plan. Break it on purpose An agent receives "Add duplicate email protection" and opens a pull request. The code is clean, it has a passing test, and the reviewer approves. A week later the mobile app breaks: signups now return 200, and repeats raise a 500 instead of the documented 409. Using this lesson, what was missing before the first edit, and what would have caught it? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Plan before edit is built in. Claude Code's plan mode reads files and proposes a plan, but makes no edits until you approve it. Cursor, Copilot and Codex have similar planning steps. Spec-driven development. GitHub Spec Kit runs Spec → Plan → Tasks → Implement, and each phase writes a Markdown file the next one reads. Kiro's specs are requirements.md (user stories and acceptance criteria), design.md and tasks.md . Receipts over recollection. Coding agents cite files and line ranges in their plans. The SWE-agent work showed that the interface the agent works through, including how it searches and views files, changes its success rate. On your laptop : a frame is a text file. The validator is standard library, and the whole lesson runs on CPU. Sources: Claude Code, Common workflows (plan mode) , GitHub Spec Kit , Kiro, Specs , Yang et al., SWE-agent (arXiv:2405.15793) . Recap What to keep from this lesson Frame before editing: goal, facts with receipts, allowed and forbidden paths, acceptance, unknowns. A vague request leaves many reasonable but incompatible implementations open. Write the acceptance test first. It moved the small model more than prose did. Check receipts against the code. A model's own frame needs checking most. Stop reconnaissance when every decision is evidenced, delegated or listed as unknown. Model ordering as dependencies instead of prose sequence. Detect missing facts, unknown dependencies, and cycles before editing. Separate steps that can run together from steps that must wait. Before you start Needs : Phase 14 lesson 43 Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 65 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A plan is not a prettier to-do list. It is a dependency graph in which every change has a reason and every terminal node has proof. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.135 · AI system design: the method, estimates and budgets Why Agent Plans Fail In plain words first A plan is a small graph. Each work item says what changes, which repository lines justify it, what it waits for, and which command proves it is done. From that graph you get the order ( waves : items in the same wave can run together), a check before any edit (missing receipts, unknown dependencies, cycles), and a way to resume after an interruption. System-design method and estimates are covered in Lesson 14.135 (linked above). This lesson asks a small model for plans, runs them through the lesson's validator, and then executes a hand-written plan across two sessions. Weak plans repeat the request in future tense: Update the API. Add tests. Update documentation. Nothing in that list says what was found, why those files are correct, which contract changes first, or what can happen concurrently. An agent can follow every step and still create rework. A strong plan makes five commitments for each work item: Commitment Purpose Identifier Stable reference for dependencies and handoff Change The smallest behavior or contract change Evidence Repository facts that justify the change Dependencies Work that must be true first Proof The exact check that closes the item Plan the Contract Before Its Implementations When multiple surfaces depend on the same behavior, define the behavior first. Tests, implementation, documentation, and integration can then share one contract instead of inventing four versions. The graph exposes safe concurrency. Implementation and documentation can proceed together after the contract is fixed. Integration waits for both. Evidence Changes the Plan Repository evidence is not decoration. It should be capable of changing the work: An existing helper removes a planned new abstraction. A compatibility test forces a migration step. A deployment constraint moves a schema change into another task. A public response type changes the order of implementation and documentation. If the evidence cannot change the plan, it is probably not evidence for that decision. Design for Interruption Coding-agent sessions end unexpectedly. A resumable plan has work items small enough that another session can determine: which item is complete; which proof ran; which artifacts changed; which dependencies are now unblocked; what the next safe item is. Do not encode state only in checked boxes inside a chat. Store the plan next to the work. Plan Validation Reject the plan before execution when: an identifier is duplicated; a work item has no evidence; a work item has no proof; a dependency names an unknown item; the graph contains a cycle; the first irreversible action occurs before the relevant uncertainty is resolved. The first five checks are mechanical. The last requires judgment and should be called out explicitly. The same idea as a formula Waves are levels of the graph. An item's wave is one more than the deepest wave among its dependencies: max ​ w ( j ) , w ( i ) = 1 if deps ( i ) = ∅ . A cycle has no finite , which is why execution_waves() stops on one. Parallel time is the sum of the slowest item per wave. With durations ​ , ​ = i ∑ ​ t i ​ , T waves ​ = k ∑ ​ i ∈ W k ​ max ​ t i ​ . The number of waves is the length of the longest dependency chain, the critical path of PERT and CPM. No amount of parallel work makes the plan shorter than that chain. Explain the mechanism Your session ends without warning in the middle of a multi-step change, and a colleague picks it up the next morning. What must they be able to find, and where? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. They need to see which items are done, which proof ran for each one, which files changed, which dependencies are now unblocked, and what the next safe item is. That state lives next to the work, in the repository, as small items with explicit proof, not as checked boxes inside a chat. Design for interruption. Sessions end unexpectedly. A resumable plan has work items small enough that another person, or another agent, can determine the state of each one from the artifacts alone. The five things they must be able to read: which item is complete; which proof ran and what it returned; which artifacts changed; which dependencies are now unblocked; what the next safe item is. Why chat is the wrong place. A checked box in a conversation says that someone believed an item was done. It does not say which command proved it or which files it touched. The next person either trusts the box or redoes the work. A plan stored next to the code, with one identifier per item and the proof command written down, lets them verify instead of trust. The habit. I stop at item boundaries when I can. When I cannot, the plan still shows the last proof that passed, so the resume point is the first item whose proof has not run. Plausible wrong answers. "Write a summary message at the end of the session." The session can end before the summary; the state must exist as the work proceeds. "The git log is enough." Commits show what changed, not which proof ran or which item is next. "Only the person who started can finish it." That is the failure the plan should prevent. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Where do you keep the plan? Expected: in the repository next to the work, as the source of truth, with any rendering such as a Markdown view generated from it. (level 2) An item is marked done but has no proof recorded. What does the colleague do? Expected: treat it as not done and run its proof; a box without proof is a belief. (level 2) Why does item size matter for resumption? Expected: a small item either finished or did not; a large half-done item forces the next person to reconstruct where it stopped. Where it is taught. The evidence-backed plan lesson covers designing a plan for interruption and storing it next to the work. Debug a failure A teammate, or a coding agent, hands you this plan for a change to a public API: update the endpoint, add tests, update the documentation. They want approval to start. What do you ask for before you say yes, and what would make you reject the plan outright? Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. That list repeats the request in future tense. I ask for five things on each item: a stable identifier, the smallest change, the repository facts that justify it, the items it depends on, and the exact check that closes it. I reject a plan with a duplicate identifier, an item without evidence or proof, a dependency on an unknown item, a cycle, or an irreversible step scheduled before the uncertainty it depends on is resolved. Why the three-line plan fails. Nothing in it says what was found in the repository, why those files are the right ones, which contract changes first, or what can run at the same time. Someone can complete every line and still create rework. The five commitments. Commitment Purpose Identifier A stable reference for dependencies and handoff Change The smallest behavior or contract change Evidence Repository facts that justify the change Dependencies Work that must be true first Proof The exact check that closes the item Order by dependency, not by prose. When several surfaces depend on one behavior, the contract comes first. Tests, implementation and documentation then share one definition instead of inventing four. A dependency graph also shows safe concurrency: implementation and documentation can proceed together after the contract is fixed, and the integration gate waits for both. Evidence must be able to change the plan. An existing helper removes a planned abstraction. A compatibility test forces a migration step. A deployment constraint moves a schema change into another task. If a piece of evidence cannot change the plan, it is decoration, not evidence. The rejection list. The first five checks are mechanical: duplicate identifiers, items without evidence, items without proof, unknown dependencies, cycles. The last check needs judgment: does the first irreversible action, such as a migration or a public release, happen before the relevant uncertainty is resolved? I call that one out explicitly in the review. Plausible wrong answers. "Trust the author and review the result instead." Rework found at review time costs more than a plan rejected before editing. "A longer plan is a better plan." Length adds nothing; evidence and proof on each item do. "Dependencies are obvious from the order of the list." Prose order hides which steps can run together and which must wait. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) One item lists two proof commands. What do you do? Expected: split it into two items, because one item needs one clear completion proof. (level 2) Two items depend on each other. What does that usually hide? Expected: an unresolved product or design disagreement; the cycle is the symptom, the missing decision is the cause. (level 3) The plan sits in a chat thread as checked boxes. Why is that a problem? Expected: a session can end at any moment, and another person cannot see which proof ran or which item is now unblocked; the plan belongs next to the work. (level 3) A migration item needs a human approval. How do you express that in the graph? Expected: as an explicit item with the approval as its proof, which every dependent item waits for. Lesson 14.66 · Multi-agent systems Lesson 14.111 · Deep Agents: a harness on LangGraph The Parallelism Test In plain words first Delegation means handing parts of one change to separate workers, whether agents or people. It only saves time when the parts are truly independent: each worker owns files nobody else touches, has its own proof, and works to an interface fixed before anyone starts (the merge contract ). An integrator then checks each handoff against its unit, merges in dependency order and runs the whole gate. Multi-agent systems and harnesses are covered in Lessons 14.66 and 14.111 (linked above). This lesson runs two model workers in two real git worktrees, with and without a merge contract. Do not delegate because more agents are available. Delegate when at least one of these is true: two investigations can answer different unknowns independently; two implementations own disjoint files and contracts; a reviewer can inspect a completed artifact without changing it; a slow external check can run while local work continues. Keep work serial when agents need the same files, the same unresolved decision, or the same mutable environment. A Work Unit Is a Contract Each delegated unit needs: Field Meaning Goal One observable result Owner One accountable worker Paths Exclusive write ownership Dependencies Completed units required before starting Proof Exact evidence returned to the integrator Handoff Files changed, decisions made, remaining risk “Handle the backend” is not a work unit. “Implement the duplicate check in app/accounts.py and prove it with the focused account test” is. Isolation Has Three Layers Filesystem isolation: separate worktrees or sandboxes prevent accidental shared edits. Ownership isolation: contracts prevent two workers from intentionally editing the same path. State isolation: separate logs and outputs prevent one worker from overwriting another worker’s evidence. Filesystem isolation does not solve ownership. Two clean worktrees can still produce conflicting designs. The merge contract must resolve shared interfaces before work begins. The Integrator Does Not Rebuild the Work The integrator should: confirm each handoff matches its assigned scope; read the proof output, not just the worker’s summary; combine changes in dependency order; run the full cross-unit gate; reject hidden scope expansion; record conflicts as new decisions, not silent edits. If integration requires rewriting most of a worker’s result, the original decomposition was wrong. Human and Agent Roles Delegation does not remove human judgment. The human still owns choices that change public behavior, risk, authority, or irreversible cost. Agents can own bounded investigation, implementation, verification, and review. This is calibrated autonomy: the system grants freedom where evidence and rollback are strong, and requires a checkpoint where consequence is high. Weigh a trade-off Your organization wants to let coding agents merge changes without a human in the loop for a class of tasks. You are asked to write the policy that says which decisions an agent may make on its own. How do you draw that line, and how does it move over time? Level 4 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The line follows consequence and reversibility, not task difficulty. A human keeps the choices that change public behavior, risk, authority or irreversible cost; an agent owns bounded investigation, implementation, verification and review. I express that as locked, bounded and delegated decisions in each task contract, and I widen the delegated set only where evidence and rollback are strong, which is calibrated autonomy rather than a fixed switch. Calibrated autonomy. The system grants freedom where evidence and rollback are strong and requires a checkpoint where consequence is high. That is a property of each decision, so the policy is written per decision class, not per task or per model. Human-owned and agent-owned. Human keeps Agent may own Changes to public behavior or compatibility Local structure, names, reversible refactors Changes to risk or safety posture Bounded investigation that returns a fact table Grants of authority or access Implementation inside exclusive paths with proof Irreversible cost: migrations, deletions, spend Verification and read-only review of finished artifacts The three modes make it executable. Each decision in a task contract is locked, bounded or delegated. Locked decisions carry a human checkpoint. Bounded decisions state the limits, such as a dependency allowlist or a retry range, and the agent proposes inside them. Delegated decisions require the agent to explain the choice and prove the result. The mode is chosen from consequence and reversibility, and the reason is recorded so a later team can revise it. How the line moves. Autonomy expands on evidence. When a class of delegated decisions has a strong proof layer, a clean rollback and a window without incidents, a bounded decision can become delegated. When an incident shows a missing control, the move goes the other way until the control exists. The policy itself is a control with an owner and a review date. What never moves. Proof must match the claim. A unit test does not prove a public interface path, and an agent's summary does not replace reading the proof output. The integrator reads the proof, not the story. Plausible wrong answers. "Let the agent decide easy tasks and keep the hard ones." Difficulty is not the axis; a trivial deletion can be irreversible and a hard refactor can be reversible. "Autonomy is a single setting per team." Each decision class has its own consequence and reversibility, so one switch is wrong in both directions. "A passing test suite is enough to merge anything." The suite proves local contracts; public behavior, authority and irreversible cost need their own proof and a human checkpoint. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) An agent proposes a dependency outside the allowlist with a good argument. What happens? Expected: the bounded decision escalates to a human; the argument is input to the decision, not a permission. (level 4) How do you widen autonomy for a decision class safely? Expected: show the proof layer, the rollback and an incident-free window for that class, then change the mode and record the evidence and the reviewer. (level 4) What evidence would make you narrow autonomy again? Expected: an incident that a lower-level control did not catch, which shows the proof layer was weaker than the policy assumed. Where it is taught. The delegation lesson defines calibrated autonomy and the specification lesson gives the three decision modes. Weigh a trade-off Your manager wants a feature finished faster and suggests that you run two coding agents, or two engineers, in parallel on it. Tell me about a time you had to make that call. How did you decide, and what did you put in place before anyone started? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. I delegate only when the work is really independent: two investigations that answer different unknowns, two implementations with disjoint files and contracts, a reviewer who only reads, or a slow external check that runs while local work continues. When the parts need the same files, the same open decision or the same mutable environment, I keep them serial, because a parallel split then converts one clear task into a coordination problem. Before anyone starts, each unit gets a goal, an owner, exclusive write paths, dependencies, a proof and a handoff. The parallelism test. More available workers is not a reason. The split is justified when at least one of these holds: two investigations can answer different unknowns on their own; two implementations own disjoint files and contracts; a reviewer can inspect a finished artifact without changing it; a slow external check can run while local work continues. A work unit is a contract. "Handle the backend" is not a unit. "Implement the duplicate check in one named file and prove it with the focused account test" is. Each unit records the goal, one accountable owner, exclusive paths, completed units it waits for, the exact evidence it returns, and a handoff with the files changed, the decisions made and the remaining risk. Three layers of isolation. Filesystem: separate worktrees or sandboxes stop accidental shared edits. Ownership: the contract stops two workers from editing the same path on purpose. State: separate logs and outputs stop one worker from overwriting another's evidence. Filesystem isolation does not solve ownership. Two clean worktrees can still produce two conflicting designs. The merge contract has to settle shared interfaces before work begins. What the integrator does. The integrator confirms each handoff matches its scope, reads the proof output rather than the summary, combines changes in dependency order, runs the full cross-unit gate, rejects hidden scope growth, and records conflicts as new decisions instead of silent edits. If integration means rewriting most of a worker's result, the split was wrong. The call I made. The time this mattered most, the two halves looked independent but both needed the same response type to change. I ran one short unit to fix that contract first, then let the two implementations run in parallel against it. The serial step was shorter than the merge conflict it prevented. Plausible wrong answers. "Two agents are always faster than one." Parallel work saves wall time only when the pieces are independent; otherwise it raises the failure rate. "Separate worktrees solve the conflicts." They prevent accidental shared edits, not two conflicting designs of one interface. "The integrator fixes whatever does not fit." If most of a result must be rewritten at integration, the original split was the mistake. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) A docs unit asks to own the whole application directory. Lesson 14.147 · The LLMOps lifecycle and safe releases Corrections Are Evidence In plain words first Each time you correct an agent ("don't edit that file", "keep the function name"), you have found a gap in the system around it. The ratchet turns that correction into something permanent at the earliest layer that can stop it happening again: a test, a scope rule, an automated check, an example, or a human decision. A reminder in chat is only the last resort. Release discipline and the LLMOps loop are covered in Lesson 14.147 (linked above). This lesson feeds the lesson's ratchet the real corrections this course made in 14.40 to 14.45, then measures two versions of one control. When you tell an agent “do not edit that file,” you have learned that the scope boundary was not executable. When you say “this output shape is wrong,” you have learned that an example or test was missing. When setup fails again, you have learned that environment knowledge belongs in automation. Treat the correction as an observation about the work system, not as a prompt-writing failure. Promote to the Earliest Effective Layer Use this order: Recurring failure Durable destination Wrong result or regression Test or evaluation Off-scope or unsafe action Scope or permission policy Repeated setup or command mistake Automation or tool Repeated output-format mistake Canonical example plus validator Ambiguous local convention Instruction with a scenario check Product disagreement Human decision record Earlier controls are cheaper. A type that prevents an invalid state is stronger than a review comment that catches it later. A focused test is stronger than a paragraph asking the agent to remember. The Ratchet Record Capture: symptom; root cause; consequence; recurrence count; chosen control; verification for the control; owner; date to review or retire it. Do not promote every one-off preference. Promote a correction when recurrence or consequence justifies permanent complexity. Separate Cause from Symptom “The agent edited README” is a symptom. Possible causes include: the task allowed the repository root; docs were implicitly considered safe; the plan bundled implementation and documentation; two workers had overlapping ownership. Each cause belongs to a different control. A rule that merely repeats the symptom will fail in the next slightly different case. Controls Also Decay Old controls can conflict, bloat context, and encode a system that no longer exists. Every promoted rule needs a retirement check. Remove or rewrite it when: the underlying architecture changed; a stronger executable control replaced it; the failure has not recurred across a meaningful window; the control creates more friction than the risk it prevents. The goal is not the longest instruction file. It is the smallest system that preserves hard-won judgment. The same idea as a formula Promote when expected cost beats upkeep. A correction recurs at rate per month, costs each time, and the control stops a fraction of recurrences while costing a month to keep: context, maintenance, friction. Promote it when A severe first failure (large ) clears the bar with small. A cosmetic preference rarely does. Fingerprints group causes, not wordings. Two causes with token sets and count as one when their Jaccard overlap ∣ A ∩ B ∣ ​ ≥ τ . Set too low and unrelated failures merge. Set it too high and every paraphrase becomes its own rule. Explain the mechanism For the third time this month you have told a coding agent not to edit the project README during a feature change. Each time it apologized and fixed the run. Tell me what you do now, and why the fix is not a better prompt. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A correction that lives in chat fixes one run. I treat the repeat as evidence about the work system: the scope boundary was not executable. I find the cause behind the symptom, then put a control at the earliest layer that can stop the recurrence, which here is a scope or permission policy rather than another paragraph in the instructions. The control gets an owner, a verification and a date to review or retire it. Separate the cause from the symptom. "The agent edited the README" is a symptom. The cause can be any of these: the task allowed writes to the repository root; documentation was treated as safe by default; the plan bundled implementation and documentation in one item; two workers had overlapping ownership. Each cause belongs to a different control. A rule that only repeats the symptom fails in the next slightly different case. Promote to the earliest effective layer. Recurring failure Durable destination Wrong result or regression Test or evaluation Off-scope or unsafe action Scope or permission policy Repeated setup or command mistake Automation or tool Repeated output-format mistake Canonical example plus validator Ambiguous local convention Instruction with a scenario check Product disagreement Human decision record Earlier controls are cheaper. A permission that makes the write impossible is stronger than a review comment that catches it later, and a focused test is stronger than a paragraph that asks the agent to remember. The record. For each promoted correction I capture the symptom, the root cause, the consequence, the recurrence count, the chosen control, how the control is verified, the owner, and a date to review or retire it. Not every one-off preference gets promoted. Recurrence or consequence has to justify permanent complexity. Why not a better prompt. The prompt was already clear three times. The failure is that the boundary depended on the agent reading and remembering. A policy that refuses the write does not depend on memory. Plausible wrong answers. "Add the rule in capital letters at the top of the instructions." The instruction already existed; a louder copy still depends on the agent reading it. "Promote every correction so nothing is lost." Controls accumulate, conflict and bloat context; promotion needs recurrence or consequence. "The agent is the problem, switch models." The boundary was not executable; a different model meets the same missing control. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Two corrections use different words for the same cause. How do you keep them from becoming two rules? Expected: normalize them to a stable fingerprint of the cause, so they collapse into one control without merging unrelated failures. (level 2) A first-time failure deleted customer data. Does it wait for recurrence? Expected: no; consequence weighting lets a severe first occurrence be promoted at once. (level 3) When would you remove the control you added? Expected: when the architecture changed, a stronger executable control replaced it, the failure has not recurred across a meaningful window, or the control blocks more legitimate work than the risk it prevents. (level 3) What is the smallest system you aim for? Expected: the smallest set of controls that preserves the hard-won judgment, not the longest instruction file. Where it is taught. The feedback-to-system lesson gives the destination table, the ratchet record and the retirement checks. Weigh a trade-off A team's agent instruction file has grown for a year. Rules contradict each other, the context is heavy, and nobody remembers why half of them exist. You are asked to clean it up. How do you decide what stays, what goes, and what you will not touch yet? Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Every control needs a retirement condition, and retirement needs evidence like any other change. I review each rule against four questions: did the architecture or workflow it protected change, did a stronger executable control replace it, has the failure stayed away across a meaningful window, and does the rule block legitimate work more often than it prevents harm. A rule that passes none of those stays, and a rule I cannot trace to a cause gets an owner and a review date before it gets deleted. Why the file grew. Each rule was a correction promoted into prose. Prose is the weakest durable layer. Over a year the rules encoded a system that no longer exists, started to conflict, and now consume context on every run. The goal is not the longest instruction file. It is the smallest system that preserves hard-won judgment. The review. Question If yes Did the architecture or workflow change? The rule protects a system that is gone; retire it Did a type, a test or a permission replace it? Delete the prose and keep the executable control Has the failure not recurred across the window? Retire it, and note the window as the evidence Does it block legitimate work more than it prevents harm? Rewrite it narrower or retire it Replace before delete. For a rule that still protects a real risk, the better move is often promotion rather than retirement: a prose rule about output shape becomes an example plus a validator, a prose rule about files becomes a scope policy. I delete the sentence only after proving the stronger control exists and fires. What I do not touch yet. A rule with no recorded cause and no owner is a gap in the record, not a candidate for deletion. I give it an owner and a review date, and I look for the correction that created it. Deleting it because it feels old is the mistake the lesson warns against. Guard against regrowth. Every new control gets an owner, a verification, a review or expiry window and a retirement condition when it is created. Without that, the file fills again in a year. Plausible wrong answers. "Delete everything older than a year and see what breaks." Retirement needs evidence; a silent failure can take months to appear. "Keep all of it, context is cheap." Stale rules conflict, encode a dead system and bloat every run. "Rewrite the whole file from scratch." The file holds judgment that was paid for; the job is to move it to stronger layers, not to lose it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Two rules contradict each other. What do you do first? Expected: find the cause behind each; a contradiction usually means one of them protects a system or decision that changed. (level 3) A rule has not fired in months. Is that enough to delete it? Expected: only if the window is meaningful for that failure and the risk it protected is still visible elsewhere; low frequency with high consequence can keep a rule alive. (level 4) How do you show that a deletion was safe? Expected: the stronger control that replaced it fires on the original failure case, and the recurrence stays absent across the review window. (level 4) What stops the file from growing back? Expected: a creation rule that every control carries an owner, a verification and a retirement condition, with periodic review. Where it is taught. The feedback-to-system lesson gives the retirement checks and the feedback ratchet lesson gives the ownership and expiry fields. Lesson 14.162 · From pilot to value: use cases, the business case and the operating model Output Is Not Outcome In plain words first An output is the thing you build, such as an assistant, a dashboard or a summary email. An outcome is what changes for a person: "the on-call engineer finds the failing service within two minutes". Write the outcome first, as a six-part frame (user, situation, current behaviour, desired outcome, constraints, non-goals), and keep the output out of it. Otherwise the first idea becomes the scope before anyone has checked it. Getting from pilot to value is covered in Lesson 14.162 (linked above). This lesson measures how often solution names leak into outcome statements, and how well two detectors catch them. “Build an incident assistant” names an output. It does not say who needs it, what becomes better, or what must remain safe. An outcome frame says: When a production alert arrives, the on-call engineer identifies the failing service and a safe next action within two minutes, while diagnosis remains read-only and auditable. That sentence can be satisfied by software, a runbook, a data repair, or a smaller interface change. It keeps the team attached to the result rather than the first artifact someone imagined. The Six-Part Frame Part Question User Who experiences the problem directly? Situation When and where does it occur? Current behavior What happens today, including workarounds? Desired outcome What observable state should improve? Constraints Which safety, policy, cost, or compatibility limits are fixed? Non-goals What tempting adjacent work is excluded? Find Solution Leakage Outcome statements leak solutions when they contain a product form, interface, model choice, framework, or architecture that has not been earned by evidence. “Users receive a weekly AI summary” leaks the summary and cadence. “Users understand account changes before approval” states the result. “Deploy a vector database” leaks infrastructure. “Relevant policy evidence is available during review” states a capability. Constraints can name technology when compatibility truly fixes it. Record why it is fixed. Constraints Protect the Outcome Constraints are not implementation details. They are part of the real-world goal: no production writes during diagnosis; response within the incident time budget; existing audit events remain authoritative; no new runtime dependency; accessibility behavior remains intact. A build that reaches the outcome by violating a constraint has not reached the outcome. Non-Goals Create a Boundary Non-goals prevent a useful slice from turning into a platform. Good non-goals are concrete enough to reject work: no automatic remediation; no new alert-routing system; no replacement of the incident commander; no historical analytics in this slice. The same idea as a formula A detector is judged on both kinds of error. Over labelled statements, a leak detector has TP ​ , precision = TP + FP TP ​ , where TP counts leaks flagged, FN leaks missed and FP clean statements flagged. Which error is cheaper here? A missed leak (FN) lets an output harden into scope, and costs a project. A false alarm (FP) costs a minute of a person's review. So a leak check should favour recall and route its flags to a person, not block automatically. Worked example Two detectors, fourteen statements Seven statements leak a solution and seven do not. The lesson's validate() looks for the exact proposed-output name, "incident assistant". It flags "use the incident assistant" and nothing else: recall , with no false alarms. The lexicon flags all seven leaks, so recall is . It also flags "a support agent resolves…" (a human agent) and "the nightly build stays green", so precision is . For a check that a person reviews, 2 false alarms are cheap and 6 missed leaks are not. The lexicon is the better first pass. "Users get a weekly summary from a model" leaks the summary and the cadence. "Users understand account changes before approval" states the result. A constraint can name a technology when compatibility really fixes it. I record why it is fixed. Constraints and non-goals do real work. Constraints are part of the goal. No production writes during diagnosis, a response inside the incident time budget, and no new runtime dependency all remove whole classes of solutions. Non-goals keep the first slice from growing into a platform: no automatic remediation, no new alert routing, no replacement of the incident commander. Plausible wrong answers. "Start with the interface and refine the goal later." The interface is one output. It ties the team to the first artifact before anyone knows what must improve. "Constraints are implementation details for later." A build that reaches the outcome and breaks a constraint has not reached the outcome. "Non-goals are optional." Without them, a useful slice grows into a platform before the first result is measured. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) How do you tell an outcome from an output? Expected: an outcome names an observable change for a user; an output names an artifact such as a page, a tool or a model. (level 2) The manager insists on a chat interface. Where does that go in the frame? Expected: into the constraints only when policy or compatibility fixes it, with the reason written down; otherwise it waits for evidence. (level 2) Name two non-goals that keep the first slice small. Expected: no automatic fix of the incident and no new alert routing, for example; each one must be concrete enough to reject work. (level 3) What is the first observation that would show the desired outcome is wrong? Expected: a measured time to find the failing service that is already short, which means the frame targets a problem that does not exist. Where it is taught. The outcome frame lesson gives the six-part frame and the leakage check. Lesson 14.162 · From pilot to value: use cases, the business case and the operating model Start with the Current System In plain words first Before designing anything, write down what people actually do today: each step, who does it, what triggers it, where it is slow, who has authority, and what evidence shows it happens. Evidence has strengths. Direct records (logs, recordings) and artifacts (tickets, runbooks) are stronger than what people report, which is stronger than what the team infers. Getting from pilot to value is covered in Lesson 14.162 (linked above). This lesson rebuilds an incident workflow from tool logs, compares it with the interview, and checks a small model's summary of the same logs. Do not begin by asking what features people want. Begin by reconstructing what happens now. For each step, record: Field Example Actor On-call engineer Trigger Production alert arrives Action Opens alert, then searches dashboards Input Alert payload and deployment record Output Candidate service and owner Friction Context switching across three tools Authority Incident commander approves a write Evidence Screen recording, incident log, runbook The workflow is larger than the screen. It includes waiting, copy-paste, side channels, approval, error recovery, and the steps people have stopped noticing. Evidence Has Strength Use a simple evidence ladder: Direct behavior: observation, trace, recording, or system event. Artifact: ticket, runbook, log, form, or completed output. Reported behavior: a person describes what they do. Inference: the team concludes what probably happens. All four can be useful. Only the first two prove current behavior directly. Label the rest so confidence does not silently inflate. Search for Four Things Friction: repeated effort, delay, re-entry, or recovery. Hidden state: facts carried in memory, chat, or personal notes. Authority: the person or system allowed to make a consequential change. Exceptions: the case where the normal workflow stops being normal. AI features often fail at handoffs and exceptions because the happy path was the only path shaped. Do Not Average Away Disagreement Two users can perform different workflows for good reasons. Preserve the variants until you understand whether they represent: different roles; different risk levels; legacy and current process; expertise differences; a genuine policy disagreement. An averaged workflow can describe nobody. The same idea as a formula Where the time goes is a sum of gaps. For one incident with events at times ​ < t 1 ​ < ⋯ < t m ​ , the time attributed to step is the gap ​ = t k ​ − t k − 1 ​ , and the total is ​ − t 0 ​ = ∑ k ​ g k ​ . Over many incidents, compare steps by their median gap. A median is not pulled about by one stuck incident the way a mean is. How much rests on evidence. The lesson's direct-evidence ratio is # direct evidence items ​ . An interview alone gives . Each step backed by a log event raises it. The largest gap is the approval wait: minutes, 43% of the 19.2-minute total. The owner lookup adds . The interview's three steps (open, check dashboard, roll back) have no gaps to measure, and . Explain the mechanism A customer lead spends an hour describing how their support team handles a refund request. You now have to decide what the first version of an assistant does. Tell me how you treat that hour of description, and what you do next. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. An interview is reported behavior, which is the third rung of a four-rung ladder. I label every claim from the hour by its rung, then look for direct evidence for the claims that matter most: a trace, a recording, a ticket or a completed form. The steps that stay unproven remain visible as open claims instead of turning into requirements. The ladder. Direct behavior: an observation, a trace, a recording or a system event. An artifact: a ticket, a runbook, a log, a form or a finished output. Reported behavior: a person describes what they do. Inference: the team concludes what probably happens. All four help. Only the first two prove current behavior. When I write the workflow down, each step carries its rung, so confidence does not grow on its own. What I reconstruct. I do not begin with feature wishes. I rebuild what happens now, step by step, with the actor, the trigger, the action, the input, the output, the friction, who holds authority for a consequential change, and the evidence. The workflow is larger than the screen. It includes waiting, copy and paste, side channels, approvals, error recovery and steps people have stopped noticing. Four things I search for. Friction: repeated effort, delay, re-entry or recovery. Hidden state: facts carried in memory, chat or personal notes. Authority: the person or system allowed to make the consequential change. Exceptions: the case where the normal path stops being normal. Assistants fail most often at handoffs and exceptions, because only the happy path was shaped. So the first thing I ask for after the interview is one real trace of an exception. How this changes the first version. A step with direct evidence can become a requirement. A step with only reported evidence becomes an assumption to test. The description from the hour tells me where to look, not what to build. Plausible wrong answers. "The customer knows their process, so the interview is the requirement." A description is reported behavior; it is useful but it does not prove what happens. "Average the descriptions from several people into one workflow." An averaged workflow can describe nobody; the variants must stay separate until their cause is known. "Infer the missing steps from similar teams." Inference is the weakest rung and must stay labeled as a guess. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) The lead says "we always check the order history first." How do you confirm that? Expected: ask for a recording or a log of three real cases and mark the claim as reported until one of them shows it. (level 2) What is the direct-evidence ratio and why track it? Expected: the share of workflow steps backed by observation or an artifact; a low ratio means the model of the workflow is mostly belief. (level 3) You can only observe the happy path. What is the risk? Expected: the exception path, where most failures live, stays unshaped, so the assistant breaks at the handoff that matters. (level 3) A proposed feature removes a visible step. What do you check before you accept it? Expected: whether hidden work behind that step still exists, so the feature only moves the effort somewhere invisible. Where it is taught. The workflow discovery lesson gives the evidence ladder and the step record. Weigh a trade-off Two senior analysts on the same team show you how they triage a flagged transaction. Their steps differ in order, in the tools they open, and in who they ask before they act. Your deadline allows one workflow in the first version. What do you do with the disagreement? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. I keep both variants separate until I know why they differ. The difference can come from different roles, different risk levels, a legacy process next to a current one, a difference in expertise, or a real policy disagreement, and each of those leads to a different product. An averaged workflow can describe nobody, so the first version targets one variant on purpose and names the other as a known gap. Why not average. Two people can perform different workflows for good reasons. Merging their steps into one path produces a sequence that neither of them follows. The assistant then fails at the first handoff or exception, which is where these features fail most. What the difference can mean. Cause What it tells the build Different roles Two user types, maybe two outcome frames Different risk levels The branch is a feature, not noise Legacy and current process One variant may be retiring; confirm with the owner Expertise difference The expert path may be the target and the other the training gap Policy disagreement A human decision is needed before any build How I resolve it. Record both variants as ordered steps with evidence and the rung of that evidence. Find where the branch begins and which authority boundary each variant crosses. Ask the owner of the process which cause applies; if it is a policy disagreement, that decision goes to a human and the build waits for it. Pick one variant for the first slice by risk and frequency, and write the other as a non-goal with the reason. Where the exception hides. Often one analyst's "extra" step is the exception path the other analyst has stopped noticing. I ask for a real case where the normal path failed before I call a step optional. Plausible wrong answers. "Merge the two into one standard process." The averaged workflow may describe nobody and breaks at the handoff. "Follow the more senior person." Seniority is not evidence; the cause of the difference decides. "Treat the extra steps as optional and skip them." The extra step is often the exception path that carries most of the risk. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) One analyst asks a supervisor before acting and the other does not. What is that step? Expected: an authority boundary; the build must respect it, and the two variants may differ in risk level or role. (level 2) You can only ship one path. How do you choose? Expected: by the risk and the frequency of each variant, with the other recorded as a named gap, not by averaging. (level 3) The owner says both are fine. What do you record? Expected: that the policy allows both, with the evidence, so the assistant does not force one on everybody. (level 3) How do you keep the second variant from disappearing from the plan? Expected: write it as a non-goal with its reason and a review point, so it stays visible as a decision instead of an omission. Where it is taught. The workflow discovery lesson explains why disagreement must not be averaged away and lists the causes behind variants. Lesson 14.151 · Design review and the practitioner playbook Every Build Contains Bets In plain words first Every feature rests on things the team believes but has not checked: "the alert says which service failed", "engineers will trust the answer". Write each one as a statement that could turn out false, and score three things: how bad it is if false ( impact ), how weak the evidence is ( uncertainty ), and how costly it is to learn late ( irreversibility ). Then test the riskiest open one first, with a pass mark written down before the test runs. Design review and the practitioner playbook are covered in Lesson 14.151 (linked above). This lesson maps the incident agent's assumptions from 14.48 and runs the top experiment for real. An incident tool may depend on all of these being true: alert context contains enough information to identify a service; engineers trust a recommendation they did not derive themselves; the desired response time matters operationally; required data can be accessed without unsafe authority; the workflow happens often enough to justify maintenance. These are not implementation tasks. They are conditions for the build to be valuable, usable, feasible, and safe. Assumption Classes Class Question Value Will the outcome matter enough? Usability Can the user understand and act on it? Feasibility Can the system produce it with available data and constraints? Viability Can the organization sustain cost, ownership, and operation? Safety Can it fail without unacceptable consequence? Write assumptions as falsifiable statements. “The feature is useful” cannot be tested. “Eight of ten on-call engineers identify the correct service faster with the read-only result” can. Risk Is Not One Number The lab uses three dimensions from one to five: Impact: damage if the assumption is false. Uncertainty: weakness of current evidence. Irreversibility: cost of learning after commitment. The example score multiplies impact and uncertainty, then adds irreversibility. The formula is not universal. Its purpose is to force the team to state why one unknown should be resolved before another. Design an Experiment, Not a Confirmation Ritual A useful test has: a claim that could be false; a population or realistic sample; an observable result; a threshold decided before the result; a next decision for pass, fail, and ambiguous evidence. Avoid tests that only demonstrate that the team can build the idea. Reversibility Changes Order High-consequence, irreversible choices need earlier evidence. A read-only replay can precede a production integration. A temporary adapter can precede a data migration. A human-approved recommendation can precede automatic action. The shape of the build should follow the shape of uncertainty. The same idea as a formula The lesson's score. With impact , uncertainty and irreversibility , each from 1 to 5: Here only adds, so it breaks ties. Under an irreversible bet dominates. Try a few rules and see whether the top item changes. A threshold turns a test into a decision. Fix the pass mark out of before the run. With and = 8 , an observed 10 of 10 has a rough 95% lower bound on the true rate of about (rule of three). That holds only for alerts like the ones sampled. Worked example Two rules, one top item "Alert context is enough" scores : (lesson), (product). "The agent may roll back without approval" scores : (lesson), (product). So the lesson's rule tests the alert first, and the product rule puts automatic rollback first. The second one is not answered by an experiment at all. It is answered by a decision: keep approval. Pairwise, the rules agree on 5 of 6 orderings (83%). They disagree only on which of those two comes first. Its job is to force the team to say why one unknown must be resolved before another. Irreversible, high-consequence choices need earlier evidence: a read-only replay can precede a production integration, and a human-approved recommendation can precede automatic action. An experiment, not a confirmation ritual. A useful test has a claim that could be false, a realistic sample, an observable result, a threshold decided before the result, and a next decision for pass, fail and ambiguous evidence. A demo that only shows the team can build the idea is not a test. Plausible wrong answers. "Build the first roadmap item; the order was agreed." Agreement on order is not evidence that the riskiest assumption holds. "Ship something small and see what happens." A small build without a claim, a threshold and a next decision learns nothing. "Risk is just how likely it is to fail." Impact and irreversibility change the order even when the probability is the same. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) The roadmap owner says the ranking already reflects risk. How do you check? Expected: compare the risk ranking with the roadmap order and explain each mismatch; where they differ, one of them is wrong about the evidence. (level 3) Write a threshold that would stop the build. Lesson 14.134 · Designing a production agent: specs, contracts and failure modes Two Bad Extremes In plain words first A good spec tells an agent what must hold and leaves the rest to it. It has six parts: the outcome, invariants (what must always stay true), examples, non-goals, a decision policy and proof. The decision policy sorts every choice into three modes. Locked choices are the human's (production writes). Bounded choices are the agent's within limits (at most five sources). Delegated choices are the agent's to make and explain (which source to query first). Specs, contracts and failure modes are covered in Lesson 14.134 (linked above). This lesson compiles the lesson's spec, shows what its schema cannot catch, and then enforces it around a real agent loop. An underspecified task asks an agent to guess the system. An overspecified task asks it to transcribe a design that may already be wrong. The useful middle is an executable contract: Surface Purpose Outcome The observable result Invariants Conditions that must always remain true Examples Concrete cases that reveal intent Non-goals Adjacent behavior intentionally excluded Decision policy Which choices are locked, bounded, or delegated Proof Evidence required before completion Three Decision Modes Locked: the agent must not choose. Use for public compatibility, authority, safety, irreversible cost, or a product commitment. Bounded: the agent may choose inside explicit limits. Use for search budgets, retry counts, allowed dependencies, or a known interface family. Delegated: the agent owns the choice and must explain it. Use for local structure, names, reversible refactors, and implementation details. Specify Behavior Through Examples Examples compress intent better than adjectives. “Helpful,” “robust,” and “production-ready” are not executable. A small set of normal, edge, failure, and forbidden examples gives both the builder and verifier something concrete. Examples do not replace invariants. One passing case cannot prove a universal safety rule. Proof Must Match the Claim A unit test proves a local function contract. A wire test proves serialization and transport behavior. A browser journey proves an interface path. A replay set proves behavior over representative cases. An audit log proves that authority boundaries held. Do not accept a lower layer as proof of a higher-layer claim. Preserve Unknowns Deliberately A specification can say “the implementation may choose any read-only source that returns within the time budget.” That is not vagueness. It is an intentional delegated decision with a boundary and proof. Specifications should evolve when evidence changes. Preserve the reason behind locked and bounded choices so later teams can revise them without archaeology. The same idea as a formula Choose the mode by consequence and reversibility. For a decision with consequence if chosen wrongly and recovery cost , the expected harm of letting the agent choose with error rate is roughly . Delegate when that is below the cost of a human checkpoint. Lock when it is far above, and bound when a limit can cap : A spec is executable when every invariant has a monitor. For an invariant and a run's trace , the monitor ​ ( τ ) is true or false and leaves a receipt. The proof "zero production writes over replays" is n ​ m read-only ​ ( τ k ​ ) . Even a careful agent with carries an expected harm far above , a few minutes of a commander's time. So the decision is locked. "Which source first" is cheap and reversible: a wasted read costs seconds. It is delegated. "How many sources" caps by bounding calls to 5. It is bounded. In the replay, one model tried rollback five times on one incident. The lock turned each attempt into a refused call, and the monitor recorded "0 writes executed, 5 refused". Lesson 14.133 · What production means: the stack and the readiness review Lesson 14.162 · From pilot to value: use cases, the business case and the operating model Three Different Questions In plain words first Prototype, pilot and production answer different questions. A prototype asks whether the idea works at all, on recorded or fake data, and can be thrown away. A pilot asks whether it works safely for a named group with real data, limited authority and a way back. Production is when the organisation takes ongoing responsibility: an SLO, someone on call, security review, monitoring and a retirement plan. The risk is stage drift , where a prototype gains users, data or authority without gaining an owner. What production means and the readiness review are covered in Lesson 14.133, and pilot-to-value in 14.2 (linked above). This lesson stages the incident agent's next steps and makes the stage enforceable in code. Stage Primary question Prototype Can this mechanism produce the evidence at all? Pilot Does it work safely with a bounded real audience and real conditions? Production Can we own it continuously at the promised reliability and risk level? A prototype can be technically complete and still be disposable. A pilot can use production data while remaining limited in audience and authority. Production begins when the organization accepts ongoing responsibility. Prototype Use a prototype when the unknown does not require real users or real data. Keep it: discardable; isolated; narrow in behavior; explicit about the learning question; free of false operational guarantees. Do not optimize architecture before the mechanism earns another stage. Pilot Use a pilot when the unknown requires real behavior, realistic data, or a real workflow, but consequence or readiness is not yet compatible with broad release. A pilot needs: a named audience; a human owner; bounded duration and authority; audit and rollback; outcome and guardrail thresholds; exit criteria for expand, revise, or stop. Production Production needs more than deployment: service level objective; on-call and incident ownership; security and privacy review; cost and capacity controls; rollback and recovery; continuous monitoring; a retirement path. Stage Drift Prototype code becomes dangerous when it acquires users, data, or authority without acquiring ownership. Mark prototype and pilot boundaries in configuration, access control, telemetry, and documentation. A warning banner is not enough. The stage should be observable from the system itself. Lesson 14.147 · The LLMOps lifecycle and safe releases Feedback Is Infrastructure In plain words first Every trace, failed evaluation, incident and support ticket is a signal . The ratchet turns each one into a change at the layer that owns its cause: - wrong results go to an evaluation or test; - missing facts go to the context source; - unsafe actions go to policy; - timeouts go to runtime controls; - product questions go to the backlog. Each change has an owner, a verification and a retirement condition. 14.46 did this for coding-agent corrections; this lesson does it for the product as well. The LLMOps lifecycle is covered in Lesson 14.147 (linked above). This lesson routes the signals the incident-agent story produced in 14.48 to 14.53, closes one loop with a real regression run, and writes the decision brief the practice lab asks for. A team can collect traces, evaluations, support tickets, and incident logs without learning from any of them. The missing mechanism is promotion: a defined path from observation to a durable change with an owner and proof. The loop is: observe a concrete signal; connect it to an outcome, constraint, or assumption; identify the earliest system layer that owns the cause; create a bounded change; verify that recurrence becomes less likely; review whether the control should remain. Route to the Owning Layer Signal Destination False positive, regression, wrong result Evaluation or test Missing context, duplicate work, stale fact Context source or retrieval route Unsafe action or authority gap Policy or permission boundary Timeout, retry storm, unavailable dependency Runtime control New product need or unresolved tradeoff Shaped backlog item Fix the cause at the earliest effective layer. Do not add another prompt paragraph when a test or permission can make the failure impossible. Ownership Is Part of the Control Every ratchet action needs: one owner; a priority based on consequence and recurrence; the artifact to change; the verification that proves the change; a review or expiry window; a retirement condition. An unowned improvement is an observation with better formatting. Retire Stale Controls Feedback systems accumulate policy. That policy can become contradictory and expensive. Review controls when: architecture or workflow changes; a lower-level invariant replaces a higher-level instruction; the protected failure has not appeared across the chosen window; the control blocks legitimate work more often than it prevents harm. Make Progress Within Your Authority List the unknowns and choose the cheapest reversible action that could resolve the most consequential one. State what you can decide, what is bounded by an existing agreement, and what needs authorization before execution. Defend a design You inherit a team that collects traces, evaluation scores, support tickets and incident logs for an assistant. Nobody can name a change that any of it caused. Design the mechanism that turns those signals into improvements, and tell me how you keep it from becoming another backlog. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The missing piece is promotion: a defined path from an observation to a durable change with an owner and proof. Each signal is connected to an outcome, a constraint or an assumption, traced to a root cause, and routed to the earliest layer that owns that cause, which is evaluation, context, policy, runtime or a shaped backlog item. Every resulting action carries one owner, a priority from consequence and recurrence, the artifact to change, the verification, a review window and a retirement condition, so the loop produces controls that are later re-examined rather than rules that only accumulate. The loop. Observe a concrete signal. Connect it to an outcome, a constraint or an assumption. Identify the earliest system layer that owns the cause. Create a bounded change. Verify that recurrence became less likely. Review whether the control should remain. Route to the owning layer. Signal Destination False positive, regression, wrong result Evaluation or test Missing context, duplicate work, stale fact Context source or retrieval route Unsafe action or authority gap Policy or permission boundary Timeout, retry storm, unavailable dependency Runtime control New product need or unresolved tradeoff Shaped backlog item A timeout belongs to the runtime, not to the general backlog, and a wrong answer belongs to a test, not to another prompt paragraph. The cause is fixed at the earliest effective layer. Ownership is part of the control. An unowned improvement is an observation with better formatting. Every action gets one owner, a priority based on consequence and recurrence, the artifact to change, the verification that proves the change, a review or expiry window, and a retirement condition. Why it is not a backlog. A backlog stores wishes. The ratchet stores controls with proof and expiry. Controls are reviewed when the architecture changes, when a lower-level invariant replaces a higher-level instruction, when the protected failure has stayed away across the window, or when the control blocks legitimate work more than it prevents harm. Retirement needs evidence too. Metrics close the loop. The signals only mean something against metrics defined before the result: outcome, guardrail and counter-metric, each with a threshold, a window and a source. The ratchet then changes the outcome frame, the assumptions, the slice or the measurement plan for product evidence, and the tests, context, scope or handoff for coding-agent corrections. Incidents can change both. Plausible wrong answers. "Build a dashboard so everyone can see the signals." Visibility without promotion and ownership changes nothing. "Add each lesson learned to the system prompt." Prose is the weakest layer; a permission boundary can make the unsafe action impossible, and a test can block a release that repeats the failure. "Keep every control forever since it was earned." Controls decay and conflict; each one needs a retirement condition and periodic review. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Two teams share the assistant and disagree on a tradeoff a signal exposes. Where does it go? Expected: to a shaped backlog item with a human decision owner; the ratchet does not resolve product disagreements by itself. (level 4) How do you prioritize across many signals? Expected: by consequence and recurrence together, so a severe single event and a frequent minor one both rise above a rare minor one. (level 4) What proves the loop works after a quarter? Expected: named controls that trace back to signals, verification results that show recurrence fell, and retirements with their evidence; not the volume of telemetry collected. Where it is taught. The feedback ratchet lesson gives the routing table and the ownership fields, and the success metrics lesson gives the metric contract the signals are judged against. Lesson 14.56 onwards connects the same loop to real model APIs. Why this came about Once language models could follow instructions ( Lesson 10.36 ), people wired them to tools: in 2022 the ReAct later · 14.63 paper showed a model alternating between reasoning and acting (search, look up, calculate), observing each result, and continuing. Experiments such as AutoGPT (2023) showed both the promise and the problems: impressive demos, but loops that wandered, repeated themselves and ran up large bills. In December 2024 Anthropic's guide "Building effective agents" drew a distinction that stuck: workflows , where code fixes the steps, and agents , where the model decides them, with the advice to use the simplest one that works. Andrew Ng's teaching popularised four agentic design patterns (reflection, tool use later · 14.56 , planning, multi-agent later · 14.66 collaboration), which give this block its structure. In plain words first A capable assistant with a desk and a rulebook Picture a new assistant at a desk with a phone, a computer and a calculator. You give them a task: "sort out this customer's refund". They decide what to do first (look up the order), do it, read the result, decide the next step (check the policy), and so on until the task is done, then report back. That is an agent: a language model as the decision-maker, tools as the phone and computer, and a loop that keeps going until the job is finished. The rulebook matters too: which tools they may use without asking, how long they may spend, and what needs a manager's approval. Step 1 · From one call to an agent Levels of autonomy . A single call answers once. A workflow runs model calls along a path your code fixes in advance. An agent lets the model choose its next step, tool by tool, until the task is done. Each level up handles messier tasks and costs more, varies more and needs more safeguards. One call : a prompt in, an answer out. Summarising an email, classifying a ticket. Cheapest, fastest, most predictable. Workflow : your code calls the model several times along a path you design: classify the ticket, retrieve the policy, draft a reply, check it. The model fills in each step; the code decides the order. Easy to test, because the path is known. Agent : the model decides the next step each time, including which tool to call, based on what it has seen so far. It can handle tasks whose steps you cannot list in advance, at the price of more model calls, more variation between runs, and more ways to go wrong. Multiple agents : several agents with different roles or tools pass work between them ( Lesson 14.66 ). The rule of thumb from practice: start with the simplest level that solves the task , and move up only when the task's steps genuinely cannot be fixed in advance. Step 2 · The loop The agent loop. The model reads the conversation so far and either answers or asks for a tool. Your code runs the tool and adds the result to the conversation, and the loop repeats. Your code, not the model, enforces the limits: a maximum number of steps, a budget, and approval for risky tools. The same loop as an animation: think, act, observe, and repeat until the model decides it is done. Figure: Hugging Face, Agents Course , Apache 2.0 . Every agent, however elaborate, has this core: Send the conversation so far (the task, plus every earlier tool request and result) to the model. If the model asks for a tool, your code runs it and appends the result. If the model gives a final answer, stop. Stop anyway if limits are reached: too many steps, too much cost, or a tool that needs a person's approval. Here is the loop with a scripted stand-in model and two harmless tools: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Reading this code The model only decides : it returns either a tool request or an answer. Your code acts : it looks up the tool by name, runs it, and records the result. This split is what makes agents controllable; Lesson 14.56 shows the real API version, where the model's tool request arrives as structured JSON . The conversation grows with each step, and the whole of it is sent to the model every time. That is why each step of an agent costs more than the last ( Lesson 14.61 ). max_steps is enforced by the loop, not by the model. Real agents need several such limits: steps, tokens, time, and approval for consequential tools (Lessons 14.57 and 14.60 ). A real model would not follow fixed rules: it might look up the order twice, skip the calculator, or ask the customer a question. Evaluating agents means running many cases many times ( Lesson 14.144 ). The same task as a workflow : if every refund question follows the same steps, you do not need the model to choose them. Copy What you should see Copy Cheaper, faster and fully predictable. The agent earns its extra cost only when tasks vary in ways a fixed path cannot handle: the customer has no order number, wants an exchange instead, or has three problems at once. The figure shows the five workflow patterns later · 14.62 that Lesson 14.62 builds: prompt chaining later · 14.62 , routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers later · 14.62 and evaluator-optimiser. Many production "agents" are really one of these workflows with a small agentic step inside. Step 4 · When an agent is the right tool Use an agent when Prefer a workflow or a single call when the steps depend on what you find along the way the steps are the same every time tasks are open-ended (research, debugging, multi-part requests) tasks are narrow (classify, extract, summarise) occasional extra cost and latency are acceptable cost per request and speed are critical results can be checked (tests, a human reviewer, a policy check) mistakes would be costly and hard to detect Check your mental model ✗ "An agent is a smarter model." ✓ It is an ordinary model in a loop with tools. The model decides; your code acts and enforces limits. ✗ "More autonomy is always better." ✓ Each level up adds cost, variation and risk. Use the simplest level that solves the task. ✗ "The model runs the tools." ✓ The model only asks. Your code decides whether and how to run each request, which is where safety controls live. Run the agent for the new order. Which design, agent or workflow, needed more changes? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it For each task, choose a single call, a workflow or an agent: (a) tag 50,000 incoming emails by department; (b) answer "why did my last three orders all arrive late?" using order, courier and weather data; (c) every night, summarise the day's tickets and email the summary to the team; (d) fix a failing test in a codebase. (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · A tight step limit Two tool steps are printed ( find_order , then calculator ), and the function returns "Stopped: step limit reached." because the model never got a third turn to give its answer. Step limits must leave room for the work; when one is hit, a real agent should report what it did so far rather than fail silently ( Lesson 14.57 ). Solution M1 · A second order and a new rule In the workflow, the rule already exists ( rate = 0.9 if ... > 3 else 1.0 ), so only the data changes. In the scripted model you must edit its rules to compute the rate, and with a real model you would change the instructions or the tools (for example, a refund_policy tool that returns the rate). Fixed business rules usually belong in code or tools, not in the model's judgement. Solution X1 · Choosing the level (a) a single call per email (or a small fine-tuned classifier, Lesson 7.22 ): high volume, fixed task; (b) an agent: the investigation steps depend on what each lookup reveals; (c) a workflow on a schedule: the steps never change; (d) an agent with tools to read files, edit code and run tests, because it can check its own work by running the tests ( Lesson 10.37 's verifier idea). Recap An agent is a language model that decides the next step, tools that your code runs, and a loop with limits enforced by code. Single calls, workflows and agents trade predictability and cost against flexibility; use the simplest that works. The four agentic patterns are tool use, reflection, planning and multiple agents; memory, state and evaluation support them. Each agent step resends the growing conversation, so cost and latency rise with the number of steps.
