The section The real thing runs the same function against the real Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs and lists what changes. Why this came about A model on its own can only produce text from what it learned. To let it look things up and act, OpenAI introduced function calling in June 2023, and other providers followed: the model returns a structured request to run a function, and your code runs it. This single capability is what turned chat models into the basis of agents. The problem: the model cannot see your systems A ShopKart customer writes: "Where is my order SK-1042? It was due yesterday." The answer lives in ShopKart's order service. A language model has never seen that service; it only knows what is in its training data and in the request you send. Start with the simplest thing: send the question with a good system prompt and nothing else. Copy What you should see Copy That is the stand-in being honest. A real model usually is too ("I don't have access to your order details"), and sometimes it is worse: it guesses a plausible status. Either way the customer does not get an answer, and no amount of prompt wording fixes it, because the fact is not in the request. The model needs a way to ask your code for it. That is all a tool call is. In plain words first A manager who writes errand notes A model cannot see your systems; it can only write text. Tool calling lets it write a very particular kind of text: a structured request ("run get_order_status with order_id A-1001"). Think of a manager who cannot leave the office and writes errand notes; your code is the assistant who runs each errand and brings back the result, matched to the note by its ID. The model never runs anything itself: every action passes through your code, which is where all the safety checks live. Idea 1 · Describe the tool, keep the code There are two things with the same name, and keeping them apart is most of the lesson. The function is ordinary Python that runs in your process. The tool definition is a JSON description you send to the API: a name, a description, and a JSON Schema for the arguments ( input_schema ). The model only ever sees the description. Copy What you should see Copy The function works on its own. The model will never see this code or this output unless your code sends the output back. Three things about the definition matter more than they look: The description is a prompt. The model decides whether and how to call a tool by reading it, so say what the tool does, when to use it, and what valid input looks like. "Order IDs look like SK-1042" will save you failed calls later. The schema is a contract for the arguments , not a guarantee by default: the model fills it in, and it can get it wrong. You will see that happen below, and how to check. It costs tokens on every request. The API turns your tool definitions into text the model reads, so every tool you send is paid for as input on every call, whether or not it is used. Predict before you run You send the same question again, this time with tools=[ORDER_TOOL] . Does get_order_status run during that request? What stop_reason comes back? Write your answer down, then run the next block. (Solution P1 at the end.) Idea 2 · The model asks, your code acts Send a question that the model cannot answer from memory, together with the description of one tool. Then look closely at what comes back. Print the reason the model stopped and every block of its reply: Copy What you should see Copy The response is not an answer. It is a request: a tool_use content block with an id , the tool name and the input arguments, and stop_reason is "tool_use" , which means "I stopped because I want a tool". Nothing has run. The model cannot run anything: it produced text that your code is free to act on or ignore. So your code acts. It needs a way to get from the name the model used to the function to call: Python refresher Python refresher: dispatch tables and `**` unpacking A dispatch table is a dictionary from names to functions: TOOLS = {"get_order_status": get_order_status} . Then TOOLS["get_order_status"] is the function, and adding parentheses calls it. ** unpacks a dictionary into keyword arguments: if args = {"order_id": "SK-1042"} , then f(**args) is the same as f(order_id="SK-1042") . Together, TOOLS[block.name](**block.input) calls whichever function the model named, with the arguments it chose. That one line is why the tool's input_schema property names must match the function's parameter names. Copy What you should see Copy Three appends, in this order, and each one matters: The assistant turn goes back in whole , text and tool_use blocks together. The API checks that every result answers a request it can see in the previous message. Your code runs the function. This is the only line where anything happens in the world, and it is entirely under your control: you can refuse, ask a person first, or log it. The results go back as a user message of tool_result blocks, each carrying the tool_use_id of the request it answers. The content is a string here; it can also be a list of text, image or document blocks. Idea 3 · Send the result back, get the answer Your code has now run the function and appended the result to the list of messages. Send the whole list again. The model reads its own request, sees the result underneath it, and writes the answer in ordinary text. The small show function then prints the finished conversation exactly as the API sees it, so you can count the four messages of one round trip. Copy What you should see Copy One tool call, drawn: your app sends the question and the tool's description; the model answers with a tool_use request instead of text; your code runs the function; your app sends the result back in a tool_result block matched by id; the model writes the answer. The model never runs code, and the message list grows by two entries per tool turn. That is one complete round trip: two requests to the API, one function call in your process, and a conversation that grew from one message to three. The second request contains everything: the question, the model's request and your result. The API keeps nothing between requests, so the model reads the whole list again each time. (Anthropic released message threads in public beta on 2 November 2026, which let the server hold the history for a few minutes so you send only new messages. The model still reads the full conversation and you are billed the same, and you still keep your own copy to replay when a thread expires. It is an optimization on top of this lesson, not a different mechanism.) A tool gives the model reach into your systems, and the next section is about limiting that reach. When tool calls go wrong Bad arguments, and other customers' data Fix both failures inside the tool, where they belong. The format check returns a message that tells the model how to fix its input. The ownership check uses the customer ID from your session , never from anything the model wrote, and it gives the same message for "does not exist" and "not yours", so the tool cannot be used to discover which order IDs exist. Copy What you should see Copy 6/6 on the same questions. The trace shows the correction: the first call failed validation, the error went back as a tool_result with is_error: true , and the next request carried a fixed ID. The stand-in does this with a rule; Claude's documentation says the model typically retries two or three times with corrections when a tool reports invalid or missing parameters. The retry is not free: that question now costs 781 tokens instead of about 450, which is the argument for a clear description and, on Claude, strict: true (below), so the first call is right more often. Two lines from this section are worth memorizing. Schema validity is not business validity : even when the API guarantees that order_id is a string matching your schema, only your code can check that the order exists and belongs to this customer. And identity comes from the session, not the prompt : if the tool took a customer_id argument, a customer could simply ask the model to use someone else's. Slow tools: put a deadline on every call The carrier's tracking service is having a bad day and takes three seconds to answer. Without a deadline, your customer waits as long as the slowest dependency. Python refresher Python refresher: `concurrent.futures` ThreadPoolExecutor runs functions in worker threads. pool.submit(fn, **kwargs) starts fn in a worker and returns a future , a handle to a result that is not ready yet. future.result(timeout=1.0) waits up to one second: it returns the value if the function finished, re-raises the function's exception if it failed, and raises TimeoutError if time ran out. That last case is what turns a hung dependency into an error you can handle. Copy What you should see Copy The customer gets an honest answer after one second instead of waiting three. One caveat worth knowing: Python cannot stop a running thread, so the slow call keeps going in the background until it finishes. The outer deadline protects the customer; the tool's own HTTP client should also have a timeout so the work actually stops. Retries, backoff and circuit breakers later · 14.59 come in Lesson 14.59 , and the full reliability treatment in the Production engineering and AI system design section. Two tool calls in one response Ask about two orders and the model asks for both lookups at once: two tool_use blocks in one response. (Claude does this by default; disable_parallel_tool_use: true inside tool_choice limits it to one.) The rule for the reply is strict: one user message carrying every result for that turn , results before any text. Wording varies from run to run. The model may answer without a tool, call one with a missing or invented ID, ask a clarifying question, or call two tools when you expected one. Your validation and every-request-gets-a-result rule are what keep those cases safe. Setup. An API key in the environment, a pinned model ID, and SDK versions you control. On Claude, strict: true on a tool definition enables schema validation of tool inputs. On Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, forcing a tool with tool_choice any or tool returns a 400 error; the documented alternative is auto with strict tool use. On OpenAI, set strict explicitly; strict mode later · 14.58 requires additionalProperties: false . Evaluation. Run each question several times and grade facts, not wording, exactly as run_eval does. A question that passes four times out of five is a reliability problem, not a pass ( pass^k , the Production engineering and AI system design section). Cost. Two or more requests per question, each re-sending the system prompt, the tool definitions and the growing history. Prompt caching cuts the repeated part; fewer, clearer tools cut the rest. Solutions Solution P1 · Does the function run during the request? No. stop_reason is "tool_use" and the content holds a tool_use block, but nothing ran: the API returned text describing a call it would like you to make. Only the line TOOLS[block.name](**block.input) in your code runs anything. This is the most important fact about tool calling, because it means every safety check, permission and approval lives in your code, where you can enforce it. Solution P2 · Forgetting the assistant turn The request is rejected: Copy The stand-in's wording is its own; the real API also returns a 400 invalid_request_error that names the orphaned tool_use_id . The API checks every tool_result against the tool_use blocks in the message just before it. Without the assistant turn, the result answers a question nobody can see. The fix is the first append in Idea 2: messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content}) . Solution D1 · Three bugs, one tool "delivered, ETA None" : the tool formats a field that delivered orders do not have, and the customer sees Python's None . Return structured data (JSON) with only the fields that exist, as the fixed tool does, and let the model phrase it. The crash on SK-9999 : ORDERS.get returns None for an unknown ID, and None["status"] raises TypeError . run_tool caught it, so the app survived, but the customer read an internal error message. Check for the missing order explicitly and return a message written for the model and the customer: "no order SK-9999 on this customer's account". SK-2001 leaked : there is no ownership check, so any customer can read any order by guessing IDs. This is the serious one. Check order["customer_id"] against the session, and use the same message for missing and not-yours. The fixed version is the get_order_status from Bad arguments, and other customers' data . A good habit this exercise teaches: read tool outputs as the customer will read the final answer, because the model often passes them through nearly verbatim. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism Walk me through exactly what happens when an LLM "calls a tool". Worked answer. The application sends the conversation plus tool definitions: a name, a description and a JSON Schema for the arguments. The model reads the definitions as part of its input and, if it decides a tool is needed, returns a structured request instead of a final answer: on Claude a tool_use block with an id, name and input, and stop_reason: "tool_use" . The application runs the matching function itself, then sends a new request containing the whole history plus a tool_result that references the request's id. The model reads the result and either answers or asks for another tool. The model never executes code; the API holds no state between requests unless you opt into a server-side feature; and every check lives in the application. A plausible wrong answer. "The model calls the API or function directly." It sounds right because frameworks hide the loop, but it leads to the wrong security model: if you believe the model executes calls, you look for safety in the prompt instead of in the code that actually runs them. Follow-ups. Why does the second request contain the first? What happens if a tool raises an exception? How does the model choose between two tools with similar descriptions? What does strict: true change, and what does it not? Explain the mechanism What does tool_choice control, and what would you use on Claude Sonnet 5.5? Worked answer. It controls whether and which tools the model must use: auto (the default when tools are given) lets it decide, any forces some tool, tool forces a named one, and none forbids tools. Forcing is useful for extraction, where you always want structured arguments. On Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, any and tool return a 400 error, so the documented approach is auto with strict tool use for schema-valid inputs, or structured outputs when you just need a fixed JSON shape. Parallel calls are limited with disable_parallel_tool_use inside the tool_choice object. A plausible wrong answer. "Always force the tool so the model can't skip it." On the newest Claude models that request fails outright, and even where it works, forcing a tool skips the model's thinking and removes its ability to ask a clarifying question when the input is missing. Follow-ups. When is structured output a better fit than a forced tool? How would you test that the model calls the tool when it should and not when it shouldn't? Debug a failure The API returns "tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after", but only when customers ask about two orders. Why? Worked answer. With two orders the model makes two tool calls in one response. The code appends one user message per result, so the message after the assistant turn answers only the first call and the API rejects the conversation. The fix is to collect every result for that turn into a single user message, with the tool_result blocks before any text. I would add a test with a two-call response so it cannot regress, and check the history format elsewhere, because split results also make the model less likely to make parallel calls at all. A plausible wrong answer. "The model is calling the tool twice by mistake, so disable parallel tool use." That hides the bug and makes every multi-order question slower; the model's behavior was correct and the history formatting was not. Follow-ups. What if one of the two calls times out? (Return an error result for it; never leave a call unanswered.) Should independent calls run in parallel in your code too? Debug a failure A customer was told the status of another customer's order. Where do you look, and what do you change? Worked answer. First the trace: which tool ran, with what arguments, and what it returned. The likely cause is a tool that trusts the model's arguments for identity, either by looking up any order ID or by taking a customer ID as a parameter. The fix belongs in the tool: take the customer from the authenticated session, check ownership on every call, and give the same response for missing and not-yours so IDs cannot be probed. Then add the case to the eval set as a must-not-contain check, review every other tool for the same pattern, and treat it as a security incident: find out how many lookups crossed accounts. A plausible wrong answer. "Add a line to the system prompt telling the model to only discuss the customer's own orders." Prompts are not a security boundary: a confused or manipulated model will still call the tool, and the tool will still answer. Follow-ups. How would prompt injection later · 15.24 in an order note exploit a tool like this? How do you log tool calls without logging personal data? Defend a design Why write the round trip yourself instead of using the SDK's tool runner or a framework? Worked answer. For learning and debugging, writing it once is the fastest way to understand what every framework does, and the code is about 30 lines. For production, I would happily use the tool runner or a framework when its defaults fit, because it removes boilerplate and handles details such as error results and history management. What I would not hand over is the part that carries risk: identity and ownership checks, timeouts inside tools, idempotency for writes, approvals, the cost and step caps, and evaluation. Those are the same whichever loop runs them. The simpler design wins until I need what the framework adds: streaming, persistence, human-in-the-loop later · 14.60 , or multi-agent later · 14.66 control flow (the LangChain and LangGraph section). A plausible wrong answer. "Frameworks are always better because they're maintained by experts." It ignores that a framework cannot know your permissions or your failure modes, and that its abstractions make failures harder to trace when you have never seen the underlying requests. Follow-ups. What would make you switch from your own loop to LangGraph later · 14.101 ? How would you migrate without changing behavior? (Run the same eval set before and after.) It is not a language model. Its wording is fixed, and it enforces the API's documented rules for tool results. The real thing at the end runs the same Agent class on the real Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs . Why this came about One tool call answers simple questions, but real tasks need several dependent steps. The 2022 ReAct later · 14.63 paper showed that letting a model alternate between reasoning and acting, observing each result, solved such tasks well, and the agent loop became the standard design. Its risks, loops that never end and costs that run away, came with it. The problem: one request, several dependent steps A customer writes: "My mixer arrived broken last week. Can I get a refund?" There is no order ID. The assistant has to find the order first, then decide, then act, and each step depends on the result of the one before. You cannot know in advance how many requests that takes. So the code has to keep looping until the model stops asking for tools. ShopKart now has three tools: find_orders lists the logged-in customer's orders, get_order_status is Lesson 14.56 's checked lookup, and issue_refund moves real money. Copy What you should see Copy Start with what you already have. Lesson 14.56 's answer() already loops: it allows up to four requests. Give it all three tools and the refund question: Copy What you should see Copy It worked, and that is the problem. The model found the order, asked for a refund, and the code paid INR 3,899 because the model asked. Nobody checked whether a person should approve it. And if the model had needed a fifth request, answer() would have returned a bare "Stopped" that nobody would notice. An agent loop needs three things this code lacks: an exit for every way a response can end, limits that hand the conversation to a person, and a gate in front of risky tools. In plain words first Repeat until done, with a stop button One tool call answers simple questions. Real requests need several dependent steps: look up the order, then check the refund policy, then issue the refund. The agent loop repeats: call the model, run any tools it asked for, send the results back, until it answers without asking for tools. Because the model decides when to stop, the loop needs your limits too: a maximum number of steps, a check for repeated calls, and a record of each step. Idea 1 · Every way a turn can end The loop's exit decision is stop_reason . You have used two values. The Messages API documents seven, and a loop needs an answer for each one: stop_reason What happened What the loop does end_turn The model finished Return the answer tool_use The model wants tools Run them, send the results, go round again max_tokens The reply hit your max_tokens Stop and hand over, or retry with a larger limit; a cut-off tool_use block is unusable stop_sequence One of your stop sequences appeared Treat as finished, or as your own signal pause_turn A server-side tool loop (such as web search) hit its iteration limit Send the assistant content back unchanged to let it continue refusal The model declined Stop; Anthropic's docs suggest retrying on a different Claude model model_context_window_exceeded The reply filled the context window Treat it as truncated Every turn of the agent loop ends with a stop reason, and the loop needs a decision for each one. Only tool_use continues the loop. Anything the code does not recognise must stop the run with a clear message, never fall through. The Agent below handles the two everyday values, stops cleanly on max_tokens , and stops with a message on anything it does not expect. A loop that falls through on an unknown value either crashes or, worse, keeps going. Idea 2 · Limits, a gate, and a trace Python refresher Python refresher: `dataclasses` @dataclass writes a class's __init__ for you from annotated fields: Agent(system="...", tools=TOOLS) sets self.system and self.tools , and every other field takes its default. A mutable default such as a set must be made fresh for each object with field(default_factory=set) . Otherwise all agents would share one set. __post_init__ runs right after __init__ , which makes it the place to check the configuration. Copy What you should see Copy Nothing runs yet. This block only defines the class. Read run as a list of exits. Each one ends the run with a message a person can act on, never silently: Exit Trigger Why it exists Answer end_turn The job is done Cut-off reply max_tokens Half an answer, or half a tool call, cannot be used Unknown stop Any other stop_reason Fail loudly instead of looping on something you did not plan for Repeat check The same tool with the same input a third time A stuck model asks the same question forever Token budget Input plus output tokens over token_budget A cap on cost per run that does not depend on counting steps Step limit max_steps requests The last line of defense And call_tool is the gate. The model can ask for issue_refund , but the function only runs if approve says yes. The default approve says no to everything, so a misconfigured agent fails safe. The model gets a clear error result in place of the action and tells the customer. Notice also the start-up check in __post_init__ : a risky tool name that does not exist is an error when the agent is created, not a silent hole in production. The debugging exercise shows why. Two small methods are there as hooks. call_tools runs one turn's calls, and execute is the single line that touches the world. Lesson 14.59 overrides them to run calls in parallel, put a deadline on each and retry failures, without changing the loop. The trace shows every step, and the token count climbs faster than the step count: 249 tokens after step 1, 1,110 after step 3. That is the cost of a loop. Each request re-sends the whole conversation, so step n pays for everything before it. Words in the answer are not actions. The stand-in says the refund needs a colleague's approval, and that is true here because the gate refused it. But a real model can also say "I've passed this to a colleague" when nothing was passed to anyone. If a handoff later · 14.66 matters, it must be a tool call or a ticket your code creates ( Lesson 14.60 , Lesson 14.148 ), not a sentence. Copy What you should see Copy The unguarded run made 40 requests and spent about 57,000 tokens to tell the customer nothing. The guarded one stopped at the third identical call, at under 1,000 tokens. The growth is quadratic: each request carries every earlier result, so 13 times the requests cost about 60 times the tokens. Repeat checks and token budgets are cost controls as much as reliability controls. A cut-off reply is the other quiet failure. To run the same agent on OpenAI's Responses API , write an adapter : an object with the same messages.create(...) method that translates the request on the way out and the reply on the way back. This is the pattern every multi-provider framework and gateway uses. Copy What you should see Copy (Same local test server.) The adapter is where provider differences live. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What is the agent loop, and what are its exit conditions? Worked answer. The loop sends the conversation and tool definitions to the model, and if the model asks for tools, the application runs them, appends the request and the results, and calls the model again. It repeats until the model answers. A production loop has an exit for every stop_reason : end_turn returns the answer; tool_use continues; max_tokens , refusal and anything unexpected stop with a handoff. It also has its own limits: a step limit, a token or cost budget, and a check for repeated identical calls. Every exit returns something a person can act on. A plausible wrong answer. "Loop while the response has tool calls, with a maximum of N iterations." It covers the happy path and the runaway case, but not a cut-off reply, a refusal or a stuck model making the same call. Those are exactly the failures that reach customers. Follow-ups. How do you pick N? Why does cost grow faster than the number of steps? What should the customer see when a limit is hit? Debug a failure An agent's bill tripled overnight, but traffic was flat. What do you check? Worked answer. Look at tokens per run and steps per run in the traces, not total requests. A jump in steps per run usually means a stuck pattern: a tool that started failing or returning empty results, which the model retries. Because each step re-sends the whole history, a few extra steps per run can triple the tokens. Group runs by their last tool call and its result to find the tool, fix it or make it return an explicit error, and add a repeat check and a per-run token budget so the next failure is capped. Then alert on steps per run and tokens per run, not only on total spend. A plausible wrong answer. "Switch to a cheaper model." That lowers the price per token, but the stuck loop still runs. The cause is the number of steps, not the model. Follow-ups. How would prompt caching change the cost curve? What would you put on a dashboard to catch this within an hour? Defend a design Why gate risky tools in code instead of telling the model in the prompt to ask first? Worked answer. The prompt influences what the model asks for. The gate controls what happens. A model can misread an instruction, be manipulated by text in a document or a message, or simply make a mistake, and a prompt cannot stop the function from running. A gate in the loop decides whether the function runs, using rules that read your data rather than the model's arguments, and it logs the decision. I would still describe the policy in the prompt, so the model sets expectations with the customer, but the enforcement lives in code. A plausible wrong answer. " Fine-tune the model so it always asks for confirmation." It makes good behavior more likely. It does not make bad behavior impossible, and nothing records who approved what. Follow-ups. Where would you put the gate in a multi-agent later · 14.66 system? How do you approve without making people click "yes" on everything ( Lesson 14.148 )? Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Sandbox An isolated environment where an agent's code or actions cannot reach anything important Lesson 15.25 Model Context Protocol (MCP) An open standard for connecting models to tools and data through small servers, so one integration works in many apps Lesson 16.26 LangChain A widely used open-source library of building blocks for model applications: models, prompts, tools and agents Lesson 14.93 Why this came about Writing a tool's JSON description by hand next to its code meant the two drifted apart. Libraries began generating the description from the function itself, its name, docstring and type hints, the same idea web frameworks such as FastAPI used for APIs. One source of truth for each tool became the norm. The problem: two descriptions of one function In Lessons 14.56 and 14.57 every tool was written twice: once as a Python function, and once as a JSON definition for the model. Nothing keeps the two in step. A teammate renames a parameter in a refactor, tests that call the function directly still pass, and the model keeps sending the old name: Copy What you should see Copy The agent survives because Lesson 14.57 's call_tool turns the exception into an error result, but every order lookup now fails. The fix is to have one source of truth: generate the definition from the function. In plain words first One description, written once A tool has two descriptions that must agree: the Python function your code runs, and the JSON Schema the model reads. Writing both by hand means they drift apart. Instead, read the schema out of the function: its name, its docstring and its type hints already say what it is called, what it does and what arguments it takes. A decorator can do that and register the tool, so adding a tool is writing one well-described function. Idea 1 · Read the definition out of the function A tool definition is read straight from the function. The name, the type hints and the docstring already say everything the model needs, so generating the schema from them keeps the two descriptions from drifting apart. Python refresher Python refresher: type hints and `inspect` def f(order_id: str, limit: int = 5) carries everything a schema needs. inspect.signature(f).parameters lists the parameters in order, each with its default ( inspect.Parameter.empty when there is none). typing.get_type_hints(f) maps each name to its type. inspect.getdoc(f) returns the docstring. typing.Literal["damaged", "wrong item"] is a type that allows only those values, and typing.get_args returns them. Copy What you should see Copy Each part of the function lands somewhere specific: In the function In the definition Why it matters to the model Name name How it refers to the tool First paragraph of the docstring description How it decides whether to use the tool Parameter names and type hints properties and their type What to fill in Literal[...] enum It cannot invent a reason such as "broken" (when the schema is enforced) A default value Left out of required It may omit the argument Args: lines Each property's description What a good value looks like (always) additionalProperties: false No arguments you did not define Predict before you run For def find_orders(customer_note: str, limit: int = 5, include_items: bool = False) , what will required contain, and what type will include_items get? (Solution P1.) Idea 2 · A decorator that registers tools Python refresher Python refresher: decorators A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a function. @tool() above def f means f = tool()(f) . So tool() runs first and returns register , and register(f) runs once, when Python reads the def , not when f is called. That is why a decorator can record every tool in a registry at import time. functools.wraps(fn) copies fn 's name, docstring and signature onto the wrapper, so code that inspects the wrapper still sees the original. Copy What you should see Copy Two things changed for the better. The definition is generated, so the rename in the opening example is now impossible: rename the parameter and the schema follows it. And risk is declared on the tool itself, @tool(risky=True) , with the agent's risky set read from the registry. Lesson 14.57 's debugging exercise, where a typo in a separate list of names let a refund through, cannot happen this way. Idea 3 · Check the arguments before anything runs A schema describes valid input; it does not enforce it. Unless you use a strict mode (below), the model can send an enum value that is not in the list, misspell an argument, or leave one out. Check before the approval gate and before your function: Copy What you should see Copy Each message names the argument and says how to fix it, which is what lets a model correct itself on the next request ( Lesson 14.56 's retry). The check runs before the approval gate, so nobody is asked to approve a malformed refund. Validation of the shape is not validation of the meaning. validate cannot know whether SK-1077 belongs to this customer, or whether it was delivered more than 30 days ago. Those checks stay in the function, where Lesson 14.56 put them. Tool design: what makes a tool easy to use well The model chooses and fills tools from their names, descriptions and schemas, so those are prompt text: together they are the agent-computer interface (ACI) . Anthropic's guidance on writing tools for agents ( Writing effective tools for agents , September 2025) comes down to a few rules: Name tools for the task, not the API : find_orders , not GET_orders_v2 . Namespace related tools ( orders_find , orders_refund ) when you have many. Fewer, higher-level tools. One schedule_meeting beats list_users plus list_events plus create_event when the model would always chain them. Describe when to use it and what comes back , including units, formats and limits, as you would for a new colleague. Make arguments hard to get wrong : enums, IDs that come from lookup tools rather than memory, sensible defaults. Return what the next step needs, not everything. Errors that say how to fix the call , never an empty result that looks like "nothing found". The fifth rule is the easiest to measure, because every byte a tool returns is re-read on every later step ( Lesson 14.57 ). Here is the same agent with the order service's full record, then with only the fields the answer needs: Copy What you should see Copy Identical answers, about a third fewer tokens per run. (The stand-in counts characters ÷ 4, so read the ratio.) With a real model, irrelevant fields also cost accuracy: the model has more text to misread and more chances to quote an internal field to the customer. Problems that show up in production, and the fix for each: Problem Fix Two overlapping tools ( search_orders and find_order ); the model picks either Merge them, or say in each description when not to use it Too many tools for one agent; tool choice gets worse as the list grows Give each specialist only its own tools ( Lesson 14.66 ), or load definitions on demand (below) Huge results Return a few fields by default, with a detail or limit option An empty list on error, which the model reads as "no orders" An explicit error that says what to do next IDs the model has to remember or invent Lookup tools, so IDs always come from data Large tool sets. Every definition you send is read on every request. The problem: tools are slow, and sometimes fail So far every tool answered instantly and never failed. Real ones are network calls. Python refresher Python refresher: exceptions are classes class TransientError(Exception) makes a new kind of error. except TransientError: catches only that kind, and the subclasses of it, and lets every other exception through. In plain words first Errands that run late, fail or happen twice Real tools are slow and sometimes fail. Several independent errands should run at the same time, each with a deadline. A failure the model can work around ("order not found") goes back to it as a result, not as a crash. Temporary failures get retried, waiting longer each time. And any tool that changes something must be safe to run twice, because retries and restarts will run it twice: an idempotency key lets the receiving system recognise and ignore the repeat. Idea 1 · Parallel calls, each with a deadline Three tool calls requested in one model turn. Run one after another, the turn takes the sum of their times. Run in parallel, it takes as long as the slowest, and a deadline keeps one slow tool from holding up the others: it is cancelled and reported to the model as a timeout it can react to. Lesson 14.57 left two hooks in Agent : call_tools , which runs one turn's calls, and execute , the line that calls your function. RobustAgent overrides both. Copy What you should see Copy Trace what happens for the two-order question: run (unchanged from 3.2) gets two tool_use blocks and calls call_tools . call_tools submits call_tool for each block to the pool. A call still running after its deadline becomes an error result, so the turn always has one result per request ( Lesson 14.56 's rule). Two details matter in production. Backoff (waiting longer after each failure) gives a struggling service room to recover. Jitter (a random part of the wait) stops a thousand clients that failed together from retrying together, which is how a short outage becomes a long one (the retry storm later · 14.139 in Lesson 14.139 ). Suppose the payment provider makes the refund, and then the connection drops before the reply reaches you. Your code sees a transient error and retries, as it should: Copy What you should see Copy Without a key, the retry refunded the customer twice. With a key, the provider recognized the second request and returned the first result. An idempotency key is a value that is the same on every retry of one logical operation and different for every new one. Here it is a hash of the run, the tool and its arguments. Real payment and messaging APIs accept one (often as an Idempotency-Key header) for exactly this reason. Where an API does not, store the key with the record yourself and check it before writing. After a transient failure you wait before retrying, and the wait grows with each attempt, for example 0.1, 0.2, then 0.4 seconds, capped. That gives an overloaded service time to recover instead of hitting it again at once. Jitter makes each wait random within that range. Without it, every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment, and the synchronized wave knocks the service over again. Debug a failure Customers report being refunded twice, and only during an incident with the payment provider. What happened? Worked answer. During the incident, refund requests succeeded on the provider's side but the replies timed out, so the agent's retry logic sent them again and each retry made a new refund. The fix is an idempotency key per logical refund, generated by our code from the run and the call, sent with every retry and stored with the record, so the provider (or our own table) returns the first result instead of acting twice. Then reconcile the duplicates from the provider's records, and add a test that simulates a lost reply. A plausible wrong answer. "Turn off retries for the refund tool." That trades double refunds for missing ones: a customer whose reply was lost now never hears back, and an agent or a person retries by hand anyway. Follow-ups. Where would you store idempotency keys, and for how long? What if the model itself asks for the refund twice in one run? Defend a design Why run a turn's tool calls in parallel, and when would you not? Worked answer. When the model asks for several independent lookups in one turn, running them concurrently makes the turn as slow as its slowest call instead of the sum of all of them. In the example that halved latency. I would run them sequentially when one call's result changes whether another should run, when two calls write to the same record, or when a downstream service has a low rate limit. And I would cap concurrency per tool. The model's batching is a hint, not a guarantee that the calls are independent, so the decision lives in code, per tool. A plausible wrong answer. "Always parallelize, it's free speed." It is not free for writes to the same record, for rate-limited services, or when results must be applied in order. Follow-ups. How do you keep result ordering correct? How would you do the same with asyncio instead of threads ( Lesson 14.66 )? Python refresher Python refresher: generators A function containing yield is a generator . Calling it runs nothing. It returns an object that produces values one at a time as you loop over it, pausing at each yield until the caller asks for the next value. That makes it a natural shape for an agent loop : the caller receives each event the moment it happens, and stopping the loop stops the agent. A generator can be consumed only once. In plain words first A live progress bar and an itemized bill An agent that works silently for twenty seconds feels broken, and one whose cost nobody can explain is a budget risk. So the loop yields events as it works ("calling get_order_status", text as it is written, "done") and adds up the tokens of every model call into a cost per run . Both come from the same idea: the loop reports what it is doing, step by step, instead of only returning an answer at the end. Idea 1 · The loop yields events Until now run returned only when the agent had finished, so a user saw nothing for several seconds. In an agent you usually stream the last step's text and show progress events for the steps before it. Idea 2 · Tokens and cost per run Why each step of an agent costs more than the last. Every model call re-reads the whole conversation so far, so input tokens per call rise step by step, and the total grows roughly with the square of the number of steps. Prompt caching makes the re-read part cheap; a step budget caps the total. Every response carries usage : input and output tokens for that request. Output tokens are a small share of the total, so for agents the input side, and caching it, usually matters most. In plain words first Most problems need a recipe, not a chef who improvises Before building an agent, check whether a fixed workflow will do: code decides the order of steps and a model fills in each one (classify, then extract, then route). Workflows are cheaper, faster and easier to test. An agent, where the model decides the next step, is for tasks whose path cannot be known in advance. Most production systems are workflows with one agentic step inside, built from a few standard shapes: chaining, routing, parallel steps, orchestrator and workers, and generate-then-evaluate. Start with the least autonomy that works How this connects Lesson 14.55 introduced the idea that systems sit on a scale from "your code decides everything" to "the model decides everything", and Lessons 14.56 to 14.61 built the far end of that scale: an agent loop . This lesson fills in the middle. It names the five standard arrangements of model calls where your code stays in charge, and builds each one in a few lines. The most cited practical advice in the field comes from Anthropic's Building effective agents (December 2024): find the simplest solution, and add complexity only when it measurably helps. They distinguish workflows , where code decides the path, from agents , where the model decides the path. This workflow vs. agent distinction is the first design decision. The autonomy ladder: each rung hands one more decision to the model. Climb only as far as the task needs, and only with the evidence and controls of that rung. Prompt chaining (fixed steps with gates between them), routing (classify, then send to a specialized path), parallelization (sectioning a task into independent parts, or voting over several attempts), orchestrator-workers (a model splits a task and delegates parts), evaluator-optimizer (draft, critique against criteria, revise), and plan-and-execute with re-planning. They differ in how much control the model has; start with the least autonomy that handles every known path, and give the model more only where the path cannot be known in advance. A plausible wrong answer. "Always build an agent; it can do all of these." It can, at higher cost and lower predictability. Follow-ups. When does orchestrator-workers beat a fixed parallel split? Debug a failure A plan-and-execute workflow keeps executing a stale plan after a step fails. What do you change? Worked answer. Re-plan on failure: after each step, check the result against the step's success condition, and on failure send the plan, the results so far and the error back to the planner for a revised plan, with a limit on re-plans. Also check that steps report failures as failures instead of plausible text. A plausible wrong answer. "Make the plan more detailed." A detailed plan still goes stale when the world differs from the plan. Follow-ups. How would you stop endless re-planning? Defend a design A stakeholder wants a fully autonomous agent for refunds. What do you propose? Worked answer. A workflow with the model inside it: route refund requests, look up the order and policy in fixed steps, let the model draft the explanation, decide eligibility in code, and require approval above a limit. Autonomy goes where the path truly varies, such as understanding messy customer messages. That is cheaper, easier to test and audit, and still feels intelligent to the customer. Expand autonomy later if evals show the fixed path is the bottleneck. A plausible wrong answer. "Yes, agents are the future." Refunds move money; predictability and auditability come first. Q3 What should an evaluator-optimizer loop always have? A A larger model for the critic B A maximum number of rounds and a defined outcome when it does not converge C Temperature zero D Two different providers Unbounded loops are unbounded costs. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Prompt injection Text that tricks a model into following an attacker's instructions instead of yours Lesson 15.24 Sandbox An isolated environment where an agent's code or actions cannot reach anything important Lesson 15.25 RAG Retrieval-augmented generation: find the relevant passages in your own documents, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them Lesson 10.45 Long-term memory What an agent remembers across conversations, stored outside the context window and fetched when needed Lesson 14.65 Subagent An agent that another agent delegates part of a task to, with its own instructions and context Lesson 14.66 Error analysis Reading the model's wrong outputs and grouping them by cause Lesson 14.130 Agent harness Everything around the model that makes an agent work on long tasks: the loop, tools, files, checks, memory and limits Lesson 14.67 About the model on this page The "models" on this page are scripted stand-ins Every function whose name ends in _model , and the planner , solver and replanner , are plain Python with fixed rules. They stand where a real model call would go, so each trace is identical on every run and you can study the control flow of each pattern. The tools, the executor, the checker and the search are real code. Lesson 14.57 showed how to connect the same loops to a real model API. Why this came about The first tool-using models answered in one shot and failed on anything needing several steps. In 2022 the ReAct paper showed that letting a model alternate between a short written thought, one action and the observation that came back solved multi-step questions far more reliably. But ReAct calls the model after every single step, and on long tasks it can wander or lose the goal. Through 2023 researchers proposed fixes, each trading something: plan-and-execute and ReWOO plan first to save calls; Reflexion has the model learn from a failed attempt; Tree of Thoughts and LATS search over several lines of reasoning; CodeAct has the model write code instead of single tool calls . Since 2024, reasoning models ( Lesson 10.37 ) do much of this planning internally, so these patterns matter today mainly as ways to structure the code around a model: where it is called, what it sees, and what checks it. In plain words first Asking for directions at every corner, or planning the trip There are two ways to drive to an unfamiliar address. You can stop at every corner and ask which way next: slow, but you recover easily from a closed road. Or you can plan the whole route before leaving: fast, but if a road is closed the plan is useless until you re-plan. Agents face the same choice. Reacting step by step adapts well and costs many model calls; planning first is cheaper and easier to review, and needs a way to notice surprises. Two more ideas sit on top: checking your work against something concrete before handing it in (reflection), and trying several routes on paper and keeping the best (search). The task for this lesson One customer question that needs several lookups and a little arithmetic. Three tools, each a plain function: Copy The correct answer needs: the customer's orders, each order's status and price, the cancellation rule for each status, and a sum. The work_out function is the last reasoning step; every pattern below must gather the facts it needs. Three shapes of control. ReAct asks the model after every observation, so it adapts well and costs the most calls. Plan-and-execute asks once for a plan, lets code run it, and asks once more for the answer; it needs a re-plan step for surprises. Reflection adds a check after a draft and feeds concrete findings back. Step 1 · ReAct: think, act, observe, repeat In ReAct the model is called once per step. Each call sees the question and everything that has happened so far, writes a short thought , and chooses one action . Your code runs the action and appends the observation . This is the agent loop of Lesson 14.57 with the model's reasoning made visible. Copy What you should see Copy Eight model calls for one question. Notice the last line: every call re-reads the whole history, so the text the model reads grows with each step. The total grows roughly with the square of the number of steps ( Lesson 14.61 measured this as cost). In exchange, ReAct never committed to anything in advance: had list_orders returned five orders, or one, it would simply have carried on. Reading this output Reading this trace Thought lines are text the model writes for its own benefit: stating what is missing before choosing an action makes the next action better ( Lesson 10.37 ). With reasoning models this happens in a hidden thinking phase and you see only the action. One action per call is the classic form. Modern APIs let a model request several tool calls in one turn ( Lesson 14.59 ), which would let it fetch the three orders together and cut the calls from eight to four. The loop stops when the model returns an answer, or at max_steps . The limit is enforced by your code, never by the model ( Lesson 14.55 ). Step 2 · Plan-and-execute: decide the steps once If the steps can be known in advance, ask the model once for a plan , let ordinary code execute it, and ask the model once more to write the answer from the results. The plan here is a small data structure; steps can refer to the results of earlier steps: Copy What you should see Copy Two model calls instead of eight, and the model read about a ninth of the text. The plan is also something a person, or a policy check, can read and approve before anything runs , which matters when steps have consequences. This is the idea behind the "plan mode" of coding agents and the to-do lists that long-running agents keep ( Lesson 14.67 ). Reading this output ReWOO: a plan with no way back The planner above wrote for_each steps because it could not know how many orders there would be. A stricter variant, ReWOO (reasoning without observation), writes every tool call up front with placeholders such as #E1 for "the result of step 1", runs them all, and solves. It uses the fewest tokens of any pattern, because the model never re-reads observations between steps. Its weakness is in the name: it cannot react to what the tools return. Use it for fixed lookups, such as "fetch these five fields and summarise them". Step 3 · When the plan meets a surprise Plans are written before the facts are known. Here the customer has a brand-new order that the order system has not synced yet: Copy What you should see Copy The executor ran the plan faithfully and one lookup came back not found . A solver that assumes every step succeeded crashes (or, worse with a real model, confidently reports on an order it knows nothing about). The fix has two parts: code that checks each step's result against what the plan expected, and a re-plan call that is made only when something is off. Here re-planning drops the missing order and tells the customer. That third model call was spent only because it was needed, which is the practical advantage over ReAct. ReAct Plan-and-execute ReWOO Model calls on this task 8 (4 with parallel tool calls) 2, plus 1 per surprise 2 Adapts to tool results At every step Only when a check triggers a re-plan No Can a person review the steps first? No, they do not exist yet Yes Yes Typical failure Wanders, repeats itself, loses the goal on long tasks Follows a stale plan Breaks on anything unexpected Good for Exploratory tasks where each result decides the next step Multi-step tasks with a predictable shape Fixed data-gathering Step 4 · Reflection needs something to reflect on Reflection means checking a draft and revising it. The research version, Reflexion , stores a short written lesson from a failed attempt and retries with it. Whether reflection helps depends almost entirely on what the model is given to reflect on: Copy What you should see Copy "Please improve it" changed nothing, because it told the model nothing it did not already believe. The checker recomputed the refund from the tools, found a mismatch of exactly Rs 100, and said where to look. With that, one revision fixed it. The stand-in exaggerates for clarity, but the pattern is what studies and production teams report: self-critique with no new information mostly restates the draft, and sometimes talks the model out of a correct answer. Good sources of a concrete signal, roughly from strongest to weakest: Signal Example Executing something Run the tests; run the SQL and inspect the rows; call the API in dry-run mode A rule in code Recompute the total; validate against a schema; check every cited passage exists Retrieved evidence Does each claim appear in the documents that were retrieved? ( Lesson 14.72 ) A second model with a rubric A grader that scores tone, completeness and policy points and must quote the problem ( Lesson 14.143 ) The same model, same prompt, "are you sure?" Weak: no new information Lesson 14.62 built this as the evaluator-optimiser workflow. The rule to remember is that the evaluator must be able to see something the writer could not. Step 5 · Search: try several plans, keep the best ReAct and plan-and-execute follow one line of reasoning. Tree of Thoughts and LATS (language agent tree search) explore several: generate a few candidate next steps, score each partial result, keep the most promising, and repeat. The task below shows why that can matter. Three coupons can be applied to a Rs 2,400 basket, and the order changes the result: Searching over plans. Each node is a partial plan (which coupons have been applied, and the price so far). Greedy search keeps only the cheapest state at each depth, takes the 20% coupon first, and can then never use the Rs 300 coupon, which needs a price of at least Rs 2,000. Keeping two states at each depth finds the better order. Copy What you should see Copy With a beam width of 1 the search is greedy : it takes the 20% coupon first because that gives the biggest immediate saving, and then the Rs 300 coupon no longer applies. Keeping the two best states at each depth finds the order that saves Rs 240 more. Keeping all six finds the same answer and evaluates almost twice as many states. In a real agent every "state evaluated" is at least one model call to propose it and often another to score it, so search multiplies cost by the beam width times the depth. Reading this output When search is worth it Search pays off when three things are true: a wrong early choice is expensive to undo, partial results can be scored reliably (here, the price; in coding, the tests), and you can afford many times the cost of a single run. That describes some coding, theorem-proving and planning problems. It does not describe most business agents, where a reasoning model in a plain loop is the better first choice, and where actions on real systems cannot be tried and undone. Reasoning models perform a form of this search internally during their thinking phase, at a price you pay in thinking tokens. Step 6 · CodeAct: let the model write the loop Every pattern so far spends model calls on control flow : "now fetch the next order". A model that can write code can express the whole control flow in one reply. In CodeAct , the tools are functions and the model's action is a short program that calls them: Copy What you should see Copy One model call, and the loop over orders, the lookups and the arithmetic all ran as ordinary code. The intermediate results never passed through the model's context at all, which is why this pattern (also called programmatic tool calling or "code mode") is spreading in agents that work with many tools or large tool results. smolagents ( Lesson 14.125 ) is built around it. Watch out Code written by a model must run in a sandbox The exec call above runs a fixed string that this lesson wrote, with almost every built-in function removed. Real model output is untrusted input: it can contain mistakes, and text from a web page or document can talk a model into writing harmful code ( prompt injection later · 15.24 , Lesson 15.24 ). Emptying __builtins__ is not a security boundary in Python. Production systems run model-written code in an isolated sandbox later · 15.25 : a container or micro-VM with no credentials, no network except what you allow, and time and memory limits ( Lesson 15.25 ). First, reasoning models have absorbed much of this : prompts that force "think step by step" or elaborate plan formats often make them worse, not better ( Lesson 11.25 ). Try the plain loop with a strong model before adding structure. Second, every pattern adds model calls, and the only way to know whether one earned its cost is to run your evaluation set with and without it ( Lesson 14.144 ). The agent improvement loop Like RAG later · 10.45 , agents improve in a loop: trace real runs, find the most common failure, apply the matching fix, re-run the evals. The table maps symptoms to fixes in the order most teams try them. Notice how often the fix is a tool, an instruction or a piece of code rather than a bigger model. Choose by scenario The agent is not reliable enough: what to try next # If you see this Try this If that doesn't work Watch out in production 1 It picks the wrong tool, or none Rewrite tool names and descriptions: when to use, when not to; (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · One more order ReAct makes 9 calls: one more get_order , and no extra cancel_policy because "packed" has already been looked up. Plan-and-execute still makes 2: the for_each step simply runs once more in code. The total becomes Rs 3,697 (1,299 + 799 + 1,599). The cost of ReAct grows with the size of the task; the cost of a plan grows only when the shape of the task changes. Solution B1 · A silent skip The answer lists the two cancellable orders and says nothing about SK-49001. The customer, who asked about all their orders, is told a total that silently leaves one out, and nobody is alerted that the order system is behind. A crash is visible and gets fixed; a silently wrong answer is repeated to every affected customer. Surprises should be surfaced: to the model (re-plan), to the user (a note), and to your logs. Solution D1 · Reflection without a signal "Improve it" gives the model no new information, so it rewrites in place. It rarely finds errors it could not see the first time. Reflection helps when the critique carries a concrete signal: a failing test, a schema error, a policy check, a missing citation. Use the improvement loop instead: read the failing traces, label why each failed, and fix the cause (context, tools, instructions), measured on the evaluation set. If a check exists for the common failure, run it and feed its message back, as Step 4 does. Solution M1 · A wider tree There are now 24 orders in which to apply four coupons. Beam width 2 may or may not contain the best path, depending on how the intermediate prices rank: a path that looks third-best after one step is dropped even if it would have won. Compare with search(2400, 24) . No beam width short of "everything" is guaranteed, which is why search needs a scoring function that predicts final quality, not only current quality, and why wider beams buy reliability with cost. Solution X1 · Matching patterns to tasks (a) A workflow or ReWOO: a fixed query and a summary; check that the ten amounts in the summary match the query result. (b) ReAct with a reasoning model: each finding decides the next lookup; add a step budget and require the answer to cite the records it used. (c) Any loop plus reflection with execution as the signal: run the query on a sample database and feed errors or suspicious results back ( Lesson 14.80 ). (d) Search, or better, an optimisation library called as a tool: the score (total cost) is exact, and a solver will beat a language model at combinatorics. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism Compare ReAct, plan-and-execute and reflection. Worked answer. ReAct interleaves reasoning with tool calls and observations, deciding one step at a time; it adapts well, costs a model call per step, and can wander. Plan-and-execute writes a plan first and has code execute it, which is cheaper, more predictable and reviewable, and needs checks plus re-planning when steps fail. Reflection critiques an output and revises it; it helps when the critique has a concrete signal, such as tests or a rubric. Modern reasoning models do much of this internally, so the patterns now mostly shape the harness later · 14.67 around the model. A plausible wrong answer. "They are different model architectures." They are prompting and control patterns over the same models. Follow-ups. Where does a reasoning model's internal thinking replace these patterns? Debug a failure An agent's plans look good but it often stops before finishing. What do you check? Worked answer. The stop conditions: step limits and budgets that are too tight, a planner that marks steps done without checking results, or a final step that is skipped when a tool returns an error. Read traces of unfinished runs, check whether each step's success condition was verified, and add a final check that the goal is met before answering. A plausible wrong answer. "The model is lazy." Stopping early is almost always a limit or a missing success check. Follow-ups. How would you make "goal met" checkable? Defend a design Should every agent have a planner? Worked answer. No. Short tasks with one or two tool calls do better with a plain loop; a planner adds a call and a structure that must be kept in sync with reality. Planners pay off for long, multi-step tasks where order matters and progress must be visible, especially across context resets ( Lesson 14.67 ). Decide with evaluations on the actual tasks. A plausible wrong answer. "Yes, planning always improves reasoning." It improves some long tasks and slows down short ones. Follow-ups. How would you show a plan to the user, and when would you not? Recap ReAct calls the model once per step and re-reads the whole history each time: most adaptable, most expensive. Plan-and-execute spends one call on a plan and one on the answer; code runs the steps. Add checks and a re-plan step for surprises. ReWOO is the same with no way to adapt. Reflection works when the check gives the model new, concrete information. Search keeps several partial plans alive; it needs a reliable score and multiplies cost. CodeAct replaces many small tool-call turns with one program, and requires a sandbox. Start with a plain loop and a strong model; add a pattern only when your evaluation set shows it helps. Managing short-term memory, deciding what stays, what is condensed and what is dropped, became a core part of building agents. In plain words first What is in your head right now Short-term memory is the working memory of one conversation: the messages so far, tool results, what the agent is in the middle of. It lives in the run's state and is sent to the model every turn, so it must be kept within budget by trimming, summarizing or clearing old tool results. The memory pipeline is the set of steps that decide what is kept, what is condensed and what is passed to the model on each call. Memory design Memory type Holds Lives in Example Working memory (short-term) The current conversation and task state The context window , plus a checkpoint store This chat's messages Semantic memory later · 14.65 Facts about users and the world A key-value or document store, often with vector search later · 14.71 "Prefers answers in Hindi" Episodic memory later · 14.65 Past experiences and outcomes A store of past cases, retrieved as examples "Last time this error happened, the fix was X" Procedural memory How to do things Prompts, skills, instructions "Always add LIMIT to SQL" The first row is what you have had since Lesson 14.57 : the list of messages. The other three rows are long-term memory later · 14.65 , kept outside the context window and brought in when needed. Short-term memory (left) is the message history of one conversation, saved as checkpoints so the conversation can resume. Long-term memory (right) is a separate store of facts that outlives the conversation and is shared by all of a user's conversations. Both end up in the same place: the model's context. Figure: LangChain documentation , MIT . This lesson builds short-term memory in code, and Lesson 14.65 builds the long-term kinds. Three design decisions apply to every memory: When to write : during the conversation (the agent calls a remember tool; immediate but adds latency) or after it (a background job extracts facts, called memory consolidation ; better quality, one session late). The figure below shows both. How to scope : always put the tenant and the user in the key, so one customer can never read another's memory. How to keep it healthy : timestamps, sources, updates instead of duplicates, expiry, and a way for users to see and delete what is stored. Memory has two paths: the write path runs after a conversation; the read path runs on every turn. The memory pipeline Every long-term memory system, managed or not, has the same five stages: Stage Question Typical implementation Extract What in this conversation is worth remembering? An LLM call that turns turns into candidate facts, with a type and importance Consolidate Is it new, an update, or a duplicate? Similarity search against existing memories, then add, update or skip Store Where, and scoped to whom? A store keyed by tenant and user, with embeddings for search Retrieve What is relevant to this turn? Similarity plus recency plus importance, filtered by scope Forget What must expire or be deleted? Time-to-live, user deletion requests, decay Step 1 · Short-term memory: a token-budgeted buffer with a running summary Short-term memory is the current conversation. In Lesson 11.20 you saw that the API keeps nothing between calls, so "the conversation" is just a list of messages that your code resends every turn. Left alone, that list grows until it is slow, expensive and finally too long for the context window. There are only three things you can do about it: cut old messages off (cheap, and the agent forgets them completely), summarise them (costs a model call, keeps the gist), or both. The two ways to shorten a conversation. Filtering (bottom) simply drops the oldest messages. Summarising (top) replaces them with one short summary message, written by a model, and keeps the recent messages word for word. Figure: LangChain documentation , MIT . The standard design does both: it keeps the last few turns verbatim and folds older turns into a running summary , so the agent remembers the gist of a long session without paying for every word. Lesson 11.27 called this move compaction ; here it becomes a reusable class. Copy What you should see Copy The first three turns were folded into the summary; the facts survived. A real summarizer is an LLM call with a prompt such as "update the summary with anything the agent will need later: facts, decisions, open questions"; it costs tokens, so fold several turns at once and run it in the background where you can. In production When summaries lose what mattered Summaries paraphrase, and paraphrase is where order IDs, amounts, dates and promises get lost or changed ("about INR 2,500" for INR 2,499). Keep a small structured state next to the summary for facts that must survive verbatim (customer ID, order IDs, amounts, decisions, promises made), and have the summarizer update that state rather than prose. Test it: ask about a turn-two detail at turn twenty. Check your mental model ✗ "Short-term memory is the same as long-term memory with a time limit." ✓ Short-term is one conversation's working state; long-term is distilled later · 14.132 facts kept across conversations. ✗ "Trimming is always safe." ✓ Cutting between a tool call and its result breaks the conversation; trim by whole turns. ✗ "Keeping everything gives the best answers." ✓ Old, irrelevant history adds cost and distracts the model. Exercises Predict before you run A ConversationBuffer with a small token budget receives ten turns. Which turns are kept word for word, and where do the others go? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Set the buffer's budget below the size of a single long turn, such as a pasted invoice. What does the buffer do with it, and what should it do? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise Debugging exercise: the summary forgot the order ID After twelve turns, the agent asks the customer for their order ID again, although they gave it in turn 2. The running summary reads "Customer has a delivery problem." Find the cause in the memory pipeline and fix it. (Solution D1.) Make it your own Change the summary step so it always keeps a structured "facts" section (order IDs, amounts, promises made) separate from the free-text summary, and show it surviving ten turns. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Recent turns verbatim, older ones summarized The most recent turns that fit in the budget are kept word for word; older turns are folded into the running summary, which is kept at the front. The model sees the summary, then the recent turns, then the new message, so recent detail is exact and older detail is compressed. Solution B1 · One turn bigger than the budget A buffer that only drops whole turns either keeps the oversized turn and exceeds the budget, or drops it immediately and loses it. Better: store the large content outside the conversation (a file or a document store), keep a short reference and summary in the turn, and retrieve the details when needed. Solution D1 · Summaries must keep identifiers The summarizer compressed the facts the conversation depends on. Instruct it to keep identifiers, amounts, dates and commitments verbatim, or extract them into structured state that is never summarized (the modify exercise). Then test with long conversations that refer back to early facts. Solution M1 · Facts outside the summary Keep facts: dict next to summary: str , update facts with a small extraction step after each turn, and render both at the front of the context. Facts are replaced, not summarized, so the order ID from turn 2 is still exact at turn 12. LangGraph's typed state ( Lesson 14.101 ) is the production form of the same idea. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What is short-term memory in an agent, and how do you keep it within budget? Worked answer. It is the context of the current conversation or task: recent messages, tool results and working state, sent with each call. Keep it within budget by keeping recent turns verbatim, summarizing older ones, clearing old tool results, keeping key facts in structured state, and moving durable facts to long-term memory. Never cut between a tool call and its result. A plausible wrong answer. "The model remembers the conversation." The application resends it every time ( Lesson 11.20 ). Follow-ups. How do you test that summaries keep what matters? Debug a failure Users say the assistant "forgets" things mid-conversation. Where do you look? Worked answer. At the context of the call where it forgot: whether the fact was still there, summarized away or trimmed, or buried among long tool results. Check the summarization prompt and the trimming boundary, and whether the thread or session ID changed between turns, which would start a new conversation. A plausible wrong answer. "Use a model with a longer context window." The fact was probably removed by your code, not the window. Follow-ups. How would you log enough to debug this without storing personal data unnecessarily? Defend a design Summarize history, or trim it? Worked answer. Trim when old turns rarely matter, such as short support chats, because it is cheap and exact. Summarize when the conversation builds on earlier decisions, such as long tasks and agents, and keep structured facts outside the summary so identifiers survive. Many systems do both: trim tool output aggressively, summarize dialogue. A plausible wrong answer. "Always summarize, it keeps everything." Summaries lose detail and cost a model call. Follow-ups. A In the system prompt for everyone B Semantic memory, keyed by tenant and user C Episodic memory D Only in the current conversation It is a fact about the user that should persist across sessions, scoped to that user.
