Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Durable execution Running a long task so that every completed step is saved and a crash resumes from the last one Lesson 14.140 Memory Bank Vertex AI's managed long-term memory service Lesson 14.120 LangGraph A library for building agents as graphs of steps with saved state, so runs can pause, resume and branch Lesson 14.101 LangChain A widely used open-source library of building blocks for model applications: models, prompts, tools and agents Lesson 14.93 Deep agent An agent with a harness for long tasks: files, subagents, planning and permissions Lesson 14.111 Sandbox An isolated environment where an agent's code or actions cannot reach anything important Lesson 15.25 Model Context Protocol (MCP) An open standard for connecting models to tools and data through small servers, so one integration works in many apps Lesson 16.26 Durable wait A workflow paused for an external event, stored in the database Lesson 14.140 Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. In plain words first How to use these questions These questions check whether the chapter's ideas have really landed. Read each question, then answer it in your own words (out loud, on paper, or to a colleague) before opening the model answer: a one-sentence definition, then how it works, then what it means in practice. Compare with the model answer and the plausible wrong answer, and note any follow-up you could not answer. If a question feels unfamiliar, go back to the lesson that teaches it. Teams can also use these as discussion prompts in a study group. Foundations and agent design Junior What is an AI agent, and how is it different from a chatbot? An agent is a model running in a loop: it decides on an action (usually a tool call ), observes the result, and repeats until the goal is met or a limit is reached. A chatbot answers one turn at a time without acting. The practical definition, from Anthropic and Simon Willison, is "an LLM running tools in a loop to achieve a goal". Agents add autonomy, so they also add cost, latency and risk. Junior Explain tool calling end to end. You send the model a list of tools (name, description, JSON schema of parameters). The model returns a structured tool call instead of text. Your code validates the arguments, runs the tool, and sends the result back as a tool message. The model then answers or calls another tool. The model never runs anything itself; your code is the only executor, which is where permissions and checks live. Mid When would you use a workflow instead of an agent? When the steps are known in advance: extraction pipelines, classification then routing, fixed approval flows. Workflows are cheaper, faster, testable step by step and predictable. Use an agent when the path depends on what the model finds (research, troubleshooting, open-ended support). Most production systems are workflows with an agentic step inside. Mid What is context engineering, and why did the term replace prompt engineering? Prompt engineering is wording instructions. Context engineering is deciding everything that goes into the model's window at each step: instructions, tools, retrieved documents, memory, history and tool results, within a token budget. Agents run many steps, so what to select, compress, isolate or drop matters more than phrasing. Failure modes include context poisoning , distraction, confusion and clash. Senior Single agent or multi-agent? Walk me through how you decide. Start with one agent. Move to several only when (a) the work is broad and parallel, like research across many sources, (b) tool sets or permissions must be separated, or (c) context would overflow. Multi-agent systems cost much more (Anthropic measured about 15 times the tokens of chat) and lose context between agents (Cognition's argument). If you split, give each subagent a precise objective, output format and boundaries, and avoid splitting work whose parts must agree, such as one codebase change. Senior How do you make a long-running agent reliable? Externalize state: a progress file or task list, checkpoints after each step, durable execution later · 14.140 so a crash resumes instead of restarting, idempotency keys on side effects, step and token budgets, and human approval for high-impact actions. Compact or summarize context periodically and keep the goal recited near the end. Treat the agent as a stateless reducer over an event log so pause and resume are simple. Junior What is the ReAct pattern? ReAct (reason plus act) interleaves reasoning steps with tool calls: think about what to do, call a tool, read the observation, think again. It was introduced in a 2022 paper and is the basis of nearly every tool-calling agent loop . Native tool calling made the format implicit: the model's tool call is the "act", and the tool result is the "observation". Mid What kinds of memory does an agent have? Short-term memory is the conversation and working state in the current context window or thread. Long-term memory persists across sessions and comes in three flavors borrowed from psychology: semantic (facts about the user or domain), episodic (past interactions and their outcomes, often used as examples) and procedural (learned instructions or rules, sometimes the agent's own updated prompt). Long-term memory needs extraction, deduplication, provenance, expiry and per-user isolation, and it is an attack surface ( memory poisoning ). Managed options include AgentCore Memory, Vertex AI Memory Bank later · 14.120 , Foundry memory, LangGraph later · 14.101 stores, Mem0 and Zep. Mid What are the common workflow patterns before you reach for an agent? From Anthropic's "Building effective agents": prompt chaining (fixed sequence with checks between steps), routing (classify then dispatch), parallelization (sectioning or voting), orchestrator-workers (a model splits work dynamically) and evaluator-optimizer (generate, critique, revise). Each is easier to test and cheaper than a free agent. Good designs say which one fits the problem and why. Mid How do you design good tools for an agent? Few tools that match real tasks rather than one per API endpoint; clear names with namespaces; descriptions that say when to use the tool and when not to; typed, constrained parameters (enums, formats); compact, meaningful results (names, not opaque IDs); errors that tell the model what to do next; idempotency on write tools; and permissions enforced inside the tool. Then evaluate tool use on real tasks and refine descriptions from the failures. Senior What is a "deep agent" or agent harness, and how is it different from a ReAct loop? A harness wraps the basic loop with what long tasks need: a planning tool (a to-do list the agent maintains), a file system for notes and artifacts, subagents with their own context for isolated subtasks, context compaction , and detailed system prompts . Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, Deep Research and LangChain later · 14.93 's Deep Agents later · 14.111 follow this shape. It lets agents work for hours on coding or research while keeping each model call's context focused. Senior How do computer-use and browser agents work, and what are their risks? The model receives screenshots (and sometimes the accessibility tree or DOM), and returns actions such as click, type and scroll, executed by a harness in a browser or virtual machine. They reach systems without APIs, but they are slower, costlier and less reliable than API tools, and every web page is untrusted input that can carry injected instructions. Run them in isolated sandboxes later · 15.25 with no stored credentials beyond what the task needs, restrict domains, require confirmation for purchases, logins and sending, and prefer an API or MCP later · 16.26 tool whenever one exists. Senior How would you add human-in-the-loop to an agent without making it unusable? Classify actions by risk: read-only runs freely, reversible low-impact actions run with notification, irreversible or high-value actions need approval. Show the reviewer the exact action and arguments plus the agent's reason, and let them edit, approve or reject. Implement the pause as durable state (an interrupt with a checkpointer or a durable wait later · 14.140 ) so approvals can take hours. Track approval rates: actions approved 99% of the time are candidates for automation with monitoring, frequently rejected ones point to agent errors. Senior How do structured outputs work, and can you rely on them? Providers offer constrained decoding : the model can only produce tokens that keep the output valid against a JSON schema, so the result always parses. That guarantees syntax, not meaning: fields can still be wrong, so validate values ( Pydantic , business rules) and retry with the error on failure. Without native support, ask for JSON, validate, and repair. Keep schemas small and descriptive; enums and field descriptions improve accuracy. Senior An agent works in demos but picks the wrong tools and loops in production. What do you change first? Read the failing traces before changing anything. Wrong tool choice usually means overlapping or vague tool descriptions, or too many tools in one agent: rewrite descriptions with when to use and when not to, merge overlaps, and split tools across specialists if the list is long. Loops usually mean no stop criteria and errors hidden from the model: add a step budget, explicit "after two failures, tell the user" instructions, repeated-call detection in code, and keep errors visible. Then move any fixed sequence into a workflow, enforce business rules in tools, and add the failing traces to the eval set so the fix is measured and stays fixed. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Vector database A store that finds the vectors nearest to a query vector quickly Lesson 14.71 Hybrid search Running keyword search and vector search together and merging the results Lesson 5.38 Reranker A second, slower and more accurate model that reorders the top search results Lesson 5.38 Multi-hop A question whose answer needs facts connected through intermediate entities Lesson 14.88 Index (LlamaIndex) The object that splits documents into passages, embeds them and stores the vectors for search Lesson 14.124 BM25 The standard keyword-ranking formula: rare matching words count more, and repeats count less each time Lesson 5.37 Contextual retrieval Prepending a short description of the source to each chunk before indexing Lesson 14.75 Why this came about Search engines return documents; models need short, focused passages that fit in a prompt. Early RAG cut documents into fixed-size pieces and lost meaning at the cuts, so chunking strategies that respect structure and keep context became an important design choice. In plain words first Cutting a book into index cards Search works on pieces, not whole documents. Chunking cuts documents into passages small enough to be specific and large enough to make sense on their own, ideally along natural boundaries such as sections, with a little overlap and with the document's title and headings kept as metadata. Chunk size is a trade: small chunks find precise facts but lose context; large ones keep context but dilute the match. Chunking in code Documents are too long to put whole into every prompt, and long passages dilute the embedding . Chunking splits them into retrievable pieces. The function below does recursive chunking : paragraphs first, then sentences, until each piece is under a size limit. Chunking, drawn: fixed-size chunks cut through a table and a heading; structure-aware chunks follow the document's sections, keep the table whole, and carry a short header that says where they came from. Copy What you should see Copy Chunking strategy How it splits Good for Watch out Fixed size Every N tokens, with overlap Quick baselines Cuts sentences and tables in half Recursive (above) Paragraphs, then sentences, then words, until under a size Most prose; the common default Ignores document structure Structure-aware Headings, sections, list items, table rows Manuals, policies, HTML, Markdown Needs good parsing first Semantic chunking Starts a new chunk when meaning shifts (embedding distance jumps) Long unstructured text Slower; gains are often small Late chunking Embeds the whole document first, then pools token vectors per chunk, so each chunk "knows" its context Long documents with many cross-references Needs a long-context embedding model that supports it Page-level or document-level No splitting Short documents; multimodal page retrieval Large contexts Industry practice Chunk size is a tuning knob, not a constant Practitioners consistently report that parsing quality and chunk boundaries matter more than the choice of vector database later · 14.71 . Start around 200 to 500 tokens with modest overlap, keep tables and code blocks whole, store the section heading with every chunk, and tune against a retrieval eval ( Lesson 14.72 ) rather than by intuition. In production Chunking problems you will meet, and what to do Answers quote half a rule ("refundable within 30 days" without "for damaged items"): chunks are cutting through the sentence that carries the condition. Split on headings and paragraphs first, add a small overlap, and prepend the section heading to every chunk. Tables answered wrongly : fixed-size and semantic splitters cut tables into pieces that mean nothing alone. Keep each table whole (or one row per chunk with the header repeated) and convert it to Markdown before indexing. Precise questions match, but the answer lacks context : chunks are too small. Rather than making every chunk bigger, match on small chunks and hand the model the parent section (small-to-big, below and in Lesson 14.75 ). Broad questions retrieve the wrong section : chunks are too big, so one vector averages several topics. Split further or add per-section summaries as separate entries. Semantic chunking was slower to ingest and not better : common. Its gains over good structure-aware splitting are often small; try it only on long, unstructured text and keep it if your eval says so. Every change means a re-index : so tune chunking last, after hybrid search later · 5.38 , headers and reranking later · 5.38 , and compare the new index side by side with the old one on the same questions. The chunking families used in production The recursive splitter above is the default, and the table in the previous step names the common alternatives. Production systems use a few more, and practitioners refer to them by name. Here is the full set, grouped by what they decide: where to cut , what to index , and what to return . Family What it decides How it works Use when Cost and watch-outs Fixed size (sliding window) Where to cut Every N tokens, stepping forward by N minus the overlap Baselines, uniform prose Cuts mid-sentence and mid-table; overlap of 10 to 20% duplicates storage Recursive Where to cut Try paragraph breaks, then sentences, then words until each piece fits The default for prose Ignores headings; a section can straddle two chunks Structure-aware (Markdown / HTML header splitting) Where to cut Split on headings, keep the heading path as metadata; tables, lists and code blocks stay whole Manuals, policies, wikis, anything a parser turned into Markdown Only as good as the parser ( Lesson 4.29 ) Code-aware (AST splitting) Where to cut Split on function, class and method boundaries from the language's syntax tree Repositories, notebooks, SQL files Needs a parser per language (tree-sitter); giant functions still need a fallback Semantic Where to cut Embed sentences; cut where the distance between neighbours jumps Long unstructured text with topic shifts One embedding call per sentence at ingest; gains over structure-aware are often small Agentic (model-decided) Where to cut A model reads the document and emits boundaries and titles Messy documents with no structure, high-value corpora Slowest and most expensive; propositions can drift from the source wording Contextual (header or model-written context) What to index Prepend the document title, section path, or a model-written summary of where the chunk sits Almost always; page-image retrieval ( Lesson 4.29 ) Large contexts; precise questions match poorly Three of these change the index shape rather than the cut, so they are worth seeing in code. All three reuse DOCS and chunk() from the previous step. Hierarchical parent-child chunks Index small pieces for matching; store, for each, the ID of the larger piece it came from; return the parent. The "parent" can be a paragraph, a section, or the document. This is what Bedrock Knowledge Bases call hierarchical chunking , and what Lesson 14.75 uses for small-to-big retrieval. Copy What you should see Copy Match at the sentence level (sharp), return the chunk or the document (enough context). Which level to return is a per-corpus decision: return the chunk for FAQs, the section for manuals, and cap the total so three sentence hits in one section do not return it three times (deduplicate on the parent ID). Sentence window A variant that needs no hierarchy: index single sentences and, at answer time, return each hit with its neighbours. Cheaper than parents when documents have no sections. Copy What you should see Copy A window of one or two sentences is usually enough for "what does this rule say" questions; it fails when the condition lives several sentences away, which is when parent-child wins. Proposition chunks Index facts, not passages. A model rewrites each chunk into standalone statements with pronouns resolved and context filled in; each proposition is indexed and points back to its chunk. The stand-in below does the rewrite by rule so the block runs offline; the real prompt is in the docstring. Copy What you should see Copy Each proposition carries its subject, so "UPI refunds usually arrive in 2 days" is findable from "how fast is a UPI refund" without the chunk's other sentences diluting the embedding. The first proposition shows the weakness of a rule-based stand-in (a title turned into a "fact"); a model would drop it. Costs: one model call per chunk at ingest, and roughly three to five times as many index rows. Return the source chunk, not the proposition, so the answer quotes real text. Code-aware and Markdown-header splitting, in one line each Both are "structure-aware" with a specific parser. For Markdown, langchain_text_splitters.MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter splits on # , ## , ### and stores the heading path in each chunk's metadata, which is exactly the "section path" header that contextual chunking wants. For code, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter.from_language(Language.PYTHON, ...) splits on class and def boundaries first; for full syntax-tree splitting, tree-sitter based splitters (for example in LlamaIndex later · 14.124 's CodeSplitter ) cut at function and class nodes and fall back to lines inside oversized functions. Copy What you should see Copy The Markdown splitter kept the heading path with each chunk; the Python splitter cut at the class boundary, not in the middle of a method. Choosing, in order Parse well first ( Lesson 4.29 ): structure-aware splitting needs headings and tables to exist. Default : structure-aware where there is structure, recursive where there is not, 200 to 500 tokens, 10 to 20% overlap, tables and code whole. Always add context : the heading path or title on every chunk (contextual, cheap version). Then shape the index : parent-child when precise matches lack context; sentence window for dense technical text without sections; propositions for fact-heavy prose when you can afford the ingest cost; summary-as-chunk for tables and long sections. Only with an eval ( Lesson 14.77 ): semantic, agentic and late chunking. They are slower to ingest and their gains are corpus-specific; keep them if recall@k goes up, not because they sound advanced. Managed services expose the same choices as settings: Bedrock Knowledge Bases offer fixed, hierarchical, semantic, none and custom (Lambda) chunking; most vector databases and frameworks ship the splitters above. The decision is yours either way. Choose by scenario Chunking by document type, and what to try when it is not enough If your documents are... Chunk like this If retrieval is still poor, try Can backfire when Short FAQ entries or product cards One chunk per entry, no splitting Add the question and category as metadata Entries are long and cover several questions Long, structured documents (policies, manuals, contracts) Split on headings; match small chunks and return the parent section Prepend the heading path to each chunk Parsing lost the headings, so the splitter has nothing to follow: fix parsing first Uniform prose (articles, transcripts) Fixed size, about 300 to 500 tokens, 10 to 20% overlap, at sentence ends Semantic chunking, or per-section summaries Overlap too large: near-duplicate chunks crowd the top results Mixed-topic text (long emails, meeting notes) Semantic chunking: cut where the topic changes Summarize each section and index the summaries too Ingestion gets slower; measure whether it pays Tables Whole table, or one row per chunk with the header repeated, as Markdown A table-level summary as an extra entry Very wide tables exceed the embedding model's input limit Source code Split by function and class Index docstrings and file paths as metadata Splitting by lines cuts functions in half Scanned or complex PDFs Layout-aware parsing first, then chunk the Markdown Retrieve page images directly ( Lesson 4.29 ) OCR errors in numbers go unnoticed: spot-check against the source Managed knowledge bases expose the same choices as settings (fixed, hierarchical, semantic or no chunking, and custom chunking functions); the decision logic is the same wherever you build. Check your mental model ✗ "Smaller chunks are always more precise." ✓ Too small and a chunk loses the context that makes it findable and understandable. ✗ "Chunking by fixed character count is fine." ✓ Splitting mid-sentence or mid-table hurts; split on structure where you can. ✗ "Chunks do not need metadata." ✓ Source, section and date are what make citations, filters and freshness possible. ✗ "Parent-child chunking and semantic chunking solve the same problem." ✓ Semantic chunking decides where to cut; parent-child decides what to index (small) and what to return (large). You can use both. ✗ "Proposition chunking replaces the chunks." ✓ Propositions are indexed for matching; the source chunk is still what you return and cite. Exercises Predict before you run With chunk(text, max_words=40, overlap_sentences=1) , what happens to a single sentence that is 60 words long? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Set overlap_sentences=0 and ask "Can I get a refund for a damaged item after 7 days?" Which part of the refund policy might the retrieved chunk lose? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise After switching to 400-word chunks, precise questions such as "What is the COD fee?" got worse while broad ones improved. Explain, and suggest a design that serves both. (Solution D1.) Make it your own Prepend each chunk's document title to its text before indexing, and compare retrieval on the the Retrieval (RAG) section questions with and without it. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Long sentences It becomes a chunk of its own, over the limit, because the function splits only at sentence boundaries. Real splitters fall back to smaller separators (clauses, words) or token limits for such cases. Solution B1 · Conditions split from rules The condition ("Damaged or defective items are always refundable, even after 7 days") can end up in a different chunk from the time limit ("if reported within 30 days"), so an answer quotes half a rule. Overlap and structure-aware chunking keep conditions with their rules. Solution D1 · One vector averages a whole chunk A large chunk's embedding averages several topics, so a precise question matches it less sharply. Use small chunks for matching and return the larger parent section to the model (small-to-big, Lesson 14.75 ), and keep the eval set for both kinds of question. Solution M1 · Context headers A header such as "[Refund policy]" gives every chunk the topic its sentences assume, which helps both BM25 later · 5.37 and embeddings; Lesson 14.75 measures the effect as contextual retrieval later · 14.75 . Keep the change only if the eval improves. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How do you choose a chunking strategy? Worked answer. Start from the documents' structure: split on headings and paragraphs, keep tables and code whole, add modest overlap, and store the section heading with each chunk. Choose size by the questions: precise questions want small chunks, broad ones larger. Then tune against a retrieval eval, because the right size depends on the corpus. A plausible wrong answer. "Use 512 tokens; that is standard." A default is a starting point, not a decision. Follow-ups. When does semantic chunking help? Explain the mechanism Explain parent-child (hierarchical) chunking, sentence-window retrieval and proposition chunking, and when you would pick each. Worked answer. All three separate what you match on from what you hand the model . Parent-child indexes small pieces (sentences or paragraphs), each pointing to a larger parent (section or document); you match small and return the parent, deduplicated by parent ID. Pick it for long structured documents such as manuals and policies. Sentence window indexes single sentences and returns each hit with its k neighbours; no hierarchy is needed, so it suits dense technical text without sections, and it fails when the condition sits several sentences away. Proposition chunking has a model rewrite each chunk into standalone facts, indexes the facts and returns the source chunk; it helps fact and multi-hop questions over prose at the cost of a model call per chunk and three to five times as many index rows. In every case the eval set decides: measure recall@k and answer quality before and after. A plausible wrong answer. "They are all ways of making chunks smaller." Smaller matching units, yes, but the point is returning a larger or better-contextualized unit than you matched. Follow-ups. How do you stop three sentence hits from returning the same section three times? What does parent-child cost in storage? Debug a failure Answers cite the right document but quote an incomplete rule. Why? Worked answer. The chunk boundary cut the rule from its condition or exception. Check the stored chunks for that document: if the condition is in the next chunk, add overlap, split on structure, or retrieve neighbors of the top chunk. A plausible wrong answer. "The model truncated the answer." The model quoted what it received. Follow-ups. How would you test chunk boundaries automatically? Defend a design Re-chunking means re-indexing the whole corpus. When is it worth it? Worked answer. When the eval shows chunking is the cause of failures that cheaper fixes (headers, hybrid search, reranking) do not solve. Build the new index beside the old one, compare on the same questions, and switch only if it wins. Tune chunking late because it is the most expensive knob to change. A plausible wrong answer. "Whenever a new chunking method is published." Only measured gains justify a re-index. Follow-ups. How would you migrate indexes without downtime? Check your understanding Q1 What do parent-child chunking, sentence-window retrieval and proposition chunking have in common? A They all make chunks larger B They separate what you match on from what you hand to the model C They remove the need for embeddings D They only work on tables Each one matches on a small unit and returns a larger or cleaner one. Q2 Answers cite the right document but quote an incomplete rule. What is the likely cause? A The embedding model is too small B A chunk boundary cut the rule off from its condition or exception C The temperature is too high D The document was never indexed Read the stored chunks. If the condition sits in the next chunk, add overlap, split on structure, or retrieve the neighbours of the top chunk. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in HNSW A layered graph of nearest neighbors navigated greedily Lesson 14.74 Hybrid search Running keyword search and vector search together and merging the results Lesson 5.38 Reranker A second, slower and more accurate model that reorders the top search results Lesson 5.38 pgvector The Postgres extension for vector columns and indexes Lesson 14.74 Exact search (flat index) Comparing the query with every vector; the ground truth Lesson 14.74 Inverted file index (IVF) Clustering vectors and searching only the nearest clusters Lesson 14.74 Why this came about Keyword search cannot match different words with the same meaning. From 2013, word embeddings ( word2vec , Lesson 5.33 ) showed that a neural network could place words with similar meanings close together in a space of a few hundred dimensions. In 2019, Sentence-BERT did the same for whole sentences, using a transformer trained so that sentences with the same meaning get nearby vectors. Search by meaning became practical: embed every passage once, embed each question when it arrives, and return the nearest passages. This dense retrieval became the default first step of RAG , and embedding models have improved steadily since, with larger models, many languages and longer inputs. In plain words first Coordinates for meaning An embedding model turns a piece of text into a list of numbers, which you can think of as coordinates on a map with hundreds of directions instead of two. The model has been trained so that texts with similar meanings land close together. Searching by meaning is then geometry: turn the question into coordinates, and find the stored passages nearest to it. That finds "refund" for "money back" without a single shared word. It can also blur things that must be exact, such as codes and names, and it will always return its nearest neighbours even when nothing relevant exists. Step 1 · Closeness as an angle An embedding is a vector: a list of numbers representing a text's meaning. Two texts are compared with cosine similarity , which measures the angle between their vectors: 1 means pointing the same way, 0 means unrelated, negative means opposite. A toy example with three numbers per text: Copy What you should see Copy "Refund" is close to "money back" and far from "shipping", even though the words differ. That is the whole idea behind semantic search. Embeddings put meaning on a map: texts about refunds land near each other, so a question lands near its answer. Similarity is the angle between vectors (cosine), not the words they share. Step 2 · A real embedding model Now the real thing. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is a small, widely used open embedding model: a 6-layer transformer encoder ( Lesson 7.22 ) with 22 million parameters that runs comfortably on a laptop processor. It turns any text into 384 numbers: Copy What you should see Copy Four sentences became a table of 4 rows and 384 columns. No single number means anything on its own; the meaning is in the direction of the whole vector. normalize_embeddings=True scales every vector to length 1, which makes cosine similarity the same as a plain dot product ( Lesson 1.23 ). Compare every sentence with every other: Copy What you should see Copy The two refund sentences score 0.63 with each other without sharing a meaningful word, and the two parcel sentences score 0.76. Across the groups, similarities are near zero. This is what "captures meaning" looks like in numbers. Reading this output How does a model learn to do this? An embedding model is trained on hundreds of millions of text pairs that belong together: a question and its answer, a title and its article, two phrasings of one sentence. Training pulls the vectors of each pair together and pushes them away from the other texts in the batch ( contrastive learning , Lesson 7.22 ). Nothing tells the model what "refund" means; it learns that texts about getting money back tend to be paired with each other. Lesson 3.22 fine-tunes such a model on your own data. Step 3 · Vector search over the chunks Embed every chunk once (in production this happens when documents are indexed), then for each question embed it and take the chunks with the highest dot products: Copy What you should see Copy These are the questions keyword search could not answer in Lesson 5.37 . "stop my purchase" now finds the cancellation chunk, "pay when it arrives" finds cash on delivery, and a question about the courier finds shipping. The last question works for both, because it shares the rare words "dead" and "box" with the chunk. Reading this output Brute force is fine, up to a point minilm_vecs @ q compares the question with every chunk: one matrix multiplication . For a few hundred thousand chunks that still takes milliseconds. Beyond that, systems use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes such as HNSW later · 14.74 that look at a small fraction of the vectors, and store the vectors in a vector database . Lesson 14.74 builds those. Step 4 · What vector search gets wrong Vectors measure closeness of meaning, and that causes two typical failures. Here are five error messages whose codes differ by a digit or two: Copy What you should see Copy For "E-4021 error", the right entry and a different one are tied at the top to two decimal places: to the embedding model these codes all look much alike. For "E-4210", a code that does not exist , vector search confidently returns its nearest neighbour, E-4201, with a similarity as high as many correct matches. Keyword search, with a tokeniser that keeps each code whole, gives an exact match in the first case and correctly finds nothing in the second. Two rules follow, and both will come back throughout this chapter: Vector search always returns something. There is no natural "no match". If the similarity of the best result is low for your model and data, treat it as "not found", and choose that threshold by measurement, not by guessing. Exact identifiers belong to keyword search or filters. Order numbers, SKUs, error codes, names and dates should be matched exactly. Step 5 · The model has a maximum input length An embedding model reads a limited number of tokens and silently ignores the rest: Copy What you should see Copy The text is 611 tokens long and this model reads 256. The sentence with the code is at the very end, so it was never read, and the similarity to the question is about zero. Embedded on its own, the same ending matches. This is one of the two reasons for chunking ( Lesson 14.70 ): a chunk must fit the embedding model's input, and one vector can only summarise so much. Newer embedding models accept 8,000 tokens or more, but a single vector for a long, mixed text is still a blurry summary. Step 6 · The lab's stand-in embedder The rest of this chapter's lab must run in seconds, offline, and give identical numbers on every machine. So from here on it uses a tiny stand-in instead of a neural model: LSA (latent semantic analysis), which compresses TF-IDF vectors ( Lesson 5.32 ) with a matrix factorisation. It captures which words tend to occur together in this corpus , and nothing more. Copy How much weaker is it than the real model? Copy What you should see Copy The stand-in gets the easy case and misses the two paraphrases, because it has only ever seen these nine chunks and has no idea that "purchase" relates to "order". The real model learned that from a billion sentence pairs. Keep this in mind when later lessons report numbers: the methods ( hybrid search later · 5.38 , reranking later · 5.38 , evaluation) are what transfer, and a real embedding model makes each of them work better. The box below shows the swap. Tip Swapping in a real embedding model To use the real model in the lab, define search_dense = search_minilm . To use a hosted model, replace the embedding call; the rest of the pipeline stays the same. For example with OpenAI (not run here, needs a key): Copy On AWS use a Bedrock embedding model (Amazon Titan or Cohere Embed) through bedrock-runtime ; on Google, the Gemini embedding model through google-genai ; on Azure, an embedding deployment in Foundry Models. Open models such as BGE-M3, Qwen3-Embedding and nomic-embed run locally with sentence-transformers , exactly as MiniLM did above. Choosing and using an embedding model Question What to know Which model? Shortlist by your languages, domain and budget, using a public benchmark such as MTEB only as a filter. Then decide on your own questions ( Lesson 14.72 ) How many dimensions? 384 to 1,024 is typical; up to 3,072 exists. More dimensions cost more storage and search time for a small gain. Models trained with Matryoshka learning let you keep only the first 256 or 512 numbers with little loss ( Lesson 14.74 ) How long can the input be? From 256 tokens to 8,000 and more. Know the limit and chunk below it Query and document prefixes? Many models (E5, BGE, nomic, Qwen) expect a short instruction such as query: or passage: in front of the text, and score noticeably worse without it. Read the model card Which similarity? Cosine, or dot product on normalised vectors, for almost every text model. Use the one the model was trained with Hosted or local? A hosted API is simplest; a local model keeps data in-house and has no per-call price. Either way, embedding is far cheaper than generation Can I change model later? Only by re-embedding every document. Vectors from different models, or different versions of one model, cannot be compared Check your mental model ✗ "Similar vectors mean a correct answer." ✓ They mean similar wording or topic; the passage may still not answer the question. ✗ "If nothing relevant exists, vector search returns nothing." ✓ It always returns its nearest neighbours. You must decide what counts as too far. ✗ "Any embedding model works with any stored vectors." ✓ Query and documents must be embedded with the same model and version. ✗ "Embeddings replace keyword search." ✓ They complement it; hybrid search usually beats either alone. The model families you will meet Model family Open? Notes OpenAI text-embedding-3 (small, large) Closed Matryoshka (dimensions can be shortened) Google Gemini embedding Closed Multilingual, Matryoshka; on Vertex AI or the Gemini API Cohere Embed v4 Closed Long context, multimodal, available on Bedrock and Azure Voyage AI Closed Strong general and domain models (law, finance, code) Amazon Titan / Nova embeddings Closed Native on Bedrock BGE-M3 (BAAI) Open (MIT) Dense, sparse and multi-vector in one model; 100+ languages Qwen3-Embedding Open (Apache 2.0) Strong multilingual and code retrieval; several sizes nomic-embed Open Small, runs on CPU Choose on your own retrieval eval. The public MTEB leaderboard is a shortlist: its averages mix many tasks, and your domain and languages matter more. For Indian deployments, test Hindi, Hinglish and regional-language queries explicitly. Matryoshka embeddings let you store shorter vectors (say 256 instead of 3,072 numbers) at a small quality cost, cutting storage and search cost. In production Embedding model mistakes seen in production Different models for documents and queries , or a model upgrade on one side only: similarity scores become meaningless. Version the embedding model with the index and change both together. Changing models in place : re-embedding a large corpus takes hours to days. Build a new index beside the old one, evaluate, then switch an alias. Choosing from the leaderboard alone : an English-heavy model can look strong on MTEB and fail on Hindi or domain jargon. Test on 50 real questions per language before deciding. Ignoring input limits : chunks longer than the model's maximum input are silently truncated, so the end of the chunk is never searchable. Where the vectors are stored In this lesson the vectors sit in a NumPy array. A real system keeps them in a vector store : a database, or a feature of one, that saves each vector with its text and metadata and can find the nearest ones quickly. Store Choose it when pgvector later · 14.74 (Postgres) You already run Postgres and have up to tens of millions of vectors. SQL joins and filters for free. The most common sensible default. Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus You need rich filtering, built-in hybrid search or very large scale, and can run another service Pinecone You want fully managed, zero operations OpenSearch, Elasticsearch You already run them for search; strong BM25 plus vectors in one engine LanceDB, Chroma Local, embedded or prototype use Turbopuffer, S3 Vectors Very large, cost-sensitive collections on object storage, accepting slower cold queries Cloud-native (below) You want retrieval managed inside your cloud's security boundary Under the hood most use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes, usually HNSW (a navigable graph), trading a little recall for large speedups. Tune them, and always measure recall against exact search later · 14.74 on a sample. Lesson 14.74 opens these indexes up: IVF later · 14.74 , HNSW, quantization , filtering and sizing, with code. In production Vector store choices that hurt later The vector store rarely decides answer quality; operations decide whether you regret it. The usual regrets: no hybrid or keyword support, so it has to be bolted on; weak filtering, so permission and tenant filters become slow post-filters; no way to build a new index beside the old one, so every re-embedding is a risky in-place migration; and a separate system the data team cannot govern. Choose the store that already sits next to your data and permissions unless measurements say otherwise. Exercises Predict before you run Two sentences, "Refunds reach UPI in 2 days" and "UPI refunds take two days", are embedded with MiniLM. Will their cosine similarity be close to 1, close to 0, or negative, and how would BM25 score one against the other? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Embed the chunks with MiniLM and the queries with the LSA stand-in (pad or cut the vectors so the sizes match). What happens to search? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise After normalizing chunk vectors but not query vectors, the scores changed but the ranking did not. Using the definition of cosine similarity, explain why, and say when forgetting to normalise does change the ranking. (Solution D1.) Make it your own Set search_dense = search_minilm and write five questions of your own about the ShopKart help pages, each phrased without the words the pages use. How many does vector search answer in its top result, and how many does search_bm25 ? (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Same meaning, different words High, close to 1, because they mean the same thing. BM25 gives partial credit only for the shared words ("UPI", and "refunds" in both; "2" does not match "two", and "reach" does not match "take"). That difference is why vectors find paraphrases. Solution B1 · Vectors from different models are incomparable Results become close to random. Each model has its own space: direction 17 in one has nothing to do with direction 17 in the other, even when the sizes match. Always embed queries and documents with the same model and version, store the model name with the index, and re-embed everything when you change it. Solution D1 · Normalization and dot products With every chunk vector at length 1, the dot product with an unnormalised query equals the cosine multiplied by the query's length, which is the same for every chunk, so the order is unchanged. If the chunk vectors are not normalised, longer vectors get higher dot products regardless of direction, and the ranking changes. Normalise consistently, and use the metric the index expects. Solution M1 · Paraphrase questions Expect vector search to answer most of them and keyword search few, because you removed the shared words on purpose. Now write five questions that quote exact figures or terms from the pages ("INR 499", "OTP") and compare again: keyword search recovers. Real question sets contain both kinds, which is the argument for Lesson 5.38 . Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What is an embedding, and how does vector search find relevant passages? Worked answer. An embedding model maps text to a vector so that texts with similar meaning are close, usually by cosine similarity. Documents are embedded once and stored; a query is embedded at search time, and the nearest vectors are returned, exactly or with an approximate index ( Lesson 14.74 ). It finds paraphrases that keyword search misses, and blurs exact tokens such as IDs. A plausible wrong answer. "Embeddings understand the text." They encode similarity learned in training, which can miss domain terms and negation. Follow-ups. How are embedding models trained ( Lesson 3.22 )? Debug a failure Vector search returns passages about the right topic but the wrong product. What do you try? Worked answer. Embeddings capture topic more than exact identity, so add keyword search for names and IDs (hybrid, Lesson 5.38 ), add metadata filters by product, and rerank the candidates. Check whether chunks carry the product name at all. A plausible wrong answer. "Use a bigger embedding model." It may help a little; identity matching is a keyword and metadata problem. Follow-ups. How would you add product filters from the question? Defend a design Which embedding model would you choose for ShopKart? Worked answer. Shortlist by language coverage (English, Hindi, Hinglish), domain, dimension and cost, hosting needs (API or self-hosted for data residency), and benchmark scores as a filter only. Then decide on ShopKart's own eval set , because public leaderboards rarely match a specific corpus. A plausible wrong answer. "The top of the leaderboard." Leaderboards measure other data. Follow-ups. When would you fine-tune an embedding model? Recap An embedding model turns text into a vector; texts with similar meaning get vectors pointing in similar directions, measured by cosine similarity. Vector search embeds chunks once and each question on arrival, and returns the nearest chunks. It bridges different words with the same meaning. It blurs exact identifiers, always returns something, and ignores text beyond the model's input limit. Queries and documents must use the same model; changing the model means re-embedding everything. The lab continues with a small offline stand-in; a real model makes every later method work better. Check your understanding Q1 Why can vector search match "stop my purchase" to a chunk about cancelling an order? A It expands the query with a synonym dictionary B The embedding model places texts with similar meaning close together, whatever the words C It ignores the words and matches the length D It asks a language model to rewrite the question Closeness in the embedding space reflects meaning learned from many paired texts. Q2 A user searches for an error code that does not exist. What does plain vector search return? A Nothing B An error C The nearest entries anyway, with similarity scores that may look reasonable D A keyword search fallback Nearest-neighbour search has no built-in notion of "no match"; you must set a threshold or use exact matching. Q3 You upgrade to a newer embedding model. What must you do with the stored document vectors? A Nothing; vectors are interchangeable B Multiply them by a correction factor C Re-embed every document with the new model D Normalise them again Each model defines its own vector space; old and new vectors cannot be compared. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in GraphRAG Retrieval that uses a knowledge graph built from the documents, to answer questions that span many of them Lesson 14.88 Semantic ranker Azure AI Search's cross-encoder reranker Lesson 14.155 Agent Search Google's managed enterprise search (formerly Vertex AI Search) Lesson 14.157 Query engine A retriever plus the model call that answers from what was retrieved Lesson 14.124 Why this came about Early RAG systems were judged by reading answers, which hid whether failures came from search or from the model. Measuring retrieval with labeled questions (recall, ranks) and requiring citations in answers separated the two problems and made improvement systematic. In plain words first Check the search before blaming the answer A RAG system has two halves that fail differently: retrieval (did we find the right passages?) and generation (did the model use them faithfully?). Measure them separately. For retrieval, label which passages answer each test question and compute recall at k (did a right one appear in the top k?) and ranks. For generation, require citations so every claim points to a passage you can check. Evaluate the two halves separately A wrong RAG answer has one of two causes, and the fix differs completely: What to measure in a RAG system, and where: retrieval metrics check the evidence, generation metrics check the answer against that evidence and the question, and the whole is judged against a reference. Retrieval failed : the right passage was not in the context. Fix chunking , search, rewriting or the content itself. Generation failed : the passage was there, but the model ignored it, misread it or added things. Fix the prompt, the model or the context order. So measure both, per question. Step 1 · Measure before you tune You now have three searches: keyword ( Lesson 5.37 ), vector ( Lesson 14.71 ) and hybrid ( Lesson 5.38 ). Which is best on these documents? Reading a few results and forming an impression is how teams fool themselves. The reliable way takes ten minutes: Write down some questions in the words a real customer would use. Next to each, write the ID of the chunk that answers it. This pair list is a labelled question set . You will also hear it called a gold set or ground truth. Run every question through each search and count how often the right chunk comes back. Two numbers summarise the result: Recall@k is the share of questions whose right chunk appears in the top k results. Recall@3 = 0.88 means that for 88% of the questions, the right chunk was among the first three. Reciprocal rank scores one question by where the right chunk landed: 1 if it was first, 1/2 if second, 1/3 if third, 0 if it was not found. The mean over all questions is the mean reciprocal rank ( MRR ) . It rewards putting the right chunk near the top, not just somewhere in the list. Copy What you should see Copy On this tiny set, hybrid beats both. Eight questions prove nothing statistically; the habit of measuring is the point. Lesson 14.77 builds a proper evaluation set . For RAG, watch recall first: the model cannot use or cite a passage that was never retrieved. MRR matters next, because the passages at the top of the prompt get the most attention and because a better ranking lets you send fewer passages. Step 2 · Four retrieval metrics, for questions with more than one right chunk Step 1 assumed one right chunk per question. Real questions often have several: "what does delivery cost?" is answered by the standard-shipping chunk and the express-delivery chunk together. With a set of relevant chunks, four metrics are in common use, and you will see all four in papers, tools and vendor dashboards: Metric The question it answers Read it as Precision@k Of the top k results, what share is relevant? How much of what the model reads is useful Recall@k Of all the relevant chunks, what share is in the top k? How much of what the model needs is there MRR How high is the first relevant result? 1 for rank 1, 1/2 for rank 2, and so on nDCG @k Are the relevant results near the top, all of them? 1.0 for the ideal order, lower as relevant results sink nDCG (normalised discounted cumulative gain) is the only one that needs arithmetic to understand. Each relevant result earns a gain that shrinks with its rank: 1 / log2(rank + 1) , which is 1.0 at rank 1, 0.63 at rank 2 and 0.5 at rank 3. Add the gains (that is the DCG), then divide by the best total any ordering could have earned, so the result lies between 0 and 1. The functions below have their own names so that they do not replace Step 1's one-answer versions, which later lessons keep using. Copy What you should see Copy Check each number against the list. The top three results hold two relevant chunks, so precision@3 is 2/3. Both relevant chunks are in the top three, so recall@3 is 1.0. The first relevant chunk is at rank 1, so MRR is 1.0. For nDCG, the relevant chunks sit at ranks 1 and 3 and earn 1.0 + 0.5 = 1.5; the ideal order would put them at ranks 1 and 2 and earn 1.0 + 0.63 = 1.63; 1.5 / 1.63 = 0.92. Which to watch? For RAG, recall@k first, for the reason in Step 1. Use precision when prompts are getting long and you want to send fewer passages, and nDCG when you are comparing rerankers , because it is the one that notices every change in order. Step 3 · Generate with citations, then check them Retrieval has found the passages. Now the model writes the answer from them. Two rules make that answer checkable: The prompt contains only the retrieved passages , each wrapped in a tag that carries its ID, and it tells the model to answer from those passages alone and to say it does not know when they do not contain the answer. Every claim cites a passage ID in square brackets, such as [refund-policy#1] . With those two rules, ordinary code can check an answer: every cited ID must be one of the passages that was actually sent, and an answer with no citation at all is suspect. So that this step runs without an API key , the model's reply is written in by hand below; to use a real model, send prompt with the client from Lesson 11.20 . Copy What you should see Copy The reply cited one passage twice, that passage was among the three retrieved, and nothing was left uncited. Be clear about what this check proves. It catches two failures cheaply: an answer that cites a source that was never retrieved (an invented reference), and an answer with no citation. It does not prove that the cited passage really supports the sentence next to it. Checking that needs a reader, human or model, and is the faithfulness metric of Lesson 14.77 . From this pipeline to a production system You now have every part of a working RAG pipeline: parsing ( Lesson 4.29 ), chunking (4.3), keyword and vector search (4.4, 4.5), fusion and reranking (4.6), and in this lesson measurement and cited answers. The boxes below collect what changes when the same pipeline runs for real users. On the platforms RAG on the platforms AWS : Bedrock Knowledge Bases manages ingestion, chunking (fixed, hierarchical, semantic or custom via Lambda), embeddings and retrieval over vector stores including S3 Vectors (generally available since December 2025, up to two billion vectors per index), OpenSearch Serverless, Aurora PostgreSQL and Neptune Analytics (for GraphRAG later · 14.88 ). It offers reranking models and RetrieveAndGenerate . Amazon Kendra closed to new customers in July 2026; new enterprise-search work goes to Knowledge Bases or Amazon Quick ( Lesson 14.153 ). Azure : Azure AI Search provides hybrid search , the semantic ranker later · 14.155 and integrated vectorization. Its agentic retrieval (knowledge bases over knowledge sources, with LLM query planning) is generally available in a minimal form (API version 2026-04-01), with planning and answer synthesis in preview. Google Cloud : Agent Search later · 14.157 (formerly Vertex AI Search) for out-of-the-box search, RAG Engine for a managed pipeline, Vector Search and Agent Retrieval for your own index, plus the Ranking API, Check Grounding API and Document AI Layout Parser . Databricks : AI Search (called Vector Search until June 2026) syncs indexes from Delta tables, supports hybrid and full-text search with an optional reranker, and respects Unity Catalog permissions. In production Design a RAG system right from day one Most RAG systems that struggle in production were missing one of these from the start, and each is far cheaper to build in than to retrofit: 1. A labeled question set before any tuning : 30 to 100 real questions with the chunks that answer them, split by question type. Without it, every later change is a guess. 2. Parsing you have looked at : open twenty parsed documents and read them. Most quality problems start here. 3. Chunks with context : every chunk carries its document title, section path, date and source URL, both as metadata and in the indexed text. 4. Hybrid search from the start : keyword plus vectors. Codes, names and exact terms are a large share of real questions. 5. Filters for permissions and tenants inside the search , never after it ( Lesson 14.73 ). 6. Versioned indexes behind an alias , so re-chunking or a new embedding model is a side-by-side switch, not a migration. 7. Citations in every answer and a refusal path ("I couldn't find that in our policies"), so wrong answers are visible and missing content becomes a ticket, not a hallucination . 8. Incremental ingestion with deletions , so stale and removed documents leave the index ( Lesson 14.73 ). 9. Traces of query, retrieved chunks and answer , so every complaint leads to one inspectable run ( Lesson 14.145 ). From the field Uber: fix the documents before tuning the retriever Uber's internal on-call copilot, Genie, answered security and privacy questions from policy documents. Their write-up on the improved version (May 2025) starts with ingestion, not models: they moved source documents from PDFs to Google Docs because the structure survived extraction, had an LLM convert tables into Markdown, kept table chunks intact through chunking, and attached a summary, keywords and generated FAQs to every chunk as metadata for keyword search. Together with the agentic retrieval steps described in Lesson 14.76 , the redesign raised acceptable answers by a relative 27% and cut incorrect advice by a relative 60% on a golden set of more than 100 questions over 40-plus policy documents. Solutions Solution P1 · Read the metrics recall@1 = 0, recall@3 = 1, reciprocal rank = 1/3. Recall@k asks whether the answer is anywhere in the top k; MRR rewards putting it first. Solution D1 · Generation, not retrieval Retrieval mostly finds the answer, so the loss is in generation: the model ignores, misreads or overrides the context. Solution M1 · Measure abstention Gold entries with no chunk need an abstention metric: the share of such questions where the answer says it cannot find the information, rather than inventing one. Without them, an eval rewards confident guessing. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How do you evaluate a RAG system? Worked answer. In two halves. Retrieval: recall@k, MRR and nDCG against labeled relevant chunks. Generation: faithfulness to the retrieved context, answer correctness, citation validity, and abstention on unanswerable questions. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Eval case One test question with a written rule for what a correct answer must and must not contain Lesson 14.131 Foundry IQ Knowledge bases with agentic retrieval, built on Azure AI Search Lesson 14.155 Agent Search Google's managed enterprise search (formerly Vertex AI Search) Lesson 14.157 Post-filtering Filtering results after an approximate search, which can drop everything Lesson 14.74 Filtered search Applying the filter during the index search Lesson 14.74 Why this came about Company assistants quickly ran into access control: a search index built from everyone's documents could show a user something they were not allowed to see, and outdated policies kept being quoted. Permission filters inside the search and freshness tracking became requirements for enterprise RAG . In plain words first Only the documents you are allowed to see, and only current ones A RAG system must never show a user a passage they are not allowed to read, and should not answer from an outdated policy. So permissions and freshness are filters inside the search, not afterthoughts: each chunk carries who may see it and when it is valid, and the search only considers chunks the current user may see and that are current. Filtering after retrieval can leave too few results, or leak information. Permission-aware and multi-tenant retrieval The enterprise requirement most demos skip: a user must never receive a passage they are not allowed to read, because once it is in the prompt, the model can repeat it. Two words first. An access control list (ACL) is the list of who may read a document: particular people, or more often groups such as "support" or "finance". A tenant is one customer of a system that serves many: if ShopKart and MegaMart both use the same assistant product, each is a tenant, and one tenant's documents must never appear in another's answers. Capture access control lists (ACLs) at ingestion : store allowed users, groups or roles as metadata on every chunk. Filter at query time, inside the search engine : pass the caller's groups as a mandatory filter. Never retrieve everything and filter afterwards in application code, which is slow and easy to get wrong. Partition by tenant : a separate index or namespace per customer for strong isolation, or a mandatory tenant_id filter for many small tenants. Keep ACLs fresh : permissions change more often than documents; sync them on their own schedule. Test it : an eval case later · 14.131 where a user without access asks about a restricted document, expecting "I don't know". In production Permission bugs seen in production The leaks that actually happen: a cache or semantic cache keyed only on the question, so one user's answer is served to another; summaries or generated FAQs created from restricted documents and stored without the source's ACL; a "search all" admin tool reachable by the agent; and permissions copied once at ingestion and never resynced after someone changes teams. Put tenant and group IDs into every cache key, inherit ACLs onto every derived artifact, and make the permission test above part of CI. On the platforms Built-in permission trimming Most enterprise retrieval services can trim results by the caller's identity: Azure AI Search and Foundry IQ later · 14.155 with document-level access control, Bedrock Knowledge Bases with metadata filters and Amazon Quick with ACL-aware connectors, Agent Search later · 14.157 (formerly Vertex AI Search) with data-source access control, and Databricks AI Search through Unity Catalog. Check each connector, since support varies by source. See the leak, and the fix, in code The rules above are easy to agree with and easy to get wrong. This small example makes the difference concrete. Five chunks about refunds carry two labels each, written when the documents were ingested: the tenant (which company the chunk belongs to) and the groups allowed to read it. The same question is then asked by two people, through three versions of the search function. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output search_unfiltered leaks. A customer asking about fraud cases is shown the finance team's exceptions document and the agents' approval limits. Once those passages are in the prompt, the model will happily summarise them. search_post_filter does not leak, but it starves. It searches everything, keeps the top 2, and then throws away what the user may not see. For the customer, both top results were restricted, so nothing is left, even though a public refund page exists that would have answered the question. With real data this shows up as "the bot says it does not know" for exactly the users with the fewest permissions. Asking for more results before filtering helps a little and never fully fixes it. search_pre_filter is the correct shape. It removes what the user may not read first, and ranks what remains. The customer gets the public page; the agent gets the agents' page and the public page. Neither sees the finance documents. In a real system "remove first" does not mean a Python list comprehension. It means passing the tenant and the groups as a filter inside the search engine's query , so the engine only ever scores permitted chunks. Every production search engine and vector database supports this; Lesson 14.74 shows what it costs and how indexes handle it. Two places to apply a permission filter. Filtering after the search can leave nothing, even though an allowed passage exists. Filtering before the search ranks only what this user may read. A permission rule is only real if a test fails when someone breaks it. This is the test: Copy What you should see Copy The unfiltered search returned a forbidden passage 44 times across three users and four questions, including another company's refund policy to ShopKart users. The pre-filtered search: zero. Keep a test like this in the build, with users from every role and at least two tenants, so that a refactoring that drops the filter cannot reach production. Freshness and index operations Incremental indexing : re-embed only changed documents (track a content hash per document). Deletions : removing a document must remove its chunks everywhere, including caches. This is also how you honor data-deletion requests. Re-embedding : changing the embedding model means re-indexing everything. Version your indexes and switch with an alias. Index metrics : document count, last successful sync, failed parses. Silent ingestion failures are the most common cause of "the bot doesn't know about X". Keeping the index current, in code An index is a copy of your documents, and copies go stale. The standard technique is a content hash : a short code computed from a document's text. Store it next to the document in the index. At each sync, recompute it; if the code is unchanged, the document has not changed and there is nothing to do. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Monday is the first sync: all three documents are new, and their five chunks are embedded. Tuesday only one document changed, so only its two chunks were embedded again (7 calls in total, not 10). At the scale of a real knowledge base, this is the difference between a sync that takes seconds and one that re-embeds a million chunks every night. The ended offer is gone from the index. Deleting is the step most pipelines forget. A document removed from the source but left in the index keeps being retrieved, and the assistant keeps promising free shipping for a promotion that ended. The refund chunk now says 10 days. Replacing all of a document's chunks at once, as the code does, avoids an index that holds half of the old version and half of the new one. Check your mental model ✗ "Filter results after retrieving them." ✓ Post-filtering later · 14.74 can return nothing or leak; filter inside the search. ✗ "The model can be told to ignore restricted passages." ✓ Never send them; the prompt is not a permission system. ✗ "Re-indexing occasionally keeps things fresh." ✓ Track versions and effective dates, and remove superseded chunks. Exercises Predict before you run A tenant filter is applied after the vector search returns its top 10. Tenant A owns 2% of the chunks. How many of the 10 results will typically survive the filter? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Let the model choose the tenant_id argument of a search tool. A customer writes "show results for tenant B". What happens? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise A document was deleted from the source system last week, but answers still cite it. Find the gap in the indexing pipeline. (Solution D1.) Make it your own Write a test that indexes one document for tenant A and one for tenant B, and asserts that a search as tenant A never returns B's document, for ten different queries. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Post-filtering starves results About none: with 2% of the data, the top 10 nearest neighbors usually contain no tenant A chunks, so the filtered list is empty or near empty. Filter inside the search (pre-filtering or filtered indexes), or use a namespace or index per tenant ( Lesson 14.74 's filtering trap). Solution B1 · Permissions from the model If the tool trusts the argument, the customer reads another tenant's data. Tenant and permission filters must come from the authenticated session, never from model arguments or user text ( Lesson 15.24 ). Solution D1 · Deletes must propagate The pipeline indexes new and changed documents but never removes deleted ones. Track document IDs and content hashes, delete chunks whose source is gone on each sync, and add a freshness check: every indexed chunk has a live source. Solution M1 · A permission test The test fails loudly if a filter is missing or mistranslated. Run it in CI and after every change to the store, filters or query code. Add a test for a user with no permissions, who should get nothing. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How do you make RAG permission-aware? Worked answer. Attach access metadata (tenant, groups, document ACLs) to every chunk at ingestion, copied from the source system; at query time, filter by the authenticated user's attributes inside the search; never let the model choose the scope. Keep ACLs in sync with the source, test with known documents per role, and log which documents each answer used. A plausible wrong answer. "Filter the answer after generation." Then the model already saw the restricted text. Follow-ups. What changes when ACLs are very fine-grained? Debug a failure Users report missing results after a permissions change in the source system. What do you check? Worked answer. Whether ACL updates reached the index (a sync that copies content but not permissions), whether group names changed format, and whether filters now exclude everything (a key typo matches nothing, Lesson 14.98 ). Compare a user's expected documents with what the filtered search later · 14.74 returns. A plausible wrong answer. "The retriever is broken." It is probably filtering correctly on stale or wrong ACLs. Follow-ups. How would you monitor ACL drift? Defend a design One shared index with tenant filters, or one index per tenant? Worked answer. Shared with filters when tenants are many and small, and the store supports efficient filtered search; per-tenant indexes or namespaces when tenants are large, have different data residency, or need hard isolation and easy deletion. Many systems mix: namespaces for large customers, shared for the long tail. A plausible wrong answer. "Always per tenant, it is safer." It can become thousands of small indexes that are expensive to run. Follow-ups. How do you delete all of one tenant's data quickly? The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Amazon S3 Vectors Vector storage and query built into S3, at low cost Lesson 14.153 Lesson 14.71 used vector search as a black box with nine chunks. At nine chunks, comparing the query with every vector is instant. At nine hundred million, it is the most expensive part of your system, and the index settings decide both your bill and your recall. This lesson opens the box with FAISS , the open-source library from Meta that many vector databases build on, so you can see exactly what the settings in pgvector , OpenSearch, Qdrant, Milvus, S3 Vectors or Azure AI Search are doing. Copy Why this came about Comparing a query with every stored vector is too slow for millions of documents. Approximate nearest-neighbor indexes ( HNSW , IVF , quantization ), developed for image and recommendation search, were adopted by vector databases, which boomed with RAG in 2023. In plain words first How to find the nearest neighbors fast Comparing a query with every stored vector is exact but slow at millions of vectors. Vector indexes trade a little accuracy for a lot of speed: graph-based indexes (HNSW) hop between nearby points, cluster-based ones (IVF) search only the closest clusters, and quantization shrinks vectors to save memory. Each has settings that move the balance between speed, memory and recall. Step 1 · Exact search, and the ground truth for everything else Exact (brute-force, "flat") search compares the query with every vector. It is the reference that every faster index is measured against. With normalized vectors, the inner product equals cosine similarity . Copy What you should see Copy Distance Formula idea Use when Cosine Angle between vectors Text embeddings (the default); equals inner product after normalization Inner product (dot) Sum of products Normalized vectors, or models trained for dot product Euclidean (L2) Straight-line distance Some image and older models; check the model card Use the metric the embedding model was trained with. Mixing them (L2 on vectors meant for cosine, unnormalized) quietly lowers recall. Step 2 · IVF: search only the nearest clusters An inverted file index (IVF) clusters the vectors with k-means into nlist lists. A query is compared with the cluster centres, then only with the vectors in the nprobe closest clusters. More probes, more recall, more work. Copy What you should see Copy With one probe the index compares about 1% of the vectors and misses a third of the true neighbors; eight probes get essentially everything at 7% of the work. A common starting point is nlist near the square root of the number of vectors and nprobe tuned for the recall you need. IVF needs training data that looks like the data you will add, and re-training when the distribution drifts. Step 3 · HNSW: navigate a graph HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world) links each vector to its nearest neighbors in a layered graph. A search enters at the top layer and greedily walks toward the query, layer by layer. It is the default index in pgvector, OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and most managed services, because it gives high recall at low latency without training. How a vector index finds neighbors fast (HNSW): a few long-range links on the top layer get close quickly, and denser lower layers refine the search, so a query visits a tiny share of the vectors. Setting Meaning Effect M Links per node Higher: better recall, more memory efConstruction Candidates considered while building Higher: better graph, slower build efSearch ( ef_search ) Candidates considered per query The main runtime knob: recall versus latency Copy What you should see Copy HNSW reaches near-perfect recall while touching about 2% of the collection, and the work grows slowly with efSearch . Its costs are memory (the graph links add to every vector) and slow, memory-hungry builds and deletes on very large collections, which is why IVF and disk-based indexes (DiskANN, used in Azure Cosmos DB and others) remain common at billion scale. Step 4 · Quantization: smaller vectors, then rescore Vectors are usually stored as 32-bit floats: a 1,536-dimension embedding is 6 KB, and a hundred million of them is 600 GB before any index. Quantization compresses them: Method Size per value How Typical recall impact float32 4 bytes None Reference float16 / bfloat16 2 bytes Lower precision Negligible Scalar quantization (int8) 1 byte Map each dimension's range to 256 levels Small Product quantization (PQ) Fractions of a byte Split the vector into sub-vectors, store the nearest of 256 learned centroids for each Large without rescoring Binary 1 bit Keep only the sign of each dimension Large without rescoring The standard pattern is compress for the first pass, rescore with full vectors : search a compressed index for many candidates, then re-rank the shortlist with exact distances (FAISS calls it refinement; OpenSearch, Qdrant and Elasticsearch call it rescoring or oversampling). Copy What you should see Copy int8 cuts memory by 4x for a small recall loss. PQ cuts it by 10x but, alone, finds less than half the true neighbors; rescoring a 10x shortlist with full vectors brings recall back to almost perfect. The rescoring copy can live on cheaper storage (SSD or object storage) while the compressed index stays in memory, which is how large managed services keep costs down. Step 5 · The filtering trap Real queries filter: this tenant's documents, this language, documents the user may read ( Lesson 14.73 ). There are two ways to combine a filter with approximate search, and one of them silently loses results: Post-filtering : find the top k, then drop those that fail the filter. If the filter is selective, few or none survive. Filtered search : apply the filter during the index walk, so only matching vectors are returned. Engines support it (pgvector iterative scans, Qdrant payload indexes, OpenSearch efficient filtering, Pinecone metadata filters, FAISS ID selectors), but a graph index still struggles when very few nodes match. Exact scan of the matching subset : when the filter leaves few vectors, skip the index and compare against all of them. Good engines switch to this automatically below a selectivity threshold. Copy What you should see Copy With a filter that keeps 1% of the data, post-filtering returned almost nothing: a tenant would see "no results" for questions their own documents answer, the most common production vector-search bug. Filtered HNSW does better but needs a much larger efSearch , because the graph walk passes through many non-matching nodes. For a small matching set, an exact scan of those 203 vectors is both perfect and cheap. Test your store with your most selective real filters, check how it plans filtered queries, and for large tenants use separate indexes or namespaces so the problem never arises.
