It decides whether the index fits in memory, which instance class you need, and whether object-storage-based stores (S3 Vectors, Turbopuffer, LanceDB on object storage) are worth their slower cold queries. Copy What you should see Copy Two levers dominate: fewer dimensions (Matryoshka embeddings, Lesson 14.71 , let you shorten vectors) and fewer bytes per dimension (quantization). Ten million documents fit comfortably on one large Postgres or OpenSearch node with either lever; half a billion needs quantization plus a distributed or disk-based store. pgvector in production Most teams' first production vector store is Postgres with pgvector , because it adds vectors to a database they already run, with SQL filters, joins, transactions and backups. Copy Hybrid search in Postgres pairs this with full-text search ( tsvector with a GIN index, or the BM25 extensions such as ParadeDB's pg_search ) and fuses the two lists with RRF in SQL or application code. Choosing a vector store Workload Good fits Why Up to tens of millions of vectors, existing Postgres pgvector (RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Neon, Supabase, Databricks Lakebase) One database, SQL filters and joins, transactions Search-heavy apps with keyword, facets and vectors OpenSearch , Elasticsearch , Azure AI Search , Vespa Mature BM25, hybrid, filtering and relevance tuning Dedicated, filter-heavy vector workloads Qdrant , Weaviate , Milvus / Zilliz Rich payload filters, quantization, multi-tenancy features Fully managed, minimal operations Pinecone , Turbopuffer , cloud-native services Serverless scaling and pricing Huge, rarely queried collections at low cost Amazon S3 Vectors later · 14.153 , Turbopuffer, LanceDB on object storage Storage priced like object storage; slower cold queries Inside a data platform Databricks AI Search (formerly Vector Search), BigQuery vector search , AlloyDB AI No data movement; governance from the platform Local, embedded, prototypes Chroma , LanceDB , FAISS , sqlite-vec Zero infrastructure Operating a vector index Version indexes and switch with an alias. Changing the embedding model, dimensions or chunking means a full re-index; build the new index beside the old one, evaluate it, then move the alias. Measure recall continuously. Sample a few hundred real queries, compute the exact top-k offline, and track the index's recall against it after every parameter change or growth milestone. Plan for deletes. HNSW deletions leave tombstones that degrade the graph; schedule compaction or rebuilds, and verify that deleted documents really disappear ( Lesson 14.73 ). Back up the source, not just the index. Keep chunks and embeddings in durable storage (a table or object store), so an index can always be rebuilt. Watch the usual database metrics : memory headroom, p95 latency per filter type, ingestion lag, and the "no results" rate per tenant. Industry practice What experienced teams say about vector databases The consistent advice from practitioners is that the choice of vector database matters less than chunking, hybrid search, filtering and evaluation. Start with the store you already operate (very often Postgres or OpenSearch, or your data platform's native search), measure recall and latency on your own data, and move to a dedicated engine only when a measured limit forces it: scale, filtering performance or cost. In production Design a vector index right from day one Store chunks, metadata and embeddings in durable storage you control (a table or object store), so any index can be rebuilt. Record the embedding model and version with every vector. Put tenant and permission fields on every record and test the most selective filter you will run. Build new indexes beside old ones and switch with an alias. Track recall against exact search on a few hundred real queries, and re-check it at every growth milestone. Exercises Predict before you run HNSW's ef_search is raised from 16 to 128. What happens to recall and to latency? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Quantize vectors to 8 bits and skip the rescoring step. What happens to recall, and what does rescoring with full-precision vectors fix? (Solution B1.) Solutions Solution P1 · The recall-latency dial Recall rises toward exact search and latency rises, because the search explores more of the graph. The right value is the smallest that meets your recall target at your latency budget, measured against exact search as ground truth. Solution B1 · Quantization needs rescoring Recall drops, because compressed distances misorder close candidates. Rescoring the top candidates with the original vectors restores most of it at a small cost, which is why production systems keep full vectors for rescoring. Solution D1 · The filtering trap Filtering after the graph search discards most candidates, and the graph walk may not reach enough matching vectors. Fixes: filter during traversal (filtered HNSW), raise ef_search for filtered queries, or keep a separate index or partition for the rare category. Solution M1 · Size before you buy Float32: 50M × 1,024 × 4 bytes ≈ 205 GB, plus graph overhead. 8-bit in memory: about 51 GB plus the graph, with full vectors on disk for rescoring. The difference decides between one large machine and a cluster. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How do IVF and HNSW indexes work, and what are their trade-offs? Worked answer. IVF clusters vectors and searches only the nearest clusters ( nprobe controls how many), which is memory-efficient and fast to build. HNSW builds a layered proximity graph and walks it ( ef_search controls breadth), giving high recall at low latency with more memory and slower builds. Both trade recall for speed, and both are tuned against exact search. A plausible wrong answer. "HNSW is always better." It uses more memory and handles deletes and filters less gracefully. Follow-ups. When is exact search good enough? Debug a failure Recall dropped after the index was rebuilt with the same data. What do you check? Worked answer. The build and search parameters ( M , ef_construction , ef_search , nlist , nprobe ), the distance metric, whether vectors were normalized the same way, and whether the embedding model version changed. Compare against exact search on a sample to measure recall directly. A plausible wrong answer. "Approximate search is random." It is deterministic enough to measure and tune. Follow-ups. How would you monitor recall in production? Defend a design pgvector in your existing Postgres, or a dedicated vector database? Worked answer. pgvector when the corpus fits (millions, not billions), you want transactions, joins and permissions in one place, and the team already runs Postgres. A dedicated store for very large scale, heavy filtered search, multi-tenant isolation features or managed scaling. Measure recall and latency on your data. A plausible wrong answer. "Dedicated vector databases are faster, so always use one." Operational simplicity often matters more at moderate scale. Follow-ups. What would make you migrate later? Run those blocks first. Where each technique in this lesson acts. Three of them change what you index, four change the question before the search, and three work on the results after it. The step numbers are the code steps below. Why this came about Basic RAG reached a ceiling on harder questions. A wave of techniques from 2023 and 2024 improved either the query (rewriting, decomposition, hypothetical answers) or the passages (contextual chunks, parent documents, summaries), each aimed at a specific failure. In plain words first Better questions, better pieces When basic retrieval falls short, two kinds of fixes help. Improve the question : rewrite it, split it into sub-questions, or generate a hypothetical answer to search with. Improve the pieces : add context to each chunk before embedding it, keep small chunks for matching but return their larger parent section, or store summaries. Each fix targets a specific failure, so measure before adopting it. Contextual retrieval A chunk like "Express delivery costs INR 99" loses its context once it is cut out of the document. Anthropic's contextual retrieval (2024) asks a model to write a short context for each chunk ("This is from ShopKart's shipping policy, about delivery charges") and prepends it before embedding and keyword indexing. In their tests, failed retrievals dropped by 35% with contextual embeddings , 49% when combined with contextual BM25 , and up to 67% with reranking added. Prompt caching makes the per-chunk model calls affordable, since the whole document is the cached prefix. The cheapest version prepends the document title and section heading, and already helps: Copy What you should see Copy A one-line context header raised keyword MRR from 0.64 to 0.78 on this set, and rewriting the user's vague "faster delivery" into the corpus's word "express" moved the right chunk to the top. Query transformation Users write short, vague or compound questions. Transform them before retrieval: Technique What the model does Helps when Multi-query (above) Writes several phrasings; results are fused Vocabulary mismatch between users and documents HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings) Writes a fake answer and searches with that Short questions against long technical documents Step-back prompting Asks a more general question first ("what is the refund policy?") Specific questions that need general rules Query decomposition Splits "compare A and B" into sub-questions Multi-part and comparative questions Self-query / metadata extraction Turns "laptop policies from 2025" into a filter year=2025 plus a search Structured attributes hidden in natural language Each adds a model call and latency. Add them when your eval shows a matching failure type, not by default. In production Query transformation in production Rewrites help most on short, vague questions and hurt on precise ones: a rewrite of "error E-4012 on checkout" may drop the code that mattered. Keep the user's original query as one of the searches, cache rewrites for repeated questions, and log the rewritten queries so you can see when they drift. For conversations, the most valuable rewrite is often the simplest: turn a follow-up ("and for COD orders?") into a standalone question before searching. Small-to-big retrieval Small chunks match precisely; big chunks give the model enough context to answer. Small-to-big (also called parent-document retrieval ) gets both: index sentences or small chunks, but when one matches, return its parent section or a window of neighbors to the model. Store a parent_id with every chunk to make this a lookup. In production When small-to-big backfires Returning whole parent sections can multiply prompt size, and with it cost and the chance that the model latches onto the wrong paragraph. Cap the parent size, return a window of neighboring chunks instead of a whole section for long documents, and check faithfulness , not just recall, after switching it on. Long context or RAG? Context windows of a million tokens or more make it tempting to put everything in the prompt. Cache-augmented generation (CAG) does exactly that for small, stable corpora: load the whole knowledge base once, cache it, and answer from it. Choose long context or CAG when Choose RAG when The corpus is small (fits comfortably) and stable The corpus is large or changes often Questions need the whole document (summaries, cross-references) Questions need a few specific facts You can cache the prefix You need per-user permissions on content Latency of a long prefill is acceptable Cost per question must be low In practice they combine: retrieve a few relevant whole documents rather than tiny chunks, and let a long-context model read them. The retrieval improvement loop Improving RAG is a loop, not a one-time choice: measure, find the biggest failure type, apply the matching fix, measure again. The table is the loop's lookup step. Work down it in order, because the early rows are cheap and do not require re-indexing, while the later ones do. Choose by scenario Accuracy is not good enough: what to try, in what order # If you see this Try this If that doesn't move the number Watch out in production 1 A whole group of questions fails whatever you try Check whether the answer is in the corpus at all (an inventory problem) Add or fix the content; no retriever finds what is missing Teams lose weeks tuning retrieval for content that was never ingested 2 The right chunk is in the top 50 but not the top 5 Rerank a wide candidate list Let the reranker see titles and sections; reweight hybrid scores Reranking adds latency per query; budget it, especially for voice 3 The right chunk is never retrieved; questions contain codes, names or exact terms Hybrid search : keyword plus vectors, fused with RRF Prepend titles and section paths so the keywords appear in the chunk Some vector stores accept a "hybrid" setting but silently fall back to vectors only: verify with a keyword-only test question 4 Chunks are retrieved but meaningless alone ("it costs INR 99") Metadata prepend: document title, section path, product, date Have a model write one or two sentences of context per chunk (contextual retrieval) Generated context can be wrong; spot-check it, and regenerate when documents change 5 Users use different words from the documents ("faster delivery" for "express") Multi-query rewriting, then fuse HyDE; a synonym list built from failed queries Rewrites can drift from the user's intent; keep the original query as one of the searches 6 Multi-part or comparative questions get half answers Decompose into sub-questions; keep the top results of each An agentic retrieval loop ( Lesson 14.76 ) Fusing sub-question results with RRF can bury the specific answers (Step 2) 7 Results from the wrong product, year, region or tenant Metadata filters Extract filters from the question (self-query) Over-strict filters return nothing; fall back to unfiltered search with a warning 8 Old documents outrank current ones A recency boost, or a date filter for "latest" questions Remove superseded documents at ingestion Boosts that are too strong bury the canonical policy page under newer chatter 9 The top results are near-duplicates MMR (Step 5) Deduplicate at ingestion Aggressive dedup removes legitimate versions (regional policies) 10 Tables, figures or scans answered wrongly Layout-aware parsing ( Lesson 4.29 ) Retrieve page images and let a multimodal model read them Image-based retrieval costs more per query 11 Precise matches lack enough context to answer Small-to-big: match small chunks, return the parent section Larger chunks for that document type only Parents that are too large waste tokens and dilute the prompt 12 Still stuck after all of the above Re-chunk for the failing document types and compare side by side A better embedding model for your languages and domain Both force a full re-index; do them last and behind an alias Change one thing at a time, re-run the same labeled questions, and keep a short log of what each change did. That log becomes your team's playbook for the next system. Step by step: the advanced techniques in code The blocks below continue the lab from Lessons 14.70 to 14.72 . Each technique is measured on the same GOLD questions, so you can see what it buys on this corpus, and the habit carries over to yours. Step 1 · Reranking the top candidates The two-stage retrieval pattern: retrieve generously with hybrid search, then rerank the candidates with a more expensive scorer and keep the best few. A real reranker is a cross-encoder model (Cohere Rerank, Voyage, BGE reranker, Bedrock or Azure semantic ranking). The stand-in below scores each candidate by IDF-weighted overlap with the query plus a phrase bonus, which is enough to show the mechanics and the measurement. Copy What you should see Copy The crude stand-in leaves recall@1 unchanged and lifts MRR a little, by moving correct chunks up within the top few. That matters because the top few passages are what the model reads most carefully, and because a better top-3 lets you send fewer chunks (cheaper, less distraction). A real cross-encoder reads meaning, not just shared words, so expect clearly larger gains on paraphrased questions; its cost is a model call over every candidate, so keep the candidate pool to 20 to 100. Step 2 · HyDE and query decomposition HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings) searches with a model-written answer instead of the question, because an answer looks more like the documents than a question does. Query decomposition splits a compound question into parts, retrieves for each, and fuses the results so no part is crowded out. Copy What you should see Copy Two lessons. HyDE fixed the first question: the plain query ranked the shipping chunk first, while the hypothetical answer, written in the corpus's own words ("cash on delivery", "fee"), put the COD chunk on top. Decomposition shows a trap: fusing the sub-question results with RRF lost the refund chunks, because RRF rewards documents that appear in several lists, and generic chunks (shipping, warranty) matched both halves weakly. For decomposed questions, take the top results of each part instead, as the last line does. Each technique adds a model call, so turn it on for the question types your eval shows failing. Step 3 · Small-to-big (parent-document) retrieval Index small pieces for precise matching, but return the larger parent to the model so it has enough context to answer. Copy What you should see Copy The best match was the precise sentence about UPI refunds ( refund-policy#1/s2 , second here because BM25 also liked the word "refund" in the first chunk); in both cases the model receives the whole chunk around the matched sentence, not just one line. Step 4 · Metadata filters from the question (self-query) Questions often contain structured constraints: a document type, a date, a product category. Self-query retrieval extracts them into a filter and searches only the matching subset, which is both more precise and cheaper. Copy What you should see Copy The filter ran inside the search (only payment chunks were scored), which is the same rule that made permission filtering safe in Lesson 14.73 : filter first, then rank. Step 5 · Diversity with maximal marginal relevance When several chunks say nearly the same thing (overlapping chunks, the same policy copied into an FAQ page, old and new versions of a document), the top-k wastes slots on repeats. Maximal marginal relevance (MMR) picks each next result to be relevant to the query but different from what is already selected. Copy What you should see Copy The FAQ page and the policy chunk are 89% similar, so relevance-only ranking spent two of three slots on the same content. MMR kept one, then used the freed slot for the warranty chunk, which covers dead-on-arrival replacements. lam trades relevance (1.0) against diversity (0.0): tune it on your eval set , because too low a value starts pulling in irrelevant chunks. Most vector stores and LangChain later · 14.93 retrievers offer MMR as a search option. Step 6 · Diagnose, then choose the fix The loop above starts with a diagnosis, and one test separates the two big families of failure. Retrieve wide (top 10 here; top 50 on a real corpus). If the right chunk appears in the wide list but not in the top 3, it is a ranking problem (rows 2, 9 and 11 of the loop). If it is not in the wide list at all, it is a recall problem , and the fix is upstream: content, vocabulary, search type or chunking (rows 1, 3 to 8, 10 and 12). Copy What you should see Copy BM25 ranked one answer fourth: a ranking problem, which hybrid search and reranking both fixed. The Andaman question fails for every retriever, because the corpus has no delivery-areas page: an inventory problem, row 1 of the loop, and no amount of tuning will fix it. On a real system, run this over your full labeled set after every change, and track the three counts over time. Industry practice Inventory problems versus capability problems Jason Liu, whose Systematically Improving RAG Applications course is widely followed, separates failures into inventory problems (the information is not in the index at all: add or fix content) and capability problems (it is there but the system cannot find or combine it: improve retrieval, add tools such as date filters or comparisons). He recommends clustering real user questions into segments, measuring satisfaction per segment, and fixing the high-volume, low-satisfaction segments first. Fixing an inventory problem with a better retriever wastes weeks. From the field Anthropic: what contextual retrieval and reranking bought, in numbers Anthropic's contextual retrieval write-up (September 2024) measured the failure rate of top-20 retrieval across several datasets. The baseline failed 5.7% of the time. Prepending model-written context to each chunk before embedding cut failures to 3.7%; adding the same context to BM25 cut them to 2.9%; and reranking the results cut them to 1.9%, a 67% reduction overall. The context costs about $1.02 per million document tokens to generate once, using prompt caching. The lesson that generalizes: the cheap ingestion-time fix and the reranker stack, so measure each step rather than picking one. Source: Anthropic Engineering, "Introducing Contextual Retrieval" . Code to study NirDiamant/RAG_Techniques : reranking, query rewriting, contextual chunking and more, side by side Hands-on lab Lab 7 · Fix the failures you measured Take the questions your Lab 6 retriever missed. Label each as an inventory problem or a capability problem. Add contextual headers to your chunks and re-measure. Then add multi-query rewrites for the two worst questions. Run the diagnosis from Step 6 on your own questions before and after each change, and keep the three counts (answered, ranked too low, not retrieved) in a short log. Go deeper (optional) Other retrieval techniques you will hear named The methods in this lesson are the ones that most often pay off. A few more appear in papers, talks and vendor documentation: RAPTOR : cluster the chunks, summarise each cluster with a model, cluster the summaries, and so on, building a tree. Index every level. Broad questions match the summaries and specific ones match the leaves. Useful for long documents where the answer is spread across sections; the cost is many summarisation calls at indexing time. RAG-Fusion : generate several rewrites of the question, search for each, and merge the results with reciprocal rank fusion ( Lesson 5.38 ). It is multi-query retrieval with RRF. Late chunking : embed the whole document with a long-context embedding model first, then pool the token vectors per chunk, so each chunk's vector carries context from the rest of the document ( Lesson 14.70 ). Late interaction ( ColBERT , ColPali later · 4.31 ): one vector per token or image patch, matched at query time (Lessons 5.38 and 4.31 ). Learned sparse retrieval ( SPLADE , ELSER): a model-made keyword index that also matches related words ( Lesson 5.37 ). Self-RAG later · 14.76 and corrective RAG later · 14.76 : the model judges whether retrieval was needed and whether the results are good enough, and searches again if not ( Lesson 14.76 ). GraphRAG later · 14.88 and LightRAG : retrieval over entities and relationships extracted from the documents ( Lesson 14.88 ). Cache-augmented generation : put a small, stable corpus in the prompt and cache it, with no retrieval at all ( Lesson 14.78 ). Treat each as a hypothesis to test on your evaluation set, not as an upgrade to install. Check your mental model ✗ "Advanced techniques always beat the basics." ✓ Each adds cost and complexity; adopt one only when it fixes a measured failure. ✗ "Query rewriting cannot hurt." ✓ A rewrite can drift from what the user meant; keep the original query too. ✗ "Bigger chunks solve missing context." ✓ Return parent sections, or add context to small chunks, instead. Exercises Predict before you run Contextual retrieval adds a one-line header to each chunk before indexing. Will it help BM25, vector search , or both? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Use HyDE (embed a hypothetical answer instead of the question) for "What is ShopKart's COD fee?". What happens if the model's guess says INR 50? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise Query decomposition splits "Compare COD and UPI refunds" into two sub-queries, but the final answer only covers UPI. Where do you look? (Solution D1.) Make it your own Implement small-to-big: match on sentence-level chunks, then return the whole parent section to the model, and compare answer completeness on questions with conditions. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Both, for different reasons Both: BM25 gains the header's words ("Refund policy"), and the embedding gains the topic the chunk's sentences assumed. The lesson's measurement shows the keyword gain; measure the vector gain on your own data. Solution B1 · HyDE embeds a guess The hypothetical answer is only used for matching, so a wrong number usually still finds the COD chunk. But the guess can steer retrieval toward wrong topics for unfamiliar domains. Never show the hypothetical answer, and compare HyDE with plain retrieval on the eval. Solution D1 · Each sub-query must be answered Check what each sub-query retrieved: the COD sub-query may have retrieved nothing relevant, and the generator answered with what it had. Require an answer per sub-question, and show missing parts explicitly. Solution M1 · Match small, read big Keep a parent ID on each small chunk, retrieve by small chunks, deduplicate parents, and pass parents to the model. Expect better completeness on rules with conditions, at the cost of more context tokens. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism Name advanced retrieval techniques and when each helps. Worked answer. Contextual chunk headers or contextual retrieval (chunks lack context), query rewriting and expansion (vocabulary mismatch), HyDE (short or abstract questions), decomposition (multi-part questions), small-to-big (precise matching with complete context), metadata filters from the question (self-query), and MMR for diversity. Each fixes a specific failure; pick by diagnosing failures first (Step 8). A plausible wrong answer. "Use all of them." Each adds latency and cost and can hurt other questions. Follow-ups. How do you decide which technique to try first? Debug a failure After adding query rewriting, some answers got worse. Why? Worked answer. The rewrite changed the meaning (dropped a constraint, added an assumption) or translated a Hinglish question badly. Log original and rewritten queries, compare retrieval for both on the eval, and retrieve with both and fuse rather than replacing the original. A plausible wrong answer. "Rewriting always helps." It helps vague queries and can damage precise ones. Follow-ups. How would you evaluate a rewriter on its own? Defend a design Long context or RAG for a 500-page policy manual? Worked answer. If the manual is stable and questions are occasional, long context with caching can be simpler and comparable in quality. For frequent questions, many users, permissions, citations and updates, RAG is cheaper and easier to maintain. Many teams combine them: retrieve sections, then give the model whole sections. A plausible wrong answer. "Long context makes RAG obsolete." Cost, latency and the lost-in-the-middle effect remain. Follow-ups. How would you compare them fairly? A A larger embedding B A short description of where the chunk comes from, prepended before indexing C A link to the original document D A summary of the whole corpus The chunk keeps its context after being cut out, which helps both BM25 and vectors. Q2 When is cache-augmented generation (long context with caching) a better choice than RAG? A A small, stable corpus where questions need whole-document understanding B A large corpus that changes hourly C Content with per-user permissions D Very tight cost per question Long context suits small, stable, holistic tasks. Q3 Users ask about a product launched last week and the bot says it doesn't know. The launch notes were never ingested. What kind of problem is this? A An inventory problem B A capability problem C A reranking problem D A chunk-size problem The content is missing; no retriever can find it. Q4 When fusing results for a decomposed question, why can RRF lose the right chunks? A RRF needs calibrated scores B RRF rewards documents appearing in several lists, so generic chunks that weakly match every part can outrank the specific answers C RRF only works with two lists D Decomposition always fails Take the top results of each sub-question instead. Q5 What does maximal marginal relevance trade off? A Speed against cost B Relevance to the query against redundancy with results already chosen C Recall against precision of the embedding model D Keyword against vector scores It stops near-duplicates from filling the top-k. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Multi-hop A question whose answer needs facts connected through intermediate entities Lesson 14.88 LLM-as-a-judge Using a model with a rubric to grade another model's output Lesson 14.77 Contextual grounding checks Guardrail checks that an answer is supported by its source and relevant Lesson 14.153 Groundedness detection Checking that an answer is supported by its sources Lesson 14.155 Cypher The pattern-matching query language of Neo4j and openCypher databases Lesson 14.84 LangChain A widely used open-source library of building blocks for model applications: models, prompts, tools and agents Lesson 14.93 LangGraph A library for building agents as graphs of steps with saved state, so runs can pause, resume and branch Lesson 14.101 Why this came about Single-shot retrieval had no way to recover when it fetched the wrong passages. Giving retrieval decisions to an agent, which can grade results, rewrite the query, try again or say it does not know ( Self-RAG and Corrective RAG , 2023 and 2024), made RAG more robust at the cost of more model calls. In plain words first A researcher who checks their sources Plain RAG retrieves once and hopes. Agentic RAG adds decisions: should we search at all, are the results relevant, should we rewrite the query and try again, is the answer supported by the sources? Corrective RAG grades retrieved passages and retries or falls back when they are poor; self-checking RAG verifies the answer before showing it. Each check is a model call, so the loop needs limits. From pipeline to agent Classic RAG always retrieves once, then answers. Agentic RAG gives retrieval to an agent as one or more tools, so the model decides: whether to retrieve at all ("hi" needs no search) where to look (policies index, product catalog, SQL warehouse, web) how to rephrase the query, and whether to try again when it has enough evidence to answer The trade-off is the usual one for agents: better on hard, multi-step questions; slower, costlier and less predictable on easy ones. Many production systems route easy questions to a fixed pipeline and only hard ones to the agent. In production What goes wrong with agentic RAG in production Over-searching : the agent calls retrieval five times for a question one search would answer. Cap retrieval calls per turn, and route simple questions to the fixed pipeline before the agent sees them. Loops on missing content : when the answer is not in the corpus, the agent keeps rephrasing. Give it an explicit "not found, say so" path after two or three tries. Latency users notice : each retrieval round trip adds a model call. Stream a status message ("checking the refund policy...") and measure p95, not the average. Inconsistent answers across runs : different search paths find different evidence. Evaluate with repeated runs ( pass^k ), not single runs. If agentic RAG is not beating plain RAG on your eval , the usual reason is that the plain pipeline was never tuned. Go back to the Lesson 14.75 loop first. Self-correcting retrieval The Corrective RAG (CRAG) pattern adds a grader between retrieval and generation. Here it is with the lab's search functions and a grader you can replace with a model call: Agentic retrieval as a loop: the model decides whether to retrieve, grades what came back, rewrites the query if the evidence is weak, and answers only when it can cite. Copy What you should see Copy The first question failed the grader, was rewritten into the corpus's vocabulary, and succeeded. The second correctly found nothing, so the answer step should say "I don't know" instead of improvising. Other agentic retrieval patterns you will meet: Pattern Idea Self-RAG The model checks its own answer for support and usefulness, and retrieves again if needed Adaptive RAG A router picks no retrieval, one-shot retrieval or iterative retrieval per question Multi-hop retrieval Answer one sub-question, use the result to form the next query ("who supplies our top product?" then "what incidents did that supplier have?") Deep research An agent plans, searches many sources in parallel, reads, and writes a cited report ( Lesson 14.62 's orchestrator-workers pattern) Federated retrieval One agent with tools over several sources: documents, SQL, tickets, web Step by step: agentic retrieval in code The blocks continue the lab from Lessons 14.70 to 14.72 . Where a model makes a decision (route, rewrite, extract, verify), a small stand-in function makes the same decision deterministically and the real prompt is described in its docstring, so the control flow is visible and runnable. Step 1 · Adaptive routing: decide whether and how to retrieve Not every question needs retrieval, and some need several rounds. An adaptive RAG router picks the strategy per question, which saves cost on easy questions and spends it on hard ones. Copy What you should see Copy In production the router is a cheap model call with a few examples, measured on its own eval set ( Lesson 14.62 's routing pattern). Step 2 · Multi-hop retrieval A multi-hop later · 14.88 question needs a fact from one passage to know what to search next. The cancellation policy says cancelled prepaid orders are refunded; only then do you know to look up refund timing. Copy What you should see Copy The first hop found the cancellation rule ("cancelled prepaid orders are refunded in full"); the second used that to fetch the UPI timing ("UPI refunds usually arrive in 2 days"). Bound the hops, and log each query: the sequence of queries is the most useful debugging signal in agentic RAG. Step 3 · Verify the answer against the evidence Self-RAG and similar patterns check the draft answer before it is sent: split it into claims, check each claim against the retrieved passages, and revise or abstain if any is unsupported. Here the support check is word overlap; in production it is an LLM judge later · 14.77 or an NLI model, or a platform service (Bedrock contextual grounding checks later · 14.153 , Azure groundedness detection later · 14.155 , Google's Check Grounding API). Copy What you should see Copy The voucher is a hallucination : nothing in the evidence promises it. Drop or rewrite unsupported claims before sending, and count them: the unsupported-claim rate is a production quality metric you can alert on. Step 4 · Rewrite with the failure in view corrective_search in the first block of this lesson takes a fixed list of rewrites. A real rewriter is a model call, and the mistake to avoid is giving it only the question: it then produces the same query twice. Give it what was tried and what came back. Copy What you should see Copy The first query failed the grader (the corpus never says "speedy" or "parcel"), the rewriter saw that and produced "express delivery cost", which hit. What makes the second attempt better than a blind retry is that the rewriter knows which words were already tried and what they surfaced. One more rule for the real thing: the stand-in grader is word overlap, so it must score the rewritten query, but a model grader should be shown the user's original question alongside the passages, so a rewrite that drifts away from the intent cannot pass. Step 5 · Condense follow-up questions before retrieving In a chat, the second question is "and how long does that take?". Retrieval on those words finds nothing useful. Rewrite it to stand alone first, using the history; this is the one model call that belongs before retrieve . Copy What you should see Copy As asked, "Is there a fee for that?" retrieves the cash-on-delivery chunk (the only one with the word "fee"), which would produce a confident wrong answer; condensed, it retrieves the cancellation policy. The second question already stood alone and was left as it was. Store the history in the agent's state or read it from the thread's messages, and condense only when the question is not self-contained, so you do not pay a model call on every turn. Step 6 · When verification fails, regenerate once with the feedback Step 3 drops unsupported claims. Cheaper and usually better: send the failed claims back to the writer as feedback and let it try once more; fall back only if the second draft fails too. Copy What you should see Copy One retry, with the exact failing sentences in the prompt, never a loop: a writer that failed twice with feedback is unlikely to pass on the third attempt, and every attempt costs tokens. Log regenerated and still_unsupported as metrics; a rising regeneration rate usually means retrieval got worse, not that the writer did. Step 7 · A small deep-research loop Deep research combines everything: plan sub-questions, retrieve for each in parallel, take notes with citations, and write a report whose every claim is checked. This version uses the lab corpus and the verification step from Step 3. Copy What you should see Copy The structure is right (parallel research, citations, verification), and the output shows why quality depends on each piece: every note is a real sentence with a valid citation, so verification passes, yet the first note gives the general 7-day window instead of the 30-day rule for damaged items, the second gives refund timing in general rather than for UPI, and the third answers a neighbouring question. Citation checks prove support, not relevance. Real deep-research agents fix this with a model that reads the whole passage and extracts the sentence that answers the sub-question, and a final review step against the plan. The same idea drawn as a graph you will be able to build in the LangChain and LangGraph section: decide whether to retrieve, grade what came back, and either rewrite the question or generate the answer. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in LangChain A widely used open-source library of building blocks for model applications: models, prompts, tools and agents Lesson 14.93 Cohen's kappa Agreement between two raters beyond chance Lesson 14.143 Microsoft Foundry Microsoft's platform for models, agents, knowledge and governance (formerly Azure AI Foundry) Lesson 14.155 Groundedness detection Checking that an answer is supported by its sources Lesson 14.155 JSONL A file with one JSON object per line Lesson 7.25 Why this came about Judging RAG answers by eye did not scale, and word-overlap metrics did not capture correctness. Frameworks such as RAGAS (2023) introduced component metrics for retrieval and generation, often scored by a model acting as judge, so RAG systems could be tested on every change. In plain words first Grading the open-book exam Evaluating RAG means checking both halves on a fixed set of questions: did retrieval bring the right passages ( context precision and recall), and is the answer faithful to them and relevant to the question ( faithfulness , answer relevance ). Many of these are scored by a model acting as judge, which itself must be checked against human labels before you trust it. Generation metrics These need a judge (a model, or people) because they are about meaning. The names come from RAGAS and are now industry vocabulary: Metric Question it answers Needs Faithfulness (groundedness) Is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved context? Question, answer, contexts Answer relevance Does the answer address the question? Question, answer Context precision Are the retrieved passages relevant, with the useful ones ranked first? Question, contexts, reference Context recall Does the retrieved context contain everything the reference answer needs? Question, contexts, reference answer Answer correctness Does the answer match the reference? Answer, reference TruLens calls the first three together the RAG triad : context relevance, groundedness and answer relevance. If all three are high, the answer is very likely trustworthy. What each RAG metric compares. Three corners are produced on every question; the reference answer exists only in your evaluation set. A low score on one edge tells you which stage to fix. Running RAGAS and DeepEval Both are open-source libraries that use an LLM as the judge ( LLM-as-a-judge ). Code below was checked against RAGAS 0.4.3 and DeepEval 4.3 (imports and function signatures), not run against a live judge. Copy Watch out A dependency clash you may hit RAGAS 0.4.3 imports an old LangChain later · 14.93 module. With the newest langchain-community it fails with No module named 'langchain_community.chat_models.vertexai' . Pin langchain-community<0.4 in the environment you use for evals ( uv add "langchain-community<0.4" ), or keep evals in their own environment. Eval tooling often lags the libraries around it, which is one reason teams keep a separate eval environment. Copy Step by step: a RAG evaluation harness you own Libraries are useful, but the teams with the most reliable RAG systems own a small harness : their questions, their metrics, their judge, calibrated against their experts, running in CI. The blocks below build one over the Lessons 5.38 and 14.75 retrievers. Step 1 · Generate a test set, including the hard cases Start from the corpus: for each chunk, ask a model for questions that the chunk answers, then add the variations real users produce. The generator here is a stand-in that applies the same transformations a prompted model would. Copy What you should see Copy Synthetic questions are a starting point; they are usually easier than real ones because they reuse the passage's words. That is why the set mixes in real phrasing, typos, Hinglish and questions with no answer. Replace synthetic items with real traffic as it arrives. Step 2 · Per-segment metrics with confidence intervals Averages hide failing segments, and small eval sets give noisy numbers. Report each metric per question type, with a bootstrap confidence interval (resample the questions many times and see how much the metric moves). Copy What you should see Copy Three findings. Hybrid and reranked retrieval reach 1.0 in every segment, while BM25 loses ground on generated and misspelled questions. BM25's interval is wide (0.76 to 1.0): with 25 answerable questions, a difference of a few points is noise, so grow the set before trusting small gains. And the Hinglish question passes only because it contains the English words "refund" and "UPI"; a question written fully in Hindi or in Devanagari script would fail with these word tokenizers ( Lesson 5.37 ), so add those cases before you claim the system works for Indian users. Step 3 · An LLM judge for faithfulness, and calibrating it Generation metrics need a judge. A good faithfulness judge splits the answer into claims and checks each against the context; that is what RAGAS does internally. Whatever judge you use, do judge calibration : label a sample yourself and measure agreement. Cohen's kappa later · 14.143 measures agreement beyond chance (1.0 perfect, 0 no better than chance; above about 0.6 is usually acceptable for a judge). Copy What you should see Copy The judge agrees with the human on 7 of 8. Its one miss is a false positive: "INR 49" against a context that says INR 99 passes, because word overlap cannot see a wrong number. That case belongs in the judge's own test set . Real LLM judges handle numbers far better but have their own blind spots (long answers, partial support, hedged claims), so keep measuring agreement whenever the judge prompt or model changes ( Lesson 14.143 ). Step 4 · Measure abstention A RAG system must say "I don't know" when the corpus has no answer, and must not say it when the answer is there. Treat abstention as a classifier and measure both errors. Copy What you should see Copy Both unanswerable questions were caught, at the cost of one false abstention: "faster delivery" shares no strong word with the passage about express delivery, the same vocabulary gap Lesson 14.75 's query rewriting fixes. Move the threshold and watch the trade-off; then decide with the business which error is worse. For a support bot, a false abstention means a human handles the question; a missed abstention means a confident wrong answer. Step 5 · A regression gate for CI The harness becomes useful when it runs on every change and blocks regressions against a stored baseline. Copy What you should see Copy A change that looked harmless dropped recall on real and misspelled questions, and the gate caught it before users did. Store the baseline in the repository next to the eval set, and update it deliberately when a change is accepted. Building the eval set Synthetic questions first : for each chunk, ask a model to write one or two questions that the chunk answers. That gives labeled (question, correct chunk) pairs before any users exist. Aim for retrieval recall of 80 to 90% on these before launch. Make them realistic : vary phrasing, add typos and Hinglish, add multi-part questions and questions with no answer in the corpus (to test abstention). Add real traffic after launch: sample questions from logs, especially those with negative feedback, and have experts write reference answers. Segment : tag questions by type (policy, product, order-specific, comparison) and report metrics per segment. Averages hide the segment that is failing. Re-run on every change to chunking , embeddings , prompts or models, and block releases that regress ( Lesson 14.143 ). In production Eval-set mistakes that make scores lie Synthetic questions that copy the chunk's wording : retrieval looks excellent because the question shares every keyword with its answer. Ask the generator to paraphrase, use synonyms and write the way customers write, and keep real questions as the majority once you have traffic. No unanswerable questions : the system is never tested on saying "I don't know", which is where hallucinations hurt most. A frozen set : the set stops matching what users ask. Add a sample of new production questions every month. One average for everything : a 90% average can hide a 40% segment (order-specific or Hindi questions, say). Always report per segment. Judges nobody checked : an LLM judge that agrees with experts 60% of the time makes every comparison noise. Calibrate first ( Lesson 14.143 ). Exercises Predict before you run System A scores 82% and system B 85% on 100 questions. Can you conclude B is better? What does a confidence interval tell you? (Solution P1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Small samples, wide intervals Not yet: on 100 questions, the 95% interval for each score is roughly plus or minus 7 to 8 points, so the difference can be noise. Use a paired comparison on the same questions, more questions, or report the interval with the score (Step 2). Solution B1 · Synthetic tests flatter the system Questions mirror the chunk's wording, so retrieval is easy and the set misses real users' phrasing, typos, Hinglish and unanswerable questions. Mix in real questions, add the hard cases on purpose, and have people review a sample. Solution D1 · Judges drift too The judge changed, not the system. Pin the judge model and prompt, re-calibrate against human labels after any change, and track judge agreement as a metric of its own. Solution M1 · Segments reveal hidden failures Overall averages hide small groups. Tag each question with its segment, compute each metric per segment with intervals, and gate releases on the worst important segment, not just the average. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What are RAGAS-style generation metrics, and what do they measure? Worked answer. Faithfulness (claims supported by the retrieved context), answer relevance (the answer addresses the question), context precision and recall (whether retrieved passages are relevant and cover the needed information), and answer correctness against references. Most use an LLM judge, so they need calibration against human labels. A plausible wrong answer. "They measure accuracy." Faithfulness can be perfect for a wrong answer if the context was wrong. Follow-ups. When would you trust an LLM judge? Debug a failure Your eval shows no regressions, but users complain after a release. Why? Worked answer. The eval set does not represent current traffic: new topics, phrasings or languages, or the failing cases were never added. Sample production questions, label them, add failures to the set, and segment by question type. A plausible wrong answer. "Users are wrong." Users are the ground truth the eval set is meant to approximate. Follow-ups. How would you keep the eval set fresh? Defend a design RAGAS, DeepEval, or your own harness? Worked answer. Libraries for standard metrics and fast setup; your own harness when you need control: your segments, your judges, intervals, and integration with your release gates. Many teams use library metrics inside their own harness. The question set matters more than the library. A plausible wrong answer. "A library is enough; no labels needed." Without labeled data, metrics have nothing to calibrate against. Follow-ups. What would block a release in your harness? Check your understanding Q1 What does faithfulness measure? A Whether the answer matches a reference answer B Whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context C Whether the right chunk was retrieved D Whether the answer is polite Faithfulness (groundedness) is about support, not correctness against a reference. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Knowledge graph Facts stored as things and the named relationships between them Lesson 14.83 GraphRAG Retrieval that uses a knowledge graph built from the documents, to answer questions that span many of them Lesson 14.88 Why this came about Vector search needs an embedding pipeline and can miss structure. With larger context windows and capable agents, some teams found that navigating documents directly, through tables of contents, file trees or plain text search as coding agents do, worked better for well-structured collections. In plain words first Reading the table of contents instead of searching Not every retrieval needs embeddings. For structured or well-organized collections, an agent can navigate: read a table of contents or a document tree, open the relevant section, follow links, or search with plain text tools. This vectorless retrieval avoids embedding pipelines and can be more precise for long, structured documents, at the cost of more model calls. What the term means Vectorless RAG is retrieval-augmented generation in which no embedding similarity is used to find the context. The term became popular in 2025 with PageIndex, but it covers several older and newer ideas. What they share: they find information by structure, exact matching or model reasoning rather than by "nearest vector". Approach How it finds context Best for Keyword and full-text search BM25 in OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, Postgres full-text Codes, names, exact phrases; a strong baseline that is often underrated Reasoning over a document tree An LLM reads a table of contents with summaries and navigates down to the right section Long structured documents: filings, contracts, manuals, regulations Agentic search with tools The agent lists, greps and reads files like a developer Codebases, wikis, folders of documents Structured retrieval Text-to-SQL, APIs, knowledge graph later · 14.83 queries Facts that live in tables and systems of record Long context with caching ( CAG ) No retrieval at all: the whole corpus is in the cached prompt Small, stable corpora Reasoning over a document tree PageIndex (Vectify AI, open source) builds a hierarchical "table of contents" index of a long document, with a summary at every node. At question time an LLM reads the top-level summaries, picks the branch most likely to hold the answer, and moves down level by level, like a person using a manual's contents page. Its authors report 98.7% accuracy on FinanceBench, a benchmark of questions over financial filings. That is a vendor-reported result, so verify on your own documents. The approach also leaves an explainable trail: the path it took. Vectorless retrieval over a document tree: the model reads the table of contents, picks a branch, and drills down to the section that answers, like a person using an index. No embeddings, and the path explains the answer. Here is the core idea in 30 lines. A keyword scorer stands in for the LLM so it runs offline; the real prompt is shown. Copy What you should see Copy With an LLM as the chooser, the navigator handles questions that share no words with the headings ("how much does the platform keep from an electronics sale?") by reasoning about what each section covers. Costs to weigh: building the tree needs an LLM pass to write summaries, and each question makes one model call per tree level. It pays off for long, structured, repeatedly queried documents, and loses to vector search for broad search across thousands of short documents. Agentic search with ordinary tools Coding agents such as Claude Code popularized another vectorless approach: no index at all. The agent uses ls , grep and read tools on files, exactly as a developer would, and iterates. With modern models this often beats a vector index on codebases and technical wikis, because exact identifiers matter and the agent can follow references. Copy What you should see Copy Give these three functions to any agent from the LangChain and LangGraph and Other agent frameworks, compared sections as tools, and it can answer questions over a folder with no index to build or keep in sync. The cost is more model calls per question, so it suits low-volume, high-value questions. Step by step: vectorless retrieval you can deploy Step 1 · Build the tree from a document's own headings Hand-writing a table of contents does not scale. Most long documents already have structure (Markdown or HTML headings, PDF bookmarks, numbered sections), so the index can be built automatically, with an LLM writing the node summaries. Here the summary is the first sentence of each section, standing in for that model call. Copy What you should see Copy The same navigate function from above works on the generated tree. For PDFs, PageIndex and similar tools detect the structure from the layout (and with an LLM, from the text itself when there are no headings). Step 2 · Beam navigation with a leaf check A greedy navigator that picks one branch per level fails when an early choice is wrong. Two standard fixes: keep the top few branches at each level (a beam), and check the leaf before answering, backtracking to the next candidate if it does not contain the answer. Copy What you should see Copy The greedy navigator matched the word "seller" in the wrong place and ended in the onboarding documents; the beam navigator rejected that leaf, backtracked to the next branch, and found the penalty rule. The leaf check is also why the beam navigator can return nothing: when no leaf passes, say "not found" rather than guessing. A beam of 2 roughly doubles model calls in the worst case, which is usually still far fewer tokens than reading the whole document. Step 3 · Long context with caching: the cost arithmetic Cache-augmented generation skips retrieval: put the whole corpus in a cached prompt prefix and ask questions against it. Whether that is cheaper than RAG is arithmetic, so do the arithmetic. Copy What you should see Copy Even with cached input at a tenth of the normal price, reading the whole corpus on every question costs more than retrieving 3,000 relevant tokens, and the gap grows with corpus size. CAG wins on quality for small corpora where questions need the whole picture, and on simplicity; it rarely wins on cost. Plug in your own prices and cache lifetimes (they differ by provider). Step 4 · Route each question to the right retriever Teams with mature systems run several retrievers and route between them by query type, as the practice box below describes. The router is a cheap classifier; here, rules. Copy What you should see Copy An agent with all four retrievers as tools makes the same choice itself ( agentic RAG , Lesson 14.76 ); a router is cheaper and more predictable when the categories are stable. Choosing an approach Your content and questions Start with Many short documents, natural-language questions Hybrid search ( Lesson 5.38 ) Few long, structured documents, precise questions Tree navigation (PageIndex style), or long context with caching Codebases, technical wikis, identifiers everywhere Agentic file search, plus BM25 Facts in databases and systems of record Text-to-SQL or APIs as tools Relationship and global questions GraphRAG later · 14.88 ( Lesson 14.76 ) Small and stable corpus Long context with caching Industry practice Embeddings are a tool, not the definition of RAG The common thread among teams with mature RAG systems is that they choose retrieval by query type, and many end up with several retrievers behind a router: keyword for codes, vectors for paraphrases, SQL for numbers, navigation for long documents. "Vector database first" is a habit from 2023, not a requirement. In production Where vectorless approaches disappoint Tree navigation depends entirely on good headings and section summaries; on documents with vague or missing headings it wanders, and every level costs a model call, so deep trees get slow. Agentic file search with grep is excellent for code and identifiers but spends many tool calls on natural-language questions. Long context with caching is simple, but the cost of every uncached question and the time to first token grow with the document. Most teams that adopt these keep a hybrid retriever as the fallback and route by question type. Solutions Solution P1 · Reasoning over structure Four choices, so four model calls, against embedding the whole document once. Tree navigation trades calls for following the document's own structure, which helps long, well-organized documents. Solution B1 · Errors compound down the tree Every later choice is inside the wrong branch, so the answer comes from the wrong section. Recover with backtracking (try the next-best branch when the leaf does not answer), or by exploring the top two branches. Solution D1 · Tools need text to search PDFs must be parsed to text first, and grep matches exact words, so paraphrased questions miss. Agentic search with ordinary tools works best on well-named, text-based corpora such as code and Markdown. Solution M1 · Backtracking Keep the ranked choices at each level, check the leaf, and on failure try the next-ranked sibling, with a limit on backtracks. Measure how many questions need it. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Text-to-SQL Having a model turn a question in plain language into a database query Lesson 14.80 Semantic layer Agreed definitions of business metrics and tables that a data agent queries instead of raw tables Lesson 14.80 Why this came about As RAG systems went into production, wrong answers were reported without any indication of where they came from. A stage-by-stage debugging method, checking parsing, chunking , indexing, retrieval and generation in order, emerged from that experience. In plain words first Debug from the beginning of the pipeline When a RAG answer is wrong, walk the pipeline in order and look at evidence at each stage: was the document parsed correctly, chunked sensibly, indexed and current, retrieved for this question, ranked near the top, and then used faithfully by the model? Checking retrieval before generation splits the problem in half quickly. Debugging a RAG answer, stage by stage A wrong RAG answer was broken at one of a small number of stages, and each stage leaves a different trace. Work from the input end: a fix downstream cannot repair what was lost upstream. Run the same question through each stage and look at the intermediate output before changing anything. A RAG answer passes through eight stages, and a wrong answer was broken at exactly one of them. Read the symptom, go to that stage, and look at what it produced before changing anything. Symptom in the answer Stage to check What to look at Usual fix (lesson) Numbers or table values are wrong or missing Parsing The extracted text of the source page next to the original Layout-aware parsing; verify tables against the source ( Lesson 4.29 ) The right document is found but the answer is partial Chunking Whether the needed sentences ended up in one chunk Larger or structure-aware chunks; small-to-big retrieval ( Lesson 14.70 , Lesson 14.75 ) An exact term (a product code, an error string) is missed Keyword retrieval BM25 results for the query alone Hybrid search ( Lesson 5.38 ) A paraphrased question is missed Vector retrieval Top-k by cosine similarity , and the embedding model 's language coverage A better embedding model, query rewriting, or fine-tuning embeddings ( Lesson 14.71 , Lesson 14.75 , Lesson 3.22 ) The right chunk is retrieved but ranked below distractors Ranking Ranks before and after reranking A reranker; fewer, better chunks in the context ( Lesson 5.38 ) The answer contradicts or goes beyond the retrieved text Generation Claim-by-claim support against the cited chunks Stricter citation instructions, a faithfulness check, abstention ( Lesson 14.72 , Lesson 14.77 ) A user sees a document they should not Permissions The filter applied before retrieval Filter by identity and tenant before the search, never after ( Lesson 14.73 ) An answer is out of date Freshness Index timestamps against source timestamps Incremental indexing and deletes ( Lesson 14.73 ) Keep every debugged case. Each one becomes a row in the evaluation set from Lesson 14.72 , so the same failure cannot come back unnoticed. A tracer you can run The table says where to look. This function does the looking: it follows one question through the pipeline built in Lessons 14.70 to 5.38 and reports where the passage that holds the answer was found, and at which stage it was lost. You tell it which chunk should be found; it tells you what happened to it. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Each block is one question. Each row is one stage, with the rank at which the right chunk stood (1 is best) and which chunk came top. The damaged-item question. The right chunk is at rank 1 or 2 at every stage and is among the three sent to the model. Retrieval is fine. If the final answer were wrong, you would stop looking at search and read the prompt and the answer instead. "How do I get my money back?" with only one chunk allowed in the prompt ( k=1 ). Vector search had the right chunk first, keyword search had it third, and after fusion and reranking it was second. With k=1 it missed the prompt. Nothing was lost in retrieval; it was ranked just too low. The cheap fix is a larger k. The better fix is to ask why the reranker prefers the other chunk. The Nepal question. Nothing in the index answers it, yet every stage still returns something, because search always returns its closest match. The tracer cannot judge the answer; it reminds you to check that the system says "I do not know" instead of answering from the shipping chunk. The warranty question. The chunk it was told to look for does not exist under that name. In a real system this is the commonest finding of all: the document was never ingested, failed to parse, or was chunked so that the answer straddles two chunks. No search setting can find what is not there. A tracer like this takes twenty lines, and it turns "the bot gave a bad answer" into "the right chunk was at rank 4 after reranking and only 3 go in". Run it on every reported failure before touching a prompt. From the field: what teams learn about RAG From Jason Liu ( Systematically improving RAG ), the year of building authors and the Retrieval (RAG) section: Measure retrieval separately from generation (recall and precision at k on a labeled set) before tuning prompts. Segment your questions by type and volume; build specialized retrieval (or tools) for the large, failing segments instead of one ever-larger pipeline. Hybrid search and a reranker are the default, not an optimization; keyword search alone is a strong baseline. Structure and metadata beat clever chunking : titles, dates, filters and document types often matter more than chunk size. Use tools, not just retrieval, for structured data : text-to-SQL later · 14.80 over a semantic layer later · 14.80 for numbers (Lessons 14.158 and 13.50 ), search for documents. Agentic and vectorless retrieval (Lessons 14.76 and 14.78 ) help when questions need several hops or when documents have strong structure; they cost more tokens, so measure the gain. Check your mental model ✗ "Start by changing the prompt." ✓ Start by checking what was retrieved; most failures are upstream. ✗ "One failing question shows the cause." ✓ Group failures; patterns point to the stage at fault. ✗ "A fix is done when the reported question works." ✓ Add it to the test set and check nothing else broke. Break it on purpose Fix a bad answer by adding the correct sentence to the system prompt . Why is that not a fix? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise Answers alternate between two refund windows. Both documents are in the index. Which stage-by-stage check finds the cause, and what is the fix? (Solution D1.) Make it your own Write a debugging checklist for one failed RAG answer, with one command or query per stage: corpus, parsing, chunking, retrieval, ranking, prompt, generation, citation check. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Retrieval before generation First, whether the answer exists in the corpus at all; second, whether retrieval returned it for this question. Only then the prompt and the model. Most RAG failures are found in the first two. Solution B1 · Patches hide the cause It fixes one question and hides the pipeline failure (a missing document, a bad chunk, a retrieval miss) that will break related questions. Fix the stage that failed, and add the question to the eval set. Solution D1 · Conflicting sources Retrieval returns both an old and a new policy chunk. Check the retrieved passages and their sources and dates. Remove or mark superseded documents at ingestion, prefer the newest by metadata, and tell the model how to handle conflicts. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Prompt injection Text that tricks a model into following an attacker's instructions instead of yours Lesson 15.24 Model Context Protocol (MCP) An open standard for connecting models to tools and data through small servers, so one integration works in many apps Lesson 13.46 Knowledge graph Facts stored as things and the named relationships between them Lesson 14.83 The numbers that businesses ask about live in tables, not documents. "How many orders were late in Pune last week?" cannot be answered by retrieving passages; it needs a query. Text-to-SQL turns a question into SQL, runs it and explains the result. It is one of the most requested enterprise agent patterns, and one of the easiest to get dangerously wrong, so this lesson builds it with every safeguard in place. The database is SQLite, so everything runs offline; where a model writes SQL, a stand-in returns what a model would, including its typical mistakes. Why this came about Many business questions are about numbers stored in databases, which passages cannot answer. Models turned out to be good at writing SQL, and text-to-SQL became a major use case, along with the need to validate queries, run them safely and use semantic layers so terms mean what the business means. In plain words first Translating questions into SQL, carefully For questions about numbers in a database, the model writes a query instead of reading passages: find the relevant tables, write SQL, check it, run it with read-only permissions, and explain the result. Each step guards against a known failure: wrong tables, invented columns, huge scans, or a destructive statement. A semantic layer that defines business terms such as "active customer" makes the model far more accurate. Step 1 · A database with realistic traps Real schemas have cryptic column names, codes instead of labels and several tables to join. The lab database has all three. Copy What you should see Copy Step 2 · A semantic layer: business meaning in one place A model that sees only ord.stat_cd and amt_inr has to guess what "revenue", "late" or "delivered" mean, and different guesses give different numbers. A semantic layer defines them once: tables with descriptions, joins, dimensions and metrics with exact SQL, plus verified queries for the most important questions. This is what Databricks metric views, dbt's semantic layer, Cube and LookML provide; here it is a dictionary. Copy What you should see Copy "Sales by location" became the defined revenue metric, with the rule that only delivered orders count. Without that line, a model would happily sum every order, including cancellations and returns, and report a number several times too high (Step 6 measures it), which nobody would notice until finance did. Step 3 · Schema linking: show the model only what it needs Enterprise warehouses have thousands of tables; putting them all in the prompt is expensive and confuses the model. Schema linking selects the relevant tables and columns first, by matching the question against table and column descriptions (with embeddings or a model call in production). Text-to-SQL by narrowing (as in Uber's QueryGPT): each step shrinks what the model must read, from thousands of tables to a few columns, so generation sees a small, relevant schema. Copy What you should see Copy Step 4 · Validate every query before it runs Model-written SQL is untrusted input. Parse it with a real SQL parser (here sqlglot ) and enforce rules on the parsed tree, not with string matching: exactly one statement, and it must be a SELECT only allowlisted tables a row limit, added if missing the caller's tenant filter, injected into the query so it cannot be forgotten or bypassed Copy What you should see Copy Validation is one layer. The others are just as important: connect with a read-only database role that can see only the allowed schemas (so even a validator bug cannot write), and let the database enforce row-level security where it supports it (Postgres row-level security, Databricks row filters). Step 4b · Verify the tenant filter cannot be bypassed Step 4 injects cust.tenant_id = 1 into the outer WHERE . Before trusting it, attack it. Three queries a model (or a prompt injection later · 15.24 ) could produce: Copy What you should see Copy Three holes. The scalar subquery counts all 40 customers across both tenants, while the outer filter scopes only the rows it sits on (30 rows, each carrying the leaked total). The CTE named ord reads cust for both tenants, and the outer filter on the real cust cannot touch it; the row cap trims the output to 200, but every one of those rows crosses the tenant line (the full result is 40 cities × 30 rows). The alias case is not a leak but a failure: cust.tenant_id does not exist once the table is called c . The fix: refuse CTEs, and apply the filter to every SELECT scope using the alias that scope actually uses. Any scope that does not read cust is refused, which also closes subqueries over other tables. Copy What you should see Copy The scalar subquery now counts only tenant 1 (the inner SELECT got its own filter), the CTE is refused, the alias works, LIMIT 50000 became LIMIT 200 , and the ordinary query is unchanged. Keep these four in a test file and run them on every change and every sqlglot upgrade: version 30 renamed the from and with argument keys to from_ and with_ , which silently breaks code that reads them. Derived tables in FROM ( SELECT ... FROM (SELECT ...) t ) are refused by the same rule because the outer scope sees no cust ; that is a deliberate loss of some legitimate queries in exchange for a rule you can reason about. Step 4c · Cost pre-check and a warehouse-level timeout The next step adds a timeout inside the Python process ( run_with_timeout , in Step 5), which cancels a query that runs too long. That protects this process; it does not protect the warehouse from a query that your process forgot about, or from a second client. Two more layers, both on the database side: Compile before you run. EXPLAIN parses and plans without executing. On SQLite it is cheap and catches bad columns; on Snowflake, EXPLAIN USING TABULAR also reports partitionsAssigned and bytesAssigned , which is an upper-bound estimate of what the query will scan, so you can refuse anything above a budget before spending a credit. A timeout the database enforces. On Snowflake, set STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS on the warehouse the agent uses (and in the session if you like; when both are set, the lowest non-zero value wins). Postgres has statement_timeout ; Databricks SQL warehouses have STATEMENT_TIMEOUT as well. The agent's warehouse should also be its own, small, with a resource monitor, so a runaway query cannot starve anyone else. Copy What you should see Copy Put explain_check between validate and run_with_timeout in Step 5's loop; its message goes back to the writer like any other error. On Snowflake replace the step-count stand-in with a check on bytesAssigned from EXPLAIN USING TABULAR , and keep the warehouse timeout regardless: the pre-check estimates, the timeout enforces. Step 5 · Generate, execute, self-correct The agent loop : build the prompt from the semantic context and linked schema, generate SQL, validate, execute with a timeout, and if anything fails, send the error back for one or two repair attempts. The generator below plays a model that makes a classic first mistake (forgetting the status-code lookup) and fixes it when shown the error. Copy What you should see Copy The database's own error message ("no such column") was enough for the repair. Two more practices from production systems: show the SQL next to the answer so analysts can check it, and answer only from the result set (the summarizing model gets the rows, not freedom to add numbers). Step 6 · Evaluate by execution accuracy Two correct queries can look completely different, so comparing SQL strings is useless. Execution accuracy runs the generated query and a gold query and compares the result sets. Public benchmarks (Spider 2.0, BIRD) use the same idea; your own set of verified questions matters more. Copy What you should see Copy The last line is why the semantic layer exists: the naive query is valid SQL, runs without error, and overstates Pune's revenue more than threefold. An eval set of verified questions with gold SQL catches this class of silent error; a "did it run?" check never will. Google Cloud : BigQuery data agents and the Conversational Analytics API, Looker's semantic model ( Lesson 15.30 ). Azure : Fabric data agents over lakehouses, warehouses and Power BI semantic models, usable from Foundry agents ( Lesson 14.156 ). AWS : Bedrock Knowledge Bases structured data (natural language to SQL over Redshift and the Glue catalog) and Amazon Quick for business users ( Lesson 14.153 ). In production Design a text-to-SQL system right from day one Scope by domain : one curated subject area per assistant (orders, payments, marketing), not the whole warehouse. A semantic layer before prompts : table and column descriptions, synonyms, sample values for low-cardinality columns, metric definitions, and a few verified queries. This is where most accuracy comes from. Read-only execution as the user's role , with row limits, timeouts and cost limits, so permissions and masking apply automatically. Show the SQL and the assumptions with every answer, and ask a clarifying question when a term is ambiguous. An eval set of real questions with verified results , scored by comparing result sets. Logging of question, SQL, row count and user , so wrong answers can be traced and turned into new verified queries. The first prototype retrieved tables and sample SQL by similarity and degraded as tables were added. The version that worked chains narrow agents: an intent agent maps the question to a business-domain workspace, a table agent proposes tables for the user to confirm, and a column-prune agent trims schemas that were 40,000 to 60,000 tokens. Evaluation uses a golden set with verified intent, tables and SQL, scoring each stage separately. In a limited release, 78% of users said it cut their query-writing time. Uber Engineering Pinterest (2024): table selection by vector search over table summaries and summaries of historical queries, weighting table documentation more heavily, then an LLM picks the final tables for the user to confirm. Table search hit rate rose from 40% without documentation to about 90% with it, and first-shot acceptance of generated SQL rose from 20% to over 40%. Chen et al., arXiv Swiggy, Hermes (India, 2026 write-up): a Slack-based analyst over the company's data warehouse. Historical SQL was explained in natural language by an LLM, indexed, and retrieved as few-shot examples; a ReAct -style orchestrator checks completeness, looks up metadata, asks clarifying questions and attaches assumptions and confidence to every answer. The team reports SQL accuracy rising from 54% to 93% across versions.
