Frameworks appeared to package it, and many competed. Knowing what you built by hand in the Talking to models: APIs, messages, prompts and context and Agents from first principles sections lets you judge what a framework actually saves you. In plain words first Hand tools first, then power tools A framework packages the code every agent needs: the loop, tool plumbing, state, persistence, streaming, approvals, tracing . You wrote much of that by hand in the Talking to models: APIs, messages, prompts and context and Agents from first principles sections, so you know what each piece does. A framework saves that work and adds tested features, at the cost of learning its abstractions and depending on its choices. Use one when its features match what you need; write plain code when they do not. Four kinds of thing, all called "agent frameworks" Vendors use the word "framework" for products that solve different problems. Sorting them first saves weeks of confused comparisons. The four kinds of ' agent framework ' stack rather than compete: agent logic in a framework or harness, a durable runtime underneath when the process must survive failures, and a managed platform (or your own Kubernetes) around all of it. A typical enterprise build is: an agent framework or harness for the agent logic, a runtime underneath when the process must be durable, and a managed platform (or your own Kubernetes) to host it. LangChain later · 14.93 's documentation uses the same three-way split of runtimes, frameworks and harnesses . Do you need a framework at all? Often not at first. Anthropic's Building effective agents advises starting with direct model API calls, because many patterns are a few lines of code, and frameworks can hide the prompts and responses you need to see when debugging. You built a complete agent in about 80 lines in Lesson 14.57 . Reach for a framework when you need what it does well and would otherwise rebuild: durable state, approval pauses, streaming to a UI, multi-agent routing, tracing, or integration with a cloud's managed services. Industry practice What the adoption data says Datadog's State of AI Engineering report (April 2026) found that the share of organizations using an agent framework roughly doubled in a year, from about 9% to 18%, with LangChain, LangGraph, Pydantic AI and the Vercel AI SDK named most often. The same report warns that frameworks add operational complexity, and recommends using agent telemetry to find framework logic that a simpler custom workflow could replace. Two lessons: most teams still build without a framework, and the ones that adopt one should measure what it costs them. How this connects Where the side-by-side comparison is This lesson sorts the landscape and sets up the lab. It does not yet compare the frameworks with each other, because a comparison table means little before you have used any of them. The order from here is: LangChain and LangGraph in depth (the rest of this chapter), then the same ShopKart agent in eight other frameworks (the Other agent frameworks, compared section), and only then the side-by-side table and the method for choosing, in Lesson 14.127 . In plain words first The two names you will see most in this chapter LangChain is an open-source library of building blocks for applications that use language models: one interface to many model providers, prompt templates later · 14.94 , tools, structured output and a ready-made agent loop . Lessons 14.93 to 14.99 teach it. LangGraph is a second library from the same company, one level lower. It runs an agent as a graph: steps (nodes) connected by arrows (edges), with the state saved after every step so that a run can pause for a person, survive a crash and resume. LangChain's agent loop is itself built on LangGraph. Lessons 14.101 to 14.112 teach it. You do not need either to build an agent, as the Agents from first principles section showed. They are taught in depth here because they are the most widely used, and because every idea in them (the loop, tools, state, checkpoints, approvals, streaming) is one you have already built by hand. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What kinds of things are called agent frameworks? Worked answer. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What does a LangChain chat model give you over calling a provider's SDK directly? Worked answer. One interface across providers: the same message types in, an AIMessage out with standard usage_metadata and content blocks, and the same invoke , stream and batch methods, plus fallbacks, rate limiters and callbacks for tracing . That makes switching providers a configuration change and lets the rest of LangChain and LangGraph later · 14.101 work with any model. The cost is a layer between you and the provider: a brand-new provider feature may arrive in the SDK before the integration supports it, and debugging means knowing what the integration sent. Second, how the code reads usage: joining chunk text loses metadata, so merge chunks with + or use a usage callback. Third, whether the endpoint returns usage at all; some local servers do not. I would also make the pipeline fail loudly on missing usage instead of recording zero. A plausible wrong answer. "The provider is not billing streamed calls." Copy Why this came about Early LangChain code chained steps through special classes that were hard to inspect and stream. In 2023 LangChain introduced the Runnable interface and its pipe syntax ( LCEL ), so any step, a prompt, a model or a parser, could be composed and would support invoke, stream and batch the same way. The problem: glue code around every call ShopKart's support reply is a fixed pipeline: build messages from a template, call the model, take the text. Written by hand it is a few lines: Copy What you should see Copy That works. What it does not give you, without more code: streaming the text as it is generated, running many inputs in parallel, a trace that shows each step, and a way to swap the model or add a step without rewriting the function. A runnable is any LangChain component with the same methods as a chat model ( invoke , stream , batch and async versions). Prompts, models, parsers and your own functions are all runnables, and joining them gives you those methods for the whole pipeline. In plain words first Pipes between machines A runnable is anything with invoke : a prompt template , a model, a parser, a function. The | pipe connects them so the output of one becomes the input of the next, like machines on a production line: template fills in the message, the model replies, the parser pulls out the text. The chain itself is a runnable too, so it also has invoke , stream and batch for free. Idea 1 · A prompt template is a runnable that builds messages A prompt template is a prompt with named holes in it. You write the fixed parts once, mark the variable parts in curly brackets, and fill them in at call time. MessagesPlaceholder is a hole for a whole list of earlier messages. Build one and ask it which variables it expects: Copy What you should see Copy The template found its own variables. MessagesPlaceholder is where a list of earlier messages goes, which is how chat history enters a fixed prompt ( Lesson 11.27 covers how much history to keep). A template fails loudly when a variable is missing, which is what you want: Copy What you should see Copy A placeholder that may be empty can be declared with MessagesPlaceholder("history", optional=True) . Literal braces in a template, for example in a JSON example, must be doubled: {{ and }} . Idea 2 · The pipe joins runnables into a chain A chain built with the pipe operator. Each runnable takes one kind of value and returns another, and the pipe passes each output to the next step. Because every step has the same interface, the whole chain can be invoked once, streamed, run on a batch, or traced, without extra code. The LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) is the | operator: the output of the left side becomes the input of the right side. Copy What you should see Copy The chain is exactly the three calls written out: a dictionary goes into the prompt, a ChatPromptValue (the messages) goes into the model, an AIMessage goes into the parser, and a string comes out. Knowing the type between each pair of steps is most of what you need to debug a chain: almost every chain error is a step receiving a type it does not expect. And the whole chain has the runnable methods, with no extra code: Copy What you should see Copy Streaming passes through: the parser turns each AIMessageChunk into a piece of text as it arrives. Idea 3 · Parallel steps, and adding keys as data flows A dictionary of runnables is a RunnableParallel : every value gets the same input, they run at the same time, and the result is a dictionary. Plain functions become runnables with RunnableLambda : Copy What you should see Copy RunnablePassthrough.assign is the common shape for multi-step pipelines: keep everything you had and add the result of a step under a new key, so later steps can use both. It is how traces get readable names, how you filter runs by prompt version, and how your own code observes each step: Copy What you should see Copy LangChain added its own tag ( seq:step:2 , the model is the second step) to yours. Add one ordinary function at the end of a chain: Copy What you should see Copy A RunnableLambda needs its whole input before it can run, so the chain waited for the full reply and produced one chunk. With a real model, that turns a reply whose first words appear in a fraction of a second into one that appears all at once after several seconds. Steps after the model must be streaming-aware, or streaming quietly stops; the debugging exercise below fixes it. When a chain is the wrong tool A chain has a fixed order. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What is a runnable, and what does LCEL give you? Worked answer. A runnable is LangChain's common interface: anything with invoke , stream , batch and async versions, plus config for callbacks, tags and metadata. Prompts, models, parsers, retrievers and wrapped functions are all runnables. LCEL composes them with | into a sequence and with dictionaries into parallel steps, and the composite is itself a runnable, so streaming, batching, async and tracing work for the whole pipeline without extra code. I use it for fixed pipelines; agents and branching workflows go in LangGraph. A plausible wrong answer. "LCEL is LangChain's agent framework ." LCEL composes fixed steps; it has no loop in which the model decides what happens next. Follow-ups. What type flows between a prompt and a model, and between a model and a string parser? Debug a failure Streaming worked in development, but after a new step was added, users see the whole reply at once. Where do you look? Worked answer. At the new step and anything after the model. A RunnableLambda or any step that needs its whole input blocks the stream; it must be a streaming transform ( RunnableGenerator , or a parser that supports streaming). I would also check the infrastructure, because proxies that buffer responses cause the same symptom ( Lesson 11.22 ), by comparing chunk counts at the chain and at the client. A plausible wrong answer. "The model stopped streaming." The model still streams; something after it is collecting the chunks. Follow-ups. How would you test that a chain still streams? Defend a design A teammate wants to write all pipelines as plain Python functions instead of LCEL. Do you agree? Worked answer. For a short pipeline that never needs streaming or batching, plain functions are clearer and easier to debug, and I would accept them. Once the pipeline needs streaming through several steps, parallel steps, retries or fallbacks per step, or per-step tracing, LCEL gives those consistently, and the alternative is rebuilding them by hand. The deciding questions are which of those features we need, and whether the team can read LCEL fluently. A plausible wrong answer. "LCEL is always better because it is the framework's way." Abstraction is only worth it for the features you actually use. Follow-ups. Where would you draw the line between a chain and a LangGraph graph? If the model keeps answering in plain text, the run can loop until the recursion limit later · 14.96 ProviderStrategy(Schema) Sends the schema as the provider's native response_format , and parses the JSON reply One attempt: bad JSON or a provider that rejects the schema raises. A Union of schemas is refused when the agent is built AutoStrategy (a bare schema) Chooses before each model call: ProviderStrategy when the model's profile says structured_output is supported (or the model name is on a known list), ToolStrategy otherwise As whichever strategy it chose; a failure never switches strategy mid-run So the same agent code can behave differently on two providers: the bare schema resolved to a different strategy. In production, choose explicitly, set a recursion limit you can afford for ToolStrategy , and catch the error from ProviderStrategy . Small models are the weak spot: the AI Engineering from Scratch LangChain manual found a 4-billion-parameter local model returned no object from ToolStrategy in 39 of 39 tasks, while a plain extraction call with with_structured_output did as well as the best strategy on every model it tried. When the agent does not need tools for the final step, a separate extraction call is often the most reliable design. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How does a LangChain tool get from a Python function to the model, and back? Worked answer. @tool builds a schema from the function's name, docstring and type hints, or from an args_schema Pydantic model. bind_tools sends those definitions, in the provider's format, with each request. The model replies with tool calls, which LangChain normalizes into AIMessage.tool_calls with a name, parsed arguments and an ID. Invoking the tool with a call validates the arguments, runs the function and returns a ToolMessage carrying the call's ID, and that message goes back in the history for the next request. A plausible wrong answer. "The model runs the Python function." The model only asks; your process runs the function and sends the result back. Follow-ups. What happens if one of two parallel tool calls gets no ToolMessage ? Debug a failure An agent calls the right tool with a wrong argument format about one time in ten. What do you do? Worked answer. Read the schema the model actually receives ( convert_to_openai_tool ), and check that the description and the field descriptions say what a valid value looks like, with an example. Add the constraint to the schema, such as a pattern for IDs, and turn on the provider's strict mode if it supports that schema. Keep validation in the tool, return the validation error as a result so the model can retry, and measure the retry rate on a set of real questions before and after. A plausible wrong answer. "Lower the temperature ." It may reduce variety, but it does not tell the model what a valid argument is. Follow-ups. When would you normalize the argument in code instead of rejecting it? Defend a design Should tool errors raise, or be returned to the model? Worked answer. Return errors the model can act on: not found, already shipped, a malformed argument, a rate limit with a retry time. Raise errors that mean the system is broken or the action is unsafe to retry blindly: a missing credential, an unknown internal failure, a refused approval that a person must see. The model can recover from the first kind; the second kind should stop the run and alert someone, because a model retrying against a broken system wastes money and can repeat side effects. A plausible wrong answer. "Always return errors, so the agent never crashes." An agent that never stops can loop on a broken dependency and hide an outage. Follow-ups. Copy Why this came about LangChain's early agent classes were rigid and hard to customize, so in 2024 most teams moved agents to LangGraph later · 14.101 's prebuilt ReAct agent. LangChain 1.0 (2025) made that the standard create_agent , built on LangGraph, so simple agents and complex graphs share one runtime. The problem: the loop you wrote in Lesson 14.57 Your Agent class called the model, ran the tools it asked for, sent the results back and repeated until the model answered or a limit was hit, with a trace of every step. Every agent framework ships that loop. LangChain's is create_agent , and it runs on LangGraph, so the same agent later gains checkpoints, human approval and streaming without being rewritten. In plain words first Your loop, packaged An agent is a loop: ask the model, run the tools it asks for, send back the results, repeat until it answers in plain text (Lessons 14.56 and 14.57 ). create_agent is that loop, packaged: it builds a small LangGraph graph with a model node, a tools node and a rule that loops between them. Because it is a graph, the same agent can later save its progress, pause for approval and stream, without being rewritten. Idea 1 · An agent in one call create_agent takes a model, a list of tools and a system prompt , and returns a working agent: the whole loop from Lesson 14.57 , already written. Ask it about two orders and print every message it produced, so you can see the loop's steps in the result. Copy What you should see Copy The result is the agent's state , a dictionary whose messages key holds the whole run: your question, the model's turn with two tool calls , one ToolMessage per call, and the answer. This is the same sequence you built by hand in Lesson 14.95 and in Lesson 14.56 . When an agent gives a wrong answer, this list is the first thing to read. Idea 2 · The loop is a graph The agent that create_agent returned is not a special object. It is a small graph, the kind you will build by hand from Lesson 14.100 onward. Ask it for its nodes and edges: The loop that create_agent builds for you. The model either asks for tools, reads their results (the observation) and goes round again, or returns the final result. Figure: LangChain documentation , MIT . Copy What you should see Copy create_agent returned a compiled LangGraph graph with two working nodes. model calls the model. A conditional edge later · 14.100 then checks the reply: tool calls go to tools , which runs them and goes back to model ; no tool calls go to the end. That is Lesson 14.57 's while loop drawn as a graph, and Lessons 14.101 and 14.102 build the same graph yourself. Streaming shows each node's output as it finishes, which is how a UI shows "checking your order…" while the agent works: Copy What you should see Copy stream_mode="updates" yields what each node changed. Other modes ( values for the whole state, messages for tokens) are covered in Lesson 14.106 . Idea 3 · Limits Your Lesson 14.57 agent had max_steps . A LangGraph run has a recursion limit : the maximum number of steps (node runs) before it stops with an error. One round trip with one tool call takes three steps (model, tools, model), so a limit of 2 cannot finish: Copy What you should see Copy The default limit is high (10,000 in langgraph 1.2), so set your own per run in config , based on the longest run you expect. Idea 5 · Conversations: a checkpointer and a thread The agent keeps nothing between invoke calls unless you give it a checkpointer , which saves the state after every step, and a thread ID , which names the conversation: Copy What you should see Copy The second turn started from the four messages of the first. InMemorySaver loses everything when the process stops; Lesson 14.103 covers database checkpointers, resuming after a crash, and going back to an earlier step. A checkpointer is also what lets an agent pause for a person's approval and continue later (Lessons 14.97 and 14.104 ). Measure it: what each question costs The messages show how many model calls and tool calls a run made, which is where its cost and latency come from ( Lesson 14.61 ): Copy What you should see Copy A greeting costs one model call; any question that needs a lookup costs at least two, however many tools run in parallel. That is why an agent is the wrong tool when every request takes the same fixed steps: a chain ( Lesson 14.94 ) makes one call where an agent makes two or more. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What does create_agent actually run? Worked answer. A LangGraph graph with a model node and a tools node. The model node calls the chat model with the system prompt, the messages and the bound tools. A conditional edge sends a reply with tool calls to the tools node, which runs them, in parallel when there are several, and appends ToolMessage s; then control returns to the model. A reply without tool calls ends the run, or, with response_format , produces a structured response. Because it is a graph, checkpointers, streaming, interrupts and middleware all apply to it. A plausible wrong answer. "It is a chain that calls tools." A chain has a fixed order; the agent decides at every step whether to call more tools. Follow-ups. Where would you add a step that runs before every model call? Debug a failure An agent sometimes fails with GraphRecursionError. What do you check? Worked answer. Whether the run was legitimately long or looping. In the trace I look for the same tool called with the same arguments again and again, which usually means a result the model cannot use: an empty result, an error it does not understand, or a result message that does not match the call. I fix the tool's result, add a repeat check or call limits, and set recursion_limit from the longest legitimate run plus a margin, so loops fail fast. A plausible wrong answer. "Raise the recursion limit." That turns a fast failure into a slow, expensive one. Follow-ups. How would you end a run gracefully at the limit instead of raising ( Lesson 14.97 )? Worked answer. create_agent when the work is one model choosing among tools in a loop, plus the standard extras that middleware covers: approval, summarization, limits, fallbacks. My own graph when the control flow is mine to decide: fixed steps before or after the agent, routing between specialists, parallel branches that merge, or a workflow where the model only fills in parts. Often both: a custom graph whose nodes include create_agent agents. A plausible wrong answer. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in LangGraph A library for building agents as graphs of steps with saved state, so runs can pause, resume and branch Lesson 14.101 Sandbox An isolated environment where an agent's code or actions cannot reach anything important Lesson 15.25 About the model on this page The model on this page is the lab rig chat is a real LangChain chat model pointed at mockllm ( Lesson 14.92 ), which follows fixed rules. Everything around the model, the middleware , interrupts and checkpoints, is the real library. Copy Why this came about Teams kept forking create_agent to add trimming, retries, approvals or model switching. Following the pattern web frameworks used for decades, LangChain 1.0 added middleware : hooks around each model and tool call , so behaviour can be added without rewriting the loop. The problem: the agent loop needs hooks The plain create_agent loop from Lesson 14.96 cancels an order the moment a customer asks. Production agents need more than the loop: a person approving risky actions, a cap on how many model calls a run may make, history that is summarized before it overflows the context window , personal data kept away from the model. In Lesson 14.57 you added risky and approve hooks to your own Agent class for this. Middleware is LangChain's set of hooks around the loop, and a library of ready-made ones. Idea 1 · Where middleware runs Middleware is code that runs at fixed points of the agent loop : before the model is called, around the model call, around each tool call, and after the model replies. The four small functions below do nothing except print a line when they run. Attach them to an agent, ask one question, and the printout shows you the order of the hooks. Where middleware runs in the agent loop. Node-style hooks (before and after) run at fixed points and can read or change the state. Wrap-style hooks surround the model call or a tool call, so they can change the request, retry it, replace the result, or skip the call entirely. Copy What you should see Copy Read the output as a timeline. Each model call is surrounded by before_model , wrap_model_call (which receives a handler ; calling it is the model call) and after_model . Each tool call runs inside wrap_tool_call . There are also before_agent and after_agent , which run once per invocation. Every built-in middleware below is made of these hooks: Hook Runs Typical use before_agent , after_agent Once per invoke Load or save per-user data, final checks before_model Before every model call Trim or summarize history, redact input wrap_model_call Around every model call Retries, fallbacks, choosing a model or tools per call, dynamic prompts after_model After every model call Approval of tool calls, limits, output checks wrap_tool_call Around every tool call Retries, timing, error handling, logging Hooks can also change things, not just watch: a before_model hook can return {"messages": ...} to update the state, and a wrap_model_call hook can change request (its messages, tools or model) before calling handler . There are two shapes of hook, and the difference explains most of what follows: In plain words first Checkpoints on a road, and wrappers around a call Node-style hooks ( before_agent , before_model , after_model , after_agent ) are checkpoints the agent passes: your function sees the state and may return changes to it, or a jump. What they return is saved in the agent's state. Wrap-style hooks ( wrap_model_call , wrap_tool_call ) wrap one call, like a decorator ( Lesson 0.23 ). Your function gets the request about to be sent and a handler that performs it; you may change the request, call the handler, retry it, or skip it. Changes to the request affect that call only and are not saved. The same loop in plain Python, with the hook points marked, shows where each runs: Copy What you should see Copy Plain Python above LangChain middleware before_model(messages) at the top of the loop @before_model , receiving state and runtime wrap_model(call_model) returning a wrapper @wrap_model_call , receiving request and handler inner(messages) inside the wrapper handler(request) : the real call, through any inner middleware The while True loop The graph create_agent builds A request carries messages , system_message , tools , model , state and runtime (with context and store ); request.override(...) returns a copy with some of them replaced. Idea 2 · Human approval: pause, decide, resume Some tools should not run until a person agrees. HumanInTheLoopMiddleware names those tools. When the model asks for one, the run stops and returns a description of the pending call. Your application shows it to a person and then resumes the same run with their decision. Because the run has to be found again later, the agent needs a checkpointer and a thread ID. Watch a cancellation pause and then continue: Copy What you should see Copy The model asked to cancel; HumanInTheLoopMiddleware stopped the run in its after_model hook, before the tool ran, and returned an interrupt describing the request. The checkpointer saved the state, and next shows where the run will continue. Nothing is waiting in memory: the decision can come minutes or days later, from another process, such as an approval dashboard. You resume by invoking the same thread with a Command : Copy What you should see Copy A rejection becomes a ToolMessage with your reason, so the model can tell the customer what happens next; an approval runs the tool. This is Lesson 14.60 's waiting_for_approval and decide , built on LangGraph later · 14.101 's interrupt and Command , which Lesson 14.104 uses directly. In plain words first Two places, two people Approval needs two decisions, by two people, at two times. At setup, the developer writes the policy in interrupt_on : which tools pause, and which answers a reviewer may give. At run time, the reviewer decides each case , and that answer goes into Command(resume=...) . The policy, one entry per tool: interrupt_on value Meaning False , or the tool left out Never pause True Pause, and allow all four decisions {"allowed_decisions": [...]} Pause, and allow only those {..., "when": fn} Pause only when fn(request) returns True for this call {..., "description": "..."} The text the reviewer sees The reviewer's four decisions: Decision Shape What the model sees approve {"type": "approve"} The tool's real result edit {"type": "edit", "edited_action": {"name": "cancel_order", "args": {...}}} The result of the edited call, plus a note that a reviewer changed it reject {"type": "reject", "message": "..."} An error result: "User rejected the tool call..." respond {"type": "respond", "message": "..."} Your text as a successful result, as if the tool returned it Never use respond to deny: the model would believe the action succeeded. It is for tools that ask the customer a question, where the reviewer's reply is the answer. The resume shape depends on interrupt_mode . The default, "batched" , is what you just used: one pause per model turn, whose value lists every gated call under action_requests , answered with {"decisions": [...]} , one decision per action, in the same order . With "per_call" , each gated call is its own pause, answered by interrupt ID. A when function narrows the gate to the risky calls, here high-value orders only: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output A-1003 is not in HIGH_VALUE , so when returned False and the tool ran without a pause. A-1002 paused. In per-call mode the interrupt's value describes one call: type ( "tool_approval" ), name , args , plus tool_call_id and description . The resume maps that interrupt's ID to one decision. In batched mode the same answer would be {"decisions": [{"type": "approve"}]} . Mixing up the two shapes is the most common approval bug. when runs again on resume, so it must give the same answer for the same call: no clocks or lookups that can change. Idea 3 · Limits that end a run gracefully Lesson 14.57 's loop had a step limit so that a confused agent could not run for ever. The middleware version is a pair of counters: one for model calls, one for tool calls. With exit_behavior="end" the run stops cleanly with what it has so far, without raising an error. Here the limit is set to one model call, so that you can see it trigger: Copy What you should see Copy With run_limit=1 the agent ran the tool but was not allowed a second model call, so the middleware ended the run with a message instead of raising. exit_behavior="error" raises instead, which suits batch jobs where a half-answered run should fail loudly. thread_limit caps calls across a whole conversation, and ToolCallLimitMiddleware does the same for one tool or for all of them. Compare recursion_limit ( Lesson 14.96 ), which counts graph steps and always raises. Idea 4 · Summaries before the context overflows Lesson 11.27 compacted long conversations by hand. SummarizationMiddleware does it in before_model : when the history passes a trigger, older messages are replaced by a summary written by a model you choose, and the most recent ones are kept as they are. Copy What you should see Copy The thread stays at four messages: a summary, then the recent turn. The lab rig's "summary" is its fixed sentence; a real model writes one, guided by a default prompt that asks for the session's intent, decisions, artifacts and next steps. Triggers can be a message count, a token count, or a fraction of the model's context window. The middleware never splits a tool call from its result, which would break the conversation ( Lesson 14.56 's rule). Idea 5 · Personal data never reaches the model PIIMiddleware finds personal data in the messages, such as an email address, and replaces it before the request leaves your process. To prove that it works, a second small middleware prints exactly what the model is about to receive: Copy What you should see Copy The email address was replaced before the first model call (it prints twice because the agent made two model calls, both with the redacted text). Strategies are redact , mask (keep the last characters), hash and block (raise). Built-in detectors cover email, credit card, IP, MAC address and URL; you can pass your own regex or function, for example for Indian phone numbers or PAN numbers. Because redaction changed the message in the state, the original address is not saved in checkpoints either. Lesson 15.23 covers what pattern-based detection misses. The order of middleware When several middleware wrap the same call, the order of the list matters. The first one listed is the outermost: it sees the request first and the response last, like the layers of an onion. Three tagging functions make the nesting visible: Copy What you should see Copy The first middleware in the list is the outermost: its before_* hooks run first and its after_* hooks run last, like nested function calls. Order is a design decision. Put redaction before anything that logs messages, or the log holds the personal data. Put retries inside fallbacks, so a model is retried before you give up on it. LangChain splits the job into swappable parts: a splitter cuts documents into chunks, an embedding model turns text into numbers so similar meanings are close, a vector store keeps and searches those numbers, and a retriever is anything you can ask for relevant chunks. You built each part by hand in the Retrieval (RAG) section; here each becomes a component you can swap without rewriting the rest. Idea 1 · Split documents, keep their metadata LangChain's splitters do the chunking of Lesson 14.70 . Their useful extra is that every chunk keeps the metadata of the document it came from (the source, and here the start position), which is what citations and filters need later. Split the help-centre pages and look at three chunks: Copy What you should see Copy RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter is Lesson 14.70 's recursive chunking : try the first separator, and split further with the next only when a piece is still over chunk_size . And every chunk kept its document's metadata, plus a start_index , so a citation can point to the exact place in the source. Idea 2 · Embeddings behind an interface Every embedding model in LangChain has the same two methods: embed_documents for the texts you index and embed_query for a question. Every integration ( OpenAIEmbeddings , BedrockEmbeddings , GoogleGenerativeAIEmbeddings , HuggingFaceEmbeddings , CohereEmbeddings ) implements the same two, so swapping models is one line. Copy Why this came about Testing code that calls a model is slow, costly and non-deterministic, and debugging an agent without seeing its steps is guesswork. Fake models for tests, callbacks and LangSmith tracing (2023) were developed to make LLM applications testable and observable. The problem: tests that call a model are slow, costly and flaky A test that calls a real model costs money, takes seconds, and can fail because the model worded something differently. But most agent bugs are not about wording: a tool is not registered, a result is not matched to its call, a middleware is in the wrong order, an approval is never resumed. Those bugs can be tested with a fake model that returns replies you script, so the test checks your code and nothing else. Quality, whether the real model chooses well, is a separate question for evals . LangChain ships fake chat models. The obvious one fails with an agent: Copy What you should see Copy create_agent binds the tools to the model before its first call, and GenericFakeChatModel does not implement bind_tools . In plain words first A stand-in actor for rehearsals Tests that call a real model are slow, cost money and change their answers from run to run. So tests replace the model with a scripted stand-in that returns exactly the replies you wrote, the way a director rehearses with a stand-in actor. Then the test checks what your code did with those replies: which tools ran, with what arguments, in what order. Callbacks and tracing are the recording side: a callback is a function LangChain calls at each event (model start, tool end), and a trace in LangSmith is the full recording of a run. Idea 1 · A scripted model that accepts tools A test should not depend on what a real model happens to say today. A scripted model is a stand-in that replays a list of replies you wrote in advance, including the tool calls . This small class adds one method to LangChain's fake chat model so that create_agent accepts it. The agent built on it behaves the same way on every run: Copy What you should see Copy The fake returned the scripted tool call, the real tools node ran your real tool, and the fake returned the scripted answer. Everything except the model's choices was real, which is exactly what a unit test should exercise. Idea 2 · Tests that check behavior, not wording With the model scripted, a test can assert what the agent did : which tool it called, with which arguments, what the tool returned and what reached the user. These are ordinary pytest functions. Note what they do not check: the exact wording of a real model's reply, which changes from run to run. Copy What you should see Copy The assertions check what matters: which tool ran with which arguments, what result went back, and what the run ended with. Run them with pytest like any other tests; they take milliseconds, so they can run on every commit. Building a tiny graph engine by hand shows what LangGraph adds before you use it. In plain words first A graph is a loop with names on the steps An agent loop , a workflow, a pipeline with branches: all are steps connected by rules about what runs next. An execution graph writes that down explicitly: nodes are the steps, edges are the rules, and a shared state carries the data between them. Building a tiny engine by hand in this lesson shows what LangGraph really does: run the next node, merge its result into the state, save a checkpoint, decide where to go. Orchestration graphs: why agents became state machines An agent loop ( Lesson 14.57 ) lets the model decide every step. A state graph writes the control flow down: nodes are functions that read and update a shared state, edges say what runs next, and conditional edges choose the next node from the state. Cycles allow retries and loops, a checkpoint after each node makes runs resumable, and an interrupt pauses the graph for a person. The model still makes decisions inside nodes, but the shape of the process is code you can test, draw and review. This is the design behind LangGraph, and the reason "least autonomy that works" ( Lesson 14.62 ) is easy to express: a workflow is a graph with few branches, an agent is a graph with a loop. The refund workflow as a state graph: conditional edges branch on state, a loop retries the lookup, the approval node can pause the run, and every step is checkpointed. Hands-on · A state-graph engine, from scratch Before using LangGraph, build its core yourself. It is about forty lines. A graph holds named nodes (functions that take the state and return an update), edges (what runs next) and conditional edges (a function that looks at the state and picks the next node). The engine starts at the first node and keeps going until it reaches the end. Read the class, then the refund workflow built with it underneath. Copy What you should see Copy The linter catches the orphan node before anything runs: in a large graph, unreachable nodes, edges to missing nodes and branches with no path to END are real bugs. The run loops once on lookup (the order service failed the first time), decides that 7,999 needs approval and pauses, with every step checkpointed. The process could now stop for hours. When a person approves, the run resumes from the last checkpoint, the approval node runs again and sees the approval, and the refund completes. The step budget turns an accidental infinite cycle into an error instead of a bill. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up StateGraph LangGraph's graph builder: nodes and edges over a typed state Idea 1 Reducer A function that says how an update to a state key combines with its current value Idea 3 About the model on this page No model on this page Every node here is a plain Python function, so the graphs run identically every time. LangGraph does not need a model at all; models are just one thing a node can call ( Lesson 14.102 ). Copy Why this came about Agents built with simple chains could not branch, loop or wait, so in January 2024 LangChain released LangGraph , describing agents as graphs of nodes over shared state, with reducers to merge updates safely. The problem: your engine merges state with dict.update The engine you wrote in Lesson 14.100 ran one node at a time and merged each node's output into the state with {**state, **update} . That is fine until two things happen. Two nodes run in parallel and write the same key: which value wins? And some keys should accumulate rather than be replaced, like a conversation's messages or a list of checks. LangGraph's answer is a typed state with a reducer per key, and it gives you the rest of the engine, checkpoints, interrupts and streaming, on the same model. In plain words first A shared case file and a rule per field A LangGraph graph is a set of functions ( nodes ) that work on one shared dictionary (the state ), connected by edges that say what runs next. A node never returns the whole state; it returns only the keys it changed, and LangGraph merges them in. For most keys, merging means "replace". For some, such as a list of messages or log lines, it should mean "add to the end"; the per-key rule that decides is a reducer . Your Lesson 14.100 engine merged with dict.update ; reducers are what make parallel nodes and chat histories work. Idea 1 · State, nodes, edges The refund workflow from Lesson 14.100 , its first three steps, in LangGraph: Copy What you should see Copy Four parts, and you have seen each one before. The state schema ( RefundState ) names the keys the graph carries. Each node is a function that takes the current state and returns only the keys it changes, a partial update. Edges say what runs next; START and END are the entry and the exit. compile() checks the structure (an edge to a missing node fails here, like your engine's lint ) and returns a runnable, with invoke , stream and batch ( Lesson 14.94 ). Idea 2 · Watch the state change graph.stream runs the graph and hands you something after every step. Ask for values and you get the whole state each time; ask for updates and you get only what the node that just ran returned. Run the same input both ways and compare: Copy What you should see Copy stream_mode="values" yields the whole state after each step; stream_mode="updates" yields only what each node returned, keyed by node name. The updates view is the one to read when debugging: it shows exactly which node wrote which value. You can also draw the graph: Copy What you should see Copy Idea 3 · Parallel nodes and reducers State and reducers. Each node returns only the keys it wants to change. With no reducer, the new value replaces the old one. With a reducer, LangGraph combines the old value and the update, which is what lets two nodes that ran in parallel both add to the same list without one overwriting the other. After the lookup, ShopKart wants two independent checks, fraud and stock, which can run at the same time. Two edges out of one node make both targets run in the same step, and a list of sources on an edge waits for all of them: Copy What you should see Copy Both nodes wrote checks in the same step, and LangGraph refuses to guess which one wins. That is better than your engine, where the last one silently overwrote the first. Say how the updates combine with a reducer , a function from (old value, new value) to the merged value, attached to the key with Annotated : Copy What you should see Copy Without a reducer, a key's new value replaces the old one. With operator.add on a list, updates are appended. Any two-argument function works, for example a dictionary merge or "keep the maximum". Idea 4 · The messages reducer Conversations need a smarter reducer than appending, so LangGraph ships add_messages : Copy What you should see Copy It appends new messages, replaces a message that has the same ID (useful when a streamed message is finished, or a person edits a tool call before approving it), and deletes on RemoveMessage , which is how you trim history ( Lesson 14.105 ). MessagesState is a ready-made state with messages: Annotated[list, add_messages] , and create_agent 's state is built on it. Idea 5 · A public interface, private internals A graph's callers should not depend on its internal keys. Give it an input schema and an output schema: Copy What you should see Copy Callers send a message and get a decision; intent and order stay inside. This matters when the graph becomes a node inside another graph ( Lesson 14.107 ) or a deployed API ( Lesson 14.108 ), where internal keys would otherwise become part of the contract. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What are state, nodes, edges and reducers in LangGraph? Worked answer. The state is a typed dictionary that the graph carries from step to step. Nodes are functions that read the state and return a partial update. Edges decide which nodes run next, fixed or conditional, and several edges from one node run their targets in parallel in the same step. Reducers decide how an update is merged into a key: by default it replaces, and with a reducer such as operator.add or add_messages it accumulates. Two parallel writes to a key without a reducer are an error rather than a silent overwrite. A plausible wrong answer. "Nodes pass their output to the next node." Nodes write to the shared state; any later node can read any key. Follow-ups. When would you write a custom reducer? Debug a failure A key in your state keeps growing with duplicate entries. Where do you look? Worked answer. At the nodes that write that key. With an appending reducer, a node that returns the whole current list instead of only its new entries duplicates everything, and a node that mutates the state in place makes it worse. I would stream with stream_mode="updates" to see which node returned which value, then fix the node to return only its additions. A plausible wrong answer. "LangGraph is replaying steps." The duplicates come from what the nodes return, not from the runtime. Follow-ups. How would you remove old entries from such a key? Defend a design Why use LangGraph's state model instead of passing values between functions? Worked answer. Because the runtime needs to own the state to do the hard parts: save it after every step so a run can resume after a crash or a pause for approval, run nodes in parallel and merge their results deterministically, stream each update, and replay or fork from any earlier step. Passing values between functions is simpler for a short fixed pipeline, and there I would use plain code or LCEL . Once a workflow is long-running, branching or needs approvals, a shared, typed, checkpointed state is what makes those features possible. A plausible wrong answer. "It is just the LangGraph way of writing code." The state model exists because checkpointing and parallelism need it. Follow-ups. What should and should not go into graph state ( Lesson 14.103 )? Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Conditional edge An edge whose target is chosen by a router function after a node runs Idea 1 ToolNode A prebuilt LangGraph node that runs every tool call in the last message Idea 4 ReAct The reason, act, observe loop: model, then tools, then model again Idea 4 Runtime context Per-run values such as the user, passed to nodes but not saved in state Idea 5 About the model on this page What is real and what is a stand-in The graphs are real LangGraph . Most nodes are plain functions; the order service that fails twice is simulated with a counter. The agent in Idea 4 uses the lab rig ( Lesson 14.92 ) as its model. Why this came about Agents need to choose paths and repeat steps until done. Conditional edges, loops with limits and Command gave LangGraph explicit control flow, and the agent loop itself became one small graph. The problem: real workflows branch and repeat The refund workflow from Lesson 14.100 is not a straight line. A question that is not about a refund goes to a person. The order service sometimes fails, so the lookup is retried, but not forever. And the agent loop itself, model then tools then model again, is a cycle that ends when the model stops asking for tools. Edges that always go to the same node cannot express any of that. In plain words first A dispatcher, a loop and a self-routing worker Real workflows branch and repeat. A conditional edge is a dispatcher after a node: it reads the state and names the next node. A loop is an edge back to an earlier node with a rule to stop. A node can also route itself by returning a Command (update the state and go there). And context carries per-run values such as the customer, which never change during the run and are never saved. Idea 1 · Conditional edges An ordinary edge always goes to the same node. A conditional edge calls a small function, the router , which reads the state and returns the name of the node to run next. In this refund workflow a classify node records the customer's intent, and the router sends refund requests one way and everything else another: Conditional edges, drawn. A diamond is a function that reads the state and names the next node: here the document type picks one path, and a second check picks the tool. Figure: Hugging Face, Agents Course , Apache 2.0 . The checkpointers are the real libraries, including a real SQLite database file. Copy Why this came about Agents that ran in memory lost everything on a crash or redeploy. LangGraph built in checkpointers from the start, borrowing durable execution from workflow engines, so every step is saved and runs can resume, be inspected and be replayed. The problem: runs outlive processes A refund run waits for an order service that is down, or for a person's approval that comes tomorrow. Meanwhile the process restarts for a deploy. In Lesson 14.60 you wrote run state to JSON files after every step so that a run could resume; in Lesson 14.100 your engine appended checkpoints to a list. LangGraph does this for every graph with a checkpointer : after every step, the whole state, what runs next and some metadata are saved, grouped by thread . The idea in plain words In plain words first Autosave with named save slots A checkpointer saves a copy of the state after every step, the way a game autosaves. The thread ID is the name of the save slot: call the graph again with the same thread ID and it loads that slot and carries on; a new thread ID is a new game. Each saved copy is a checkpoint . The whole idea in plain Python: Copy What you should see Copy Plain Python above LangGraph The saved dictionary A checkpointer: InMemorySaver() , or SQLite and Postgres savers thread_id {"configurable": {"thread_id": "..."}} in the config Loading the latest snapshot Done for you on every invoke Appending after each step Done for you after every step saved["chat-1"] graph.get_state_history(config) What LangGraph adds is everything hard to write yourself: real databases, the full history for going back (Idea 4), and records of unfinished work so a crashed or paused run can continue (Idea 3 and Lesson 14.104 ). A checkpoint holds the whole state , not just messages: every key, what runs next, and metadata. Idea 1 · A checkpointer and a thread Compile the same kind of graph with a checkpointer and it saves the state after every step. The saves are filed under a thread ID that you pass with each call. Run the graph, then ask for the saved state of that thread: everything the run produced is still there, along with which node would run next. Checkpoints and threads. With a checkpointer, LangGraph saves the full state after every step, filed under a thread_id. Invoking again with the same thread_id continues from the last checkpoint, in the same process or a new one. Any earlier checkpoint can be loaded, and running from it starts a new branch without erasing the original. Copy What you should see Copy get_state returns a snapshot of the thread's latest checkpoint: the state's values , the nodes that will run next (none: the run finished), and metadata such as the step number. The thread ID in config chooses the thread; one thread per conversation or per case is the usual design ( Lesson 14.96 used one per customer conversation). Idea 2 · The history of a thread The checkpointer keeps every save, not only the latest. get_state_history returns them newest first. Each one records which step it was, which node was due to run next, and what the state held at that moment: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Read it from the bottom up to replay the run: - step -1 , next ('__start__',) , no keys: the input arrived but is not in the state yet. - step 0 , next ('classify',) : the input was written into the state ( msg ); classify is due. - steps 1 and 2 : each node finished and added its key ( intent , then order ); next names the node due after it. - step 3 , next () : refund finished; nothing is left to run. next is the column to read when debugging: empty means the run finished; a node name means it stopped before that node, because it crashed or is waiting for a person. One checkpoint per step, newest first: before anything ran (step -1), and after each node. This is what makes LangGraph runs debuggable after the fact: for any run, you can see the state at every step, not just the end. Idea 3 · Crash, then resume in a new process Now the order service is down, and the checkpoints go to a database file: Copy What you should see Copy The run failed in lookup . The checkpoint after classify was saved, and the snapshot records that lookup is next and why it failed. Now the service comes back, and a new process, with a new graph object and only the database in common, continues the thread: Copy What you should see Copy Invoking with None as input means "no new input, continue this thread". classify did not run again; lookup ran a second time, now successfully, and the run finished. That is durable execution : a run's progress survives failures and restarts, and only unfinished work is redone. In production the database is Postgres ( PostgresSaver from langgraph-checkpoint-postgres , which needs setup() once to create its tables), or the platform's built-in persistence ( Lesson 14.108 ). Idea 4 · Time travel: go back and branch A reviewer finds that the refund amount should have been INR 4,999. Go back to the checkpoint before refund , correct the state there, and run from that point: Copy What you should see Copy update_state writes a new checkpoint that branches from the old one (a fork ); the original history is kept, which is why the thread now has more checkpoints. Invoking with the fork's config runs only what came after that point. Uses: replaying a failed production run from just before the failure with a fix, testing "what if the tool had returned this", and letting a person correct an agent's state before it continues. What to keep in state Checkpoints save the state after every step, so the state's contents decide the cost and the risk: Keep : what the run must remember after a pause: messages, decisions, IDs, results of expensive steps. Do not keep : database connections, clients and secrets (pass them as context, Lesson 14.102 ), and large blobs such as files or images (store them elsewhere and keep a reference). Serialization : values must be serializable by the checkpointer's serializer, which handles JSON types, LangChain messages, Pydantic models and dataclasses. Checkpointers can encrypt state at rest with an encrypted serializer. Retention : every step of every thread is stored; plan deletion of old threads, both for cost and for data-protection rules ( Lesson 15.26 ). Solution D1 · A node is the unit of retry The money was sent, then the same node failed on the ledger. The last checkpoint was before the node, so the resume ran the whole node again and sent the money a second time. Two fixes, best together: put each side effect in its own node, so a later failure does not repeat it, and make the side effect itself idempotent with a key the payment provider checks ( Lesson 14.59 ). Worked answer. After every step, it saves the graph's state, the next nodes to run, pending writes and metadata, keyed by thread ID. That enables conversation memory across calls, resuming after a failure or restart from the last completed step, pausing for human input and resuming later, inspecting the state at every step of a past run, and forking from an earlier checkpoint to replay with changes. In production it is backed by a database such as Postgres. A plausible wrong answer. "It caches model calls." It saves the graph's state; caching model responses is a separate feature. Follow-ups. What should never be put in checkpointed state? Debug a failure After a resume, a customer got two confirmation emails. What happened, and how do you prevent it? Worked answer. The email was sent inside a node that then failed, or was interrupted, before the node finished. A resume reruns the whole node, so the email went out again. Prevent it by putting each external side effect in its own node at the end of what it depends on, by making side effects idempotent with a key the receiving system checks, and by recording "sent" in state immediately after the side effect. Then test the failure by making the step after the side effect fail. A plausible wrong answer. "LangGraph replayed the whole run." Only the unfinished node was rerun; the node design caused the duplicate. Follow-ups. How would you handle a side effect that cannot be made idempotent? Defend a design Durable execution in LangGraph checkpoints, or a workflow engine such as Temporal? Worked answer. LangGraph's checkpoints when the durability needed is the agent's own: conversation state, pauses for approval, resume after a crash, replay for debugging, all inside one graph. A workflow engine when the process spans many services, needs retries with timers over days, strict exactly-once activity semantics and mature operational tooling, or the organization already runs one; the agent can then run as an activity inside it ( Lesson 14.140 ). They also combine: a Temporal workflow that calls a LangGraph agent per step. A plausible wrong answer. "Checkpoints make LangGraph exactly-once." They make progress durable; side effects can still repeat unless nodes are idempotent. Follow-ups. Where would the approval wait live in each design? Why this came about Companies wanted people to approve risky agent actions, which means pausing for hours without losing state. LangGraph 's interrupt and Command(resume=...) (2024) built that on top of checkpoints. The problem: a decision that only a person may make A refund of INR 7,999 is above what ShopKart lets an agent approve alone. The run must stop, show a person what it wants to do, wait, possibly for hours, and continue with their decision, even if the process restarts in between. Your Lesson 14.100 engine did this with an interrupt flag in the state and a resume that patched the state by hand. LangGraph's interrupt function does it inside a node. The idea in plain words In plain words first Save the case and wait for a signature Human in the loop means: stop before the risky step, save everything, show a person what you want to do, and wait. When they answer, possibly hours later on another server, continue with their answer. Two consequences explain every rule in this lesson. Pausing needs somewhere to save the run while it waits: the checkpointer and thread from Lesson 14.103 . And LangGraph cannot freeze a Python function halfway through, so the paused node starts again from its first line when the run continues; the second time, the pause call returns the answer instead of stopping. The state is checkpointed, so the pause can last a second or a week. Here a refund above a limit asks for approval: Pausing for a person. When a node calls interrupt(), LangGraph saves the state and returns to your code with the question. Nothing is running while the person decides. Resuming with Command(resume=answer) starts that node again from its first line, and this time interrupt() returns the answer instead of pausing. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output version="v2" makes invoke return an object with two parts: out.value (the state so far) and out.interrupts (the pauses). Each interrupt has .value , exactly the dictionary passed to interrupt(...) , and .id , which you need when several pauses wait at once (Idea 4). next: ('approval',) means the run stopped inside approval and will re-enter it on resume. finish has not run. Calling interrupt(payload) stopped the run: the checkpointer saved the state, the payload came back to the caller (in out.interrupts with version="v2" , or under the __interrupt__ key with the default output), and the snapshot shows approval as the next node. The payload can be any serializable value; make it everything the person needs to decide, because they will see nothing else. In plain words first Signing every order, or watching the dashboard Human in the loop : the agent stops and waits for a person before a step. Like a manager who must sign every purchase order. Human on the loop : the agent runs on its own while people supervise: alerts, sampled reviews, the power to correct or stop a run. In the loop On the loop The agent Waits for a decision Keeps running The person Approver or editor Supervisor or auditor Blocks the work? Yes No Catches mistakes Before they happen During or after Best for Irreversible, costly or regulated actions Reversible, low-impact, high-volume actions In LangGraph, in the loop is interrupt in a node or HumanInTheLoopMiddleware ( Lesson 14.97 ), with a durable checkpointer. On the loop is not one feature: it is built from tracing ( Lesson 14.108 ), alerts on errors and spend, a review queue fed by sampled runs, and the ability to cancel a run or correct its state with update_state ( Lesson 14.103 ). How production systems use both: Risk tiers. Reading data and drafting replies run on their own and are monitored. Medium-risk actions run with sampled review afterwards. Refunds above a limit, cancellations of shipped orders, deletes and emails to customers need approval. Conditional gates. A when function ( Lesson 14.97 ) or a check in the node pauses only the risky cases, such as refunds above INR 5,000. Escalation on doubt. The agent pauses when a validator or guardrail later · 15.23 flags its output, not on every step. Asynchronous review. The pause is saved in Postgres; the request goes to a dashboard, Slack or email; someone answers hours later, and the run resumes on the same thread. Sampling audits. Reviewers check a share of autonomous actions; findings become evaluation cases and can tighten or relax the tiers. Controls for unattended work. A kill switch later · 15.26 , rate limits, spend and action budgets, anomaly alerts, and an audit log of who approved what. A trust ladder. Start with approval on most actions, collect the decisions, and move an action to on-the-loop only when it is approved almost every time and errors stay rare. Each mode has a typical failure. In the loop: delays, and reviewer fatigue , where people approve the fiftieth request without reading it; every pause needs a timeout and a safe default (deny or escalate). On the loop: a mistake lands before anyone notices, so it suits only actions that can be undone, and only when someone actually watches the alerts. That is the safe way to make an interrupt conditional. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How does interrupt work in LangGraph? Worked answer. Calling interrupt(payload) inside a node raises a special signal; the runtime saves a checkpoint, records the pending interrupt and returns the payload to the caller. The run is then finished from the process's point of view. To continue, the caller invokes the same thread with Command(resume=value) ; the runtime reruns the node from its start, and this time interrupt returns value . It requires a checkpointer, and because the node reruns, code before the interrupt must have no side effects. A plausible wrong answer. "The node waits on a blocking call until someone answers." Nothing blocks; the run ends and restarts from the checkpoint, which is why approvals can take days. Follow-ups. How are several interrupts in one node matched to answers? Debug a failure Approvals sometimes apply to the wrong refund. What would you check? Worked answer. How the approval reaches the run: the decision must resume the exact thread that paused, so the approval request must carry the thread ID, and the resume must be a Command , not new input. Then the payload: the person must see the order ID and amount from the state at the moment of the pause, not values looked up again later. Finally, conditional interrupts: a node whose branch changes between pause and resume can match an answer to a different interrupt. I would log thread ID, interrupt ID, payload and decision for every approval. A plausible wrong answer. "Two people clicked at the same time." Possible, but the common causes are a missing thread ID or a payload that did not show what was being approved. Follow-ups. How would you expire an approval that nobody answered? Defend a design interrupt in your own graph, or HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on create_agent? Worked answer. The middleware when the thing to approve is an agent's tool call: it already offers approve, edit, reject and respond, per tool, with a standard payload. interrupt in my own node when the decision is part of a workflow rather than a tool call, for example a refund over a limit, a missing piece of information only the customer has, or several sign-offs in parallel, or when the payload or validation is specific to the business. Both use the same mechanism and both need a checkpointer and an approval service. A plausible wrong answer. "Middleware for everything." Some decisions are not tool calls and have nothing for the middleware to hook into. Follow-ups. What would your approval service's API look like? It is not a language model. The trimming, middleware, store and namespaces are the real libraries. Copy Why this came about Users wanted agents that remember them across conversations, while long conversations outgrew context windows . LangGraph added a long-term store beside per-thread checkpoints, and middleware for trimming, summarizing and clearing context. The problem: two kinds of memory A checkpointer gives each thread its conversation ( Lesson 14.103 ). That raises two problems. A thread keeps growing, and every model call resends all of it, until it no longer fits or costs too much. And some facts belong to the customer, not to one conversation: "reply in Hindi", "refunds to UPI, please". Next week's conversation is a new thread and should still know them. Lesson 14.64 called these short-term and long-term memory. LangGraph handles the first in the thread's messages and the second in a store . In plain words In plain words first Your head and your notebook Short-term memory is what is in your head during one meeting: what was said a minute ago, what you are halfway through. When the meeting ends, it is gone. Long-term memory is the notebook you carry between meetings: a few short notes about each person ("replies in Hindi", "refunds to UPI"). You read it before the next meeting, even weeks later. In LangGraph the "head" is the thread's state, saved by the checkpointer under a thread_id ( Lesson 14.103 ). The "notebook" is a separate database called the store . A new thread starts with an empty head but the same notebook. The notebook fits in plain Python, as a dictionary that outlives each conversation: Copy What you should see Copy Every long-term memory system, LangGraph's included, is this notebook plus answers to four questions: whose page is it (the namespace ), how to find the right note among hundreds (search by meaning), who decides when to read and write (your code or the model), and when notes are written (during or after the conversation). This lesson answers them in that order, after first dealing with the head that keeps growing. Plain Python above LangGraph notebook A store: InMemoryStore() here, PostgresStore in production "C-42" as the page A namespace tuple: ("customers", "C-42", "profile") remember(...) , recall(...) store.put(namespace, key, value) , store.search(namespace, query=...) monday , tuesday Two threads, each saved by the checkpointer What a memory is, and what it is not. A memory is not a saved question and answer; the checkpointer already keeps the raw conversation. A memory is a short fact distilled later · 14.132 from conversations. From "I'm ordering a gift for my mother, please send refunds to UPI, and keep it short", three memories are worth keeping: "Buys gifts for family", "Refunds to UPI", "Prefers short replies". In one line: the checkpointer keeps what was said; the store keeps what was learned from it. Question Options Where in this lesson What kind of memory? Fact or preference (semantic), past episode, procedure or rule Lesson 14.65 has the full taxonomy How is it read? Automatically by your code every turn, or on demand by the model through a tool Ideas 5 and 6 When is it written? During the conversation (the "hot path"), or after it by a background job Idea 7 The three choices are independent: any kind of memory can be read either way and written at either time. Trim the saved thread, or only what the model sees There are two places to apply that trim, and the difference matters more than the trim itself. In plain words first The archive and the photocopy Option A, change the saved thread. Delete old messages from the state. The checkpointer saves the shorter version, and the deleted turns are gone from the thread for good. Like shredding the old pages of a case file. Option B, change only the request. Just before each model call, send a trimmed copy . The saved thread stays complete. Like photocopying the last few pages for the model while the full file stays in the archive. Middleware ( Lesson 14.97 ) gives you both. A @before_model hook returns state updates, so its RemoveMessage really deletes. A @wrap_model_call hook receives the request about to be sent, and request.override(messages=...) changes that one request only: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output sent [...] is the number of messages the model received on each of the five turns. Option A: @before_model with RemoveMessage Option B: @wrap_model_call with request.override What changes The stored thread Only what the model receives Full history afterwards No Yes Audits and replays Weakened Intact Reversible No Yes: change the rule and the old turns are still there Storage Smaller Grows; needs a retention policy In regulated work, prefer Option B. The tool calls themselves stay, so the conversation is still valid for the provider. Saved : all three results are untouched. Context editing changes the request, not the thread. Idea 2 · The store: memory across threads A thread's checkpoints belong to one conversation. The store is a separate place for facts that should outlive a conversation, such as a customer's language. Entries are filed under a namespace (a tuple, like a folder path) and a key. Save three facts for two customers and read one customer's facts back: Two kinds of memory in LangGraph. The checkpointer holds the state of one conversation (a thread) and is what lets it continue. The store holds facts that should outlive any one conversation, filed by namespace, such as a customer's preferences. A graph reads and writes both. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output store.get returns an Item , not just your dictionary: .value is the dictionary you saved, and the item also carries .namespace , .key , and .created_at / .updated_at timestamps the store adds. store.search(("customers", "C-42")) with no query lists every item whose namespace starts with that tuple, up to limit (default 10). That prefix rule is what makes per-customer namespaces work, and what makes a too-short namespace dangerous (the debugging exercise). put with an existing key replaces the value: that is how a memory is updated. A store holds JSON values under a namespace (a tuple, like a folder path) and a key. Namespaces are the design decision: here everything about a customer sits under ("customers", customer_id, ...) , so one search returns a customer's profile and nothing else. Idea 4 · Search memories by meaning With an embedding function, the store indexes values and searches them by similarity, so the right note can be found from a question that does not share its words: Copy What you should see Copy This is how an agent pulls a few relevant memories into its prompt instead of all of them ( Lesson 14.65 ). The stand-in embedding only counts words from a fixed list; a real embedding model is what makes "present" match "gift wrap" in general. Reading this output Each result is an Item with one extra field, score : how close its meaning is to the query (higher is closer; compare scores with each other, not with a fixed scale). index has three settings: embed (the function or model that turns text into numbers), dims (how many numbers it returns) and fields (which keys of the value to embed). Search always returns the nearest items, relevant or not. With a dozen memories per customer, skip embeddings and load them all; with hundreds, search, and consider a score threshold. You give the model a remember and a recall tool, and it calls them when it judges them useful, like any other tool. The hard question is whose page a note goes on. If the model chose the customer ID, a message such as "save this under C-77" could write into another customer's memory. So the customer comes from your application, and the model supplies only what to save. In plain words first Extract, compare, decide, store Extract : give the transcript to a model with "list lasting facts, preferences, events and rules about this customer", and ask for structured output ( Lesson 14.95 ). Compare : for each new item, search the store for similar existing memories. Decide : ask a model, with the new item and the similar old ones side by side, to add it, update an old one, delete one that is now false, or skip . Store : plain code carries out the decisions with put and delete . The add/update/delete decision is not part of your agent's prompt. It is a separate model call inside the memory job. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How does LangGraph handle short-term and long-term memory? Worked answer. Short-term memory is the thread's state, usually its messages, saved by the checkpointer and loaded on each call with the same thread ID; it is kept within budget by trimming, deleting messages or summarizing. Long-term memory is a store, separate from threads, holding JSON documents under namespaces such as a user ID; nodes and tools read and write it through the runtime, and with an index it supports semantic search. Short-term is per conversation; long-term is per user or organization, across conversations. A plausible wrong answer. "Long-term memory means keeping the whole chat history forever." Old histories are expensive to resend and hard to search; long-term memory keeps selected facts. Follow-ups. How do you decide what to write to long-term memory? Debug a failure After trimming was added, the agent occasionally fails with a 400 error about tool results. Why? Worked answer. The trim boundary sometimes falls between an assistant message with tool calls and its tool results, leaving results without their calls, which providers reject. Set start_on="human" (and keep the system message), or trim by whole turns, and add a test with a long history ending in a tool call. If turns are large because of tool results, clear old tool results instead of whole turns. A plausible wrong answer. "The model is producing bad tool calls." The calls were fine; the trimming removed them. Follow-ups. How would you trim when a single tool result is larger than the budget? Defend a design Should an agent decide for itself what to remember? Worked answer. Partly. The model is good at spotting candidate facts, so I let it propose memories, through a tool or an extraction step, but the application decides the namespace from authentication, filters what categories may be stored, records when and where each fact came from, and lets the customer see and delete it. The problem: one graph for everything does not scale ShopKart's support system grows: refunds, tracking, cancellations, returns, each with its own rules, owned by different teams. Send fans a list out to as many copies of a node as there are items and gathers the results with a reducer. A supervisor is a routing node that passes control to specialist agents and receives it back.
