Retries, timeouts, handlers and caching are the real LangGraph features. Copy Why this came about Agents in production met flaky APIs, slow tools and partial failures. LangGraph added declarative retries, timeouts, error handlers and caching per node, bringing reliability patterns from distributed systems into the graph. The problem: one flaky service fails the whole run ShopKart's refund workflow calls a payment service that fails now and then, an order service that sometimes hangs, and a courier API that can be down for an hour. In Lesson 14.59 you wrote retry loops with backoff, deadlines and an idempotency key around each call. In a LangGraph graph, each of those is a setting on a node, so the policy is visible in the graph definition and applied the same way every time. In plain words first Plans for when things go wrong Every outside service fails sometimes. Each failure needs its own response, the way a careful person handles a bad phone line: retry if the line dropped, wait a little longer each time; hang up after a timeout ; when retries run out, an error handler does something sensible instead of crashing; a saga undoes steps already done when a later step fails; a cache avoids paying twice for the same work; and a graceful ending stops before a step limit with the best answer so far. Idea 1 · Retry the errors a retry can fix A RetryPolicy attached to a node tells LangGraph to run the node again when it raises one of the listed errors, waiting a little longer each time. The node below fails twice with a connection error and then succeeds, so the policy has something to do: Copy What you should see Copy The node failed twice with a ConnectionError , and LangGraph ran it again after a short wait each time ( initial_interval , multiplied by backoff_factor after each failure, capped by max_interval ; jitter adds randomness so many runs do not retry at the same moment). The third attempt succeeded. The important argument is retry_on : a dropped connection may work a second later, but a bad request never will. By default LangGraph retries most exceptions except obvious programming errors; be explicit for anything with side effects. Idea 2 · When retries run out: an error handler Some failures will not pass however often you retry. For those, a node can name an error handler : a function that receives the state and the error, and returns a Command that updates the state and chooses where the run goes next. Here a rejected payment routes to a node that tells the customer, and the run finishes normally: Copy What you should see Copy A RuntimeError is not in retry_on , so there was no retry; the error handler received the state and a NodeError (which node failed, and the exception), and returned a Command that recorded what happened and moved on to notify . The run finished with a useful state instead of an exception. Handlers are where you decide between "tell the customer", "try another route" and "park it for a person". Idea 3 · Timeouts, and why sync nodes cannot have them A hanging service is worse than a failing one: the run waits forever. Try a timeout on an ordinary function: Copy What you should see Copy LangGraph refuses at compile time, because Python cannot safely stop a running synchronous function from the outside. Make the node async , and the timeout works, with the same error handler mechanism: Copy What you should see Copy For synchronous code, set a timeout on the client inside the node instead (the HTTP library's or the SDK 's timeout ), so the call itself gives up. Idea 4 · The saga: undo what already happened A return takes three steps: reserve a pickup slot, send the refund, book the courier. If the courier fails after the refund was sent, stopping is the worst outcome: money gone, nothing collected. A saga gives the failing step a handler that runs compensating actions for the steps before it, in reverse order: The saga pattern on a product return. Each step that changes the outside world has a matching undo. When a later step fails, the handler runs the undos for the completed steps in reverse order, so nothing is left half done. Copy What you should see Copy Each compensation must itself be safe to repeat ( Lesson 14.59 's idempotency), because a crash during the undo will run it again on resume ( Lesson 14.103 ). Idea 5 · Cache expensive nodes If a node is expensive and gives the same answer for the same input, give it a CachePolicy . LangGraph then stores the node's result, keyed by its input, and skips the node while the entry is fresh. The list lookups records every real execution, so you can count how many calls the cache saved: Copy What you should see Copy Four runs, two node executions: the second and fourth runs for A-1077 reused the cached result, keyed by the node's input. ttl (seconds) sets how long a result stays valid; pass a key_func to choose what the key is built from. Cache only nodes whose output depends on their input alone, such as a policy lookup or a classification, never one with side effects. Idea 6 · End gracefully before the recursion limit The recursion limit ( Lesson 14.102 ) stops a runaway loop with an exception. Sometimes you would rather wrap up with the best answer so far. A RemainingSteps key is a managed value : LangGraph fills it with the number of steps left, and a router can act on it: Copy What you should see Copy With a limit of 8, the loop searched six times and then ended with an honest message rather than a GraphRecursionError . Idea 7 · Long work: idle timeouts and heartbeats A hard timeout is the wrong tool for work that is slow but healthy, such as exporting thousands of orders. LangGraph 1.2 adds TimeoutPolicy with two limits: run_timeout , a hard cap that never resets, and idle_timeout , which resets every time the node shows progress. Writes, stream output and callbacks count as progress, and a node can say so itself with runtime.heartbeat() : Copy What you should see Copy Four chunks of 0.15 seconds each passed, because every heartbeat reset the 0.4-second idle timer; the hang after them was caught 0.4 seconds later, long before the 3-second hard cap. A NodeTimeoutError goes to the retry policy and then to the error handler like any other failure. Use refresh_on="heartbeat" in the policy when only your own heartbeats should count as progress. Idea 8 · Stop cleanly for a deploy: drain A deploy sends your process a shutdown signal while runs are in the middle of their work. Killing them leaves each run wherever it was. LangGraph 1.2 lets a run stop at the next superstep boundary instead: pass a RunControl to the run, and call request_drain() from your shutdown handler. The run saves a checkpoint, raises GraphDrained , and resumes later from exactly that point: Copy What you should see Copy The drain was requested while reconcile was running. LangGraph let that step finish, saved the checkpoint, and stopped before report . The resumed run, which in production starts on a new worker after the deploy, ran only report . Drain needs a checkpointer, and it waits for the current step, so give nodes timeouts shorter than your platform's shutdown grace period. A model client retrying 6 times inside a node retrying 3 times inside middleware retrying 2 times makes 36 calls for one failure. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How do you make a LangGraph workflow resilient to failing services? Worked answer. Per node: a RetryPolicy with backoff, jitter and an explicit retry_on list of transient errors; timeouts on async nodes or on clients; an error handler that returns a Command to recover, notify, compensate or park the run; caching for expensive pure nodes. Across the graph: checkpoints so runs resume after crashes, RemainingSteps or limits so loops end gracefully, idempotent side effects so retries and resumes are safe, and a dead-letter queue for runs nothing can fix. Retries at several layers multiplied: the SDK's own retries, a node RetryPolicy , and middleware or application retries. Keep retries in one layer, use backoff with jitter, add a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing provider for a while ( Lesson 14.59 ), and fall back or fail fast when it is open. A plausible wrong answer. "Increase max_attempts so more requests succeed." That makes the storm bigger. Follow-ups. Which layer should own retries in a LangGraph agent? Copy Why this came about Tools needed to update agent state, not only return text, and companies wanted to share tools across agents through MCP. LangChain added tools that return state updates, MCP adapters and more powerful middleware to meet both needs. The problem: tools that only return text So far every tool returned a string for the model to read. Real agents need more. A tool that identifies the customer should remember them for the rest of the conversation, so later tools use the right account without the model passing the ID around. Tools should come from the systems that own them, over MCP, not be copied into every agent. And some rules need to act on the loop itself: stop the run, count calls across the conversation, or send hard questions to a stronger model. In plain words first Tools that change things, tools from elsewhere, rules on the loop So far tools only returned text. Here a tool can update the agent's state (remember the selected customer), tools can come from other teams' MCP servers instead of being copied into every agent, and middleware can act on the loop itself: stop a run, keep its own counters, or choose a different model per call. Idea 1 · A tool that writes to the state This tool finds a customer by email. An ordinary tool would return a sentence. This one returns a Command that does two things: it stores the customer's ID in the agent's state, and it supplies the ToolMessage the model is waiting for. A second tool then reads the ID from the state, so the model never has to repeat it. Two kinds of tool. An ordinary tool returns text that only the model reads. A tool that returns a Command also writes to the graph's state, so later nodes, tools and middleware can use what it found. Copy What you should see Copy ToolRuntime is a parameter LangChain fills in and hides from the model: it carries the agent's state , the tool_call_id , the run's context and the store ( Lesson 14.105 ). select_customer returned a Command that set customer_id in the state, and open_orders read it from runtime.state . The model never saw or passed the ID, which is also safer: an ID kept in the state cannot be changed by a manipulated tool argument. The state key is declared in a custom state_schema . runtime. field What it holds Set by state The agent's current state, including messages and your own keys The graph context Per-run data such as the signed-in customer ( context_schema= ) Your application, on each call store Long-term memory across threads ( Lesson 14.105 ) store= on create_agent config The run's config, including thread_id The caller tool_call_id The ID of this tool call The model's request stream_writer A function that sends progress to custom streaming ( Lesson 14.106 ) The graph Why the ToolMessage inside the Command ? Normally LangChain turns a tool's return value into a ToolMessage carrying the call's ID, which the provider requires: every tool call needs a matching result. A tool that returns a Command takes over that job, so it must include the ToolMessage itself, with runtime.tool_call_id . Leave it out and the next model call fails, which is the debugging exercise. Idea 2 · Tools from an MCP server How this connects MCP in five lines, and where it is taught The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is taught in the Protocols section; this section only uses it, so here is all you need. An MCP server is a small program that offers tools (and sometimes data and prompt templates ) in a standard format. Any agent that speaks MCP can connect to the server, ask "what tools do you have?", and call them, without code written for that particular server. The team that owns a system writes its server once, and every agent in the company can use it. The connection is either a local subprocess (called stdio ) or a web address. If you would like to see a server built before you connect to one, read Lesson 16.26 first. It takes 25 minutes and needs only Lesson 14.58 . langchain.mcp connects to MCP servers and turns their tools into LangChain tools. It has been part of langchain itself since 1.4 (install langchain[mcp] ) and replaces the older langchain-mcp-adapters package. MCPAdapter decides the transport from what you give it: a URL string means a remote server over HTTP, a Path means a local script started as a subprocess, and you can also pass an in-process FastMCP server, a fastmcp.Client , or a dictionary of several servers. Copy Copy Why this came about Coding agents in 2025 showed that long tasks need a harness: files, planning, subagents and context compaction . LangChain released Deep Agents as an open harness built on create_agent and middleware. The problem: long tasks need more than a loop "Investigate why last night's refund export failed and write an incident note" is not one question. It needs a plan, notes that outlive the context window , side investigations that should not flood the main conversation with log lines, and limits on what the agent may change. Lesson 14.67 called this a harness : the loop plus planning, files, subagents and context management. deepagents is LangChain's harness, built on create_agent and LangGraph , so everything from this chapter (checkpoints, interrupts, streaming, middleware) still applies. In plain words first The engine and the car The model is an engine; create_agent adds a steering wheel, a loop that lets it call tools. A harness is the rest of the car, the parts long trips need: a place to keep notes and large results (files), the ability to send a helper on an errand who reports back (subagents), a route plan (a to-do list), automatic summarizing when the context fills up, and fences around what it may change (permissions). Deep Agents is LangChain's harness, built from middleware on LangGraph. Idea 1 · What the harness gives the model Create a deep agent with no tools of your own and ask what tools the model was offered anyway. The list that prints is the harness: a file system, a to-do list and a way to start subagents, added before you wrote anything. Copy The parts of a harness, grouped by job: somewhere to act (the execution environment), a way to keep the context small (context management), a way to hand work off (delegation), and a way for people to step in (steering). Figure: LangChain documentation , MIT . What you should see Copy File tools ( ls , read_file , write_file , edit_file , delete , glob , grep ) and task , which delegates work to a subagent . Large tool results can be written to files instead of kept in the conversation, which is the harness's main context-management trick: the agent keeps a short reference and reads back only what it needs. Idea 2 · Files as working memory The harness gives the agent files. By default they live in the agent's state, not on your disk, so they are saved with the conversation and cost nothing while they are not being read. The scripted model writes a short report to a file and reads it back: Copy What you should see Copy By default the files live in the agent's state (a "state backend"), so they are saved with the thread's checkpoints and survive restarts, but are private to that thread. Other backends store them elsewhere: StoreBackend in the long-term store ( Lesson 14.105 ), so files survive across conversations; FilesystemBackend on a real disk; CompositeBackend to route paths, for example /memories/ to the store and everything else to the state; and sandbox later · 15.25 backends for running code. Watch out Host-access backends: for your laptop, not for a server Two backends touch the real machine. FilesystemBackend(root_dir="./work") reads and writes real files; LocalShellBackend(root_dir="./work") adds an execute tool that runs shell commands with your user's permissions and no sandbox. They exist so that a coding assistant can edit the project on your own computer. Do not put them behind a web server, an API or anything multi-tenant: the agent can read any file it can reach ( .env , keys), and once there is a shell, path rules are no protection at all. In deepagents 0.7.41 virtual_mode defaults to True , which blocks .. and paths outside root_dir ; the docs page still describes the older default, so set it explicitly, and treat it as a guardrail later · 15.23 , not a sandbox. The library's own advice: approval middleware on every call when you use these locally, and a sandbox backend ( Lesson 15.25 ) when the agent must run code for other people. Large results are offloaded for you A tool result above a threshold (20,000 tokens by default) never enters the context. The harness writes it to /large_tool_results/<tool_call_id> and hands the model a short note with a preview and the path; the model reads back only the part it needs. The same happens to conversation history when the harness summarizes: the folded-away messages go to /conversation_history/<session_id>.md . Copy What you should see Copy The 216,000-character log was saved, not sent. With artifacts_root="/scratch/" on a CompositeBackend , both offload folders move under /scratch/ , so a /memories/ route or a project folder never fills up with logs. Idea 3 · Subagents with their own context A subagent is a second agent that the main agent can start with the task tool. It gets its own instructions, its own tools and a fresh, empty context. It does the noisy work, such as reading long logs, and returns only a summary, so the main agent's context stays small. Define one that reads logs, and have the main agent hand it a job: Copy What you should see Copy The main agent called task , the log-reader subagent ran with its own system prompt , tools and model, and only its final answer came back as the tool result. The log lines it read never entered the main conversation. That isolation is the point: each subagent has a clean, focused context, and the main agent stays short. Give subagents fewer tools and narrower prompts than the main agent, and a cheaper model where the task allows ( Lesson 14.107 compares this with other multi-agent shapes). Idea 4 · Planning with a to-do list Long tasks drift. A to-do list that the agent writes and updates keeps the plan in front of the model at every step. With TodoListMiddleware the model gets a write_todos tool, and the list is stored in the state where your application can show it: Copy What you should see Copy In deepagents 0.7 the to-do tool is not in the default tool set; add TodoListMiddleware when the work benefits from an explicit plan. The list is part of the state, so it is checkpointed, visible to a UI and readable after a restart, which is what lets a long task continue where it stopped. Idea 5 · Limit what the agent may change An agent that can write files needs limits on where. Permissions are a list of rules, checked in order: this one allows writing under /reports/ and denies writing anywhere else. The scripted model tries both a forbidden write and an allowed one: Copy What you should see Copy FilesystemPermission rules allow, deny or interrupt (ask a person, Lesson 14.104 ) for reads and writes by path pattern. The agent may write reports and nothing else; its attempt to change the payment config came back as an error it can read. Combine this with interrupt_on for risky tools, and run real file and shell backends inside a sandbox ( Lesson 15.25 ). Idea 6 · Skills and rules files Two file conventions from coding agents are built in. A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md : YAML front matter ( name , description ) and then the procedure. The harness lists only names and descriptions in the system prompt and the model reads the full file when a task matches ( progressive disclosure ), so long procedures cost nothing until needed. A memory file ( AGENTS.md style) is loaded whole into the system prompt on every run, inside an <agent_memory> block, with instructions to update it with edit_file when the user corrects the agent. Copy What you should see Copy With the default state backend the files come in through invoke(files=...) ; with FilesystemBackend(root_dir=...) the same paths are read from disk, which is how a team checks its skills and rules into git. Skills are cached per thread; after editing one, invoke with "skills_metadata": None to reload. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What is a deep agent, and what does the deepagents library add to create_agent? Worked answer. A deep agent is an agent with a harness for long tasks: a virtual file system for notes and large results, subagents with isolated contexts launched through a task tool, optional planning with a to-do list, pluggable storage backends, permissions on files, and human approval on tools. deepagents packages these as middleware on top of create_agent , so the result is a LangGraph graph with checkpoints, streaming and interrupts. Depth : Core. Time : about 50 minutes. Checked on 22 November 2026 with langgraph 1.2.24, langchain 1.5.2 and fastapi 0.162.0. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Cassette Recorded model replies replayed in tests instead of calling the model Idea 4 About the model on this page The model on this page is the lab rig chat is a real LangChain chat model pointed at mockllm ( Lesson 14.92 ). The FastAPI service runs for real, called through FastAPI's test client, and the checkpoints go to a real SQLite file. Copy Copy Why this came about Some companies cannot use a hosted agent service and need agents inside their own APIs and infrastructure. This lesson builds the serving layer by hand with FastAPI, showing what the platform would otherwise provide. The problem: you need the API without the platform Lesson 14.108 's Agent Server gives you threads, runs, interrupts and streaming over HTTP. Some teams cannot use it: the platform team runs everything on its own FastAPI stack, the license or data rules do not fit, or the agent is one feature inside an existing service. Then you build the thin service yourself. The hard parts are not the HTTP routes; they are durable state, approvals that resume the right run, and making sure one customer can never reach another's conversation. In plain words first Building the counter yourself Agent Server gives you a ready-made service. Sometimes you need your own: your company's API conventions, an existing web app, or a platform you already run. Then your web framework (FastAPI here) receives requests, checks who is calling, picks the right thread for that customer, calls the compiled graph, and streams the result back. Everything Agent Server did for you becomes a few lines you own, which is the point and the cost. Idea 1 · An agent behind your own API This is a complete small service: a FastAPI application with two routes in front of the agent from Lesson 14.97 . One route takes a customer's message and runs the agent; the other takes a person's decision on a paused action and resumes the run. Conversations are saved in SQLite, so they survive a restart. Read the two route functions first; the rest is set-up. Copy Two routes cover a conversation with approvals. A message runs the agent; if the agent pauses for approval, the route returns the pending action instead of a reply. A decision resumes the paused run with a Command ( Lesson 14.104 ). Calling it as a client would: Copy What you should see Copy The checkpointer is a database, so a paused cancellation survives a deploy, and the decision can come from another worker. In production, use PostgresSaver (or AsyncPostgresSaver with an async service), and move long runs to a background worker so the HTTP request does not wait for the whole agent. Idea 2 · Keep customers apart Keeping customers apart in your own service. The customer comes from the verified token, never from the URL, and it becomes part of every key the agent's storage uses. The thread ID is built from the authenticated customer and the conversation, never from the URL alone: Copy What you should see Copy Meera used Ravi's conversation number and found nothing to approve, because her requests address C-77:1 , not C-42:1 . An unknown token is refused before the agent runs. This is the same rule as memory namespaces ( Lesson 14.105 ): identity comes from authentication, and every key that stores customer data includes it. On Agent Server, the equivalent is a custom auth handler ( @auth.authenticate to identify the user, @auth.on to add an owner filter to threads), configured in langgraph.json . Idea 3 · Front ends and the v3 event stream LangGraph 1.2 added stream_events(version="v3") , which returns a run object with separate views over one event stream, instead of filtering chunks by mode yourself: Copy What you should see Copy The first model call produced no text, because it only asked for a tool; the second streamed the answer. Other views include values (state snapshots), tool_calls , subgraphs , interrupts and output . In langgraph 1.2.24 this API prints a warning that it is experimental, so pin your version if you adopt it, and keep the stable stream modes of Lesson 14.106 for code that must not change. Two things to know before you build on it. First, read each view as it arrives. A loop that reads all of a reasoning model 's thinking before it starts reading the answer will show the answer only at the end, even though its tokens arrived on time; the LangChain manual measured an answer appearing about 9 seconds late this way. Read views concurrently, or iterate the raw events. Second, from langchain-core 1.7 (October 2026) a streaming tool call arrives as tool-call-delta events that carry only the new part of the arguments, where older versions repeated all the arguments so far. Upgrade clients before servers: Python clients need langchain-core 1.6.13 or later, and the JavaScript framework packages ( @langchain/react and its siblings) 1.2.6 or later. For React front ends, LangGraph's useStream hook (from @langchain/langgraph-sdk/react ) connects to an Agent Server or a compatible API, and gives the component the messages as they stream, the thread, interrupts waiting for approval, a submit function and loading state: Copy LangChain's Agent Chat UI is a ready-made interface built on it, useful for internal tools and testing. Idea 4 · Tests in CI: record once, replay forever Tests that call a real model are slow and flaky; tests with hand-written scripts ( Lesson 14.99 ) drift from what the real model does. A cassette records the real model's replies once and replays them in CI: Copy What you should see Copy The replay used no network, but your tools ran again, so the test still checks your code. Re-record when you change the model or the prompt, and review the new cassette like code. Idea 5 · Evals as a pull-request gate The last check before a change is merged: run a fixed set of questions with known answers through the agent, compute the share it gets right, and fail the build if that share is under a threshold. Debugging exercise Debugging exercise: an approved refund that was never sent In a variation of the desk, approvals are resumed by a nightly job. One night the job resumed every waiting thread with input={"messages": [...]} containing the text "approved". The next morning, no refunds had been sent and every thread was still waiting. Using Lessons 14.104 and 14.108 , explain what happened and what the job must send instead. (Solution D1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Trace one turn redact replaces the email; triage sees "refund" and an order ID and routes to refund ; find_order finds INR 899; approve auto-approves it under the silver limit, so there is no interrupt; issue_refund sends it and replies. Saved: the redacted message, the route, the order ID, the amount, the outcome and the reply, as checkpoints on the new thread. Nothing goes to the store, because no preference was stated. Solution B1 · Order is a security property Every turn still gets an answer, but triage and anything it calls now see the original message, and if triage saved anything or logged it, the email leaks. The saved thread still ends up redacted, so the audit's email count stays 0, which is exactly why the order bug is easy to miss: the audit checks the wrong place. Guardrails go first, and tests should check what each node received, not only what was saved. Solution D1 · Input is not a resume Sending input to a waiting thread starts a new run from START . Each thread's new message went through redact and triage again; if it was routed to the refund flow, it paused at a new interrupt, and if not, it was answered as a new question. Either way, no interrupt was answered, so no refund was sent. The job must resume each thread with Command(resume={"approved": True}) (or command={"resume": ...} over the API), using the stored thread ID, and should log the interrupt it answered. Solution M1 · A returns route Add "returns" to the router (when the text contains "return" and an order ID), a node that looks up the status and replies "Return started for …" only when it is delivered , and an edge from it to END . Test it like test_redaction_replaces_the_message : call the node directly with a delivered order and with a processing one, and assert on the reply. Then add a routing test that sends both messages through triage . Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What is the difference between LangChain and LangGraph, and how do they fit together? Worked answer. LangChain is the component layer: chat model integrations, messages, prompts, tools, structured output, retrievers, and create_agent with middleware. LangGraph is the runtime underneath: a graph of nodes over a typed state, with checkpoints, interrupts, streaming, subgraphs and durable execution later · 14.140 . create_agent returns a LangGraph graph, so a team can start with LangChain's agent and drop to LangGraph when it needs custom control flow, using the same components inside its nodes. LangSmith is the separate platform for tracing, evaluation and deployment. A plausible wrong answer. "LangGraph replaced LangChain." They are layers; LangChain 1.x agents run on LangGraph. Follow-ups. Which LangChain pieces would you still use inside a hand-written LangGraph graph? Explain the mechanism Walk through what happens, step by step, when a LangGraph agent with a checkpointer handles one user message. Worked answer. The caller invokes the graph with the new message and a thread ID. The checkpointer loads the thread's last state, and the add_messages reducer appends the message. The model node calls the model with the history and bound tools; a checkpoint is saved. The conditional edge sees tool calls and goes to the tools node, which runs them in parallel and appends ToolMessage s; another checkpoint. Back to the model, which answers without tool calls; the edge goes to END and the final state is saved and returned. Middleware hooks run around the model and tool calls, and an interrupt at any point saves the state and returns its payload instead. A plausible wrong answer. "The agent keeps the conversation in memory between calls." The process keeps nothing; the checkpointer loads and saves it per thread. Follow-ups. How many checkpoints does that run write, and what is in each? Debug a failure Users of a LangGraph chat app sometimes see another user's earlier messages. What do you check? Worked answer. Thread identity first: how the app chooses the thread ID. A constant, a reused ID, or one derived from something users share, such as a session cookie that is not per user, puts two users on one thread. Then the store's namespaces, which must include the user ID from authentication. Then caching or streaming layers that might mix responses. I would reproduce it with two test users, check which thread each request used in the traces, and add a test that two users never share a thread or a namespace. A plausible wrong answer. "The model remembered the other user." Models keep nothing between calls; the state was shared. Follow-ups. How would you clean up after the leak was fixed? Debug a failure A LangGraph workflow sends duplicate emails after deploys. Why, and how do you fix it? Worked answer. A deploy stops runs mid-node, and on resume the interrupted node runs again from its start. If the email is sent inside a node that then does more work, or before an interrupt , it is sent again. Put the send in its own node so that it is checkpointed as soon as it finishes, make it idempotent with a key the email service or an outbox table checks, and record that it was sent in state. Test it by failing the step after the send. A plausible wrong answer. "Checkpoints should prevent repeats." They prevent repeating finished nodes, not the inside of an unfinished one. Follow-ups. How would graceful shutdown during deploys reduce this? Defend a design Would you choose LangGraph for a new production agent? What are the alternatives and trade-offs? Worked answer. For an agent that needs durable state, human approval, streaming and some custom control flow, yes: those are LangGraph's core, they are hard to build well, and the code is portable across hosting options. The trade-offs are another abstraction to learn and debug, version churn in a fast-moving ecosystem, and the commercial platform being separate from the open-source library. Alternatives: a provider SDK such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or the Claude Agent SDK for simpler agents tied to one provider, a workflow engine such as Temporal for long cross-service processes, or plain code with a checkpoint table for small agents. I would decide with a spike that builds our hardest path, approval and resume, in the top two candidates ( Lesson 14.127 ). A plausible wrong answer. "Frameworks are unnecessary; just write the loop." The loop is easy; durable pauses, resumes, parallel tool calls and streaming are not. Follow-ups. What would you pin and test to manage upgrades? Defend a design create_agent with middleware, or a custom StateGraph, for ShopKart's desk? Worked answer. Both, in layers, as in this capstone: the desk is a custom graph, because its control flow is ours (guardrail first, routing, a refund workflow with business rules and an approval), and the specialists inside it are create_agent agents, because a model choosing among a few tools is exactly what that loop does well. If the whole desk were one agent with a few tools, I would use create_agent alone with approval and limit middleware, and move to a custom graph only when a requirement did not fit the middleware hooks. A plausible wrong answer. "One giant agent with every tool and a long prompt." It is simpler to start, but harder to control, test and secure as rules grow. Follow-ups. Which parts of the desk would you evaluate separately? Explain the mechanism Why LangGraph? What does it give you that a while loop does not? Worked answer. A while loop is fine until the agent must survive a crash, pause for days for an approval, run steps in parallel and merge their results, stream progress, be replayed from any step for debugging, or be composed with other agents. LangGraph gives all of these on one model: typed state with reducers, nodes and edges including cycles, checkpoints per thread, interrupt and Command , stream modes , subgraphs, retry and cache policies, and a server runtime. The loop's logic is small; durable, observable, controllable execution is what you would otherwise rebuild. A plausible wrong answer. "It makes agents smarter." The model's intelligence is unchanged; the runtime makes behavior controllable. Follow-ups. Name a case where you would not use LangGraph. Explain the mechanism Compare LangGraph with the OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI and a workflow engine such as Temporal. Worked answer. LangGraph is a low-level, provider-neutral runtime: you design the graph, and get checkpoints, interrupts and streaming. The OpenAI Agents SDK is higher level and smaller: agents, handoffs , guardrails and sessions with less control-flow design, best with OpenAI models. CrewAI organizes role-based agents into crews and flows, quick for multi-role pipelines with less fine-grained control. Temporal is a general durable workflow engine for long, cross-service processes; it is not LLM -specific, and an agent can run as an activity inside it. Choose by how much control flow you must own and how long-lived and cross-service the process is. A plausible wrong answer. "They all do the same thing." They sit at different levels of abstraction. Follow-ups. How would you combine LangGraph and Temporal? Debug a failure An agent works in a notebook, and in production half the approvals never complete. Walk through your investigation. Worked answer. Check how approvals resume: the thread ID must be the paused thread's, built from the user, and the resume must be a Command , not new input. Check persistence: a database checkpointer shared by all workers, not InMemorySaver per process. Check deploys: renamed nodes or state keys break old checkpoints. Check timeouts: pending approvals without SLAs or reminders. Then add a dashboard of threads waiting at an interrupt, with their age. A plausible wrong answer. "The approvers are slow." Possibly, but the common causes are plumbing. Follow-ups. How would you migrate pending approvals across a breaking deploy? Mentioned here, taught later 1 Durable execution This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Durable execution Running a long task so that every completed step is saved and a crash resumes from the last one Lesson 14.140 About the model on this page The model on this page Idea 2 uses the lab rig from Lesson 14.92 , so the agent run is the same every time. Everything else is plain LangGraph with no model: the nodes are small functions, so you can see the runtime itself. Why this came about LangGraph runs a graph the way Google's Pregel system (2010) ran large graph computations: in rounds called supersteps, where every active node runs and all their messages are delivered together at the end of the round. That design makes parallel work predictable and gives a natural place to save a checkpoint. In 2025 and 2026, teams running agents for days and over thousands of steps found the edges of that design: write collisions that break a thread, side effects that repeat after a crash, and checkpoints that grow with the square of the conversation. LangGraph 1.2 (May 2026) added DeltaChannel and durability controls to address the last two. The problem: the graph works in tests and fails in production Three surprises reach every team that runs LangGraph for real. Two parallel nodes write the same key, and from then on every read of that thread fails, even the admin page that tries to look at it. A refund tool runs, the process is killed by a deploy a moment later, and the resumed run refunds the customer a second time. A long research thread that holds 100 KB of messages turns out to use 5 MB in the database. None of these are bugs in your nodes. They come from how the runtime plans, merges and saves each step, and each one has a clear fix once you can see the machinery. In plain words first A meeting with minutes Picture a meeting where everyone works at the same time, then the secretary collects all the notes at once and writes the minutes. That round is a superstep . Each topic in the minutes has a rule for combining notes: some topics keep one answer and complain if two people wrote different ones ( LastValue ), others add every note to a list ( a reducer ). After each round the minutes are filed ( a checkpoint ). If the building is evacuated mid-round, whoever had not handed in their note does that part of the work again, which is fine for thinking and not fine for sending money. And if every set of minutes is a full copy of all earlier minutes, the filing cabinet fills fast ( DeltaChannel files only the new notes). Idea 1 · One superstep: plan, run, update Every LangGraph run is a loop of supersteps. Plan : find the nodes whose input changed since they last ran. Run : execute all of them, in parallel. Update : apply all their writes at once, then save a checkpoint. A node never sees a write from its own superstep; it reads the state as it was at the end of the previous one. The update phase has a rule worth testing. Two nodes run in parallel and each appends to one list. One is slow and one is fast: Copy What you should see Copy The nodes finished in different orders, and the state was ['a', 'b'] both times. Before applying anything, the update phase sorts the tasks by their task path , a stable name the planner gave each task, and hands the writes to each reducer in that order. So the result never depends on which node was faster: you can test it, and two replicas of your service compute the same state. The other side of the rule: if your reducer keeps only the last value, the winner is the task whose path sorts last, not the one that finished last. Idea 2 · Watch an agent's supersteps create_agent ( Lesson 14.96 ) is a graph too, so its run is a series of supersteps. A checkpointer records one checkpoint per superstep, with the nodes planned for the next one: Copy What you should see Copy Five checkpoints for one question. Step -1 holds the input, step 0 the question in the state, step 1 the model's reply with two tool calls . Look at next after step 1: ('tools', 'tools') . create_agent turns each tool call into its own task with Send ( Lesson 14.107 ), so both lookups run in the same superstep, side by side, and both results land together at step 2. Step 3 has nothing next: the model answered without asking for a tool, so the loop stopped. The animated plate in Lesson 14.96 draws this same run. Idea 3 · Channels: how each key combines writes Every key of the state is stored in a channel , an object with one job: take all the writes for that key in one superstep and produce the new value. A key with no reducer gets a LastValue channel; a key with a reducer gets a BinaryOperatorAggregate . LangGraph also uses channels internally: a Topic collects the Send tasks, and an EphemeralValue carries the input and routing signals, then clears. You can drive them directly: Copy What you should see Copy Read the rows as the rules of the state. A plain key keeps its value when no node writes it, and refuses two writes in one step. A key with a reducer folds every write in (here 1 + 2 + 3 = 6). A Topic holds a step's items and clears when nobody writes. An EphemeralValue lives for one step only. The row to remember is the first one: two nodes that write a plain key in the same superstep raise InvalidUpdateError . Idea 4 · A collision that breaks a thread, and the repair The error itself is easy to understand. What happens to the thread afterwards is not. Two shipping nodes run in parallel and both set carrier , a key with no reducer, on a graph with a checkpointer: Copy What you should see Copy Both nodes ran before the error, because the collision is found in the update phase. Their outputs were already saved as pending writes of the checkpoint the step started from. Now every read of the thread replays those two writes into the same LastValue channel and raises again: get_state fails, a resume fails, a new message to the thread fails. Retrying does not help, and editing the state with update_state does not either, because the pending writes are still there. The repair is a schema with a reducer for that key, compiled against the same checkpointer: Copy What you should see Copy The saved writes now combine, the thread reads again, and the resume finished without running either node again : no model call or tool call was paid twice. The lesson for production: give a reducer to every key that two nodes can write in the same superstep, before you deploy, and add a test that runs parallel branches on a checkpointer. Idea 5 · What a checkpoint saves, and when A checkpointer has two write calls. put_writes saves the output of one finished task, as soon as it finishes. put saves the whole checkpoint at the end of the superstep. The durability mode of a run ( durability= on invoke and stream ) decides when they happen: Copy What you should see Copy Mode What is saved during the run What the run waits for After a crash "exit" Nothing until the run ends, fails or pauses at an interrupt Nothing The whole run starts again from the input; there is no history for time travel "async" (the default) Every checkpoint and every task's writes, in the background Nothing Repeats a task that had just finished, and any step after the last saved checkpoint "sync" The same as async Each checkpoint's put , before the next step starts Repeats a task that had just finished sync is the safest of the three, and it is still not a guarantee. put_writes for a finished task runs in the background in every mode, and sync only waits for the checkpoint at the end of the step. A task that returned a few milliseconds before the process died can lose its writes and run again on resume. The AI Engineering from Scratch LangChain manual measured exactly this: with a crash right after a node returned, the node ran again in 97 of 100 trials in sync mode and 95 of 100 in async mode; with 0.2 seconds between the return and the crash, it never did. One more trap from the same source: durability="sync" on a graph with no checkpointer raises an AttributeError instead of warning, so pass it only with a checkpointer. Idea 6 · Side effects: a checkpoint cannot undo them So a node can run twice. That is harmless for thinking and harmful for anything that changes the world: a refund, an email, a stock reservation. The script below pays a refund and is killed right after the payment, before the node returns, the way a deploy or an out-of-memory kill would do it. Save it next to your code: Copy Now crash it, resume it in a new process, and count the payments, first without a key and then with one: Copy What you should see Copy Without a key, the resume ran pay from its first line, because its writes were never saved, and the customer was refunded twice even in sync mode. With a key, the node first checked its own records, found the payment and skipped it. The rules, the same as Lesson 14.59 's: Give every side effect an idempotency key built from things that are the same on a re-run: the thread ID, the node, the order ID. Never use a timestamp or a random number. Check your records before acting, or let the service do it: most payment APIs accept an idempotency key and refuse a duplicate. Keep approvals and model calls out of the node that acts . A node that asks for approval with interrupt() and then pays will, after a crash, ask the reviewer again and may pay again ( Lesson 14.104 ). Idea 7 · Checkpoints grow with the square of a thread A checkpoint stores the state as it is after the step, so a list key is stored in full in every checkpoint. A thread of 100 steps that adds one item per step stores 1 + 2 + ... + 100 items in total. Measure it with a reader that adds one 1 KB page per step: Copy What you should see Copy The content was about 100 KB (the writes table stores each page once). The plain thread's checkpoints held about 5.2 MB, fifty times the content, and the number grows with the square of the thread's length. DeltaChannel , new in LangGraph 1.2 and still marked beta, stores only each step's writes plus a full snapshot every snapshot_frequency steps (100 by default), and rebuilds the value on read: about 160 KB here, a thirtieth of the plain thread. Its reducer receives every write of a step in one call, which is why append_all takes a list of batches. For an agent, swap the message channel by passing create_agent(..., state_schema=...) a subclass of AgentState whose messages key uses a DeltaChannel . Summarising long threads ( Lesson 14.105 ) helps too, because it shortens what every checkpoint has to hold. In the same manual's measurements, the framework's own work (planning, merging, saving) took under half a percent of a real agent's time; the model took the rest. Spend optimisation effort on bytes and model calls, not on the loop. Idea 8 · What survives a round trip through a checkpoint Everything in the state goes through the checkpointer's serializer ( JsonPlusSerializer , which writes msgpack) and comes back on the next step, after a resume, or on another server. Most values come back as they went in. Some do not: Copy What you should see Copy A node that calls .most_common() on a Counter works on the first step and fails after a resume, because what came back is a plain dict . A time zone comes back as a fixed offset, which is wrong across a daylight-saving change. A plain class cannot be saved at all. Keep state to plain JSON -like values, Pydantic models, dataclasses, enums and LangChain messages, and convert at the edges. Loading also has a security side. A checkpoint row names the type to rebuild, so whoever can write to your checkpoint database can choose what your process constructs. Treat the checkpoint store as trusted infrastructure, never as user input, and in production set LANGGRAPH_STRICT_MSGPACK=true , which makes the loader return raw fields instead of building classes that are not on its allow list. Putting it together Symptom Cause Fix InvalidUpdateError: At key 'x': Can receive only one value per step , then every read of the thread fails Two tasks wrote a key with no reducer in one superstep Add a reducer to the key and recompile on the same checkpointer; add a parallel-branch test Parallel results in an unexpected order The update phase applies writes in task-path order, not finish order Do not depend on which task finished first; sort explicitly if order matters A refund or email happened twice after a crash or deploy A node with a side effect ran again on resume An idempotency key and a records check in the node, or at the service No history to go back to The run used durability="exit" Use "async" (the default) or "sync" The checkpoint database grows far faster than the conversation Every checkpoint holds the whole message list DeltaChannel for long lists, summarisation, retention policies A value has the wrong type after a resume The serializer cannot round-trip that type Plain JSON-like types, Pydantic models, dataclasses In production The runtime in production Test with a checkpointer : many of these failures appear only when state is saved and reloaded. Run your graph tests on InMemorySaver and at least one test that resumes in a new process on SQLite or Postgres. Deploys are crashes : a rolling deploy kills processes mid-step. Combine RunControl.request_drain() on shutdown ( Lesson 14.109 ), which stops at the next superstep boundary with a resumable checkpoint, with idempotent side effects for the steps that were running. Retention : decide how long to keep checkpoint history per thread, and prune old checkpoints, or the database grows without limit even with DeltaChannel . Watch the bytes : alert on checkpoint size per thread, the same way you alert on token usage. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How does LangGraph execute a graph, step by step? Worked answer. In supersteps, after Google's Pregel model. Each superstep plans the tasks whose trigger channels changed since they last ran (plus one task per pending Send ), runs them in parallel, then applies all their writes at once through each key's channel, sorted by task path, and saves a checkpoint. A node reads the state as of the previous superstep, never a sibling's write from the same one. The run ends when a step plans no task, or at the recursion limit , which counts supersteps. A plausible wrong answer. "Nodes run one after another along the edges, and each sees the previous node's output immediately." That misses parallel steps and the all-at-once update. Follow-ups. Why does the update phase sort tasks before applying their writes? Debug a failure After adding a second branch, one customer's thread fails on every request with InvalidUpdateError, even reads. What happened, and how do you fix it without losing the conversation? Worked answer. Two tasks wrote a key with no reducer in the same superstep. The runtime raised in the update phase after both had run, and their writes were saved as pending writes, so every read replays the collision. Fix the schema with a reducer for that key (or make only one branch write it), recompile against the same checkpointer, and the thread reads and resumes without rerunning the nodes. Add a test that runs the parallel branches on a checkpointer. A plausible wrong answer. "Delete the thread." That loses the customer's history and does not stop the next thread from breaking. Follow-ups. Why does update_state not repair it? Defend a design Is durability="sync" enough to make a refund agent safe to retry after crashes? Worked answer. No. sync waits for each checkpoint, but a task that finished just before a crash can still lose its writes and run again, and a model can also simply ask for the same action twice. Safety comes from the side effect: an idempotency key built from stable values, checked against your records or passed to a provider that refuses duplicates, with the approval step in a separate node. Choose sync when losing a completed step is expensive, and keep the key either way. A plausible wrong answer. "Yes, sync writes every checkpoint before continuing." That confuses the checkpoint with the task's own writes. Follow-ups. Where should the idempotency key come from? Check yourself Predict the merge order of parallel writes, and explain it. Repair a thread broken by a write collision without rerunning its nodes. Choose a durability mode and say what a crash repeats in it. Make a side effect safe to run twice. A Only that run fails; the next one works B The colliding writes are saved, so reads and resumes keep failing until the key gets a reducer C LangGraph keeps the first write D The checkpointer deletes the thread Recompile with a reducer on the same checkpointer to repair it. Q3 Which durability mode keeps no checkpoint history during a run? A "exit" B "async" C "sync" D All of them keep history exit saves once, when the run ends or pauses. Mentioned here, taught later 1 Model Context Protocol (MCP) This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Model Context Protocol (MCP) An open standard for connecting models to tools and data through small servers, so one integration works in many apps Lesson 16.26 About the model on this page No model on this page The examples use LangGraph 's in-memory store and SQLite, so they run anywhere. The text says where Postgres or the Agent Server does the same job in production. Why this came about Lesson 14.112 put an agent behind your own API. The next problems appear only with traffic: a second worker process, a second customer, a customer who sends two messages before the first answer arrives. LangGraph's savers and stores do not know about users or workers; they store what you give them. These rules came from teams running agents as multi-user services in 2025 and 2026, and several of them were collected and measured in the AI Engineering from Scratch LangChain manual. The problem: a graph that is correct, run by a service that is not Your agent passes every test. In production, two requests for the same conversation reach two worker processes and both write to one checkpoint chain. A memory tool built its store prefix from a user ID that a client sent, and a crafted ID listed everyone's memories. A customer typed "also, cancel the other order" while the first run was still calling tools. None of this is in the graph; all of it is in how the service runs the graph. In plain words first One booking clerk per file A travel agency keeps one paper file per customer. Two clerks must never work on the same file at once, so the file gets a "taken" slip, and if a clerk goes home sick the slip is removed. Files of different customers sit in labelled drawers, and the clerk reads the label from the customer's ID card, not from what the customer says. And when a customer phones again while their booking is being made, the office needs a rule: wait, replace, or drop the second call. Idea 1 · One run per thread, across workers Within one process, a lock in memory is enough. With several processes, the lock must live where every process can see it, and it must be released when a process dies. Here is the pattern with a SQLite table, where a primary key refuses a second holder: Copy What you should see Copy One request ran and the other was refused with a 409, which the client turns into "still working on your last message". The weakness of this table is the crash case: a worker that dies holding the row leaves the thread locked until someone deletes it. In production on Postgres, use an advisory lock instead: pg_try_advisory_lock(hashtextextended(thread_id, 0)) on a connection the worker holds for its locks. Postgres releases it automatically when that worker's session ends, so a crashed worker frees its threads with no timer. Two details matter: hold lock connections outside the pool your checkpointer uses, or many held locks starve checkpoint writes; and an advisory lock can be taken again by the same session, so also track held thread IDs inside the worker. Adding workers buys availability, not speed, when the model server is the bottleneck. Measure where the time goes (Lessons 11.18 and 14.137 ) before adding processes. Idea 2 · Double texting: a new message while a run is going The lock answers "never run twice at once". It does not say what to do with the second message. LangGraph's Agent Server ( Lesson 14.108 ) makes this a per-request choice, the multitask strategy of a run: Strategy What happens to the run in progress What happens to the new message Use it for reject Continues Refused with an error Forms and workflows where a second message is a mistake enqueue Continues Runs after it, on the updated thread Chat, where every message should be answered in order (a common default for chat front ends) interrupt Stops at its next step; its progress is kept Runs now, seeing what the first run did "Also, cancel the other order" rollback Stops and is deleted as if it never ran Runs now on the state before it "Sorry, wrong order number" With your own service ( Lesson 14.112 ), you implement the same choice around your lock: reject is the 409 above, enqueue is a per-thread queue, and interrupt uses RunControl.request_drain() ( Lesson 14.109 ) on the running run before starting the new one. Whatever you choose, a side effect that already happened stays happened, so interrupt and rollback need the idempotency keys of Lesson 14.115 . Idea 3 · Keep users apart: the store, the savers and the approver A checkpointer stores threads by ID, and a store stores items by namespace. Neither knows who a user is. Two users' memories in one store: Copy What you should see Copy A search is a prefix match. Build the namespace from the full user ID, and any code path that searches a shorter prefix sees everyone. So: take the user ID from the authenticated request and pass it to tools through the run context ( ToolRuntime.context , Lesson 14.110 ), never as a tool argument the model fills in; refuse IDs that are empty or contain wildcard characters; and never expose list_namespaces or a raw search to users. The same goes for threads: keep your own table of which user owns which thread, check it on every route, and answer 404 (not 403) for someone else's thread, so the response does not confirm that the ID exists. Four other defaults to change before a multi-user launch: Boundary The default Change it to Loading checkpoints The loader rebuilds the classes a checkpoint row names LANGGRAPH_STRICT_MSGPACK=true , and a checkpoint database only your service can write ( Lesson 14.115 ) Tool approvals HumanInTheLoopMiddleware batches all calls of one model turn into one review interrupt_mode="per_call" (LangChain 1.4.6 and later): one review per call, answered by interrupt ID, with edits validated against the tool's schema so an edit cannot turn one tool into another MCP later · 16.26 servers MCPAdapter starts a local script when given a Path Never build the target from user input; a bare string is treated as a URL and refused if it is not one, so keep it that way ( Lesson 14.110 ) Tracing Traces hold prompts, tool arguments and results Redact before tracing ( Lesson 14.145 ), and check which runs actually leave the machine; the LangChain manual found that tracing_context(enabled="local") still sent agent runs to LangSmith , while enabled=False sent none And the approver is a separate identity: the customer who owns a thread must not be the person who approves its refund. Idea 4 · What the framework costs Running an agent through create_agent and LangGraph adds planning, merging and checkpointing around each model call. Measured against a hand-written loop on the same model, the AI Engineering from Scratch manual found about 5 ms per model call and no extra tokens; on the course lab rig, a two-call agent run took about 10 ms outside the model, and 10.3 ms with an in-memory checkpointer. A real model call takes hundreds or thousands of milliseconds, so the framework is rarely where the cost is. The costs that grow are elsewhere: Cost Why it grows What to do Input tokens per call Every call resends the whole thread Summarise or trim ( Lesson 14.105 ); cache the stable prefix ( Lesson 11.23 ) Checkpoint storage Every checkpoint holds the full message list DeltaChannel , retention policies ( Lesson 14.115 ) Harness prompts A Deep Agent sends its tool and planning instructions on every call Use the simplest harness that passes your evals ( Lesson 14.111 ) A failing trace endpoint Retries and timeouts on telemetry slow every run Send traces asynchronously, with a short timeout and a sample rate To price a conversation, measure token counts per turn on your real traffic, multiply by the provider's prices, and add storage and compute; do not estimate from the number of messages ( Lesson 14.142 ). In production Running it for real Workers : one lock per thread across processes (advisory locks on Postgres), a per-thread queue or strategy for double texting , and graceful drain on shutdown. Isolation : owner check on every thread route, user ID from auth into the run context, store namespaces built server-side. Safe defaults : strict msgpack loading, per-call approvals, no user-controlled MCP targets, redacted traces. Budget : alert on tokens per conversation and checkpoint bytes per thread, not only on errors. Solutions Solution P1 · Prefixes match whole parts An empty list: namespaces match by whole tuple elements, and "u-ra" is not the element "u-ravi" . The danger is in your code, not the store: if a route accepted a user ID and searched ("users",) when the ID was empty, or built a shorter prefix by mistake, it would return everyone's items. Validate the ID and build the full namespace in one function that every tool uses. Solution B1 · A lock that outlives its holder The row stays in the table, so every later request for thread-77 gets "409 busy" forever, until someone deletes the row. A Postgres advisory lock belongs to the database session that took it, so when the worker process dies, its connection closes and Postgres frees the lock at once. With a table lock you need a lease: store a timestamp, and let another worker take a lock older than the longest possible run. Solution M1 · A queue per thread Copy Copy A real service keeps the queue in the database next to the lock, so a message survives a crash, and the worker that releases the lock checks the queue before letting go. Check your understanding Defend a design Your agent service needs to scale. Do you add uvicorn workers or not? Worked answer. First find the bottleneck. If the model server or provider rate limit is the ceiling, more workers add availability and failover but not throughput; scale the model side or reduce tokens instead. If CPU-bound work in your service is the ceiling, workers help. Either way, more workers need a cross-process lock per thread (a Postgres advisory lock) and a database-backed queue for double texting, because in-memory locks no longer protect a thread. A plausible wrong answer. "Yes, more workers always mean more requests per second." Not when every request waits on the same model server. Follow-ups. How would you measure where the time goes? Debug a failure A customer reports seeing another customer's preferences in a reply. Where do you look? Worked answer. At how the store namespace and the thread ID reach the code. Check that the user ID comes from authentication into the run context, not from a tool argument or the request body; that every store access builds the full namespace in one shared function; that no tool can search a shorter prefix; and that every thread route checks ownership. Then search the traces for the tool call that read the wrong namespace. A plausible wrong answer. "The model hallucinated it." Possible, but a real cross-user leak must be ruled out first. Follow-ups. Why answer 404 rather than 403 for another user's thread? Check yourself Lock a thread across workers, and say what frees the lock when a worker dies. Pick a double-texting strategy for chat, for a form and for a correction. Keep store namespaces and threads per user, with the user ID from authentication. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Sandbox An isolated environment where an agent's code or actions cannot reach anything important Lesson 15.25 Why this came about After LangChain , the model providers themselves began shipping agent frameworks . OpenAI's experimental Swarm (2024) became the Agents SDK in March 2025: a small set of primitives (agents, tools, handoffs, guardrails, sessions) with tracing built in. It shows the same loop through a provider's eyes. In plain words first The same loop, from another vendor Every agent framework packages the same ideas you built in the Agents from first principles section: a model with instructions, tools, a loop, memory of the conversation, approvals and guardrails. The OpenAI Agents SDK names them Agent , function tools , Runner , sessions , approvals and guardrails . Reading it as a mapping ("this is the agent loop , this is the checkpointer") makes any framework quick to learn. What it is The OpenAI Agents SDK (Python and TypeScript, MIT licensed) is OpenAI's production successor to its experimental Swarm project. It keeps a small set of primitives: agents (a model with instructions and tools), handoffs (one agent passing the conversation to another), guardrails (checks that run alongside the agent), sessions (conversation memory) and tracing (on by default). Since April 2026 it also includes a sandbox harness : agents that read and write files, run shell commands and apply patches inside isolated containers from providers such as E2B, Modal, Daytona, Cloudflare and Vercel, with state stored outside the container so a lost sandbox later · 15.25 does not lose the run. It works with any model: OpenAI models natively through the Responses API , and others through any Chat Completions-compatible endpoint or the LiteLLM extension. Copy One run in the OpenAI Agents SDK. The Runner drives the loop you wrote in the Agents from first principles section; guardrails check the input and the final output, a tool that needs approval pauses the run, and the session keeps the conversation between runs. Step 1 · An agent with tools The same support agent you have built several times, now in the OpenAI Agents SDK. Three things to notice as you read. @function_tool turns a function into a tool, as @tool did in LangChain. Agent(...) only describes the agent: its name, instructions, model and tools. Runner.run(agent, question) is what runs the loop. The model here is the lab rig, so the code needs no key. Copy What you should see Copy With an OpenAI key, drop the model= argument (the default is a current OpenAI model over the Responses API) or pass model="gpt-5.5" . For other providers, point AsyncOpenAI at their OpenAI-compatible endpoint , or install openai-agents[litellm] and use LitellmModel . Runner.run is the async entry point; Runner.run_sync wraps it, and Runner.run_streamed streams events for a UI. The SDK runs the loop for you: call the model, run tools (in parallel when the model asks for several), repeat until a final answer or max_turns . Step 2 · Sessions and human approval Two additions. A session stores the conversation, so that the next message on the same session continues it. And cancel_order was declared with needs_approval=True , so a run that reaches it stops and reports what is waiting. Your code approves or rejects each waiting call and runs the agent again from the saved state: Copy What you should see Copy The run did not block a thread while waiting. to_state() gives you an object you can serialize to a database, which is how approvals survive a restart or wait for a reviewer in another time zone. Session backends include SQLite, Redis, SQLAlchemy (any SQL database), encrypted sessions, and OpenAIConversationsSession , which stores history in OpenAI's Conversations API. Step 3 · Guardrails Guardrails run in parallel with the agent and stop the run when they trip, so they add little latency. Input guardrails check the first agent's input; output guardrails check the final answer; tool guardrails wrap individual tools. Copy What you should see Copy A real input guardrail usually calls a small, cheap model (for example "is this request about ShopKart orders?") through its own Runner.run , so the expensive agent is stopped as soon as the check fails. An output guardrail checks the final answer before the customer sees it. Here a tool result leaks a staff email address, and the guardrail stops it: Copy What you should see Copy In production, catch the exception and send a safe fallback ("Let me connect you with a colleague") rather than an error. Tool guardrails ( @tool_input_guardrail , @tool_output_guardrail ) apply the same idea to one tool's arguments or result, which is the place to stop a leak like this one before the model even sees it. In production Guardrail details that matter in production Input guardrails run only for the first agent in a run, and output guardrails only on the agent that produces the final output, so a check you attach to a specialist that receives a handoff will not run on the user's input. By default guardrails run in parallel with the agent, which saves latency but means the agent may already have spent tokens, or called a tool, before a tripwire fires. For checks that must block side effects, set run_in_parallel=False on that guardrail, or put the check inside the tool itself. And cancel A-1002", how many tool calls will run before the first pause, and what does result.interruptions contain? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Resume the paused run with a new SQLiteSession("customer-43") instead of the session the run started with. What does the agent remember, and what happens to the pending approval? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise Debugging exercise: the guardrail that never fires A teammate added no_card_numbers as an input guardrail on the refunds agent, which receives conversations by handoff from the triage agent. A customer pasted a card number to the triage agent, the conversation was handed off, and the guardrail did not trip. Explain why, and where the check must go. (Solution D1.) Make it your own Add an output guardrail that blocks any reply containing an order ID that was not in the customer's message or in a tool result of this run. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Tools run until the approval The model asks for both status lookups and the cancellation. The lookups run; the cancellation does not, because needs_approval=True pauses the run first. result.interruptions holds one approval item for cancel_order with its arguments, and the run state , saved with result.to_state() , is what you resume after state.approve(...) or state.reject(...) . Solution B1 · The session is the memory A new session has none of the conversation, so the agent has no history for that run. The pending approval lives in the run state, not the session, so resuming the saved state still continues the cancellation, but any later turn on the new session starts without context. Keep one session per conversation, keyed by an ID you store, exactly like a LangGraph thread ( Lesson 14.103 ). Solution D1 · Input guardrails run only for the first agent In the Agents SDK, input guardrails run only when their agent is the first agent of the run, and output guardrails only on the agent that produces the final output. The refunds agent was not first, so its input guardrail never ran. Put input checks on the entry agent (or check before calling Runner.run ), and use tool guardrails for checks that must run wherever a tool is called. Solution M1 · An output guardrail with run data Collect the order IDs from the input and from the run's tool results ( result.new_items , or a run hook that records tool outputs into the run context ), then in the guardrail compare them with the IDs in the output and trip on any unknown ID. This catches invented IDs, a common hallucination in support replies, at the cost of one regex pass per reply. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What are the core primitives of the OpenAI Agents SDK? Worked answer. Agents (instructions, a model, tools, handoffs, guardrails and an optional output type), a Runner that executes the loop ( run , run_sync , run_streamed ), function tools built from Python functions, sessions for conversation memory, guardrails on input, output and tools that can stop a run with a tripwire, handoffs that transfer the conversation to another agent, and built-in tracing. Approvals pause a run before a tool marked needs_approval , with a serializable run state to resume later. A plausible wrong answer. "It only works with OpenAI models." Through its model interfaces and LiteLLM it can call other providers, though some features are OpenAI-specific. Follow-ups. How does a handoff differ from calling an agent as a tool? Debug a failure A run raises InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered for normal questions after a prompt change. How do you investigate? Worked answer. Look at the guardrail's own output in the trace: guardrails that call a model return a reason along with the tripwire. Check whether the guardrail agent's prompt or model changed, and run it alone on a set of normal and malicious inputs to measure false positives. Then tune it, and in production catch the exception and send a safe reply instead of an error. A plausible wrong answer. "Remove the guardrail." That hides the false positives and the attacks together. Follow-ups. How would you run guardrails in parallel with the main agent to save latency? Defend a design OpenAI Agents SDK or LangGraph for a support agent? Worked answer. The Agents SDK when the team is on OpenAI models and wants a small, readable API with sessions, guardrails, handoffs and tracing built in. LangGraph when the workflow needs custom control flow, durable pauses that span days with a checkpointed graph state, time travel , or provider-neutral components. Both can do approvals and multi-agent hand-offs; the difference is how much of the control flow you want to own. I would build the hardest path, approval and resume, in both before choosing ( Lesson 14.127 ). A plausible wrong answer. "The vendor SDK is always better for that vendor's models." It is convenient, not automatically better; requirements decide. Follow-ups. What would make you switch later, and how expensive would it be?
