Strands Agents (2025) took a model-driven approach: give the model tools and a prompt, and let it decide the steps, with AWS integration for production. In plain words first A model, tools and a prompt; the model decides the rest Strands Agents, from AWS, leans on the model to plan: you give it a model, tools and a prompt, and its loop lets the model choose steps, with less graph-style control flow than LangGraph . It integrates closely with AWS services and deployment on AgentCore. Read it as the same loop with a different philosophy: more trust in the model, less explicit structure. What it is Strands Agents is an open-source SDK that AWS released in May 2025 after using it internally for products such as Amazon Q Developer and AWS Glue. Its philosophy is model-driven : give a capable model a prompt and tools and let it plan, instead of scripting the steps. Around that loop it adds production plumbing: hooks, interrupts for human approval, session managers, steering plugins, OpenTelemetry later · 14.145 tracing , MCP later · 16.26 and A2A later · 16.29 support, and four multi-agent patterns. There are Python and TypeScript SDKs. The default model provider is Amazon Bedrock, but Strands supports Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, LiteLLM, Ollama , llama.cpp , Mistral, Writer and others, and it routes between models with a model router later · 14.155 . Copy Step 1 · Tools and an approval hook The ShopKart agent again, in Strands. @tool and Agent(...) will look familiar by now. What is new is the hook : a small class that Strands calls at fixed moments of the loop. This one listens for the moment before a tool runs, pauses the run when the tool is cancel_order , and waits for a person's answer. It is the approval gate of Lesson 14.60 written as a plug-in. Copy What you should see Copy callback_handler=None turns off the default behavior of printing the stream to the console. For real models: BedrockModel(model_id=...) with your AWS credentials (Bedrock is the default when you pass a model ID string), AnthropicModel , OpenAIModel(model_id="gpt-5.5") , GeminiModel or LiteLLMModel . For the common case, the built-in HumanInTheLoop intervention ( from strands.vended_interventions import HumanInTheLoop ) does the same approval pause without writing a hook. A session manager ( FileSessionManager , S3SessionManager , or AgentCore Memory) saves the conversation and any pending interrupts, so the answer can arrive later, on a different server. Step 2 · Structured output Pass a Pydantic model as structured_output_model and Strands registers it as a tool the model must call, validates the arguments, and puts the object on result.structured_output . If validation fails, the error goes back to the model so it can correct itself. Copy What you should see Copy The scripted model always answers False for booleans; a real model would mark this one urgent. The older agent.structured_output(Model, prompt) method still works but is deprecated in favor of this argument, which also works with tools in the same run. Step 3 · Sessions, state and the context window Two separate concerns, and Strands keeps them separate. A session manager persists the conversation and the agent's key-value state ( agent state ) so a new process can pick up where the last left off. A conversation manager decides what stays in the context window as the conversation grows. Copy What you should see Copy Each question here takes four messages (the question, the tool call , the tool result, the answer). The window allows six, but keeping six would start the context with an orphaned tool result, which models reject, so the manager trims to four. SummarizingConversationManager summarizes old turns instead of dropping them; NullConversationManager keeps everything until the model's limit. Step 4 · Steering: rules at the moment they matter Long system prompts full of rules get diluted as the conversation grows. Strands' steering plugins check the agent at decision points instead: before a tool runs ( steer_before_tool ) and after the model answers ( steer_after_model ). A handler returns Proceed , Guide (cancel and tell the model why) or Interrupt (ask a human). Copy What you should see Copy The cancel never ran; the model received the reason and, with a real model, would offer a return instead. Industry practice Steering versus prompts, with numbers In a March 2026 evaluation published by the Strands team (600 runs per approach on a customer-service task), agents using steering handlers passed 100% of cases, against 82.5% for simple instructions, 80.8% for a scripted workflow and 99.8% for a long standard-operating-procedure prompt, while using about two-thirds fewer input tokens than the SOP prompt. It is a vendor's own benchmark, but the principle generalizes: enforce rules at the point of action, in code or with a focused check, rather than by adding paragraphs to the prompt. In production Steering and hooks in production Steering handlers run at every decision point, so keep them fast and deterministic: a slow handler (one that calls a model on every tool call) adds latency to every step. Make each handler's Guide message tell the model what to do instead, or it will retry the same blocked action. And log every Guide and interrupt: a rule that fires constantly is usually a sign the tool or prompt should change, not just the steering. Step 5 · Streaming and MCP tools stream_async yields events as they happen: text deltas ( data ), the tool being called ( current_tool_use ), each complete message, and the final result . That is what a chat UI or an SSE endpoint consumes. Copy What you should see Copy Any MCP server becomes a set of Strands tools through MCPClient . This starts a small stdio server (built with the official mcp SDK) as a child process, lists its tools, and gives them to an agent: Copy What you should see Copy For a remote server, swap stdio_client for streamablehttp_client(url, headers=...) . Calls must happen inside the with block, because that is where the connection lives; for long-running services, pass the MCPClient itself in tools=[...] and Strands manages its lifecycle. Step 6 · Four multi-agent patterns The four multi-agent patterns in Strands, by who decides what runs next. In the first two a model decides; in the last two your code does. Pattern How it works Strands API Agents as tools An orchestrator calls specialist agents like functions Wrap an agent call in a @tool function Swarm Agents hand work to each other autonomously, sharing context Swarm([agent_a, agent_b, ...]) with handoff and iteration limits Graph A fixed or conditional flow between agents GraphBuilder with nodes, edges and conditions Workflow A task list with dependencies, run in order or in parallel The workflow tool in strands-agents-tools Copy What you should see Copy A swarm is the autonomous counterpart: each agent gets a handoff_to_agent tool and decides who works next, sharing one context. Copy What you should see Copy The scripted model never calls handoff_to_agent , so triage finished the job alone. A real model would usually hand off, giving ['triage', 'orders'] . The limits are the important part: max_handoffs and max_iterations stop two agents from passing a task back and forth forever, the classic swarm failure. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Agent2Agent (A2A) An open protocol that lets agents built by different teams or vendors hand tasks to each other Lesson 16.29 Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Google's platform for building, scaling, governing and optimizing agents (formerly Vertex AI) Lesson 14.157 Model Context Protocol (MCP) An open standard for connecting models to tools and data through small servers, so one integration works in many apps Lesson 16.26 OpenTelemetry The open standard for collecting traces, metrics and logs from software Lesson 14.145 Eval case One test question with a written rule for what a correct answer must and must not contain Lesson 14.131 Why this came about Google needed a framework that worked closely with Gemini and Google Cloud and supported multi-agent systems. The Agent Development Kit (April 2025) provided agents, workflow agents and sessions, alongside the A2A later · 16.29 protocol for agents to talk to each other. In plain words first Google's way of packaging the same parts The Agent Development Kit (ADK) packages agents, tools, sessions and multi-agent composition, with workflow agents for sequences, loops and parallel steps, and close integration with Google's models and cloud. It supports protocols such as A2A. Map each concept to what you know: agents are the loop, sessions are threads, workflow agents are fixed graphs. What it is The Agent Development Kit (ADK) is Google's open-source framework (Apache 2.0) for building agents, available for Python, TypeScript, Go and Java. It powers agents inside Google products and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform later · 14.157 ( Lesson 14.157 ). It is optimized for Gemini but model-agnostic: other providers plug in through LiteLLM, and Anthropic, Llama and others are available through Vertex AI Model Garden. ADK's building blocks: an agent is a model with instructions and tools, and agents are combined into workflows, either as a graph or as agents that delegate to each other. Figure: Google Agent Development Kit documentation , Apache 2.0 . ADK 2.0 became stable in May 2026 and added a graph workflow runtime next to the original agent classes. It also rebuilt sessions around events, so storage from 1.x is not compatible: follow the migration guide before upgrading an existing deployment. Copy Watch out Small dependency surprise LiteLLM imports the mcp package when it calls a model. Without it, you get No module named 'mcp' wrapped in an APIConnectionError , which looks like a network problem. Installing mcp fixes it. Step 1 · An agent, a runner and a confirmation ADK separates three things. The agent holds the instructions, the model and the tools. The runner executes it and keeps the sessions. And what comes out is a stream of events : each model reply, tool call and tool result is one event . The tool cancel_order is wrapped so that it asks for confirmation before it runs. The model is the lab rig, reached through ADK's LiteLLM adapter. The ADK runtime. The runner sits between the user and your agent logic: it asks the agent for the next event, saves what the event changed through the session, artifact and memory services, and passes the event on to the user. Figure: Google Agent Development Kit documentation , Apache 2.0 . Copy What you should see Copy With Gemini, pass model="gemini-flash-latest" (or a pinned version) and set GOOGLE_API_KEY , or the Vertex AI variables, instead of using LiteLlm . Everything in ADK is an event : user messages, model turns, tool calls, confirmations and state changes all arrive as events from the runner. Confirmation requests are ordinary function-call events named adk_request_confirmation , so any client (web UI, Slack bot, API caller) can answer them. Tool confirmation is still marked experimental and, at the time of writing, does not work with the database and Vertex AI session services. Step 2 · Sessions, state and memory Service Holds Implementations Session service One conversation's events and its state dictionary In-memory, database (SQL), Agent Platform Sessions Memory service Long-term knowledge searchable across sessions In-memory, Agent Platform Memory Bank (formerly Vertex AI Memory Bank) Artifact service Files the agent produces or reads In-memory, Google Cloud Storage State keys use prefixes for scope: no prefix for the session, user: across a user's sessions, app: for the whole app, temp: for the current turn. Tools load_memory and preload_memory connect agents to the memory service. Callbacks and scoped state in code Two features you will use in every real ADK agent: callbacks that enforce rules at the point of action, and state that tools read and write through ToolContext , with prefixes that decide how long a value lives. Copy What you should see Copy The shipped order was never cancelled, whatever the model decided; the injection attempt never reached the model; and the user: -scoped value followed the customer into a new session while the session counter did not. Callbacks are ADK's equivalent of LangChain middleware and Strands hooks: put rules there, not in the prompt. In production Sessions and state in production InMemorySessionService and InMemoryRunner lose every session on restart; use the database or Agent Platform session services from the first deployment (Step 4 shows the database service). Choose state prefixes deliberately: an unprefixed key lives for one session, user: follows the user everywhere and app: is shared by everyone, so a value written with the wrong prefix leaks across users. Keep large objects in the artifact service rather than in state, which is loaded with every event. Step 3 · Workflow agents and graph workflows The three workflow agents: a sequence runs sub-agents one after another, a loop repeats them until a condition is met, and a parallel agent runs them at the same time. Figure: Google Agent Development Kit documentation , Apache 2.0 . ADK has two ways to fix the control flow: Workflow agents (since 1.0): SequentialAgent , ParallelAgent and LoopAgent run sub-agents in a fixed pattern. In ADK 2.13 they still work but emit a deprecation warning in favour of Workflow ; keep them for existing code, use Workflow for new code (one limitation at the time of writing: a Workflow cannot yet be a sub-agent of an LLM agent). Graph workflows (ADK 2): a Workflow whose edges connect functions and agents, with routes, fan-out and fan-in, retries and human-input nodes. Copy What you should see Copy Each node's output becomes the next node's input. A router must pass output=node_input explicitly, otherwise the chosen node receives nothing. Any node can be an Agent , so a graph can mix deterministic functions with model-driven steps. Fan-out and fan-in work the same way: a tuple of nodes runs in parallel, and a JoinNode waits for all of them and passes their outputs on as one dictionary keyed by node name. Here an LLM agent and two deterministic checks run side by side: Copy What you should see Copy The chain syntax ("START", a, b, c) is shorthand for edges START to a, a to b and b to c; a tuple element fans out. Set max_concurrency on the workflow to cap how many nodes run at once. Step 4 · Callbacks, plugins and tools Where callbacks run: before and after the agent as a whole, and before and after each model call and each tool call inside it. Figure: Google Agent Development Kit documentation , Apache 2.0 . Callbacks on an agent: before_agent_callback , before_model_callback , after_model_callback , before_tool_callback , after_tool_callback and error callbacks. Return a value to short-circuit the step, for example to block a tool or answer from a cache. Plugins apply the same hooks globally to every agent in a runner: logging, policy checks, caching. In plain words first A crew with roles and tasks CrewAI describes work as a team: agents with roles and goals, tasks assigned to them, and a process (sequential or managed by a lead agent) that runs the crew . Flows add explicit, event-driven control for production. It is quick to express role-based collaboration, at the cost of less fine-grained control over each step than a graph. CrewAI: role-based crews and event-driven flows Best fit : quick multi-agent prototypes and business-process automation, especially for teams who think in roles ("researcher", "writer", "reviewer"). CrewAI has two layers. Crews are teams of agents, each with a role, goal and backstory, working through tasks in a sequential or hierarchical (manager-led) process. Flows are event-driven workflows ( @start , @listen , @router ) with typed state, persistence and human feedback, which can call crews as steps. A crew: agents with roles, tools and memory work through tasks, and the last task's result is the outcome. Figure: CrewAI documentation , MIT . A flow : steps of ordinary code that share state and call a crew where judgement is needed. Crews give agents more freedom; flows give you more control. Figure: CrewAI documentation , MIT . Idea What it means, in one line Taught in OpenTelemetry The open standard for collecting traces, metrics and logs from software Lesson 14.145 Model Context Protocol (MCP) An open standard for connecting models to tools and data through small servers, so one integration works in many apps Lesson 16.26 Agent2Agent (A2A) An open protocol that lets agents built by different teams or vendors hand tasks to each other Lesson 16.29 Durable execution Running a long task so that every completed step is saved and a crash resumes from the last one Lesson 14.140 Why this came about Python developers who liked Pydantic 's typed models wanted the same safety for agents. Pydantic AI (late 2024) came from the Pydantic team: typed tools, typed outputs and dependency injection , in the style of FastAPI. In plain words first Type safety for agents Pydantic AI, from the makers of Pydantic, treats an agent like well-typed Python: tools and outputs are typed, dependencies are injected into tools, and results are validated. If you like FastAPI-style code, it feels familiar. It covers the same loop, tools, structured output and streaming, with a strong focus on correctness and testing. Pydantic AI: type-safe agents Best fit : Python services where types, validation, testing and dependency injection matter, and teams already using Pydantic and FastAPI. What Pydantic AI adds around a model call. Dependencies carry your application's data to the tools without the model seeing it, and the reply must pass validation against the output type before your code receives it. Copy Copy What you should see Copy r.output is a validated Answer , not text. If the model returns something invalid, Pydantic AI sends the validation error back and asks it to retry. Approvals use deferred tools : a tool marked requires_approval=True ends the run with a list of pending calls, and you continue with your decisions. Copy What you should see Copy Dependencies: what a tool needs that the model must not choose The tools above read ORDERS , a variable that happens to be in scope. A real tool needs a database connection, and it needs to know which customer is asking. Neither may come from the model: a model that can pass any customer_id can read any customer's orders. Dependency injection means your code hands these things to the run, and the framework hands them to each tool. You declare one type that holds them ( deps_type= ), pass a value on each run ( deps= ), and a tool reads them from its first parameter, the run context . Copy The model sees one argument for this tool, order_id . The context parameter is left out of the schema it is sent, so the customer check cannot be talked around. Testing an agent without calling a model Because the tools take their data from deps , a test can pass a small fake. Because the model can be swapped for one run, the test needs no network and costs nothing. Pydantic AI ships two stand-in models. TestModel calls every tool once with made-up arguments that fit the schema, then returns text: it checks that the agent is wired together. FunctionModel lets a function you write play the model, so the test can ask for one exact tool call . Copy What you should see Copy The same question about the same order gives two answers, and the difference comes only from deps . Solutions Solution P1 · Validation, then a retry Pydantic AI validates the output against Triage ; urgency=7 fails the le=5 constraint, so the validation error is sent back to the model as a retry prompt, up to the agent's retry limit, before an exception reaches your code. That is Lesson 11.21 's validate-and-repair loop , built in. Output validators ( @agent.output_validator ) add business rules to the same loop. Solution B1 · Missing dependencies fail when a tool needs them The run starts without complaint. ctx.deps is then None , so the error appears only when a tool or a system-prompt function reads from it: with this lesson's order_status tool it is AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'orders' , raised in the middle of the run. Pass deps= on every run; typed dependencies are the point, and a type checker such as mypy or pyright flags the call before it runs. Solution D1 · TestModel, FunctionModel and override Use with agent.override(model=TestModel()): in the test, which calls every tool and returns schema-valid output without a network call, or FunctionModel to script exactly what the model returns. Set ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False (from pydantic_ai.models ) in the test setup so any accidental real call fails loudly. Keep real-model checks in evals . Solution M1 · Dependencies make tools testable Declare @dataclass class ShopKartDeps: db: OrdersDB , set deps_type=ShopKartDeps , and write the tool as def get_order_status(ctx: RunContext[ShopKartDeps], order_id: str) -> str: return ctx.deps.db.status(order_id) . In the test, pass deps=ShopKartDeps(db=FakeOrdersDB({...})) with TestModel , and assert on the tool's effect. The same pattern injects HTTP clients and per-user settings. The retry messages in the trace: which field failed validation, and why. Often the schema is too strict or ambiguous for the model (an enum with unclear values, a required field the input lacks), or an output validator's rule is impossible for some inputs. l0708: Course home / Phase 14 · AI Agents: Design and Engineering LlamaIndex and DSPy From Zero to Agents Lesson 14.124 30 min Compare Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Run a LlamaIndex agent, build an index over documents, retrieve from it and update it when a document changes Declare a DSPy signature and module, and explain what an optimizer does to the prompt Say when each of the two is the right choice Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.96 , Lesson 11.28 Depth : Comparative Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Signature / optimizer A declared input-output spec / a search for better prompts against a metric DSPy Index (LlamaIndex) The object that splits documents into passages, embeds them and stores the vectors for search An index over your documents Nodes (LlamaIndex) The passages a document is split into, as stored in an index An index over your documents Query engine A retriever plus the model call that answers from what was retrieved An index over your documents Why this came about LlamaIndex (2022) began as a way to connect models to private data, and grew into a framework for retrieval-centered agents. DSPy (from Stanford, 2023) took a different path: treat prompts as programs that are optimized automatically against a metric, instead of hand-tuned. In plain words first A data framework and a prompt compiler LlamaIndex started as a toolkit for connecting models to your data (loading, indexing, retrieval) and now includes agents and workflows; reach for it when retrieval is the heart of the system. DSPy treats prompts as programs to optimize: you declare what each step takes and returns, give examples and a metric, and it searches for prompts or examples that score best, instead of you hand-tuning text. LlamaIndex: data-first agents and workflows Best fit : agents whose main job is to work over documents and data, building on LlamaIndex's ingestion, indexing and parsing (LlamaParse). A LlamaIndex workflow drawn as a graph: steps (the boxes) are connected by the events they emit and receive, and the run ends at a stop event. Figure: Hugging Face, Agents Course , Apache 2.0 . Copy Copy What you should see Copy Agents here are Workflows : event-driven steps where each step consumes one event type and emits another. FunctionAgent , ReActAgent and CodeActAgent are prebuilt; AgentWorkflow coordinates several agents with handoffs . Workflows are ephemeral by default; snapshot the context or use the DBOS-backed runtime for durability. The part LlamaIndex is named for: an index over your documents The agent above could have been written in any library of this chapter. What LlamaIndex adds is everything around documents. Its central object is the index : you hand it documents, and it splits them into passages (it calls them nodes ), embeds each one and stores the vectors, which is the ingestion half of the pipeline you built by hand in Lesson 14.72 . From an index you get a retriever , which returns the best passages for a question, or a query engine , which retrieves and then asks the model to answer from what it found. The code builds an index over three policy snippets and retrieves from it. So that it runs offline, the embedding model is a toy that counts ten chosen words. In a real project you would pass a real embedding model ( Lesson 14.71 ) in the same place and change nothing else. Copy What you should see Copy The first two lines are the retriever's answer: the refund policy scores highest, and each hit knows which document it came from. The last two lines show the part that matters in production. The policy changed from 30 to 45 days, and refresh_ref_docs compared every document with what the index held, re-embedded the one that had changed ( True ) and left the other two alone. The index still holds three documents, and the search now returns the 45-day text. This only works because each document was given an ID. Without one, loading the documents again adds a second copy of each, and the index starts returning the old policy beside the new one. That is the usual cause of "the assistant quotes a rule we changed last month". DSPy: programming instead of prompting Best fit : pipelines with a clear quality metric, where you want prompts (and few-shot examples) optimized automatically instead of hand-tuned. DSPy (from Stanford NLP) separates what a step should do from how it is prompted. You declare a signature (inputs, outputs, a docstring), wrap it in a module ( Predict , ChainOfThought , ReAct ), and an optimizer (such as MIPROv2 or GEPA) searches for instructions and examples that maximize your metric on a training set. Change the model, re-run the optimizer, and the prompts adapt. Copy Copy What you should see Copy urgent came back as a real boolean: DSPy parses outputs into the declared types. The optimization step (for example dspy.MIPROv2(metric=my_metric).compile(triage, trainset=examples) ) needs a real model and 20 or more labeled examples. What a DSPy optimizer actually does The example above ran a module without optimising it, because optimisation needs a real model. It is the part that makes DSPy different from every other library in this chapter, so here is what happens when you call an optimizer, step by step. What a DSPy optimizer does when you call it. It searches over prompts for your program, using your examples and your metric to keep score, and hands back the best one it found. You supply three things: the program (the triage module), a training set (say, 40 customer messages with the correct category and urgency), and a metric (a function that returns 1 if a prediction matches the label and 0 if not). Step What the optimizer does In plain words 1 Runs your program on the training examples and keeps the runs that the metric scores as correct Collects worked examples that are known to be right 2 Asks a model to write several candidate instructions for each step, from the signature, the code and the examples Drafts different ways of wording the prompt 3 Builds candidate prompts: one instruction plus a few of the collected examples Combines an instruction with few-shot examples ( Lesson 11.25 ) 4 Runs each candidate on a batch of training examples and scores it with your metric Measures every candidate, instead of trusting anyone's taste 5 Uses the scores to choose which combinations to try next, and repeats Searches, spending model calls where they look most promising 6 Returns your program with the best instruction and examples filled in The "compiled" program; you save it and load it in production The result of compiling is nothing mysterious. It is a prompt, with an instruction and a few examples, that you can print and read. What changed is how it was found: by search against a metric on your data, not by a person editing text and eyeballing three outputs. That has three consequences worth knowing before you adopt it: It needs what all evaluation needs. No labelled examples and no metric, no optimisation. Teams that already have an evaluation set ( Lesson 11.19 ) get the most from DSPy; teams that do not must build one first, which is worth doing anyway. It costs model calls. An optimisation run makes hundreds to thousands of calls. That is a one-off cost per model and per program change, paid again whenever you switch models. It can overfit. Forty training examples can be fitted by a prompt that then does worse on new messages. Hold out examples the optimizer never sees, and report the score on those ( Lesson 2.26 explained why). When to reach for it: a pipeline with a clear, checkable output (a classification, an extraction, a retrieval step with known right answers), where prompts are being hand-tuned again and again as models change. When not to: open-ended writing or conversation, where no metric captures "good". Check your mental model ✗ "LlamaIndex is only a vector database wrapper." ✓ It covers ingestion, indexing, retrieval, agents and workflows. ✗ "DSPy writes prompts for free." ✓ It needs a metric and examples, and its optimization runs many model calls. ✗ "Optimized prompts transfer to any model." ✓ Re-optimize or re-evaluate when you change models. Solutions Solution P1 · Different jobs DSPy: it compiles a program by optimizing prompts and examples against a metric. LlamaIndex focuses on data ingestion, indexing and retrieval. Solution B1 · Small optimization sets overfit The optimized prompts fit those examples and may generalize poorly. Use more examples and a held-out set. Solution D1 · Ingestion pipelines Whether the ingestion pipeline uses document IDs and caching to update changed documents and delete removed ones. Solution M1 · Metrics drive DSPy A function returning a score per example; DSPy optimizers search prompts and demonstrations to maximize it on a training set, validated on a held-out set. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Sandbox An isolated environment where an agent's code or actions cannot reach anything important Lesson 15.25 Why this came about Research in 2024 showed that agents writing short programs, instead of one JSON tool call per step, could do more in fewer steps. Hugging Face's smolagents (late 2024) made code agents simple to try, with sandboxes later · 15.25 to run their code safely. In plain words first Agents that write small programs instead of single calls Most agents call one tool per step as JSON. smolagents popularized code agents: the model writes a short Python snippet that can call several tools, loop and filter, which the framework runs and returns. That takes fewer steps and is more expressive, but running model-written code demands a sandbox. smolagents: agents that act in code Best fit : research, open-model agents and code-acting agents, where a minimal, hackable library is a feature. Hugging Face's smolagents keeps the core small. Its signature agent is the CodeAgent : instead of one JSON tool call per step, the model writes a short Python snippet that calls tools, loops and computes, which takes fewer steps on complex tasks (the CodeAct idea from Lesson 14.63 ). Code runs in a local restricted interpreter or, for real isolation, in E2B, Docker, Modal or WebAssembly sandboxes. ToolCallingAgent does classic tool calling. Copy Copy What you should see Copy smolagents requires an Args: section in tool docstrings and ends every run with a built-in final_answer tool. The part that is different: an agent whose actions are code The example above used smolagents' ordinary tool-calling agent, which works like every agent so far. The library's own idea is the CodeAgent . Lesson 14.63 introduced it as CodeAct: instead of asking for one tool call and waiting for the result, the model writes a short Python program, and the library runs it. Tools are ordinary functions the program can call, so one model reply can loop over several orders, combine the results and compute an answer. How CodeAgent.run() works: the task goes into memory, the model writes a block of Python, the block is executed, and what it printed is added to memory for the next step, until the code calls final_answer . Figure: Hugging Face documentation , Apache 2.0 . To show exactly what the library does with such a reply, the model here is a scripted stand-in that returns one prepared reply. Everything after that (finding the code, running it, calling the tool, returning the answer) is the real library. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The question needed three lookups, a comparison and a count. A tool-calling agent would have needed at least two model calls (one to request the three lookups, one to read the results and answer), and the model would have done the counting in its head. Here there was one model call. The loop and the arithmetic were done by Python, which does not miscount. Look at what the scripted reply contains: a line of reasoning, then code between <code> tags. The library extracts the code, runs it in its own small Python interpreter with the tools available as functions, and treats the call to final_answer(...) as the end of the run. If the code had printed something instead, that output would have gone back to the model as the observation for its next step. Running code that a model wrote is the obvious risk. The library's first line of defence is that its interpreter is not ordinary Python: it allows a short list of safe modules and refuses the rest. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The first reply tried import os to list the machine's files. The interpreter refused, and the error went back to the model as an observation, exactly as a failed tool call would. The second scripted reply then gave up gracefully. Two cautions. First, a restricted interpreter is a filter, not a wall. The smolagents documentation says plainly that it is not a security boundary, and recommends running code agents inside a real sandbox (a container or a remote sandbox service) for anything beyond experiments; Lesson 15.25 covers sandboxes. Second, the tools themselves are still the main risk: a code agent with a delete_order tool can call it in a loop. Check your mental model ✗ "It is a chat API." ✓ It is a full agent harness with tools, files, permissions and hooks. ✗ "It can safely run with all permissions." ✓ Restrict tools, directories and commands; use hooks and approvals. ✗ "It replaces LangGraph for every use." ✓ It fits workspace-style agents; explicit business workflows may still suit a graph better. In depth: permissions, hooks, subagents and sessions The Claude Agent SDK's power is its built-in tools: it can read and edit files and run shell commands. So most of the work of using it safely is deciding what it may do. These are the controls, with names checked against claude-agent-sdk 0.2.178 (not run here: the SDK drives the Claude Code engine, which needs an API key ): The six checks a tool call passes in the Claude Agent SDK, in the order the SDK applies them. A call can be blocked at three of them and approved at three; anything still undecided at the end goes to your can_use_tool function. The SDK applies the checks in a fixed order (checked against the SDK's permissions documentation in November 2026): hooks first, then deny rules, ask rules, the permission mode, allow rules, and last your can_use_tool function. Three things follow from that order, and each one surprises people: allowed_tools approves; it does not restrict. Tools you leave off the list still exist. A call to one of them falls through to the permission mode and then to can_use_tool . To take a tool away from the model, name it in disallowed_tools . A call that is approved early never reaches can_use_tool . In the example below, Bash is in allowed_tools , so only_reports_folder is never asked about a shell command. That is why the dangerous-command check is a PreToolUse hook: hooks run before everything else, on every call. A deny rule wins in every mode, and allowed_tools does not limit bypassPermissions . That mode approves every tool that is not denied, listed or not. For an agent that runs with nobody watching, pair a short allowed_tools list with permission_mode="dontAsk" : listed tools run, and anything that would have asked a person is refused. Copy Control What it decides Use it for allowed_tools , disallowed_tools Which tools run without asking, and which never exist The first and simplest boundary permission_mode The default for everything else: ask ( default ), refuse instead of asking ( dontAsk ), accept edits, plan only, let a classifier decide ( auto ), or bypass plan for read-only analysis; dontAsk for unattended agents; never bypassPermissions outside a sandbox can_use_tool A function that allows or denies each remaining tool call , optionally changing its input Path and argument rules, human approval Hooks ( PreToolUse , PostToolUse and others) Code that runs at fixed points of the loop Blocking commands, audit logs, redaction agents Subagents with their own prompts and tool lists Narrow tasks with fewer permissions and a separate context sandbox , cwd , add_dirs Where it can act Containing file and shell access max_turns , max_budget_usd How long and how expensive a run may be Runaway protection resume , fork_session , session_id Continuing or branching an earlier session Long tasks across requests; trying an alternative Two production rules. Run it in a container or sandbox with only the files and network it needs, because a shell tool can do anything the process can ( Lesson 15.25 ). And set setting_sources explicitly: by default the engine can load settings, memory files and tools from the machine it runs on, which makes behavior depend on whoever's laptop or server it is. Solutions Solution P1 · Nobody to ask Bash is not pre-approved, so the default mode wants to ask for permission, and in a service there is no person to ask: the call is denied (or the run stops waiting, depending on how the host handles permission prompts). Decide permissions in code for services: pre-approve what is safe, deny the rest, and use can_use_tool to route the rest to an approval system. Five years of agent frameworks on one line. Each wave fixed what the one before it got wrong, and by 2026 the frameworks have converged on the same parts. When What appeared What it taught the field Late 2022 LangChain and LlamaIndex : chains of prompts, the first "agents" that parsed tool calls out of model text Composing model calls is useful; parsing free text for actions is fragile Spring 2023 AutoGPT and BabyAGI : a model in an open-ended loop that writes its own task list Autonomy without checks wanders, repeats itself and burns money. Industry practice Keep the seams clean, whatever you pick Teams that switch frameworks painlessly have one thing in common: the framework touches little. Two other kinds of generative AI show up in real projects often enough to deserve their own module: voice agents , which put an agent on a phone line or in an app's microphone, and generative media , which creates images, audio and video. Both reuse everything else in the course (tools, retrieval, guardrails later · 15.23 , evals ), and both add constraints of their own. Why this came about Voice assistants existed for years but were rigid. In 2024 realtime speech models made natural, low-latency spoken conversations with language models possible, creating voice agents with their own latency and interruption challenges. In plain words first A conversation where a second of silence is too long Voice agents must answer within about a second, so latency drives the design. The pipeline design chains speech-to-text, a normal text agent and text-to-speech, streaming at every stage; it gives control and any model. Speech-to-speech models hear and speak directly, with fewer parts and lower latency, but fewer choices. Both must handle interruptions, when the user starts talking over the agent. Voice agents: two architectures Two ways to build a voice agent. The cascade is debuggable and swappable; speech-to-speech is faster and more natural. The latency budget decides, and turn detection sits in front of both. The cascaded design as a concrete device: a small model listens for the wake word, speech-to-text transcribes the question, a language model writes the answer, and text-to-speech reads it out. The legend shows which steps can run on the device and which in the cloud. Figure: Hugging Face, Audio Course , Apache 2.0 . Architecture How it works Strengths Trade-offs Cascaded pipeline Speech-to-text (STT), then a text LLM with tools, then text-to-speech (TTS), all streaming Use any LLM and your existing text agent; transcripts for logging and evals; swap each part independently More hops, so more latency; tone of voice is lost in the transcript Speech-to-speech model (realtime) One model hears audio and speaks audio, with tool calling Lowest latency; hears tone, hesitation and interruptions; more natural prosody Fewer model choices; harder to inspect and evaluate; audio tokens cost more Realtime speech models and APIs include OpenAI's Realtime API, Gemini Live, Amazon Nova Sonic on Bedrock and Azure's Voice Live. Frameworks that handle the media plumbing (streaming audio, voice activity detection , interruptions, telephony) include Pipecat , LiveKit Agents and Vapi-style managed platforms; telephony arrives through providers such as Twilio, Exotel or Amazon Connect. Transport matters: WebRTC handles jitter and packet loss for browsers and mobile apps; WebSockets are simpler for server-to-server audio. An eval set of real call audio in your callers' languages, accents and noise levels. Step 1 · The latency budget People expect a reply within roughly a second of finishing a sentence; much more and they start talking again or assume the line dropped. Add up a turn stage by stage: Copy What you should see Copy Three lessons. Streaming everything is not optional: waiting for each stage to finish more than doubles the delay. Endpointing (deciding that the caller has finished) is often the biggest single cost, which is why voice stacks add a small turn-detection model that listens for the end of a thought, not just silence. And the LLM's time to first token matters far more than its total generation time, which favors fast models, short system prompts with prompt caching, and tools that answer in milliseconds. Speech-to-speech models win on raw latency; cascades win on control. Step 2 · Speak while the model is still thinking TTS should start on the first natural phrase, not the full answer. A small chunker sits between the LLM stream and the TTS engine: Copy What you should see Copy Chunking at punctuation keeps intonation natural; chunks of one or two words sound robotic. Write voice prompts differently from chat prompts: short sentences, no markdown, no lists or URLs, numbers and order IDs in a form the TTS reads well ("A, ten oh one"), and a confirmation read back before any action ("I'll cancel order A-1002. Shall I go ahead?"). Step 3 · Turn-taking and interruptions Voice activity detection (VAD) finds speech in the audio stream. The silence threshold that ends a turn is a trade-off: short thresholds cut people off mid-thought, long ones feel sluggish. Here is energy-based VAD on synthetic audio: Copy What you should see Copy The caller stopped at 1.1 seconds; every rule adds its silence on top. Production systems use trained VAD models (Silero VAD, WebRTC VAD) that ignore background noise, plus semantic turn detection that waits longer after "my order number is..." than after a complete question. Barge-in is the other half: when the caller starts speaking while the agent talks, stop TTS playback immediately, cancel the pending LLM generation, and keep only what the caller actually heard in the conversation history, or the agent will "remember" saying things the caller never heard. Voice agents in production Evaluate on audio, not just text : word error rate on names, order IDs, addresses and numbers in your callers' accents and languages (Indian English, Hindi and code-mixed Hinglish behave very differently from benchmark audio); task completion; latency percentiles per turn; interruption handling. Simulated callers ( Lesson 14.143 ) can be voiced with TTS to test end to end. Languages : check STT and TTS quality per language and dialect before committing; Azure Speech, Google Cloud Speech, Amazon Transcribe and Polly, and Indian providers such as Sarvam AI cover Indian languages to different degrees. Safety and compliance : announce recording and AI use at the start of the call, verify identity before revealing account data, redact PII in transcripts, hand off to a person on request or on emergencies, and guard against voice prompt injection later · 15.24 (a caller can say "ignore your instructions" as easily as type it). Cost : audio is billed per minute or per audio token at each stage; long calls with long contexts add up, so trim history and summarize. Check your mental model ✗ "Voice agents are text agents with a microphone." ✓ Latency, interruptions and spoken-style answers change the design. ✗ "Speech-to-speech is always better." ✓ It is simpler and faster; pipelines give more control and easier tracing . ✗ "Long, detailed answers are fine in voice." ✓ Short sentences and no tables or lists suit speech. Exercises Predict before you run The latency budget allots 300 ms each to speech recognition, the model's first token and speech synthesis. If the model needs 900 ms for its first sentence, where can you win time without a faster model? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Use a fixed 1.5-second silence to decide that the caller finished speaking. What do callers experience? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise The agent keeps talking when the caller interrupts. What is missing? (Solution D1.) Make it your own Change speakable_chunks to never split inside numbers or order IDs such as SK-1042, and test it on a reply that contains both. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Overlap the stages Stream: start synthesizing the first speakable chunk as soon as it is complete (Step 2), and start recognition early with streaming ASR. Fillers or short acknowledgments also hide latency. Solution B1 · Turn-taking needs more than silence Long pauses before every reply, and interruptions when callers pause mid-sentence. Use voice activity detection with adaptive or semantic end-of-turn detection, as end_of_turn begins to do. Solution D1 · Barge-in Detecting speech while the agent speaks, stopping playback, cancelling pending synthesis, and telling the model it was interrupted, with what was actually heard. Solution M1 · Speak whole units Treat numbers, IDs and abbreviations as unbreakable, and split on sentence or clause boundaries. Spoken IDs also need formatting: read SK-1042 as "S K one zero four two". Check your understanding Explain the mechanism Compare pipeline and speech-to-speech voice agents. Worked answer. A pipeline chains speech recognition, a text model and speech synthesis: flexible, debuggable, any model, but latency adds up per stage. Speech-to-speech models process audio directly, with lower latency and better prosody, but less control, fewer model choices and harder evaluation. Both need streaming, turn-taking and interruption handling. A plausible wrong answer. "Speech-to-speech is always better." It trades control and observability for latency. Follow-ups. How would you evaluate a voice agent? Debug a failure Callers say the agent sounds slow, although each stage meets its budget in tests. What do you check? Worked answer. End-to-end timing on real calls: network jitter, telephony codecs, end-of-turn detection waits, and the time to the first spoken chunk rather than first token. Log timestamps at each stage per turn. A plausible wrong answer. "Use a faster model." Measure the whole path first. Follow-ups. What is a good target for response latency? Defend a design Should ShopKart deploy a voice agent for order support? Worked answer. For high-volume, simple calls (order status, delivery dates) with a clear handoff to people, yes, if it meets latency and accuracy targets and supports the languages callers use. Refunds and complaints may stay with people. Pilot on a slice of calls with measured outcomes. A plausible wrong answer. "Replace the call center." Voice agents handle the routine share well and the rest poorly. Follow-ups. What would you measure in the pilot? This lesson loads the model saved in Lesson 3.23 from the shopkart-ft/full folder, so run that lesson first. Lesson 2.25 (measuring models honestly) and Lesson 2.26 (overfitting and leakage) are the background. Depth : Core. Time : about 70 minutes; the last experiment trains three short models and takes roughly 10 to 15 minutes on a laptop processor. Next : Lesson 3.25 shrinks and ships the best model. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Error analysis Reading the model's wrong outputs and grouping them by cause Improving any model Stratified sampling Sampling so that each category keeps its share Building evaluation sets Why this came about Training a model became easy long before evaluating one did. With a few lines of configuration anyone can produce a fine-tuned model and a falling loss curve, and the hard question moved to what happens afterwards: is it better than what we had, where does it fail, and why? Teams that fine-tune successfully report spending most of their effort on evaluation sets , error analysis and data repair, and very little on training settings. This lesson is that part of the work, on the model you trained two lessons ago, which scored 100% on validation and 42.5% on the test set . In plain words first Marking the exam paper properly A single score is like a single exam mark. It tells you whether there is a problem and nothing about what the problem is. A good teacher looks at which questions were missed, what was written instead of the right answer, and whether the student misread the instructions. Then the teacher changes what is taught, not how loudly. Evaluating a fine-tune is the same: split the score up, read the wrong answers, check that the model is being asked in the way it was taught, and fix the training material. Step 1 · Look past the average The test score of the fully fine-tuned model was 42.5% fully correct. Split it by the true intent of each ticket, and by field: Copy What you should see Copy The average hid two very different situations. Order numbers and urgency are right on every test ticket in every class: that part of the task is solved. The whole problem is the intent , and even there one class is perfect while the other four are mostly wrong. A model that is 100% right on one class and poor on the rest is not "42% accurate"; it is doing something specific, and the next step is to find out what. The fully fine-tuned model's test score, split by the true intent of each ticket. The average of 42.5% hid one class that looks solved and four that are mostly wrong, and the solved one is only the model's default guess. Step 2 · Read what it says instead For every ticket with the wrong intent, count which intent the model gave, and read a few: Copy What you should see Copy Now the behaviour is clear. When the model does not recognise a phrasing, it almost always answers order_status . That is why order_status scored 100% in Step 1: not because the model understands those tickets better, but because that is its default guess. The examples show why the guess is tempting: the test phrasings mention an order number and a product, as most order_status training tickets do, and say "refund", "cancel" or "exchange" in words the model never saw ("reimbursed", "drop this order", "trade this"). A second finding: for other tickets the model sometimes invents an intent that is not one of the five ( pay , payable ). Nothing in a language model limits it to your list of labels. Reading this output Two fixes that do not involve training Constrain the output. Validate the reply against the allowed values and treat anything else as a failure to be retried or escalated ( Lesson 11.21 ). Serving systems can also force the output to follow a JSON schema while it is generated ( constrained decoding ), which makes an invented label impossible. Use confidence. A model that is unsure spreads its probability across several labels. Reading the probability of the chosen intent token lets you send low-confidence tickets to a person or to a larger model. This is a cascade , and it is how small tuned models are usually deployed ( Lesson 14.142 ). Step 3 · Is the model being asked the way it was trained? Before blaming the data, rule out the commonest cause of "it worked in training and not in production": the input format. Evaluate the same model on tickets it handles perfectly, changing only how the prompt is built: Copy What you should see Copy Two results, and they teach different things. The system message made no difference here. Every training example had the same system message, so it carried no information and the model learned to ignore it; you saw the same thing in Lesson 3.23 , when the model answered a geography question in JSON with no system message at all. Do not rely on this. A model fine-tuned with several different system messages, or less heavily, depends on them, and the safe rule is unchanged: send in production exactly what you trained on. Without the chat template the model is useless. The same weights, given the ticket as plain text, continue it as if it were the start of a letter, and not one reply is JSON. The markers <|im_start|>user , <|im_end|> and <|im_start|>assistant are how the model knows that a question has ended and its answer should begin. Template mismatches are easy to cause without noticing, because serving tools apply a chat template for you and may not use yours: Where it goes wrong What happens The serving tool has its own template for the model, or a default one The model sees markers it was not trained on; quality drops a little or a lot The generation prompt (the final <|im_start|>assistant ) is missing The model continues the user's message instead of answering The end-of-turn token is not set as a stop token The model answers correctly, then keeps generating A beginning-of-text token is added twice Subtle quality loss You trained on raw strings but serve with a chat endpoint (or the reverse) Like the last row of the output above The test is always the same: print the exact string or token ids that reach the model in production, and compare them with what apply_chat_template produced in training. Step 4 · An experiment: variety against volume The diagnosis from Steps 1 and 2 is that the training data has too few ways of saying each thing. That is a claim, and claims should be tested. Train three models that differ only in their data, and score all three on the same 40 test tickets (whose phrasings are in none of the training sets): Copy What you should see Copy Ignore the step 1 lines, which are the training function reporting its first step. Read the other three lines as an experiment. Same volume, more variety (first line against second): with 320 tickets in both cases, going from 2 to 8 phrasings per intent took the test score from 30% to 90%. Nothing about the model, the training settings or the number of examples changed. A quarter of the volume, with variety (third line): 80 varied tickets beat 320 uniform ones by a wide margin. The model, the code and the hyperparameters were never the problem. No learning rate would have turned 30% into 90%. This is what practitioners mean by "fine-tuning is a data problem", and it is the reason Lesson 7.25 spent so long on the dataset. Watch out How sure are these numbers? The test set has 40 tickets, so each ticket is worth 2.5 points, and a different random seed would move each result by a few points ( Lesson 2.25 ). A jump from 30% to 90% is far outside that noise. A difference of 5 points between two settings would not be, and you would need a larger test set, or several runs with different seeds, before believing it. Size your test set for the smallest difference you care about. Step 5 · Where things stand, and the decision Every result from the workshop, on the same test tickets: Approach Test, all correct What it costs to run Notes Base 135M model, instructions only 0% Tiny Cannot produce the format Base 135M model, five examples in the prompt 15% Tiny, but 7 times the prompt tokens Format fixed, content wrong Full fine-tune, 4 phrasings per intent 42.5% Tiny Memorised its training phrasings LoRA on all linear layers, 4 phrasings 60% Tiny Generalised better from the same data Full fine-tune, 8 phrasings per intent 90% Tiny Better data, half the training steps A large hosted model with a good prompt not measured here; expect high Hundreds of times more per ticket The alternative to beat Is 90% good enough? That is not a modelling question. It depends on what a wrong route costs (a refund request sent to the wrong queue is delayed; a cancellation missed may ship an unwanted parcel), on what the current process achieves, and on whether errors can be caught downstream. Usual next steps from here: Replace templates with real tickets , labelled by a large model and reviewed by people ( Lesson 7.25 , Step 8). Real variety is far greater than ten phrasings. Add the hard cases on purpose: two requests in one ticket, no order number, mixed Hindi and English, sarcasm, tickets that are not requests at all. Constrain the intent to the allowed list, and route low-confidence tickets to a larger model. Measure the large-model alternative on the same test set, and compare cost at your volume ( Lesson 3.25 ). A debugging checklist Symptom Most likely causes What to do Great validation score, poor test or production score Training data lacks variety; leakage between training and validation Error analysis as in Steps 1 and 2; add varied and real examples; deduplicate Worked in the notebook, poor when served Chat template or system message differs; quantisation ; wrong stop token Compare the exact input strings; evaluate the served model on the test set Correct answer followed by extra text End-of-turn token missing from the labels or the stop list Include it in training targets; set stop tokens Output not in the allowed set Nothing constrains a language model's output Validation with retry; constrained decoding; more examples of edge cases Loss does not fall Learning rate too low; labels all masked; weights frozen Print trainable parameter count and a batch of labels; raise the rate Loss jumps or is nan Learning rate too high; bad examples (empty, enormous) Lower the rate; add warm-up and clipping; inspect the longest and shortest examples Loss near zero immediately The answer is visible in the prompt; duplicates Check encode ; check for leakage Training loss falls, validation loss rises Overfitting Fewer epochs; more data; lower LoRA rank; early stopping The model lost general abilities Catastrophic forgetting Fewer steps; LoRA; mix in general examples; regression tests Results change between runs Small test set; sampling at generation time Fix seeds; evaluate with greedy decoding ; larger test set Good on average, bad for one group or language That group is rare in the training data Per-group scores ( Lesson 10.41 ); targeted data The order in which to spend effort, from experience across many teams: data first (coverage, correctness, format), then how long you train (stop when validation stops improving), then the learning rate , and only then method details such as LoRA rank. Check your mental model ✗ "One accuracy number describes a model." ✓ Split it by class and by field, and read the errors. The average here hid one perfect class and four failing ones. ✗ "If the score is low, train longer or tune the learning rate." ✓ First find out what is wrong. Here more variety in the data tripled the score with the same settings and half the steps. ✗ "The fine-tuned model will only output the labels I trained it on." ✓ It can produce any text. Validate or constrain the output. ✗ "A model that works in my notebook will work the same when served." ✓ Only if the served input, token for token, matches the training format. Exercises Predict before you run In Step 4, add a fourth experiment: dict(n_train=320, phrasings=1) . Before running, predict its test score relative to the 2-phrasing result, and say which intent you expect it to default to. (Solution P1.) Make it your own Write constrained_reply(model, row) : call reply , parse the JSON, and if the intent is not one of INTENTS replace it with "other" . Re-score the Lesson 3.23 model on the test set. How much does this cheap fix gain, and for which class? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it A team's fine-tuned support model scores 94% on their evaluation set. After release, agents report that it handles billing questions badly. The evaluation set has 500 examples sampled at random from last year's tickets, of which 12 are about billing. What is wrong with the evaluation, and what would you change? (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · One phrasing per intent Expect a score at or below the 2-phrasing result, close to what you would get by always answering one intent (20% for five balanced classes, plus whatever the default class contributes). With a single sentence pattern per intent, the model has learned five strings and nothing about meaning. Which default it picks depends on which training pattern the test phrasings most resemble on the surface. Solution M1 · Constraining the output pred = json.loads(reply(...)); pred["intent"] = pred["intent"] if pred.get("intent") in INTENTS else "other" . The invented intents all occurred on other tickets, so mapping them to other makes those tickets correct: other improves by several tickets and the overall score by a few points, at no training cost. The larger failure, defaulting to order_status , is untouched, because those outputs are valid labels. Constraints fix invalid outputs, not wrong ones. Solution X1 · An evaluation set that hides a group Twelve billing examples cannot measure billing quality: one error moves that group's score by 8 points, and the overall 94% would barely change if all twelve were wrong. Random sampling reproduces the frequency of topics, not their importance. Build the set by stratified sampling : a minimum number per category (say 50), including rare but costly ones; report scores per category with a minimum bar for each; and add every production failure to the set as it is found ( Lesson 14.143 ). Recap Break scores down by class and by field, and read the wrong answers. Averages hide default guesses and invented labels. Check the format: the chat template is a hard requirement, and what reaches the model in production must match training exactly. A controlled experiment showed that variety in the training data, not volume or settings, decided generalisation: 30% to 90% with the same number of tickets. Constrain outputs and use confidence to catch what the model cannot do. Debug in the order data, training length, learning rate, method details, and size the test set for the differences you need to see. Check your understanding Q1 A fine-tuned classifier scores 100% on one class and about 30% on the other four. What is the most likely explanation? A The first class is easier B The model answers the first class by default whenever it is unsure C The test set is too small to tell D The learning rate was too high A default guess is always right for its own class and wrong for the rest; the confusion counts confirm it. Q2 In the variety experiment, 80 varied tickets beat 320 uniform ones. What is the lesson? A Smaller datasets are always better B The model was too small for 320 tickets C Coverage of the ways an input can be phrased matters more than the number of examples D Training for fewer steps improves accuracy Extra examples that repeat the same patterns add little; new patterns add a lot. Q3 A fine-tuned model answers perfectly in your notebook but writes rambling text when served. What do you check first? A Whether the GPU is too slow B Whether the serving stack applies the same chat template and stop tokens as training C Whether the training loss reached zero D Whether the LoRA rank was high enough Compare the exact prompt string that reaches the model in each place; a template or stop-token mismatch is the usual cause. l1104: Course home / Phase 14 · AI Agents: Design and Engineering Data curation and the data flywheel From Zero to Agents Lesson 14.131 35 min Go deeper Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Name the stages of the data flywheel and say what each one produces Turn production traces into training data and eval cases, with lineage and privacy controls, and keep the two from overlapping Decide when customising a model is worth it, and which method fits the goal Before you start Needs : Lesson 3.25 Depth : Deepen Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) Training on input-output examples Customization LoRA / QLoRA Training small adapter weights / on a quantized base model Parameter-efficient tuning Distillation Training a small model on a large model's outputs Cost and latency Preference tuning (DPO) Training from pairs of better and worse answers Tone, helpfulness Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) Training with a grader or verifiable reward Checkable tasks Lineage Tracking where each training example came from source_trace Grader A function that scores an answer, the core of RFT Step 6 Eval case One test question with a written rule for what a correct answer must and must not contain Failed traces become eval cases Why this came about Teams found that improving data improved models and systems more than most other changes. The data flywheel , using production feedback to build better datasets that improve the system, became a central practice for AI products. In plain words first Better data beats more data The data you train or evaluate on decides what you get. Curation means collecting relevant examples, cleaning them, removing duplicates and sensitive data, labeling carefully, and balancing hard and easy cases. The data flywheel is the production loop that keeps improving it: production traces and user feedback reveal failures, failures become labeled examples, examples improve prompts, evaluations or models, and the cycle repeats. The flywheel Every production run is data. The data flywheel turns it into improvement: log traces with feedback → mine failures and good examples → label (people and calibrated judges) → grow the eval set → fix with prompts, tools and retrieval, or train → release through the eval gate → repeat. Most loops end at "fix with prompts and tools". Training is for the cases that remain. The data flywheel. Production traffic becomes evaluation cases and, when needed, training data; each release then produces better traffic to learn from. Most turns of the wheel end with a prompt, tool or retrieval fix, not with training. Step 1 · From traces to a dataset Your tracing store already holds what a training set needs: real inputs, the outputs your system gave, and signals about which outputs were good (user feedback, eval results). The code turns five traces into training examples in four moves: keep only the ones that passed, remove near-duplicates, mask personal data, and write the result in the chat format that fine-tuning services accept, with a pointer back to the trace each example came from. Copy What you should see Copy The chat-format JSONL ( messages with roles) is what almost every fine-tuning service accepts. Lineage ( source_trace ) lets you delete training examples when a customer exercises their right to erasure , and audit where a behavior came from. Make sure your terms with customers allow using their data for training before you do. The other half: failed traces become eval cases Step 1 used the traces that went well. The traces that went badly are worth more, because each one is a mistake your system really made. They do not go into training data. They go into the eval set , the fixed list of test questions (first met in Lesson 11.19 ) that every change must pass before release. For each failed trace, a person writes down what a correct answer must say and must not say. From then on, that mistake is checked automatically on every release. The code continues from Step 1. It turns the failed trace t4 (the invented insurance offer) into an eval case , shows that the old answer fails it and a corrected answer passes, and then checks one more thing: that no question sits in both datasets. Copy What you should see Copy The last two lines are the part teams forget. Trace t1 asked "Where is A-1001?", and so does an eval case. A model fine-tuned on t1 would pass that case by memory, and the eval score would rise without the model getting any better. This is data leakage , the problem you met with train and test splits in Lesson 2.26 , and the rule that prevents it is simple: when a question is in the eval set, it stays out of the training data. The check uses the same norm function as the duplicate filter, so "where is A-1001 ?" counts as the same question. Step 2 · When to customize a model The workshop showed how to fine-tune; this table is about whether to, and which method fits. Customize only after prompts, retrieval, tools and model choice are exhausted, and only with an eval set to prove the gain. Lesson 14.132 works through the three methods below that the workshop did not use. Goal Method Teach a format, style or narrow task with many examples Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) , usually parameter-efficient ( LoRA , QLoRA ) Make a small model behave like a large one on your task (cost and latency) Distillation : generate outputs with the large model, fine-tune the small one on them Prefer some answers over others (tone, helpfulness) Preference tuning (DPO and variants) from pairs of better and worse answers Improve on tasks with checkable outcomes (correct SQL, passing tests, right classification) Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) with a grader or verifiable reward Add knowledge that changes Not fine-tuning: use retrieval (the Retrieval (RAG) section) Costs that teams underestimate: building and cleaning data, evaluating every candidate, hosting the custom model (often provisioned capacity), and re-doing it all when a better base model ships. Check your mental model ✗ "More data always helps." ✓ Noisy or duplicated data can make results worse. ✗ "Production data can be used as is." ✓ Remove personal data and check consent and licensing first. ✗ "The flywheel runs by itself." ✓ It needs labeling, review and ownership to turn failures into improvements. Exercises Predict before you run A training set has 30% near-duplicate support replies. What happens to the fine-tuned model, and what is the fix? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Use production conversations for training without filtering. What gets into the model? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise The data flywheel collects thumbs-up answers for training, and the model becomes more confident but not more correct. Why? (Solution D1.) Make it your own Design a flywheel for ShopKart: what is logged, how examples are selected and labeled, how they enter evals and training, and how quality is checked. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Duplicates skew training It over-learns the repeated replies, and an eval that shares duplicates looks better than reality. Deduplicate (exact and near-duplicate), and split train and test after deduplication. Solution B1 · Data hygiene Personal data, wrong agent answers, abusive messages and prompt injections . Filter for quality and policy, remove personal data, and keep only conversations with good outcomes. Solution D1 · Feedback is not ground truth Users reward confident, pleasant answers, not necessarily correct ones. Verify feedback-selected examples against ground truth before training, and include corrected failures. Solution M1 · A flywheel with checks Log inputs, outputs, tool calls and outcomes; select failures and uncertain cases; label them; add them to the eval set first; train only after the eval shows a gap; check for regressions before release. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What is a data flywheel, and what makes it work? Worked answer. A loop where production use generates data (failures, corrections, outcomes) that improves the system's evals, prompts, retrieval and models, which improves the product and brings more use. It works when data is selected for informativeness, labeled reliably, privacy-filtered, and used first to measure and only then to train. A plausible wrong answer. "Collect everything and fine-tune on it." Unfiltered data teaches errors. Follow-ups. What would you log to make it possible? Debug a failure After retraining on new data, quality for one customer segment dropped. What do you check? Worked answer. The new data's mix: whether that segment was under-represented or labeled differently, and whether the eval covers it. Rebalance, relabel and segment the eval. A plausible wrong answer. "The model is worse." The data changed the balance. Follow-ups. How would you catch this before release? Defend a design Synthetic data or real data for training? Worked answer. Real data for distribution and edge cases; synthetic data to fill gaps (rare intents, languages) and to scale, with quality checks and a held-out real eval. Pure synthetic training risks narrow, repetitive behavior. A plausible wrong answer. "Synthetic is cheaper, so use it only." It inherits the generator's blind spots. Follow-ups. How would you check synthetic data quality? Check your understanding Q1 Where should a failed production trace go? A Into the training data B Into the eval set, as a case every release must pass C Nowhere, because it is noise D Into the system prompt Good traces can become training examples. A failed trace is a mistake the system really made, so it becomes an eval case. Q2 An eval question also appears in the training data. What goes wrong? A The model can pass it from memory, so the score rises without the model getting better B Training becomes slower C The eval becomes too hard D Nothing goes wrong This is data leakage. When a question is in the eval set, it stays out of the training data.
