Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Custom Model Import Serving open-weight models you trained elsewhere through Bedrock Lesson 14.153 Microsoft Foundry Microsoft's platform for models, agents, knowledge and governance (formerly Azure AI Foundry) Lesson 14.155 Why this came about Full fine-tuning of large models was too expensive for most teams. LoRA (2021) made tuning cheap by training small add-on matrices, and distillation let small models learn tasks from large ones, putting model customization within reach of ordinary teams. In plain words first Adjusting a model instead of only instructing it When prompts and retrieval are not enough, you can change the model itself. Fine-tuning trains it further on your examples; LoRA does that cheaply by training small extra matrices instead of all the weights; distillation trains a small model to imitate a large one on your task, cutting cost and latency. Each needs a good dataset and an evaluation that proves the tuned model beats the simpler options. How this connects Where this lesson sits The workshop (Lessons 7.25 to 3.25 ) took one task from a baseline measurement through a full fine-tune, a LoRA adapter, error analysis , quantisation and serving. Lesson 14.131 showed how production traffic becomes training data and when customising a model is worth it at all. This lesson completes the picture with the methods the workshop did not use: distillation , preference tuning and reinforcement fine-tuning , then the tools and managed services that run them. Its steps continue the numbering of Lesson 14.131 (Steps 1 and 2 are there). Step 3 · Where LoRA sits among the methods You trained a LoRA adapter in Lesson 3.24 , so this step is a recap and a map. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes the model's weights and learns a small update for each chosen layer as the product of two thin matrices, B @ A . Training touches a few percent of the parameters, the result is a file of a few megabytes, and one base model can serve many adapters. LoRA, drawn: the big pretrained weight matrix W stays frozen; training learns two thin matrices B and A whose product is a low-rank update, so only a tiny fraction of parameters change and the adapter can be swapped per task. LoRA is a way of doing supervised fine-tuning : you show the model inputs with the outputs you want. The rest of this lesson covers what supervised fine-tuning on your own examples does not give you: You want Supervised fine-tuning needs The method in this lesson A cheap, fast model for a step that a large model already does well Thousands of labelled examples, which you may not have Distillation (Step 4): the large model writes the labels Answers in the style people prefer One "correct" answer per input, when really some answers are just better than others Preference tuning (Step 5): learn from pairs of better and worse answers Better results on a task where answers can be checked by a program Example answers, when all you have is a way to check them Reinforcement fine-tuning (Step 6): learn from a grader's scores Each of these can be trained with LoRA adapters too: LoRA decides which weights change, and the method decides what signal they learn from. In production Fine-tuning projects that disappoint The usual reasons: the gap was knowledge, which retrieval would have fixed; the training data repeated the system's own mistakes because it came from unreviewed traces ; the evaluation set leaked into training, so the gain disappeared in production; or a better base model shipped a month later and beat the tuned one. Start from a held-out, human-labeled eval set, compare against the best prompt-only baseline and the newest base model, and keep the frontier model behind the same alias as a fallback. Step 4 · Distillation: a small model for a high-volume step The most common customization that pays for itself: a frontier model labels your traffic for one narrow step (here, intent routing), and a tiny model learns to imitate it: Copy What you should see Copy The student even beat its teacher here, because a model trained on many labels averages out the teacher's random slips. Do not expect that on real traffic: these template messages are easy, and real students usually land a few points below the teacher. That is why the evaluation set must be labeled by people (the gold labels here), never by the teacher alone. When the student is unsure (low predicted probability), fall back to the teacher: a cascade ( Lesson 14.142 ) that keeps quality while most calls cost nothing. For generative steps, distill into a small LLM with SFT instead of a classifier; Bedrock, Foundry and OpenAI offer managed distillation. Step 5 · Preference pairs and pre-upload checks Preference tuning ( DPO and its variants) learns from pairs: for the same prompt, which answer was better. Pairs come from A/B comparisons, reviewer choices, or a rejected draft and its human-edited replacement. Whatever the method, validate the file before uploading; a rejected training job after an hour in a queue is the most avoidable delay in fine-tuning: Copy What you should see Copy The second feedback item produced no pair: both answers were liked, so there is nothing to prefer. The prompt / chosen / rejected format with chat messages is what TRL's DPOTrainer and most managed services accept. Step 6 · Reinforcement fine-tuning starts with a grader Reinforcement fine-tuning ( RFT ; GRPO is the common open-source algorithm) lets the model try several answers per prompt and rewards the good ones. It needs no example answers at all, only a grader : a function that scores an answer. For SQL, the grader runs the query and compares the rows: Copy What you should see Copy The fourth query is written differently from the reference and still scores 1.0, because the grader checks results, not text. That is what makes RFT powerful for tasks with checkable outcomes (SQL, code that must pass tests, extraction that must match a schema, classification) and useless for tasks without them. Most of the work is the grader: models are very good at finding its loopholes ( reward hacking ), so test it on wrong answers that look right before training, and keep a held-out eval set that the grader never sees. Step 7 · The same steps with open-source trainers On a GPU machine, Hugging Face TRL and PEFT run these methods on open-weight models . This script trains a LoRA adapter with SFT on the JSONL from Step 1, then shows how the Step 6 grader plugs into GRPO: Copy assistant_only_loss needs a chat template that marks assistant turns (most recent instruction models have one). Unsloth and Axolotl wrap the same trainers with faster kernels and YAML configs. Whatever the tool, the evaluation step is not optional: compare the tuned model with the base model and the frontier model on your held-out set before anything ships. From the field Checkr: a fine-tuned small model beat GPT-4 on the hard 2% Checkr classifies records from background checks into 230 categories. A logistic regression model handled 98% of records; the remaining 2% were hard cases. Its engineers compared approaches on those cases (October 2024): GPT-4 with a prompt reached 81.8% accuracy at about 15 seconds per call; adding retrieved examples ( RAG ) made it worse, 79.3%, because similar-looking examples pulled the model toward wrong labels; a fine-tuned Llama-2 7B reached 85%; and a Llama-3 8B fine-tuned with LoRA reached 90%, with production latency around 0.15 seconds and inference cost about five times lower than GPT-4. Two lessons travel well: RAG is not automatically an improvement for classification, and a narrow, high-volume step is exactly where a small tuned model pays off. Source: Rubrik and Predibase blog . Solutions Solution P1 · Parameter-efficient fine-tuning A tiny fraction, well under 1%. Training is cheaper, fits on smaller GPUs, and adapters are small files that can be swapped per task on one base model. Solution B1 · Distillation data decides coverage The student never saw hard cases and fails on them. Distill on a representative and challenging input set, including the hard cases the student must handle. Solution D1 · Train and serve must match The chat template, tokenizer and system prompt used in serving against training, whether the adapter was merged or loaded correctly, and quantization differences. Template mismatches are the most common cause. Solution M1 · A decision with numbers Compare accuracy on the eval set, cost per thousand requests, latency and maintenance for each option; choose fine-tuning or distillation only if it meets accuracy at clearly lower cost or latency. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism When would you fine-tune, distill, or just prompt? Worked answer. Prompt (with retrieval) first: cheapest to change. Fine-tune when you need consistent format, style or narrow skill that prompting cannot reach, or a smaller model at the same quality. Distill when a large model is accurate but too slow or expensive, training a smaller model on its outputs. Measure each against the eval set and the total cost of ownership. A plausible wrong answer. "Fine-tune to make it smarter." Fine-tuning shapes behavior; it rarely adds general capability. Follow-ups. What does QLoRA add to LoRA? Debug a failure A fine-tuned small model matches the large one on the eval but fails in production. Why? Worked answer. The eval set does not cover production's variety, so the small model's narrower competence is hidden. Add production samples, especially rare intents, and monitor fallback rates. A plausible wrong answer. "The small model is unstable." It is narrower; the eval was too narrow to show it. Follow-ups. When would you route back to the large model? Defend a design Managed fine-tuning API or self-hosted training? Worked answer. Managed for speed and simplicity when the provider supports your model and data terms; self-hosted for open models you must run yourself, data that cannot leave, or specialized methods. The deciding factors are data governance, model choice and the team's capacity. A plausible wrong answer. "Self-hosted is always cheaper." Not counting the team's time. Follow-ups. The gap between demo and production became the central engineering problem, and this chapter covers the practices that close it. In plain words first A demo is a prototype; production is a promise A demo works when you run it. A production system works for thousands of people you never meet, at any hour, within a budget, and you can explain what it did afterwards. That requires a whole stack around the model: gateways, identity, tools, memory, evaluation, observability, deployment and incident response. A readiness review checks each layer before launch. Most agents never reach production, and most of the ones that do reach it the hard way: a demo that worked on Friday becomes an incident on Monday. The model is rarely the reason. The reasons are the things around it: an action nobody bounded, a retry nobody budgeted, a failure nobody could see, a change nobody could roll back. This part of the course is about those things. It treats agents in production as its own discipline, end to end. Earlier chapters built the pieces: the loop ( Lesson 14.57 ), patterns ( Lesson 14.62 ), harnesses ( Lesson 14.67 ), frameworks (the LangChain and LangGraph and Other agent frameworks, compared sections), protocols (the Protocols section) and security (the Safety, security and governance section). This chapter assembles them into a system you can run, and adds what only shows up once real users, real data and real money are involved. What "in production" means for an agent A chatbot is in production when it answers. An agent is in production when it acts , so the bar is higher. Use seven properties, and write each down with a number before launch: Property What it means Typical evidence Correct enough It completes the tasks it is for, at a measured rate that the business accepts Task success on an eval suite built from real cases; pass^k for reliability ( Lesson 14.144 ) Bounded It can only do what it is meant to do, with the rights of the person it acts for Tool allow-list, scoped credentials, approval policy, budgets ( Lesson 14.138 ) Reliable It finishes, or fails cleanly and recoverably, when dependencies misbehave Timeouts, retries with budgets, idempotency , checkpoints, compensation ( Lesson 14.139 ) Observable Every run can be reconstructed: what it saw, decided, called and cost Traces with model and tool spans, linked to user, version and outcome ( Lesson 14.146 ) Affordable Cost per successful task is known and inside budget at expected volume Unit economics from traces, caps per run and per tenant ( Lesson 14.141 ) Changeable Prompts, models and tools can change without surprises, and roll back in minutes Versioned releases, shadow and canary, a kill switch ( Lesson 14.147 ) Owned A named team is on call for it, and people know how to take over Owner, runbook, escalation path, human handoff ( Lesson 14.148 ) The last one is the one demos skip. An agent with no owner is a production incident waiting for a date. Agentic AI concept The production gap is a systems gap Teams that ship agents successfully describe the same shift: from " prompt engineering " to "systems engineering". The model call is one component in a distributed system that also has queues, credentials, state, retries, approvals and telemetry. Treat the agent as a non-deterministic service inside a deterministic shell: everything around the model is ordinary, testable, boring software, and that is what makes the model safe to use. The production agent stack Every serious deployment ends up with roughly the same layers, whatever the vendor. Learn the layers, and every product becomes "an option for layer X". Hands-on · A production readiness review, as code A production readiness review (PRR) is the checklist an SRE team runs before it agrees to carry the pager for a service. For agents, write it as code so it runs in CI on every release, and so the bar is the same for every team. The review takes an agent manifest , the one document that describes the agent, and returns blocking and advisory findings. Copy What you should see Copy The agent passes its own evals , which is what the team would have pointed to. The review finds what would have caused the first incident: no one is on call, the suite is too small to trust, the refund tool can pay twice and pays without approval, and there is no cost cap or kill switch. Fix the manifest the way the team would, and run the review again: Copy What you should see Copy Note what changed: no prompt was edited. Every fix is in the system around the model. Teams began writing specifications first, with contracts for tools, budgets and failure handling, the same discipline as other critical software. In plain words first A specification before the code Designing a production agent starts with writing down what it must and must not do: its users, the tasks it handles, its tools and their permissions, the shape of its inputs and outputs, its budgets for cost and time, and how each likely failure is handled. That specification becomes the contract for building, testing and reviewing the agent. Most production incidents with agents were designed in. Nobody decided what the agent must never do, so nothing stopped it; nobody decided what "done" meant, so it stopped too early or never; a tool returned 40,000 rows, so the context overflowed. These decisions are cheap on a whiteboard and expensive in an incident review. This lesson is the whiteboard. The agent spec: one page, decided before code The spec is the agent's charter. It is short, it is versioned with the code, and every reviewer reads it first. A good spec answers twelve questions: # Question Example (a refund agent) Why it matters later 1 Who are the users, and through which channel? Support staff in the helpdesk; customers via chat for status only Identity, latency budget, tone, who can approve 2 Which intents are in scope? Order status, refund eligibility, refund under 5,000 INR, address change before dispatch Eval suite shape; routing 3 What is explicitly out of scope? Legal threats, chargebacks, account deletion These become escalations and refusal tests 4 What is the autonomy level per intent? Status L3, refund L2, address change L2 ( Lesson 14.133 ) Approval design, release plan 5 What may it never do? Refund twice for one order; refund above order value; change a dispatched order Hard rules become hooks and tool checks, not prompt lines 6 Which tools, with which effects? get_order (read), issue_refund (write, money), notify (write, external) Risk tiers, scopes, approvals ( Lesson 14.138 ) 7 Which data may it see, and whose? The requesting customer's orders only; no card data Delegated identity; redaction; tenant isolation 8 What does success mean, as numbers? 90% correct resolution on the suite; under 2% wrong refunds; p95 under 60 seconds The release gate ( Lesson 14.144 ) 9 What are the budgets per run? 12 steps, 0.40 USD, 120 seconds Runaway loops and bills 10 When does it escalate, to whom, with what? Uncertain, out of scope, or angry customer: to tier 2 with a handoff summary Handoff quality ( Lesson 14.148 ) 11 What happens when a dependency is down? Orders API down: say so, create a callback ticket, never guess Degraded modes ( Lesson 14.139 ) 12 Who owns it? Payments AI team; on-call rotation; product owner Incidents, changes, sunsetting Tip Write the "never" list first Questions 3 and 5 are the ones teams skip and regret. Each "never" line should map to something that enforces it: a tool argument check, a policy rule, a hook, a database constraint. If you cannot name the enforcer, the line is a hope, not a rule. Choose the shape with the least autonomy that works Lesson 14.62 covers the patterns. In production, decide the shape per intent , and prefer the most deterministic shape that meets the quality bar: If the intent is... Shape Why Fixed steps every time (status lookup, form filling) A workflow : code calls the model for the fuzzy step only Cheapest, fastest, easiest to test and audit A few known paths chosen by the request A router to small workflows or narrow agents Each path is evaluated and released separately Open-ended, but within one domain and toolset A single agent with a bounded loop Flexible without coordination costs Several distinct skills, contexts or permissions Specialists behind a supervisor, or handoffs Separate contexts and scopes; each specialist testable ( Lesson 14.66 ) Long, verifiable work (code, research, migrations) An agent inside a harness with a spine and a verifier Finishes across context windows ( Lesson 14.67 ) From the field Factory and Two Sigma: shape and scope follow purpose Factory describes the multi-agent architecture behind its coding product as three roles: an orchestrator, workers and validators, connected by validation contracts and structured handoffs, with adversarial verification. It argues for serial over parallel execution where work depends on earlier results, and for choosing the model per role ( talk , 19 min). Two Sigma's John Feminella lists, among five controls for giving agents real autonomy, tool access that follows an agent's declared purpose : the purpose in the spec decides the tools, not the other way round ( talk , 19 min). Tool contracts: the agent-computer interface, hardened Lesson 14.58 covers tool design for model accuracy. Production adds a second reader: the systems the tool touches. A production tool contract has eight parts: Part Rule Failure it prevents Name and description One verb, one object; say when to use it and when not to The model picking a near-duplicate tool Typed arguments Enums for closed sets, formats for IDs and dates, bounds for amounts Hallucinated values that pass as strings Effect class Declare read, write, external (sends something out) or destructive Approvals and retries applied to the wrong tools Idempotency Writes take an idempotency key ; the tool returns the original result on a repeat Double refunds after a retry or resume Bounded output Page, truncate and summarize; never return unbounded rows Context overflow and cost spikes Actionable errors Errors say what went wrong and what to do next, in words the model can act on Retry loops on errors that will never succeed Dry run Writes support dry_run=true to preview the effect Approvals without a clear picture of the change Version and owner Contracts are versioned; breaking changes get a new version A tool that changed shape silently breaking agents The linter below checks tool definitions against these rules. Run it in CI next to your MCP server or tool registry. Copy What you should see Copy refund_order is the tool most teams have somewhere: added early, loosely typed, never removed, and now a near-duplicate of the real refund tool. Delete it or hide it from the agent; an agent cannot misuse a tool it never sees. Where state lives An agent run touches four kinds of state. Mixing them up is the root of many production bugs: Four kinds of state in one agent run, by how long they must last and who may trust them. The classic bug is at the far left: treating the transcript as the truth about what happened in the business system on the far right. State Lives in Example Rule Conversation The context window and transcript What the user said, recent tool results Disposable; can be summarized or truncated Run state A durable store owned by the runtime (checkpoints) Step reached, plan, pending approval, idempotency keys used Survives crashes; one writer; versioned schema Memory A memory store with provenance ( Lesson 14.65 ) Customer prefers email; resolved issue history Written deliberately, scoped per user or tenant, expirable System of record The business system (orders, CRM, ledger) Refund issued, address changed The truth. The agent reads it before acting and never infers it from the transcript The most common mistake is treating the transcript as the system of record: "I already refunded this" because the transcript says so, when the refund call actually timed out. Always re-read the system of record before a write, and let idempotency keys make the write safe to repeat. Failure mode and effects analysis, for agents FMEA is an engineering method from aerospace and automotive: list how each part can fail, score each failure for severity , likelihood and detectability (1 to 5, where 5 is worst and for detectability means "hard to notice"), multiply into a risk priority number (RPN), and fix from the top. It fits agents well because their failures are many, varied and easy to overlook. Copy What you should see Copy Two lessons hide in the ranking. Detectability matters as much as severity: a double refund that nobody notices for a week scores higher than a loud outage. And most mitigations are not prompts: they are keys, bounds, versions and budgets. Solutions Solution P1 · Specs as contracts Inputs: a customer message and the signed-in customer. Outputs: an answer citing policy, or a handoff. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Durable execution Running a long task so that every completed step is saved and a crash resumes from the last one Lesson 14.140 AI gateway One service that every model call passes through, for keys, routing, limits, fallbacks, logging and cost tracking Lesson 14.136 Senior AI engineering, architect and forward deployed roles now share one expectation: given a business problem, you can lay out the whole system, not just the prompt or the retriever. This lesson pulls the rest of the course together into that skill. Everything here applies equally to a team whiteboard session, a client workshop and an architecture review board. Why this came about As AI systems became core products, teams and design reviews needed a method for designing them. A repeatable approach, requirements, estimates, design, risks and evaluation, emerged from system design practice and was adapted to models' costs and uncertainties. In plain words first Ask, estimate, design, then defend AI system design follows a repeatable method: clarify requirements and what success means; estimate volumes, tokens, cost and latency to find what actually constrains you; design the flow with code where rules are known and models where they are not; then go through risks (failure, security, privacy) and how you will evaluate and roll it out. The estimates often decide the design. What is different about AI system design Classic system design is about data, traffic and failure. AI system design keeps all of that and adds five things that change the architecture: Difference Consequence for the design Outputs are probabilistic Quality is a requirement with a number, measured by an eval suite; the design includes how it is measured and gated Cost scales with tokens, not requests Cost per outcome is a first-class requirement; context size, caching and model routing are architecture decisions Latency is dominated by model calls The number of sequential model calls is the main latency lever; streaming is a requirement, not a nicety The system acts on untrusted text Security boundaries follow data flow (untrusted content, private data, external actions), not just network zones Models change underneath you Version pinning, gateways, evals on upgrade and fallbacks are part of the design, not operations afterthoughts The method: nine steps, said out loud Use the same sequence every time. In a 45-minute design discussion, spend roughly the minutes shown; in a client workshop, the same steps take a day. The nine-step system design method from Lesson 14.135 as a timeline for a 45-minute design session: most time goes to clarifying, designing knowledge and tools, and defending trade-offs. # Step Minutes Questions to answer 1 Clarify the problem 5 Who are the users, what tasks, which actions are allowed, what is out of scope, what does a wrong answer cost? 2 Define success and constraints 4 Quality metric and target, latency (first token and total), cost per outcome, availability, data residency, compliance 3 Estimate 4 Volume, peak rate, tokens, cost, quotas, storage (Step 1 below) 4 Choose the shape 4 Workflow, single agent, router plus agents, or multi-agent ; the least autonomy that works ( Lesson 14.62 ) 5 Design knowledge and tools 7 Retrieval type, structured data, tools with risk levels, permissions, memory 6 Draw the architecture 6 The reference architecture below, adapted; the request path step by step 7 Safety and governance 4 Trifecta check, approvals, guardrails , identity, residency, audit 8 Operate and evolve 4 Evals and release gates, tracing , dashboards, cost controls, rollout and rollback, model upgrades 9 Trade-offs, failure modes and what next 7 What you chose and against what, what breaks first at 10 times the load, what you would build next Say each step's decision with its reason and trade-off ("a router plus one agent, because 70% of traffic is three fixed intents; the trade-off is maintaining the router, which I would evaluate separately"). Reviewers judge the reasoning more than the boxes. The reference architecture Almost every production agentic system is a variation of this picture. Learn it once, then adapt it per problem by removing what the problem does not need. A reference architecture for a production agentic system: every arrow out of the orchestrator passes a gateway, and every layer emits traces. Copy What you should see Copy Three conclusions fall out immediately. Peak traffic needs about four deployments' worth of token quota, so the design needs a gateway that load-balances across deployments or Regions. Input tokens dominate cost even with 70% cached, so prompt caching and compact tool results are requirements, not optimizations. And the vector index fits on one node even in float32 , so a dedicated vector database is not justified by size. The prices and quota here are illustrative; in a real estimate, state your assumptions and move on. Step 2 · Budget latency along the critical path Users feel the time to the first visible token. Write the request path as hops with their p95 times, mark which run in parallel, and add up the critical path : Copy What you should see Copy The design fits the budget with little margin, and the two cheapest wins are architectural: route the common intents with rules instead of a model call, and keep the main model's prompt prefix stable so caching shortens time to first token . Running the order lookup alongside retrieval already removed one hop. Step 3 · Compose availability Every component in series multiplies its availability; alternatives in parallel multiply their failure probabilities. Model providers are often the least available component, so the design question is what happens when one is down: Copy What you should see Copy A second provider behind the gateway removes most of the downtime; a degraded mode (answer common questions from a cached FAQ when search is down, switch to read-only when tools fail) removes more. AI gateways emerged in 2023 and 2024 to centralize access, cost control, logging and failover, and model routing followed to send each request to the right model. In plain words first One front door for every model call When many teams call many models, an AI gateway sits in between: one place for keys, rate limits, logging, cost tracking, caching, safety filters and failover. Model routing chooses which model serves each request, for example a cheap one for simple requests and a strong one for hard ones, or a backup when the main provider is down. Why a gateway Without one, every team holds its own provider keys, picks its own models, and nobody knows what the company spends or sends to whom. An AI gateway (or LLM gateway) is a proxy that every model call goes through. It gives you, in one place: An LLM gateway is one door to every model: it checks the key and budget, applies policy and redaction, routes by task, falls back when a provider fails, caches, and logs every call for cost and audit. Capability What it does One API, many providers Applications call one OpenAI-style endpoint with a model alias ; the gateway translates to Bedrock, Azure, Vertex, Anthropic, OpenAI or self-hosted models Routing and fallbacks Primary and backup deployments, cross-region and cross-provider failover, load balancing, latency- or cost-based routing Keys and access Provider keys stay in the gateway; teams get their own virtual keys with allowed models Budgets and limits Spend limits per team, key or user; request and token rate limits Caching Exact-match and semantic caches Guardrails Central input and output checks ( Lesson 15.23 ) Logging and cost attribution Every call, tokens and cost tagged by team, app and user, exported to your observability stack Policy Approved models only, data-residency rules, PII handling It is also the cleanest seam for changing models: swap the deployment behind an alias, run evals , and no application code changes. LLM gateway, MCP gateway, agent gateway: one control plane The terms overlap, so it helps to separate the traffic each one governs: Gateway Traffic it governs Typical policies Covered in LLM gateway (or AI gateway, model gateway) Application or agent → model providers Routing, fallbacks, virtual keys, budgets, token limits, caching, PII redaction , logging This lesson MCP gateway Agent → tool servers Server allowlists, per-agent tool allowlists, auth to backends, tool-definition pinning, audit Lesson 16.28 Agent gateway Agent → agent ( A2A ) and front end → agent (AG-UI) Agent registry, identity, task limits, routing between agents Lesson 16.29 In 2026 these are converging into one control plane: Azure API Management, Kong, agentgateway, Bedrock AgentCore Gateway and Google's Agent Gateway each cover more than one kind of traffic, and enterprise platform teams increasingly run a single policy layer for models, tools and agents. The design principle is the same for all three: every call from an agent to anything outside it passes one point where identity, policy, cost and audit are enforced. Step 1 · A teaching-sized gateway Fifty lines show what the products do inside: Copy What you should see Copy Notice the waste: every request still tries the dead primary first. Real gateways add a cooldown ( circuit breaker ): after a few failures, skip that deployment for a while. Here is that circuit breaker , the standard fix. It has three states: closed (send traffic), open (skip the deployment until a cooldown ends) and half-open (let one trial request through to see whether it has recovered): Copy What you should see Copy After two failures the primary was skipped, so requests stopped paying the timeout. At 40 seconds one trial request found it still down, and the breaker opened again straight away. Production gateways track breakers per deployment and per error type: a 429 (rate limited) deserves a short cooldown and maybe a different region; a 400 (bad request) should not open the breaker at all, because the next deployment will reject it too. In production Gateway pitfalls seen in production The gateway becomes the outage : one instance, no health checks, and every agent stops when it does. Run it highly available, with its own SLOs later · 14.139 , and keep a documented emergency bypass. Added latency on every call : heavy plugins (PII scanning, logging of full payloads) on the hot path. Measure the gateway's own overhead and move slow work off the request path. Streaming broken by the proxy : buffering turns token streams into one late response. Test streaming through the gateway, not only directly. Fallbacks that change behavior silently : traffic shifts to a different model during an incident and quality drops. Log the model that actually served each call and evaluate every fallback ( Lesson 14.93 ). Budgets that cut off a critical flow : a hard limit hits the support agent at peak. Alert well before the limit and set separate budgets for critical and experimental traffic. Step 2 · LiteLLM's router, in code LiteLLM (open source) is the most widely used self-hosted gateway. Its Router gives an application fallbacks, retries, cooldowns and load balancing; its proxy server adds keys, budgets, logging and a UI for a whole company. Copy What you should see Copy Several deployments can share one model_name ; the router then load-balances across them ( routing_strategy options include simple shuffle, least busy, latency-based and cost-based). The proxy takes the same ideas as configuration: Copy Teams then get virtual keys with their own models and budgets ( POST /key/generate with models , max_budget and budget_duration ), and applications point any OpenAI-compatible SDK at the proxy URL. Cost attribution is the feature finance asks about first. LiteLLM computes the response cost ( response_cost ) for every call from its price table (or from prices you set per deployment, as here), and a callback can attribute it to a team from request metadata: Copy What you should see Copy 50 input tokens at $3 per million plus 20 output tokens at $15 per million is $0.00045 per call. Success callbacks run in a background thread, hence the short sleep before reading the totals. The proxy does this attribution for you per virtual key , team and user, and stores it in its database for the spend dashboards. Step 3 · A gateway as a service: virtual keys, limits and redaction Applications should not know provider keys exist. Here is a gateway as an HTTP service that any OpenAI SDK can call: it authenticates virtual keys , enforces each team's model allowlist and a tokens-per-minute limit, redacts personal data before the request leaves, and holds the only real provider key: Copy What you should see Copy Every rule a platform team cares about lives in one place: the intern key cannot reach the expensive model, a made-up key gets nothing, the support team hit its token limit on the third call and got a standard 429 with Retry-After (which the OpenAI SDK's retry logic understands), and the provider never saw the customer's email or phone number. Limits on tokens , not just requests, matter for LLM traffic, because one request can cost a thousand times more than another. Production gateways keep these counters in Redis so every gateway replica sees the same totals. Watch out Pin and verify your gateway The gateway holds every provider credential, so it is the most valuable target in the stack. LiteLLM itself was hit by a supply-chain attack in March 2026 ( Lesson 15.25 ). Pin exact versions with hashes, build images from a reviewed lockfile, keep provider keys in a secrets manager, and restrict the gateway's network egress to the providers it needs. Step 4 · Semantic caching, measured honestly An exact-match cache only helps when users send identical requests. A semantic cache reuses an answer when a new question means the same thing, judged by embedding similarity. It can cut cost sharply on FAQ-style traffic, and it can also serve confidently wrong answers: Copy What you should see Copy At the looser threshold, the cache answered a UPI PIN question with password instructions, and it never matched the real paraphrase. A good embedding model ranks paraphrases much higher than this lexical stand-in, but near-misses like "reset password" and "reset UPI PIN" stay close for every model. So: evaluate a semantic cache on labeled pairs (same meaning and different meaning) like any classifier; scope entries by tenant and, for personal answers, by user; expire entries when content changes; and keep it off for anything permission-dependent or time-sensitive. In production Semantic caching: where it helps, where it hurts It helps on high-volume FAQ-style traffic with stable answers (store hours, return windows), and it hurts anywhere the answer depends on who is asking or when: order status, balances, eligibility. Scope cache entries by tenant and, for personal answers, by user; set short lifetimes for anything that changes; invalidate when the source document changes; and measure the false-hit rate on labeled question pairs before turning it on. Industry practice Gateways are platform infrastructure Platform teams that run agents for many product teams usually make the gateway mandatory: no direct provider keys in applications. From the field Uber's GenAI Gateway: one door for every team Uber's machine-learning platform team built a GenAI Gateway (2024) as the single entry point for all large language model use at Uber, across external vendors and Uber-hosted open models. Requests pass through a PII redactor that replaces sensitive values with placeholders before they reach third-party vendors and restores them in the response; every call is authenticated, metered and logged for cost attribution, security audits and quality evaluation, and each use case is reviewed by the security team before it gets access. At the time of the write-up it served close to 30 customer teams and about 16 million queries a month. Source: Uber Engineering . Running models yourself became an option for cost, control and privacy. In plain words first Renting the oven, or building your own Calling a hosted model is renting someone else's oven; self-hosting is buying one. Running a model yourself means GPUs with enough memory for the weights and the per-request cache, a serving engine that batches many requests together, and the operations to keep it up. It can win on cost at high volume, on data control, or for fine-tuned models, and loses on effort and flexibility. A GPU you pay for around the clock but use 15% of the time is far more expensive per token than an API. Step 1 · Size the memory GPU memory holds two big things: the weights and the KV cache (the attention keys and values of every token in every active conversation). The KV cache is what limits how many users one GPU serves. Copy What you should see Copy The 8B model needs about 50 GB for 32 users at 8k tokens of context: more than half of it is KV cache, not weights. That is why long contexts and many concurrent users drive serving cost, and why the techniques below exist. Modern models use grouped-query attention , with far fewer key-value heads than attention heads (8 instead of 32 here), which already shrinks the KV cache fourfold. Add 10 to 20% headroom for activations and runtime overhead. Step 2 · Quantization, by hand Quantization stores weights in fewer bits: each block of weights is divided by a scale, rounded to a small integer, and multiplied back at run time. Two choices decide the quality: how many bits, and how many weights share one scale. Real models also have a few outlier channels with much larger values, and those outliers are what make low-bit quantization hard: Copy What you should see Copy With one scale per row, the outlier column sets the scale for the whole row, so all the ordinary weights get squeezed into a handful of integer levels; at 4 bits that destroys the layer. Giving every 128 weights their own scale, group-wise quantization (what GPTQ and AWQ do, plus smarter rounding and outlier handling) cuts the error by more than four times at almost the same size. This toy exaggerates the errors (production methods calibrate on real data), but the lesson holds: never accept a quantized model on perplexity alone; run your own evals , especially for tool calling and structured output , which degrade first. Step 3 · Continuous batching, simulated A GPU produces one token for every request in the batch at each decode step, so the question is when new requests may join. Static batching waits for the whole batch to finish. Continuous batching admits a waiting request the moment any slot frees up: Static versus continuous batching: with static batching the GPU waits for the longest request in a batch; continuous batching slots a new request in the moment one finishes, so throughput rises at the same latency. Copy What you should see Copy One 400-token request held three slots hostage under static batching: the short requests that arrived later waited for it to finish. With continuous batching they flowed through the free slots, and mean latency fell by more than three times on the same hardware. Every modern engine (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM) does this; it is one reason a hand-rolled transformers server is so much slower than vLLM. Step 4 · Prefix caching: why agents love it An agent re-sends its whole context on every step: system prompt , tool definitions and the growing history. Without caching, the server recomputes all of it every time. Prefix caching keeps the KV cache of the shared prefix and computes only what is new. Hosted APIs offer the same thing as prompt caching , billed at a discount: Copy What you should see Copy That is why context engineering advice says to keep the start of the prompt stable: put instructions and tool definitions first, append history, and never insert a timestamp or a per-request value near the top, which would break the cache for everything after it. Discounts and rules differ by provider (explicit cache breakpoints , minimum lengths, cache lifetimes), so check the current pricing page; the prices above are illustrative. In production Self-hosting surprises Quantization that passes benchmarks and fails your task : tool calling and JSON output often degrade first. Re-run your own evals after every quantization or engine change. Out-of-memory under real traffic : long prompts from a few users exhaust the KV cache. Set max-model-len and concurrency from the memory math in Step 1, with headroom. Cold starts : loading a large model takes minutes, so scale-to-zero can make the first user wait. Keep a warm minimum and scale on queue depth. Chat templates : a wrong or missing chat template makes a good model look broken. Use the template shipped with the model and test tool calling end to end. A load test is a short script. This one runs against a fake GPU server that takes 200 ms of prefill, 20 ms per token, and serves at most four requests at a time, then reports the numbers in the table: Copy What you should see Copy Your timings will differ slightly with machine load. This is the shape every real server shows. Throughput rises with concurrency until the hardware is full, then stays flat, while queueing makes time to first token climb: at 16 concurrent users throughput is unchanged, but only 4 of 16 requests met the 0.5 s target. Goodput, not throughput, tells you the capacity of one replica, and that number sets the autoscaling threshold. (On a real GPU the inter-token latency also rises as the batch grows; this fake keeps it fixed to make the queueing visible.) Step 8 · Self-host or call an API: the break-even Put your measured throughput into a cost model and find the break-even utilization before deciding: Copy What you should see Copy With these illustrative numbers one GPU must stay busy well over half of every hour of every day before it beats the API, and real traffic has nights and weekends. Reserved or spot GPUs, bigger batches and smaller quantized models move the line; so do engineering time and the cost of the evals you must re-run on every engine upgrade. Self-hosting wins on control and data locality far more often than on price. Industry practice Self-hosting, honestly Teams that self-host successfully usually do it for a narrow reason (data that cannot leave, a fine-tuned small model at very high volume, or latency at the edge), keep frontier tasks on hosted APIs behind the same gateway, and run the serving stack like any critical service: autoscaling on queue depth, capacity planning with the memory math above, and evals whenever the model, quantization or engine version changes. From the field Character.AI: serving cost is an architecture decision Character.AI, one of the highest-traffic chat services, reported in June 2024 that it served around 20,000 queries per second and had cut serving cost by at least 33 times since its 2022 launch, to under one cent per hour of conversation. Its leadership attributed this to work on the attention KV cache (the memory-bound part of serving covered in this lesson), better caching of conversation state between turns, and other model and serving changes they designed together rather than separately. You will rarely redesign a model's attention yourself, but the lesson transfers to every self-hosting decision: memory for the KV cache, cache hits across turns and quantization usually decide cost more than raw GPU price. Solutions Solution P1 · Memory and latency KV-cache memory (context length times concurrent requests) and the latency each user experiences. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Policy engine Deterministic rules on tool calls, enforced at the Gateway Lesson 14.153 Why this came about Agents act on behalf of users, which created a classic security problem: an agent with broad access can be tricked into acting for the wrong person (the confused deputy). Identity, delegated permissions and governed tool platforms became essential parts of production agent design. In plain words first Every action has an owner An agent acts on someone's behalf, so every tool call must answer: who is the agent, which user is it acting for, and is that user allowed to do this? A tool platform centralizes the answers: tools are registered with owners and risk levels, credentials are issued per user and per call with narrow scopes, permissions are checked in code at each call, and every action is logged. Agents fail safely when their permissions are designed, and dangerously when their permissions are inherited. The common pattern in early deployments is the dangerous one: the agent runs with a developer's personal token, a static API key in an environment variable, or an over-privileged service account. Every tool call then carries more rights than the task needs, nobody can tell the agent's actions from a person's, and a single prompt injection or confused plan can use all of them. From the field A valid key deleted production Speakeasy's Sagar Batchu tells the story of a coding agent that tried to fix a problem in staging and deleted a production database and its backup instead. It did this with valid credentials: nothing was hacked, and every individual permission check passed. His conclusion for regulated industries is a control layer in which every action is tied to an identity, checked against policy in real time, never allowed to exceed its owner's rights, and recorded for compliance ( talk , AI Engineer, 21 min). Keycard's Kamil Potrec lists what proper agent authentication requires: per-agent identity, delegation, short-lived scoped credentials, federation with legacy systems, policy and audit, and he compares SDK -based and gateway-based ways to keep credentials out of the agent's reach ( talk , 19 min). Who is acting: three identities on every call Identity Question it answers Example Subject (the user, or the business owner of a background job) On whose behalf? Priya, support agent, tenant shopkart-in Actor (the agent, as a registered workload) Which software is doing it? refund-agent version 0.4, registered by payments-ai Session (the run) Which task, approved by whom? Run r-8812 , refund approved by Priya at 10:42 The credential presented to a tool should carry all three. OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693, introduced in Lesson 15.25 ) is the standard way: the agent exchanges the user's token for a new, short-lived token whose sub is the user and whose act (actor) claim names the agent. The tool, or the gateway in front of it, sees both and can decide accordingly. The effective permission of the call is the intersection of three sets: what the user is allowed to do (their own role and data), what the agent is allowed to do (its declared purpose and scopes in the registry), what this task needs (the scopes requested for this run). An agent should never be able to do something the user could not do themselves, and a user should not gain powers by asking an agent. The permission of one tool call is the overlap of three sets: what the user may do, what the agent is registered to do, and what this task asked for. The token that reaches the tool names all three. Hands-on · Delegated, scoped, short-lived credentials A delegated credential is a short-lived token that lets the agent act for one user, with a subset of that user's rights, for one purpose. The code below mints and verifies a token the way a token-exchange service would. Real systems use signed JWTs and a standard OAuth server; the logic is the same: intersect scopes, bind the audience, set a short expiry, and name the actor. Copy What you should see Copy Two things to notice. customers:read was requested and Priya has it, but the refund agent's registered purpose does not include it, so it is not granted. And Priya cannot hand the fixit agent db:admin because she does not have it herself: the agent cannot exceed its user. Watch out Keep credentials out of the model's reach The model should never see a token, key or password, in its context, in a tool result or in a file it can read. Hold credentials in the runtime or the gateway and attach them to outgoing calls there. Anything in context can be repeated, logged, or extracted by an injected instruction. Hands-on · A policy decision point in front of every tool call Scopes say what is possible. Policy says what is allowed now , given the arguments, the environment, the amount and the risk. Put a policy decision point (PDP) between the harness and the tools, ideally in the gateway so every framework gets it. It returns one of three answers, always with a reason: allow, deny, or require approval. Copy What you should see Copy The fourth and fifth calls are the Speakeasy incident in miniature: the credentials would have worked, but the policy knows the task is about staging and refuses anything aimed at production, and it never lets an agent destroy production data unattended. Real deployments express these rules in a policy engine later · 14.153 such as Open Policy Agent or Cedar, version them with the agent, and test them like code. The tool platform: registry and gateway When more than one team builds agents, tools become a shared platform. Run it like one: Capability What it does Why it matters Tool registry Every tool has an owner, a versioned contract ( Lesson 14.134 ), an effect class, a risk tier and scopes Reviews happen once per tool, not once per agent Review and approval New tools and breaking changes pass security and owner review before agents can see them Stops "temporary" admin tools reaching production agents MCP gateway One entry point for agents to reach tools: authentication, token exchange, policy, rate limits, logging Every framework gets the same controls ( Lesson 14.136 covers the gateway family) Per-agent allow-lists Agents see only the tools their declared purpose needs Smaller tool lists are both safer and more accurate Rate limits and quotas per tool Caps calls per agent, per user, per minute A looping agent cannot hammer a downstream system Tool fingerprinting Pins the exact tool definitions an agent was evaluated with ( Lesson 16.28 ) Detects a tool whose description or schema changed silently Kill switches per tool Disables one tool for all agents in seconds The fastest containment in an incident ( Lesson 14.146 ) Hands-on · An audit log the agent cannot rewrite Compliance teams ask two questions after an incident: what happened, and can you prove the record is complete? A hash chain answers the second. Each entry stores the hash of the previous one, so editing or deleting any entry breaks every hash after it. Store the log outside the agent's reach, and anchor the latest hash somewhere separate (a write-once bucket, a ledger table) every few minutes. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Durable execution Running a long task so that every completed step is saved and a crash resumes from the last one Lesson 14.140 Why this came about Production agents met every failure distributed systems know, plus new ones such as loops and invalid tool calls . Reliability engineering adapted timeouts, retries, fallbacks, circuit breakers and graceful degradation to agents. In plain words first Assume every part will fail sometimes Models time out, providers have outages, tools return errors, agents loop. Reliability engineering plans a response for each: timeouts and retries with backoff for temporary failures, fallbacks for outages, idempotency so retries are safe, circuit breakers to stop hammering a broken service, limits on steps and spend, and graceful degradation so users get a useful partial answer instead of an error. A web request that fails is retried and forgotten. An agent task that fails halfway may have charged a card, sent an email and reserved stock, and then stopped. Agents run longer, touch more systems and take actions with side effects, so ordinary reliability engineering matters more for them, not less. The good news is that almost none of it is new: it is distributed-systems practice applied to a non-deterministic caller. How agent runs fail Class Examples First defense Covered in Model Malformed tool call, refusal, wrong plan, invented value Schema validation and repair; verifier step; bounds in tools Lesson 11.21 , Lesson 14.67 Provider Outage, rate limit, quota exhaustion, latency spike, silent model change Gateway fallbacks, quotas, pinned versions Lesson 14.136 , Lesson 14.141 Tool Timeout, 5xx, 429, partial result, changed schema Timeouts, retries with budgets, contract tests This lesson, Lesson 14.134 Side effects Duplicate action on retry, half-finished multi-step change Idempotency keys , sagas with compensation This lesson Loop Stuck repeating a call, oscillating between two plans, never declaring done Step budgets, repeated-call detection, progress checks Lesson 14.67 , Lesson 14.146 Context Overflow, lost instructions, stale data from earlier in the run Compaction , re-reading the system of record before acting Lesson 11.27 Runtime Process crash, deploy mid-run, pod eviction Durable checkpoints and resume Lesson 14.140 Human Approval never comes, reviewer unavailable Approval deadlines and escalation paths Lesson 14.148 Timeouts, retries and the retry storm Every call an agent makes needs a timeout. Without one, a hung tool holds the run, its context and its quota forever. With one, the next question is whether to retry, and here agents make a classic failure worse. A retry storm happens when a dependency slows down or fails, every caller retries immediately, and the retries multiply the load on exactly the system that is struggling. Agents amplify it in two ways: a single task makes many calls, and a model that sees an error often decides on its own to try again, on top of whatever retries the code does. The dependency recovers, the backlog of retries arrives at once, and it falls over again. A retry storm, drawn from the Lesson 14.139 simulation: when the service comes back, naive clients send every queued retry at once and knock it over again; backoff with jitter and a client-side rate limit spread the load. The patterns that prevent it: Pattern What it does Rule of thumb Timeout Bounds every call Set per tool from its p99, not a global default Retry only what can succeed Retries 429, 503 and timeouts; never 400 or 403 Actionable errors from tools make this decision easy ( Lesson 14.134 ) Exponential backoff with jitter Spreads retries out in time Double the wait each try, add randomness, cap it Retry budget Caps retries as a share of first attempts, per client 10 to 25% of requests; beyond that, stop retrying and back off Adaptive rate limit (backpressure) Clients slow down when they see errors, and queue instead of sending Halve the send rate on failure, add one on success (AIMD, as in TCP) Circuit breaker After many failures, fail fast for a while instead of calling Open on error rate over a window; probe before closing One retry layer Retries happen in exactly one place Tell the model "the system retries for you" and do not let it loop on errors The simulation below runs 1,800 agent tasks of three tool calls each against a service that is down for 90 seconds and can serve 8 calls a second. The naive client retries at once, up to five times. The hardened client queues work behind an adaptive rate limit, backs off with jitter, keeps each task's checkpoint and gives up only after a deadline. Copy What you should see Copy The naive client loses about one task in ten, and a few of those stopped halfway with side effects already done. The hardened client loses none and wastes fewer calls, at a price you must design for: during and after the outage, tasks wait in the queue, so the slowest 5% take minutes. That is the honest trade-off. A user would rather hear "your refund is queued and will finish in a few minutes" than receive a half-done refund, so pair backpressure with a status message and an expected time ( Lesson 14.148 ). Tip Tell the model who retries If the harness retries a failed tool call, say so in the tool result ("temporarily unavailable; the system will retry; continue with other work or wait"). Otherwise the model may retry on its own, re-plan around a transient error or give up. One retry layer, in code, is easier to reason about than two, one of them a language model. Side effects: idempotency, checkpoints and sagas Three patterns, used together, make multi-step actions safe. Idempotency keys. Every write carries a key derived from the business action (order and refund sequence, not a random UUID per attempt). The system of record stores the key and returns the original result on a repeat. A retry, a resume after a crash or a model that calls the tool twice then does no harm. Checkpoints. The runtime records each completed step durably before starting the next ( Lesson 14.140 covers durable execution later · 14.140 with LangGraph checkpointers, Temporal and DBOS). A crashed run resumes from its last checkpoint, and idempotency makes repeating the step in flight safe. Sagas with compensation. When a multi-step change fails partway, undo the completed steps in reverse order with compensating actions : refund the charge, release the stock, cancel the shipment label. A saga does not give you a database transaction across systems; it gives you a defined way back. Copy What you should see Copy Run 1 ends with no money taken and no stock held. Run 2 resumes without charging twice. Run 3 is the case prompts cannot prevent: the model starts the whole task again, and every step replays harmlessly because the keys are business keys. The ledger shows each effect exactly once. Watch out Some actions cannot be compensated An email cannot be unsent and a payment to an outside bank may not be reversible. Order the saga so that irreversible steps come last , after everything that can fail has succeeded, and put an approval before them when the stakes are high ( Lesson 14.148 ). The Citibank-Revlon payment error described in Lesson 14.148 is the case where the irreversible step came with a confusing interface. Degraded modes: fail cleanly and tell the truth When a dependency is down, an agent has three bad options (hang, guess, or fail silently) and one good one: degrade on purpose. Decide each degraded mode in the spec (question 11 in Lesson 14.134 ): Dependency down Degraded mode What the user hears Primary model Gateway falls back to a second provider or a smaller model, with a stricter scope Nothing, or "replies may be shorter right now" All models Static answers for top intents; a ticket for the rest "Our assistant is unavailable; we have logged your request as T-4411" A read tool (orders API) Say what is unknown; offer a callback "I can't see order status right now; I'll message you when I can" A write tool (payments) Queue the action durably; confirm when done "Your refund is queued and will complete within the hour" Retrieval index Answer only from tools and structured data; refuse policy questions "I can't check the policy right now; a colleague will follow up" Never let the agent fill the gap with a guess. An agent that invents an order status during an outage turns an availability incident into a trust incident. Reliability objectives for agents Write service level objectives for what users experience, not only for the infrastructure. A service level objective (SLO) is a target you commit to, stated as a number over a period: "95% of refund requests are resolved correctly within two minutes, measured over 30 days". The gap between the target and perfection is the error budget : at 95%, one request in twenty may fail before the objective is broken. The budget turns reliability into something you can spend and track: while there is budget left you can ship changes, and when it is burning fast you stop and fix. Lesson 14.145 shows how to measure SLOs from traces and alert on the burn rate. For agents, write SLOs like these: Indicator Definition Example objective Task success rate Tasks completed correctly, per intent, from evals and sampled production review 95% for order status, 90% for refunds, over 28 days Clean failure rate Failed tasks that ended in escalation or a queued action, never half-done 100% of failures clean Time to complete p95 from request to final answer or action, per intent Status under 10 s; refunds under 2 min Escalation rate Tasks handed to a person Under 15%, and every escalation has a complete handoff Cost per successful task Model and tool cost, divided by successes Under 0.30 USD for refunds Use error budgets exactly as for any service ( Lesson 14.145 ): when the budget is burning, freeze risky changes and spend the time on reliability. Solutions Solution P1 · Availability multiplies About 99.4% (0.999 × 0.995), worse than either. Fallbacks, caching and degraded modes are how you raise it. Solution B1 · Retry storms Retries multiply load on the struggling provider and on your quotas, making the outage worse and costs higher. Use exponential backoff with jitter, limits, circuit breakers and fallbacks ( Lesson 14.59 ). Solution D1 · Visible degradation Logging and alerting on which model served each request, and a dashboard of fallback rates. Degradation should be a known state, not a silent one. Solution M1 · SLOs for an agent Availability of answered requests, p95 time to first token and p95 total time, and a quality SLO from sampled evaluations or resolution rate. Each with an error budget and alerts. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How do you engineer reliability for an agent? Worked answer. Set SLOs for availability, latency and quality; design for dependency failures with timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, fallbacks and degraded modes; make tools idempotent; limit runs; monitor and alert on error budgets; and rehearse incidents. A plausible wrong answer. "Use a reliable provider." Your agent's reliability is the product of all its dependencies. Follow-ups. What is a degraded mode for a support agent? It is noisier than availability, so use rolling windows and clear thresholds. A plausible wrong answer. "Only availability and latency are SLOs." Then a confidently wrong agent is "healthy". Three rules make it production-shaped: stream events (not just text) so the UI can show progress, keep session state outside the worker, and turn off proxy buffering so tokens are not held back: Copy What you should see Copy Server-Sent Events work through most load balancers and need no special client; WebSockets suit apps that also push from the client mid-answer, such as voice. The event types here ( status , tool , delta , done ) are a small version of what AG-UI standardizes ( Lesson 16.29 ). Replace SESSIONS with Redis or a database table keyed by session, and any replica can serve the next turn. Durable execution: survive the crash A long agent run will meet a deploy, a crash, a timeout or a provider outage. Durable execution records each completed step in a database; after a failure the workflow resumes from the last completed step instead of starting over, so expensive or irreversible steps are not repeated. LangGraph 's checkpointers do this for graph runs (the LangChain and LangGraph section). The same idea exists as general-purpose engines: Durable execution: each completed step is recorded before the next starts, so a crash mid-run resumes at the failed step instead of starting over, and idempotent steps make the repeat harmless. Engine Model Temporal Workflows as code with deterministic replay; activities hold side effects. Widely used for business processes; integrations with the OpenAI Agents SDK , Pydantic AI and others DBOS A library: decorate functions as workflows and steps; state checkpoints in Postgres (SQLite for development). No separate server Restate , Inngest Durable functions and event-driven workflows AWS Step Functions , Lambda durable functions (announced at re:Invent 2025: checkpointed steps, waits and callbacks for up to a year) Managed on AWS Azure Durable Functions and Durable Task Managed on Azure; Microsoft Agent Framework hosts durable agents on it Google Cloud Workflows Managed orchestration on Google Cloud A crash, for real: the program below starts a refund workflow in a child process that dies after the refund call, then restarts and lets DBOS recover. Copy Copy What you should see Copy (DBOS also prints a few start-up log lines.) After the restart, the refund API was not called again: its result came from the checkpoint, and only the unfinished email step ran. Without durable execution, a naive retry would have refunded the customer twice. Durable execution also gives you durable waits . A workflow can pause for a human decision for days without holding a thread or a process; the wait is a row in the database, and whichever process receives the decision resumes it: Copy What you should see Copy The first process exited while the workflow was waiting. The second process recovered it, skipped the already-checkpointed draft step, delivered the approval with DBOS.send , and the workflow finished. This is the pattern behind "approve in Slack tomorrow": the approval button calls send with the workflow ID. Temporal (signals), Step Functions (task tokens), Durable Functions (external events) and LangGraph ( interrupt with a checkpointer) offer the same capability. Idempotency completes the picture. Steps can still run twice (a step that crashed midway is retried), so every side effect needs an idempotency key the downstream system honors, such as the workflow ID plus step name sent as an Idempotency-Key header to a payments API. Here is the failure it prevents, the most common way agents double-charge or double-refund: the call succeeds, but the response is lost, so the caller retries: Copy What you should see Copy Without a key, the retry created a second refund. With a key built from the workflow ID and step name, the API recognized the retry and returned the first result. If a downstream system does not support idempotency keys, keep your own record of completed side effects and check it before calling. Releasing safely Technique How Shadow Run the new version on copies of real traffic; compare outputs and costs; users see only the old version Canary Send 1 to 10% of traffic to the new version; watch online evals , errors, cost; then ramp Feature flags Switch prompts, models or tools per tenant without a deploy A/B test Measure business outcomes (resolution rate, CSAT) between versions with enough traffic for significance Rollback Keep the previous release (code, prompts, model aliases, index) one switch away Version pinning for in-flight runs Long runs started on version N finish on N, or migrate deliberately; durable state schemas must stay compatible Automate the canary decision ( canary analysis ), so a bad release rolls back at 3 a.m. without waiting for someone to notice. Compare the canary with the baseline on quality, latency and cost, and require enough traffic before deciding: Copy What you should see Copy The second canary's fail rate (6.3%) is slightly above the baseline's (6.0%), but well within noise, so it promotes. The third (9.5%) is more than four standard errors worse. Tools such as Argo Rollouts and Flagger run this analysis loop for Kubernetes deployments; for prompt and model changes behind feature flags, a scheduled job like this one, reading from your observability store, does the same. Industry practice How production teams deploy agents Teams with mature agent operations separate the agent's "brain" (prompts, model choices, tools) from its infrastructure, so that most changes ship as configuration through the eval gate, not as code deploys. They default to asynchronous, durable execution for anything longer than a few seconds, make every side effect idempotent, and rehearse failure: kill workers mid-run in staging and confirm runs complete correctly. In production Deployment problems that bite agents specifically Timeouts at the load balancer : a 60-second idle timeout kills long agent turns mid-stream. Stream progress events, or move long work to a job with polling or webhooks. State in worker memory : a deploy or autoscale drops conversations. Keep sessions and checkpoints in a database from the first release. Retries that repeat side effects : a retried request refunds twice. Idempotency keys on every write (this lesson). Rate limits during traffic spikes : every worker retries at once. Client-side rate limiting, backoff with jitter, and a fallback deployment through the gateway. Model or prompt changes shipped like config, without evals : the most common cause of quality incidents. Put every behavior change through the same gate as code ( Lesson 14.147 ). Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Provisioned throughput Reserved model capacity for steady load Lesson 14.142 Batch APIs Discounted asynchronous processing Lesson 14.142 Why this came about Successful agent products hit provider rate limits and served many customers with uneven load. Capacity planning, queues and per-tenant limits became necessary to scale fairly and keep customers' data apart. In plain words first Many customers sharing the same kitchen At scale, the limits are provider quotas (requests and tokens per minute ), concurrency, and fairness between customers. Scaling means queueing work, controlling concurrency, giving each tenant budgets and limits so one heavy customer cannot starve the rest, and keeping each tenant's data, memory and caches strictly separate. Scaling Model calls dominate latency; run independent tool calls and sub-agents in parallel . Scale workers on queue depth , not CPU: agent workers mostly wait on I/O. Respect provider rate limits with client-side limiting and backoff; spread load across regions and deployments through the gateway. Put per-run ceilings on steps, tokens and wall-clock time. Keep conversation and workflow state in a database, never in worker memory, so any worker can continue any run. Backoff deserves code, because the naive version (retry immediately, or every second) turns a provider's rate limit into an outage. Use exponential backoff with jitter , and obey Retry-After when the provider sends it: Copy What you should see Copy The first two waits are random draws below 0.5 s and 1 s ("full jitter"), so a thousand workers hitting the same 429 do not all retry at the same instant; the third wait is the 4 seconds the provider asked for. The SDKs from OpenAI and Anthropic do this for you ( max_retries ), and so do gateways; write it yourself for tools and internal APIs. Choose by scenario Something is wrong in production: the response playbook Signal First move Then Error rate spikes after a release Roll back the release (prompt, model mapping, index alias, code) Diff the release manifests and replay failing traces Provider errors or rate limits Fail over through the gateway to the backup deployment Raise quotas or spread across Regions Quality drops (judge scores, complaints) with no errors Compare traces before and after; check for a model or index change Canary any fix before full rollout Cost spikes Find the top runs by cost; cap steps and tokens per run Look for loops, tool results that ballooned, or a cache that stopped hitting Latency rises Check queue depth and provider latency per model Scale workers on queue depth; shift traffic to faster deployments A harmful action happened Kill switch to read-only mode ( Lesson 15.26 ) Incident review, regression test, then re-enable gradually A web service scales with requests. An agent service scales with runs , and a run is long (seconds to hours), bursty, stateful and expensive: each one holds context, makes several model calls and may wait on tools or people. That changes the arithmetic and the architecture. Lesson 14.140 covered where agents run and how they survive crashes; this lesson is about what happens when there are many of them. Size it before you build it Two numbers decide most of the design: Runs in flight = arrival rate x time per run ( Little's law ). It sets the number of workers, the memory for contexts and the connections to tools. Tokens per minute at peak = arrival rate x tokens per run. It is checked against the provider's TPM quota , which is often the first thing to run out. Copy What you should see Copy Five pods handle the doubled traffic easily; the token quota does not. A second region halves the headroom, and a system prompt that grew by 5,000 tokens takes it to less than half of what is needed, with no change in traffic. This is the most common scaling surprise with agents: prompt changes are capacity changes . Treat input tokens per step as a capacity number, review it in every release, and reserve quota ( provisioned throughput later · 14.142 , committed capacity) before a launch rather than after the first 429s. The runtime shape that scales Concern Pattern Why Long runs Accept the request, enqueue the run, return a run ID; stream progress to the user Web servers should not hold a socket open for minutes; queues absorb bursts ( Lesson 14.140 ) Bursts A durable queue in front of a pool of workers that autoscale on queue depth Scale on the work waiting, not on CPU, which idles while waiting for models Different urgency Separate lanes : interactive, background and batch, each with its own workers and quota share A nightly batch must never slow down a customer conversation State Run state in a durable store keyed by run ID, not in the worker's memory Any worker can resume any run; deploys do not lose work Slow tools Bulkheads: a separate pool and timeout per slow dependency One slow tool cannot exhaust every worker ( Lesson 14.139 ) Quota All model traffic through the gateway, which enforces per-team and per-tenant shares Quota becomes something you allocate, not something you discover ( Lesson 14.136 ) Overload Admission control : reject or defer new batch work when queue age or quota use crosses a threshold; keep interactive lanes open Shedding load early keeps the service usable for the work that matters Hands-on · Fair scheduling across tenants In a multi-tenant agent product, one large customer's batch job can fill the queue and make every other customer wait. The simulation below runs three tenants on 20 workers. At one minute, bigco submits 900 batch runs. First-in, first-out scheduling lets that burst delay everyone; round-robin across tenants with a concurrency cap per tenant keeps the others fast. One queue against one queue per tenant. In the lesson's simulation a single customer's batch of 900 runs makes everyone wait over twenty minutes; with per-tenant queues and a cap, the small tenants wait seconds and the batch waits for itself. Copy What you should see Copy With a single queue, the two small tenants wait more than twenty minutes for interactive work because a batch arrived first. With per-tenant queues and caps, their p95 wait drops to seconds and the tenant that sent the burst absorbs the delay. In production, put batch work in its own lane with its own quota as well, and show bigco an honest completion estimate. Cost and latency levers, in order of payoff Lever Typical effect What it can break Prompt caching with a stable prefix Large input-cost and latency cuts on agents, which are input-heavy ( Lesson 14.142 , Lesson 14.163 ) Anything that changes the prefix: timestamps, reordered tools Shorter context : compact tool results, prune history, load detail on demand Fewer tokens per step, better accuracy Lost facts if pruning is careless; keep the system of record as truth Model routing : a small model for routine steps, a large one for hard ones Lower cost per task Quality on the hard tail; route by evidence from evals Fewer sequential steps : parallel tool calls, code that does deterministic work Lower latency Harder debugging if parallel calls interact Batch APIs later · 14.142 for work that can wait About half the price at major providers Latency of hours; use only in batch lanes Semantic or result caching for repeated questions Large savings on repetitive traffic Stale or wrong answers if keys ignore user, permissions or time Self-hosting a tuned small model for a high-volume step Lower cost at high, steady volume You now run GPUs ( Lesson 14.137 ) What breaks at ten times the load Ask this in every design review ( Lesson 14.151 ). For agents the usual order is: provider quota and rate limits, then a tool or database that was sized for human traffic (agents call tools far more often than people click), then cost, then queue latency for interactive users, and only then your own servers.
