Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Batch inference Asynchronous model jobs over JSONL files in S3, at a discount Lesson 14.154 Why this came about Agent costs surprised many teams, because each task makes several calls and resends growing context. Cost engineering, measuring cost per task and applying caching, routing and step reduction, became a standard discipline. In plain words first Paying for what you use, knowingly Agent cost is the sum of every model call (input and output tokens, with the input re-sent each step) plus tools and infrastructure. Cost engineering measures cost per successful task, then pulls the big levers: fewer steps, shorter inputs, caching repeated prefixes, cheaper models where they are good enough, and limits that stop runaway runs. Cost is per run, not per call An agent run makes several model calls, and each call re-reads the system prompt , tool definitions and a growing history. That is why agents cost 5 to 50 times more than a single chat answer, and why the levers below are mostly about not re-reading tokens . Why agents are input-heavy: every step re-reads the whole growing context. Cumulative input tokens grow with the square of the steps; caching the stable part turns most of that into cheap cached reads. Copy What you should see Copy Prompt caching halved the cost without changing a word of the output. A cascade is cheap only if few requests escalate: at 60% escalation it costs almost as much as using the strong model always, plus extra latency. Measure the escalation rate before adopting one. The levers, roughly in order of payoff Lever How Watch out Prompt caching Keep the stable prefix (instructions, tools, documents) identical and first; dynamic content last Any change early in the prompt (a timestamp!) breaks the cache Shorter context Trim and summarize history, return compact tool results, retrieve less but better Losing facts the agent needs Fewer steps Better tools that do more per call; parallel tool calls ; plan once Over-merged tools are harder for models to use Right-size models Small models for routing, extraction and formatting; strong models where reasoning matters Validate per step on evals Reasoning effort Use low effort or no extended thinking where it adds nothing Hard steps degrade quietly Batch APIs Offline work (evals, enrichment, summaries) through batch endpoints, typically at about half price Hours of latency Caching answers Exact and semantic caches for repeated questions ( Lesson 14.136 ) Wrong or stale answers Provisioned throughput or committed use Discounts for steady, predictable volume Paying for idle capacity Self-hosting At very high, steady volume ( Lesson 14.137 ) Operations cost and quality Latency follows the same levers: fewer sequential model calls, smaller contexts, streaming, parallel tools, and prefix caching (which also cuts time to first token ). Hands-on · Shorter context: compact tool results The cheapest token is one the model never reads. Tool results are the usual culprit: an internal API returns everything it knows, and that blob then sits in the context for every remaining step of the run: Copy What you should see Copy A thirtyfold reduction, and usually better answers: the model no longer has to find three useful fields among audit logs and status codes. Anthropic's tool-writing guidance recommends exactly this (return meaningful, compact context; offer a response_format parameter for "concise" versus "detailed" when the model sometimes needs more). The character-count estimate is rough; count with your provider's tokenizer or the usage field for real numbers. In production Cost cuts that backfire A cheaper model that retries more : more failed tool calls and clarifications can make the cheap model cost more per resolved task. Always compare cost per successful outcome, not per call. Over-trimmed context : dropping history saves tokens and causes the agent to ask the user again. Trim tool results first, pinned facts last. Caching personal answers : savings on paper, privacy incident in practice. Batch for interactive work : users wait hours. Batch only work nobody is waiting for. Hands-on · Right-size models with a router A router sends each request to the cheapest model likely to handle it. Choosing its threshold is a measurement, not a guess: label a sample with whether each model succeeds, then trace the quality and cost of every threshold: Copy What you should see Copy Routing at 0.50 keeps 95.3% quality, within 1.4 points of always using the strong model, at about a third of the cost. Whether those points are worth $0.04 per run is a product decision; this table is what makes it a decision instead of an argument. Routers can be a small classifier, an embedding similarity to known-hard examples, or the small model's own confidence; RouteLLM and the gateways in Lesson 14.136 provide ready-made ones. Hands-on · Batch what does not need an answer now Evaluations, enrichment, nightly summaries and backfills do not need a reply in seconds. Batch APIs take a file of requests and return results within hours, typically at about half price: Copy What you should see Copy That line format is OpenAI's Batch API; Anthropic's Message Batches, Bedrock batch inference later · 14.154 , Vertex AI batch prediction and Azure's global batch deployments take similar files. Batch runs also stay out of your real-time rate limits, which protects interactive traffic during a large backfill. FinOps for AI FinOps is the practice of making engineering teams accountable for cloud spend with shared data. For AI: Attribution : tag every model call with team, application, feature, tenant and environment (at the gateway, Lesson 14.136 ), and report cost per unit of value : per resolved ticket, per report, per active user. Budgets and alerts : per team and per tenant, with anomaly detection on daily spend and a hard ceiling per run. Forecasting : traffic times cost per run, per model, with scenarios for model price changes. Showback or chargeback : teams see (or pay) for what they use. Review cadence : a monthly look at the biggest cost drivers, with the eval suite ready to test cheaper options. The FinOps Foundation publishes guidance on managing AI spend, and its FOCUS standard for billing data helps combine costs from several cloud and AI providers in one view. Hands-on · Unit economics from usage records Attribution starts with one row per run, tagged with team, feature, model and outcome. From there, cost per resolved outcome falls out: Copy What you should see Copy Order status is almost free. The refunds feature costs seventy times more per resolution, partly because the failed run still has to be paid for, and it is only three times cheaper than a person. That is where to spend optimization effort, and the failed run is where to look first. Hands-on · Catch a spend spike the day it happens A loop bug or an abusive tenant shows up as a sudden jump in daily spend. Compare each day with a robust baseline (the median and median absolute deviation of the previous week, which one old spike cannot distort): Copy What you should see Copy Daily is the slowest useful cadence; the per-run ceiling ( Lesson 14.57 ) and per-tenant budgets at the gateway ( Lesson 14.136 ) stop runaway spend within minutes. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, Azure Cost Management alerts and Google Cloud budget alerts do this for cloud bills; run your own on the gateway's per-team data, which arrives sooner and in more detail. Industry practice Unit economics decide what you build Teams that keep AI programs funded report cost per business outcome next to quality: "₹4 per resolved support conversation at 92% resolution, against ₹60 for a human-handled one." That framing turns cost work into product decisions (is a cheaper model at 89% resolution better value?) and catches agents that look cheap per call but expensive per outcome. Choose by scenario Cost is too high: the order to work through Step Lever Typical effect Check before you ship it 1 Measure cost per resolved outcome, per feature and per step Shows where the money goes Tags on every call ( Lesson 14.136 ) 2 Prompt caching: stable prefix first, dynamic content last Large on agents, which are input-heavy Cache-hit rate in usage data 3 Trim context: compact tool results, summarize old turns Often the largest single cut on long runs Quality on the eval set 4 Route easy requests to a small model Large if most traffic is easy Quality per route (this lesson's router table) 5 Batch anything that can wait About half price on supported APIs Latency is acceptable for the use 6 Cache whole answers for repeated questions Depends on repetition False-hit rate on labeled pairs ( Lesson 14.136 ) 7 Fine-tune or distill a small model for one high-volume step Large for narrow tasks Held-out eval against the current model ( Lesson 14.132 ) 8 Provisioned capacity or self-hosting for steady load Depends on utilization Break-even utilization ( Lesson 14.137 ) Most teams get the bulk of their savings from steps 2 to 4 without touching model weights. From the field Manus: agents are input-heavy, so caching decides the bill Manus reports an average input-to-output token ratio of about 100:1 for its agent, because every step re-reads a growing context while producing a short action. With Claude Sonnet, cached input cost 0.30 USD per million tokens against 3 USD uncached at the time, so the share of input served from cache dominated cost and also time to first token. That is why the team treats KV-cache hit rate as its key production metric, keeps prompts append-only, and avoids anything that changes the start of the prompt between steps. Solutions Solution P1 · Measure the cost drivers It depends on where tokens go. Measure input versus output tokens, cacheable share and calls per task; for agents with long system prompts and tools, caching often wins first. Solution B1 · Cost per outcome It can rise: more retries, longer conversations and more handoffs to people. Measure cost per resolved task, not per call. Solution D1 · Hidden growth Context growth (longer histories, larger tool results), more tool loops, lower cache hit rates after a prompt change, and retries. Measure tokens and calls per task, find the drivers, then apply levers: prompt caching, shorter prompts and outputs, routing easy steps to smaller models, batching non-urgent work, trimming context and tool results, limiting loops, and caching results. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Microsoft Foundry Microsoft's platform for models, agents, knowledge and governance (formerly Azure AI Foundry) Lesson 14.155 Why this came about Traditional testing did not fit non-deterministic outputs, and judging by eye did not scale. Evaluation practices for LLM systems ( test sets , behavioral checks, model judges) developed rapidly from 2023 into an expected part of shipping AI. In plain words first Tests for something that answers differently each time Ordinary tests check exact outputs. AI outputs vary, so evaluation checks properties on a fixed set of examples: correct fields, required citations, the right tools called, scored by code where possible and by a calibrated model judge where not. Versions are compared on the same set, cost and latency are recorded alongside quality, and failures from production are added to the set. The kinds of evaluation Axis Options When Offline (before release, on a dataset) / online (on live traffic, sampled) Granularity Unit (one step, one tool, one prompt) / trajectory (the path of tool calls ) / end-to-end (the outcome) Reference Reference-based (compare with an expected answer) / reference-free (judge against a rubric) Grader Code (exact checks, regex, schema, SQL result match) / LLM judge / human Interaction Single turn / multi-turn , often with a simulated user Prefer the cheapest grader that can decide: code where possible, a judge where meaning matters, people to calibrate both. Step 1 · Start with error analysis, not metrics Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar, whose evals course has trained thousands of AI engineers, teach a process borrowed from qualitative research: Collect a few dozen to a hundred real (or realistic synthetic) traces . Open coding : a domain expert reads each trace and writes a short note about the first thing that went wrong. Axial coding : group the notes into a failure taxonomy and count each category. Fix the biggest categories; write an eval for each one that should never come back. Repeat until new traces stop revealing new failure types. Generic metrics ("helpfulness 4.2") rarely point to a fix. Failure categories from your own traces do ("cites the 7-day policy for damaged items, which allow 30 days"). Step 2 · An eval harness you can read in one screen An evaluation harness has four parts, and this one fits on a screen so that you can see all of them: a set of test cases with what a right answer must contain, a function that runs the system on each case, graders that score the results, and a comparison of an automated judge with a human expert's labels. Read the numbered comments in order. Copy What you should see Copy Three lessons are in the numbers. The judge agrees with the expert 90% of the time, but Cohen's kappa (agreement beyond chance) is 0.76: good, not perfect, so keep sampling its decisions for human review. The improvement interval excludes zero, but with six cases it is wide; real suites need dozens to hundreds of cases per important segment. And the gate checks regressions per case , not just the average (a bootstrap over cases gives the interval above), because a better average can hide a newly broken case. Step 3 · LLM judges that deserve trust Calibrating an LLM judge: compare its labels with people's on the same sample. Agreement above chance (Cohen's kappa) tells you whether the judge can stand in for reviewers; the off-diagonal cells tell you how it fails. Binary or small scales, with a written rubric : "pass" or "fail" against explicit criteria is more reliable than 1-to-10 scores. One judge per failure mode , written from your error analysis , rather than one judge for "quality". Calibrate : label 50 to 100 examples yourself, measure the judge's agreement (precision and recall on "fail", or kappa), and iterate on the judge prompt until it is acceptable. Re-check after changing the judge model. Know the biases : position bias in pairwise comparisons (swap the order and average), verbosity bias, self-preference for the judge's own model family. Give the judge the evidence : the retrieved context, the tool results, the policy text. A judge without the facts guesses. A calibrated judge is still wrong sometimes, and its errors are usually lopsided: judges tend to pass answers that a careful expert would fail. Once you know the judge's true-positive rate (how often it passes truly good answers) and true-negative rate (how often it fails truly bad ones), you can correct the pass rate it reports in production: Copy What you should see Copy The raw judge overstated quality by eleven points, because it lets 43% of bad answers through. The Rogan-Gladen correction , borrowed from epidemiology (imperfect medical tests), recovers the true rate from the judge's known error rates. Two cautions: it is only as good as the calibration set (label at least 50 to 100 examples, with enough failures), and it falls apart when the judge is close to random ( tpr + tnr near 1). The open-source judgy library from Shreya Shankar's group adds confidence intervals. Position bias is the other judge error worth testing for in pairwise comparisons. Show each pair in both orders, and count a win only when the verdicts agree: Copy What you should see Copy Answer A really is better here (the judge prefers concise answers), but depending on the order you show it, A wins either 100% or 73% of the time. Swapping and requiring agreement gives an honest result and a measure of the judge's inconsistency (35% of pairs). The same check exposes verbosity bias: give the judge two equally correct answers of different lengths. In production Judge failures seen in production The judge drifts : a provider updates the judge model and scores shift with no change to your system. Pin the judge model version and re-calibrate when you change it. Judges grading their own family's outputs score them higher (self-preference). Use a judge from a different family when comparing models. Scores without evidence : a judge asked "is this correct?" without the policy text guesses. Always pass the sources, tool results and rubric. One "quality" score hides everything : binary judges per failure mode are easier to calibrate and point to a fix. Nobody looks at the disagreements : the cases where judge and human disagree are where your rubric is unclear; review them weekly. Step 4 · Agents need extra kinds of evals Eval What it checks Note Trajectory Right tools, right arguments, sensible order, no forbidden calls Exact, subset, unordered or judged matching Multi-turn with simulated users Clarifying questions, policy compliance over a conversation A model plays the customer from a persona and goal (the τ-bench approach) Side-effect checks The final state of the world: was the order really cancelled, and only that order? Run against a sandbox or fake backend and inspect it Repeated runs Reliability ( pass^k ) Run each case several times Safety and red-team suites Injection, data leakage , policy violations Lesson 15.25 Cost and latency Budgets per case Fail a case that passes but costs ten times more A multi-turn eval with a simulated customer tests behavior that only exists across turns, such as "always confirm before cancelling". The customer here is scripted for clarity; in practice it is an LLM given a persona and a goal (the τ-bench approach), and a second check reads the whole conversation: Copy What you should see Copy Every single-turn answer from impatient_agent looks helpful. Only the conversation shows that it cancelled a shipped order and ignored a customer who changed their mind, which is why policy-heavy agents need conversation-level evals. Side-effect checks look at what the agent changed rather than what it said. Run each version against a fresh fake backend, diff the state, and compare with the exact change the case expects: Copy What you should see Copy Version 1 would have passed an answer-only eval ("your order is cancelled" is true), while silently cancelling someone else's order too. "Exactly these changes, and nothing else" is the assertion to write for every tool with side effects. Step 5 · Wire it into delivery Pre-merge : a fast suite (tens of cases, code checks, mocked tools) on every pull request. Pre-release : the full suite with real models, repeated runs and judges; compare against the current production version; block on regressions. Canary : online evals on sampled live traffic for the new version before full rollout. Continuous : sampled online judging and feedback dashboards; new failures from production go into the dataset. The pre-merge suite is ordinary test code. Writing evals as pytest tests gets you parametrized cases, clear failure messages, xfail for known gaps with a ticket number, and an exit code CI already understands: Copy What you should see Copy The failing case is the behavior this release was meant to add, so the gate is doing its job. xfail keeps a known failure visible without blocking every merge, and turns into an "unexpected pass" the day someone fixes it. DeepEval and promptfoo build on the same idea, adding LLM-judged assertions and reports. Tools Tool Notes promptfoo YAML test suites with assertions, LLM graders and red-team plugins; runs in CI; language-agnostic DeepEval Pytest-style tests with many built-in metrics, including agent and RAG metrics RAGAS RAG-focused metrics and test-set generation ( Lesson 14.77 ) Inspect (UK AI Security Institute) A rigorous framework for agent and model evaluations, with sandboxed tools OpenAI Evals , agentevals and openevals ( LangChain ) Eval frameworks and ready-made evaluators, including trajectory matching MLflow , LangSmith , Braintrust , Langfuse , Arize Datasets, experiments and judges, connected to traces Cloud services Amazon Bedrock Evaluations (models, Knowledge Bases, agents), Microsoft Foundry later · 14.155 evaluations and red-teaming agent, Vertex AI Gen AI evaluation service, Databricks Agent Evaluation Industry practice What experienced teams agree on Across published guidance from Anthropic, OpenAI, Hamel Husain, Eugene Yan and others, a few points recur: look at your data before building metrics; write evals from observed failures; prefer simple binary checks; calibrate judges against people; treat the eval set as a product that grows from production; and remember that evals are the main way to move fast safely, because they make every model upgrade and prompt change a measurable experiment instead of a gamble. From the field Shopify: judges you can trust, and a simulator before release Shopify's Sidekick team (August 2025) replaced curated "golden" examples with ground-truth sets sampled from real merchant conversations and labeled by at least three product experts. Human agreement (measured with Cohen's kappa, Kendall's tau and Pearson correlation) set the ceiling for what an LLM judge could reach. Iterating on the judge prompt raised one judge's kappa from 0.02 to 0.61, against a human-to-human baseline of 0.69; their practical test was whether reviewers could tell the judge's labels from a human's. Before release, an LLM-powered merchant simulator replays the goals of real conversations against candidate versions. When they later trained with reinforcement learning , the model found loopholes in the rewards, such as using customer tags as a catch-all filter instead of the right field, which they fixed with gated rewards that combine procedural checks with judges. From the field: evaluation, what the experts actually do From Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar ( Your AI product needs evals , A field guide to rapidly improving AI products , 2024 to 2025), Anthropic ( Demystifying evals for AI agents , January 2026), and Eugene Yan: Error analysis first. Read real traces, write open notes, cluster them into failure categories, and count. The categories tell you which evals to build. Build a simple trace viewer for your domain; it speeds up review more than any generic dashboard. Copy What you should see Copy The same agent looks nearly perfect or unreliable depending on the metric. If a customer talks to it five times a week, the second column is their experience. Solutions Solution P1 · Paired comparisons Likely yes: a sign test on 182 decided pairs (112 against 70) is significant at the usual levels. A Kappa is easier to compute B Kappa corrects for agreement that would happen by chance C Raw agreement is always wrong D Kappa measures latency High raw agreement can come from imbalanced labels. A Release; the average improved B Block or review: a per-case regression can hide behind a better average C Delete the failing case D Lower the threshold Gate on regressions , not only on averages. A A tone judge B A side-effect check on the final state of a sandboxed backend C BLEU score D Time to first token Agents act; check what they changed. A The judge is accurate; trust 72% B The judge lets many bad answers through, so the true pass rate is lower; correct it with its error rates C The true rate is higher D Error rates cannot be measured The Rogan-Gladen correction gave about 61%. A Use a bigger judge model B Show each pair in both orders and count a win only when the verdicts agree C Always show the new version first D Lower the temperature Inconsistent verdicts become ties, and their rate measures the bias. A 75% B 99% C About 42% D 25% 0.75 cubed is about 0.42, which is what a repeat customer experiences. Benchmarks and methods for agents (such as tau-bench, 2024) introduced trajectory checks and simulated users. In plain words first Grading the journey as well as the destination For agents, a right final answer reached by a wrong path is still a problem: too many steps, a skipped approval, an unnecessary risky call. End-to-end agent evaluation scores the outcome and the trajectory (which tools, in what order, with what arguments), often in a simulated environment with a scripted user, and runs each case several times because agents vary. Lesson 14.143 covers evaluation in depth: error analysis , harnesses , judges and CI. Lesson 14.77 covers RAG . This lesson adds what is specific to agents that act : the answer is not the reply, it is what changed in the world, and the same task can succeed on Monday and fail on Tuesday with the same inputs. Three things to grade What Question Grader Example Outcome Is the world in the right state at the end? Code that inspects the environment The order shows exactly one refund of 1,200 INR; the in-transit order shows none Trajectory Did it get there in an acceptable way? Rules over the sequence of calls; sometimes a judge Read the order before refunding; never call a forbidden tool; at most 8 steps Interaction Did the person get what they needed, politely and truthfully? Rubric judge calibrated with people ( Lesson 14.143 ) It explained why the refund was refused and offered the next step Grade outcomes with code whenever you can: it is cheap, exact and does not drift. This is the core idea of τ-bench and its successor τ²-bench from Sierra: tasks in domains such as retail and airline support, a simulated user, and success judged by comparing the final database state with the expected one. Reliability is a separate number Run each task several times. An agent that solves a task in 7 of 10 trials has a 70% pass@1, but the chance that it succeeds on four independent attempts in a row (what four different customers experience) is far lower. τ-bench reports this as pass^k : the probability that all k trials succeed, estimated without bias from n trials with c successes as C(c, k) / C(n, k). Report both: pass@1 says how capable the agent is; pass^k says how dependable it is. pass@k and pass^k from the same agent: pass@k (any of k tries succeeds) rises with k, which flatters the agent; pass^k (all k tries succeed) falls with k, which is what a user who comes back k times experiences. Hands-on · A task suite judged by final state Grading by the resulting state of the system rather than by the reply text is called final-state grading . The environment below is a tiny order database. Each task is a user request, an expected final state and a "critical" flag. The two agent versions stand in for real ones: correct most of the time, with version-specific mistakes, as real agents have. Copy What you should see Copy Version 2 looks better on every summary number: pass^1 and pass^4 are both higher, and it fixed v1's habit of acting without reading the order. Look at the per-task line before celebrating. Hands-on · A release gate that reads per task Averages hide the one regression that matters. Gate on rules that encode the business risk: no new failures on critical tasks, no drop in reliability, and an honest statement of how much evidence the comparison has. Copy What you should see Copy Version 2 is blocked: in one trial out of ten it refunded 18,000 INR that should have gone to a person, a failure v1 never had. Three tasks improved, but no amount of improvement elsewhere pays for a new way to lose money. And six tasks cannot show a significant difference between versions in either direction; a real suite needs hundreds of tasks, weighted towards the critical ones. Public benchmarks, read carefully Benchmarks tell you how models and harnesses compare on someone else's tasks. Use them to shortlist models and to learn evaluation design; never as evidence that your agent works. Solutions Solution P1 · Outcomes and trajectories No. Trajectory evaluation (tool calls, order, count) or cost metrics catch it. Agents need both outcome and process measures. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Application Insights Azure Monitor's tracing and telemetry service Lesson 14.156 Request-response logging Saving model inputs and outputs to BigQuery Lesson 15.30 Why this came about Debugging AI systems required seeing every model call and tool step, which logs did not show. LLM observability tools (2023 onward) adapted distributed tracing , and OpenTelemetry added conventions for generative AI . In plain words first A flight recorder for every run You cannot fix what you cannot see. Observability for agents means recording each run as a trace : every model call with its inputs, outputs, tokens and timing, every tool call and its result, linked to the user, prompt version and model. Metrics and alerts are built on top: error rates, latency, cost, tool failures, loops. Sensitive data must be kept out of traces or masked. Logs, traces, metrics, and what is different for agents A trace of one agent run as a waterfall: each bar is a span with its duration. The model calls dominate, the knowledge-base search is the slow tool, and the run's cost and tokens roll up to the top span. Signal Answers Agent-specific content Traces What happened in this run, step by step, and how long each step took? Model calls, tool calls, retrieval, guardrail decisions, handoffs , approvals Metrics How is the system doing overall? Tokens and cost per run, tool error rate, steps per run, escalation rate, judge scores Logs What exactly was said and decided? Prompts and responses (redacted), tool arguments and results, policy blocks Feedback and evals Was the outcome good? Thumbs, corrections, resolution outcome, online judge scores For agents, the trace is the primary unit: almost every question ("why did it refund that order?", "why was this run slow?", "why did cost spike?") starts from one. Step 1 · Instrument with OpenTelemetry Framework integrations ( Lesson 14.118 's tracing, Strands, ADK, MAF, LangSmith , MLflow autolog) produce spans for you. Underneath, the vendor-neutral standard is OpenTelemetry. Here is the shape of a well-instrumented agent, written by hand so you see every attribute: What a trace of one agent run looks like in a tracing tool: the run at the top, each step inside it, and each model call and tool call inside its step. Every row is a span. Figure: Hugging Face, Agents Course , Apache 2.0 . Copy What you should see Copy One trace, one root span per agent run, a child per model call and tool call, token counts on each model span. Replace InMemorySpanExporter with an OTLP exporter and the same spans appear in any backend. Prompt and response text are left out on purpose: the conventions make content capture opt-in. Step 2 · What to log, and what not to Decision Recommendation Content capture Capture prompts and responses where you need them for debugging and evals, with PII redaction before storage ( Lesson 15.23 ), restricted access and an audit trail Identifiers Pseudonymous user and tenant IDs on every span; never emails, phone numbers or names as attributes Sampling Keep 100% of errors, blocked requests, negative feedback and slow or expensive runs; sample the rest (for example 10%) Retention Short for full content (for example 30 days), longer for metrics and redacted metadata; align with privacy law and contracts Correlation Put the trace ID in every log line and in your support tickets, so "this customer had a bad answer" leads to one trace Cost attribution Tag spans with team, app, feature and model, so costs roll up ( Lesson 14.142 ) Erasure Make traces deletable by user ID; tracing stores are personal-data stores ( Lesson 15.26 ) Three of those rows in code. First, content capture that is off by default and redacted when on. The environment variable is the one OpenTelemetry's GenAI instrumentations use: Copy What you should see Copy Redact before the attribute is set, not in the backend: once raw text leaves the process it is in your collector, your vendor and their backups. Regexes catch the obvious formats; for names and addresses, run a recognizer such as Presidio ( Lesson 15.23 ) in the collector or the instrumentation. Second, tail-based sampling : decide whether to keep a trace after it finishes, when you know whether it was interesting. (Head-based sampling decides at the start, so it drops errors as readily as successes.) Copy What you should see Copy Every error, block, complaint and outlier was kept, plus a 10% random sample of the ordinary runs for baselines. The OpenTelemetry Collector's tail_sampling processor implements the same rules as configuration; most LLM observability vendors offer equivalent filters at ingestion. Third, correlation : put the trace ID on every log line, so a log entry, a support ticket or an alert leads to exactly one trace: Copy What you should see Copy Your trace ID will differ. OpenTelemetry's logging instrumentation ( opentelemetry-instrumentation-logging ) adds the same fields automatically and can ship the logs over OTLP next to the traces. Here they are computed from the 10,000 runs above, followed by the alerting method most SRE teams now use, error-budget burn rate : alert when the rate of failures would exhaust the month's allowance much too fast, checked over a long and a short window together so one bad minute does not page anyone: Copy What you should see Copy A burn rate of 19 means the last hour consumed error budget nineteen times faster than the SLO allows; sustained, the month's budget would be gone in under two days. l1214: Course home / Phase 14 · AI Agents: Design and Engineering AgentOps: triage, replay and incidents From Zero to Agents Lesson 14.146 105 min Core Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Choose the signals that tell you an agent is healthy, in four layers from user outcomes down to infrastructure Triage a day of traces in minutes: loops, budget breaches, runs with no answer, cost outliers and failing tools Group errors into signatures and tie a regression to the release that introduced it Reproduce a bad run exactly by replaying its recorded tool results, and prove the fix against the same evidence Run an agent incident from the first five minutes to a blameless postmortem that adds a permanent check Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.145 Depth : Core Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up AgentOps Operating agents in production: observing decisions as well as systems Introduction Error signature An error message normalized so that occurrences of the same problem group together Error signatures Replay Re-running an agent against the tool results a trace recorded, to reproduce a failure exactly Replay Blameless postmortem A review of an incident that looks for system fixes rather than people to blame Postmortems Why this came about As agents ran in production, incidents became routine: loops, bad answers, cost spikes. AgentOps borrowed incident practice from site reliability engineering (triage, replay , post-mortems) and adapted it to agents. In plain words first From an alert to a fix, with evidence When an agent misbehaves in production, AgentOps is the routine for handling it: triage the alert, find affected runs, replay a failing trace to reproduce it, identify the stage that failed, fix and test the fix against the replay, then add the case to the evaluation set and write up what happened. Good traces and replay tools turn incidents into tests. Lesson 14.145 showed how to instrument an LLM application. This lesson is about operating an agent once it is live: what to look at every morning, what should wake someone up, how to find the one run in ten thousand that went wrong, and what to do in the first five minutes of an incident. The word for this practice is AgentOps . It is ordinary site reliability engineering, with one addition: the thing you are operating makes decisions, so you must observe its decisions as well as its latency. Four layers of signals Four layers of signals, and the path from an alert to a fix. Start reading from the top: an agent can be green on every infrastructure chart while telling customers the wrong thing. Layer What it tells you Examples Where it comes from Outcomes Is the agent doing the job? Task success per intent, escalation rate, user override rate, complaints, refunds reversed Online evals on sampled traces, business systems, feedback ( Lesson 14.144 ) Behavior Is it doing the job the right way? Steps per run, repeated calls, tools used per intent, policy denials, approval rate, unverified claims Trace analysis, policy decision logs ( Lesson 14.138 ) Cost and latency Can we afford it, and do users wait? Cost per successful task, tokens per run, cache hit rate , time to first token , p95 task time Spans with usage attributes, gateway logs ( Lesson 14.142 ) Infrastructure Are the parts up? Provider errors and rate limits, tool error rates and latency, queue depth, worker saturation Gateway, tool services, runtime metrics ( Lesson 14.136 , Lesson 14.141 ) Most teams start at the bottom because infrastructure metrics are easy. Start at the top instead. An agent can be green on every infrastructure metric while confidently telling customers the wrong thing; only the outcome and behavior layers catch that. Tip Put the release on every span Tag each trace with the release bundle (prompt, model, tool and policy versions, Lesson 14.147 ), the tenant, the intent and the outcome. Without the release tag you cannot answer the first question of every incident: "what changed?" Traces are the source of truth A trace per run, in the shape of the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions ( Lesson 14.145 ), is what makes everything else possible: one invoke_agent span for the run, with chat spans for model calls and execute_tool spans for tool calls beneath it. Three operating decisions matter: Sampling. Keep every trace for errors, escalations, policy denials, cost outliers and the first days of a new release (tail sampling, decided after the run ends). Sample the healthy rest. Content capture. Prompts and tool results contain personal data. Store them where access is controlled and retention is short, or redact them at the collector, and record that choice ( Lesson 15.26 ). Linking. Carry the trace ID into tickets, approvals and the business record ("refund R-88 was issued by run r-0204"), so a complaint can be traced back to the decisions that caused it. Hands-on · Triage a day of runs The first job every morning is to find the runs that went wrong in ways no error message reports. The script below generates 300 synthetic runs in the shape of OpenTelemetry GenAI spans (in production you would query your tracing backend), with release 0.5 introduced at run 200. It flags loops, step-budget breaches, runs that ended without an answer and cost outliers, and computes an error rate per tool. Copy What you should see Copy The same eight runs trip four detectors: a loop is a budget breach, a missing answer and a cost outlier at once, which is why loop detection pays for itself ( Lesson 14.67 ). The tool table points at search_kb , with an error rate several times the others. Neither problem raised an exception in the agent; both are visible only in traces. Hands-on · Error signatures, and what changed Raw error messages contain order numbers, shard IDs and request IDs, so ten thousand errors look like ten thousand different problems. Normalizing them into signatures groups them, and splitting the counts by release answers "what changed?" in one line. Copy What you should see Copy The orders-API errors are old noise spread across both releases. The search_kb timeouts exist only in 0.5, so the release introduced them, perhaps a longer query or a new index. That is a rollback decision you can make in minutes ( Lesson 14.147 ), before anyone has worked out the root cause. Hands-on · Replay a bad run exactly A user complains that the agent said their refund was completed when it was not. Re-running the conversation against live systems will not reproduce it: the model samples differently, the knowledge base is up again and the order has moved on. Instead, replay the run: feed the agent the tool results the trace recorded, in order, and check that it asks for the same things. The bug then reproduces every time, and the fix can be proven against the same evidence before it ships. Copy What you should see Copy Release 0.5 turned a knowledge-base timeout into a false claim of success; the fix says what is known and what is not. The claims_unverified_success check is a few lines of code, and it now belongs in the eval suite ( Lesson 14.144 ) and in an online check on live traces, so this class of failure cannot come back silently. With a real model, replay the recorded model outputs too when you need an exact reproduction, or replay only the tool results and run the model several times to see how often the failure occurs. Alerts: what pages, and what waits Signal Page someone now Ticket for business hours Harmful action or data exposure detected (policy violation, PII in output, unapproved write) Yes, always Task success error budget burning fast ( Lesson 14.145 burn-rate alerts) Yes Slow burn A tool or provider failing for most runs Yes, if there is no fallback If degraded mode is working Loop or step-budget breaches above baseline Yes Cost per successful task above budget If the spend cap is about to trip Otherwise New error signature after a release Yes, and check the canary ( Lesson 14.147 ) Override or escalation rate drifting up Yes, with a sample of runs to read Page on what users and the business feel; everything else is a ticket. An agent team that pages on every tool timeout learns to ignore pages. Incident response for agents Agent incidents have one feature ordinary incidents lack: the system may still be acting while you investigate. So the first minutes are about stopping harm, not finding the cause. Severity Agent examples Response SEV1 Wrong or unauthorized actions in the world (payments, deletions, messages), data leaking to the wrong user Kill switch or disable the affected tools now; page the owner and security; preserve evidence SEV2 Wrong answers at scale, an intent failing broadly, a runaway spend Roll back the release or route the intent to people; communicate a workaround SEV3 Degraded quality or latency with a working fallback Fix in hours; watch the error budget The first five minutes of a SEV1 or SEV2: Stop the bleeding. Use the controls you built before launch: the kill switch, per-tool disable flags, routing an intent to people, or rolling back the release bundle ( Lesson 14.138 , Lesson 14.147 ). Prefer the narrowest control that stops the harm. Preserve the evidence. Pin the traces, approvals and policy logs for affected runs so retention does not delete them. Find the blast radius. Query traces for every run with the same signature, release and tool, and list the affected users and records. Agents act on many records; the list is the input to remediation. Communicate. Tell support what users will see and what to say; for data or money, involve the people who own those obligations. Remediate the effects , not only the cause: reverse the duplicate refunds, contact the users who received wrong information. Postmortems that ratchet Run a blameless postmortem for every SEV1 and SEV2. For agents, add three questions to the usual timeline, root cause and actions: Which check would have caught this before release? Add it to the eval suite ( Lesson 14.144 ), so the release gate now blocks this failure. Which control would have contained it sooner? A tighter permission, an approval, a lower spend cap or a narrower kill switch ( Lesson 14.138 ). Which signal would have shown it earlier? An online check, a new alert or a dashboard panel. Each answer becomes a permanent rule, test or hook: the same ratchet that Lesson 14.67 applies to harnesses , applied to operations. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What is AgentOps? Worked answer. Operating agents in production: monitoring behavior and quality, triaging failures by category, replaying runs from traces, managing incidents with runbooks and kill switches, and turning every failure into tests and fixes. The team that owns it, with runbooks, dashboards and the authority to disable capabilities; platform teams for shared infrastructure. A To hide errors from users B So thousands of messages with different IDs group into a few problems you can count and tie to a release C To make logs smaller D Because OpenTelemetry requires it Grouping turns noise into a short list of problems, and the release split shows what changed. LLMOps extended MLOps release practices (versioning, evaluation gates, gradual rollout, rollback) to every such change. In plain words first Releasing changes you cannot fully predict Changing a prompt, model, tool or retrieval setting changes behaviour in ways tests may not catch. The LLMOps lifecycle treats every such change as a release: version it, evaluate it offline against the current version, roll it out gradually ( shadow mode , then a small share of traffic), watch online metrics, and keep a fast way to roll back. From MLOps to LLMOps to AgentOps MLOps grew up around models you train: data pipelines, feature stores, training runs, model registries, drift monitoring. LLMOps keeps the discipline but moves the center of gravity: most teams do not train the model, so the things you build and change are prompts, retrieval, tools, guardrails and model choice , and quality is judged by evals rather than one accuracy number. AgentOps adds what agents bring: multi-step traces , tool side effects, approvals, long-running state and per-run cost that varies tenfold. Frame : the task, the users, what "good" means, risk tier ( Lesson 15.26 ), cost and latency budgets. Prototype : smallest thing that works, often in a notebook against a hosted model. An agent's behavior is set by more than its code: the prompt, the model version, the tool definitions , the permission policy, the retrieval index and the harness settings all change what it does. Any one of them can change on a Tuesday afternoon. Shipping safely means versioning them together, gating each change by its risk, and being able to undo it in minutes. The first half of this lesson introduced the lifecycle and its tools; this half turns them into a change process for agents: a release manifest, gates and a staged rollout. The release bundle A release bundle is an immutable, versioned set of everything that defines behavior: prompt and its template version, model and its dated version, tool definitions and their schemas, policy (permissions, approval thresholds, budgets), retrieval configuration (index version, chunking, reranker ) and harness settings (step budget, stop conditions). The bundle ID goes on every trace ( Lesson 14.146 ). Rolling back means pointing traffic at the previous bundle, never editing a prompt in place. Watch out Hot-fixing a prompt in production The fastest way to break an agent is an "urgent one-line prompt fix" applied outside the release process. It skips the eval suite, has no bundle ID, cannot be rolled back cleanly and makes the next incident's "what changed?" unanswerable. Make the safe path fast instead: a small prompt change through the eval gate and a canary should take an hour, not a week. Hands-on · Gates follow what changed Different changes carry different risks. A model change can alter everything; a policy change can widen what the agent is allowed to do. The plan below diffs two bundles and lists the gates the change must pass. Copy What you should see Copy This change touches three parts at once, and one of them adds a write tool. In practice, split it: ship the model change first behind the existing tools, then add issue_refund with its own approval and evals. Smaller bundles make failures attributable. Hands-on · Shadow mode: compare decisions on live traffic Shadow mode sends a copy of live requests to the candidate. Its tool writes are stubbed and its replies are discarded, so users see nothing; you compare what it decided with what production decided. For agents, decisions (which tool, which arguments, escalate or not) are far easier to compare than prose, and a new write that production would not have made is the finding that matters most. Copy What you should see Copy The candidate agrees on status questions but issues refunds above the 5,000 limit that production escalated: a policy violation the offline suite missed, found before a single user saw it. The policy disagreements cut the other way: there, production sometimes answered from memory and the candidate searched the knowledge base. A disagreement is a question, not a verdict, so read a sample of each kind before deciding. Two rules for shadows: stub every write (shadow traffic must never touch the world), and remember that shadows double model cost for the traffic they cover, so shadow a sample. Canaries, flags and the kill switch After shadow mode, a canary sends a small share of real traffic to the candidate and widens it in steps. Decide the stop rules before starting: Shipping a change safely: offline evals gate it, shadow mode compares its decisions on copied live traffic with writes stubbed, a canary widens real traffic in steps with stop rules, and the previous bundle stays warm for rollback. Stage Traffic Stop and roll back if Minimum evidence before widening Internal Staff and test tenants Any critical eval case fails A day of use Canary 1 5% of one low-risk tenant or intent Task success falls beyond the noise band; any new write-related error signature; cost per task up more than 20% Enough runs for the comparison test in Lesson 14.140 Canary 2 25% across tenants Same, plus escalation or override rate rising A full weekly cycle for seasonal traffic General 100% Error budget burning ( Lesson 14.146 ) Keep the previous bundle warm for a week Use feature flags for capabilities (a new tool, a new intent) so they can be turned off without a release, and keep a kill switch that stops all agent actions and routes work to people. Test both regularly; a kill switch nobody has used is a hope, not a control. Model upgrades are migrations Provider model versions change behavior even when the vendor calls them compatible: different tool-calling habits, different verbosity, different refusals and different token use. Treat an upgrade as a migration project: Pin dated model versions in every bundle. Never point production at a floating alias such as "latest". Run the full suite with repeated trials on the new model, plus cost and latency, per intent ( Lesson 14.144 ). Re-tune before you judge. Prompts tuned for one model often need adjustment for another; budget time for it. Shadow, then canary , as above. Watch tokens, not just price. A new model at the same list price can cost much more if it writes longer answers or takes more steps. Track deprecation dates for every pinned model, and start the migration well before the old version is retired. Versioning of every component that changes behavior (prompts, models, retrieval data, tools, configs), evaluation gates, staged releases with canaries and rollback, monitoring of quality, safety and cost, data and feedback loops, and governance records. l1216: Course home / Phase 14 · AI Agents: Design and Engineering Humans in charge: approvals and handoffs From Zero to Agents Lesson 14.148 95 min Go deeper Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Route each action to the lightest review that matches its risk: automatic, notify, approve or two-person approval Design approvals people actually read, and detect when they have become a rubber stamp Hand work to a person with a complete packet, so the customer never repeats themselves Set approval deadlines and escalation paths so a missing reviewer does not stall or silently drop work Design the interface so users can see what the agent did, correct it and take over Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.138 Depth : Deepen Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Approval tier The level of human review an action needs, set by its risk Approval tiers Rubber-stamping Approvals given without real review, usually because the queue is badly designed Hands-on Handoff packet The structured summary a person needs to take over a case without re-asking the customer Handoffs Why this came about As agents took consequential actions, organizations needed people to approve, review and take over. Human-in-the-loop design moved from a debugging feature to a product and compliance requirement, with lessons about reviewer fatigue and escalation. In plain words first Deciding who signs, and how Some actions need a person: approve before, review after, or take over the conversation. Designing this well means deciding by risk which actions need approval, giving reviewers the context to decide quickly, handling timeouts and absent reviewers, recording who approved what, and watching for reviewer fatigue, where people approve without reading. Human-in-the-loop blocks until a person decides; human-on-the-loop lets work continue under supervision. "Human in the loop" is easy to say and hard to do well. Put a person in front of every action and they will approve hundreds a day without reading them; put nobody there and one bad decision reaches the world. The design question is where people add judgment, what they need to see to exercise it, and what happens when they are not there. Lesson 14.60 introduced approval levels and Lesson 16.29 the protocols (AG-UI, interrupts) that carry them; this lesson is about designing the human side. Approval tiers by risk Give every action an approval tier , set by its risk, before the agent can take it. Approval tiers as a risk map: reversibility on one axis, value on the other. Most actions sit in the corner that needs no review, which is what lets people review the rest carefully. Tier When What the person does Example Automatic Low value, reversible, within policy Nothing; it is logged and sampled for review Order status, small refunds on known customers Notify after Reversible, moderate value Can undo within a window A refund of a few thousand rupees, a calendar change Approve before Irreversible, high value, new counterparty or outside normal policy Reads a summary with evidence and approves or rejects A large refund, a payment to a new account, an email to a customer list Two-person approval Irreversible and very high value Two people approve independently Moving large sums, deleting production data Hands-on · Approval routing, and approvals that are real The script routes a day of actions to tiers, then checks reviewer behavior. An approval only protects you if the reviewer actually decides; a reviewer who approves almost everything in two seconds is a sign that the queue is badly designed, not that the reviewer is careless. Copy What you should see Copy Routing by risk cuts reviews from 2,000 to a few hundred, which is what makes careful review possible at all. The second check flags one reviewer as a rubber stamp. The fix is usually the queue, not the person: too many low-risk items, summaries that bury the one thing that matters, or targets that reward speed. Make approvals rarer, show the deciding fact first ("new account, first payment, INR 90,000"), and sample approved items for audit. From the field Every control "worked" In 2020 Citibank accidentally paid about USD 900 million to Revlon's lenders instead of an interest payment of about USD 8 million. Two Sigma's John Feminella uses the case to show that the procedure, the warning popup and three human approvers all functioned as designed, and the payment still went out, because the interface did not make the consequence clear to the people approving it. His recommendations for agents: a registry of agents, review proportional to risk, tool access that follows each agent's declared purpose, shared evaluations across the firm, and classifiers that route only the approvals that matter to people ( What a $900M Bank Error Teaches Us About AI Agents , 19 min). What an approval screen must show The decision in one line , with the consequence: "Refund INR 7,999 to Priya's original card; cannot be reversed after 24 hours." Why the agent proposes it , with evidence links (order, photo, policy section), not the agent's whole transcript. What is unusual : above limit, new counterparty, outside business hours, different from the customer's history. The alternatives : approve, edit (change the amount), reject with a reason, or take over. A deadline and what happens if nobody decides. Rejections and edits are training data: log the reason, and review them weekly to improve the agent or the policy ( Lesson 14.131 ). Hands-on · A handoff packet nobody has to re-ask When the agent escalates, the person who takes over should not need to read the transcript or ask the customer again. The packet below has a fixed set of fields, and the function reports any that are missing so the escalation can be blocked until it is complete. Copy What you should see Copy The colleague can approve in one step, with the evidence attached and the trace one click away. Make the packet a contract: an escalation without it is a bug, counted on the dashboard ( Lesson 14.146 ). When the human is not there Situation Bad default Better design Approval not given in time Work waits forever, or proceeds silently A deadline per tier; then escalate to a backup approver, or cancel and tell the user Reviewer queue grows Reviewers approve faster and read less Admission control on actions needing approval; raise thresholds only with evidence Out of hours Agent acts anyway, or stops all work Business-hours policy per action; queue high-risk actions, keep low-risk ones running Customer asks for a person Agent keeps trying Always honor it, with the handoff packet Person takes over mid-task Agent and person both act Explicit ownership change: the agent stops acting on that case and records why Design for oversight in the interface Users stay in charge when they can see what the agent did (an activity log in plain words, with links), correct it (edit a draft, undo an action within its window) and stop it (a visible pause or take-over control). Show progress for long runs, and say honestly when something is queued or waiting for a person. These are product requirements, not polish: they are what lets people trust an agent with more autonomy over time. Solutions Solution P1 · Rubber-stamping Reviewers are not really reviewing; approval fatigue makes the control ineffective. Raise the threshold, show reviewers what matters, sample-audit decisions and automate safe cases. Solution B1 · Handoffs need context Repeating everything to the person. Pass a summary, the conversation, the facts gathered and the attempted actions. Solution D1 · Approval SLAs Deadlines, reminders and escalation for pending approvals, and a default action (decline with a message) when they expire. Solution M1 · An approval screen Order, amount, policy check result, customer history, the agent's reasoning summary; approve, edit amount, reject with reason; log decision, reviewer, time and outcome. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How do you design human oversight for agents? Worked answer. Decide which actions need approval by risk, design reviewer tools with the right context and decisions, set SLAs and escalation, measure reviewer quality and load to avoid rubber-stamping, design smooth handoffs to people, and use decisions as training and eval data. A plausible wrong answer. "Add an approve button." Oversight that is not designed becomes a formality. Follow-ups. How do you prevent approval fatigue? Debug a failure After adding approvals, customer satisfaction fell. Why? Worked answer. Waiting: approvals added delays without communication. Show status to customers, set SLAs, and auto-approve low-risk cases. A plausible wrong answer. "Customers dislike AI." They dislike waiting without updates. Follow-ups. Which cases would you auto-approve? Defend a design When should a human be in the loop, on the loop, or out of the loop? Worked answer. In the loop (approve each action) for high-risk, irreversible actions; on the loop (monitor and intervene) for medium risk at volume; out of the loop for low-risk, reversible tasks with audits. Revisit as evals and incident history build trust. A plausible wrong answer. "Always in the loop for safety." It does not scale and becomes rubber-stamping. Follow-ups. A Replace the reviewer B Redesign the queue: fewer, risk-routed approvals with the deciding fact shown first, plus audit samples C Remove approvals entirely D Add a second identical approval Rubber-stamping is usually a queue design problem. Q2 What lesson does the Citibank-Revlon payment teach about approvals? A Approvals always prevent errors B Procedures, warnings and approvers can all function and still fail if the interface hides the consequence C Banks should not use software D One approver is enough The approval must make the consequence unmistakable. Q3 What must a handoff to a person include? A The raw transcript only B Customer, goal, what was done, evidence, the open question, a suggested next step and the trace ID C Only the customer's name D Nothing; the person will ask the customer A complete packet means the customer never repeats themselves. Q4 An approval for a high-risk action is not given within its deadline. What should happen? A The agent proceeds anyway B The work waits indefinitely C It escalates to a backup approver, or is cancelled with the user told, as the policy for that tier says D The request is deleted silently Every approval needs a deadline and a defined outcome when it passes. l1217: Course home / Phase 14 · AI Agents: Design and Engineering Platforms and multi-agent systems at scale From Zero to Agents Lesson 14.149 105 min Go deeper Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Recognize why multi-agent systems fail, using the MAST taxonomy, and design against the common failure modes Choose a coordination pattern (orchestrator and workers, pipeline, choreography) and make handoffs contracts, not conversations Build the paved path: the platform pieces that let many teams ship agents safely without rebuilding them Run an agent registry that enforces ownership, purpose-bound tool access, evals, budgets and a kill switch before deploy Organize teams and governance so the platform speeds teams up instead of becoming a queue Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.147 Depth : Deepen Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up MAST The Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy: 14 failure modes in three groups Why multi-agent systems fail Silent handoff failure A vague, untyped or stale result passed between agents and built on unnoticed Handoffs Paved path A platform that makes the safe way to ship an agent the easy way The paved path Agent registry The record of every agent's owner, purpose, tools, data and risk tier Registry Why this came about Large companies ended up with many agents built by many teams, each reinventing identity, tools and evaluation. Internal agent platforms and registries emerged to provide those once, and to govern how agents call each other. In plain words first From one agent to an agent platform When many teams build many agents, shared needs appear: a registry of agents and tools, common identity and permissions, gateways, evaluation and observability, and rules for how agents call each other. A platform provides these once so each team does not rebuild them, and multi-agent systems at scale depend on it to stay understandable and safe. One agent in production is a product. Fifty agents across a company are a distributed system and an organizational problem. This lesson covers both: how systems of agents fail and how to make them hold together, and the shared platform that lets many teams ship agents without each team relearning every lesson in this part. Why multi-agent systems fail Researchers at UC Berkeley studied the traces of popular multi-agent frameworks and published MAST , the Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy, with 14 failure modes in three groups ( Cemri et al., "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" ; code and annotated traces ). Their central finding is that most failures come from system design and coordination, not from the underlying model being too weak. Group Failure modes The design answer Specification issues Disobeying the task specification; disobeying the role specification; step repetition; loss of conversation history; being unaware of termination conditions Precise specs per agent ( Lesson 14.134 ); explicit stop conditions and step budgets ( Lesson 14.67 ); state outside the conversation Inter-agent misalignment Conversation reset; failing to ask for clarification; task derailment; information withholding; ignoring another agent's input; a mismatch between reasoning and action Structured handoffs with contracts (below); one owner of the plan; clarification as an explicit tool Task verification Premature termination; no or incomplete verification; incorrect verification Independent verifiers with their own criteria; outcome checks in code ( Lesson 14.144 ) Read the first column as a checklist for design reviews: for each mode, where in your system is it prevented or detected? Tip Fewer agents first Before splitting work across agents, check that one agent with good tools and a good harness cannot do it ( Lesson 14.66 ). Multi-agent systems earn their cost when work truly parallelizes (research across many sources), when roles need different permissions or models, or when an independent verifier is worth its price. They cost more tokens, more latency and more ways to fail. Coordination patterns The orchestrator pattern in its simplest form: a coordinator agent routes each request to the subagent that fits and gathers what comes back. Figure: Google Cloud Architecture Center , CC BY 4.0 . Pattern How it works Good for Watch for Orchestrator and workers One agent plans and delegates; workers return structured results; the orchestrator decides Research, complex tasks with separable parts The orchestrator becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure Pipeline Fixed stages, each an agent or code, passing typed outputs Document processing, content workflows Errors propagate silently between stages unless every handoff is checked Maker and checker One agent produces, an independent one verifies against criteria Code, analysis, anything with checkable outputs Checkers that share the maker's blind spots; give them different context or models Choreography Agents react to events on a bus, with no central plan Loosely coupled teams' agents, long-running business processes Untraceable decisions; needs strong event contracts and tracing across agents A handoff design for customer support: a triage agent passes the customer to the specialist that fits, specialists can pass to each other, and any of them can escalate to a person. Every arrow in this picture is a handoff that needs a contract. Figure: Microsoft, Azure Architecture Center , CC BY 4.0 . Hands-on · Handoffs as contracts Most multi-agent bugs are silent handoff failures : one agent passes along a vague, untyped or stale result and the next one builds on it confidently. Treat every handoff like an API: a schema, required provenance and a freshness limit, checked in code before the next agent sees it. Copy What you should see Copy The second result is a string where a number should be and has no source, so the writer agent would have quoted "about 4%" with nothing behind it. The third is real but forty days old. Rejected handoffs go back to the producing agent with the reason, which is cheaper than finding the error in a report the CFO has already read. Contracts also make multi-agent traces readable, because every hop has a known shape. From the field Multi-agent systems that ship Factory's Luke Alvoeiro describes the architecture behind its coding droids: an orchestrator, workers and validators; validation contracts and structured handoffs; adversarial verification; a preference for serial over parallel steps when work interacts; and a model chosen per role ( The Multi-Agent Architecture That Actually Ships , 19 min). Databricks' Sandipan Bhaumik argues that 50 agents are a distributed-systems problem, with silent handoff failures, stale data and untraceable decisions as the typical faults, and data contracts plus a deliberate choice between orchestration and choreography as the cure ( talk , 26 min). The paved path: an agent platform When several teams build agents, each one rebuilds identity, gateways, tracing, evals and approvals, differently and with gaps. Each agent declares an owner, a purpose and its tools; the check below blocks deploys that lack the basics and flags tools that do not fit the declared purpose. Copy What you should see Copy The finance helper can propose journal entries but has also been given email, which its purpose does not need: an exit for data that nobody decided to open ( Lesson 15.24 ). The growth experiment has no owner, no evals and access to customer exports for writing marketing copy: exactly the agent that causes an incident and has nobody to page. Run the check in the deploy pipeline, so compliance is the default rather than a review meeting. Teams and governance A platform team owns the paved path as a product, with internal users and a roadmap. Its success measure is how fast product teams ship safe agents, not how many requests it approves. Product teams own their agents end to end: spec, evals, on-call and outcomes. Risk tiers set the review. Low-risk agents on the paved path deploy without a meeting; high-risk ones (money, health, legal, customer data at scale) get a design review and a sign-off from the people who own those risks ( Lesson 15.26 ). Shared learning. Postmortems, eval cases and new failure checks go into the shared platform so every team benefits from each incident ( Lesson 14.146 ). From the field Paved paths in practice Credit Karma's platform registers an agent through a portal that provisions identity, memory, traces, evals and secrets; deploys it as a scanned container on Kubernetes; routes tools through a central MCP gateway ; and keeps tracking tables for model use, tool calls , cost and eval results ( talk , 29 min). LinkedIn's agent platform, built on LangGraph , standardized a Python service framework, asynchronous messaging between agents, layered memory and a central skill registry ( How LinkedIn Built Their First AI Agent for Hiring with LangGraph ). Uber's GenAI Gateway put every model call behind one door with redaction, metering and logging ( Lesson 14.136 ). Read each one for the reasoning behind the choices, not just the final diagram. Worked design 1 · A support assistant at 50,000 conversations a day Worked design: a support assistant at 50,000 conversations a day. Deterministic paths take most traffic; the agent handles the rest; writes are idempotent and gated. Clarify : order status, cancellations of unshipped orders, refunds (automatic up to INR 2,000, approval above), policy questions; English, Hindi and Hinglish; chat and voice later. Success : 60% resolved without a person; under 1% wrong resolutions; p95 first token under 2 seconds; under INR 10 per resolved conversation; 99.7% availability. Estimate : Step 1's numbers: about 17 model calls per second at peak, four deployments of quota, prompt caching essential. Shape : an intent router sends the frequent, fixed intents (order status, FAQ) to deterministic flows, policy questions to cited RAG , and the rest to one agent with a step budget. A multi-agent design adds cost and handoff errors without a measured need. Tools : read tools through an MCP gateway with the customer ID taken from the session; cancel and refund as durable workflows with idempotency keys ; refunds above the limit pause for approval. Safety : customer messages and reviews are untrusted; the agent holds private data and can act, so outbound actions are limited to the customer's own orders, links in answers are allowlisted, and every write is checked in code. Operate : eval set by intent with pass^3 gates in CI; online judges on 5% of traffic; dashboards for resolution rate, handoff rate, p95 and cost per resolved conversation; canary releases. Trade-offs : the router is a component to maintain and evaluate, but it removes a model call from 70% of traffic; durable workflows add infrastructure, but a lost refund is worse. At 10 times the load : token quota and cost first, then the human desk's capacity for handoffs; the answer is more caching, smaller models for more intents, and moving automation per intent as quality allows. Worked design 2 · A multi-tenant enterprise knowledge assistant Worked design: a multi-tenant knowledge assistant. Permissions are enforced inside retrieval; every cache and index is keyed by tenant. Clarify : 200 client companies, each with its own documents in SharePoint, Google Drive and wikis; users must only see what they could open in the source system. Success : answer accuracy over 85% on each tenant's labeled set, zero cross-tenant or cross-permission leaks, answers with citations or an explicit "not found", fresh within an hour of a document change. Key decisions : permissions enforced inside retrieval with the user's groups from the identity provider, synced hourly; separate indexes for the largest tenants and a mandatory tenant_id filter for small ones; every cache key includes tenant and user; versioned indexes behind aliases so re-chunking is a side-by-side switch. Failure modes to design for : stale ACLs after someone changes teams, derived artifacts (summaries, FAQs) losing the source's permissions, selective filters returning nothing from post-filtered vector search ( Lesson 14.74 ), and documents that fail to parse silently. Trade-offs : per-tenant indexes isolate well but cost more to operate; shared indexes with filters are cheaper but make every filter bug a potential leak, which is why the permission test runs in CI. Worked design 3 · A text-to-SQL analytics agent Shape : a semantic layer per business domain (metrics, synonyms, sample values, verified queries ) is the core component, not the model; the agent selects the domain, generates SQL against it, validates and runs it read-only under the user's role, and returns the SQL, the assumptions and a chart. Numbers that matter : warehouse cost per query and a row limit, not tokens; a query timeout; caching of frequent questions. Evaluation : verified question and result pairs per domain, compared by result set ( Lesson 14.80 ). Platform fit : Genie on Databricks, data agents in BigQuery, or your own agent over dbt or Cube metrics elsewhere. Failure modes : wrong tables in large schemas (narrow by domain), wrong metric definitions (one definition, owned by the data team), ambiguous questions answered confidently (ask, or state assumptions). Worked design 4 · A document-processing pipeline Shape : asynchronous and batch, not chat. Documents arrive on a queue; each passes classify, parse, extract to a schema, validate against business rules and route: straight through when every field is confident and valid, to a reviewer otherwise. Numbers : documents per day and pages per document set throughput and cost; batch inference later · 14.154 APIs cut model cost; reviewer capacity sets how low the straight-through rate can be before the backlog grows. Key decisions : prebuilt extractors for standard formats, a multimodal model for the long tail; every field carries its source page and confidence; idempotent processing so a retried document is not booked twice. Evaluation : field-level accuracy against reviewer corrections, monitored per document source because a vendor's template change breaks one source at a time. In plain words first Reviewing a design like a practitioner A design review asks the questions that production will ask anyway: what happens when this fails, who can see this data, what does it cost at ten times the volume, how will we know it works, and how do we roll back. The practitioner playbook collects the lessons teams learned the hard way, so you can check a design against them before building. Review a design like an architecture board The same checks catch most of the gaps that later become incidents. Encode them, and run them against any design, including your own: What a design review checks, grouped by the question behind it. The code in this step runs the same checks against a written design and reports each gap with a severity, so that the review is repeatable. The cancellation finding is a question rather than a defect: cancelling an unshipped order is reversible, so no approval may be the right call, and the review makes someone say so.
