Multi-agent by default : impressive diagrams with five agents for a problem a router and one agent would solve, at several times the cost and with more failure points. Evaluation drawn as a box called "evals" : say what is measured, on what data, with which threshold, and what it blocks. Security as a perimeter : firewalls around the system while untrusted text flows straight into an agent with credentials. Draw the data flow and check the trifecta. The happy path only : no answer to "what happens when the model provider is down", "when retrieval finds nothing", or "when the user changes their mind halfway through a refund". Presenting a design In a 45-minute design session : spend the first ten minutes on clarifying, success metrics and numbers before drawing anything; draw the reference architecture adapted to the problem; walk one request through it end to end; then invite the others into the trade-offs ("I would start with a router plus one agent; if routing accuracy turned out low, I would..."). Leave five minutes for failure modes and what you would build next. Silence while you think is fine; silence while you draw is not, so narrate. To leadership or a client (one slide and five minutes): the problem in business terms and its current cost; the architecture as five or six boxes, not thirty; the evidence (pilot or eval results, and what the error cases are); the cost per outcome next to today's cost; the risks and their controls; the decision you need from them. Keep the detailed architecture in the appendix for the technical reviewers. Practice Design Design an AI assistant for relationship managers at a bank that drafts client meeting briefs from CRM, portfolio and market data. Clarify: 2,000 relationship managers, briefs before each meeting, read-only, no advice sent to clients without review; regulated data. Success: briefs rated usable without major edits 80% of the time, every number traceable to a source, generated within a minute, no data leaving the bank's cloud account. Estimate: a few thousand briefs a day, batchable the night before. Shape: a workflow, not an agent: fetch CRM notes, portfolio positions and relevant market news in parallel, summarize each with citations, assemble a brief with a fixed template, check every number against its source. Safety: the market-news step reads untrusted text, so it has no access to client data and returns only structured summaries ( dual-LLM pattern); briefs are drafts for the manager. Operate: managers' edits are the main quality signal; evaluate numeric accuracy automatically; models inside the bank's tenancy. Trade-off: a workflow is less flexible than an agent but auditable, which a regulator will ask about. Design Design an agent that reconciles payments against invoices for a mid-size company every night. Clarify: about 30,000 transactions a night from bank feeds and the ERP; matches must be exact; mismatches go to accountants by morning. Shape: deterministic matching rules first (amount, reference, date window) handle most items; an agent handles the remainder by reading remittance emails and partial references, proposing matches with evidence, never posting them. Durable, resumable batch with a progress log so a failure at 3 a.m. resumes rather than restarts; idempotent writes of proposed matches. Success: share auto-matched by rules, precision of agent proposals accepted by accountants, completion before 7 a.m. Safety: remittance emails are untrusted; the agent has read-only access and writes only proposals. Trade-off: rules are cheaper and exact; the agent is for the long tail, measured by acceptance rate. Design Design an internal platform so 30 product teams can ship agents safely. A paved road rather than a shared agent: an LLM gateway with virtual keys, budgets and model allowlists; an MCP gateway with an approved server registry and per-agent tool allowlists; a deployment template with durable execution , tracing and guardrail defaults; an evaluation service with CI integration and release gates; a prompt registry ; and an AI system register fed automatically from gateway traffic. Tenancy and cost attribution per team at the gateway. Success is time for a new team to ship a governed agent and the share of model traffic through the gateway. Trade-off: the platform becomes a critical dependency, so it needs its own SLOs and an emergency bypass. Design Your design must serve customers in India and the EU with data staying in each region. What changes? Two regional stacks with the same code: models, indexes, logs, traces and memory in each region; a router at the edge by customer residency; no cross-region calls on the request path. Check model and feature availability in both regions first, because a model missing in one region forces a different choice there, and keep the eval suite per region. Shared components such as prompt registries and dashboards hold no personal data. Document the data flows for both DPDP and GDPR reviews, and test residency mechanically (egress rules, region checks in CI). From the field: shipping and running AI products Plan around experiments, not features (Hamel Husain): time-boxed experiments with clear success criteria give stakeholders decision points without promising outcomes nobody can guarantee. Solutions Solution P1 · Review checklists "What is the worst action this agent can take, and what bounds it?" Every design review should ask about blast radius. Solution B1 · Review early Changes are expensive after launch, and risks are already live. Review at design time with a short checklist, and again before launch. Solution D1 · Turn findings into defaults Encode common findings into platform defaults, templates and automated checks, so teams start correct. Solution M1 · A review checklist Task and success metric; evals; worst action and its bounds; permissions; untrusted inputs; failure modes; cost per task; observability; data handling; ownership and on-call. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What should a design review of an AI agent cover? Worked answer. Purpose and success metrics, structure (workflow or agent), evaluation plan, safety and security (permissions, injection, data), reliability and failure modes, cost and scale, observability, governance and ownership. The goal is to find expensive mistakes early. A plausible wrong answer. "Code quality." Design reviews are about system risks. Follow-ups. Who should attend? Add the failure mode to the checklist, share the postmortem, and check whether the review had the right people and information. A plausible wrong answer. "Reviews do not work." l1220: Course home / Phase 14 · AI Agents: Design and Engineering Check your understanding: Production engineering and AI system design From Zero to Agents Lesson 14.152 35 min Core Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Test your understanding of LLMOps and system design: answer each question in your own words before opening the model answer Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.150 Depth : Core Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up System design round An interview where you design a system end to end and discuss trade-offs Interviews Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. In plain words first How to use these questions These questions check whether the chapter's ideas have really landed. Read each question, then answer it in your own words (out loud, on paper, or to a colleague) before opening the model answer: a one-sentence definition, then how it works, then what it means in practice. Compare with the model answer and the plausible wrong answer, and note any follow-up you could not answer. If a question feels unfamiliar, go back to the lesson that teaches it. Teams can also use these as discussion prompts in a study group. LLMOps, evaluation and model customization Mid What is different about LLMOps compared with MLOps? You usually do not train the model; you version prompts, tools, retrieval settings and model choices. Outputs are open-ended, so evaluation needs judges and human review, not only accuracy. Behavior is non-deterministic, so you test consistency. Cost and latency vary per request with tokens. Observability centres on traces of multi-step runs. Safety and security are part of every release. Senior How do you know a prompt or model change did not make things worse? A regression set that gates CI (near 100% expected), capability evals to track improvements, several trials per case to measure consistency, judges calibrated against experts, and an online comparison after release: canary or shadow traffic, online judge scores, user feedback, cost and latency. Change one thing at a time, and keep a rollback. Senior How do you cut an agent's cost by half without hurting quality? Measure first: cost per resolved task broken down by model, step and tool. Then prompt caching (stable prefix), routing easy requests to smaller models (with evals proving they pass), trimming tool definitions and tool outputs, fewer steps through better tools, batch APIs for offline work, semantic caching for repeated questions, and provisioned capacity for steady load. Re-run evals after each change. Mid What do you put on an agent's dashboard? Error rate, p50 and p95 latency and time to first token , steps and tool calls per run, tokens and cost per run and per tenant, escalation and approval rates, guardrail blocks, online judge scores and user feedback, retrieval no-result rate. Alert on SLO breaches, cost spikes and quality drops. Every metric links back to traces. Junior What is the difference between pass@k and pass^k? pass@k is the probability that at least one of k attempts succeeds; it suits tasks where you can pick the best attempt, such as code checked by tests. pass^k is the probability that all k attempts succeed; it measures consistency, which is what a customer-facing agent needs. An agent with 80% per-attempt success has pass@3 of about 99% but pass^3 of about 51%. Mid How do you build a trustworthy LLM-as-judge? One judge per failure mode, a binary verdict against a written rubric, the evidence included (context, tool results, policy), and calibration against 50 to 100 human labels, reporting true-positive and true-negative rates or Cohen's kappa . Control known biases: swap positions in pairwise comparisons, check verbosity bias, and avoid judging with the same model family when comparing models. Re-calibrate whenever the judge prompt or model changes, and correct production pass rates for the judge's known error rates. Mid What is error analysis, and why do it before writing evals? Reading a sample of real traces and noting the first thing that went wrong in each ( open coding ), then grouping the notes into a failure taxonomy and counting ( axial coding ). It tells you which failures matter and what to measure; generic metrics such as "helpfulness" rarely point to a fix. Evals written from observed failures catch regressions that actually hurt users. Mid What would you put in an agent's trace? A root span per run with user, tenant, session, release ID and outcome; a child span per model call with model, token counts, latency and finish reason; per tool call with name, arguments (redacted), result size, errors and duration; spans for retrieval, guardrail decisions, approvals and handoffs . Follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions so any backend can read them, make content capture opt-in and redacted, and keep 100% of errors and negative-feedback runs when sampling. Senior How do you roll out a new model version safely? Pin the current model version. Run the full offline suite (regression, capability, safety, cost and latency) on the candidate, several trials each. Shadow it on real traffic to compare outputs and costs, then canary it to a small share behind a flag with online judges, error and cost alerts, and an automated rollback rule. Watch for behavior changes in tool calling and refusal rates, not only quality averages. Keep the old version one switch away until the new one has run a full business cycle. Mid How do you serve an open model efficiently? Use an inference engine such as vLLM or SGLang: continuous batching , paged KV cache , prefix caching , quantization (FP8 or INT4 with group-wise methods such as AWQ or GPTQ , after checking quality on your evals), speculative decoding for latency, and tensor parallelism for large models. Size GPU memory for weights plus KV cache at your context length and concurrency. Load-test with realistic traffic and track time to first token, inter-token latency and goodput, and autoscale on queue depth. Senior p95 latency of your agent is 14 seconds and the target is 6. Where do you start? Break the 14 seconds down from traces: model time per call, number of sequential calls, tool time, queueing. Then work from the biggest item: remove sequential model calls (do fixed steps in code, merge steps), run independent tools in parallel, move routing and extraction to a small fast model, lower reasoning effort where it adds nothing, keep the prompt prefix stable for caching to cut time to first token, and stream progress so the wait feels shorter. Re-measure p95 after each change; averages hide the slow tail. System design rounds Lessons 14.135 and 14.150 teach system design in depth: the nine-step method, estimation, latency and availability budgets, the reference architecture and worked designs. The short version, for when you have to design on the spot: Clarify the users, the tasks, the actions allowed, volume, latency and the cost of a wrong answer. Define success as metrics: task success, pass^k, latency, cost per task, safety thresholds. Choose the shape : workflow, single agent, or multi-agent , and why. Design knowledge and tools : retrieval, structured data, tool list with risk levels. Add safety : guardrails, approvals, permissions, Rule of Two. Plan operations : evals in CI, tracing, monitoring, rollout and rollback, cost controls. Discuss trade-offs and what you would do next. Design Design a customer-support agent for an e-commerce company with 50,000 conversations a day. Clarify intents (order status, returns, refunds, policies) and the actions allowed. Shape: a router workflow sends simple intents to deterministic flows and the rest to one agent with order, refund and escalation tools; policies through hybrid RAG . Safety: refunds above a threshold need approval; injection screening on any customer-provided text; PII redaction in logs. Scale: stateless agent workers behind a gateway with caching and model routing; durable execution for refunds. Ops: regression evals with pass^3 gates, online judges on a sample, dashboards for resolution rate, handoff rate, p95 latency and cost per resolved conversation. Trade-off: more automation versus escalation rate; move the boundary as evidence accumulates. Design Design an internal research agent that writes reports from company documents and the web. Orchestrator with parallel research subagents (breadth justifies multi-agent), each with a clear sub-question, search tools (internal search with permissions, web search) and a token budget; a citation step that checks every claim against a source; a writer that produces the report from the collected notes. Long-running: checkpoint after each subagent, store notes in files, allow resume. Evaluate with a rubric judge (accuracy, citations, completeness, source quality) on 20 to 50 real research questions, plus human review. Security: web content is untrusted, so the research agents get no write tools. Design Design a text-to-SQL analytics agent for business users. A semantic layer (metrics, dimensions, joins, synonyms, verified queries ) is the core; the agent writes SQL against it, shows the SQL, runs it under the user's role so masking and row policies apply, and explains results with a chart. Add clarifying questions for ambiguous terms, a query cost limit, and read-only credentials. Evaluate on verified question-and-SQL pairs by comparing result sets, not SQL text. On Databricks this is Genie; elsewhere, your own agent over dbt or Cube metrics. Design Design an agent that triages and resolves IT helpdesk tickets. Clarify: ticket volume, categories (password resets, access requests, hardware, outages), systems it can act on, and what must stay human. Shape: a classifier routes tickets; deterministic automations handle the top categories (password reset through the identity provider's API with verification); an agent with read tools (knowledge base, monitoring, CMDB) drafts resolutions for the rest; access grants go through an approval workflow with the requester's manager. Safety: least-privilege service identities per tool, no free-form shell, approval for anything that changes access. Ops: measure auto-resolution rate, reopen rate, time to resolve, and escalations; evaluate drafts with a judge calibrated on resolved tickets. Trade-off: automation rate versus reopen rate. Design Design a voice agent for appointment booking at a hospital chain. Clarify: languages (Hindi, English, regional), call volume, booking rules, and what is out of scope (medical advice). Architecture: telephony into a streaming speech pipeline (speech-to-text, LLM , text-to-speech) or a speech-to-speech realtime model, with a target of under about 800 milliseconds from the end of the caller's speech to the start of the reply; barge-in support; tools for doctor schedules and bookings with confirmation read back before committing. Safety: no diagnosis, immediate handoff for emergencies, identity verification before revealing appointments, consent and recording notices, PII redaction in transcripts. Ops: task completion, handoff rate, latency percentiles per turn, word error rate on names and dates, and sampled human review. Design Design a coding agent for your company's internal repositories. Clarify: tasks (bug fixes, tests, upgrades, reviews), languages, CI, and who merges. Harness : the agent works in an isolated sandbox with a clone of the repository, tools to read and search files, edit, run tests and linters, and open a pull request; never push to protected branches. Context: repository instructions files, code search, and the issue; subagents for exploration to keep the main context clean. Safety: no production credentials, network allowlist for package registries, secrets scanning on output, human review required for merge. Evaluate on a set of past issues with their merged fixes and tests (SWE-bench style), and track PR acceptance rate and review comments in production. Design Design a document-processing agent for insurance claims. Clarify: document types (claim forms, invoices, medical bills, photos), volume, turnaround, and the decisions it may make. Pipeline: classify documents, extract fields with a layout-aware parser plus a model with a schema, validate against policy data and business rules, flag fraud signals, and route: straight-through for simple claims within limits, human adjuster review with a prepared summary for the rest. Every extracted value carries its source page and confidence; low confidence goes to review. Ops: field-level accuracy against adjuster corrections, straight-through rate, turnaround, and fairness checks across customer groups because this affects financial outcomes (likely high-risk under the EU AI Act if used in the EU). Design Design a multi-tenant agent platform for 30 product teams. Paved road rather than a shared agent: an AI gateway (model access, virtual keys, budgets, routing, logging), a tool registry of approved MCP servers behind an MCP gateway with per-agent allowlists, a managed runtime or a deployment template with durable execution, standard OpenTelemetry tracing into one backend, an evaluation service with CI integration and release gates, guardrail defaults, a prompt registry , and an AI system register fed automatically from the gateway. Tenancy: isolation of data, memory, caches and indexes per tenant; cost attribution per team. Success: time for a new team to ship a governed agent, and the share of model traffic through the gateway. A Always multi-agent B A default of one agent, the conditions that justify more, the cost and context trade-offs, and how you would measure the difference C Naming as many frameworks as possible D Refusing to choose Decision, conditions, trade-off, measurement. B "The refund tool enforces the limit and requires approval above it." C "Only the session's customer can be refunded, checked in code." D "Refunds use an idempotency key per order." Tools, identity and policy through the Gateway The Gateway is where enterprise control lives. A typical setup: Register targets: a Lambda function, an OpenAPI spec for your order API, and an existing MCP server. Industry practice A reference architecture AWS teams converge on Front door : API Gateway or an ALB with Cognito or your IdP, then AgentCore Runtime (or Lambda or ECS for simple agents). Agent : Strands or LangGraph, models through Bedrock with geographic cross-Region profiles for residency, a guardrail enforced at account level, prompt caching on. Tools : all through one AgentCore Gateway with Policy rules and Identity-managed credentials; no secrets in agent code. Knowledge : Knowledge Bases or managed knowledge bases on S3 Vectors, with OpenSearch where latency matters. State : AgentCore Memory, with DynamoDB for business state; Step Functions or Lambda durable functions for long workflows with human approvals ( Lesson 14.140 ). Ops : ADOT later · 14.154 traces into CloudWatch, invocation logging to S3 with KMS, CloudTrail, online evaluations, cost tags through application inference profiles ( Lesson 14.154 ). Accounts : separate dev, staging and prod accounts; model access and guardrails set by SCPs and enforced guardrails from the organization's security account. In production Production issues teams hit on Bedrock and AgentCore Throttling at launch : on-demand throughput is limited by per-model, per-Region quotas, and a launch-day spike returns throttling errors. Use cross-Region inference profiles, request quota increases weeks ahead, and consider provisioned throughput for steady high volume. Feature and model availability by Region : new models and features often reach US Regions first, and Mumbai availability differs by feature (the rerankers above are one example). Check availability against your data-residency rules before designing around a feature. Knowledge Base syncs are jobs : new documents are not searchable until the ingestion job finishes, and individual files can fail while the job succeeds. Read the ingestion job's statistics and alert on failed documents. Guardrails that are optional : a guardrail only applies to calls that reference it. Enforce it with the IAM condition shown in Lesson 14.154 so a code change cannot drop it. Runtime limits : managed agent runtimes have limits on session duration, payload size and concurrency; check them against your longest tasks and largest documents before committing. Deployment type Where it runs Use it for Global Standard Any Azure region with capacity Most capacity, lowest price; data at rest stays in your geography Data Zone Standard Within a data zone (for example the EU, the US, or Asia Pacific) Residency within a zone Standard (regional) One region Strict residency, for example India-only Provisioned (PTU: global, data zone or regional) Reserved throughput units Steady, high, latency-sensitive load Global and Data Zone Batch Asynchronous, within 24 hours, about half price Large offline jobs and evals The model router is itself a deployment: it sends each request to the cheapest model in its pool that can handle it, including agentic routing across OpenAI, Anthropic and open models. It is a quick cost win for mixed traffic; check its routing metadata in traces so you know which model answered. Concept How the code in this lesson runs offline Azure SDKs send HTTP requests through a pluggable transport. The Recorded helper below plugs in a transport that answers from recorded JSON , for both the azure-* SDKs and the OpenAI SDK that Foundry hands you. Your code goes through the real SDKs (request building, authentication policy, response parsing); only the network is replaced. OfflineCredential stands in for DefaultAzureCredential . To go live, drop transport= and http_client= , and use DefaultAzureCredential() . Tested with azure-ai-projects 2.9 and openai 3.39 (which is built on httpx2 ). Step 2 · Create and run a Foundry agent A prompt agent is a versioned definition (model, instructions, tools) stored in the project. You talk to it through the Responses API with a conversation that keeps the history server-side. Function tools work exactly as in Lesson 14.117 : the response contains function_call items, you run them, and send back function_call_output items. Copy With the rig in place, the agent itself is short: Copy What you should see Copy Four HTTP calls: create the agent version, open a conversation, then two turns of the tool loop. Agent versions are immutable, so you can pin production to version 1 while you test version 2. Built-in tools (file search, code interpreter, web search, Azure AI Search, SharePoint, Fabric, MCP, OpenAPI, A2A , browser automation) are declared in the same tools list and run server-side, so they do not appear in your loop. When an agent uses many tools, put them in a toolbox : a versioned bundle of tools and skills that Foundry exposes as one MCP endpoint, handles authentication for, and searches at run time ( tool search ) so only the relevant tools reach the model. Step 3 · Three ways to build agents in Foundry Kind You provide Foundry runs Choose it when Prompt agent Model, instructions, tools (portal, SDK or YAML) Everything Most single agents; fastest path Workflow A graph of agents, conditions, loops, human approvals and variables (visual designer or YAML) The orchestration and state Multi-step and multi-agent processes with clear structure Hosted agent (GA July 2026) Your own code in a container: Agent Framework, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI or anything else Hosting, scaling, identity, sessions, sandboxes , observability You need custom logic or an existing framework, with Foundry's governance Around them sit routines (GA September 2026: run an agent on a schedule or an event), memory (user, session and procedural memory managed by the service), long-running hosted agents that survive restarts, voice agents , publishing to Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot , and the Agent Optimizer , which proposes better instructions, models and tool sets from evaluation results. Industry practice Choosing between Foundry, Copilot Studio and Microsoft 365 Copilot Studio : low-code agents for business makers, with Power Platform connectors, topics and approvals. Good for internal, departmental agents; governed by Power Platform admins. Microsoft 365 Copilot extensions (declarative agents, Microsoft 365 Agents SDK): when users live in Teams and Outlook and the agent mostly works over Microsoft 365 data through Work IQ. Foundry : pro-code and production agents, custom models, evaluations, private networking, any framework. Most enterprises use all three, and register every agent in one control plane ( Lesson 14.156 ). Step 4 · Grounding with Foundry IQ and Azure AI Search Azure AI Search is the retrieval engine. It supports keyword ( BM25 ), vector and hybrid search fused with reciprocal rank fusion , plus the semantic ranker (a cross-encoder reranker ), integrated vectorization, filters and security trimming. Foundry IQ puts knowledge bases on top: a knowledge base combines several knowledge sources (search indexes, blob storage, SharePoint, OneLake, the web) and runs agentic retrieval ( Lesson 14.76 ): a model plans sub-queries, searches the sources in parallel, reranks and returns grounding data with references. Copy What you should see Copy The activity list is the knowledge base's own trace: what it planned, which sources it searched, and the tokens and time each step took. Log it. In an agent you usually attach the knowledge base as a tool instead of calling it yourself; pass the user's token ( query_source_authorization ) so results respect document permissions. Choose by scenario Tuning Azure AI Search for RAG Loop step Setting Notes Hybrid search Send both a text query and a vector query; results are fused with RRF The default for most RAG indexes Reranking Enable the semantic ranker with a semantic configuration that names the title and content fields Adds latency and is billed per query beyond the free tier; include the title field so the ranker sees context Vocabulary mismatch Query rewriting with the semantic ranker (preview) Generates rewrites of the user query before retrieval Multi-part questions Agentic retrieval through knowledge bases (Foundry IQ, Step 4) Plans sub-queries and returns grounded results; more model calls Chunks lacking context Index projections from parent documents, so each chunk carries parent fields Configure in the indexer's skillset Freshness Scoring profiles with a freshness function Combine with filters for "latest" questions Tables and layout The Document Layout skill, which outputs Markdown sections Better chunk boundaries for structured documents Step 5 · Content Safety and Prompt Shields Azure AI Content Safety provides the checks Lesson 15.23 described, as an API and as guardrails you attach to model deployments and agents in Foundry. Check What it does Harm categories Hate, sexual, violence and self-harm, each with a severity from 0 to 7, for text and images Prompt Shields Detects jailbreaks in user prompts and indirect prompt injection in documents, emails and tool results Groundedness detection Checks that an answer is supported by its sources, and can suggest a correction Protected material Detects known copyrighted text and public code in outputs Task adherence and spotlighting Flags agent tool calls that drift from the user's task; marks untrusted content so the model treats it as data Custom categories and blocklists Your own harmful-content definitions and banned terms Copy What you should see Copy The user's request was harmless; the review it asked about carried an injection. That is the indirect-injection case from Lesson 15.24 , and it is why tool results and retrieved documents must be checked too, not only user input. In production Production issues teams hit on Foundry Deployment type decides residency and capacity : Global deployments give the most capacity, Data Zone and regional deployments keep processing in a geography. Decide by data-residency rules first, then capacity. 429s under load : tokens-per-minute quotas apply per deployment and subscription. Spread load across deployments and Regions behind API Management, and use provisioned throughput (PTU) with pay-as-you-go spillover for steady traffic. Content filters blocking legitimate requests : the default filters can block ordinary support content (complaints, medical terms). Review blocked requests and adjust filter configurations per deployment. Index freshness in AI Search : indexers run on a schedule; a document uploaded now may not be searchable for hours. Check the indexer schedule and run history, and alert on indexer failures. Step 1 · Cortex AI functions: AI in SQL AI functions are the highest-leverage AI feature in Snowflake. They turn a model call into a column expression, so one SQL statement can classify, extract or summarize millions of rows, in a dynamic table that keeps itself up to date, with no agent at all. Function Job AI_COMPLETE General generation, with a model, options and structured output ( response_format as a JSON schema ); accepts images, and in 2026 audio and video AI_CLASSIFY Assign one or more labels from a list you provide AI_FILTER A yes or no condition in plain language; use it in WHERE and for a semantic join AI_AGG , AI_SUMMARIZE_AGG Aggregate many rows into one insight or summary (beyond the context window ) AI_EXTRACT Pull named fields from text or documents AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT OCR and layout extraction from PDFs and images on a stage AI_TRANSCRIBE Speech to text from audio and video files AI_REDACT Remove PII from text AI_SUMMARIZE Summarize text, images or documents AI_EMBED , AI_MULTI_EMBED , AI_SIMILARITY Embeddings for text and images (and with AI_MULTI_EMBED audio and video), and similarity AI_SENTIMENT , AI_TRANSLATE Sentiment by aspect, translation AI_COUNT_TOKENS Estimate tokens before you spend them Copy Watch out Cost control for AI functions AI functions bill in credits per token, and a careless SELECT AI_COMPLETE(...) FROM big_table can be the most expensive query of the month. Test on LIMIT 100 , estimate with AI_COUNT_TOKENS , use the smallest model that passes your evals , filter rows before calling the model, use dynamic tables so rows are processed once, and watch SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.CORTEX_AI_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY (the standard view for function spend; CORTEX_AISQL_USAGE_HISTORY still exists for per-function detail but is slated for deprecation in January 2027), plus CORTEX_AGENT_USAGE_HISTORY and the other per-service usage views. Calling AI functions needs the USE AI FUNCTIONS account privilege and the CORTEX_USER (or AI_FUNCTIONS_USER ) database role, so grant them to roles deliberately. Set budgets with alerts and per-user quotas (the only AI cost control with built-in enforcement), and restrict models with model RBAC : grant the model application roles in SNOWFLAKE.MODELS ( CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-ALL , or one role per model). The older CORTEX_MODELS_ALLOWLIST account parameter is being retired (behavior change bundle 2026_07; fully retired in January 2027), so do not build new controls on it. Step 2 · Cortex Search for documents Cortex Search is managed hybrid retrieval : it embeds your text, keeps a vector and keyword index fresh as the source table changes, and reranks results (Lessons 14.70 to 5.38 as one SQL statement). Copy Step 3 · Semantic views and Cortex Analyst for metrics Text-to-SQL fails when the model guesses what "revenue" or "late" means. A semantic view is a schema-level object that defines tables, relationships, dimensions , facts and metrics with business names, synonyms and verified example queries. Cortex Analyst uses it to write correct SQL, and the same definitions serve BI tools, so humans and agents get the same number. Copy AI_SQL_GENERATION gives Cortex Analyst standing instructions; AI_VERIFIED_QUERIES stores question-and-SQL pairs an analyst has checked. Analyst prefers a verified query when the question matches, and reports it in its response ( verified_query_used ), which is how you tell a checked answer from a generated one. Semantic View Autopilot (GA 2026) drafts semantic views from your query history and existing BI models, and the Open Semantic Interchange initiative aims to make these definitions portable across tools. Add verified queries for the questions that matter most; they are the evaluation set for Analyst. Step 4 · Cortex Agents A Cortex Agent is a schema object that holds the orchestration model, instructions, tools and limits. Cortex plans, calls tools (Analyst for numbers, Search for documents, your procedures for actions), reflects on results and answers with citations, charts and tables. The same agent serves CoWork, your app (through the REST API), Teams and Slack integrations, and outside agents (through MCP). Copy Custom tools are UDFs or stored procedures; the spec above attaches a UDF ( type: "function" , the documented form). Write actions such as a refund belong in a stored procedure with its own checks (amount limits, idempotency keys ); Snowsight lets you attach a procedure as a custom tool, and since the YAML keys for procedure-backed tools are not shown in the docs we checked (UNVERIFIED), build those in Snowsight and copy the spec it generates. Agents run with the caller's role (for REST calls, the X-Snowflake-Role header or the user's default role), and the budget caps orchestration time and tokens, not the tools' own work. Your application calls the agent with the Agent Run API , which streams server-sent events : status updates, tool calls , tool results, text deltas, tables, charts and a final response event. Authenticate with OAuth or a programmatic access token (PAT) bound to a least-privileged role; the agent then sees only what that role can see. Synchronous runs time out after 15 minutes; background: true (with a thread) allows 6 hours. Copy What you should see Copy Show the generated SQL to analysts: it makes the answer checkable. Use threads ( thread_id , parent_message_id ) for multi-turn conversations, background: true for long runs, and handle event types you do not recognize (the docs list more: response.thinking.delta , response.text.annotation , response.table , response.chart , response.map , response.warning ). This lab block runs offline against a recording. Industry practice Lessons from Cortex Agent projects Semantic views decide quality. Most wrong answers trace back to a missing metric definition, synonym or relationship, not to the model. Invest there first, and keep verified queries as your eval set. One agent per domain , with a sharp description per tool, beats one agent with every tool. CoWork lets users pick the agent. Roles are the guardrail. Run each agent under a role that sees only what its users may see; masking and row access policies then apply to every tool call automatically. Write actions go through procedures with their own checks (amount limits, idempotency keys), not through free-form SQL. Budget limits ( budget.seconds , budget.tokens ) stop runaway plans; tune them from traces . Copy Clients authenticate with Snowflake OAuth (the default) or external OAuth from your IdP ( OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER ); every tool call runs with the connecting user's default role, or a role the client requests with a session:role:<name> scope. Access to the server does not grant access to its tools: each tool needs its own grant (USAGE on the search service, SELECT on the semantic view, USAGE on the agent). Other tool types are GENERIC for UDFs and procedures (needs a config with type , warehouse and input_schema ) and CODING_AGENT ; when a server includes CORTEX_AGENT_RUN or CODING_AGENT , Snowflake adds ASYNC_AGENT_RUN_STATUS , AGENT_RUN_RESULT and ASYNC_AGENT_RUN_CANCEL for background runs . MCP for tools, A2A for agent-to-agent calls, OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions for traces, OpenAI-compatible APIs for models, and an open framework ( LangGraph , Strands, ADK, Agent Framework, OpenAI Agents SDK) for logic. In production Platform choices teams regret Choosing by demo : every platform demos well; choose by where the data, identities and users already are. Splitting one system across platforms without a reason : each boundary adds identity, networking, logging and cost work. Cross platforms deliberately, through MCP or A2A with clear ownership. Ignoring Region availability : the feature you designed around may not exist in the Region your data must stay in. Locking business logic into a platform's agent definition : keep tools, prompts and evals portable so a second platform is a port, not a rewrite. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How do you compare cloud platforms for AI agents? Worked answer. Teams can also use these as discussion prompts in a study group. Platforms Mid How would you build a governed agent on AWS? Strands or LangGraph hosted on AgentCore Runtime; models through Bedrock with a geographic inference profile and an enforced guardrail ; tools through AgentCore Gateway with Policy rules and Identity-managed credentials; knowledge in Bedrock Knowledge Bases on S3 Vectors or OpenSearch; memory in AgentCore Memory; observability through ADOT into CloudWatch; online evaluations with AgentCore Evaluations; PrivateLink, least-privilege IAM and cost tags through application inference profiles . Mid How would you build an agent over warehouse data in Snowflake? Define a semantic view (metrics, dimensions, synonyms, verified queries ) for Cortex Analyst , a Cortex Search service over documents, and a Cortex Agent that orchestrates both plus procedures for actions, with orchestration budgets. Users reach it through CoWork or the Agent Run API; outside agents through the managed MCP server. Governance comes from roles, masking and row access policies, AI guardrails and model allowlists; quality from the agent's evaluations and AI Observability; cost from the account usage views and budgets. Senior A client runs Microsoft 365, keeps data in Snowflake and serves customers on AWS. Design their agent landscape. Put each agent where its data and users are. Data agents live in Snowflake (Cortex Agents over semantic views), exposed through the managed MCP server. The customer agent runs on AWS AgentCore and calls the Snowflake tools through the Gateway. Employees reach data agents in CoWork or through Copilot. One gateway policy governs model traffic, OpenTelemetry traces flow to one observability backend, identities are federated (Entra to AWS and Snowflake), and each agent has its own least-privileged role. Mid How would you build a governed agent on Azure? A Foundry agent (prompt agent for simple cases, hosted agent built with Microsoft Agent Framework or LangGraph for code-heavy ones) using models deployed in Foundry; knowledge through Foundry IQ knowledge bases over Azure AI Search; tools through MCP and OpenAPI with Entra-managed identities ( Entra Agent ID ); Content Safety with Prompt Shields on inputs and documents; Azure API Management as the AI gateway for token limits and routing; Application Insights for OpenTelemetry traces and Foundry evaluations for quality; private networking and Purview for data governance. Mid How would you build a governed agent on Google Cloud? ADK agents deployed to Agent Runtime (formerly Vertex AI Agent Engine) with Sessions and Memory Bank ; Gemini models through Vertex AI; grounding with Agent Search or Google Search grounding; tools through MCP and Agent Gateway ; Model Armor screening prompts and responses; Cloud Trace and Cloud Logging for telemetry; the Gen AI evaluation service for quality; VPC Service Controls around data; BigQuery for analytics over interaction logs. Mid How would you build an agent on Databricks? Author it as an MLflow ResponsesAgent (with LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK or plain Python inside), tools as Unity Catalog functions and managed MCP servers, retrieval through AI Search (formerly Vector Search ), structured questions through a Genie space, models through the AI Gateway with usage tracking. Evaluate with mlflow.genai.evaluate and scorers, deploy with agents.deploy to Model Serving, and monitor with MLflow tracing and production scorers. Unity Catalog governs data, models, functions and lineage end to end. Agent Bricks offers higher-level, auto-optimized agents for common patterns. Senior Managed agent runtime or your own containers? Managed runtimes (AgentCore Runtime, Foundry Agent Service, Agent Runtime, Databricks Model Serving) give session isolation, identity, memory, observability and scaling out of the box, which shortens time to production and passes security review faster. Containers give full control over frameworks, networking, cost and portability. Choose managed when the platform matches where the data and users already are and its limits (session length, regions, supported frameworks) fit; choose containers for multi-cloud portability, unusual runtimes or very high steady volume. Either way, keep the agent code framework-thin so the choice can change. Senior How do you decide between Cortex Agents and building an agent with LangGraph on top of Snowflake? Cortex Agents win when the work is mostly questions over governed Snowflake data and documents: Cortex Analyst and Search are built in, roles and policies apply automatically, data never leaves, and business users get it through CoWork or the API. LangGraph wins when you need custom control flow, long-running stateful workflows, many non-Snowflake tools, or a specific model outside Snowflake's catalog. A router keeps predictable requests on fixed paths and lets only open-ended questions reach the agent loop; both assistants share the tools and the knowledge, and every step is traced. l1402: Course home / Phase 14 · AI Agents: Design and Engineering From pilot to value: use cases, the business case and the operating model From Zero to Agents Lesson 14.162 60 min Go deeper Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Rank candidate use cases by value, feasibility and risk, and say why the first one should be boring Write a business case as a range, with the two numbers that decide it: the automation rate and the cost of a wrong answer Compare buying a product, building on a platform and self-hosting over three years, and find the volume where the answer changes Describe who owns what once several teams build agents, and how you would measure adoption Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.142 (cost per resolved outcome) and Lesson 14.133 (what production means). Lesson 14.149 (platform teams) helps with Step 4. Python : functions and loops only. Depth : Deepen. Time : about 60 minutes. Why this came about Everything before this lesson is about building an agent that works. Most agents that work are still never used, or are used and then switched off, and the reason is rarely the model. Nobody chose the use case on purpose, nobody wrote down what it had to earn, or nobody owned it after launch. This lesson is the part of the work that happens around the engineering. In plain words first A shop decides whether to hire Think of an agent as a new member of staff. Before hiring, a sensible manager asks four questions. Which job needs doing most? What will the hire cost, and what will the work be worth? Should we hire, or pay an agency? Who will manage this person? An AI system gets the same four questions, and this lesson takes them in that order. From an idea to a system that earns its keep: five decisions in order, and one measurement, the pilot, that the later ones depend on. The pilot exists to replace the estimates in the business case with numbers. The problem: a good demo is not a business case ShopKart's support assistant from the capstone answers order questions well. A director now asks three things the demo cannot answer: Why this use case first? What is it worth, and when does it pay back? Should we have bought one? Each has an honest answer made of a few numbers, and each answer is a range, because the numbers that matter are not known until the system runs. Step 1 · Choose the use case List the candidates and score each on three things. Value is the work it could take over, in money per month. Feasibility asks whether the data exists and whether an answer can be checked: an answer you cannot check cannot be evaluated, and a system you cannot evaluate cannot be improved. Harm is how bad a wrong answer is. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The first use case is the boring one. Order status wins by a factor of twelve: the volume is high, the answer is in a database, it can be checked exactly, and a wrong answer costs little. The exciting candidate, contract review, comes last, because few contracts arrive and nobody can cheaply check a review. The score is a way to argue, not a verdict. The inputs are estimates. Its use is that a team must write down volume, checkability and harm for every candidate, and those three numbers are where the disagreements are. Harm sets the level of autonomy, not only the order. Credit-limit changes can still be a good second project as a draft for a person to approve ( Lesson 14.148 ). High harm rules out acting alone. It does not rule out helping. Step 2 · Write the business case as a range A business case has a one-off cost to build and a monthly result. The monthly result depends mostly on the automation rate : the share of cases the system resolves with no person involved. It is the number you know least before launch, so compute the case for several values of it. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The same system loses money or pays back in eight months. At 30% automation the running cost is larger than the saving. At 75% the build is paid for in under a year. Nothing about the model changed between those rows. Present the range, and say which automation rate the pilot must show before the next stage is funded. Escalated cases cost extra. A case the system tried and then handed over was paid for twice: once for the model, once for the person. This is why a low automation rate is worse than it looks. Wrong answers can cancel the saving. At 60% automation, moving from 1% to 6% wrong resolutions turns a profit of 486,000 into a loss. Each wrong resolution costs INR 250 to find and put right, against a saving of about INR 16 on a good one. The eval set and the release gate of the Production engineering and AI system design section are what protect the business case. Every input is a measurement you will have. Volume and human cost come from today's operation. Automation rate, error rate and AI cost per case come from the pilot, in the form of Lesson 14.142 's cost per resolved outcome . Watch out The automation rate is not the goal A system can raise its automation rate by refusing to hand over, and customers pay for it. Report the automation rate together with a quality measure such as wrong resolutions, repeat contacts or satisfaction, and an escape route to a person that works ( Lesson 14.148 ). Klarna's public account of its assistant, in Lesson 14.66 , is the standard case study. Step 3 · Build, buy or both There are three routes to the same job. A product is quick to start and is priced per resolution. Building on a cloud agent platform (the Cloud platforms, compared section) costs more up front and less per resolution. Hosting the model yourself ( Lesson 14.137 ) costs the most to set up and run, and the least per resolution. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Volume decides between buying and building. A price per resolution is cheap at low volume and expensive at high volume. At ShopKart's 72,000 resolutions a month, building on a platform is cheaper over three years. At 20,000, buying is. Self-hosting loses here on cost. Its low price per resolution does not repay the fixed cost at this volume. Teams usually self-host for other reasons: data that may not leave, latency, or a fine-tuned small model ( Lesson 3.25 ). Cost is one of four questions. The others often decide: Question Points toward buying Points toward building Is this work what makes your company different? No: it is the same job everywhere, such as password resets Yes: your policies, data and tools are the product How much must it connect to your own systems? A little, through connectors the product already has Deeply: your order system, your approvals, your permissions Who must be able to change it, and how fast? A business team, through settings Engineers, in code, with your own evals and release gates What must you be able to prove? The vendor's certifications are enough You need your own traces , audit log and data controls Many organisations do both: they buy for common work, and build where their own data and rules are the point. Before you sign for a product, ask the questions of Lesson 14.151 's design review: where the data goes and whether it is used for training, what happens when the service is down, how you get your traces and your data out, and what a wrong answer costs under the contract. Step 4 · The operating model: who owns what One team with one agent needs no operating model. The second and third team make the same decisions again, differently, unless someone owns the shared parts. The arrangement that most organisations reach has three layers: Layer Owns Does not own A central platform team (often called a centre of excellence at the start) The paved path of Lesson 14.149 : gateway, identity, runtime, tracing, eval tooling, the agent registry, shared guardrails The use cases Product teams Their agent end to end: the use case, the eval set, the release gate, on-call, the outcome metric The platform Risk, legal and security The tiering rules of Lesson 15.26 and the review for high-risk tiers Day-to-day releases of low-risk agents Two rules keep this working. Each agent has one named owner who is on call for it, and the registry refuses agents without one. Low-risk agents on the paved path ship without a committee, so that the review time goes to the few systems that need it. Step 5 · Adoption: the part nobody budgets for A system that works and is not used earns nothing. Treat adoption as something you measure, in the same way as quality: Measure use, not availability. Count the share of eligible work that goes through the system each week, and the share of users who come back. A flat line after launch is a finding. Put it where the work already happens. An assistant inside the support console is used. The same assistant on a separate page is forgotten. Show what it did. People trust a system whose work they can see, correct and stop ( Lesson 14.148 ). Hidden automation is switched off after its first visible mistake. Give the people affected a say. Support agents know which answers are wrong and why. Their corrections are your best eval cases ( Lesson 14.131 ), and a team that helped shape a tool uses it. Retire what is not used. Every agent left running costs money and attention. The registry of Lesson 14.149 should show usage, and unused agents should be removed. A maturity ladder Use this to say where an organisation is and what the next step is. Each step adds one thing. Stage What exists What to add next 1 · Experiments Demos by individuals, no shared tooling One use case chosen on purpose, with a metric (Step 1) 2 · One system in production An eval set, a release gate, an owner on call A business case measured against the pilot (Step 2) 3 · Several systems Each team built its own stack A shared platform and a registry (Step 4, Lesson 14.149 ) 4 · A platform Paved path, tiered review, cost per outcome by team Adoption and outcome metrics reviewed like revenue (Step 5) 5 · Managed like a product line Use cases are added and retired on evidence Keep the evidence honest Check your mental model ✗ "Start with the most impressive use case." ✓ Start with the one that has high volume, an answer you can check, and a low cost when it is wrong. ✗ "A business case is one number." ✓ It is a range that depends on the automation rate and the error cost, and the pilot's job is to narrow it. ✗ "Buying is always cheaper than building." ✓ It is cheaper at low volume. A price per resolution grows with success. ✗ "Once it works, people will use it." ✓ Adoption is measured and worked on, like quality. Exercises Predict before you run In Step 2, the AI cost per case doubles from INR 1.2 to INR 2.4. At 60% automation, does the net result fall by more or by less than a doubling of the error rate from 1% to 2%? Work it out, then check with the function. (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Give "supplier contract review" a checkability of 0.9 in Step 1 and run the ranking again. Where does it land, and what would have to be true in the real world for that number to be honest? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise A team reports an automation rate of 82% and a strong business case. Three months later, repeat contacts are up by a third. What was measured wrongly, and what would you add to the report? (Solution D1.) Make it your own Replace the candidates in Step 1 with five from your own organisation, using real volumes. Then fill in Step 2 for the top one and write down the automation rate at which it pays back within twelve months. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · AI cost against error rate Doubling the AI cost adds INR 1.2 for every one of the 120,000 cases, resolved or not: 144,000 a month. Doubling the error rate adds 72,000 resolved cases x 1% x INR 250 = 180,000 a month. The error rate hurts more, although the AI cost is the number people watch. With these inputs the net falls from 486,000 to 342,000 in the first case and to 306,000 in the second. Solution B1 · An honest checkability With checkability 0.9 its feasibility becomes 0.45 and its score 23,625, which moves it above credit-limit changes and still far below order status, because only 400 contracts arrive a month. For 0.9 to be honest, you would need a set of contracts already reviewed by lawyers, with the issues marked, so that a review can be graded against them. Building that set is the real first project. Solution D1 · Automation that customers paid for The automation rate counted every conversation that ended without a handover as resolved, including the ones where the customer gave up and wrote in again. Report resolution confirmed by an outcome (the order was found, the refund was issued, no repeat contact within some days), and show the automation rate next to repeat contacts and wrong resolutions. Then check whether the handover to a person works. Solution M1 · Your own case There is no single answer. A good one names where each input came from (a report, a sample, an estimate), gives the payback at three automation rates, and states which rate the pilot must reach. If the top candidate has high harm, the answer should also say what the person in the loop approves. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How would you choose the first AI use case for a team? Worked answer. List the candidates and write down, for each, the monthly volume, the time each case takes today, whether the data exists, whether an answer can be checked, and what a wrong answer costs. Start with high volume, a checkable answer and low harm, because that system can be evaluated and improved, and its mistakes are cheap while the team learns. Keep the high-harm candidates as drafts for a person to approve. A plausible wrong answer. "Pick the one the leadership is most excited about." Excitement tracks novelty. The exciting cases tend to have low volume and answers nobody can check. Follow-ups. What would make you choose a lower-scoring use case first? How do you find volume if nobody measures it? Debug a failure The pilot worked and the rollout is losing money. Where do you look? Worked answer. Compare the business case's inputs with what production shows: the automation rate, the cost per case including escalated ones, the rate and cost of wrong resolutions, and the running cost of the team. The usual finding is that the pilot ran on easy cases, so the automation rate fell on real traffic, or that wrong resolutions were not counted at all. A plausible wrong answer. "Switch to a cheaper model." The model's price is rarely the largest term. A cheaper model that resolves fewer cases makes the result worse. Follow-ups. Which of these numbers can you measure in the first week? What would you show a finance director? Defend a design Defend building over buying for ShopKart's support assistant. Worked answer. At 72,000 resolutions a month the platform route is cheaper over three years than a product priced per resolution, and the gap widens as volume grows. The assistant must call ShopKart's own order and refund systems under ShopKart's permissions and approval rules, engineers need to change it weekly behind their own release gate, and the company wants its own traces and audit log. Each of those points toward building. I would still buy for work that is the same everywhere. A plausible wrong answer. "We should own all our AI." Ownership has a running cost: an on-call rota, evals, upgrades. It is worth paying where the work is specific to the company. Follow-ups. At what volume would you reverse the decision? What would you ask a vendor before signing? Check yourself Rank five use cases and defend the first choice in two sentences. Compute a payback period at three automation rates. Q2 Why present a business case at several automation rates? Lesson 14.151 summarizes what the field keeps teaching, and Lesson 14.135 gives you the method for designing a system; here you apply that method to problems real companies faced, with their real numbers, and check yourself against what they shipped. Why this came about Much of what works in production is learned by teams before it reaches documentation. Talks, case studies and post-mortems are where those lessons appear first. In plain words first Learning from people who shipped Talks, case studies and post-mortems from teams running agents in production show what the documentation does not: what failed, what they measured, what they would do differently. Use them as design drills: read the problem, sketch your own design, then compare with what the team actually built and why. How to learn from a practitioner talk Most people watch a conference talk passively and keep one quote. Engineers who get better from talks watch actively, in three passes: When What to do Why it works Before you press play Read the title and write the one question you want answered ("How do they evaluate a multi-step agent?") A question turns 20 minutes of video into one usable answer When the problem is stated Pause. Spend five minutes sketching your own design with the nine steps from Lesson 14.135 , at least steps 1 to 5 Comparing your design with theirs is where the learning happens; agreeing with a slide teaches little At the end Fill in a decision log (below) and note one thing you would do differently in your own system The log is what you will remember and reuse in design reviews Copy Watch out Read talks critically Survivorship bias : conference talks describe systems that worked well enough to present. The failed projects rarely get a slot, so the base rate of success is lower than it looks. Self-reported numbers : a "60% reduction" usually comes from the team's own benchmark, at one point in time. Treat numbers as evidence of direction, and ask what was measured against what. Incentives : a vendor's talk about its own product is still useful, but separate the general lesson (narrow the context) from the product pitch (buy our context engine). Model generation : an architecture designed around 2024 models may be overbuilt for 2026 models. Ask which parts exist because the model was weak, and which because the problem is hard. The second kind lasts. The watch list The talks below were chosen for one reason each: they show how a production system was actually built, or teach a technique you will use.
