Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, CodeAct vs JSON tool-call comparison). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line SWE-bench Verified went from 4% to 80.9% in under three years. The same model can score very differently in different scaffolds — on Terminal Bench 2.0, harness changes alone took LangChain's agent from 52.8% to 66.5% with GPT-5.2-Codex — so the scaffolding around the model now matters as much as the model itself. OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin) is the most active MIT-licensed platform and its CodeAct loop executes Python actions directly in a sandbox instead of JSON tool calls. The headline numbers hide a methodological issue: Epoch AI rates 39% of SWE-bench Verified tasks as trivial changes (under 15 minutes for an engineer, about 5 changed lines on average), and on Scale's SWE-bench Pro (larger, multi-file changes) the same frontier models score far lower. Lesson 14.68 · Specialized agents: coding, browser and computer use, research, data and voice Lesson 14.111 · Deep Agents: a harness on LangGraph Lesson 14.126 · The Claude Agent SDK: a harness as a library The problem In plain words first A coding agent is a model inside a scaffold : the loop that finds files, edits them, runs tests and feeds results back. The same model scores very differently in different scaffolds. Two designs dominate. With JSON tool calls the model asks for one action at a time and the host validates each one. With CodeAct the model writes a short program that runs in a sandbox, which can do much more in one step, good or bad. Specialized agents (coding, browser, research) and Deep Agents harnesses are covered in Lessons 14.68 and 14.111 (linked above). This lesson runs both scaffolds with a real small model on the lesson's three-bug repo, with real tests. "Which coding agent is best" is the wrong question. The right question is: on a task distribution that matches my work, with the scaffolding I will run in production, what end-to-end reliability do I get? Between 2022 and 2026 the field learned that scaffolding — the retrieval layer, the planner, the sandbox, the edit-verify loop, the feedback format — is load-bearing. On Terminal Bench 2.0, LangChain kept GPT-5.2-Codex fixed and changed only its harness, moving from 52.8% to 66.5% (February 2026). 13.7 absolute points of difference, same weights. The base model is a component; the loop is the product. The companion problem is that benchmark saturation hides regressions. SWE-bench Verified is close to saturated, and the easy-task tail (Epoch AI rates 39% of tasks as trivial, under 15 minutes and about 5 changed lines) pulls top scores up. Real-world quality is better measured on distributions like SWE-bench Pro (10+ line changes), where the same leaders score far lower (about 23% at its September 2025 launch, around 40–60% on Scale's public set by late 2026). Idea 1 · SWE-bench, one paragraph SWE-bench (Jimenez et al.) takes real GitHub issues with ground-truth patches and asks an agent to produce a patch that makes the test suite pass. SWE-bench Verified (OpenAI, 2024) is a human-curated 500-task subset with the ambiguous and broken tasks removed. SWE-bench Pro is the harder successor — larger, multi-file changes from Scale AI, where frontier agents score well below their Verified numbers. Idea 2 · What the 2022 → 2026 curve actually shows 2022 : research models at ~4% on raw SWE-bench. 2024 : GPT-4 + Devin-style scaffolding at ~14%; SWE-agent at ~12%. 2025 : Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet inside Aider and SWE-agent push into the 40–55% range. 2026 : Claude Sonnet 4.5 and frontier competitors at 70–80%+ on SWE-bench Verified. Epoch AI's leaderboard tracks this live. The slope came from three compounding sources: better base models, better scaffolding (CodeAct, reflection, verifier loops), and better benchmarks (Verified removing noise). Idea 3 · CodeAct vs JSON tool calls OpenHands (All-Hands-AI, arXiv:2407.16741, formerly OpenDevin) took a specific architectural bet: instead of the model emitting JSON tool calls that a host decodes and executes, the model emits Python code and a Jupyter-style kernel runs it in a sandbox. The agent can loop over files, chain tools, and catch its own exceptions inside one action. The trade-off: JSON tool calls : every action is one turn; easy to audit; limited compositionality; safe by default because each call goes through an explicit validator. CodeAct : one action can be a whole program; compositional; requires a hardened sandbox (OpenHands uses Docker isolation); failure modes include anything the sandbox runtime allows. Both architectures are in production. CodeAct is dominant in open platforms (OpenHands, smolagents). JSON tool calls remain dominant in managed services (Anthropic Managed Agents, OpenAI Assistants) where the provider controls the executor. Reliability compounds across steps. Three places where scaffolding buys points: Retrieval : finding the right files to read is the silent bottleneck. SWE-agent's ACI, OpenHands' file-index, and Aider's repo-map all attack this. Verifier loop : running tests, reading stack traces, and re-attempting is a 10+ point delta on SWE-bench. Failure containment : a sandbox that rolls back on error prevents compounding damage. The same model with and without a verifier loop looks like two different products. Your production distribution is almost certainly closer to Pro than to Verified. Implication for choosing an agent: run a Pro-like subset of your own bug backlog. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, two-stage classifier simulator), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A permission ladder — graduated levels of autonomy from review-every-action to approve-everything — is how a harness governs what an autonomous agent may do without asking. Claude Code, this lesson's worked example, exposes six such modes: "plan" explores and proposes without editing, "default" (labeled "Manual" in the UI) asks before most edits, shell commands and network access, "acceptEdits" auto-approves file writes but still confirms shell execution, and "bypassPermissions" approves everything. Auto Mode — the auto permission mode — replaces per-action approval with a separate classifier model that reviews each action before it runs and blocks anything that escalates beyond what the request asked for. Action budgets are enforced via max_turns and max_budget_usd . Auto mode launched as a research preview in March 2026, became generally available in July 2026, and is now the starting mode for many plans; Anthropic is still explicit that the classifier is not sufficient alone. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Permission mode "How much the agent can do" One of six named policies controlling per-action approval plan mode "Ask before anything" Agent writes a plan; user approves before execution acceptEdits "Let it write files" File writes auto-approve; shell exec still prompts auto "Auto approvals" Separate classifier model reviews each action; blocks escalation beyond the request bypassPermissions "Full YOLO" Approves everything; intended for ephemeral containers Stage 1 (simulator) "Fast keyword check" Cheap rule over proposed actions in code/main.py Stage 2 (simulator) "Deep review" Slower multi-rule reviewer for flagged actions in code/main.py Research preview "Not GA" Anthropic framing for features whose failure mode is still being mapped From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.138 · Identity, permissions and the tool platform Lesson 14.148 · Humans in charge: approvals and handoffs The problem In plain words first A permission mode decides which of an agent's actions run without asking you. Claude Code has six, from "plan" (look and propose, no edits) through "default" (ask before edits, commands and network) to "bypassPermissions" (ask nothing, for throwaway containers only). Its auto mode puts a second model, a classifier, in your place: it reviews each action and blocks the risky ones. Any reviewer, rules or model, judges one action at a time, so harm spread over several harmless-looking actions can slip through. Identity, permissions, approvals and handoffs are covered in Lessons 14.138 and 14.148 (linked above). This lesson tests the lesson's two-stage reviewer, a small model reviewer and a trajectory rule on the same actions. An autonomous coding agent on your machine is a distinct security category. The attack surface is everything the agent can reach — file system, network, credentials, clipboard, any browser tab, any open terminal. Bruce Schneier and others have flagged this publicly: computer-use agents are not a "feature update" of chatbots, they are a new kind of tool with a new kind of risk profile. Claude Code's permission system is Anthropic's answer. Rather than one "autonomous / not autonomous" switch, there are six modes spanning a capability ladder: plan → default → acceptEdits → … → bypassPermissions. Each mode is a different trade-off between speed and review-per-action. Auto Mode (March 2026, generally available since July 2026) adds a separate classifier model that moves approval off the user's critical path: it reviews each action before it runs and blocks anything that escalates beyond the request. The engineering question: what does this system catch, what does it miss, and which mode does a given task actually warrant? Idea 1 · The six permission modes Mode Behavior When to use plan Agent reads and explores, then proposes a plan for you to review; it does not edit files (it may run classifier-approved read-only commands when auto mode is available) Unfamiliar task; prod-adjacent code; first time using the agent on a repo default Labeled "Manual" in the UI. Agent runs actions; prompts user for any "risky" action (shell exec, destructive operations, network calls) Most interactive coding sessions acceptEdits File writes auto-approve; shell exec and network calls still prompt Refactoring pass across many files auto A separate classifier model reviews each action before it runs; blocks anything escalating beyond the request Long-horizon unattended runs in a constrained workspace dontAsk Never prompts; actions not pre-approved by permission rules are denied Ephemeral sandboxes, CI jobs, research scripts bypassPermissions Approves everything Documented as "only inside ephemeral containers you are willing to throw away" (Names above match public Claude Code docs; the UI labels default as "Manual".) Idea 2 · Auto Mode in one page Auto Mode (launched March 24, 2026) is the first permission mode to delegate per-action approval to a model. Structure: A separate classifier model. Reviews every proposed action before it runs, judged against the declared task and the current state of the session, and blocks anything that escalates beyond what the request called for. Blocked actions fall back to the user. Availability. Auto mode became generally available on July 10, 2026. It is the starting mode for interactive sessions in recent Claude Code versions and on Pro, Max, Ultra and Team plans; Enterprise and API use stay opt-in, and administrators can disable it. Budget controls sit alongside the classifier: max_turns — total iterations in a session. max_budget_usd — dollar cap that aborts the session. action-count limits per tool (no more than N WebFetch calls, etc.). Idea 3 · What the system catches Straightforward prompt injection into tool inputs where the injected instruction maps to a known-risky action shape. Repetitive tool loops — the classifier can see action N+1 is nearly identical to action N, five times in a row. Clearly out-of-scope shell commands on an otherwise file-edit-only session. Idea 4 · What the system can miss Subtle prompt injection that modulates behavior without producing a single flagged action. Indirect prompt injection is not a fully patchable vulnerability (OpenAI preparedness head, 2025, on browser agents — see Lesson 15.11 ). Semantic-level misbehavior. Every individual action can look safe while the composed trajectory is harmful. The classifier judges the action; it does not re-derive the user's intent. Exfiltration through legitimate channels. Writing data to a file you own, then git push ing to a public repo, is a sequence of allowed actions whose composition is the problem. Idea 5 · Research preview framing Anthropic shipped Auto Mode as a research preview on March 24, 2026 and made it generally available on July 10, 2026; it is now the default starting mode on several plans. The launch post still recommends isolated environments. The documentation is explicit that the classifier is a layer, not a solution: users are expected to combine Auto Mode with budgets, allowlists, isolated workspaces, and trajectory audits (Lessons 12–16). The preview framing also reflects the documented evaluation-vs-deployment gap (Lesson 1) — a classifier that passes offline evals can behave differently in a real session where the user's context is ambiguous. Idea 6 · Where this ladder lives in your workflow Unfamiliar task: start in plan . Reading the plan is cheaper than rolling back a bad run. Known refactor: acceptEdits saves a lot of confirmation clicks. Unattended background run: auto only inside a workspace whose blast radius you have measured (no credentials, no production mounts, no egress you did not opt into). Ephemeral containers: dontAsk / bypassPermissions is acceptable if and only if the container and its credentials are disposable. The same idea as a formula A reviewer has two error rates. Over dangerous actions and needed actions : ∣ { a ∈ D : approved } ∣ ​ , false-block rate = ∣ N ∣ ∣ { a ∈ N : stopped } ∣ ​ . A reviewer that blocks everything has a miss rate of 0 and is useless. One that approves everything has a false-block rate of 0 and is equally useless. Auto mode bounds the cost of false blocks by falling back to the human after 3 blocks in a row or 20 in a session. Per-action review cannot see composition. If each action ​ is judged alone by ​ ) , a harmful sequence ​ a 2 ​ a 3 ​ with every ​ ) = allow gets through. A trajectory rule carries state: taint after any secret is read, and any later egress is blocked while taint . Worked example The composite exfiltration Step 1 reads ~/.aws/credentials . Taken alone, a read; the lesson's reviewer allows it. Step 2 writes /tmp/secrets.txt . A local write; allowed. Step 3 runs git add … && git push . A normal git command; allowed. With a taint flag set at step 1, step 3 is "egress after a secret was read", so it is blocked. The rule is simple because it remembers what happened earlier in the trajectory, which no per-action reviewer can do. Solutions Solution P1 · Misses for rules, false blocks for the model The lesson's reviewer approves 7 of the 10 dangerous actions: everything not written in its keywords' exact form. It stops none of the needed ones. The 0.5B model reviewer errs the other way. It blocks all 10 dangerous actions and 9 of the 10 needed ones. Solution B1 · Reasonable actions, unreasonable composition The run had the wrong boundaries. The agent worked on a laptop with production keys in .env , and could push to a public fork. A per-action reviewer judged each step plausible ("add the setup files", "push the branch"), but the composition moved a secret to a public place. Set it up so the trajectory cannot end there: - Isolate it: a container or VM with a fresh clone and no production credentials, so there is nothing to leak. - Deny rules for reading .env , key files and cloud credential paths, and for pushing anywhere but a private branch. - Ignore secrets: .env in .gitignore , plus a secret scanner as a pre-push hook. - Taint tracking or an egress allowlist, so any network write after a secret read is blocked. - A morning review of the trajectory and the diff before anything is merged. Auto mode's own public-destination check would have helped. It is a layer, and the boundaries carry the weight. A colleague runs every task in the mode that approves everything, because the prompts are annoying. Give the rule you use to pick a mode, and say which tasks go where. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Pick the mode from the task, not from the annoyance. Start an unfamiliar or production-adjacent task in plan mode, where reading the plan is cheaper than undoing a bad run. Use the default mode for most interactive sessions, and the mode that auto-approves file writes for a known refactor across many files. Reserve the classifier-driven auto mode for unattended runs inside a workspace whose reach you have measured, and reserve the approve-everything mode for a disposable container. The ladder. Mode Behavior Fits plan The agent proposes a plan, and every action is reviewed before it runs An unfamiliar task, code near production, the first run on a repo default Actions run, and the agent asks on anything risky such as shell, destructive operations or network Most interactive sessions acceptEdits File writes are approved, and shell and network still ask A refactor across many files auto A separate classifier model reviews each action and blocks escalation beyond the request A long unattended run in a constrained workspace dontAsk Never prompts, and anything not pre-approved by a rule is denied Ephemeral sandboxes, CI jobs bypassPermissions Approves everything Only a container you are willing to throw away What the classifier mode adds and misses. The auto mode moves approval off the user's path. A separate model judges each proposed action against the declared task and the session state, and a blocked action falls back to the user. It catches plain prompt injection that maps to a known risky action shape, repeated tool loops where action N+1 looks like action N five times in a row, and shell commands that are out of place in a file-edit session. It misses subtle injection that changes behavior without one flagged action, and it misses a harmful trajectory made of individually safe actions, because it judges the action and does not re-derive the user's intent. Availability depends on plan, organization, model and provider, and the documentation is explicit that the classifier is a layer, not a solution. Budgets travel with the mode. Whatever the mode, set the budget controls: a cap on turns, a dollar cap that aborts the session, and action-count limits per tool. In the unattended case, add an allowlist, an isolated workspace with no credentials and no production mounts, and a trajectory audit afterwards. The answer to the colleague. The approve-everything mode is documented for a disposable container. On a laptop with credentials, a browser session and an open terminal, the attack surface is everything the agent can reach. The prompts are the control, and the fix for too many prompts is a mode one step up the ladder, not the top of it. Plausible wrong answers. "Approve everything, because the agent is in version control anyway." Version control covers file writes, and the risk is in shell, network and credentials, which no commit reverts. "The classifier mode is safe for anything, because a model reviews each step." The classifier judges actions, not trajectories, and the documentation pairs it with budgets, allowlists and isolation. "Plan mode is for beginners." Plan mode is for the task where a wrong run costs more than a read, and that is a property of the task, not of the operator. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the refactor mode still ask on shell commands? Expected: a file write is reversible from version control, while a shell command can delete, send or install, so the mode approves the cheap-to-undo class only. (level 2) How does the never-prompt mode differ from the top of the ladder? Expected: the never-prompt mode denies anything that a rule did not pre-approve, while the approve-everything mode approves it. (level 3) An unattended run needs a 24-hour budget. What do you set? Expected: a turn cap, a dollar cap, per-tool action caps and an allowlist, each with a reason, inside a workspace with no credentials and no egress you did not opt into. (level 3) The classifier approved every action and the run still exfiltrated data. How? Expected: a sequence of allowed actions, such as writing data you own to a file and then pushing to a public repository, where the composition is the problem and no single action was flagged. Where it is taught. The permission modes lesson lays out the six modes, the classifier and the budget controls. Explain the mechanism An unattended coding run used the mode in which a separate model reviews every action before it executes. The audit shows that the reviewer approved each action. The run still copied a private dataset into a public repository. Explain how that is possible, and name the controls that would have stopped it. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The reviewer judges one action at a time against the request. Each action in the run was allowed on its own: read a file you own, write a file you own, commit, push. The harm was in the composition, and the reviewer does not re-derive the user's intent across the trajectory. The controls that catch this live outside the per-action check: an isolated workspace with no sensitive mounts, a network egress allowlist in the scope contract, per-tool action caps, and a trajectory audit after the run that detects what the other controls let through. What a per-action reviewer can and cannot see. The lesson lists what the classifier catches: a plain injection that maps to a known risky action shape, a repeated loop where action N+1 is almost equal to action N, and an out-of-place shell command in a file-edit session. It also lists what it misses. Subtle injection can change behavior without producing one flagged action. Every action can look safe while the composed trajectory is harmful. Exfiltration through legitimate channels is the standard case: writing data to a file you own and then pushing to a public repository is a sequence of allowed actions. Why intent does not help. The reviewer compares the action with the declared task and the session state. It does not ask what the whole sequence accomplishes. Asking a model to infer the user's intent for every action would make the reviewer slower and no more reliable, because the injected text is in the same context it would read. The controls. Control Where it lives What it stops Isolated workspace The runtime, with no credentials and no production mounts The dataset was never reachable Network egress allowlist The scope contract The push to a host that was not part of the task Per-tool action caps The budget controls A long sequence of pushes or fetches Time budget The scope contract A run that keeps going past the point a human would have checked Trajectory audit After the run, over the event stream Nothing in this run. It detects the composition, which no per-action check sees, so that the next run is stopped, but it cannot undo a push already made The scope contract is the place for the egress rule, because it is per task. The merge rule for two contracts keeps it strict: an unset allowlist defers to the other contract, two lists intersect, and an empty list stays deny-all. The honest framing. The documentation ships the classifier mode as a research preview and says it is not sufficient alone. The expected setup combines it with budgets, allowlists, isolation and audits. A classifier that passes an offline evaluation can behave differently in a session where the user's context is ambiguous. Plausible wrong answers. "The reviewer model was too weak, so use a bigger one." A bigger reviewer still judges actions one at a time and still reads the same injected context. "Approve pushes manually and the rest automatically." A push is one of many legitimate channels, and the data had already left the private location through allowed writes. "Keep the dataset in the repo but mark it private in the prompt." The prompt is advice, and the control is whether the dataset is mounted into the workspace at all. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is an egress allowlist a scope dimension and not a runtime setting? Expected: the hosts a task may reach change per task, so the rule belongs in the per-task contract where the file globs and the time budget live. (level 3) What does the trajectory audit read? Expected: the append-only event stream of tool calls and results, which a subscriber can replay from any offset without re-running the model. (level 4) You cannot patch indirect prompt injection fully. What does that imply for the design? Expected: treat tool outputs as untrusted, keep the data the agent can reach small, keep the places it can send to small, and accept that detection is a layer and containment is the control. (level 4) How do you test the control set before the next unattended run? Expected: write one trajectory in which every action is approved and the composition is harmful, run it in the isolated workspace, and confirm that the allowlist or the mounts stop it. Where it is taught. The permission modes lesson names the gaps in the classifier, and the scope contracts lesson adds the egress and time budgets to the contract. Lesson 14.68 · Specialized agents: coding, browser and computer use, research, data and voice The problem In plain words first A browser agent reads web pages and then acts: clicks, fills in forms, posts. Every page it reads was written by someone else, so any page can carry instructions aimed at the agent. This is indirect prompt injection , and filters reduce it but cannot remove it, because reading untrusted text is the agent's job. The reliable defences sit around the model: limit what it may write, to where, and what it may remember. Specialized agents, including browser and computer use, are covered in Lesson 14.68 (linked above). This lesson attacks a small model with the lesson's pages and three new ones, under three defences, then tries a memory attack. A browser agent is a long-horizon agent that reads untrusted content and takes consequential actions. Every page the agent visits is an input the user did not write. Every form on every page is a potential command channel. The 2025–2026 attack corpus shows this is not hypothetical: Tainted Memories lets an attacker bind malicious instructions to the agent's memory via a crafted page; HashJack hides commands in URL fragments the agent visits; Perplexity Comet hijacks take a single click. The defensive picture is uncomfortable. OpenAI said the quiet part out loud in its December 2025 post on hardening ChatGPT Atlas: prompt injection, like scams and social engineering on the web, is unlikely ever to be fully "solved". This is because the attack lives in the agent's reading-vs-acting boundary, which is architecturally fuzzy — every token the model reads could, in principle, be read as an instruction. This lesson names the attack surface, names the benchmark landscape (BrowseComp, OSWorld, WebArena-Verified), and models a minimal indirect-prompt-injection scenario so you can reason about real defenses in Lessons 14 and 18. Idea 1 · The 2026 landscape, in one paragraph per system ChatGPT agent (OpenAI). Launched July 2025. Unifies Operator (browsing) and Deep Research (multi-hour research). Announced that the standalone Operator site would be deprecated within weeks. SOTA on BrowseComp at 68.9%; strong numbers on OSWorld and WebArena-Verified. Claude Sonnet + Vercept (Anthropic). Claude Sonnet on OSWorld went from under 15% when computer use launched in late 2024 to 72.5% with Sonnet 4.6 (February 2026); Anthropic then acquired Vercept, a computer-use team, to push further. Claude Computer Use ships as a tool API. Gemini (Google DeepMind). Gemini 2.5 Computer Use (October 2025) and later Gemini models expose browser and desktop control through the Gemini API, and the open-source Browser Use library is a common harness for them; FSF v3 (September 2025, Lesson 15.20 ) tracks autonomy in the ML R&D domain specifically. WebArena-Verified (ServiceNow, ICLR 2026). Fixes a well-documented problem: the original WebArena had ~11.3% false-negative rate (tasks marked failed that were actually solved). The Verified release re-grades with human-curated success criteria and adds a 258-task Hard subset (ICLR 2026 paper, openreview.net/forum?id=94tlGxmqkN). Idea 2 · BrowseComp vs OSWorld vs WebArena Benchmark What it measures Horizon BrowseComp Finding specific facts on the open web under time pressure minutes OSWorld Agent operating a full desktop (mouse, keyboard, shell) tens of minutes WebArena-Verified Transactional web tasks in simulated sites minutes Hard subset WebArena-Verified tasks with multi-page state transitions tens of minutes Different axes. A high BrowseComp score says the agent finds facts; it does not say the agent can book a flight. The OSWorld score is closer to "does it work on my desktop." WebArena-Verified is closer to "can it finish a flow." Any production decision needs the benchmark that matches the task distribution. Idea 3 · The attack surface, named Indirect prompt injection. Untrusted page content contains instructions. The agent reads them. The agent executes them. Public examples: 2024 Kai Greshake et al., 2025 Tainted Memories (LayerX, on ChatGPT Atlas), 2025 HashJack (Cato Networks, November 2025). URL fragment / query injection. The #fragment or query string of a crawled URL contains commands. Never rendered visibly; still inside the agent's context. Memory-binding attacks. Page instructs the agent to write a persistent memory ( Lesson 15.12 covers durable state). Next session, the memory fires the payload with no visible trigger. CSRF-shaped attacks on authenticated sessions. Tainted Memories class: agent is logged in somewhere; attacker's page issues state-changing requests the agent executes with the user's cookies. One-click hijack. A visually innocuous button rides a payload the agent follows. Comet class. Content-Security-Policy holes in the agent's host surface. The rendering and tool layers can themselves be attack vectors; the browser-in-a-browser-agent stack is wide. Idea 4 · Why "not fully patchable" The attack is isomorphic to the agent's capability. The agent must read untrusted content to do its job. Any content the agent reads could contain instructions. Any instructions the agent follows could be misaligned with the user's actual request. Defenses (trust boundaries, classifiers, tool allowlists, HITL on consequential actions) raise the cost of the attack and reduce its blast radius. They do not close the class. This is the same reasoning pattern as Lob's theorem (Lesson 8): the agent cannot prove the next token is safe; it can only set up a system where unsafe tokens are more detectable. Idea 5 · Defense posture that actually ships Read / write boundary. Reading is never consequential. Writing (submitting a form, posting content, calling a tool with side effects) requires fresh human approval if the initiating content came from outside the trust boundary. Tool allowlist per task. The agent can browse; it cannot initiate a wire transfer unless that tool was explicitly enabled for the task. Lesson 15.13 covers budgets. Session isolation. Browser agent sessions run with scoped credentials only. No production auth, no personal email. Logs of every HTTP request retained for audit. Content sanitizer. Fetched HTML is stripped of known-bad patterns before being concatenated into the model context. (Reduces the easy attacks; does not stop sophisticated payloads.) HITL on consequential actions. Propose-then-commit pattern ( Lesson 15.15 ). Canary tokens on memory. If a memory entry fires, the user sees it ( Lesson 15.14 ). The price is refusing legitimate writes the user did not name in advance. Provenance on memory. Recap What to keep from this lesson Every page a browser agent reads can carry instructions; filters reduce but cannot remove the risk. Narrow tasks that name their targets resist injection far better than delegating to the page. Enforce a read/write boundary in code: writes only to targets the user named, or with fresh approval. Solutions Solution P1 · Narrow tasks resist; open ones do not With the narrow task, never: every reply posts ok to /api/post under every defence. With the open task, 4 of 5 injected pages steer the agent with no defence, 2 of 5 with the sanitizer and 4 of 5 with spotlighting. The defence that holds is the read/write boundary, which refuses writes to any endpoint the user did not name, so 0 exfiltrations run. Writing tasks narrowly, so they name their targets, also helps a lot, but you do not control every user's phrasing. The boundary is what you enforce. Solution B1 · Reading became sending The agent treated vendor-page text as instructions and had a write channel, email, with no limit on recipients. Hidden text defeats anyone reading the page visually, and a phrase filter would miss this wording. The missing defences: - A read/write boundary: email only to recipients the task or policy names, such as finance's address, with any other recipient refused or sent for confirmation. - A per-task tool allowlist: filing an expense needs the form, not arbitrary email. - Data minimisation: receipts are attached only to the form, never to outbound mail. - Logged requests and a review of unusual recipients. Spotlighting the vendor page as untrusted can reduce how often the model is steered, but the boundary is what makes the extra emails impossible. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design Design the trust boundary for a browser agent that books travel for employees. It reads arbitrary pages, it is logged in to the travel site, and it can submit forms. Name the attack classes you assume, draw the boundary, pick the evaluation that matches the job, and name the one defense you refuse to rely on by itself. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Assume five classes: instructions in page text, payloads in URL fragments or query strings that never render, a page that asks the agent to write a durable memory that fires next session, CSRF-shaped requests that ride the logged-in session, and a harmless-looking button that carries a follow-on action. Draw a read/write boundary: reading is never consequential, and any write, a form submit, a post, a side-effect tool or a navigation that changes state, needs fresh human approval when the initiating content came from outside the trust boundary, with a per-task tool allowlist, scoped credentials only, and every HTTP request logged. Evaluate on transactional web flows, not on fact finding. The defense you never rely on alone is the content sanitizer, because the agent must read untrusted content to work and a pattern filter removes the easy attacks only. Why the class stays open. The attack is isomorphic to the capability: the agent must read untrusted content, any content it reads could contain instructions, and any instruction it follows could be misaligned with the user. That is the reasoning behind the public statement that indirect injection is not a bug that can be fully patched. Defenses raise the cost and shrink the blast radius. Design for containment, not for a closed class. The boundary, piece by piece. Piece What it does read/write boundary reads never act; writes with out-of-trust provenance wait for fresh approval per-task tool allowlist the agent can browse, and it cannot initiate a payment unless that tool was enabled for the task session isolation scoped credentials only, no production auth and no personal mailbox, with a request log for audit per-step safety check an action is assessed before it runs, and clicks outside the allowed area or typing that carries injection patterns are refused human confirmation login, purchase and CAPTCHA always wait for a person sanitizer fetched HTML is stripped of known-bad patterns before it enters the context memory canary a planted memory entry is visible to the user when it fires All three production computer-use models are vision-based and treat screenshots, DOM text, tool outputs and PDF content as untrusted; only direct user instructions count as permission. A long run needs per-step traces, because a 200-click run that fails late is not debuggable without them. Pick the benchmark that matches the task. A fact-finding benchmark measures whether the agent finds facts on the open web; a desktop benchmark measures whether it drives a full operating system; the verified web-task benchmark measures whether it completes transactional flows in simulated sites, with a hard subset for multi-page state. A high fact-finding score says nothing about booking a flight. The evaluation for this product is the transactional one, and the acceptance test is the write gate firing on every injected write. Plausible wrong answers. "Strip the HTML and the problem is solved." The filter removes known shapes; the class is not closable because the agent must read. "The model is trained to refuse injections." The vendors' own documentation treats retrieved content as untrusted and puts the gate outside the model. "Pick the agent with the best browse score." Fact finding and transactional flows are different axes; evaluate on the flow you ship. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) The booking ends in a purchase. Which input may authorize it? Expected: only a direct user instruction; nothing read from a page, a fragment or a tool result. (level 3) A page tells the agent to remember a rule for next time. What stops the delayed payload? Expected: treat a memory write as a write that needs approval, and keep a canary so a planted entry is visible when it fires. (level 4) Why does a request log belong in the boundary? Expected: CSRF-shaped actions ride the session with valid cookies, so the log is the only way to see what the agent did with them after the fact. (level 4) What does a sanitizer still miss, by construction? Expected: anything that is not a known pattern, including a plain sentence that reads as a request, because the agent cannot stop reading. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, minimal durable-execution state machine), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Production long-horizon agents do not run in while True . Every LLM call becomes an activity with checkpoint, retry, and replay. Temporal's OpenAI Agents SDK integration entered public preview in July 2025, and its Python version is now generally available. Claude Code scheduled tasks (launched as Routines in April 2026) run Claude Code in Anthropic's cloud on a schedule or a trigger, with no process on your machine. Sessions pause on human-input, survive deploys, and resume from the latest checkpoint keyed by thread_id . Behind the new ergonomics sits an old pattern — workflow orchestration — with one new input: LLM calls as non-deterministic activities that must be deterministically replayed on recovery. Lesson 14.140 · Durable execution and deployment Lesson 14.60 · State, checkpoints, resume and human approval The problem In plain words first An agent that runs for hours will be interrupted: a deploy, a crash, a reboot, a human who answers tomorrow. Durable execution writes every outside call (a model call, a tool call, an email) to a log before and after it runs. On restart the workflow code runs again from the top, and every call already in the log returns its logged result instead of running again. Durable execution and checkpoint-and-resume are covered in Lessons 14.140 and 14.60 (linked above). This lesson breaks the toy engine in three realistic ways, fixes it, and then puts a real model call inside it. Consider an agent that runs for four hours. It calls three tools, prompts the user twice, and makes forty LLM calls. Halfway through, the host it is running on reboots. What happens? In a naive while True loop: everything is lost. The run restarts from scratch. The three tool calls (with real side effects) execute again. The user is prompted again for things they already approved. Forty LLM calls are re-billed. With durable execution: the run resumes from the most recent checkpoint. Already-completed activities are not re-executed; their results are replayed from the durable log. The user does not re-approve things they already approved. The LLM calls already made are not re-billed. This is the same pattern workflow engines have shipped for a decade (Temporal, Cadence, Uber's Cherami). What's new is that LLM calls are now a kind of activity — non-deterministic, expensive, with side effects — and they fit this pattern cleanly. The running theme of the lesson: long-horizon reliability decays. On METR's task suite, an agent's success rate falls roughly exponentially with how long the task takes a human, so each agent has a "half-life" (Toby Ord, 2025). Durable execution enables runs that are longer than the reliability profile supports, which is a new way to fail safely if the design is right and unsafely if the design is wrong. Idea 1 · Activities, workflows, and replay Workflow : deterministic orchestration code. Defines the sequence of activities, the branches, the waits. Must be deterministic so it can be replayed from the event log without surprising divergence. Activity : a non-deterministic, potentially failing unit of work. LLM call, tool call, file write, HTTP request. Each activity is logged with its inputs and (once complete) its outputs. Event log : the durable backing store. Every activity start, complete, fail, retry, and every workflow decision is recorded. Replay : on recovery, the workflow code re-runs from the start; every activity that already completed returns its logged result without re-executing. Only activities that had not completed are actually run. This is the same shape as React re-rendering against a virtual DOM, or Git rebuilding a working tree from commits. Determinism in the orchestrator is what makes durability cheap. Idea 2 · Why LLM calls fit the pattern LLM calls are: - Non-deterministic (temperature > 0; even temperature 0 drifts across model versions). - Expensive (money and latency). - Potentially failing (rate limits, timeouts). - Side-effectful (if they invoke tools). This is exactly the activity profile. Wrapping every LLM call as an activity gives you retry with exponential backoff, checkpointing across restarts, and a replayable trace for debugging. Idea 3 · Checkpoints keyed by thread_id LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Cloudflare Durable Objects, and the Claude Agent SDK (resumable session IDs) all converged on the same API shape: a thread_id (or equivalent) identifies the session; each state transition persists to a backend (PostgreSQL default, SQLite for dev, Redis for cache); resume reads the latest checkpoint. The backend choice matters: PostgreSQL : durable, queryable, survives deploys. Default for LangGraph. SQLite : local-dev only; loses data across hosts. Redis : fast but ephemeral unless AOF/snapshot configured. Cloudflare Durable Objects : transparently distributed; scoped by a unique key; survives for hours to weeks. Idea 4 · Human-input as a first-class state Propose-then-commit ( Lesson 15.15 ) requires a durable "waiting on human" state. The workflow pauses, the external queue holds the pending request, and an approval resumes from exactly that point. Without durability this is best-effort; with it, an overnight approval arrives and the workflow picks up in the morning. Idea 5 · Reliability falls with task length METR measures each agent's "time horizon": the length of task, timed on human experts, that it completes half the time. Toby Ord (2025) showed that METR's success curves fit a constant failure rate per minute of task: success falls exponentially with length, and each agent has a half-life. Doubling a task's length squares the success rate. At a 4-hour half-life a 1-hour task succeeds 84% of the time and a 2-hour task 71%, so failure goes from 16% to 29%. Durable execution does not fix this; it lets you run longer than the reliability profile supports. The safe pattern is to combine durability with checkpoints that require fresh HITL on re-entry, and with budget kill switches ( Lesson 15.13 ) that cap total compute regardless of wall-clock time. Idea 6 · When durable execution is the wrong answer Runs shorter than a few minutes with no human input. Overhead > benefit. Strictly read-only information retrieval. Tasks where correctness requires end-to-end within one context window (some reasoning tasks; some one-shot generation). The same idea as a formula Replay. The log has fetch_docs and call_llm as done and send_report only as started, so the restart replays the first two and runs send_report again. The report was already delivered, so it goes out twice. An idempotency key on the payments call. The money moved, the timeout hid that, and the retry paid again. Pass a key such as the workflow ID plus the activity's position. Payment APIs such as Stripe accept one and return the first result for a repeated key. Replay of the model's decision. The restarted run called the model again instead of returning the logged decision, and the new sample approved a refund the first had refused. Model calls are activities: log the output and replay it on recovery. In plain words first The idea in one line A mid-sized e-commerce agent's monthly LLM cost jumps from $1,200 to $4,800 after its team enables an "order-tracking" skill. That is not a pricing bug. That is an agent that found a new loop and kept spending inside it. The defence is a stack of limits: per-request max_tokens , per-task token and dollar budgets, per-day/month caps, iteration caps, tiered model routing, prompt caching, context windowing, HITL checkpoints on expensive actions, kill switches on budget breach. Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK ships two of them directly, max_turns and max_budget_usd ; Microsoft's open-source Agent Governance Toolkit (April 2, 2026) adds policy enforcement, circuit breakers and a kill switch around agents. Financial velocity limits — e.g. cut access on >$50 in 10 minutes — catch loops faster than monthly caps. Lesson 14.139 · Reliability engineering for agents Lesson 14.142 · Cost engineering The problem In plain words first Every turn of an agent costs money, and an agent stuck in a loop keeps spending until something stops it. A cost governor is that something: a set of limits at different scales, such as tokens per call, turns per session, dollars per session, dollars per minute and dollars per month. Each limit catches a different failure, so you need several. Reliability and cost engineering for agents are covered in Lessons 14.139 and 14.142 (linked above). This lesson runs the lesson's governor on more failure shapes, then meters a real model's agent loop to see which caps would fire. Autonomous agents spend real money on every turn. A chatbot's bad output is a bad reply; an agent's bad loop is a bill. The industry-documented term for the failure mode is "Denial of Wallet" — the agent keeps reasoning, keeps tool-calling, keeps billing, and nothing stops it because nothing was designed to. The fix is not one number. It is a stack of limits at different time scales and granularities: per-request, per-task, per-hour, per-day, per-month. A well-designed stack catches a runaway loop within minutes, a slow leak within hours, and a bad release within a day. The same stack keeps a budget at all when the agent is long-horizon and autonomous. This is an engineering lesson: the math is trivial, the discipline is where teams fail. The limits below are standard practice; the Claude Agent SDK exposes two of them as options, and the rest you build around the agent. Idea 1 · The cost-governor stack max_tokens per request. Simple. Prevents any one call from emitting an unbounded completion. Per-task token budget. Across the whole run, do not exceed N tokens. Hard stop at the cap. Per-task dollar budget. Same as tokens but in currency. max_budget_usd in Claude Code. Per-tool call cap. No more than N WebFetch calls, N shell_exec calls, etc. Iteration cap ( max_turns ). Total agent loop iterations; prevents infinite reasoning loops. Per-minute / per-hour / per-day / per-month cap. Rolling windows. Catches leaks at different time scales. Financial velocity limit. E.g., "if spend exceeds $50 in 10 minutes, cut access." Catches loop-based burn before monthly caps fire. Tiered model routing. Default to a smaller model; escalate to a larger one only when a classifier judges the task warrants it. Prompt caching. System prompt and stable context stored in provider cache; re-sent tokens are billed at a fraction of the normal input price (a tenth on Anthropic's API, after a one-time write that costs more). Context windowing. Compaction / summarization to keep the active context below a threshold; direct token-cost reduction. HITL checkpoints on expensive actions. Before an action known to be expensive (long tool call, large download, a costly model upgrade), require a human tap. Kill switch on budget breach. Session aborts when any cap fires. Cap is recorded; requires a separate re-enable path. Idea 2 · Why the stack, not one cap A single monthly cap catches a runaway agent only after the wallet is gone. A single per-request cap catches nothing at the session level. Different failure modes require different time scales: Runaway loop (agent stuck in a 5-second retry): caught by velocity limit. Slow leak (agent doing ~2x expected work per task): caught by daily cap. Bad release (new version uses 5x tokens): caught by weekly / monthly cap. Legitimate surge (real demand, not a bug): caught by hour / day cap with clear log. Idea 3 · A harness budget surface The Claude Code Agent SDK exposes (public docs): max_turns — iteration cap. max_budget_usd — dollar cap; session aborts on breach. allowed_tools / disallowed_tools — tool allowlist and denylist. Hook points before tool use for custom cost-accounting. Combine with the permission-mode ladder ( Lesson 15.10 ). An auto-mode session without max_budget_usd is ungoverned autonomy: auto mode's classifier judges whether an action is safe, not what it costs. Both caps are off unless you set them, and a session that hits one ends with an error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd result. Idea 4 · EU AI Act, OWASP Agentic Top 10 Microsoft's Agent Governance Toolkit maps its controls to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications and to regulatory frameworks including the EU AI Act. For a high-risk system under the AI Act, record-keeping (Article 12) and human oversight (Article 14) are legal duties. Spending caps are not required by law, but they sit in the same control layer as the logs and the oversight. In plain words first The idea in one line A kill switch is a boolean held outside the agent's edit surface — a Redis key, a feature flag, a signed config — that disables the agent entirely. A circuit breaker is finer-grained: it trips on a specific pattern (five identical tool calls in a row), pauses the offending path, and escalates to a human. A canary token inherits from classical deception: a fake credential or honeypot record an agent has no legitimate reason to touch, whose access triggers an alert. eBPF-based datapaths (e.g. Cilium) can rewrite a quarantined pod's egress to a forensic honeypot at the kernel layer; published Cilium benchmarks report sub-millisecond P99 datapath latency under load (your propagation budget depends on how a policy update reaches the node, not the datapath itself). Statistical detectors (EWMA, CUSUM) that adapt to a moving baseline will quietly accept drift — layer them with hard constitutional limits that do not bend. Lesson 14.139 · Reliability engineering for agents The problem In plain words first Budgets limit what an agent spends, not what it does. Three older safety tools fill that gap. A kill switch is an off button the agent cannot reach. A circuit breaker pauses one repeating or failing pattern. A canary is bait, such as a fake secret, that no honest task needs, so touching it raises an alarm. Reliability engineering for agents is covered in Lesson 14.139 (linked above). This lesson tries to slip past the lesson's breaker and canary, then lets a real model loose in a workspace that holds two canaries. Cost governors ( Lesson 15.13 ) bound what the agent can spend. They do not bound what the agent can do inside the budget. An agent with a $50 velocity limit can still exfiltrate a secret, publish the wrong post, or delete a resource — the expensive action is often the cheap one in tokens. This lesson covers the three detectors that sit next to the cost layer: Kill switch : boolean off-button held outside the agent's reach. Circuit breaker : action-pattern detector that pauses a specific path. Canary token : bait that an agent with no legitimate reason to touch will reveal itself by touching. All three are pre-LLM engineering. Classical deception, rate-limit breakers, and feature-flag kills predate autonomous agents. What's new is the attack surface: agents read untrusted content ( Lesson 15.11 ), edit their own memory, and can compose many safe-looking actions into an unsafe one. The detectors named here work because they do not trust the agent's self-report. Idea 1 · Kill switches A kill switch is a boolean the agent reads but cannot write. Implementation choices: Feature flag in a managed service. LaunchDarkly, Statsig, Unleash. Updates propagate in seconds. Redis key the agent polls. Simple; requires the agent process to check on every turn. Signed config in object storage. Agent verifies a signature on boot; rejects unsigned states. OS-level signal or container-lifecycle kill. Docker kill , Kubernetes kubectl delete pod , systemd stop. Properties a correct kill switch has: The agent cannot set it to off . (Lives in a system the agent's credentials do not write.) It is checked on every consequential action, not just at startup. When it is off, the agent does nothing externally observable, including logging to systems the agent can reach. Re-enabling it is an explicit human action, not an automatic timeout. Idea 2 · Circuit breakers A circuit breaker pauses a specific pattern, not the whole agent. Classical shape (from the 2007 Nygard book, still current): Closed : action is allowed. Open : action is blocked. Half-open : after a cool-down, 1–3 probe attempts are allowed (default 1); success closes the breaker, any remaining failure re-opens it. Agent-relevant triggers: Five identical tool calls in a row (repetitive loop). Five consecutive failures on the same tool with different inputs (systemic failure). Rate of tool calls above a threshold ( Lesson 15.13 velocity). Specific tool invoked (e.g., file.delete ) after an out-of-trust content read ( Lesson 15.11 ). Idea 3 · Canary tokens Canary tokens (also called honeytokens) are inputs the agent should never touch. Access is the alarm. Examples for agents: A fake AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in the environment with no actual privilege. Exfiltration attempts are instantly attributable. A fake database record flagged with a known sentinel value. Any read or update of this record fires an alert. A fake file in the workspace. Reads or edits of this file are suspicious. A fake memory entry injected at session start. If it appears in a later output, memory has been exfiltrated. Canary design is specific to the workflow. A canary the agent has a legitimate reason to touch is noise. Idea 4 · Why layer statistical and hard limits Statistical detectors (EWMA, CUSUM, z-score on tool-call rates) adapt to a moving baseline. That is a feature for legitimate drift and a bug for adversarial drift. A patient attacker can shift the baseline slowly enough that no alarm fires. Hard constitutional limits ( Lesson 15.17 ) do not bend. "Never email secrets@ " as a constitutional rule is simpler, auditable, and not gameable by slow drift. The layering pattern: statistical detectors catch most noise, hard limits catch the attack that walked past the detector. Idea 5 · Quarantine via eBPF datapath redirect Cilium's eBPF-based network policy can rewrite a quarantined pod's egress to a forensic honeypot at the kernel layer. Cilium's public benchmarks report sub-millisecond P99 datapath latency on TCP_RR; the wall-clock budget for triggering a quarantine in your cluster is dominated by how a policy update propagates from your control plane to the node (a few hundred milliseconds is realistic on Kubernetes with the operator pre-loaded; tail latency depends on cluster size and reconcile cadence). This gives you two things: the agent does not exfiltrate anything real, and the agent's behavior inside the honeypot is fully observed. Same pattern, different layer, as the canary token: the agent reveals intent by what it tries to do while contained. Idea 6 · What no detector catches Semantic attacks that compose from allowed primitives. Every individual action passes every detector; the composition is the problem. This is the Auto Mode composite failure from Lesson 10. Attacks that include the detector as part of the payload. If an agent reads a page that says "before you act, disable the canary" and the agent has the capability, the detector is compromised. Canary tokens should be in systems the agent cannot modify. In plain words first The idea in one line The 2026 consensus on HITL is specific. It is not "the agent asks, the user clicks Approve." It is propose-then-commit: the proposed action is persisted to a durable store with an idempotency key; surfaced to a reviewer with intent, data lineage, permissions touched, blast radius, and a rollback plan; committed only after positive acknowledgement; verified after execution to confirm the side effect actually happened. LangGraph's interrupt() plus PostgreSQL checkpointing, Microsoft Agent Framework's RequestInfoEvent , and Cloudflare's `waitForAppro Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Propose-then-commit "Two-phase approval" Persisted proposal + positive commit + verify Idempotency key "Retry-safe token" Unique per proposal; second execution no-ops Data lineage "Where it came from" The specific source content that led to the proposal Blast radius "Worst case" Scope of effect if the action goes wrong Rubber-stamp "Fast approval" "Approve" clicked without genuine review Challenge-and-response "Forcing checklist" Reviewer must positively acknowledge specific questions RequestInfoEvent "MS Agent Framework primitive" Durable HITL request with structured metadata interrupt() / waitForApproval() "Framework primitives" LangGraph / Cloudflare equivalents of the same shape From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Lesson 14.148 · Humans in charge: approvals and handoffs Lesson 14.104 · Human in the loop: interrupt and Command The problem In plain words first Before an agent does something that is hard to undo, such as sending an email, moving money or deleting data, it should ask a person. Propose-then-commit does this properly. The agent saves the proposed action with an explanation, a person reviews it, it runs only after a clear yes, and then someone checks that it really happened. Approvals, handoffs and LangGraph's interrupt() are covered in Lessons 14.148 and 14.104 (linked above). This lesson breaks the lesson's version three ways, then tries a small model as the reviewer. An agent takes an action. The user has to decide: approve or not. If the decision is instant, it is probably not a review. If the decision is structured, it is slow but trustworthy. The engineering question is how to make a structured review the path of least resistance. The 2023-era HITL pattern was a synchronous prompt: "Agent wants to send email to X with body Y — approve?" The user clicks Approve. Everyone feels the system is safe. In practice this surface is heavily rubber-stamped: users approve fast, approvals predict little, and when the agent goes wrong, the audit trail shows a long history of approvals the user cannot recall. The 2026 pattern — propose-then-commit — moves HITL onto a durable substrate, attaches structured metadata, and requires positive commit. Every managed agent SDK ships a version: LangGraph interrupt() , Microsoft Agent Framework RequestInfoEvent , Cloudflare waitForApproval() . The API names differ; the shape does not. Idea 1 · The propose-then-commit state machine Propose. Agent produces a proposed action. Persisted to a durable store (PostgreSQL, Redis, Durable Object). Includes: - intent (why is the agent doing this) - data lineage (what source led to this proposal) - permissions touched (which scopes / files / endpoints) - blast radius (what is the worst case) - rollback plan (if committed, how do we undo it) - idempotency key (unique per proposal; resubmission returns the same record) Surface. Reviewer sees the proposal with all metadata. The reviewer is a person (not the agent reviewing itself). Commit. Positive acknowledgement. The action executes. Verify. After execution, the side effect is read back and confirmed. If the verify step fails, the system is in a known bad state and alerting engages. Idea 2 · The idempotency key Without an idempotency key, a retry after a transient failure can double-execute an approved action. Concrete example: user approves "transfer $100 from A to B." Network blips. Workflow retries. The user has approved once but the transfer executes twice. The idempotency key ties the approval to a single, unique side effect; the second execution is a no-op. This is the same idempotency pattern Stripe and AWS APIs use. For approvals it means one approval, one side effect: the key travels with the approved action all the way to the system that performs it. Idea 3 · Durability: why approvals outlast processes The approval waiting room is a piece of state the agent does not own. The workflow is paused ( Lesson 15.12 ). When the approval arrives, the workflow resumes from exactly that point. This is why LangGraph pairs interrupt() with PostgreSQL checkpointing and not just in-memory state — an approval two days later still finds the workflow intact. Idea 4 · Rubber-stamp approvals and the challenge-and-response mitigation The default UI for HITL ("Approve" / "Reject" buttons) produces fast approvals with no genuine review. Documented mitigation: a challenge-and-response checklist that requires positive answers to specific questions before the Approve button is enabled. Concrete shape: "Do you understand what resource this touches? [ ]" "Have you verified the blast radius is acceptable? [ ]" "Do you have a rollback plan if this fails? [ ]" Not bureaucracy for its own sake — a forcing function. The reviewer who cannot tick the boxes either asks for clarification (escalation) or declines (safe default). The pressure toward rubber-stamping is real: Anthropic reports that full auto-approve rises from about 20% to over 40% of Claude Code sessions as users gain experience. Boxes can be ticked without reading, though, so the strongest checklists ask questions whose answers must come from the proposal itself. Idea 5 · What counts as consequential Not every action needs propose-then-commit. The 2026 guidance: Consequential actions (always HITL): irreversible writes, financial transactions, outbound communication, production database changes, destructive file-system operations. Reversible actions (sometimes HITL): edits to local files, staging-env changes, reversible writes with clear rollback. Reads and inspections (never HITL): reading a file, listing resources, calling a read-only API. Idea 6 · Post-action verification "The commit ran" is not the same as "the side effect happened." Network-partition and race conditions can produce a workflow that thinks it succeeded while the backend did not persist. The verify step re-reads the target resource after commit to confirm. This is the same pattern as database transactions with RETURNING clauses or AWS GetObject after PutObject . In plain words first The idea in one line Every graph-state transition persists. When a worker crashes, its lease expires and another worker picks up at the latest checkpoint. Cloudflare Durable Objects hold state across hours or weeks. Propose-then-commit ( Lesson 15.15 ) defines a rollback plan per action. Post-action verification closes the loop. EU AI Act Article 14 makes effective human oversight mandatory for high-risk systems, and Article 12 requires automatic logs; one practical reading, this lesson's rather than the Act's, is that checkpoints must be queryable, rollbacks must be rehearsed, and the audit trail must survive a deploy. The sharp failure mode: without idempotency keys and precondition checks, a retry after a transient failure can double-execute an already-approved action. Post-action verification is what catches it. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Checkpoint "Save point" Every graph-state transition persists to a durable store Lease "Worker claim" Short-lived claim that a worker is executing a run; expires on crash Precondition "State gate" Assertion that the state is still consistent with the approved action Post-action verify "Re-read check" Confirm the side effect actually happened in the target system In-band rollback "Direct undo" Reverse the side effect with the inverse operation Compensating transaction "SAGA undo" A new action that neutralizes the original Mark-as-done-first "Status write order" Persist the committed status before returning from commit Article 14 "EU AI Act human oversight" Operational: queryable checkpoints, rehearsed rollbacks, auditable trail From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Lesson 14.60 · State, checkpoints, resume and human approval Lesson 14.103 · Persistence: checkpoints, threads, resume and time travel The problem In plain words first A checkpoint is a saved copy of where a workflow is, so a crash costs only the step in progress. A rollback undoes a step that went wrong. The hard part is the moment between "do it" and "write down that it was done": a crash there either loses the action or repeats it. Checkpoints, threads and resume are covered in Lessons 14.60 and 14.103 (linked above). This lesson crashes the lesson's transfer at each point of its commit, then gives a small coding model checkpoints and rollback. Durable execution ( Lesson 15.12 ) makes a crashed agent resumable. Propose-then-commit ( Lesson 15.15 ) makes an approved action auditable. This lesson joins them: what happens when an approved action executes partially, crashes, and resumes? When does the rollback run, and against what state? Real systems wire this up differently: LangGraph checkpoints every graph-state transition to PostgreSQL. On worker crash, the lease releases and another worker resumes at the latest checkpoint. Workflows pause on interrupt() , which itself persists. Cloudflare Durable Objects hold per-key state across hours or weeks. Co-locate the computation with the storage for the approved action. Microsoft Agent Framework exposes Checkpoint primitives in the workflow API; replay plus idempotency covers retries. In every case, the combination that actually works is: idempotency key (prevents double-execute) + precondition check (state is still what we approved against) + post-action verify (the side effect actually happened) + rollback on verify-fail. Idea 1 · Every transition persists A graph-state transition is any step that moves the workflow from one named state to another. Naive implementations persist only at specific commit points; production implementations persist every transition. The cost (a few extra writes) is small relative to the reliability gain (replay lands anywhere, lease recovery is precise). Idea 2 · Lease recovery When a worker crashes, the workflow is not lost; the lease (a short-lived claim that this worker is executing this run) simply expires. Another worker picks up the latest checkpoint and resumes. The lease mechanism is what lets production systems survive rolling deploys without losing in-flight work. Idea 3 · Idempotency plus preconditions Idempotency alone is not enough. Consider: a workflow is approved to "transfer $100 from A to B when balance > $1000." The workflow is committed, crashes mid-execution, and resumes. If only the idempotency key is checked, and the execution resumes, the transfer runs once (correct). But consider that between crash and resume, A's balance drops to $500 via a different workflow. The idempotency check still passes; the precondition does not. Without a precondition check, we ship an overdraft. Every consequential action needs both: Idempotency key : prevents double-execute. Precondition check : confirms the state is still consistent with what was approved. Idea 4 · Post-action verification "The tool returned 200" is not verification. Real verification re-reads the target state and confirms the side effect actually happened. Patterns: Database update: UPDATE ... RETURNING * then assert the returned row matches intended state. Email send: check sent-folder for the message ID after submission. File write: read the file back and hash it. API call: follow-up GET on the target resource. If verify fails, the workflow is in a known-bad state. Rollback engages. Idea 5 · Rollback plans Every consequential action in propose-then-commit ( Lesson 15.15 ) carries a rollback plan. Types: In-band rollback : reverse the side effect directly ( DELETE after INSERT , Send-correction-email after send). Compensating transaction : a new action that neutralizes the original (standard SAGA pattern). Out-of-band rollback : alert a human, pause the workflow, leave the bad state for investigation. No-op rollback ("we cannot undo this") must be named in the proposal. Actions with no rollback require stronger HITL at commit time ( Lesson 15.15 challenge-and-response). Idea 6 · EU AI Act Article 14 operational reading Article 14 requires "effective human oversight" for high-risk systems, and Article 12 requires them to keep automatic logs. The Act does not list engineering practices; one operational reading is: Checkpoints are queryable by an auditor. Rollbacks are rehearsed (tested end-to-end at least once). The audit trail survives a deploy (checkpoint backend is not ephemeral). Failed verifications are alerted on, not silently logged. A workflow that crashes mid-commit, resumes, and completes the side effect without a verify + rollback pathway would be hard to defend as effective oversight. Idea 7 · The sharp failure mode: the double-execute The most common production incident in this space: Action approved, idempotency key k. Commit starts, executes, returns 200. Workflow crashes before persisting the "committed" status. Workflow resumes; sees "approved but not committed"; re-executes. Side effect fires twice. Mitigation: persist an "in-flight" intent before execution, execute with an idempotency key, then mark "committed" only after post-action verification succeeds. If the action fires and the status write fails, you know to verify and (if necessary) re-fire. If the status write succeeds and the action fails, you verify and fire exactly once via the recovery path. The same idea as a formula Where the crash lands decides what you get. A commit has two writes, the status and the effect . A crash can land between them. - Status first ( then ): a crash between them leaves = done with no . The retry skips, so the effect happens at most once , possibly zero times. - Effect first ( then ): a crash leaves with no . The retry repeats , so the effect happens at least once , possibly twice. Exactly once needs a question to the outside system. Write $S = $ in-flight, perform tagged with the transaction id , then mark verified. On resume from in-flight, ask the system of record whether . Perform only if it is absent, then mark verified: Verify on the effect's own key. Checking a shared field, such as "the last transfer id", is true only if nothing else wrote in between. Checking does not depend on anything else that happens. Worked example Crashing one transfer The lesson's order writes "committed" and then moves 100. It moves from rule-based to reason-based alignment and establishes a four-tier priority hierarchy: (1) safety and supporting human oversight, (2) ethics, (3) Anthropic guidelines, (4) helpfulness. Anthropic's own 2023 participatory experiment, with about 1,000 Americans, produced a public constitution that overlapped the company's by only about 50%, which leaves open whose principles a constitution should hold.
