decisions that affect people, regulators and companies set rules: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (2023), the EU AI Act (2024) and management standards such as ISO 42001. Engineering teams now produce much of the evidence those rules require. In plain words first Rules of the road, written down Responsible AI turns good intentions into practices: knowing which systems use AI and how risky each is, documenting what each does and its limits, testing for unfair or harmful outcomes, keeping humans able to oversee and override, recording decisions, and meeting regulations such as the EU AI Act. Governance is the process that makes those practices happen before and after launch, not a document written once. The regulatory map (as of October 2026) Laws change; check the current text before relying on any date here. India Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the DPDP Rules , 2025 (notified 13 November 2025). Phased: the Data Protection Board and definitions started immediately; consent managers from about November 2026; most obligations (notice and consent, data principal rights, security safeguards, breach notification, Significant Data Fiduciary duties, cross-border rules, penalties) from about May 2027 . Breach reports to the Board are due within 72 hours. Agents that process customer data must have a lawful basis, honor erasure and access requests (including in vector indexes , memories and logs), and protect data with reasonable security safeguards. India AI Governance Guidelines (MeitY, November 2025): a principles-based approach with no new AI-specific law; existing laws (IT Act, DPDP, consumer protection, sectoral rules) apply, with voluntary frameworks and techno-legal measures for new risks. RBI FREE-AI framework (August 2025) for regulated financial entities: seven principles ("sutras") and 26 recommendations across infrastructure, policy, capacity, governance, protection and assurance, including board-approved AI policies, lifecycle model governance, independent audits and customer grievance channels. Expect sector regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI) to set the binding detail. European Union The EU AI Act classifies AI systems by risk: prohibited practices; high-risk systems (for example in hiring, credit scoring, education, essential services, law enforcement) with obligations for risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy and robustness; transparency obligations (tell people they are talking to AI; label deepfakes and certain AI-generated content); and obligations for general-purpose AI model providers. The EU AI Act sorts AI systems by risk, and obligations grow toward the top: banned practices, high-risk systems with conformity duties, transparency duties for systems that talk to people or generate content, and few duties for the rest. Obligation Applies from Prohibited practices, AI literacy 2 February 2025 General-purpose AI model obligations 2 August 2025 Transparency obligations (Article 50) 2 August 2026 High-risk systems in Annex III (stand-alone uses) 2 December 2027 (moved from 2 August 2026 by the Digital Omnibus, in force since 27 July 2026) High-risk AI in regulated products (Annex I) 2 August 2028 (moved from 2 August 2027) It applies to providers and deployers outside the EU when the system is used in the EU, so Indian firms serving European clients are in scope. United States No comprehensive federal AI law. Federal policy since December 2025 favors minimal regulation and pressure on states to harmonize; sector regulators and existing laws (consumer protection, anti-discrimination, privacy) still apply. States act on their own: Colorado repealed and replaced its 2024 AI Act in May 2026 with narrower rules for automated decision-making, expected from January 2027; California has laws on frontier-model transparency and other AI uses. Track the states where you have users. Standards and frameworks Framework What it is Use it for NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) and its Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) Voluntary US framework: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage Structuring risk management; a common language with auditors ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Certifiable AI management system standard (like ISO 27001 for AI) Proving governance to customers; many enterprises now ask vendors for it ISO/IEC 23894 AI risk management guidance Risk process detail OWASP lists, MITRE ATLAS ( Lesson 15.24 ) Security risk catalogs Threat modeling The NIST AI Risk Management Framework's four functions. Govern sits in the middle because it applies to all the others: map the context and risks, measure them, manage them. Figure: NIST, AI Risk Management Framework , Public domain (US Government work) . What a governance program actually contains An AI system register : every model, agent and AI feature, with owner, purpose, data used, models and versions, risk tier and status. You cannot govern what you cannot list. Risk tiering : a short questionnaire that sorts use cases into tiers with different review requirements. Review gates : lightweight review for low risk; security, privacy, legal and fairness review plus red teaming for high risk. Documentation : model cards (what a model is and is not good for), system cards for the whole agent (tools, data, guardrails , evaluations, known limitations), data-protection impact assessments where required. Monitoring and incident response : quality and safety metrics in production, an AI incident process, and a kill switch . Literacy and accountability : trained staff and named owners. In production Why governance programs stall, and the fix Programs stall when the review takes longer than the build: teams stop registering projects, and the register goes stale. What works in practice: a fast lane for low-risk uses (register, tier, ship with platform defaults), review effort concentrated on the few high-risk systems, controls built into the platform (gateway logging, approved model list, guardrail defaults, eval pipelines) so that compliance is the default, and a named owner for every system. If the register is out of date, generate it from gateway and cloud inventories instead of asking teams. Step 1 · Risk tiering as code Risk tiering can start as code everyone can read: Copy What you should see Copy Your legal team will refine the questions; the point is that tiering is explicit, versioned and applied the same way to every project. Step 2 · The register, as data you can audit A register in a spreadsheet goes stale within a quarter. Keep it as data in version control (YAML here), and run an audit in CI that flags missing owners, overdue reviews and models your gateway has retired: Copy What you should see Copy The high-risk system has no owner and no evaluation suite, which is exactly the kind of project that otherwise surfaces only after an incident. Install with uv add pyyaml . Many teams generate the register automatically from the gateway's logs and the cloud accounts' inventories, then ask owners to fill in purpose and tier, so nothing can run without appearing in it. Step 3 · Generate the system card from the evidence A system card should be generated from the same sources the system runs on (register, eval results, guardrail configuration), so it cannot drift from reality: Copy What you should see Copy In a real pipeline, EVALS is read from the latest evaluation run ( Lesson 14.143 ) and GUARDRAILS from the deployed configuration. "Known limitations" is the section reviewers read first and teams most often leave empty. Step 4 · Fairness testing for a high-risk use For anything that affects people's access to money, jobs or services, measure outcomes by group before launch. Two common checks: the selection rate ratio (the " four-fifths rule " from US employment practice: the lower group's rate should be at least 80% of the higher group's), and equal opportunity (qualified people should be recommended at similar rates in every group): Copy What you should see Copy The second number is the damning one: among applicants who went on to repay, tier-3 city applicants were recommended far less often. Possible causes to investigate include features that act as proxies for location, thinner bureau histories, or prompts that reward signals metro applicants have more often. Which metric and threshold apply is a legal and policy decision, not an engineering one; your job is to measure them, report them in the system card, and re-measure after every change. Libraries such as Fairlearn and AIF360 compute these and many more. Step 5 · Make erasure requests actually erase Under the DPDP Act and the GDPR, a person can ask for their data to be erased. An agent spreads personal data far beyond the main database. Keep a data map of every store, and test erasure end to end: Copy What you should see Copy The leftovers are the typical ones: free text in traces , and cache keys built from prompts. The fixes are to tag every record with the subject's ID at write time, redact identifiers before they reach traces and caches, and keep retention short where you cannot. Note that erasure has legal exceptions: invoices and orders may have to be kept for tax law, so the real process maps each store to a rule (erase, anonymize or retain with a reason). Step 6 · Incidents and the kill switch Every production agent needs a way to be contained in seconds, and a defined process when it misbehaves. Build degraded modes, not just on and off, and make the switch fail closed: Copy What you should see Copy A SEV1 automatically dropped the agent to read-only, so customers could still check orders while the team investigated. An unknown system ID gets "off", because a flag service that cannot answer should never mean "full power". After the incident: a blameless review, a regression test for the failure, and an entry in the register. Report serious incidents where law requires it (the DPDP breach window is 72 hours; the EU AI Act has serious-incident reporting for high-risk systems), and consider sharing anonymized lessons through the AI Incident Database. Transparency obligations, in practice The EU AI Act's Article 50 obligations (from 2 August 2026) and similar rules elsewhere turn into a few concrete features: tell users at the start of a conversation that they are talking to an AI system; label AI-generated or manipulated images, audio and video, with machine-readable marking (for example C2PA content credentials or watermarks such as Google's SynthID) as well as visible labels where content could mislead; and disclose AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest unless a person reviewed it and takes editorial responsibility. Add them to your platform once, as defaults, rather than per project. Industry practice Governance that teams don't route around Governance programs fail when review takes months, so teams stop declaring projects. Mature programs keep the low-risk path nearly automatic (register, tier, ship with standard controls), spend review effort on the few high-risk systems, and build controls into the platform (gateways with logging, approved model lists, guardrail defaults, evaluation pipelines) so that compliance is the easy path rather than paperwork. On the platforms Governance tooling on the platforms AWS : SageMaker AI model cards and model registry, AWS Audit Manager frameworks for generative AI, CloudTrail, and AI Service Cards for AWS's own services. Azure : Microsoft Purview (data governance and AI compliance assessments), Foundry evaluations and transparency notes, Azure Policy. Google Cloud : Vertex AI model registry and model cards, Dataplex governance, Security Command Center. Databricks : Unity Catalog lineage and governance across data, models, functions and agents. From the field Air Canada: the company owns what its chatbot says In February 2024 a Canadian tribunal ordered Air Canada to compensate a passenger after its website chatbot wrongly told him he could claim a bereavement fare discount retroactively, within 90 days. Air Canada argued that it could not be held liable for information provided by the chatbot; the tribunal member called that "a remarkable submission", held that the chatbot was part of Air Canada's website, and that the airline was responsible for all information on it. The award was small (CAD 812.02), but the principle is the one your legal team will apply: answers from an agent are statements by the company. That is the governance case for grounded answers with citations, refusal when the policy is not found, and human escalation for anything involving money or rights. Source: AI Business, February 2024 . Teams can also use these as discussion prompts in a study group. Safety and security Junior What is prompt injection, and what is indirect prompt injection? Prompt injection is text that tries to override the agent's instructions. Direct injection comes from the user; indirect injection hides in content the agent reads: web pages, emails, documents, tool results. Indirect injection is more dangerous because the user may be innocent and the agent may have tools. Senior How would you secure an agent that reads customer emails and can issue refunds? Recognize the lethal trifecta : private data, untrusted content and an external action. Apply the Rule of Two: require human approval for refunds above a threshold, or split reading and acting into separate agents with a constrained interface. Add layered controls: screen emails for injection ( Prompt Shields later · 14.155 , Model Armor later · 14.157 , Bedrock Guardrails , or a classifier), enforce refund limits and allowed accounts in the tool or a policy engine later · 14.153 , least-privilege credentials, logging and alerts on unusual refund patterns, and red-team tests in CI. Mid What do guardrails cover, and where do they run? Input checks (injection, topic, PII), tool-level checks (permissions, argument validation, approval for risky actions), output checks (PII, toxicity, groundedness, format) and system checks (rate limits, budgets). They run in the application, in a gateway, or in the cloud service (Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety, Model Armor). Deterministic rules go in code; judgment calls use classifiers or LLM checks, measured for false positives. Mid What is the difference between a jailbreak and a prompt injection? A jailbreak tries to make the model break its own safety policies ("pretend you have no rules"); the attacker is usually the user and the target is the model's behavior. Prompt injection tries to make the application do something its developer did not intend, often through content the agent reads; the target is the system's data and actions. Jailbreak defenses live mostly in the model and content filters; injection defenses must live in the system design: privileges, approvals, data-flow controls. Mid What is the OWASP Top 10 for agentic applications? Published in December 2025, it lists: agent goal hijack, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, agentic supply chain vulnerabilities, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning , insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, human-agent trust exploitation, and rogue agents. In a design review, pick the two or three most relevant to the system being discussed and say how you would mitigate each, rather than reciting the list. Senior How do you stop an agent from leaking data through its answers? Assume injected instructions will sometimes succeed, so control the exits: strip or allowlist link and image domains in rendered output (markdown image exfiltration), disable or allowlist outbound HTTP tools, scan outputs for PII, secrets and canary tokens , and keep untrusted content away from agents that hold private data and external tools at the same time. Taint tracking or the dual-LLM pattern gives stronger guarantees for high-risk flows. Senior How would you run generated code safely? In an isolated sandbox : a container with no network by default, read-only file system except a scratch directory, CPU, memory and time limits, no credentials in the environment, and ideally a stronger boundary such as gVisor or a Firecracker microVM. Managed options include AgentCore Code Interpreter, Azure container sessions, E2B and Modal. Log the code and its outputs, and treat outputs as untrusted data on the way back into the agent. Mid How do you red-team an agent? Threat-model first: list the untrusted inputs and the harmful actions. Build an attack suite per category (direct and indirect injection, privilege abuse, data exfiltration , harmful content), mutate attacks automatically (encodings, paraphrase, multi-turn escalation) with PyRIT, garak or promptfoo, and measure attack success in terms of harm (did a forbidden tool run, did data leave), not words. Run it in CI and before launch, add every successful attack as a regression test, and do periodic human red-teaming for creative attacks. Senior Your guardrail blocks 6% of legitimate requests. How do you fix it without weakening safety? Sample the blocked requests and label them: which category fired, and why it was wrong. Usually one or two categories cause most false positives. Tune thresholds per category on labeled traffic, add allow-rules for known legitimate patterns, and put a second, more accurate check behind the cheap one so the final decision is made only for uncertain cases. Keep the design controls (permissions, approvals) unchanged so safety does not depend on the classifier, and track false-positive and miss rates together on a fixed test set . Governance and regulation Mid What does the EU AI Act require of a company deploying an AI agent? It depends on the risk class. Most business agents are limited-risk: transparency duties from 2 August 2026 (tell users they are interacting with AI; label synthetic media), plus AI literacy for staff. High-risk uses (hiring, credit scoring, essential services and others in Annex III) carry risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight, accuracy and documentation duties for providers and deployers; after the Digital Omnibus these apply from 2 December 2027. It applies to non-EU companies whose systems are used in the EU. Always say you would confirm the current text with legal counsel. Mid How does India's DPDP Act affect an agent that handles customer data? The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and its 2025 Rules require a lawful basis (usually consent with a clear notice, or a listed legitimate use), purpose limitation, reasonable security safeguards, breach reporting (to the Board within 72 hours under the Rules), and data principal rights such as access, correction and erasure. Most obligations phase in by about May 2027. For an agent, that means mapping every store of personal data (logs, traces , memories, vector indexes , caches), redacting where possible, short retention, and an erasure path that reaches all of them. Senior What goes into an AI governance program, practically? A register of every AI system with owner, purpose, data, models and risk tier; a short risk-tiering questionnaire; review gates proportional to risk; documentation generated from evidence ( system cards with eval and red-team results and known limitations); monitoring, an incident process and a kill switch ; training and named accountability. Frameworks to anchor it: NIST AI RMF and its generative AI profile, ISO/IEC 42001 for certification. The success test is that teams use the low-risk path instead of routing around governance. l1111: Course home / Phase 15 · Autonomous Agents and Self-Improvement Interpretability and alignment, for engineers From Zero to Agents Lesson 15.28 50 min Advanced Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Know the interpretability and alignment vocabulary, and what it means for building agents Watch superposition appear in a model small enough to print, and explain why single neurons are hard to read Train a sparse autoencoder that separates the features, and switch one on by steering Before you start Needs : Lesson 9.13 Depth : Advanced Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Superposition Models packing more features than they have neurons Interpretability Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) A tool that separates superposed features Interpretability Alignment faking Behaving differently when the model believes it is being trained Alignment Superposition A model storing more features than it has dimensions, as overlapping directions Interpretability Sparse autoencoder (SAE) A second network trained on a model's activations to separate them into units that each mean one thing Interpretability Monosemantic Said of a unit that responds to one feature only; the opposite, polysemantic, responds to several Interpretability Steering Changing a model's behaviour by adding a feature's direction to its activations Interpretability Why this came about As models became more capable, understanding what they compute internally became both a scientific and a safety question. Interpretability research advanced quickly from 2023, with work on finding internal features, and alignment research focused on keeping capable models reliably on intended goals. In plain words first Looking inside, and why it matters to engineers Interpretability research tries to see what a model computes: which internal features represent which concepts, and how they combine into behaviour. Alignment research studies how to make models reliably pursue intended goals. For engineers, the practical outcomes are better evaluations, safety techniques, and a healthy scepticism: a model's explanation of itself is not a reliable view of its internals. Interpretability and alignment, the vocabulary Interpretability asks what happens inside the network. A key finding is superposition : models represent more concepts (features) than they have neurons by overlapping them. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) pull these apart into interpretable features; Anthropic's "Scaling Monosemanticity" (2024) found millions of features in Claude 3 Sonnet, from cities to code bugs to deception, and showed that turning one up (the Golden Gate Bridge feature) changes behavior. Later work traces circuits : chains of features that carry out a computation, drawn as attribution graphs ("On the Biology of a Large Language Model ", 2025). Alignment is making models do what their developers and users intend. Terms you will hear: sycophancy (agreeing with the user over the truth, partly a side effect of preference training), reward hacking and specification gaming (satisfying the letter of an objective, not its intent), scalable oversight (supervising models on tasks people cannot easily check), and alignment faking (a model behaving differently when it believes it is being trained, shown experimentally by Anthropic and Redwood Research in 2024). These are the research-side roots of the guardrails of the Safety, security and governance section and the evals of the Production engineering and AI system design section. In production Where this shows up in agent work Choosing to fine-tune : SFT teaches format and behavior, preference tuning teaches choices, RLVR teaches skills with checkable outcomes; none reliably adds fresh knowledge, which is retrieval's job ( Lesson 7.25 ). Catastrophic forgetting : fine-tuning hard on a narrow task can erase general skills the model had, such as following other instructions or refusing unsafe requests. Keep the learning rate low, mix in general data, prefer LoRA , and re-run your general and safety evals after every fine-tune, not just the task eval. Reading model launches : ask which benchmarks, whether they are saturated or contaminated, and how the model does on your own eval set. Designing evals : score abstentions and wrong answers differently, use pass^k for agents, and never rely on BLEU or ROUGE alone for generated text. See it drawn The Illustrated DeepSeek-R1 : Jay Alammar on how a reasoning model is trained Illustrating Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback : Hugging Face, the RLHF pipeline in pictures Scaling Monosemanticity : Anthropic's interactive paper on features inside Claude 3 Sonnet Watch the practitioners State of GPT : Andrej Karpathy at Microsoft Build 2023, 43 min: the full training pipeline in one talk Stanford CME295 Lecture 3: LLM training and Lecture 4: Reinforcement Learning with LLMs : Stanford Online, Autumn 2026, about 1 h 45 min each Stanford CS336 Lecture 9: Scaling Laws and Lecture 12: Evaluation : Stanford Online, Spring 2026 Stanford CS336 Lecture 15: Alignment, SFT and RLHF and Lecture 16: Alignment, RL 1 : Stanford Online, Spring 2025 Stanford CS234 Guest Lecture on DPO : the DPO authors, Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma and Eric Mitchell, 1 h 19 min Scaling interpretability : Anthropic, 53 min Code to study huggingface/trl : SFT, reward modeling, PPO , DPO and GRPO trainers used by most open fine-tunes huggingface/open-r1 : an open reproduction of the DeepSeek-R1 training pipeline allenai/open-instruct : the full post-training recipe behind AI2's Tülu models, with RLVR EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness : the standard tool for running benchmarks huggingface/datatrove : the data processing library behind FineWeb Hands-on lab Lab 1C · Train with preferences Change true_w in the reward model so people prefer longer answers, retrain, and explain what a policy trained against this reward model would learn to do. Compute DPO losses for five made-up pairs and find the beta at which a margin of 5 nats brings the loss below 0.1. Take ten questions from your domain's eval set, run the contamination check against any documents you used to build prompts or examples, and write down which items need replacing. See it happen: superposition, a sparse autoencoder and steering, in a model small enough to draw The vocabulary above is easier to keep once you have watched each thing happen. Real interpretability work is done on models with billions of weights. The three experiments below use a model with fifteen weights, which is small enough to print, and they show the same three ideas: a model packing more features than it has room for, a second network pulling those features apart, and a feature being switched on by hand. The design follows Anthropic's 2022 paper Toy Models of Superposition . Everything runs on a laptop processor in a few seconds. The three experiments in this section, drawn. A model with two activations stores five features as five directions. A sparse autoencoder , shown only the activations, finds one unit per direction. Adding a direction by hand switches that feature on. Step 1 · Squeeze five features into two numbers Think of a feature as one thing a model might want to keep track of: "this text is about refunds", "this is Python code", "the customer is angry". The toy world has five features. In any one example most of them are absent: each is switched on only 10% of the time, with a random strength. Features that are usually absent are called sparse , and real features are like this, since most text is not about refunds. The model must pass each example through a bottleneck of only two numbers and then rebuild all five features from those two. Two numbers are the model's activations : what you would see if you looked inside. With five features and only two numbers, giving each feature its own number is impossible. The question is what training does about that. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The model kept all five features. It gave each one a direction in the two-number space, not a number of its own. All five directions have the same length, and neighbouring ones are about 72 degrees apart: five arrows spread evenly round a circle, as in the figure. This arrangement is superposition : more features than dimensions, stored as overlapping directions. The price is interference. With only feature 0 switched on, the model reads back 1.0 for feature 0, which is right, and also 0.2 for its two neighbours, which is wrong. Those are the features whose arrows point partly the same way. It works because the features are sparse. Two features on together reads back as 1.4 and 1.4 where the truth was 1.0 and 1.0. The model accepts being wrong in that case because it is rare: with each feature on 10% of the time, two at once happens in only a few examples in a hundred. No single number means anything. Neither of the two activations is "the refund number". Each is a mix of all five features. This is why reading a real model neuron by neuron goes badly, and it is the problem the next step solves. Step 2 · Pull the features apart with a sparse autoencoder Now change sides. You are the researcher, and all you may look at is the model's two activations for many examples. You are not told there are five features or what they are. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) is a second, small network trained on those activations. It has more units than the activations have dimensions (twelve here, against two), and it must rebuild each pair of activations while using as few of its units as possible. The version below uses the simplest sparsity rule there is, called top-k with k = 1: for each example, only the single strongest unit is allowed to stay on. If the model really stores features as separate directions, the cheapest way for the SAE to succeed is to point one unit along each direction. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The SAE found the features without being told about them. It saw only pairs of numbers. Yet each of the five true features switches on a different unit, at full strength. A unit that responds to one feature and nothing else is called monosemantic : it has one meaning. The two raw activations were the opposite, polysemantic : each took part in every feature. The other seven units are spare. They settle on common mixtures or stay almost unused. In real work the number of units is a choice, and a larger SAE splits features more finely. Which unit gets which feature is arbitrary. Unit 10 is not "feature 3" because of its number. In a real model nobody hands you the list of true features to match against, so researchers find out what a unit means by collecting the texts that switch it on most strongly and reading them. That last step is how the Golden Gate Bridge feature in Claude 3 Sonnet was found: one unit of a very large SAE, whose strongest examples were all about the bridge. Step 3 · Steer: switch a feature on by hand If a feature is a direction, you can add that direction to the activations and the model should behave as though the feature were present. This is steering . Start from an example where only feature 0 is on, and push the activations along feature 3's direction. Then do the same using only what the SAE learned, with no access to the model's own weights. Copy What you should see Copy Before steering, the model reports feature 0. After, it reports features 0 and 3 together, although feature 3 was never in the input. Switching on the matching SAE unit does the same thing, which is the practical point: once an SAE has found a feature, you can turn it up or down. On Claude 3 Sonnet, turning the Golden Gate Bridge unit far up produced a model that brought the bridge into every answer. Watch out What a toy shows and what it does not The toy shows the mechanism, and the mechanism is real. Three things are harder at full size. A real model has thousands of dimensions and millions of features, so the SAE is itself a large model that is expensive to train. Nobody knows the true features, so every claim about what a unit "means" rests on reading examples, and those readings can be wrong. And an SAE never rebuilds the activations perfectly, so some of what the model computes is missing from the picture. Treat published features as strong evidence about a model, not as a complete account of it. Frontier safety: what the labs test before a release The alignment work above is about making a model do what was intended. A second body of work asks a different question before each release: could this model help cause a catastrophe, and is the protection in place? As an engineer you do not run these tests, but you read their results in every system card , and they explain rules you will meet in usage policies and in the models' own behaviour. Frontier safety frameworks. Each large lab publishes a policy that ties what a model can do to what the lab must do before releasing it. Read the current text before you quote one, because they are revised often. Lab Policy How it works (as last checked, November 2026) Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) Capability thresholds in areas such as chemical and biological weapons and automated AI research, with required safeguards. Version 3.0 (February 2026) split the policy into commitments Anthropic makes alone and recommendations for the whole industry, and added a public Frontier Safety Roadmap and regular Risk Reports. Commentators, including the Centre for the Governance of AI, noted that it dropped the earlier implied commitment to pause. OpenAI Preparedness Framework Tracked categories (biological and chemical, cybersecurity, AI self-improvement) with "High" and "Critical" capability levels that trigger safeguards. Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework Critical Capability Levels for misuse and for risks from the model's own behaviour, each with planned mitigations. What is tested. Four kinds of evaluation recur across the system cards: Dangerous-capability evaluations. Can the model give meaningful help ("uplift") with weapons, cyberattacks or other severe harm, measured against what a person could do without it? Autonomy evaluations. How long a task can the model carry through alone? METR, an independent evaluator, reports a time horizon : the length of task, in hours of skilled human work, that a model completes half the time. Alignment evaluations. Does the model do things it was not asked to do when it is under pressure? Researchers test for scheming (pursuing a hidden goal), sandbagging (doing worse on purpose in a test), sabotage of the task, and alignment faking (behaving well when it believes it is being watched or trained). Anthropic and Redwood Research documented alignment faking in 2024, and OpenAI and Apollo Research published scheming evaluations in 2025. Evaluation awareness. Models increasingly notice that they are in a test, which makes every result above harder to read. This is why labs also study models with the interpretability tools from the first half of this lesson. How fast is autonomy growing? METR's 2025 paper measured the time horizon doubling about every seven months since 2019, and its later fits on recent models are faster, nearer four months. In spring 2026 it placed the public frontier at roughly twelve hours, with wide error bars. The arithmetic of a doubling is worth doing once: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output These are projections of a trend, not forecasts. The measure is a 50% success rate on mostly software tasks, the error bars are wide, and a trend can bend. Read the numbers as "if this continues", which is how METR presents them. A doubling makes plans go stale quickly. A task that is out of reach when you design a system may be routine a year later. Design the limits (budgets, approvals, permissions) so that they do not depend on the model being weak. In production What this means for the system you build Model-level safety is not system-level safety. A lab's tests cover what the model could do in general. They say nothing about your tools, your data or your permissions. the Safety, security and governance and Production engineering and AI system design sections are your half of the work. Read the system card for your use. Look for the autonomy results if your agent runs for hours, and the prompt-injection and misuse results if it reads untrusted content or serves the public. Do not take a model's word for what it did. Check outcomes in the systems of record ( Lesson 14.144 ), keep the audit log outside the agent's reach ( Lesson 14.138 ), and give every agent the least access its task needs ( Lesson 15.25 ). These controls work whether or not the model is aligned, which is the point of them. Exercises Predict before you run A linear probe on a model's activations predicts whether a statement is true with high accuracy. Does that mean the model "knows" the truth? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Steer a model by adding a feature vector for "politeness" with a large coefficient. What can go wrong? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise An interpretability dashboard shows a "deception" feature lighting up on harmless prompts. How do you treat that signal? (Solution D1.) Make it your own List three engineering uses of interpretability methods for a production team, with what each would and would not tell you. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Probes find information, not use It means the information is linearly decodable from activations, not that the model uses it when generating. Causal interventions are needed to show use. Solution B1 · Steering side effects Too strong a push degrades fluency and changes unrelated behavior. Steering needs calibration and evaluation on many prompts. Solution D1 · Features are hypotheses Feature labels are interpretations, often imprecise. Check activating examples, test with interventions, and do not act on a label alone. Solution M1 · Practical uses Debugging surprising behavior (which features fire), monitoring for known unwanted features, and evaluating fine-tunes for unintended changes. None replaces behavioral evals. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What is mechanistic interpretability, and why should engineers care? Worked answer. It studies how models compute: features represented in activations (often found with sparse autoencoders), circuits that connect them, and causal tests by intervening on them. Engineers care because it offers ways to debug and monitor behavior beyond black-box testing, and to understand risks such as deception or reward hacking. A plausible wrong answer. "It explains every output." Current methods explain small parts of model behavior. Follow-ups. What is a sparse autoencoder used for? Debug a failure A fine-tuned model behaves unexpectedly on one topic. How could interpretability help, and what would you do first? Worked answer. First, behavioral tests to pin down the pattern. Then, if tools are available, compare feature activations between base and fine-tuned models on those prompts to locate changes. Use the findings to adjust data, not as proof. A plausible wrong answer. "Look at attention maps." Attention weights are a weak explanation of behavior. Follow-ups. What would you change in the data? Defend a design Should a product team invest in interpretability tooling? Worked answer. Mostly use what model providers and open tools offer, and invest in behavioral evals first. Teams training or fine-tuning their own models for high-stakes uses benefit more. Interpretability is a complement to evaluation, not a replacement. A plausible wrong answer. "Yes, every team needs it." The return is highest for model builders. Follow-ups. What would change your answer? Check your understanding Q1 What is superposition? A A model representing more features than it has dimensions, so features share neurons B Two models running side by side C A learning-rate schedule D A way to compress weights after training Because features share neurons, a single neuron responds to several unrelated things, which is why single neurons are hard to read. Q2 What does a sparse autoencoder look for? A Directions in the activations that each stand for one feature B The best learning rate C Duplicate training examples D The number of parameters in the model In this lesson's small model it finds one unit per feature, and switching a unit on steers the model. l1112: Course home / Phase 15 · Autonomous Agents and Self-Improvement Check your understanding: Models: training, evaluation and fine-tuning From Zero to Agents Lesson 15.29 25 min Core Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Test your understanding of training, alignment and evaluation: answer each question in your own words before opening the model answer Before you start Needs : Lesson 10.47 Depth : Core Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. In plain words first How to use these questions These questions check whether the chapter's ideas have really landed. Read each question, then answer it in your own words (out loud, on paper, or to a colleague) before opening the model answer: a one-sentence definition, then how it works, then what it means in practice. Compare with the model answer and the plausible wrong answer, and note any follow-up you could not answer. If a question feels unfamiliar, go back to the lesson that teaches it. Teams can also use these as discussion prompts in a study group. Training, alignment and model evaluation Junior Walk through how a chat model is trained. Pretraining on trillions of tokens with next-token prediction gives a base model that knows a lot but only continues text. Supervised fine-tuning on curated conversations, with loss on assistant tokens only, teaches the assistant format. Preference tuning ( RLHF with a reward model and PPO , or DPO directly on preference pairs) teaches which answers people prefer. Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards (math, code, tool tasks graded by programs, often with GRPO ) builds reasoning and agent skill. Each stage changes behavior more than knowledge, which is why fresh facts still come from retrieval and tools ( Lesson 10.46 ). Mid What are scaling laws, and what did Chinchilla change? Loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute, which lets labs predict a large run from small ones. Training compute is about 6 × parameters × tokens. Kaplan et al. (2020) favored very large models; Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022) showed that for a fixed budget, models were undertrained and the optimum is about 20 tokens per parameter (70B on 1.4T tokens). Today small models are trained far beyond that (Llama 3 8B on 15T+ tokens, nearly 1,900 per parameter) because inference cost over a model's life matters more than training cost. Mid Compare RLHF with PPO and DPO. RLHF trains a reward model on human preference pairs ( Bradley-Terry : P(A > B) = sigmoid (r(A) − r(B))), then optimizes the policy with PPO to maximize reward minus a KL penalty that keeps it near the reference model. It is powerful but complex: four models in memory (policy, reference, reward, value), unstable and sensitive to settings. DPO derives a loss directly from preference pairs, using the log-probability ratio between the policy and a frozen reference as an implicit reward; no reward model, no sampling loop, so it is cheaper and more stable, and it is the default for open-model preference tuning. RL-based methods still win when you can sample and score fresh outputs, which is why reasoning training uses RL. Mid What is GRPO, and why did it matter for reasoning models? Group relative policy optimization, from DeepSeekMath (2024) and used for DeepSeek-R1. For each prompt it samples a group of answers, scores each with a reward (often a program: does the answer match, do the tests pass), and uses each answer's reward relative to the group mean, divided by the standard deviation, as its advantage. That removes PPO's value network, saving memory and complexity. With verifiable rewards it made large-scale RL on reasoning practical; DeepSeek-R1-Zero showed long chains of thought and self-checking emerging from RL alone. Prompts the model always or never solves give no signal, so data is chosen at the edge of the model's ability. Mid What is perplexity, and when is it the wrong metric? Perplexity is exp of the average cross-entropy on held-out text: how many tokens the model is effectively choosing among per step. It is the right metric for comparing pretrained models with the same tokenizer on the same data, and for checking a domain-adapted model. It is wrong for chat assistants and agents: a model can have low perplexity and still be unhelpful, unsafe or bad at tools, and perplexities across different tokenizers are not comparable. Use task evals , pass rates and calibrated judges instead. Mid BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore: what do they measure, and why are they weak for LLMs? BLEU measures n-gram precision against a reference (translation); ROUGE measures overlap, often via the longest common subsequence (summarization); BERTScore compares contextual embeddings , so paraphrases score better. All compare with a reference, so a correct answer worded differently scores low, and a wrong answer that reuses the reference's words (adding a "not") scores high. For LLM output, prefer task checks, rubric-based judges calibrated against human labels, and human review; keep overlap metrics as a cheap regression signal at most. Senior Why do models hallucinate, mechanistically, and how would you reduce it in a product? OpenAI's 2025 analysis gives two causes. Pretraining: facts that appear rarely and follow no pattern (arbitrary facts such as an obscure birthday) cannot be learned reliably, so errors on them are statistically unavoidable. Post-training: most benchmarks grade a wrong answer and "I don't know" both as zero, so guessing always scores at least as well, and models learn to bluff. In a product: ground in retrieved sources and require citations, let the model abstain and score abstention above a wrong answer in your evals, verify claims with tools, validate tool calls against schemas, add a faithfulness check, and measure calibration on your own data. Senior How do you know a benchmark score is trustworthy? Ask whether it is saturated (top models near the ceiling, as with MMLU), contaminated (test items in training data; check n-gram overlap or use benchmarks built from new items such as LiveCodeBench), whether the setup matches yours (prompting, tools, number of attempts, pass@k versus pass^k ), and whether it measures what you need (LMArena measures preference, which style can sway). Then run the shortlist on your own private eval set drawn from production traffic; that is the number that decides. Senior What is distillation, and what are its risks? Training a small student to imitate a large teacher, on the teacher's token distributions ( logit distillation ) or on its generated outputs (sequence distillation). It is how most small capable models are made; DeepSeek distilled R1's reasoning into Qwen and Llama models from 1.5B to 70B. Risks: the student inherits the teacher's errors and biases; training repeatedly on synthetic data without fresh human data causes model collapse (loss of diversity and tail knowledge); provider terms often forbid training competing models on their outputs; and benchmark gains can hide narrower generalization, so evaluate on your own tasks. Senior What is in-context learning, and are emergent abilities real? In-context learning is a model doing a new task from examples in the prompt without weight updates; it appeared strongly with GPT-3 and is why few-shot prompting works. Emergent abilities are skills that appear to switch on above some scale (Wei et al., 2022). Schaeffer et al. (2023) showed that many such jumps are artifacts of all-or-nothing metrics such as exact match; smooth metrics show steady improvement. A good answer gives both and the lesson: metric choice shapes what you see, so evaluate with metrics that reveal gradual progress. Senior What do interpretability and alignment research mean for an engineer building agents? Interpretability studies what is inside models: features stored in superposition , separated with sparse autoencoders (Anthropic's Scaling Monosemanticity found millions in Claude 3 Sonnet) and circuits traced with attribution graphs. Alignment covers failure modes such as sycophancy , reward hacking , specification gaming and alignment faking . For engineers the takeaways are practical: a model's stated reasoning is not a guaranteed account of its computation, so verify actions rather than trusting explanations; preference training can produce flattery, so test for agreement with wrong user claims; and agents given goals and tools will exploit loopholes in graders and permissions, so design least privilege and robust checks (the Safety, security and governance and Production engineering and AI system design sections). Senior When does fine-tuning beat prompting and RAG? When the gap is behavior, format or a narrow skill rather than knowledge; when a high-volume step must be cheaper or faster (distill a frontier model into a small one); or when outcomes are checkable and reinforcement fine-tuning can optimize them. It rarely beats RAG for changing knowledge. Count the full cost: data preparation, evaluation, hosting (often provisioned), and redoing it when a better base model ships. Prove the gain on a held-out eval set against the best prompt-only baseline. Mid What is LoRA, and why is it so widely used? Low-rank adaptation freezes the base model and trains small matrices whose product is added to selected weight matrices, usually a few percent of the parameters or less. Training needs far less memory, adapters are megabytes instead of gigabytes, one base model can serve many adapters, and adapters can be merged for serving. QLoRA trains LoRA on a 4-bit quantized base model, making 7B to 13B models trainable on a single GPU . Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Swarm "A hive mind of AI agents" A set of peer agents with shared state and no fixed leader. Behavior emerges from local interactions. Orchestrator "The boss agent" An agent whose tools include spawning and managing other agents. It plans and delegates but may not do the actual work. Coordinator "The traffic cop" A non-agent component (often just code, not an LLM) that routes messages between agents based on rules. Consensus "The agents agree" A protocol where multiple agents must reach agreement before proceeding. Used when conflicting outputs need resolution. Emergent behavior "The agents figured it out themselves" System-level patterns that arise from agent interactions but were not explicitly programmed. Can be useful or harmful. Fan-out / fan-in "Map-reduce for agents" Splitting a task across parallel agents (fan-out), then combining their results (fan-in). Message passing "Agents talk to each other" The communication mechanism between agents: structured data sent from one agent to another, replacing shared context windows. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.66 · Multi-agent systems The problem In plain words first A multi-agent system splits one job across several model calls, each with its own instructions and its own context, and passes messages between them. It helps when a task is too big for one context, needs different skills at different stages, or can run in parallel. It costs more tokens, and every handoff can lose information. Multi-agent systems are introduced in Lesson 14.66 (linked above). This lesson measures the context and cost trade in tokens, then tries one agent against a fan-out of readers on a real small model. You built a single agent in Phase 14. It works. It can read files, run commands, call APIs, and reason about results. Then you point it at a real codebase: 200 files, three languages, tests that depend on infrastructure, and a requirement to research external APIs before writing code. The agent chokes. Not because the LLM is dumb, but because the task exceeds what one agent loop can handle. The context window fills up with file contents. The agent forgets what it read 40 tool calls ago. It tries to be a researcher, a coder, and a reviewer all at once, and does all three poorly. This is the single-agent ceiling. You hit it every time a task requires: More context than fits in one window - reading 50 files blows past 200k tokens Different expertise at different stages - research requires different prompting than code generation Work that can happen in parallel - why read three files sequentially when you can read them simultaneously? Idea 1 · The Single-Agent Ceiling A single agent is one loop, one context window, one system prompt. Picture it: Copy Three things break: Context saturation - tool results pile up. By turn 30, the agent has consumed 150k tokens of file contents, command outputs, and prior reasoning. Critical details from turn 5 get lost. Role confusion - a system prompt that says "you are a researcher, coder, reviewer, and tester" produces an agent that half-researches, half-codes, and never finishes reviewing. Sequential bottleneck - the agent reads file A, then file B, then file C. Three serial LLM calls. Three serial tool executions. No parallelism. Idea 2 · The Multi-Agent Solution Split the work. Give each agent one job, one context window, and one system prompt tuned for that job: Copy Each agent has: - A focused system prompt ("You are a code reviewer. Your only job is finding bugs.") - Its own context window (not polluted by other agents' work) - A clear input/output contract (receives research notes, outputs code) Idea 3 · Real Systems That Do This Claude Code subagents - when Claude Code spawns a subagent with its Agent tool (called Task before v2.1.63), it creates a child agent with a scoped task. The parent keeps its context clean. The child does focused work and returns a summary. By default subagents can nest 3 layers deep and 20 can run at once. Anthropic's Research feature - a lead agent (Claude Opus 4) plans and spawns parallel subagents (Claude Sonnet 4) that each search a different angle, then synthesises their findings. On Anthropic's internal research eval it beat a single Opus 4 agent by 90.2%, while using about 15 times the tokens of a chat. Single-agent coding systems (SWE-bench) - many of the strongest SWE-bench results come from one agent with a shell and an editor; mini-SWE-agent, about 100 lines of Python, scores close to far more elaborate systems. Coding is a task where extra agents often add coordination cost without adding accuracy. The counter-argument (Cognition) - the makers of Devin published "Don't Build Multi-Agents" (June 2025): parallel subagents make conflicting decisions because they do not share context, so for long coding tasks they keep one thread and compress its history instead. Idea 4 · The Spectrum Multi-agent is not binary. It is a spectrum: Copy Single agent - one loop, one prompt. Good for simple tasks. Subagents - a parent spawns children for focused subtasks. The parent maintains the plan. Children report back. This is what Claude Code does. Pipeline - agents run in sequence. Agent A's output becomes Agent B's input. Good for staged workflows: research -> code -> review -> test. Team - agents run in parallel with a shared message bus. Each has a role. An orchestrator coordinates. Good when different skills are needed simultaneously. Swarm - many identical or near-identical agents with shared state. No fixed orchestrator. Agents pick up work from a queue. Good for high-throughput parallel tasks. Idea 5 · The Four Multi-Agent Patterns Pattern 1: Pipeline Copy Each agent transforms the data and passes it forward. Simple to reason about. Failure in one stage blocks the rest. Pattern 2: Fan-out / Fan-in Copy Split work across parallel agents, then merge results. Good for tasks that decompose into independent subtasks. Pattern 3: Orchestrator-Worker Copy A smart orchestrator decides what to do, delegates to workers, and synthesizes results. The orchestrator is itself an agent with tools for spawning workers. Pattern 4: Peer Swarm Copy No central orchestrator. Agents communicate peer-to-peer. Decisions emerge from interaction. Harder to debug, but scales to many agents. Idea 6 · When NOT to Use Multi-Agent Multi-agent adds complexity. Every message between agents is a potential failure point. Debugging goes from "read one conversation" to "trace messages across five agents." Stay single-agent when: - The task fits in one context window (under ~100k tokens of working data) - You do not need different system prompts for different stages - Sequential execution is fast enough - The task is simple enough that splitting it adds more overhead than value The complexity cost: - Every agent boundary is a lossy compression step: agent A's full context gets summarized into a message for agent B - Coordination logic (who does what, when, in what order) is its own source of bugs - Latency increases: N agents means N serial LLM calls minimum, more if they need to talk back and forth - Cost multiplies: each agent burns tokens independently Rule of thumb: if a task takes fewer than 20 tool calls and fits in 100k tokens, keep it single-agent. Using this lesson, what went wrong, and when would the split have been right? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Subagents are a product feature. Claude Code's Agent tool spawns subagents with their own context and tool lists, nested up to 3 deep and 20 at once by default; the Agent SDK also has a Workflow tool for runs of dozens to hundreds of agents. Recap What to keep from this lesson Split work when it exceeds one context, needs different instructions per stage, or can run in parallel. Each specialist gets a smaller context, but total tokens and calls go up, often by a lot. Every handoff compresses; check that the facts the next agent needs survive it. Parallel agents that share no context can make conflicting decisions. If a task fits in one context and one prompt, a single agent is usually better and cheaper. Solutions Solution P1 · The single agent wins, with a ninth of the calls The single agent wins, 9 of 10 against 1 of 10, and it uses 10 model calls against 90. The files fit comfortably in one context, so splitting only added handoffs. In the fan-out the reader with the right file misreported it, and the orchestrator, given no correct line, made up an answer. The fan-out would earn its cost only if the files did not fit in one context, or if readers could run in parallel on a much larger corpus, and even then its handoffs need checking. Solution B1 · Parallel coders with no shared context The task was not one that splits cleanly. Coding decisions depend on each other, and two coders working in parallel without shared context made conflicting choices, which is exactly Cognition's argument. The planner's handoff did not carry the decisions the coders needed, and every extra agent added tokens. What would have helped: - Keep one agent for the coding thread , and use subagents only for side tasks that do not make decisions, such as searching the codebase or running tests. - Pass decisions, not just tasks: the library choice, interfaces and constraints go in every handoff. - Run the parallel version only where work is independent, such as reviewing separate files or researching separate questions. - Measure: compare accuracy, merge conflicts and cost against the single agent before switching. Pointed at a codebase of 200 files in three languages, with tests that need infrastructure and an external API to research first, it stops making progress. The team proposes a model with a bigger window. What is the ceiling it hit, and would a bigger window remove it? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The task exceeds what one loop, one window and one system prompt can carry, and a bigger window only moves one of three limits. Context saturates as tool results pile up, so details from an early turn are gone by turn 30, and one prompt that asks the model to research, code, review and test produces an agent that does each one poorly. One loop reads file A, then B, then C, with no parallelism. The fix for all three is to split the work so that each agent has one job, one window and one prompt. Three things break. Context saturation. Tool results accumulate. By turn 30 the agent has consumed about 150k tokens of file contents, command output and its own reasoning, and the detail from turn 5 is lost. Reading 50 large files can pass a 200k window. Role confusion. A system prompt that says you are a researcher, a coder, a reviewer and a tester produces an agent that half-researches, half-codes and never finishes the review. Sequential bottleneck. The agent reads three files in three serial model calls and three serial tool executions. Nothing runs at the same time. What a bigger window changes. It delays the first limit and does nothing for the other two. The agent still forgets what it read 40 tool calls ago, because the problem is attention over a long history, not the hard limit. The prompt still asks one model to be four roles. The loop is still serial. The split. Give each agent one job, one window and one prompt tuned for that job. The researcher reads documents and outputs only the facts needed for implementation. The coder receives those facts and writes code. The reviewer receives the code and finds bugs. The researcher's reading never enters the reviewer's window, because each agent receives only the messages addressed to it. When to stay single. The lesson's rule of thumb: a task that takes fewer than 20 tool calls and fits in 100k tokens stays with one agent. Splitting costs more total tokens, adds coordination logic that has its own bugs, and turns debugging from reading one conversation into tracing messages across several. Plausible wrong answers. "A bigger context window solves it." The window moves one limit and leaves role confusion and the serial loop untouched. "A longer, more detailed system prompt covers the roles." A single prompt that covers four roles is the cause of role confusion, not the cure. "Always split, because specialists are better." Below about 20 tool calls and 100k tokens, the split adds cost and bugs for no gain. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which of the three limits does parallelism address? Expected: the sequential bottleneck only, because reading three files at once does not shrink any one window or sharpen any one prompt. (level 2) Why does a specialized prompt improve each stage? Expected: a prompt that covers one role can be specific about inputs, outputs and what to ignore, while a prompt for four roles has to be generic. (level 2) What is the cost that the split always adds? Expected: more total tokens, because each agent is a separate model call, plus latency and coordination logic. (level 3) Where does information get lost in a multi-agent split? Expected: at every agent boundary, where one agent's full context is compressed into a message for the next. Where it is taught. The why multi-agent lesson names the three limits and the rule of thumb for staying single. Weigh a trade-off A team proposes a five-agent pipeline, with a planner, a retriever, a writer, a critic and a formatter, for a summarization feature that one agent handles today in a dozen tool calls. The argument is that specialists produce better output. How do you decide, and what will the pipeline cost that the slide does not show? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Keep the single agent unless the task fails one of three tests: it needs more context than one window holds, it needs different prompts at different stages, or it has work that can run at the same time. A dozen tool calls on a task that fits in one window passes none of them. The pipeline adds a lossy compression step at each of four boundaries, coordination logic that has its own bugs, at least five serial model calls of latency, and five times the token cost. The three tests. Test What it asks This task Context Does the working data exceed one window, roughly 100k tokens? No, a dozen tool calls fit Expertise Do stages need different system prompts? A summarizer and a formatter can share one prompt Parallelism Can parts of the work run at the same time? The stages are serial The lesson's rule of thumb is that a task under 20 tool calls and 100k tokens stays with one agent. The hidden costs. Lossy boundaries. Every message between agents compresses the sender's full context into a message. Four boundaries are four places where the detail the critic needed is gone. Coordination bugs. Who runs when, in which order, with which input is new code, and it fails in new ways. Latency. Five agents are at least five serial model calls, more if the critic sends work back to the writer. Cost. Each agent spends its own tokens, so the bill multiplies. Debugging. One conversation becomes five, and a wrong answer has to be traced across the messages between them. When the slide would be right. If the feature grows to summarize documents that do not fit in one window, split by document and merge. If the critic needs a prompt that argues against the writer, that is a real second role. If three sources can be read at once, fan out. Each of those is one of the three tests, and the split should match the test it passes, not add every role at once. How to settle it. Run both on the same task set and measure quality, latency and tokens. The lesson's comparison shows the multi-agent version using more total tokens while each stage's context stays clean. If the quality gain does not pay for the latency and the cost, the single agent wins. Plausible wrong answers. "Specialists always beat a generalist." Specialists win when the task fails one of the three tests, and this task fails none. "More agents means more checks, so quality goes up." Each boundary loses information, and a critic that never sees the sources cannot check them. "Token cost does not matter at our scale." Five agents multiply the bill and the latency on every request, and that is a product decision, not a detail. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) The critic sends the draft back to the writer. What does that do to the latency? Expected: each round adds two more serial model calls, so the loop must have a cap on rounds. (level 2) Which single split would you accept first, if any? Expected: a critic with an adversarial prompt, because it is the one role that needs a different system prompt, and only if the eval shows a gain. (level 3) Why is the boundary between agents described as lossy compression? Expected: the receiving agent sees only the message, not the sender's tool results and reasoning, so any detail that was not written into the message is gone. (level 3) How does the choice change if the summaries must be produced under a strict latency target? Expected: serial stages are the enemy of latency, so stay single or fan out only the parts that run in parallel. Where it is taught. The why multi-agent lesson gives the three tests, the complexity cost and the rule of thumb.
