a1602: Course home / Phase 16 · Multi-Agent Systems and Swarms Speech Acts and the FIPA-ACL Heritage Lesson 16.2 60 min Learn Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 16 · 01 (Why Multi-Agent) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Before MCP, before A2A, there was FIPA-ACL. Between 2000 and 2002 the Foundation for Intelligent Physical Agents (FIPA, which became an IEEE Computer Society standards committee in 2005) standardised an agent communication language with 22 communicative acts, content languages led by FIPA-SL, and a set of interaction protocols — contract net, subscribe/notify, request-when. It faded from industry because the ontology overhead was too heavy for the web, but the LLM revival of multi-agent systems is quietly reimplementing the same ideas without the formal semantics: JSON contracts stand in for performatives, natural language stands in for ontologies. This lesson reads FIPA-ACL seriously so you can see which 2026 protocol decisions are reinvention, which are novelty, and where the current wave is going to rediscover problems the 2000s already solved. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Speech act "An utterance that does something" Austin/Searle: utterances as actions. The theoretical parent of ACL. FIPA "That old XML thing" Foundation for Intelligent Physical Agents. Standardized its ACL in 2000–2002; became an IEEE Computer Society standards committee in 2005. ACL "Agent Communication Language" FIPA's envelope format: performative + content + metadata. Performative "The verb" The intent class of a message: inform , request , propose , cfp , etc. KQML "FIPA's predecessor" Knowledge Query and Manipulation Language (1993). Simpler, narrower. Ontology "Shared vocabulary" A formal definition of the concepts the content language talks about. SL0 / SL1 "FIPA content languages" Semantic Language levels 0 and 1 — the formal content language family. Contract Net "Task market" Manager issues cfp; bidders propose; manager accepts. The canonical interaction protocol. Interaction protocol "Pattern of messages" A sequence of performatives with known correctness: request-when, subscribe-notify, etc. Problem In plain words first When agents send each other messages, each message needs two parts: what the sender wants (ask, tell, offer, refuse) and what it is about. FIPA-ACL , an agent-message standard from around 2000, named the first part the performative and defined a library of them, plus protocols such as the contract net , where a manager asks for bids and awards the job. Today's MCP and A2A carry the same ideas in JSON. There is no Zero to Agents chapter on this; it builds on Lesson 16.1. This lesson tests the lesson's ACL code against the full standard, then checks whether a small model reads intent better when the performative is explicit. The 2026 agent-protocol landscape is busy: MCP for tools, A2A for agents, ACP for enterprise audit, ANP for decentralized trust, NLIP for natural-language content, plus CA-MCP and two dozen research proposals. Each spec announces itself as foundational. The honest read is that most of them are rediscovering a very specific twenty-year-old decision tree. Speech-act theory from Austin (1962) and Searle (1969) gave us "utterances are actions." KQML (1993) turned that into a wire protocol. FIPA-ACL (standardised 2000–2002) produced the reference standardization: 22 communicative acts, content languages SL0/SL1, interaction protocols for contract-net and subscribe-notify. JADE and JACK were the Java reference platforms. The effort faded around 2010 because the ontology overhead was too heavy and the web was winning. When you look at MCP's tools/call , A2A's task lifecycle, or CA-MCP's shared context store, you are looking at a softer, JSON-native rehash of FIPA decisions. Knowing the heritage tells you two things: which new "innovations" are actually reinventions, and which old failure modes the new specs will rediscover. Concept Speech acts, in one paragraph Austin noticed that some sentences do not describe the world — they change it. "I promise." "I request." "I declare." He called these performative utterances. Searle formalized five categories: assertive, directive, commissive, expressive, declarative. KQML (Finin et al., 1993) made this operational for software agents: a message is a performative (the action) plus content (what the action is about). FIPA-ACL cleaned up KQML's gaps and standardized a library of 22 communicative acts. The FIPA performatives (partial list) Performative Intent inform "I tell you P is true" request "I ask you to do X" query-if "Is P true?" query-ref "What is the value of X?" propose "I propose we do X" accept-proposal "I accept the proposal" reject-proposal "I reject the proposal" agree "I agree to do X" refuse "I refuse to do X" confirm "I confirm P is true" disconfirm "I deny P" not-understood "Your message did not parse" cfp "Call for proposals on X" subscribe "Notify me when X changes" cancel "Cancel the ongoing X" failure "I tried X and failed" The full list is in fipa00037.pdf (FIPA ACL Message Structure). The point is not to memorize it — the point is that every one of these corresponds to a primitive an LLM protocol eventually re-adds. Canonical FIPA-ACL message Copy Seven fields carry the protocol envelope; one field ( content ) carries the payload. The rest of the fields are exactly what you reinvent every time you bolt retries, threading, and ontology onto a JSON protocol. The two legacy platforms JADE (Java Agent DEvelopment framework, 1999–2020s) was the most-used FIPA-compliant runtime. Agents extended a base class, exchanged ACL messages, ran inside containers, and coordinated using "behaviors." The interaction-protocol library shipped with contract-net, subscribe-notify, request-when, and propose-accept. JACK (Agent Oriented Software, commercial) emphasized BDI (Belief-Desire-Intention) reasoning on top of FIPA messages. More formal, less adopted. Both declined once the web stack ate multi-agent use cases. MCP and A2A are the runtime "containers" of 2026. Why FIPA faded Ontology overhead. FIPA required a shared ontology to parse content . Agreeing on ontologies is a years-long standards process. The web just used HTTP + JSON. Formal semantics nobody used. SL (Semantic Language) gave rigorous truth conditions, but most production systems used free-form content and ignored the formalism. Tooling lock-in. JADE was Java-only; JACK was commercial. Polyglot teams routed around both. The internet won the stack. REST, then JSON-RPC, then gRPC replaced ACL's transport. The LLM revival is FIPA-lite Compare a FIPA request to an MCP tools/call : Copy Same envelope, different syntax. Both carry: who, whom, intent, payload, correlation id. Neither is a revolution over the other — they are different trade-offs on the same design. Ehtesham et al.'s 2025 survey ("A Survey of Agent Interoperability Protocols: MCP, ACP, A2A, ANP", arXiv:2505.02279) compares the four modern protocols. It does not discuss FIPA, so the mapping here is this lesson's reading: MCP corresponds to tool-use speech acts, A2A to agent-peer speech acts, ACP to audit-trail speech acts, ANP to decentralized-identity extensions. The new specs are ACL descendants with JSON syntax and looser semantics. The trade-off, stated plainly What FIPA gave you and modern specs drop: Formal semantics — you can prove inform implies the sender believes the content. A canonical catalog of performatives — you do not have to re-argue "should we have a cancel ?". Decades of interaction-protocol patterns — contract-net, subscribe-notify, propose-accept — with known correctness properties. What modern specs give you and FIPA did not: JSON-native payloads compatible with every modern tool. Natural-language content that LLMs can interpret without a hand-coded ontology. Web-stack transport (HTTP, SSE, WebSocket). Capability discovery via live MCP server/discover and A2A Agent Cards. Looser intent semantics for easier implementation. That is the exact trade. Interaction protocols worth porting FIPA shipped ~15 interaction protocols. Three are worth carrying forward into LLM multi-agent systems: Contract Net Protocol (CNP). Manager issues cfp (call for proposals); bidders respond with propose ; manager accepts/rejects. This is the canonical task-market pattern (Phase 16 · 16 Negotiation). Subscribe/Notify. Subscriber sends subscribe ; publisher sends inform whenever the topic changes. This is every event-bus in 2026. Request-When. "Do X when condition Y holds." Delayed-action with pre-conditions. The 2026 analog is deferred tasks in durable workflow engines (Phase 16 · 22 Production Scaling). Each maps cleanly onto modern message queues, HTTP + polling, or SSE streaming. What breaks when you drop the ontology Without a shared ontology, agents infer meaning from natural-language content. The documented 2026 failure mode is semantic drift : two agents use the same word ( "customer" ) for subtly different concepts, the receiver's agent acts on the wrong interpretation, no schema validator catches it. FIPA's ontology requirement would have rejected the message at parse time. Mitigations without going full ontology: JSON Schema on content — rejects structural errors at the wire. Typed artifacts (A2A) — rejects wrong modality. Explicit performative in the envelope — makes intent unambiguous even when content is natural language. The 2026 specs, mapped to speech-act heritage Modern spec FIPA analog What it keeps What it drops MCP tools/call request explicit intent, correlation id formal semantics, ontology MCP resources/read query-ref explicit intent, correlation id formal semantics A2A Task lifecycle contract-net + request-when async lifecycle, state transitions formal completeness guarantees A2A streaming events subscribe/notify async push typed-predicate subscription CA-MCP shared context blackboard (Hayes-Roth 1985) multi-writer shared memory logical consistency model NLIP natural-language content LLM-native schema Reading the table top to bottom, the pattern is: keep the structural primitive, drop the formalism, let LLMs paper over the ambiguity. The same idea as a formula A message is a typed act. Write a message as : performative , sender , receiver , content and ontology . The receiver's next step is a function of first, , and only then of the content. With explicit, routing needs no model. Replies point back. A reply answers if . in-reply-to = m . reply-with . Without that field, matching a reply means guessing from the conversation id and timing, and a stale reply from an earlier round is indistinguishable from a fresh one. Contract net. A manager sends to bidders , receives bids ​ , and awards to ​ score ( b i ​ ) . If the winner sends , the protocol continues with the next-best bid; the award is a ranking, not a single name. Worked example Running one contract net with a failure Three bids arrive. Scores are price plus ETA over 10: worker-a , worker-b , worker-c . worker-b has the lowest score and gets accept-proposal. worker-b then sends failure ("disk full"). The lesson's award() has no next step. Keeping the ranking means the manager re-awards to worker-a, the next-best at 4.8, without a new round of bids. Check your mental model ✗ "FIPA had twenty performatives." ✓ Its Communicative Act Library has 22. The lesson's code accepts 16 and rejects request-when , a protocol it describes. ✗ "A JSON schema makes the meaning of a field clear." ✓ {"customers": 1200} passes int whether it counts accounts or people. An ontology tag names which one. ✗ "Writing the performative into the message makes a model read intent correctly." ✓ The small model scored 5 of 12 with the envelope and 4 without; a three-line rule reading the envelope scored 12. ✗ "Modern agent protocols descend from FIPA by design." ✓ The 2025 survey of MCP, ACP, A2A and ANP does not mention FIPA; the lineage is a reading, not a citation. Predict before you run The lesson's ACLMessage validates performatives against its own set. How many of FIPA's 22 acts does it reject? And in a contract net where the winner fails, what does the lesson's award() do next? (Solution P1.) See it drawn Testing the lesson's ACL code against the standard The lesson's ACLMessage and ContractNet : its performative set against FIPA's 22 acts, matching proposals to calls for proposals with and without :in-reply-to , a schema that cannot see meaning, and a winner that fails. Runs in under a second. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The lesson's set is short of the standard. FIPA's Communicative Act Library has 22 acts; the lesson accepts 16 and rejects inform-if , inform-ref , propagate , proxy , request-when and request-whenever . Creating a request-when message, which the lesson's own text lists among the protocols worth porting, raises a ValueError. Without :in-reply-to , a stale bid counts. Three proposals arrive in conversation cn-7, one of them left over from an abandoned round, and nothing in the lesson's envelope says which call for proposals each answers. With an :in-reply-to field, 2 of 3 are kept and the stale bid, which points at a cfp this round never sent, is dropped. A schema passes a meaning error. {"customers": 1200} passes an int check, though billing counts accounts and the CRM reads people. An ontology tag ( billing-v3#Account against an expected crm-v2#Person ) turns it into not-understood before anyone acts on it. A failed winner needs a next step. worker-b wins on score (4.5) and then fails. Keeping the ranking lets the manager re-award to worker-a (4.8) at once. See it drawn Does an explicit performative help a model read intent? This block continues from the one above. Twelve messages to a coordinator, three each meaning request, inform, query-if and refuse, mostly phrased indirectly. A rule reads the envelope; Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (CPU) picks an action from plain text and from the same text in an ACL envelope, scored by calibrated likelihood. About 1 minute. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Code reading the envelope gets 12 of 12. Once the performative is a field, routing is a lookup: request means act, inform means record, query-if means answer, refuse means find someone else. The small model barely uses the label. It chose the right action for 4 of 12 plain messages and 5 of 12 with the envelope. It handled requests better with the envelope (3 of 3) but lost the informs. It got one of three yes/no questions and one of three refusals right. The point of an explicit performative is that you do not need a model for this step. Put the act in a typed field, route on it in code, and use the model for the content. Build it code/main.py implements a pure-stdlib FIPA-ACL translator. It encodes and decodes the canonical ACL envelope and shows how every MCP / A2A message shape reduces to the same seven fields. The demo: Encodes five MCP-style and A2A-style messages as FIPA-ACL. Decodes FIPA-ACL back to the modern equivalent. Runs a toy Contract Net negotiation between one manager and three bidders using cfp , propose , accept-proposal , reject-proposal . Run: Copy The output is a side-by-side trace showing each modern message in both its 2026 JSON form and its FIPA-ACL form, then a round-trip of a contract-net bid. The same protocol primitives survive the round-trip; only the syntax differs. The whole of code/main.py follows in parts. Each part runs on this page, in order, in one Python session; the last part does what python3 code/main.py does. Part 1 of 5 · ACLMessage , mcp_tools_call_to_acl Copy Part 2 of 5 · mcp_resources_read_to_acl , a2a_task_create_to_acl , a2a_subscribe_to_acl , Bid Copy Part 3 of 5 · ContractNet Copy Part 4 of 5 · demo_round_trip , demo_contract_net Copy Part 5 of 5 · run it (what python3 code/main.py does) Copy What you should see Copy Use it: the same idea with real libraries outputs/skill-fipa-mapper.md is a skill that reads any agent-protocol spec and produces the FIPA-ACL mapping. Use it before adopting a new protocol to answer: "Is this genuinely new, or is it inform with JSON syntax?" Break it on purpose Your A2A-based scheduler broadcasts a job, takes the first reply as the winning bid, and records the agent's natural-language reply ("Sure, I'll look into it") as acceptance. Two agents start the same job, and one later replies "Actually I can't, my quota is full," which nobody reads. Using this lesson, what was missing? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) MCP went stateless. The 2026-07-28 specification removes sessions and the initialize handshake; each request carries its own version, client identity and capabilities, and mid-call input uses multi round-trip requests. A2A carries tasks between agents with typed messages, artifacts and task states, close to FIPA's request and subscribe protocols (Lesson 16.12). Schemas stand in for ontologies. JSON Schema on tool inputs and outputs, and typed A2A parts, catch structural errors; meaning errors still need shared definitions. On your laptop : you can route most agent messages with a few lines of code on an explicit type field, and save the model for reading the content. Sources: MCP 2026-07-28 release , FIPA Communicative Act Library (SC00037) , Ehtesham et al., arXiv:2505.02279 , A2A protocol . Recap What to keep from this lesson Every agent message has an act (request, inform, query, refuse) and content; make the act explicit. Replies should name what they answer, so stale or duplicate replies can be dropped. A schema checks shape, not meaning; name the meaning with an ontology or shared definitions. Contract nets keep a ranking, so a failed winner can be replaced without a new round. Route on explicit fields with code; a small model reads intent poorly even when it is labelled. Practice and reference One-page references from the source repository that cover this lesson, with commands, defaults and fixes in one place. A2 Cheat sheet · Agent Communication Protocols and A2A Ship it Do not bring FIPA-ACL back. Bring back its checklist: What is the intent primitive (performative) of each message? Is there a correlation id for request-response and cancellation? Is there an explicit content language (JSON-RPC, plain text, structured typed artifact)? Are interaction protocols first-class, or are you re-implementing contract-net from scratch? What happens when two agents disagree about content meaning (semantic drift)? Document these five questions for any new protocol before you ship it into production. outputs/skill-fipa-mapper.md Copy Exercises Run code/main.py . Observe the round-trip encoding. Identify which FIPA performative corresponds to tools/call , resources/read , and A2A task creation. Extend the contract-net demo with a cancel performative that lets the manager withdraw the task mid-bid. What failure case does cancel solve that retries alone do not? Read FIPA ACL Message Structure (http://www.fipa.org/specs/fipa00037/) sections 4.1–4.3. Pick one performative not covered in this lesson and describe its modern JSON-RPC analog. Read Liu et al., arXiv:2505.02279. For each of MCP, A2A, ACP, ANP, list the FIPA performative families they keep and drop. Design a minimal JSON-Schema for the content field of a request performative in your own system. What does that schema give you that pure natural-language does not, and what does it cost? Solutions Solution P1 · Six acts rejected; no step after a failure It rejects six: inform-if , inform-ref , propagate , proxy , request-when and request-whenever . Its set has 16 of FIPA's 22. After a failure the lesson's award() has nothing: it sends one accept and the rejects, and keeps no ranking. In the run above, worker-b wins and fails; with the ranking kept, the manager re-awards to worker-a without asking for new bids. Solution B1 · No performative, no in-reply-to, no failure path Three pieces of FIPA's design were missing. An explicit performative. "Sure, I'll look into it" is not an agree or an accept-proposal ; it is an ambiguous sentence. Require a typed status field on every reply, and route on that. Reply matching and a real award step. Taking the first reply is not a contract net. Collect bids that answer this round's call ( in-reply-to ), award one, and send reject-proposal to the rest, so two agents cannot both start. A failure path. "My quota is full" is a failure or refuse . Unread, it leaves a job that nobody is doing. Treat failure as a message type that re-opens the award. a1603: Course home / Phase 16 · Multi-Agent Systems and Swarms Agent Communication Protocols Lesson 16.3 120 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Implement MCP tool discovery and invocation so agents can use tools exposed by external servers Build an A2A agent card and task endpoint that allows one agent to delegate work to another over HTTP Compare MCP (tool access), A2A (agent-to-agent), ACP (enterprise audit), and ANP (decentralized trust) and explain which protocol solves which problem Wire multiple protocols together in a single system where agents discover tools via MCP and delegate tasks via A2A Before you start Needs : Phase 14 (AI Agents: Design and Engineering), Lesson 16.01 (Why Multi-Agent) Type : Build. Time : about 120 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Agents that can't speak the same language aren't a team. They're strangers shouting into the void. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means MCP "The protocol for AI tools" A client-server protocol for agents to discover and use tools. Agent-to-tool, not agent-to-agent. A2A "Google's agent protocol" A peer-to-peer protocol for agent collaboration under the Linux Foundation. Discovery via Agent Cards, 9-state task lifecycle, streaming via SSE. Supports JSON-RPC, REST, and gRPC bindings. ACP "Enterprise agent messaging" IBM/BeeAI's REST API for agent runs with TrajectoryMetadata: every response carries the full chain of reasoning and tool calls. Merging into A2A. ANP "Decentralized agent identity" A community protocol using did:wba (DID) for cryptographic identity, HPKE for E2EE, and AI-powered meta-protocol negotiation for agents that have never seen each other. Agent Card "An agent's business card" A JSON document at /.well-known/agent-card.json describing skills, supported MIME types, security schemes, and protocol bindings. DID "Decentralized ID" W3C standard for cryptographically verifiable identities hosted on the agent's own domain. ANP uses did:wba method. TrajectoryMetadata "The audit receipt" ACP's mechanism for attaching reasoning steps, tool calls, and their inputs/outputs to every agent response. Meta-protocol "Agents negotiating how to talk" ANP's approach where agents use natural language to dynamically agree on data formats, then generate code to handle them. Task "A unit of work" A2A's stateful object tracking work from submission through completion. Immutable once terminal. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 16.29 · A2A, AG-UI and the rest of the protocol stack Lesson 16.26 · MCP: what it is, and building a server The problem In plain words first Agents built by different teams need shared message formats to work together. MCP connects an agent to tools; A2A connects agents to each other, with an Agent Card that advertises what an agent can do and a task that moves through fixed states; ACP (now merging into A2A) adds audit trails; ANP adds decentralised identity. A2A and the rest of the protocol stack, and MCP itself, are covered in Lessons 16.29 and 16.26 (linked above). This lesson validates A2A task streams and Agent Card routing in Python, then lets a small model pick the remote agent instead. You split your system into multiple agents. A researcher, a coder, a reviewer. They're great at their individual jobs. But now you need them to actually talk to each other. Your first attempt is obvious: pass strings around. The researcher returns a blob of text, the coder parses it however it can. It works until the coder misinterprets a research summary, or two agents deadlock waiting for each other, or you need agents built by different teams to collaborate. Suddenly "just pass strings" falls apart. This is the communication protocol problem. Without a shared contract for how agents exchange information, multi-agent systems are fragile, unauditable, and impossible to scale beyond a handful of agents you personally wrote. The AI ecosystem has responded with four protocols, each solving a different slice of the problem: MCP for tool access A2A for agent-to-agent collaboration ACP for enterprise auditability ANP for decentralized identity and trust This lesson goes deep. You will read real wire formats from each spec, build working implementations, and connect all four into a unified system. Idea 1 · The Protocol Landscape Think of these four protocols as layers, each addressing a different question: They're not competitors. They solve different problems at different levels. Idea 2 · MCP (Recap) MCP is covered in depth in Phase 13. Quick recap: MCP standardizes how an LLM connects to external tools and data sources. It's a client-server protocol where the agent (client) discovers and calls tools exposed by a server. MCP is agent-to-tool communication. It doesn't help agents talk to each other. Idea 3 · A2A (Agent2Agent Protocol) Created by: Google (now under Linux Foundation as lf.a2a.v1 ) Spec version: 1.0.1 Problem: How do autonomous agents collaborate, negotiate, and delegate tasks to each other? A2A is the protocol for peer-to-peer agent collaboration . Where MCP connects an agent to tools, A2A connects an agent to other agents. Each agent publishes an Agent Card at a well-known URL, and other agents discover, negotiate with, and delegate tasks to it. How A2A Works The Real Agent Card This is what an A2A Agent Card actually looks like in the wild. Served at GET /.well-known/agent-card.json : Copy Key things to notice: - Skills are what an agent can do. Each has an ID, tags, and supported input/output MIME types. This is how a client agent decides whether this remote agent can handle its request. - supportedInterfaces lists multiple protocol bindings. A single agent can speak JSON-RPC, REST, and gRPC simultaneously. - Security is built into the card: securitySchemes names each scheme and securityRequirements says which ones apply. The client knows what auth it needs before making a single request. Task Lifecycle Tasks are the core unit of work in A2A. They move through defined states (the diagram drops the TASK_STATE_ prefix that every state carries on the wire): All 8 states (the spec also defines UNSPECIFIED as a sentinel, omitted here): State Terminal? Meaning TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED No Acknowledged, not yet processing TASK_STATE_WORKING No Actively being processed TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED No Agent needs more info from client TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED No Authentication needed TASK_STATE_COMPLETED Yes Finished successfully TASK_STATE_FAILED Yes Finished with error TASK_STATE_CANCELED Yes Canceled before completion TASK_STATE_REJECTED Yes Agent declined the task Once a task reaches a terminal state, it's immutable. No further messages. Follow-ups create a new task within the same contextId . Wire Format A2A uses JSON-RPC 2.0. Here's what a real message exchange looks like: Client sends a message: Copy Agent responds with a task: Copy Streaming via SSE: Copy Idea 4 · ACP (Agent Communication Protocol) Created by: IBM / BeeAI Spec version: 0.2.0 (OpenAPI 3.1.1) Status: Merging into A2A under the Linux Foundation Problem: How do agents communicate with full auditability, session continuity, and trajectory tracking? ACP is the enterprise protocol . Unlike what many summaries claim, ACP does not use JSON-LD. It's a straightforward REST/JSON API defined via OpenAPI. What makes it special is TrajectoryMetadata : every agent response can carry a detailed log of the reasoning steps and tool calls that produced it. Agent Discovery in ACP ACP defines four discovery methods: The AgentManifest is simpler than A2A's Agent Card: Copy Run Lifecycle ACP uses "Runs" instead of "Tasks". A Run is an agent execution with three modes: Mode Behavior sync Blocking. Response contains the complete result. async Returns 202 immediately. Poll GET /runs/{id} for status. stream SSE stream. Events fire as the agent works. TrajectoryMetadata (The Audit Trail) This is ACP's key differentiator. Every message part can include metadata showing exactly what the agent did: Copy For regulated industries this is gold. Every answer comes with a provable chain of reasoning: which tools were called, what inputs were used, what outputs were received. No black box. ACP also supports CitationMetadata for source attribution: Copy Idea 5 · ANP (Agent Network Protocol) Created by: Open-source community (founded by GaoWei Chang) Repo: github.com/agent-network-protocol/AgentNetworkProtocol Problem: How do agents from different organizations trust each other without a central authority? ANP is the decentralized identity protocol . It builds trust using W3C Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and end-to-end encryption. Unlike A2A where you discover agents through known endpoints, ANP lets agents prove their identity cryptographically. ANP has three layers: DID Documents (Real Structure) ANP uses a custom DID method called did:wba (Web-Based Agent). The DID did:wba:example.com:user:alice resolves to https://example.com/user/alice/did.json : Copy Key things to notice: - Key separation is enforced. Signing keys (secp256k1) are separate from encryption keys (X25519). - humanAuthorization is unique to ANP. These keys require explicit human approval (biometric, password, HSM) before use. High-risk operations like fund transfers go through this path. - keyAgreement keys are used for HPKE end-to-end encryption (RFC 9180). - The service section links to the Agent Description document. How Trust Works in ANP ANP does not use a web-of-trust or endorsement graph. Trust is bilateral and verified per-interaction: Trust comes from three sources: 1. Domain-level TLS verifies the DID document host 2. DID cryptographic signatures verify the agent's identity 3. Principle of least trust grants only minimum permissions There's no gossip-based trust propagation or PageRank scoring. You verify each agent directly through its DID. Meta-Protocol Negotiation This is ANP's most novel feature. When two agents from different ecosystems meet, they don't need pre-agreed data formats. They negotiate in natural language: Copy The agents go back and forth (max 10 rounds) until they agree on a format, then dynamically generate code to handle it. Status values: negotiating , rejected , accepted , timeout . This means two agents that have never seen each other before can figure out how to communicate without anyone pre-defining a shared schema. Step 2 · A2A Agent Card and Registry Build agent discovery that matches the real A2A spec: Copy This is substantially richer than a simple name-to-capability map. Step 3 · A2A Task Lifecycle Build the full task state machine: Copy This implements the real A2A task lifecycle: TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED , TASK_STATE_WORKING , TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED , then a terminal state. Handlers are async generators that yield statusUpdate and artifactUpdate events, the same wrappers the SSE stream carries. Step 4 · ACP-Style Audit Trail Wrap communication with trajectory tracking: Copy Every agent execution produces a full audit entry: what went in, what came out, and the complete trajectory of tool calls and reasoning steps in between. You can query by agent, by session, or by individual run. Step 5 · ANP-Style Identity Verification Build DID-based identity and verification: Copy This mirrors the real ANP identity model: agents have DID documents with separate authentication, key agreement, and human authorization keys. The IdentityRegistry simulates DID resolution (in production this would be HTTP fetches to the agent's domain). Step 6 · Protocol Gateway Connect all four protocols into a unified system: Copy The gateway does four things in one call: 1. ANP : Verifies the caller's identity via DID signature 2. A2A : Discovers the target agent and checks capabilities 3. ACP : Wraps the execution in an audit trail with trajectory 4. A2A : Creates a task with full lifecycle tracking Step 7 · Wire It All Together Copy What Goes Wrong Protocols solve the happy path. Here's what breaks in production: Schema drift. Agent A publishes an Agent Card advertising application/json output. But the JSON schema changes between versions. Agent B parses the old format and gets garbage. Fix: version your skills and output schemas. The A2A spec supports version on Agent Cards for this reason. State machine violations. An agent handler yields a TASK_STATE_COMPLETED status update, then tries to yield more artifacts. The task is immutable. Your code silently drops the updates or throws. Fix: check terminal state before yielding. The TaskManager above enforces this with the break after terminal states. Trust resolution failures. Agent A tries to verify Agent B's DID, but Agent B's domain is down. The DID document can't be fetched. Do you fail open (accept unverified agents) or fail closed (reject everything)? ANP recommends fail closed with the principle of least trust. Trajectory bloat. ACP trajectory logging is powerful but expensive. A complex agent that makes 200 tool calls per run produces massive audit entries. Fix: log trajectory at configurable verbosity levels. Record tool names and IO for compliance, skip reasoning steps for non-regulated workloads. Discovery thundering herd. 50 agents all query GET /agents simultaneously on startup. Fix: cache Agent Cards with TTL, stagger discovery intervals, or use push-based registration instead of polling. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Real Implementations A2A is the most mature. Google's official spec is open-source under the Linux Foundation. SDKs for Python and TypeScript. If your agents need dynamic discovery and collaboration, start here. ACP is merging into A2A. IBM's BeeAI project created ACP as a REST-first alternative, but the trajectory metadata concept is being absorbed into the A2A ecosystem. Use ACP patterns (trajectory logging, run lifecycle) even if you use A2A as the transport. ANP is the most experimental. The community repo has a Python SDK (AgentConnect). The meta-protocol negotiation concept is genuinely novel. Worth watching for cross-organizational agent deployments. MCP is already covered in Phase 13. If you want agents to use tools, MCP is the standard. Picking the Right Protocol Break it on purpose Your orchestrator upgrades to an A2A 1.0 SDK, but one partner's agent still sends "state": "completed" . The orchestrator treats every unrecognised state as "still working" and waits. Tasks from that partner never finish, and a retry loop resubmits them every ten minutes. Using this lesson, what should the client have done? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) A2A 1.0 is a Linux Foundation project with typed task states ( TASK_STATE_… ), Agent Cards at /.well-known/agent-card.json , and JSON-RPC, REST and gRPC bindings. IBM's ACP is merging into it. MCP went stateless in its 2026-07-28 specification: no session handshake, each request carries its own version and capabilities, and mid-call input uses multi round-trip requests. Frameworks speak both. Google's ADK, LangGraph, CrewAI and the Claude Agent SDK can expose or call A2A agents and MCP servers through adapters. On your laptop : write a validator for the states you accept and reject anything else loudly; it is a few lines and catches version mismatches on the first message. Sources: A2A protocol , Linux Foundation, A2A's first year , MCP 2026-07-28 release , Ehtesham et al., protocol survey (arXiv:2505.02279) . Recap What to keep from this lesson MCP connects agents to tools; A2A connects agents to agents; ACP adds audit; ANP adds identity. An A2A task is a state machine; validate every update and treat terminal states as final. Route by both skill tags and accepted input types, and report "no agent" rather than guess. Version strings and state spellings differ across protocol versions; reject what you do not recognise. Code routes well on structured cards; a small model does not. In plain words first The idea in one line Four primitives, nothing more — the agent, the handoff, the shared state, the orchestrator — span a four-dimensional design space, and the major multi-agent frameworks shipping in 2026 (AutoGen, LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework) are points in it. This lesson builds them from zero, runs a toy system on all four, then maps every major framework onto the same axes so you can read any new release in one paragraph. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Agent "An LLM with tools" A (system_prompt, tools, model) triple. Stateless. Handoff "Transfer of control" A structured call that names the next agent and optional payload. Three implementations: function return, graph edge, speaker selection. Shared state "Memory" / "context" The only stateful part of a multi-agent system. Message pool or blackboard. Orchestrator "Coordinator" Whoever decides who runs next. Static graph, LLM selector, handoff-driven, or queue-driven. Primitive "Abstraction" One of the four axes every framework parameterizes. Not a framework feature. Message pool "Shared chat history" Full-history shared state. Easy to reason about, scales badly. Projected state "Scoped view" Role-specific view into shared state. Scales, requires schema design. Speaker selection "Who talks next" Orchestrator pattern where a function (often an LLM) picks the next agent from a group. Lesson 14.66 · Multi-agent systems Problem In plain words first Every multi-agent framework is built from four parts: agents (a prompt and tools), handoffs (passing control), shared state (what agents can read and write) and an orchestrator (who decides who speaks next). Frameworks differ in the defaults they choose for each. Multi-agent systems are introduced in Lesson 14.66 (linked above). This lesson stresses the lesson's four primitives where bugs live, in shared state, then lets a small model act as the orchestrator. Every six months a new multi-agent framework ships. AutoGen in 2023. CrewAI in 2024. LangGraph and OpenAI Swarm in 2024. Google ADK in April 2025. Microsoft Agent Framework RC in February 2026. Each press release claims to be "the right abstraction." If you try to learn them one at a time you will burn out. The APIs look different. The docs disagree about what an "agent" is. One framework calls its shared memory a "blackboard," another calls it a "message pool," a third calls it a "StateGraph." You start suspecting the field is just churning. It is not. Underneath the marketing, the four primitives are stable. Learn them once, read every new framework in one paragraph. Concept The four primitives Agent — a system prompt plus a tool list. Stateless; every run starts from its system prompt and the current message history. Handoff — a structured transfer of control from one agent to another. Mechanically, a tool call that returns a new agent or a graph edge that follows a condition. Shared state — any data structure that more than one agent can read (sometimes write). Message pool, blackboard, key-value store, vector memory. Orchestrator — whoever decides who speaks next. Options: an explicit graph (deterministic), an LLM speaker-selector (soft), the last speaker's handoff call (OpenAI Swarm), or a scheduler over a queue (swarm architecture). That is the entire design space. Every framework picks defaults for each axis; the rest is surface syntax. How every 2026 framework maps to it Framework Agent Handoff Shared state Orchestrator OpenAI Swarm / Agents SDK Agent(instructions, tools) tool returns Agent caller's problem the LLM's next handoff call AutoGen v0.4 / AG2 (AutoGen is now in maintenance; Microsoft Agent Framework succeeds it) ConversableAgent speaker-selector on GroupChat message pool selector function (LLM or round-robin) CrewAI Agent(role, goal, backstory) Process.Sequential / Hierarchical Task outputs chained manager LLM or static order LangGraph node function graph edge + condition StateGraph reducer the graph, deterministic Microsoft Agent Framework agent + orchestration patterns pattern-specific thread / context pattern-specific Google ADK agent + A2A card A2A task A2A artifacts host decides Surface differences look huge. Underneath: same four knobs. Why this matters Once you see the primitives, framework comparison becomes a short checklist: Does the orchestrator trust the LLM to route (Swarm) or does it pin routing in code (LangGraph)? Is shared state full-history (GroupChat) or projected (StateGraph reducer)? Can agents modify each other's prompts (CrewAI manager) or only hand off (Swarm)? Those three questions answer 80% of which framework fits a given problem. You stop shopping for "the best multi-agent framework" and start designing for the axis you actually care about. The stateless insight Every primitive except shared state is stateless. Agent is a function of (prompt, tools). Handoff is a function call. Orchestrator is a scheduler. The only stateful thing in the system is shared state. That is where all the interesting bugs live: memory poisoning ( Lesson 16.15 ), message ordering, versioning, write contention. Frameworks that hide shared state (Swarm) push the problem to the caller. Frameworks that centralize it (LangGraph checkpoint, AutoGen pool) make it inspectable but shift coordination cost onto the shared-state implementation. Anatomy of a single primitive Agent Copy No memory. No state. Two agents with the same system prompt and tools are interchangeable. Everything that looks like per-agent state is actually in shared state or the handoff protocol. Handoff Copy Three implementations dominate: Function return — the tool returns the next agent. This is the OpenAI Swarm pattern. Agents carry routing in their tool schemas. Graph edge — LangGraph. Edges are declarative. The LLM produces a value; a condition selects the next node. Speaker selection — AutoGen GroupChat. A selector function (sometimes itself an LLM call) reads the pool and picks who speaks next. Shared state Copy At minimum, a list of messages. Often more: structured artifacts (CrewAI Task outputs), typed context (LangGraph reducers), external memory (MCP, vector DB). Two topologies: full pool (every agent sees every message) and projected (agents see a role-scoped view). Full pools are simple and scale badly. Projected pools scale but require upfront schema design. Orchestrator Copy Four flavors: Static — the graph is fixed at build time (LangGraph deterministic, CrewAI Sequential). LLM-selected — an LLM reads the pool and picks the next speaker (AutoGen, CrewAI Hierarchical). Handoff-driven — the current agent decides by calling a handoff tool (Swarm). Queue-driven — workers pull from a shared queue; no explicit next-speaker (swarm architectures, Matrix). What changes between frameworks Once the primitives are fixed, the remaining design decisions are: Memory strategy — ephemeral vs durable checkpointing (LangGraph checkpointer). Safety boundary — who can approve a handoff (human-in-the-loop). Cost accounting — per-agent token budgets. Observability — tracing handoffs, persisting state for replay. All implementable on top of the primitives. None of them are new primitives. The same idea as a formula An orchestrator is a function. Agents are functions of the state they read, so any change to , such as leftovers from an earlier run or another team's messages, changes what they do. Termination is not guaranteed. A run ends when some agent returns "done" or a step limit is hit. If no path reaches "done", the run always stops at , and a limit that fails silently looks like success. Projection. A role-scoped view ​ = { m ∈ S : m . conversation = c } keeps one task's agents from reading another task's messages. Solutions Solution P1 · A silent stop, then a one-message run It returns normally after 10 messages, the last a writer's draft, with nothing to tell the caller that no agent ever said "done". The fix is to check, at the end of the loop, whether the last handoff was "done", and raise or report if not. The second run on the same state adds one message. The researcher sees its note from the first run, decides it is finished, and hands off to "done", so no new draft or review happens. Create a new state per task. Solution B1 · One pool for every customer Shared state crossed requests, and the orchestration ended without checking. One pool for every customer means agents read other customers' messages. A last_by("writer") style read picks up whichever draft came last, so summaries mention the wrong orders. Clearing it hourly does not help: requests in the same hour still mix. Agents that count what is in the pool behave differently when old messages are there; that is how some requests ended without a review. The fix is a new state object per request, or a pool keyed by conversation id with every read projected to it, plus a check at the end of each run that the review step actually happened. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism A new multi-agent framework ships every few months, each with its own vocabulary. Give the method you use to understand a new one quickly, and name the part of every such system where the hard bugs live. Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Map the framework onto four primitives: the agent, the handoff, the shared state and the orchestrator. Every framework picks a default on each axis, and the rest is surface syntax. The agent is a system prompt plus tools and is stateless, the handoff is a structured transfer of control, the orchestrator decides who runs next, and the shared state is the only stateful part of the system. That is where the difficult bugs sit: memory poisoning, message ordering, versioning and write contention. The four axes. Primitive Definition Common implementations Agent A system prompt, a tool list and a model, with no memory of its own Interchangeable with any agent that has the same prompt and tools Handoff A structured transfer of control from one agent to another A tool that returns the next agent, a graph edge with a condition, or a speaker-selection function Shared state Any data that more than one agent reads, and sometimes writes A full message pool, a topic-keyed blackboard, a typed state with reducers, external memory Orchestrator Whoever decides who speaks next A static graph, a model that picks the speaker, the current agent's handoff call, or a scheduler over a queue Three questions answer most of it. Does the orchestrator trust the model to route, or does code pin the route? Is the shared state the full history, or a projected view per role? Can agents change each other's prompts, or only hand off? The lesson claims these three answer about 80 percent of which framework fits a problem. You stop shopping for the best framework and start designing for the axis you care about. The stateless insight. The agent is a function of its prompt and tools. The handoff is a function call. The orchestrator is a scheduler. Only the shared state carries anything from one step to the next, so every interesting bug is a shared-state bug. A framework that hides the state pushes the problem to the caller. A framework that centralizes it makes the state inspectable and moves the coordination cost into the state implementation. What is not a primitive. Durable checkpointing, human approval of a handoff, per-agent token budgets and tracing are all built on top of the four. They are design decisions, not new axes. If a framework claims a fifth primitive, check whether it is a flavor of shared state you have not seen. Plausible wrong answers. "Each framework has its own architecture, so learn them one at a time." The architectures are points in one four-axis space, and learning the axes once reads every release. "The agents hold the memory." The agent is stateless by definition, and memory lives in the shared state or in the handoff payload. "The orchestrator is the smart part, so pick the framework with the best one." The orchestrator is a scheduler with four flavors, and the choice depends on how much you trust the model to route. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Two agents have the same prompt and the same tools. How do they differ? Expected: they do not, because everything that looks like per-agent state is in the shared state or the handoff. (level 2) Name the three ways a handoff is implemented. Expected: a tool that returns the next agent, a graph edge selected by a condition, and a selector function that picks the next speaker from a pool. (level 2) Full pool or projected state, which scales further and what does it cost? Expected: projected state scales further, and it costs an up-front schema so that each role's view is defined. (level 3) Before adopting a framework, what do you write first? Expected: its four-primitive mapping, and if you cannot write it, the docs are incomplete or the framework is inventing a primitive. In plain words first The idea in one line One lead agent plans and delegates; specialized workers execute in parallel contexts and report back. This is the pattern behind Anthropic's Research system (Claude Opus 4 as lead, Sonnet 4 as subagents), measured at +90.2% over single-agent Opus 4 on internal research evals. This lesson builds the supervisor pattern from the primitives and covers the 2026 engineering lessons from production deployments. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Supervisor "Lead agent" An orchestrator agent that plans, delegates, and synthesizes. Does not do the work itself. Worker "Subagent" A focused agent invoked by the supervisor with narrow scope and its own context window. Orchestrator-worker "Supervisor pattern" Same thing, different name. The 2026 literature uses both. Fresh context "Clean window" A worker's context starts from its system prompt and assigned question, not the lead's history. Rainbow deployment "Gradual rollout" Long-running stateful agents need versioned drain-and-replace, not blue-green. Token dominance "Context is the variable" 80% of research-eval variance comes from total tokens used, not model choice, per Anthropic. Scale effort "Match agent count to complexity" Lead estimates query difficulty, spawns 1 vs 10+ workers accordingly. Synthesis conflict "Workers disagree" Two workers return contradictory facts; the lead must surface disagreement, not silently pick one. This lesson breaks the lesson's lead with a failing and a slow worker, then times real model calls run in parallel on a CPU. Research is the prototypical task that single-agent systems fail. You ask "what changed in multi-agent systems between 2023 and 2026?" A single agent reads five papers sequentially, fills half its context with their text, and then has to reason about all of them together. It forgets the first paper by the time it reaches the fifth. It cannot parallelize. The supervisor pattern fixes this: one lead agent plans the search, delegates each sub-question to a worker, and synthesizes. Each worker gets its own 200k-token window for a narrow question. The lead never sees the raw papers — only the worker summaries. Anthropic's production Research system reports +90.2% on internal research evals vs a single Opus 4. The same post notes that 80% of the BrowseComp variance is explained by token usage alone . Fresh context per subagent is the main mechanism. Concept The pattern Copy The lead never reads the raw materials. The workers never see each other's work until the lead synthesizes. Each arrow is a handoff with a narrow artifact. Why it wins Three mechanisms: Fresh context per subagent. A worker exploring "FIPA-ACL heritage" does not carry the 40k tokens the lead spent planning. It gets a 200k window for one question. Specialization via prompt. The lead's prompt is "decompose and synthesize," not "research." Each worker's prompt is narrow: "find what changed in X." Focused prompts produce focused outputs. Parallelism. Workers run concurrently. Wall-clock time is roughly max(worker_times) + plan + synthesis , not sum(worker_times) . Engineering lessons (Anthropic 2025) The Anthropic post lists several production lessons that are still 2026-relevant: Scale effort to query complexity. Simple queries: one agent, 3-10 tool calls. Complex queries: 10+ agents. The lead must estimate this, not the caller. Broad then narrow. Decompose into broad sub-questions first, then spawn more workers per sub-question if the answer warrants depth. Rainbow deployments. Agents are long-running and stateful. Traditional blue-green does not work. Anthropic uses rainbow: gradual rollout of new versions while old ones drain. Token usage dominates. Anthropic reports agents using about 4× the tokens of a chat and multi-agent systems about 15×, so a multi-agent run costs roughly 4× a single agent. Only run it when the task value justifies the cost. The graph-native turn LangGraph originally shipped a langgraph-supervisor library with a high-level create_supervisor helper. If the lead generates sub-questions that do not decompose the real question, workers do precise research on the wrong target. Workers over-explore. Say what you would cut if the budget were halved. Level 4 of 4 · about 60 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The lead decomposes the question into sub-questions, scales the number of workers to the question's complexity, and synthesizes the worker summaries without reading raw sources. Each worker has a fresh context, an explicit scope, a timeout at about twice the median runtime and a token cap. Shared memory carries provenance on every entry, is append-only, and is checked by a read-only verifier that re-fetches sources and reports on its own channel. Every outbound call sits behind a circuit breaker, the system is deployed with versions side by side, and the cost model states up front that the pattern spends about 15 times the tokens of a single agent. The lead. Prompt outline: decompose, delegate, synthesize, never research directly. Scale effort to the query: a simple question gets one agent and a few tool calls, and a complex one gets more than ten workers. The lead estimates this, not the caller. Decompose broad first, then spawn deeper workers where a sub-answer warrants it. Synthesis with provenance: every claim in the answer names the worker and the source it came from. Conflict handling: when two workers return contradictory facts, re-ask with a narrower question or surface the disagreement, never pick in silence. The workers. Prompt outline: one sub-question, the sources to prefer, what is out of scope, the output shape. Fresh context per worker, so the lead's planning tokens never enter a worker's window. A timeout at about twice the median worker runtime, after which the lead re-spawns with a narrower scope or proceeds without the result. A hard token cap per worker, on the order of ten times the expected synthesis input, so one runaway worker cannot spend the budget. Shared memory. Every entry carries the writer, the timestamp, the prompt hash and the source it cites. The log is append-only; a correction supersedes and references the entry it replaces. A read-only verifier re-fetches cited sources, flags mismatches, and writes only to a verification channel that the lead and a human read. Monitor the share of writes that are supersessions as an early sign of a hallucinating writer. Failure modes and mitigations. Expected failure Mitigation The lead decomposes the wrong question Log the decomposition and compare it with the user's question before workers start Workers over-explore Explicit scope, timeout and token cap Two workers disagree Detect by canonicalized claims per sub-question; re-ask or surface Memory poisoning Provenance, append-only, read-only verifier Retry storm against a search or fetch service Circuit breakers that open at 5 to 10 percent error rate and capped retry budgets Silent wrong answer A golden set of questions with known answers, run weekly, and sampled human review Operations. Trace the lead's plan, each worker's tool calls and the synthesis, so that a wrong answer can be traced to a worker and a source. Deploy new versions beside old ones and let long-running questions finish on the version they started on. State the measured multiplier: the pattern costs about 15 times the tokens of a single agent, and about 80 percent of the quality variance on a browsing benchmark is explained by token usage. Report tokens and wall-clock beside answer quality for every question class. With half the budget. Keep the lead's scaling rule and raise the complexity that a question must reach before the lead adds workers, so that more questions go to one agent. Keep provenance and the verifier, because they are cheap and they protect the cited answer. Cut worker count per question before you cut the verifier, and cut debate rounds entirely. What we grade. The outlined prompts, the memory schema with provenance fields, the failure table with one mitigation per row, the three operational limits with the reason for each number, and a cost section that shows the multiplier rather than hiding it. "Let the lead resolve conflicts by picking the better-written answer." A silent pick hides the disagreement from the user, and the design must re-ask or surface it. "Skip the verifier, because the lead already reads the worker summaries." The lead compares summaries with each other, not with the sources, and shared summaries can share a hallucination. Expected: provenance marks the entry as uncited, the lead weighs it lower, and the verifier cannot check it, so the answer either omits it or labels it. Debug a failure In a lead-and-workers research system, two workers answered overlapping sub-questions with numbers that contradict each other. The final report contains one of the numbers and no mention of the other. The user found the second number in a source and asks why the report hid it. Where did the system fail, and what do you change? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The lead resolved a synthesis conflict by picking one side in silence, which the lesson calls the worst failure in this pattern, because the user never learns that a disagreement happened. Two upstream causes made it likely: the decomposition gave two workers the same ground, and no worker had a scope that stopped it from drifting into the other's territory. The fix is a lead that detects contradiction between worker outputs and either re-asks with a narrower question or writes the disagreement into the answer, plus provenance on every synthesized claim. Three failure modes in the pattern. Failure What happened here The lead hallucinates the plan Sub-questions overlapped, so two workers researched the same fact Workers over-explore A worker without a scope boundary drifted past its question into another's Synthesis conflict Two contradictory facts arrived, and the lead picked one without a note The third is the one the user saw. The first two made it happen. Detect the conflict without a model. The lesson asks how to detect contradiction without a model call. Canonicalize the claims: extract each number with its unit and the entity it describes, key it by sub-question, and compare. Two different values under one key is a conflict. For non-numeric claims, flag a key only when the two workers state different claims. Different cited sources alone are not a conflict. Let the lead handle a flagged key. What the lead does with a conflict. Re-ask. Spawn a worker on a tighter question aimed at the disagreement, which adds a round. Surface it. Write both values into the answer with their sources and say that they disagree. Never pick in silence. A chosen value with no note is the failure in the prompt. Prevent the overlap. Decompose broad first and narrow later, and give each worker an explicit scope in its prompt: the sub-question, what is out of scope, and the sources to prefer. Add a worker timeout at about twice the median runtime and a token cap per worker, so that a worker that wanders is cut and the lead re-spawns with a narrower question or proceeds without it. Provenance on the synthesis. Each claim in the final answer carries the worker and the source it came from. That makes the hidden second number impossible, because a claim with two sources shows two values, and it makes the post-mortem a read of the trace instead of a guess. Plausible wrong answers. "Add a rule to the lead's prompt that says be careful with numbers." The lead did not know a conflict existed, and a prompt does not compare worker outputs. "Trust the worker with the higher confidence." Confidence is not correctness, and the user still never learns that a disagreement happened. "Run three workers per sub-question and take the majority." A majority can be wrong together, it triples the cost, and the overlap that caused the conflict stays in the plan. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is a silent pick worse than a wrong pick with a note? Expected: a noted disagreement lets the reader check the sources, while a silent pick presents an unresolved fact as settled. (level 3) The re-ask adds a round and the latency target is tight. What do you do? Expected: surface the disagreement in the answer instead of re-asking, and record the key for a later run. (level 4) How do you test the conflict detector? Expected: feed it worker outputs with a planted contradiction on one key and matching values on others, and assert that exactly that key is flagged. (level 4) The two workers agree and are both wrong. What catches that? Expected: nothing in the lead, because agreement is not correctness, so an independent verifier with its own source access has to check the claim. Where it is taught. The supervisor pattern lesson names the synthesis conflict and the worker timeout and token cap. Explain the mechanism A research system with one lead agent and several worker agents beat a single agent on an internal evaluation by a wide margin. Explain the mechanism, and say which single variable explains most of the gain. Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The lead plans and decomposes the question, each worker gets a fresh window for one narrow sub-question, and the lead synthesizes the worker summaries without ever reading the raw sources. Three mechanisms carry the gain: fresh context per worker, a narrow prompt per role, and workers that run at the same time. The variable that explains most of it is total token usage, which the lesson's source puts at 80 percent of the variance on one browsing benchmark. A worker that does not carry the lead's planning tokens has room to read. The shape. The lead receives the question, splits it into sub-questions, and sends one to each worker. Each worker starts from its own system prompt and its sub-question, not from the lead's history. The workers return summaries. The lead never sees the raw material, only the summaries, and writes the answer from them. The three mechanisms. Fresh context. A worker on one sub-question does not carry the tens of thousands of tokens the lead spent planning. It has a full window for its question. The lesson's figure is a 200k window per worker against the 40k the lead already used. Specialization by prompt. The lead's prompt says decompose and synthesize. Each worker's prompt says find what changed in one thing. Narrow prompts produce narrow, usable outputs. Parallelism. Workers run concurrently, so wall-clock time is about the longest worker plus planning plus synthesis, not the sum of all workers. The gain and its price. The lesson reports a gain of 90.2 percent over the single agent on the internal evaluation, and a cost of about 15 times the tokens of a single agent. The same source says that about 80 percent of the variance on one browsing benchmark is explained by token usage alone. The pattern wins because it spends more tokens where they help, not because the lead is clever. Operational lessons that come with it. Scale the effort to the question: a simple query needs one agent and a few tool calls, and a complex one may need more than ten workers, and the lead must estimate that. Decompose broad first, then go deeper where an answer warrants it. Long-running stateful agents need a gradual deployment where old versions drain, not a hot swap. Plausible wrong answers. "The lead is a bigger model, so it is smarter." The gain tracks token usage, and the workers do the reading; a bigger lead alone changes nothing about context. "Multi-agent is cheaper because workers are small." It costs about 15 times the tokens, and it is worth it only when the task value covers that. "Give the lead the raw sources too, so it can check the workers." That fills the lead's window with what the workers already read and removes the fresh-context advantage. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why does the lead not read the raw sources? Expected: so that its window stays free for planning and synthesis, and so that each source is read once by the worker who owns it. (level 2) When does the pattern lose to a pipeline? Expected: when step two needs step one's output, because then there is no parallel work and the extra agents only add tokens. (level 2) What does the lead do when two workers disagree? Expected: it re-asks or notes the disagreement in the answer, and never picks one side in silence. (level 3) A worker drifts beyond its sub-question. What stops it? Expected: an explicit scope in its prompt, a timeout at about twice the median worker runtime, and a token cap, after which the lead re-spawns with a narrower question or proceeds without it. Where it is taught. The supervisor pattern lesson builds the lead and the parallel workers and reports the measured gain. a1606: Course home / Phase 16 · Multi-Agent Systems and Swarms Hierarchical Multi-Agent Architecture and How It Fails Lesson 16.6 60 min Learn + Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 16 · 05 (Supervisor Pattern) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Hierarchical is supervisor nested. Manager agents over sub-managers over workers. CrewAI Process.hierarchical is the textbook version: a manager_llm dynamically delegates tasks and validates outputs. The LangGraph equivalent was create_supervisor(create_supervisor(...)) with the older langgraph-supervisor helper; LangChain now recommends building supervisors from tool calls (Lesson 16.5). It is the natural pattern when the task is a real org chart. It is also the pattern most likely to collapse into managerial looping — manager agents assign work poorly, misinterpret sub-outputs, or fail to reach consensus. Sequential often beats it. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Hierarchical "Org chart pattern" Supervisors over supervisors; only leaves do work. Manager LLM "The boss" The LLM that decomposes, assigns, and validates at an internal node. Decomposition drift "The boss lost the plot" Top manager's split no longer covers the original question. Reconciliation loop "Endless meetings" Sub-managers disagree; top re-delegates; workers re-run; loop until budget exhausted. Depth-2 ceiling "Don't go deeper than 2 levels" Empirical guardrail: 3+ levels collapses observability. Canary question "Ground truth at every level" A worker that is always asked the original query unchanged, to detect drift. Provenance chain "Who said what" Trace from each synthesis back to the leaf outputs that produced it. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.107 · Subgraphs, multi-agent systems and map-reduce Problem In plain words first A hierarchy nests supervisors: a top manager delegates to sub-managers, who delegate to workers, and summaries flow back up. It fits work that really has separate teams. Each extra level is another place to misassign work or distort a summary, and errors surface only at the top. LangGraph subgraphs and multi-agent patterns are covered in Lesson 14.107 (linked above). This lesson adds a coverage check to the lesson's hierarchy, works out how reliability falls with depth, and lets a small model decide which teams a request needs. Once the supervisor pattern clicks, the natural next step is "what if the workers are themselves supervisors?" Teams have sub-teams; companies have departments of departments. Hierarchical architectures mirror that. The issue: LLM managers are not the same as human managers. A human manager has stable priors about what their reports know. An LLM manager re-reasons the org every turn from whatever is in its context. Tiny drift in that context, and the whole tree misallocates work. Concept The shape Copy Every internal node plans, delegates, and synthesizes. Only leaves do work. Where it shines Clear org mapping. If the real task is departmental ("legal review the doc, finance review the doc, engineering review the doc, then summarize for exec"), the hierarchy is explicit. Local summarization. Each sub-manager synthesizes its team's output before the top manager sees it. Top manager sees three sub-manager summaries, not fifteen worker outputs. Where it breaks Three failure modes that studies of failed multi-agent runs, such as the MAST taxonomy (Cemri et al., 2025), keep finding: Task assignment error. The manager reads the goal, hallucinates a decomposition, and delegates to the wrong sub-manager. Because the sub-manager obediently works on what it was given, the error only surfaces at the top synthesis — one level removed from where a human could have caught it. Output misinterpretation. Sub-manager returns "unable to verify claim X." Top manager summarizes as "claim X not confirmed." Meaning drifts at every level. Consensus loops. Two sub-managers disagree; top manager asks them to reconcile; they re-delegate down; workers re-run; sub-managers return slightly different answers; loop. CrewAI's Process.hierarchical guards against this with step limits, but the limit itself is now a hyperparameter. The deciding question Sequential (linear pipeline) vs hierarchical: does your task actually have independent sub-teams, or is it one linear flow pretending to be a tree? If the latter, use sequential. If the former, use hierarchical but budget explicit reconciliation rules. Role-framework implementation CrewAI's Process.hierarchical wires a manager LLM over specialist crews. The manager: receives the top-level task, assigns subtasks to crews, evaluates crew outputs, decides whether to accept, re-delegate, or iterate. Documentation: https://docs.crewai.com/en/introduction (look for "Hierarchical Process" under Core Concepts). Graph-framework implementation LangGraph uses nested create_supervisor calls. The inner supervisor has its own graph; the outer supervisor treats the inner graph as an opaque node. This is cleaner than CrewAI for debugging (you can step through each graph separately) but harder to express dynamic reshaping of the tree. Reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph-supervisor. The same idea as a formula Reliability multiplies. If each delegation or summary step is right with probability , a hierarchy of depth has steps down and summaries up, so the top answer is right with probability . At that is 90% at depth 1, 73% at depth 2 and 59% at depth 3. Coverage is a set check. Write down the set of things the request needs at intake. After the run, compare it with the set of branches that actually answered: report (asked, never answered) and (answered, never asked). A non-empty means the synthesis must not ship. Worked example Catching one mislabel The request needs engineering and legal: . The top manager delegates to engineering and finance, so . , so the check stops: the legal question was never answered. is extra work nobody asked for. The lesson's TopManager returns a 192-character synthesis either way. Only the check notices. Check your mental model ✗ "The top manager will notice if a branch is wrong." ✓ It synthesises whatever comes back. The lesson's run returned a full synthesis with the legal question unanswered. ✗ "An unknown branch name stops the run." ✓ The lesson records MISSING[legl] as text and synthesises anyway. ✗ "Adding a level adds one small risk." ✓ It adds two steps that must both go right. At 95% per step, depth 3 is right 77% of the time. ✗ "A model asked 'does this need legal?' decides well." ✓ The small model said yes to every team for every request; calibrated, it mostly said no. Predict before you run The top manager sends a request that needs engineering and legal review to engineering and finance instead. Does the lesson's TopManager raise anything? And at 90% reliability per step, what share of depth-3 answers are right? (Solution P1.) See it drawn Checking coverage and counting depth The lesson's build_hierarchy() and TopManager.run() on the right labels, a mislabel and a typo, each followed by a coverage check against what the request needs. Then for four reliabilities and four depths. Runs in under a second. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The lesson's hierarchy always returns a synthesis. With the right labels, a mislabel (finance instead of legal) and a typo ( legl ), it produces 184, 192 and 169 characters of synthesis. The typo shows up only as MISSING[legl] text inside the summary. A coverage check catches both errors. Written down at intake, "this needs engineering and legal" turns the mislabel into "legal never answered; finance was extra", and the typo into "legal never answered". Either should stop the synthesis from shipping. Depth is expensive. With 2d − 1 steps that must all go right, 99% per step still gives 95% at depth 3, but 90% per step gives 59%, and 80% gives 33%. See it drawn A small model as the decomposer This block continues from the one above. For eight requests, Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (CPU) decides which of engineering, legal and finance each needs, from the likelihood of "Yes" against "No", raw and calibrated against a request that needs no team. About 1 minute. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Raw, the model says yes to everything. Every request was sent to all three teams: no team was missed, but 11 unneeded team calls were added across 8 requests, and not one request got exactly the right set. Calibrated, it says no to nearly everything. Subtracting how strongly it says yes to "Say good morning" leaves teams only where the request pushes harder than that. It got 1 request exactly right (the licence review, legal only), missed 9 needed teams and added 1. Neither is a decomposer you can trust. A small model cannot separate "needs legal" from "might involve legal". Write the needed teams into the request schema at intake, or use a much stronger model and still check coverage after. Build it code/main.py runs a 3-level hierarchy: top manager: splits a task into "engineering" and "legal" branches, engineering sub-manager: splits into "frontend" and "backend" workers, legal sub-manager: one worker. Demo contrasts happy path (everyone agrees) against a perturbed path where the top manager's decomposition mislabels "legal" as "finance" and watches the error cascade — the sub-manager obediently does finance work, the top synthesizer reports finance findings, the original legal question goes unanswered.
