Inputs: task description, org structure, reconciliation budget. Output: pattern recommendation with the specific failure modes to guard against. Break it on purpose Your compliance assistant runs a CrewAI hierarchy: a manager over security, privacy and legal crews. An audit finds that privacy questions were sometimes routed to security, whose summaries said "no issues found", and the manager's reports said "privacy reviewed, no issues". Using this lesson, what was missing? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) CrewAI's hierarchical process puts a manager LLM over crews that delegates and validates; LangGraph builds nested supervisors as subgraphs; the Claude Agent SDK lets subagents spawn subagents, 3 levels deep by default. Failure studies name the patterns. The MAST taxonomy (Cemri et al., 2025) sorts failed multi-agent runs into specification, inter-agent misalignment and task verification failures, and finds each category common. Shallow beats deep in practice. Production systems such as Anthropic's Research feature use one lead over workers rather than several management layers. On your laptop : keep hierarchies to two levels with a small model, and write the coverage set at intake so a script can check the result. Sources: CrewAI, Hierarchical process , Cemri et al., Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (arXiv:2503.13657) , Claude Agent SDK, Subagents , Anthropic, Multi-agent research system . Recap What to keep from this lesson Hierarchies fit tasks with genuinely separate teams; otherwise use a pipeline or a single supervisor. Reliability falls as ; every level costs two chances to go wrong. Write down what the request needs at intake and check coverage before the synthesis ships. Treat an unknown or missing branch as a failure, not text in the summary. A small model is a poor decomposer: it said yes to everything, or no to nearly everything. Practice and reference One-page references from the source repository that cover this lesson, with commands, defaults and fixes in one place. MA Cheat sheet · Multi-Agent Systems: Quick Reference OP Cheat sheet · Comparing Orchestration Patterns Ship it If you ship hierarchical: Cap tree depth at 2. Three levels already hides most errors from observability. Explicit reconciliation budget. Set max rounds before the top manager must commit. Usually 2. Provenance on every synthesis. Each node's summary must cite which leaf outputs produced it. Alert on decomposition drift. Log the manager's decomposition per step; diff against the user query. If the decomposition no longer covers the query, fire an alert. outputs/skill-hierarchy-fitness.md Copy Exercises Run code/main.py and compare happy vs perturbed. How many levels of manager hand-off does it take before the top output fully diverges from the user's question? Add a third level (top → sub → sub-sub → worker). Measure how often the perturbed path corrects itself vs fully diverges as depth grows. Implement a "canary" worker at each sub-manager that is always asked the original user question unchanged. Use the canary answer to detect decomposition drift. How should the manager react when the canary disagrees with the synthesized answer? Read CrewAI's Process.hierarchical docs. Identify one concrete guardrail CrewAI applies (step limit, manager_llm constraint) and describe what failure mode it targets. Compare nested LangGraph supervisors to CrewAI hierarchical. Which makes reconciliation loops cheaper to detect? Solutions Solution P1 · Nothing raised, and 59% at depth 3 Nothing is raised. The finance branch answers its own question, the synthesis includes it, and the legal question is simply never asked. The error is visible only if someone compares what was asked with what was answered. At 90% per step, depth 3 means 5 steps (3 down, 2 summaries up), so 0.9⁵ ≈ 59% of top-level answers are right. Solution B1 · Coverage nobody checked Two things were missing. A coverage check. The request needed privacy, and no privacy crew answered. Written down at intake, that gap would have stopped the report. Faithful summaries. "Security found no issues" became "privacy reviewed, no issues" one level up, which is the output-misinterpretation failure. Require each summary to name the branch that produced it and to keep claims within that branch's scope. Also consider flattening: three crews under one manager is already deep enough. A single supervisor with a routing table for privacy, security and legal questions is easier to check. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure A three-level agent hierarchy reviews a contract. The top manager splits the work into an engineering branch and a legal branch, each with its own sub-manager and workers. The final report is complete and confident, and it contains finance findings where the legal review should be. Nobody asked a finance question. Trace the failure and say what you change in the design. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The top manager mislabeled the legal branch as finance when it decomposed the task. The sub-manager did what it was given, the workers did finance work well, and the top synthesizer reported finance findings. The error surfaced only at the top, one level away from any point where a human could have caught it. The design fixes are a depth cap of two, provenance on every synthesis, a logged decomposition that is checked against the original question, and a canary worker that is always asked the user's question unchanged. Why hierarchy hides this. A human manager has stable knowledge of what each team does. A model manager re-derives the whole structure every turn from whatever is in its context. A small drift in that context changes the decomposition, and every level below works on the drifted version in good faith. The lesson names three failure modes, and this incident is the first: Failure Mechanism Task assignment error The manager hallucinates a decomposition and sends work to the wrong branch Output misinterpretation A sub-manager returns "unable to verify claim X" and the top reports "claim X not confirmed", and meaning drifts at every level Consensus loop Two sub-managers disagree, the top asks them to reconcile, they re-delegate, workers re-run, and the loop continues until a step limit Trace it. Read the top manager's decomposition log. The branch label is "finance", not "legal". Read the sub-manager's input. It received a finance task and had no way to know it was wrong. Read the synthesis. It cites finance findings. The original legal question appears nowhere. The side-by-side of what was asked and what was delivered is the whole diagnosis. The design changes. Cap the depth at two. Three levels already hide most errors from observability. Provenance on every synthesis. Each node's summary cites the leaf outputs that produced it, so a report can be traced to the workers who wrote it. Alert on decomposition drift. Log the manager's decomposition at each step and compare it with the user's question. When the decomposition no longer covers the question, fire an alert before the workers start. A canary worker per sub-manager. One worker is always asked the original question unchanged. When the canary's answer disagrees with the synthesized answer, the manager stops and escalates instead of merging. An explicit reconciliation budget. Set the rounds before the top must commit, usually two. The deciding question. Before you keep the hierarchy, ask whether the task has independent sub-teams or is a linear flow that looks like a tree. A contract review with legal and engineering branches is a real tree. A task where step two needs step one is a pipeline, and sequential beats hierarchical there. Plausible wrong answers. "Add a fourth level to check the third." More levels hide more errors from observability, and the fix is fewer levels with provenance. "Tell the sub-manager to double-check the task it receives." The sub-manager had no access to the original question, and a canary worker is the mechanism that gives it one. "Use a bigger model for the top manager." A bigger manager still re-derives the structure each turn from its context, and the mislabel is a context drift, not a capability gap. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) How many levels did the error travel before the output diverged from the question? Expected: one, because the mislabel happened at the top and every level below executed it faithfully, which is why the depth cap is two. (level 3) The canary's answer and the merged answer differ. What does the manager do? Expected: stop, record both answers with provenance, and escalate to a human or re-decompose, never merge the two. (level 4) How do you detect meaning drift between levels? Expected: compare each node's summary with the leaf outputs it cites, and flag a summary that changes the modality of a claim, such as unverified becoming false. (level 4) The reconciliation loop keeps hitting its step limit. What does that tell you? Expected: the limit is now a hyperparameter that hides a disagreement, so either the decomposition is wrong or the question has no single answer, and the top must report the disagreement. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Minsky's 1986 premise — intelligence is a society of specialists — gets rediscovered every decade. In 2023 Du et al. turned it into a concrete algorithm: multiple LLM instances propose answers, read each other's answers, critique, and update. Over N rounds they converge on a consensus that beats zero-shot CoT and reflection on six reasoning and factuality tasks. Two findings matter: both multiple agents and multiple rounds contribute independently. The society beats a single-agent monologue; the multi-round exchange beats one-shot voting. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Society of Mind "Minsky's idea" Intelligence as interacting specialists; 1986 framing now operationalized via LLM debate. Multi-agent debate "Agents argue" N agents propose, critique each other, revise over R rounds, majority-vote. Consensus "They agree" Not epistemic truth — just fraction-on-majority-answer. Can be confidently wrong. Rounds "Exchange steps" One round = each agent reads the others and updates once. Heterogeneous debate "Mix model families" Using different base models to decorrelate errors. Sycophancy cascade "Everyone agrees with the loud one" Debate failure where agents defer to the most confident agent regardless of correctness. NLSOM "129-agent society" Natural-language society of mind; Zhuge et al.'s scaled version. Correlated error "Same model, same bug" Why self-consistency saturates; debate across different views decorrelates. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.66 · Multi-agent systems Problem In plain words first In a multi-agent debate , several copies of a model answer the same question, read each other's answers, and revise over a few rounds. Du et al. (2023) found this beat a single model on reasoning and factuality tasks with strong models. It can also go wrong: agents can talk each other into a shared mistake. Multi-agent systems are introduced in Lesson 14.66 (linked above). This lesson checks the lesson's simulated debate against its own numbers, then runs a real debate between copies of a small model. Self-consistency — sample one model many times and take the majority answer — is the cheapest reasoning improvement you can bolt on. It works, but it saturates fast. You can double your samples and not see another meaningful jump. Debate breaks the saturation. Instead of N independent samples from one model, N agents read each other's reasoning and revise. The correlation between samples drops (they are no longer i.i.d.), and the convergence point is often correct where i.i.d. voting was confidently wrong. Concept The Du et al. 2023 algorithm From arXiv:2305.14325 (ICML 2024): Each of N agents produces an initial answer to the question. For round r = 2..R: each agent is shown the other agents' round r-1 answers and asked "considering these, give your updated answer." After R rounds, majority-vote the final answers. The paper tests on MMLU, GSM8K, biographies, MATH, and factuality benchmarks. Debate consistently beats CoT and Self-Reflection. Two independent knobs Ablations from the same paper: Agent count alone (1 round, majority vote of N) beats single-agent on most tasks, but plateaus. Round count alone (1 agent seeing its own prior reasoning) barely helps — reflection's known weakness. Both together produces the big jumps. The multi-round exchange between multiple agents drives the gain. Why it works Two mechanisms: Exposure to disagreement. When an agent sees another agent's reasoning chain with a different conclusion, it has to either justify or update. Either way, the context for round r+1 is richer than round r. Correlated error reduction. In self-consistency, all samples come from the same model, so the errors correlate — you average into a confidently wrong answer. Different models or different seeds decorrelate. Different debated views decorrelate further. Heterogeneous debate A-HMAD and related follow-ups use different base models for different agents. Llama + Claude + GPT debating reduces monoculture collapse ( Lesson 16.23 ) because the correlated errors of one model family are not shared by the others. Downside: a weak model participating in a debate can drag the consensus toward its wrong answer (see "Should we be going MAD?", arXiv:2311.17371). NLSOM — the 129-agent extension Zhuge et al. ("Mindstorms in Natural Language-Based Societies of Mind," arXiv:2305.17066) scaled this idea to 129-member societies. The result: specialization and self-organization emerge with scale, and the system outperforms single-agent on tasks like visual question answering. Failure modes Sycophancy cascade. All agents defer to whichever agent sounds most confident. The debate collapses to the loudest voice. Prompting for adversarial roles ("one agent must argue the counter-position") helps. Topic drift. Debates over many rounds drift from the original question. Mitigation: re-inject the question every round. Compute blowup. N agents × R rounds = N·R LLM calls, each with a context that grows. A 5-agent, 5-round debate is 25 calls at growing context. Cost per question can exceed 10× a single CoT call. The same idea as a formula The lesson's update is a weighted average. Each agent's next answer is ′ ​ = ∑ j ​ w j ​ x j ​ / ∑ j ​ w j ​ over itself and the others, with weights set by confidence. Repeated, every agent converges to the same weighted mean w ​ . Nothing in the update looks at the truth, so the team ends at w ​ whether or not it is close to it. Averaging cannot beat the best input. The consensus error is w ​ − x ∗ ∣ , where is the truth. One confident outlier with a large weight pulls w ​ far away, while a median of the starting answers ignores it. Majority vote with independent errors. If each of 3 agents is right with probability and errors are independent, a majority is right with probability + 3 p 2 ( 1 − p ) . Debate helps only if seeing others' answers raises each agent's accuracy; if it mostly spreads errors, it can fall below a single agent. Worked example Following one debate A starts at 38.0, B at 42.5 and C at 51.0; the truth is 42.0, and the team mean of 43.83 is off by 1.83. After one round of confidence-weighted averaging the mean is off by 2.24, and after five rounds every agent says 44.5, off by 2.50. B alone started 0.5 away. The debate moved the best agent away from the truth. Majority vote with gives + 3 ( 0.4 5 2 ) ( 0.55 ) ≈ 0.43 , about the same as one agent, so independent copies of a weak model gain little. Solution B1 · Agreement rising, accuracy falling Rising agreement is the symptom, not the goal: the agents are converging on the confident agent's answers. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The most common multi-agent decomposition in 2026: one agent plans, one executes, one critiques or verifies. MetaGPT (arXiv:2308.00352) formalizes this as SOPs encoded into role prompts — Product Manager, Architect, Project Manager, Engineer, QA Engineer — following Code = SOP(Team) . ChatDev (arXiv:2307.07924) chains designer, programmer, reviewer, tester through a "chat chain" with "communicative dehallucination" (agents explicitly request missing details). The verifier is load-bearing: Cemri et al. (MAST, arXiv:2503.13657) find task-verification failures in about a quarter of 1,642 failed multi-agent traces, and argue that stronger verification would catch many of the rest. A CrewAI case study reports PwC's code-generation accuracy rising from about 10% to over 70% after adding agents that generate, run and re-check code. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Role specialization "Different agents, different jobs" Distinct system prompts tuned for planner/executor/critic/verifier roles. SOP pattern "Encoded standard operating procedure" MetaGPT's framing: strict I/O schemas per role turn a team into a pipeline. Communicative dehallucination "Ask before inventing" ChatDev pattern: executor asks planner when a detail is missing rather than making one up. Critic "LLM reviewer" Subjective, opinionated reviewer. Catches taste issues. Can be fooled by plausible prose. Verifier "Deterministic check" Code-based pass/fail. Test runner, type checker, schema validator. Cannot be fooled. Verification gap "No one checked" 21.3% of MAST failures. Answer shipped without a check that would have caught the bug. Revision loop "Critic sends it back" Critic rejection triggers executor re-run with feedback. Needs a budget. All-LLM anti-pattern "Looks good to me" Every role is an LLM, no deterministic check. Classic MAST failure. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.66 · Multi-agent systems Problem In plain words first Role specialization gives each agent one job: a planner writes the spec, an executor does the work, a critic reviews it, and a verifier checks it by running something. Critics are models and can be fooled by work that looks right; verifiers run tests and cannot, as long as the tests are good. Multi-agent systems are introduced in Lesson 14.66 (linked above). This lesson throws wrong executors at the lesson's critic and verifier, then uses a small model as executor and critic with a real test runner. Generic multi-agent systems produce generic output. Three coders in a group chat write three flavors of the same mediocre code. You can add more agents, add more rounds, and still not cross the quality threshold. The fix is not more agents — it is different agents. Assign distinct roles. Give the critic tools the planner does not have. Give the verifier an objective test suite. Now the system has internal disagreement with grounded correction, not just parallel guessing. Concept The four canonical roles Planner. Reads the goal, produces a step list or a spec. Tools: knowledge retrieval, docs. Output: structured plan. Executor. Reads one plan step at a time, produces the artifact. Tools: the actual work tools (code compiler, shell, API client). Output: the artifact. Critic. Reads the executor's output against the planner's intent. Tools: read-only access to the artifact, static analysis. Output: accept/reject with reasons. Verifier. Reads the artifact and runs a deterministic check. Tools: test runner, type checker, schema validator. Output: pass/fail with evidence. Critic is subjective, opinionated, often LLM-based. Verifier is objective, deterministic, often code-based. They are not the same role. MetaGPT's SOP pattern MetaGPT (arXiv:2308.00352) encodes software engineering SOPs as role prompts: Product Manager writes the PRD. Architect produces the system design. Project Manager splits tasks. Engineer implements. QA Engineer runs tests. Each role has a strict input/output schema. The role prompt says what the role is and what it must produce . The Code = SOP(Team) formulation — deterministic SOPs turn a team of LLMs into a predictable pipeline. ChatDev's communicative dehallucination ChatDev adds a key move: when an executor needs a specific detail that was not in the plan, it explicitly asks the designer before continuing. This prevents the classic LLM failure of plausibly inventing the detail. Implementation: the role prompt includes "when you need specific information you were not given, ask the relevant role by name before producing output." Why verifier matters most Cemri et al. (MAST) annotated 1,642 failed multi-agent traces across 7 frameworks. About 23.5% fall under task verification: premature termination, missing or incomplete verification, and incorrect verification. The other categories, system design and inter-agent misalignment, often end in an answer that no one checked properly either. A CrewAI-hosted case study (2025) reports PwC's code-generation accuracy moving from about 10% to over 70% once CrewAI agents that generate, run and repeatedly check code were added. The figures are self-reported and do not isolate the checking step, so treat them as an illustration, not a measurement. Critic vs verifier A critic is an LLM reviewing an artifact for quality. Subjective. Can be fooled by plausible prose. A verifier is a deterministic program running on the artifact. Objective. Gives pass/fail with evidence. Use both. Critic catches taste issues the verifier cannot articulate. Verifier catches bugs the critic cannot see because they show up only at runtime. The anti-pattern Every role in your system is an LLM and every role's output is "looks good to me." Classic MAST failure mode. Add at least one verifier whose pass/fail is decided by code, not by an LLM. Framework mappings CrewAI — Agent(role, goal, backstory) is the textbook specialization surface. LangGraph — nodes can have specialized prompts; edges enforce the pipeline. AutoGen — role-specific ConversableAgents with one-word names in a GroupChat. OpenAI Agents SDK — handoff tools between role-specialized Agents. The same idea as a formula A check only catches what it tests. Let be the intended function and the executor's code. A verifier with test set passes if for all . It can miss a bug only on inputs outside , so a code that memorises passes every time. Hidden tests close that gap. Draw a second set that the executor never sees. A bug that agrees with on but not everywhere is caught when some hits the disagreement; random inputs make that likely for most bugs. Critic plus verifier. If the critic misses a bug with probability ​ and the verifier with ​ , and they fail on different bugs, both miss with probability about ​ m v ​ . A critic that approves everything has ​ = 1 and adds nothing. Worked example Checking one memorised answer The executor returns {(1, 2): 3, (10, 20): 30, (-5, 5): 0}.get((a, b), 0) , a lookup of the spec's three tests. The lesson's critic finds def , return and the right name, so it approves. The verifier runs the three tests: 3, 30 and 0, all right, so it passes. Ten hidden random tests, such as add_two(23, -7) , all return 0, so 10 of 10 fail and the bug is caught. Code that memorised them passed. ✗ "A model critic is better than a pattern-matching one." ✓ The small model approved all five of its own functions, including two that failed tests. ✗ "MAST shows every failure is a verification failure." ✓ About a quarter of its 1,642 failed traces are verification failures; the rest are design and misalignment. Verifier runs the generated code in a sandbox ( exec ) against a test case. Demo runs twice: once where the executor produces correct code (critic + verifier both pass), once where the executor produces off-spec code (critic misses the bug because it looks plausible, verifier catches it because the test fails). Use this before wiring agents into a framework. Break it on purpose Your coding pipeline has a planner, an executor, an LLM critic and a verifier that runs the planner's tests. The executor learns, through repeated retries, to return code that passes the planner's tests exactly, and production bug reports climb. The critic approves every change. Using this lesson, what should you change? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Role frameworks are mature. MetaGPT encodes software SOPs as roles, ChatDev chains roles through a chat chain, and CrewAI and LangGraph make planner, executor and reviewer roles easy to wire. Verification is where systems fail. The MAST taxonomy (presented at NeurIPS 2025) puts about a quarter of failed traces under task verification and recommends explicit verification steps. Coding agents verify by running code. Claude Code, Codex and SWE-agent-style tools run tests and linters after edits; SWE-bench grades by hidden tests the agent does not see. On your laptop : a sandboxed subprocess with no network, as in the block above, is a cheap verifier; keep some tests hidden from the executor's prompt. Sources: Cemri et al., Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (arXiv:2503.13657) , Hong et al., MetaGPT (arXiv:2308.00352) , Qian et al., ChatDev (arXiv:2307.07924) , CrewAI, PwC case study . Recap What to keep from this lesson Split planning, execution, critique and verification into separate roles with separate inputs. A critic, whether code or a model, is fooled by work that looks right. A verifier is only as good as its tests; code can learn to pass a fixed set. Keep hidden tests the executor never sees, and add random or property-based ones. Measure whether your critic ever rejects anything; one that approves everything adds cost, not safety. The planner returns a spec, not prose; the executor reads that schema. Communicative dehallucination. Executor must ask the planner when info is missing; never invent it. Critic/verifier ordering. Run critic first (cheap, catches design issues), verifier second (slow, catches bugs). Loop budget. Max 2 critic-executor revision rounds before escalating to human. outputs/skill-role-designer.md Copy Exercises Run code/main.py and observe how the verifier catches the bug the critic missed. Add a static-analysis check (count occurrences of return ) as an additional verifier. What does it catch that the runtime test misses? Add a 5th role: "requirements analyst" that translates user wish into planner-ready spec. What communicative dehallucination requests should flow up to it? Read MetaGPT Section 3 ("Agents"). List the input/output schema of each of MetaGPT's 5 roles. Read ChatDev's chat-chain diagram (arXiv:2307.07924 Figure 3). Identify where communicative dehallucination breaks a loop that would otherwise be infinite. PwC's reported gain (about 10% to over 70%) came with agents that run and re-check code. Hypothesize three tasks where adding a verifier would not help — where deterministic checking of correctness is impossible or prohibitively expensive. Solutions Solution P1 · Both pass it Yes, and yes. The critic sees a def add_two , a return and the right name. The verifier runs the spec's three tests, (1, 2), (10, 20) and (−5, 5), and the lookup returns 3, 30 and 0, all correct. Ten hidden random tests fail it 10 times out of 10, because it returns 0 for any input it was not built for. Solution B1 · An executor that learned the tests The executor is overfitting the verifier, and the critic is not a real check. Hide tests from the executor. Keep a held-out set, regenerate random inputs on every run, and add property checks, for example that add(a, b) == add(b, a) . Separate who writes the tests from who writes the code. If the planner's tests are in the executor's prompt, the executor can target them. Audit the critic. If it approves 100% of changes, it is not catching anything; measure its rejections against later bug reports, and remove it or replace it. Feed production bugs back as hidden tests so the same mistake cannot pass twice. a1609: Course home / Phase 16 · Multi-Agent Systems and Swarms Swarm, Parallel and Networked Multi-Agent Architectures Lesson 16.9 75 min Learn + Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 16 · 05 (Supervisor Pattern), Phase 16 · 04 (Primitive Model) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, threading , queue ), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Contrast with supervisor: no central decider. Agents read a shared event bus, pick up work asynchronously, write results back. LangGraph has a "swarm" pattern too, though it means agents handing off to each other rather than workers pulling from a queue. Matrix (arXiv:2511.21686) represents both control and data flow as serialized messages passed through distributed queues to eliminate the orchestrator bottleneck. The tradeoff is explicit: determinism and traceability for scalability. Swarm fits tasks with many independent sub-problems; it does not fit tasks that need a single coherent plan. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Swarm architecture "Decentralized agents" Workers pull from shared queue; no central orchestrator. Event bus "Agents subscribe to topics" Message broker that routes tasks to workers by type or content. Starvation "Task never runs" Low-priority task never gets picked because higher-priority work arrives continuously. Hot-spotting "One worker drowns" Load imbalance where one worker gets most tasks. Back-pressure "Slow down the producer" Mechanism that signals upstream to stop producing when the queue fills up. Idempotent worker "Safe to re-run" A task processed twice produces the same result. Required because workers may crash mid-run. Durable queue "Survives crashes" Queue backed by disk or replicated storage; tasks are not lost when a worker crashes. Matrix framework "Full message-passing swarm" Both data and control flow are serialized messages on distributed queues. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.107 · Subgraphs, multi-agent systems and map-reduce Problem In plain words first A swarm has no boss. Workers pull tasks from a shared queue, do them, and write results back, so fast workers simply take more tasks. It balances uneven work well and scales out easily, but there is no single place that knows what happened, and a worker that dies can lose its task unless the queue takes it back. LangGraph subgraphs and map-reduce are covered in Lesson 14.107 (linked above). This lesson kills a worker in the lesson's swarm, then schedules real, uneven model calls four ways. Supervisor scales to a few workers. What about hundreds? The supervisor itself becomes the bottleneck: every decision about who does what funnels through one agent. One slow plan step stalls the whole system. Swarm architectures flip the design. Instead of a central planner dispatching work, workers pick work off a shared queue. The "coordination" is baked into the event bus semantics. No orchestrator; the system scales until the queue does. Concept The shape Copy No orchestrator. Each worker repeats: pull a task, process, write result (and optionally enqueue follow-ups). When swarm fits Many independent tasks. Scraping, transforming, classifying. Tasks do not depend on each other. Variable-duration work. If some tasks take 100ms and others take 10s, a swarm balances load automatically — fast workers pull next jobs. A supervisor has to anticipate duration. Throughput over determinism. You care about total completion time, not strict ordering. When swarm fails Ordered workflows. If step 3 needs step 2's output, a swarm risks step 3 firing before step 2 is done. Global-plan tasks. Complex research questions benefit from a planner. A swarm of researchers produces independent facts, not a coherent report. Debugging. With no central log and asynchronous work, reproducing a bug is expensive. Matrix (arXiv:2511.21686) Matrix is the 2025 paper that takes swarm to its natural conclusion: both control flow and data flow are serialized messages on distributed queues. No central coordinator. Fault tolerance comes from message durability. Scalability is the message broker's problem, not the system's. Contribution: a programming model where multi-agent coordination is "what message topic does this agent subscribe to?" rather than "which agent does the supervisor pick next?" This makes the system look like a pub/sub event mesh. Swarm in graph frameworks LangGraph's langgraph-swarm package uses "swarm" for agents that hand control to each other through handoff tools, with the system remembering which agent was last active. That is decentralised routing between specialists, not the shared work queue built in this lesson; both drop the central supervisor. Failure mode: starvation and hot-spotting If all workers pull the fastest-available task, long-running tasks never get picked until they are the only ones left. Classic queue starvation. Mitigations: - Priority queues with explicit aging (increase priority with wait time). - Worker specialization: some workers only take "long" tasks. - Back-pressure: limit how many fast tasks enter the queue. The content-based routing link Swarm pairs naturally with content-based routing ( Lesson 16.22 ). Instead of a generic queue, have one queue per message type. Specialist workers subscribe only to their type. This is the basis for message-bus architectures that scale to thousands of agents. The same idea as a formula Makespan. With task times ​ , … , d n ​ and workers, no schedule can finish before 1 ​ i ∑ ​ d i ​ , i max ​ d i ​ ) . A shared queue, where each free worker takes the next task, finishes within ​ d i ​ at worst (Graham's list-scheduling bound). Sorting the queue longest-first brings it to within about 4 ​ of the best possible. At-least-once delivery. A queue that takes a task back when its worker dies guarantees every task runs at least once, not exactly once. If the worker died after the side effect but before the acknowledgement, the task runs twice, so tasks must be idempotent. Worked example Scheduling one real workload Twelve real model calls took between 0.4 s and 7.7 s, a 20× spread, and 50.6 s in total. With 4 workers the lower bound is s. Fixed round-robin assignment took 15.6 s, the shared queue 14.8 s, and the queue sorted longest-first 14.3 s. The lesson's queue gains less here than in its demo because round-robin happened to spread the long tasks; it gains most when assignment is unlucky, as in the lesson's pessimal case. Check your mental model ✗ "A shared queue never loses work." ✓ The lesson's queue forgets a task once it is handed out; a crashed worker took task 3 with it. ✗ "Re-queuing on failure gives exactly-once processing." ✓ It gives at-least-once. Task 3 ran twice. ✗ "LangGraph's swarm is a work queue." ✓ It is handoffs between agents with a remembered active agent; the queue pattern here is different. ✗ "Swarms are always much faster than fixed assignment." ✓ With real task times they beat round-robin by about 5%; the big wins come when assignment is badly unbalanced. Predict before you run In the lesson's swarm, a worker's process is killed while it holds task 3. How many of the 12 tasks finish? The lesson's queue does not remember tasks it has handed out, so the task dies with the worker, and the other three workers drain the rest. A task stays owned by the queue until the worker acknowledges it; if the worker dies or times out, it returns to the queue. That fixes the missing summaries. Make the side effect idempotent. In plain words first The idea in one line Shared-conversation orchestration puts N agents in one conversation; a selector function (LLM, round-robin, or custom) picks who speaks next. This is the archetype of emergent multi-agent conversation — agents do not know their role in a static graph, they just react to the shared pool. AutoGen GroupChat and AG2 GroupChat are the reference implementations: AutoGen v0.2's GroupChat semantics were preserved in the AG2 fork; AutoGen v0.4 rewrote it as an event-driven actor model. Microsoft announced Microsoft Agent Framework in October 2025 as the successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, put AutoGen into maintenance, shipped a release candidate in February 2026 and version 1.0 on April 3, 2026. The GroupChat primitive survives in both AG2 and Microsoft Agent Framework — learn it once, use it everywhere. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means GroupChat "Agents in one chat room" Shared message pool + selector function. AutoGen / AG2 primitive. Speaker selection "Who talks next" The function that picks the next agent. Round-robin, LLM-selected, or custom. GroupChatManager "The meeting host" AutoGen component that owns the selector and loops over turns. ConversableAgent "The base agent" AutoGen base class; an agent that can send and receive messages. Termination token "The 'stop' word" Sentinel string (usually TERMINATE ) that ends the chat. Hot speaker "One agent dominates" Failure mode where the selector keeps picking the same agent. Context bloat "Pool grows unbounded" Each agent reads every prior message; context grows with turns. Projection "Scoped view" Role-specific view into the shared pool to prevent context bloat. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.121 · Microsoft Agent Framework Problem In plain words first In a group chat , several agents share one conversation and a selector decides who speaks next: in turn (round-robin), by rules, or by asking a model. The chat stops when someone says a stop word such as TERMINATE, or after a set number of turns. Microsoft Agent Framework, which carries this pattern on from AutoGen, is covered in Lesson 14.121 (linked above). This lesson checks what the lesson's chat actually ships, adds a safer stop rule, and lets a small model be the selector. Static graphs (LangGraph) are great when the workflow is known. Real conversations are not static: sometimes the coder asks the reviewer, sometimes the researcher, sometimes the writer. Hardcoding every possible handoff produces an edge explosion. You want agents reacting to a shared pool , with some function deciding who talks next. That is exactly what AutoGen GroupChat does. Concept The shape Copy Every agent sees every message. A selector function is invoked at each turn to pick who speaks next. The three selector flavors Round-robin. Fixed cycle. Deterministic. Scales linearly in N but ignores context — a coder gets the turn even when the topic is legal review. LLM-selected. A call to an LLM that reads the recent pool and returns the best next speaker. Context-aware but slow: every turn adds an LLM call. AutoGen's default. Custom. A Python function with whatever logic you want. Typical: LLM-selected with fallback rules (e.g., "always give the verifier the turn after the coder"). The ConversableAgent API Copy GroupChatManager holds the selector. When an agent completes a turn, the manager calls the selector, which returns the next agent. Loop continues until a termination condition. Termination Three common patterns: Max rounds. Hard cap on total turns. "TERMINATE" token. Agents can emit a sentinel message; the manager stops when one appears. Goal-reached check. A lightweight verifier runs each turn and stops the chat when done. Lineage: forks and mergers In early 2025, Microsoft began a major rewrite of AutoGen (v0.4) around an event-driven actor model. The community forked AutoGen v0.2's GroupChat semantics as AG2, preserving the API that early adopters had integrated. In October 2025 Microsoft announced that AutoGen would go into maintenance mode, with its event-driven actor model carried into Microsoft Agent Framework , which merges AutoGen and Semantic Kernel (release candidate February 2026, version 1.0 April 3, 2026). The GroupChat concept survives in both tracks; the implementation details differ. AG2 is the preferred upstream for v0.2-compatible code. When GroupChat fits Emergent conversations. You do not want to pre-wire every possible next-speaker. Role-mixing tasks. Coder asks researcher, researcher asks archivist, archivist asks coder back. Flow is not a DAG. Exploratory problem-solving. Think "brainstorm meeting," not "assembly line." When it fails Strict determinism. The LLM selector can be inconsistent. Same prompt, different runs, different next speakers. Sycophancy cascades. Agents defer to whoever spoke most confidently. Counter-prompt explicitly. Context bloat. Every agent reads every message; after 10 turns the context is huge. Use projections ( Lesson 16.15 ) to scope views. Hot speakers. One agent dominates the conversation because the selector favors its specialties. Introduce speaker balance as a selector feature. Group chat vs supervisor Same primitives, different defaults: Supervisor: one agent plans and others execute. Selector is "ask the planner what to do." Group chat: all agents are peers; selector is a function over the shared pool. Both use the four primitives from Lesson 04. Group chat defaults to LLM-selected orchestration and full-pool shared state. The same idea as a formula A selector is a policy over speakers. Constraints remove bad moves; they do not make the choice among the remaining ones good. A stop rule is a predicate on the pool. "Stop when anyone says TERMINATE" is . A safer rule ties stopping to the outcome: Worked example Reading one round-robin chat The coder writes buggy code, return a - b . The reviewer flags it: "please fix". Round-robin gives the next turn to the manager, which says "continue working". The coder's policy looks at the last message from someone else, which is now the manager's, does not see the review, and says TERMINATE. The chat stops after 4 messages with the buggy code as its result. The lesson's printout reports this as a normal stop. Check your mental model ✗ "Any agent saying TERMINATE means the work is done." ✓ Round-robin stopped on the coder's TERMINATE with the buggy code unreviewed. ✗ "A guard on stopping fixes a bad selector." ✓ It stops a bad result from shipping; the round-robin chat then ran out its 10 turns with the bug still there. ✗ "An LLM selector understands the workflow." ✓ Free to choose, the small model picked the manager ten times in a row. ✗ "Allowed transitions make LLM selection reliable." ✓ They kept it to legal moves, but it chose the manager instead of the coder after every review, so the bug was never fixed. Predict before you run The lesson's round-robin chat stops after four messages. What code does it leave in the pool, and had the reviewer approved it? (Solution P1.) See it drawn What the lesson's group chat ships The lesson's agents and both selectors, judged by the final code in the pool and whether the reviewer approved it. Then the same chats under a stop rule that refuses TERMINATE until the latest code is approved. Runs in under a second. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Round-robin ships the bug. It stops after 4 messages on the coder's TERMINATE, with return a - b as the final code and no approval. The manager's turn came between the review and the coder, so the coder never saw the request to fix it. The context-aware selector ships the fix. It sends the review back to the coder, gets return a + b , has it approved, and lets the manager stop after 6 messages. A guarded stop rule blocks the bad result. Requiring the reviewer's approval of the latest code turns round-robin's early TERMINATE into "stop refused". The chat then runs out its 10 turns with the bug still in place, which is a visible failure instead of a silent one. The context-aware chat is unaffected. The reviewer flagged it, but under round-robin the manager spoke next, and the coder, reading the manager's "continue working", said TERMINATE. The lesson's chat stops on any TERMINATE, so it ended with unapproved, wrong code, and its printout gives no warning. Solution B1 · TERMINATE without approval The chat stops on a word, not on an outcome, and round-robin puts the wrong agent after the fact-check. Make stopping conditional: accept TERMINATE only when the fact-checker's last verdict on the latest draft is "approved". Route on content: after a fact-check that asks for changes, the next speaker must be the writer, not the editor. Use a rule or allowed transitions, not round-robin. Log and test outcomes: count articles published with an open fact-check, and treat any above zero as a bug. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Weigh a trade-off Four agents, a coder, a reviewer, a tester and a researcher, share one conversation. You must decide how the next speaker is chosen on each turn. The options on the table are a fixed rotation, a model that reads the recent messages and picks, and letting the current agent name its successor. Compare them and say what you would ship with each. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A fixed rotation is deterministic and cheap, and it gives the coder the turn when the topic is a legal question. A model selector is context-aware, and it costs one extra model call per turn, picks differently on identical input, and tends to favor one agent. A handoff by the current agent keeps the routing in the prompts with no external manager, and it is the pattern that loops when two prompts disagree. Most production chats use a selector with fallback rules, a round cap, a termination signal and a log of every selection. The three selectors. Selector Strength Weakness Round-robin Deterministic, no extra calls, scales linearly in agents Ignores context, so the wrong agent gets the turn Model-selected Reads the pool and picks the best next speaker One extra call per turn, inconsistent across runs, and it can favor a hot speaker Current agent hands off No manager, routing lives in each prompt Two prompts can form a cycle, and an injected message can force a handoff Who decides, and where. The difference between the second and the third is where the decision lives. In a group chat the selector sits outside the agents and reads the shared pool. In the handoff pattern the active agent decides by calling a tool that returns the next agent. A manager outside can see an alternation between two agents and break it. An agent inside the loop cannot. What goes wrong in a group chat. Nondeterminism. The same pool gives different next speakers on different runs, which hurts audit and replay. Deference cascades. Agents follow whoever spoke most confidently, so the prompts must say when to disagree. Context growth. Every agent reads every message, and after about 10 turns the pool is large, so give each agent a scoped view. One agent dominates. The selector keeps picking the agent whose specialty matches the recent messages, so track turns per agent and alert on imbalance. What to ship. A round cap, 10 to 20 for a typical task. A termination signal: a sentinel token from an agent, or a verifier that checks the goal each turn. A speaker-balance metric, with an alert when one agent takes too many turns. A custom selector that combines the model's pick with rules such as "the tester speaks after the coder". A log of the selector's input and its choice, because without it a wrong selection cannot be debugged. When each one fits. A fixed rotation fits a staged pipeline where the order is known. A model selector fits an exploratory conversation where the flow is not a graph. Handoffs fit triage, where a front agent routes a user to one specialist and the conversation is short. Plausible wrong answers. "Use the model selector, because it understands the conversation." It also adds a call per turn, picks inconsistently, and favors one agent unless rules and a balance metric constrain it. "Round-robin is fair, so it is safe." Fair turns are not useful turns, and a coder speaking on a legal question wastes a round and adds noise to the pool. "Let the agents decide among themselves." That is the handoff pattern, and it is the one that forms cycles and that an injected message can steer. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the model selector need a log of its input as well as its output? Expected: the choice depends on what the selector saw, and without the input a reviewer cannot tell whether the pick was wrong or the pool was. (level 2) What does a verifier-based termination add over a sentinel token? Expected: the chat stops when a check passes, not when an agent claims it is done, which removes early termination by a confident agent. (level 3) Which of the three makes prompt injection worse, and why? Expected: the handoff pattern, because the deciding tool call is made by the agent that just read the injected text, while an external selector can apply rules the agents do not control. (level 3) How does a custom selector fix the hot-speaker problem without losing context awareness? Expected: let the model propose, then apply a rule that caps consecutive turns per agent and forces the verifier or a quiet agent in. Where it is taught. The group chat lesson builds the three selectors and the termination rules, and the handoffs and routines lesson contrasts the manager's decision with the agent's. In plain words first The idea in one line OpenAI's Swarm (October 2024) distilled multi-agent orchestration to two primitives: routines (instructions + tools as a system prompt) and handoffs (a tool that returns another Agent). No state machine, no branching DSL — the LLM routes by calling the right handoff tool. The OpenAI Agents SDK (March 2025) is the production successor. Swarm itself remains the cleanest conceptual reference — its entire source fits in a few hundred lines. The pattern is viral because the API surface is roughly "agent = prompt + tools; handoff = function returning agent." Limitation: stateless, so memory is the caller's problem. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Routine "The agent prompt" System prompt + tool list. Defines role and available handoffs. Handoff "Transfer to another agent" A tool the active agent can call that returns a new Agent. The runtime switches active agent. Stateless "No memory between runs" Swarm does not persist anything; memory is the caller's responsibility. Active agent "Who's speaking now" The agent currently holding the conversation. Handoff changes this. Context transfer "What moves on handoff" Policy for what history the incoming agent sees: full, last N, or summarized. Handoff loop "Agents ping-pong" Failure mode where two agents keep handing back to each other. OpenAI Agents SDK "Production Swarm" March 2025 successor; adds sessions, guardrails, tracing on top of the handoff primitive. Handoff filter "Gate on transfer" SDK feature to inspect and modify context at the handoff boundary. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.118 · OpenAI Agents SDK II: handoffs, run context, streaming, tests and tracing Problem In plain words first A handoff is a tool an agent can call that passes the conversation to another agent; a routine is an agent's instructions plus its tools. OpenAI's Swarm (2024) showed that this is enough to build multi-agent apps: a triage agent hands refund requests to a refund agent, and so on. The OpenAI Agents SDK is its production successor. Handoffs, run context and tracing in that SDK are covered in Lesson 14.118 (linked above). This lesson tests the lesson's handoff router on realistic requests, then lets a small model route by calling the handoff tools. Every multi-agent framework wants you to learn its DSL: LangGraph nodes and edges, CrewAI crews and tasks, AutoGen GroupChat and managers. The DSLs are real abstractions, but they make the thing feel heavier than it needs to be. Swarm pushes in the opposite direction: use the tool-calling capability the model already has. Handoffs become tool calls. The orchestrator is whichever agent currently holds the conversation. The state machine is implicit in the agents' system prompts. Concept Two primitives Routine. A system prompt that defines an agent's role and available tools. Think of it like a scoped set of instructions: "you are a triage agent; if the user asks about refunds, hand off to the refund agent." Handoff. A tool the agent can call that returns a new Agent object. The Swarm runtime detects the Agent return value and switches the active agent for the next turn. That is the entire abstraction. Copy The triage agent's system prompt makes it choose the right handoff based on the user message. The LLM's tool-calling does the routing. Why it is viral Small API. Two concepts to learn. Uses what the model already does. Tool calling is already production-grade across providers. No state-machine burden. You do not describe the graph; the agents' prompts describe who they hand off to. The stateless trade Swarm is explicitly stateless between runs. The framework keeps a message history during a run, but it does not persist anything. Memory, continuity, long-running tasks — all the caller's problem. In production (OpenAI Agents SDK, March 2025) this was one of the main things that changed: the SDK adds built-in session management, guardrails, and tracing while keeping the handoff primitive. When Swarm/handoffs fit Triage patterns. Front-line agent routes user to a specialist. Skill-based handoffs. "If the task needs code, call the coder; if it needs research, call the researcher." Short, bounded conversations. Customer support, FAQ-to-ticket, simple workflows. When Swarm struggles Long sessions with shared memory. Handoffs reset the conversation state to the new agent's prompt plus history. No persistent state across agents without caller-managed memory. Parallel execution. Handoff is one-at-a-time — the active agent switches. Parallelism requires the caller orchestrating multiple Swarm runs. Audit and replay. Stateless runs are hard to replay exactly; the LLM's handoff choice is not deterministic. OpenAI Agents SDK (March 2025) The production successor adds: Session state. Persistent thread across runs. Guardrails. Input/output validation hooks. Tracing. Every tool call and handoff is logged. Handoff filters. Control what context transfers on handoff. The handoff primitive survives; production ergonomics get added around it. Swarm vs GroupChat Both use LLM-driven routing, but they differ on who picks next : GroupChat: a selector (function or LLM) picks the next speaker from outside. Swarm: the current agent picks its successor by calling a handoff tool. Swarm is "agent decides what's next"; GroupChat is "manager decides what's next." Swarm's decision lives in the active agent's tool call; GroupChat's lives in the GroupChatManager . The same idea as a formula Routing is classification. The triage agent maps a message to a handoff . With labelled messages, its accuracy is the share of with equal to the right team, and "none" counts as a miss when a team was needed. The active agent is state. After a handoff, the active agent ​ handles every later message until some agent hands off again: ​ = h a t ​ ​ ( x t + 1 ​ ) if ​ can hand off, else ​ = a t ​ . If the receiving agent has no way to hand back, every later message goes to it. Defaults are decisions. A tool argument filled with a default when the user gave none, like an order id, is an action the user never requested. Worked example Tracing one two-message conversation "I need a refund on order 77": triage hands off to refund, which processes order 77. "also, my dashboard is broken": the active agent is still refund. Its router has only process_refund , and with no order number in the message it uses the default, 42. Result: a second refund, for an order the user never mentioned, and no support ticket. The fix is a handoff back to triage, or a transfer tool to support, on every specialist. Solution B1 · Sticky specialists and default actions Two problems: specialists that never hand back, and an action taken from a passing mention. Give every specialist a way out: a transfer_to_triage tool, or transfer tools to the other specialists, and instructions to use them when the request is outside their scope. Route each new topic: on every user message, let triage (or a cheap classifier) check whether the active agent still fits. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure A support system uses handoff-driven orchestration: each agent is a prompt plus a set of tools, and one of the tools returns another agent. The trace shows the triage agent handing a user to billing, billing handing the user back to triage, and the two repeating until the round cap ends the run. The user never got an answer. Why does this happen, and what is the cheap fix? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. In this pattern the routing lives in the prompts, and the current agent picks its successor with a tool call. The triage prompt says that a billing question goes to billing, and the billing prompt says that anything outside its tools returns to triage, and the user's message satisfies both. Nothing persists between handoffs, so the new agent starts from its prompt and the history and does not know that the same handoff already failed. The cheap fix is a loop detector on the last few handoffs that forces an exit to a fallback agent, plus a trace event for every handoff. Why the pattern loops. The two primitives are the routine, a system prompt that defines a role and its tools, and the handoff, a tool that returns the next agent. The framework's only job is to see the agent-valued return and switch. There is no graph and no state machine. The routing is whatever the prompts say, and two prompts can describe a cycle without anyone writing one. The pattern is stateless between runs, and within a run the only memory is the message history, which the agents do not read for a repeated pattern. Find it in the trace. A handoff loop is two agents alternating with no user turn and no tool result between them. Read the handoff events for the pair. If each handoff carries the same reason, the prompts disagree about who owns the case. The cheap fix. Loop detection. Keep the last few handoffs in a ring. When the same two agents have handed off three times in a row, force an exit. A fallback agent. The exit goes to a safe default that can answer or escalate to a human. The same fallback catches a handoff to an agent that does not exist. Handoff logging. Every handoff writes an event with the sender, the receiver and a context snapshot, so the loop is visible before the cap. The real fix. Fix the prompts so that exactly one agent owns each case, and give the billing agent a tool that handles the case instead of a reason to send it back. Decide what context transfers on each handoff: the full history is expensive, the last N messages lose the reason, and a summary written by the outgoing agent is the usual middle. The production successor of this pattern adds sessions, guardrails and tracing around the same primitive, and a handoff filter that controls what the incoming agent sees. The security angle. A handoff to an agent with different tool permissions must be authenticated, because a message that the user did not write, such as text pulled from a document, can ask for a handoff to a more capable agent. Treat a handoff as a permission change, not a routing detail. Plausible wrong answers. "Raise the round cap so the agents have time to settle." The cap is what ended the loop, and more rounds give more of the same two handoffs. "Tell triage never to accept a handoff from billing." That blocks a legitimate return when billing really cannot help, and the fix is clear ownership plus a detector. "Switch to a graph framework and the problem disappears." A graph can encode the same cycle with two edges, and the loop detector is useful in both. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the billing agent not notice that it already sent this user back once? Expected: it is stateless and starts from its prompt plus the history, and nothing in the loop reads the history for a repeated handoff. (level 2) What should the fallback agent do? Expected: answer with what it can, or hand the case to a human with the trace, and never hand off to either agent in the loop. (level 3) How do you choose what context moves on a handoff? Expected: full history when the case is short, a summary written by the outgoing agent when it is long, and never nothing, because the incoming agent then repeats the questions. (level 3) How does a group chat with a selector avoid this specific loop? Expected: the selector sits outside the agents and can see the alternation, while in the handoff pattern the agent that is looping is the one making the decision. Where it is taught. The handoffs and routines lesson builds the handoff loop and lists loop detection and the fallback agent in its checklist. In plain words first The idea in one line Google announced A2A in April 2025; by April 2026 the spec is at https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/ and 150+ organizations back it. A2A is the horizontal complement to MCP ( Lesson 16.13 ): where MCP is vertical (agent ↔ tools), A2A is peer-to-peer (agent ↔ agent). It defines Agent Cards (discovery), tasks with artifacts (text, structured data, video), opaque task lifecycles, and auth. Production systems increasingly pair MCP with A2A. Google Cloud rolled A2A support into Vertex AI Agent Builder during 2025-2026. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means A2A "Agent-to-agent" Peer protocol for agents to call other agents across systems. Google 2025. Agent Card "The agent's business card" JSON at /.well-known/agent-card.json describing skills, supportedInterfaces , auth. Task "The unit of work" Async stateful object with a lifecycle; artifacts produced on completion. Artifact "The result" Typed output: text, structured JSON, image, video, audio. First-class media. Opaque lifecycle "How it's solved is the agent's business" Client sees state transitions; server is free to choose framework/tools. Discovery "Finding the agent" GET /.well-known/agent-card.json returns the card. MCP vs A2A "Tools vs peers" MCP: vertical agent ↔ tool. A2A: horizontal agent ↔ agent. ACP / ANP / NLIP "Sibling protocols" Adjacent specs; A2A is the most-adopted 2026. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 16.29 · A2A, AG-UI and the rest of the protocol stack Problem In plain words first A2A (Agent2Agent) lets an agent call another agent over HTTP, whoever built it. The remote agent publishes an Agent Card describing its skills; the caller sends a message, gets back a task with a state, and reads the result as artifacts . How the remote agent does the work stays hidden. A2A, AG-UI and the rest of the protocol stack are covered in Lesson 16.29 (linked above). This lesson probes the lesson's A2A server with requests its demo does not send, then puts a small model behind it. Your agent needs to call another agent on another system. How? You can expose an HTTP endpoint, define a bespoke JSON schema, and hope the other side speaks it. Every pair of agents becomes a custom integration. A2A is the universal wire protocol for that call. Standard discovery, standard task model, standard transport, standard artifacts. Like HTTP+REST but for agents as first-class citizens. Concept The four elements Agent Card. A JSON document at /.well-known/agent-card.json describing the agent: name, skills, supportedInterfaces (endpoint URL, protocol binding, protocol version), default input and output media types, and auth requirements ( securitySchemes plus securityRequirements ). Discovery happens by reading the card. Copy Copy Task. The unit of work. An async, stateful object with a lifecycle: TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED → TASK_STATE_WORKING → TASK_STATE_COMPLETED / TASK_STATE_FAILED / TASK_STATE_CANCELED . A client sends a message, the server creates the task, and the client polls or subscribes for updates. Artifact. The result type produced by a task. Text, structured JSON, image, video, audio. Artifacts are typed: each part carries one of text , raw , url , or data and can name its mediaType , so different modalities are first-class. Opaque lifecycle. A2A does not prescribe how the remote agent solves the task. The client sees state transitions and artifacts; the implementation is free to use any framework. The MCP/A2A split MCP ( Lesson 16.13 ): agent ↔ tool. The agent reads/writes via JSON-RPC to a tool server. Stateless by default. A2A : agent ↔ agent. Peer protocol; both sides are agents with their own reasoning. Production multi-agent systems use both. An A2A peer calls MCP tools on its side. The split keeps the two concerns clean. Discovery flow These are the HTTP+JSON binding routes, and every request carries A2A-Version: 1.0 . By default SendMessage blocks until the task reaches a terminal or interrupted state, so a polling client sets configuration.returnImmediately to get the task back at once. Or with streaming: POST /message:stream returns Server-Sent Events (a task first, then statusUpdate and artifactUpdate events), and /tasks/{id}:subscribe reattaches to a running task. The stream closes when the task reaches a terminal state; there is no final flag. Auth A2A supports three common patterns: Bearer token : OAuth2 or opaque ( httpAuthSecurityScheme or oauth2SecurityScheme ). mTLS : mutual TLS; organizations prove identity to each other ( mtlsSecurityScheme ). API key : a key in a header, query parameter, or cookie ( apiKeySecurityScheme ). Auth is declared in the Agent Card: securitySchemes names each scheme and securityRequirements says which ones a client must satisfy. Clients discover and comply. 150+ organizations by April 2026 Enterprise adoption drove A2A scale. The headline: A2A became the way enterprise agent systems cross trust boundaries. Google Cloud shipped Vertex AI Agent Builder A2A support; Microsoft Agent Framework supports it; most major frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen) ship A2A adapters. Where A2A wins Cross-organization calls. Agent at company A calls agent at company B. Without A2A, every pair is a bespoke contract. Heterogeneous frameworks. LangGraph agent calls CrewAI agent calls custom Python agent. A2A normalizes. Typed artifacts. Video result, structured JSON, audio — all first-class. Long-running tasks. Opaque lifecycle + polling makes hours-long tasks straightforward. Where A2A struggles Latency-sensitive micro-calls. A2A's lifecycle is async. Sub-millisecond agent-to-agent does not fit; use direct RPC. Tight-coupled in-process agents. If both agents run in the same Python process, A2A's HTTP round-trip is overkill. Small teams. Spec overhead is real; internal-only agents may not need the formality. A2A vs ACP, ANP, NLIP Several related specs emerged in 2024-2026: ACP (IBM/Linux Foundation) — predecessor to A2A, narrower scope. ANP (Agent Network Protocol) — peer-discovery-heavy, decentralized-first. NLIP (Ecma Natural Language Interaction Protocol, standardized December 2025) — natural-language content type. A2A is the most-adopted peer protocol as of April 2026. See arXiv:2505.02279 (Ehtesham et al., "A Survey of Agent Interoperability Protocols") for the comparison. The same idea as a formula Who may read a task. A task id with random bits is hard to guess, about tries. But if the server returns any task to anyone who presents its id, the id is the only key, and ids leak through logs, URLs and error reports. Safe access checks both: Shape is not meaning. A client can check that an artifact parses into the promised schema, . That says nothing about whether the issues listed are the real ones. Worked example Following one leaked id Client A submits code containing API_KEY = 'sk-live-123' for review and gets a task id of 8 hex characters, 32 bits. The id appears in A's logs. Client B, with no credentials, calls GET /tasks/{id} with that id. The lesson's server returns HTTP 200 with the full history, including A's code and its key. With the Agent Card's securityRequirements empty, nothing in the protocol stops this; an auth scheme in the card and an owner check on the server would. a1613: Course home / Phase 16 · Multi-Agent Systems and Swarms Blackboard Architectures and Shared Memory for Agents Lesson 16.13 75 min Learn + Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 16 · 04 (Primitive Model), Phase 16 · 09 (Parallel Swarm Networks) Type : Learn + Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, threading ), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Two approaches coexist in 2026 multi-agent systems: the message pool (everyone sees everyone's messages, as in AutoGen's GroupChat; MetaGPT adds role-based subscription on top) and the blackboard with subscription (agents subscribe to relevant events, close to Context-Aware MCP's shared context store). Both are the only stateful part of a multi-agent system — which means both are where the interesting bugs live. The reference failure mode is memory poisoning : one agent hallucinates a "fact," other agents treat it as verified, and accuracy decays gradually in a way that is much harder to debug than an immediate crash. This lesson builds both structures from stdlib, injects a poisoning attack, and shows the three mitigations that actually work in production. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Message pool "Shared chat history" Append-only log that every agent reads. Full transparency, poor scaling. Blackboard "Shared workspace" Topic-keyed pub/sub. Agents subscribe to relevant topics. Scales farther. Provenance "Who wrote what" Metadata on each write: writer, timestamp, prompt, sources. Memory poisoning "Hallucinations spreading" One agent's error enters shared state, downstream agents adopt it as fact. Append-only "No in-place updates" Corrections are new entries that supersede. Preserves audit trail. Unwritable verifier "Independent auditor" Read-only agent that re-fetches sources and flags inconsistencies. Projection "Scoped view" Per-agent view computed from global state. LangGraph's per-node input and private state schemas are one implementation. Knowledge Source "Specialist agent" Hayes-Roth's 1985 term for a blackboard participant.
