Lesson 14.65 · Memory II: long-term, episodic and procedural memory Lesson 14.105 · Memory: trimming threads and the long-term store Problem In plain words first When several agents work on one task, they need a shared place to put what they found. A message pool is a shared log that every agent reads. A blackboard splits the shared space into topics, and each agent sees only the topics it subscribes to. Either way, one agent's mistake can be read by every other agent as a fact. Memory for a single agent (trimming threads and the long-term store) is covered in Lessons 14.65 and 14.105 (linked above). This lesson tests the lesson's pool, blackboard and verifier on writes its demo does not make, adds lineage so a flag reaches derived entries, and tries a small model as summarizer and as verifier. Multi-agent systems need a place for agents to share facts. A literal option is "pass everything in messages" — but that reinvents shared state with extra copying. Another is "give everyone a global log" — but global logs grow unbounded and poison easily. A third is "project a view per agent" — scalable but schema-heavy. When one of the agents hallucinates and writes the hallucination to shared state, every downstream agent that reads that state adopts the hallucination as fact. By the time the human notices, the reasoning chain is five steps deep and the root cause is the third message ever written. Debugging multi-agent accuracy decay is harder than debugging a crash. This is memory poisoning. MAST (Cemri et al., arXiv:2503.13657) does not name it; its closest failure modes are information withholding, ignoring other agents' input, and missing or incorrect verification. OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications (December 2025) lists it as ASI06, Memory and Context Poisoning. It is structural: any shared-memory design without provenance and an unwritable verifier will exhibit it eventually. Concept The two main topologies Full message pool. Every agent reads every message. AutoGen's GroupChat uses this. MetaGPT starts from a shared pool but lets each role subscribe to the messages its profile needs, which is closer to the blackboard below. Simple, transparent, inspectable, but does not scale past ~10 agents because each agent's context fills with other agents' work. Copy Blackboard with subscription. Agents declare interest in topics; the substrate routes only relevant messages. CA-MCP (arXiv:2601.11595) uses a central Shared Context Store that servers read, write and watch for trigger flags. Matrix (arXiv:2511.21686, from Meta) has no shared board at all: each task's state travels as a message through per-role queues. Scales further, but requires upfront schema design to make subscriptions meaningful. Copy When each wins Full pool wins when agents are few (< 10), heterogeneous, and the conversation is short-horizon. Reasoning about who said what is trivial when everyone sees everything. Blackboard wins when agents are many, homogeneous in role but numerous in instance (swarms), and the conversation is long-running. Routing saves token cost and context pollution. Production systems often mix: a small full pool at the top (planning layer), blackboards below (worker layer). Memory poisoning, in one scenario Three agents work on a research task. Agent A is a retrieval agent. Agent B is a summarizer. Agent C is an analyst. A fetches a page and writes a message to shared state: "The study reports a 42% accuracy improvement." The fetched page actually said "4.2% improvement." A hallucinated a decimal. B, reading shared state, writes: "Large 42% accuracy gain reported (source: A)." C, reading shared state, writes: "Recommend adoption — 42% lift is transformative." The final report cites a 42% number that never existed. No agent crashed. No test failed. The system "worked." The hallucination crossed from one agent's context into every downstream agent's reasoning via shared state. Why this is structural Without shared state, agent A's hallucination stays in A's context. Downstream agents would re-fetch or re-derive and might catch the error. With naive shared state, A's context becomes everyone's context, and the hallucination is laundered into fact. The problem is not shared state per se — it is shared state without provenance and without an independent verifier . Three mitigations address this: Attribute provenance on every write. Every entry in shared state records who wrote it, when, under what prompt, and (if applicable) what source the agent cited. Downstream agents read with skepticism keyed to provenance. Version writes; treat them as append-only. A correction is a new entry that supersedes the old, not an in-place update. The audit trail is preserved. Keep at least one agent that cannot write to shared state. A read-only verifier agent samples entries, re-fetches sources, and flags inconsistencies. It still reads the pool, so it can be fooled by a bad entry, but it checks each entry against the original source and cannot write, so its verdicts never feed a poisoned fact back into shared state. Blackboard precedent (Hayes-Roth, 1985) The blackboard pattern predates LLM agents by about five decades. It comes from the Hearsay-II speech-understanding system of the 1970s (Erman et al., 1980), where specialist Knowledge Sources observe a global blackboard, contribute partial solutions, and trigger other sources. Hayes-Roth (1985, "A Blackboard Architecture for Control") extended it to control: deciding which Knowledge Source acts next. CA-MCP's shared context store is the same pattern with LLM agents and MCP servers as Knowledge Sources and JSON blobs as partial solutions. The old literature has documented solutions to write contention, opportunistic control, and consistency that modern systems rediscover. Projection vs full view A pure blackboard gives every subscriber the same projection (topic-scoped). A more aggressive design is per-agent projection : each agent gets a view customized to its role. In LangGraph, nodes and subgraphs can declare their own input and private state schemas, so each sees only a slice of the graph's state. Reducers handle the other direction: how updates from several nodes merge back into the shared state. Per-agent projection scales further but needs a schema. Without one, you rebuild ad-hoc projection in every agent's prompt. Write-contention patterns Multiple agents writing simultaneously is a concurrency problem, not just an LLM problem. Three patterns work: Sequential writer (single producer). All writes go through one coordinator agent that serializes. Simple, but a bottleneck. Optimistic concurrency with versioning. Each entry has a version; writers fail on version mismatch and retry. Classic database technique. Topic partitioning. Different agents own different topics. No cross-topic contention. Requires designed partition boundaries. Many frameworks run one writer at a time, because LLM calls are slow enough that contention is rare and the bottleneck does not hurt. LangGraph runs nodes in parallel instead, and raises an INVALID_CONCURRENT_GRAPH_UPDATE error when two nodes write the same key in one step without a reducer to merge them. The unwritable verifier The most load-bearing mitigation is the read-only verifier. Implementation rules: Verifier shares state with the team (reads the blackboard or pool). Verifier has no write handle to shared state — only to a separate verification channel. Verifier independently fetches sources cited in writes. Flags disagreement. Verifier's own outputs are routed to a human or a separate decision agent, never fed back into the pool. Without this separation, the verifier's outputs become new entries in the pool, which means a poisoned pool poisons the verifier, which poisons its verifications. The same idea as a formula Lineage. Give every entry the set of entries it was built from, . An entry is tainted if it was flagged or if any parent is tainted: ⋁ ​ taint ( p ) . A flag on the root then reaches every summary and verdict built on it. Without parents, a flag stops at the entry it was put on. Two ways a verifier errs. Over writes, a verifier flags honest writes (false positives, ) and passes wrong ones (false negatives, ). Its accuracy is . Exact string matching has for cited writes and a large , since any honest paraphrase fails; it has no view of uncited writes at all. Worked example Following one flag through the pool Entry 0: the retriever writes "42% accuracy improvement", citing paper-1. Entry 1: the summarizer builds on entry 0 and cites nothing. The verifier re-fetches paper-1, sees "4.2%", and flags entry 0. The analyst reads only summaries. Entry 1 has no flag, so it recommends adoption. With lineage, entry 1 records parents , so . The analyst has no clean summary and waits for a corrected retrieval. Recap What to keep from this lesson A message pool shares everything; a blackboard shares by topic. Both let one agent's error become everyone's fact. Record provenance and lineage on every write, so a flag reaches everything built on the flagged entry. Keep the log append-only; corrections supersede, they do not overwrite. A verifier that matches text exactly flags honest paraphrases and cannot see uncited claims; check facts, not strings. Isolate subscriber failures, and let late subscribers replay a topic. Solution B1 · An uncited claim with no lineage How it got through. The analyst wrote the table from three summaries and cited no source, so the verifier, which only re-fetches cited sources, had nothing to check. Either the analyst invented the figure or a summary blended two documents; without lineage, nobody can tell which, and hiding flagged entries does nothing when no entry was flagged. What would have stopped it: - Lineage on every write: derived_from lists the entries a write was built on, so the table points at its three summaries and each summary at its sources. - Check claims, not entries: extract each number or named fact in a write and require it to appear in some ancestor or a cited source; "98%" appears in none. - Uncited claims are unverified: treat a write with no source and no parents as a draft that cannot reach a report. - Taint downstream: when any ancestor is flagged later, re-check or withdraw everything built on it. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure Three agents share a memory on a research task. A retrieval agent reads a page and writes that a study found a 42 percent improvement. The page says 4.2 percent. A summarizer builds on the entry, an analyst recommends adoption on the strength of the number, and the final report cites it. No agent crashed and no test failed. What is this failure called, why is it structural, and what are the three changes that stop it? Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. This is memory poisoning. One agent's hallucination entered the shared state, and every agent downstream read it as a verified fact, so the error was turned into evidence as it moved. It is structural because any shared memory without provenance and without an independent verifier will do this eventually. The three changes are provenance on every write, an append-only log where corrections supersede instead of overwrite, and at least one read-only verifier that re-fetches sources and reports on a separate channel. Why it is worse than a crash. Without shared state, the retrieval agent's error stays in its own context, and a downstream agent that re-fetches the page might catch it. With shared state, the first agent's context becomes everyone's context. The symptom is a slow decay of accuracy, not a failure. By the time a human notices, the reasoning chain is several steps deep and the root cause is one of the first entries ever written. The lesson places this family second in the measured taxonomy of multi-agent failures. The three mitigations. Change What it does Provenance on every write Each entry records who wrote it, when, under what prompt, and which source it cites, so a downstream reader can weigh an entry by where it came from Append-only with supersession A correction is a new entry that points at the one it replaces, so the audit trail stays and a reader can see that a value was contested A read-only verifier An agent that reads the pool, re-fetches the cited sources, flags a mismatch, and has no write handle to the pool In the lesson's demo the verifier finds that the entry does not match the fetched text, the entry is flagged, and the analyst sees the flag before it writes its verdict. Why the verifier must not write. If the verifier's output goes back into the pool, a poisoned pool poisons the verifier, and the verifier's verdicts carry the poison further. Its findings go to a human or to a separate decision agent on their own channel. It can still be fooled by a bad entry, but it checks each entry against the original source, and its mistakes never become shared facts. What to monitor. Log the share of writes that supersede an earlier entry. A rising share is early evidence that agents are correcting each other more often, which is how poisoning shows up before anyone reads a wrong report. Plausible wrong answers. "Add a line to every prompt that says to verify numbers." The summarizer and the analyst had no source to verify against, only the shared entry, and a prompt does not give them one. "Let the verifier correct the entry in place." An in-place correction destroys the audit trail and gives the verifier a write handle that a poisoned pool can turn against it. "Switch from a shared pool to passing messages." Messages are shared state with extra copying, and a wrong number in a message poisons the receiver the same way. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does provenance help a reader who cannot re-fetch the source? Expected: the reader can see that one claim rests on one retrieval with no citation, and weigh it lower than a claim with a source and a verifier flag. (level 2) What does the analyst do when it sees a flag on the entry it depends on? Expected: it withholds the recommendation or writes it with the flag attached, and the final report carries a retraction instead of the number. (level 3) Which of the three changes would topic partitioning of the memory replace? Expected: none, because partitions limit which agents read an entry, and a poisoned entry in one topic still poisons everyone subscribed to it. (level 3) The verifier itself hallucinates a mismatch. What is the damage? Expected: a false flag on a correct entry, which a human on the verification channel can clear, and no new false fact in the pool because the verifier cannot write. Where it is taught. The shared memory lesson runs the poisoning scenario with and without the read-only verifier. Weigh a trade-off A team of four agents shares one message log, and every agent reads all of it. The team is about to grow to a few dozen agents, and the context each agent carries is already large. Compare keeping the single log with moving to topics that agents subscribe to, and say how you would handle several agents writing at once. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A full pool is simple, transparent and easy to inspect, and it stops scaling at about 10 agents because each agent's window fills with the others' work. A blackboard with subscriptions routes only the relevant messages to each agent, so it scales further, and it costs an up-front schema that makes the topics meaningful. Many systems mix the two: a small pool at the planning layer and blackboards below it. For writes, most systems serialize through one writer, because model calls are slow enough that contention is rare. The two topologies. Topology Who reads what Wins when Costs Full message pool Every agent reads every message Few agents, mixed roles, short horizon Context grows with every turn, and poisoning spreads to everyone Blackboard with subscriptions Agents declare topics and receive only those Many agents, similar roles, long-running A schema must exist before the topics mean anything The pool wins when reasoning about who said what is cheap because everyone saw everything. The blackboard wins when routing saves tokens and keeps unrelated work out of each window. Projection goes one step further. A blackboard gives every subscriber of a topic the same view. A per-agent projection gives each role a view computed from the global state, which is what state reducers do in graph runtimes. It scales furthest and needs a schema, and without one each agent rebuilds its own projection in its prompt. Writes. Concurrent writes from many agents are a concurrency problem, not a model problem. Three patterns work: A single writer. All writes go through one coordinator that serializes them. Simple, and a bottleneck. Optimistic concurrency with versions. Each entry carries a version, and a write fails and retries on a mismatch. Topic partitioning. Each agent owns topics, so there is no cross-topic contention, and the partition boundaries must be designed. Most frameworks default to the single writer, because model calls are slow enough that the bottleneck does not hurt. What does not change. Both topologies are shared state, the only stateful part of the system, and both need provenance on every entry, an append-only log and a read-only verifier. Topic partitioning limits who reads a poisoned entry. It does not stop the poisoning. The pattern has a history. The blackboard predates model agents by about five decades, back to the Hearsay-II system of the 1970s. Specialist knowledge sources watch a shared board, contribute partial solutions and trigger each other. The current systems are the same pattern with model agents as the knowledge sources and structured entries as the partial solutions, and the old literature already documents write contention and consistency. Plausible wrong answers. "Keep the pool and give agents bigger windows." The pool grows with every turn from every agent, and a bigger window delays the limit without removing it. "Pass messages directly between agents instead of sharing state." Direct messages are shared state with extra copying, and they lose the inspectable log. "Partition by topic and the poisoning problem is solved." Partitions limit the spread, and an entry with no provenance and no verifier still poisons every subscriber of its topic. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) A planning layer of three agents and a worker layer of thirty. Which topology where? Expected: a full pool for the three planners, who need to see each other, and blackboards for the workers, who need only their topics. (level 2) Which poisoning scenarios does topic partitioning make harder? Expected: a poisoned entry reaches only the subscribers of its topic, so cross-topic spread is cut, while subscribers of that topic are poisoned the same way. (level 3) When would you move from a single writer to optimistic versioning? Expected: when writes are frequent enough that the coordinator's queue adds visible latency, which is rare while each write follows a slow model call. (level 3) What goes wrong when you add a blackboard without a schema? Expected: topics are named ad hoc, agents subscribe to the wrong ones or to everything, and you rebuild the full pool with more code. Where it is taught. The shared memory lesson builds both topologies and the write-contention patterns. Defend a design You are adding a checking agent to a team that shares a memory. A colleague wants the checker to fix wrong entries directly, because that is the simplest design. Specify the checker: what it reads, what it may write, where its results go, and what it can and cannot protect against. Defend the restrictions. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The checker reads the shared memory like every other agent, re-fetches the sources that entries cite, and compares. It has no write handle to the shared memory, only to a separate verification channel that a human or a decision agent reads. It cannot stop a bad entry from being written, and it can be fooled by an entry that cites no source, but its verdicts can never become a shared fact. A checker that writes into the memory is poisoned by the same memory it checks, and then its verdicts carry the poison further. The specification. Aspect Rule Reads The whole pool, or the topics it is subscribed to on a blackboard Writes Nothing in the shared memory, only entries on its own verification channel Method For each entry with a cited source, fetch the source independently and compare the content Output A finding per mismatch with the entry id and the reason, routed to a human or a separate decision agent Effect The verifier writes nothing to the pool. The caller can attach the finding to the entry as a flag, as the lesson's demo does, but the entry's content does not change, and a correction is a new entry that supersedes it In the lesson's code the verifier returns a list of findings and never touches the pool. The caller decides what to do with them. Why no write handle. Shared memory is the only stateful part of the system, and it is where poisoning happens. A verifier that writes becomes one more writer that can be wrong. Worse, it reads the pool it writes to, so a poisoned pool shapes the verifier's view, and the verifier's conclusions re-enter the pool as new facts with the authority of a check behind them. Separation breaks that cycle. The verifier can be fooled by a bad entry, but its mistakes stay on its channel. Why not fix entries in place. An in-place fix destroys the audit trail. The lesson's rule is append-only: a correction is a new entry that references the one it supersedes. With the verifier's finding attached, the record shows that a value was written, that a check disagreed, and what the check found. A reader three steps later can see the dispute. An overwritten entry shows nothing. What it protects against, and what it does not. It catches an entry that cites a source and does not match it, which is the poisoning case. It does not catch an entry with no citation, an entry whose source is itself wrong, or a wrong conclusion drawn correctly from flagged inputs. For those you need provenance so that uncited claims are weighed lower, a diversity of sources, and a decision agent that reads the findings. How it fits the rest. Provenance on every write gives the verifier something to check. The append-only log gives its findings a place to attach. The verification channel gives its output a reader that is not the pool. The three mitigations are one design. Plausible wrong answers. "Let the checker fix the entry, since it has the source." The fix overwrites the audit trail and gives the checker a write path that a poisoned pool can turn against it. "A second reviewer agent that reads the pool is enough." A reviewer that only reads the pool compares entries with each other and inherits the same poisoned facts; the verifier must re-fetch the source. "Route the verifier's findings into the pool so every agent sees them." The findings then become shared facts, and a wrong finding poisons the pool in a new way; the finding on the verification channel, keyed by entry id, is the visible signal, not a new entry in the pool. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) The verifier flags an entry that the analyst already used. What happens to the analyst's entry? Expected: it stays in the log, a new entry can supersede it with the finding as the reason, and the final report carries the retraction. (level 3) How many verifiers do you deploy? Expected: at least one, and more if the pool is partitioned by topic, with each verifier subscribed to the topics it can check. (level 4) How do you keep the verifier's source access independent? Expected: it fetches from the original location with its own tools, not from a cache that a writer filled, otherwise it checks the entry against a copy of itself. (level 4) What metric tells you the verifier is doing useful work? Expected: the share of writes that are supersessions and the share of flagged entries, read together, with a rising flag rate as an early sign of a writer that hallucinates. Where it is taught. The shared memory lesson specifies the read-only verifier and its separate channel. In plain words first The idea in one line Classical distributed-systems BFT meets stochastic LLMs. In 2025-2026 three research directions emerged: CP-WBFT (arXiv:2511.10400) weighs each vote by a confidence probe; DecentLLMs (arXiv:2507.14928) goes leaderless with parallel worker proposals and geometric-median aggregation; WBFT (arXiv:2505.05103) combines weighted voting with Hierarchical Secure Clustering to split Core and Edge nodes. The honest empirical result from "Can AI Agents Agree?" (arXiv:2603.01213) is that even scalar agreement is fragile today, and a separate study found that a single deceptive agent can drag down a Mixture-of-Agents. BFT is necessary but not sufficient. This lesson builds a minimal BFT protocol, injects three agent-specific attacks (byzantine lie, sycophantic conformity, correlated-error monoculture), and measures how each consensus variant copes. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means BFT "Byzantine fault tolerance" Castro-Liskov 1999 protocol for consensus with f < n/3 arbitrary faults. Byzantine "Any bad behavior" A node that can lie, drop messages, fail silently — anything but crash safely. Confidence probe "How sure are you?" Self-reported or calibrator-predicted probability attached to a vote. Semantic clustering "Same answer, different words" Grouping equivalent answers before counting votes. Geometric median "Robust center" The point minimizing sum of distances to sample points. Robust to outliers, unlike the mean. Monoculture "Same model, same failures" Correlated errors when agents share training data or base model. Sycophantic conformity "Agreeing with the loud voice" An agent's vote biases toward whoever spoke first/loudest. Core/Edge "Hierarchical BFT" WBFT split: high-trust Core nodes vote, Edge nodes receive the result. Bounds latency. Problem In plain words first When several agents answer the same question, you need a rule for picking one answer. Majority vote counts heads. Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) is the distributed-systems name for agreeing even when some participants lie or misbehave. With LLM agents there is an extra problem: agents built on the same model tend to make the same mistakes, so a majority can be confidently wrong. There is no Zero to Agents chapter on this; it builds on Lesson 16.7 (debate) and Lesson 16.13 (shared memory). This lesson tests the lesson's three aggregators on votes its scenarios do not try, and runs five copies of one small model as a real monoculture. You have N LLM agents each producing an answer. They disagree. Majority vote picks the wrong one because two agents are correlated (same base model, same training data, same failure modes). A third agent happens to be wrong in a novel way — so the majority is a false majority. Now add a deceptive agent: it lies on purpose. Or a sycophantic agent: it agrees with whoever spoke last. In classical BFT, the assumption is that Byzantine nodes are a fraction f < n/3 and behave arbitrarily. The 2026 reality is that LLM nodes are stochastic even when honest, correlated across models, and influenced by each other's outputs. You cannot treat them as independent Bernoulli voters. Classical BFT (PBFT, 1999) is not wrong — it is incomplete. It handles arbitrary bit-flipping. It does not handle "three honest agents share a hallucination because they share training data." This lesson builds from PBFT's foundation and layers on three 2025-2026 adaptations. Concept What classical BFT gives you Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (Castro & Liskov, OSDI 1999) tolerates f < n/3 Byzantine nodes. The protocol has three phases (pre-prepare, prepare, commit) and two primitives (signed messages, quorum certificates). Agreement on a single value among n >= 3f + 1 honest-or-malicious nodes. The guarantees are strong but assume: Independent failures. The bound f < n/3 assumes replicas fail independently; Castro and Liskov suggest running different implementations so one bug cannot take out many nodes at once. The faulty nodes themselves may collude. Honest nodes are truly honest. Correctness of honest outputs is a non-issue; the protocol only aligns disagreement. The question has a ground-truth answer. Consensus on a wrong fact is still consensus. LLM agents violate all three. Two agents running the same base model share faults. An "honest" LLM still hallucinates. And on ambiguous questions, the "truth" is what the agents decide — there is no external oracle. The three LLM-specific attacks Byzantine lie. One agent outputs a deliberately wrong answer. Classical BFT handles this if f < n/3 . Sycophantic conformity. One agent reads others' answers before voting and aligns with whoever spoke last. Not malicious, but correlates with the loudest voice. Classical BFT does not prevent this because the agent passes every signature check. Correlated-error monoculture. Three agents share a base model. They hallucinate the same wrong answer. The majority is wrong. Classical BFT does not help because all three "honestly" agree. The 2025-2026 responses CP-WBFT (arXiv:2511.10400) — confidence-probe-based weighted BFT. Each voter's answer gets a confidence, either self-reported in the prompt or read by a probe trained on the model's hidden activations. Vote weights scale with confidence. With 6 of 7 agents Byzantine, the hidden-state probe raised final accuracy from 14.29% to 100% (+85.71%) on complete graphs; gains from self-reported confidence were smaller and on one task sometimes negative. Mitigation for: sycophantic conformity, on the assumption that conforming agents have low confidence in a position they did not derive. DecentLLMs (arXiv:2507.14928) — leaderless. Worker agents propose answers in parallel, evaluator agents score every proposal, the scores are combined with the geometric median (Weiszfeld's algorithm), and the best-ranked answer wins. Robust while fewer than half the evaluators are Byzantine. Mitigation for: Byzantine lies (the geometric median ignores a minority of extreme scores); it does not fix errors that most agents share. WBFT (arXiv:2505.05103) — weighted BFT with Hierarchical Secure Clustering, for a blockchain-style network of LLMs. A leader proposes a response, followers vote on whether theirs is better, and the response is accepted with two-thirds of the weighted vote. Each weight mixes a response-quality score and a trust value. Clustering on trust and latency picks high-trust Core nodes that vote, while Edge nodes receive the result by broadcast. Mitigation for: scalability (Core consensus is small and fast) and partially for monoculture (Core can be chosen for diversity). Empirical: "Can AI Agents Agree?" (arXiv:2603.01213) The paper (Berdoz, Rugli and Wattenhofer) runs LLM agents in a synchronous, all-to-all Byzantine consensus game over a scalar value, with no stake in which value wins, across hundreds of simulations that vary model size, group size and the number of Byzantine agents. The finding is uncomfortable: Even with no adversaries, valid agreement is unreliable, and it gets worse as groups grow. A few Byzantine agents lower the success rate further. Separately, Wolf et al. (arXiv:2503.05856) found that one deceptive agent among six cut a Mixture-of-Agents' AlpacaEval 2.0 length-controlled win rate from 49.2% to 37.9%. Most failures are loss of liveness (timeouts and stalled convergence), not agreement on a wrong value. The takeaway: BFT gives you machinery to align outputs, but it does not tell you whether the aligned output is right. Combine with verification (Phase 16 · 08 role specialization), diversity (Phase 16 · 15 debate variants), and evaluator agents (Phase 16 · 24 benchmarks). The core protocol, stripped down A minimal BFT round for LLM agents: Copy The semantic clustering step is the LLM-specific twist. Two answers "the study reports 4.2%" and "4.2% improvement" are the same cluster. A naive string-equality check would miss this. In production, use a cheap embedding model or explicit canonicalization. Threshold tuning The threshold parameter decides when to accept and when to retry. Too low: you accept weak majorities. Too high: you never accept anything. A reasonable starting point is 0.5-0.67 for n=5-7 agents, higher for smaller n ; tune it on your own attack tests. Below a threshold, escalate to a human or to a different agent ensemble. Where consensus does not help Ambiguous questions. If the question has no ground truth, consensus is an opinion. Call it that. Compound questions. "Write code and explain it" — two answers. Vote on each independently. Adversarial multi-round. If agents can observe prior rounds and mimic (Du 2023 debate), they start agreeing with each other regardless of truth. Bound the rounds (2-3 typically). The same idea as a formula Majority of independent voters. Agents attach self-reported confidence. A new merchant category appears; all five agents call its payments fraud at confidence 0.9, and the block rate triples overnight. Nothing in the consensus logs looks wrong. Using this lesson, what failed, and what would you change? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Confidence from inside the model. CP-WBFT's strongest results come from a probe trained on hidden activations, not from asking the model; with open-weight models, token probabilities are a cheap step in that direction. Diversity over headcount. Mixtures of different model families and prompts are the main defence against correlated errors; five copies of one model share many mistakes. Agreement is not reliable yet. Recap What to keep from this lesson Majority vote helps only as much as voters' errors are independent; copies of one model share mistakes. Normalise answers before counting, or honest votes split and a liar wins the tie. Self-reported confidence is the voter's to set; weight by signals the voter cannot choose. A threshold can refuse a weak or wrong majority, but it cannot find the right answer; escalate. Agreement is not correctness; send the consensus to an independent verifier. Solutions Solution P1 · 42%, rejected, 42% Plurality: 42%. canonical() keeps the four honest answers apart, so all five clusters have one vote, and max returns the first cluster it saw, the liar's. CP-WBFT: rejected. The liar's 0.6 is the largest single weight, but it is only 0.6 of 3.8, under the 0.5 threshold, so no answer is returned. DecentLLMs: 42%. Every cluster has one member and no spread, so all score 1, and the tie again goes to the first vote. Solution B1 · A monoculture with self-set weights What failed. The five agents share a base model, so on an unfamiliar category they share the same mistake; different prompts do not make their errors independent. Their self-reported confidence was high and uniform, which CP-WBFT reads as strong agreement. The consensus worked exactly as designed and agreed on a wrong answer. What to change: - Diversify the voters: use models from different families or training data, so errors are less likely to coincide. - Weight by signals the voters cannot set: token probabilities or a calibrated probe, checked against labelled outcomes per category. - Watch the agreement rate: a sudden jump to unanimity on a new segment is a warning, not reassurance; route it to review. - Verify independently: send blocks on new categories to a rule-based check or a human before acting, and track the block rate per category. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Read the code Read the clustering and the plurality aggregator from the consensus lesson. Five agents vote on a percentage from a study. Three agents that share a base model answer 42% , and two agents answer 4.2% . Each of the two is more confident than any of the three, but the three still carry more confidence in total. Say what the plurality returns, what the aggregator that weighs each vote by its confidence returns, and what the canonicalization does with the answer 4.2 percent . python @dataclass class Vote: agent: str answer: str confidence: float def canonical(self) -> str: return "".join(c for c in self.answer.lower().strip() if c.isalnum() or c == "." or c == "%") def plurality(votes: list[Vote]) -> tuple[str, dict[str, int]]: counts: dict[str, int] = {} rep: dict[str, str] = {} for v in votes: key = v.canonical() counts[key] = counts.get(key, 0) + 1 rep.setdefault(key, v.answer) winner_key = max(counts, key=counts.get) return rep[winner_key], counts Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Plurality counts three votes for 42% and two for 4.2% and returns the wrong answer, because it counts heads and the wrong cluster has more heads. The confidence-weighted aggregator sums confidence per cluster and compares the top cluster's share with a threshold. The wrong cluster has the larger sum, so with a threshold of 0.5 it also returns 42% , and with a higher threshold it can return no winner. The canonicalization keeps letters, digits, dots and percent signs, so 4.2 percent becomes 4.2percent and lands in a different cluster from 4.2% , which splits the right answer's votes. What the code does. canonical lowercases the answer, strips the ends, and keeps alphanumerics, the dot and the percent sign. It is the lesson's rough semantic clustering. plurality builds a count per canonical key, keeps the first original answer per key as its representative, and returns the key with the most votes. The monoculture case. Aggregator Rule Result here Plurality Most votes Wrong, because three correlated votes beat two Confidence-weighted Sum of confidence per cluster, top cluster must pass a threshold share Wrong, because the three votes carry more total confidence, or none when the share is under the threshold Geometric-median style Score each cluster by its size and how tight its confidences are Wrong, because the cluster of three is larger and its confidences are also tight The lesson's own takeaway is the limit: no aggregator solves a wrong cluster that is both larger and more confident than the right one. That case needs diversity of models or verification, not a better vote. The canonicalization blind spot. Two agents that mean the same value can land in two clusters. 4.2% and 4.2 percent differ after canonicalization, and so would four point two percent . Every split in the right cluster helps the wrong one. In production, canonicalize numbers with their units into one form, or cluster by embedding similarity, and keep the canonical key next to the original answer in the log so a reviewer can see when a split happened. Where the two percentages come from. The values in the scenario are the memory-poisoning numbers from the shared-memory lesson: a page says 4.2 percent and a retrieval agent writes 42 percent. The consensus lesson reuses them so that the vote is over a claim with a known source, which is also what makes a verifier possible after the vote. What the plurality code cannot see. It has no idea which agents share a base model, no confidence, no source. It returns the answer with the most votes and does not check whether the voters are independent or accurate. Independence makes a right majority more likely but does not guarantee it, and the prompt's three agents share a base model, so their errors are correlated. Plausible wrong answers. "Plurality is fine as long as there are at least five agents." Three agents on one model are a majority at any size as long as they are over half, and the count never sees the correlation. "The canonicalization is good enough because it handles case and spaces." It splits 4.2% from 4.2 percent , and every split in the right cluster is a vote for the wrong one. "Higher confidence means a more correct answer, so weight by it and you are done." Weighting helps against low-confidence conformity and does nothing when the wrong cluster is also the confident one. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does plurality keep rep ? Expected: so that it can return the original answer text for the winning key, since the canonical key is a comparison form and not an answer to show. (level 3) No cluster reaches the threshold share in the weighted vote. What is the result? Expected: no winner, with the weights, so the caller retries or escalates instead of accepting a weak majority. (level 4) The sycophancy case: two agents copy the first answer they saw with low confidence. Which aggregator catches it and why? Expected: the confidence-weighted one, because the copiers carry little weight, while plurality counts them as full votes. (level 4) How would you test a replacement for canonical ? Expected: a table of answer pairs that must cluster together and pairs that must not, including unit variants and spelled-out numbers, run as a unit test. Where it is taught. Explain the mechanism Five agents answer the same factual question and vote. Three of them run the same base model and agree on a wrong answer, and the two others are right. Majority vote picks the wrong answer. A colleague says that classical fault-tolerant consensus solves this. Explain why it does not, which assumptions break, and what the recent agent-specific protocols change. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Classical consensus tolerates fewer than a third of nodes behaving arbitrarily, and it assumes that faults are independent, that honest nodes are correct, and that a ground truth exists. Three agents on a shared base model share their faults, an honest model still hallucinates, and on some questions the agents define the truth. The agent-specific variants weigh each vote by a confidence probe, aggregate leaderless proposals by a geometric median, or split agents into a core and an edge with learned trust weights. None of them makes agreement equal correctness, so the consensus output still goes to an independent verifier. What the classical protocol gives and assumes. The standard protocol reaches agreement on one value among n nodes when fewer than n divided by three are faulty, which needs n at least three f plus one. It runs three phases over signed messages and quorum certificates. Its three assumptions: Faults are independent, so faulty nodes do not coordinate. Honest nodes are correct, so the protocol only aligns disagreement. The question has a ground truth, so agreement on a wrong value is still agreement. Model agents break all three. Agents on one base model share faults. An honest agent hallucinates. And on an ambiguous question the agents decide what is true. Three attacks that pass the signature check. Attack What happens Does the classical protocol handle it A deliberate lie One agent outputs a wrong answer with high confidence Yes, while the liars are under a third Sycophantic conformity One agent reads the others and aligns with whoever spoke last No, because the agent passes every check Correlated monoculture Three agents on one model hallucinate the same answer No, because all three honestly agree The prompt's case is the third. The agent-specific responses. Confidence-weighted voting. Each voter attaches a confidence, self-reported or read by a probe trained on the model's hidden activations, and the vote weight scales with it. The paper's large gain on fully connected graphs comes from the hidden-state probe. It helps most against conformity, because an agent that adopted a position it did not derive tends to report low confidence. Leaderless aggregation by geometric median. Workers propose in parallel, evaluators score the proposals, and the answer is the geometric median of the scored positions. It is robust while the faulty fraction is under a half, and it resists outliers and pulls toward the dense cluster rather than the model-biased mean. Weighted voting with a core and an edge. Weights come from a response-quality score and a trust value. A small core reaches agreement first and the edge follows, which bounds latency and lets the core be chosen for diversity. The stripped-down round. Each agent produces an answer and a confidence. The aggregator groups answers into semantic clusters, so that two phrasings of one value count together, sums the confidence per cluster, and accepts the top cluster only when its share passes a threshold. Below the threshold it retries or escalates. The lesson's working range for the threshold is 0.5 to 0.67 with five to seven agents. Minority clusters are logged with provenance, because they are the early warning for correlated errors. The uncomfortable measurement. The lesson cites a study of scalar agreement (Berdoz, Rugli and Wattenhofer): even with no adversary, groups of LLM agents often failed to reach valid agreement, more so as groups grew, and a few Byzantine agents made it worse. A separate study found one deceptive agent among six cut a Mixture-of-Agents' AlpacaEval win rate from 49.2% to 37.9%. Consensus machinery aligns outputs. It does not tell you whether the aligned output is right. Plausible wrong answers. "Use the classical protocol with a two-thirds quorum." Three honest agents that share a hallucination form the quorum, and the protocol agrees on the wrong value. "Add more copies of the same model until the majority is right." More copies of one model add more correlated votes, and the wrong cluster grows with them. "Consensus means the answer is correct." Agreement and correctness are different measurements, and the consensus output needs a verifier that is independent of the ensemble. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Does the geometric median rescue this case? Expected: no. The median discounts outliers and moves toward the dense cluster, which helps only while the wrong cluster is under half. Here three of five votes are wrong, so the dense cluster is the wrong one and the median selects it. (level 3) The three wrong agents are also the most confident. What now? Expected: no aggregator fixes a wrong cluster that is both larger and more confident, so the system needs diversity of base models or an independent verifier. (level 4) Why bound the rounds at two or three? Expected: agents that observe earlier rounds start to mimic each other regardless of truth, so more rounds reward conformity. (level 4) What do you monitor in production? Expected: the agreement rate, where a sharp rise means conformity and a sharp fall means model drift, and the minority clusters with their provenance. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The cheapest aggregation: sample N independent agents, majority-vote. Wang et al. 2022 self-consistency did this with one model sampled N times. Multi-agent extends it with heterogeneous agents to escape monoculture — different models, different prompts, different temperatures, different contexts. Beyond majority vote, debate topology matters: MultiAgentBench (arXiv:2503.01935, ACL 2025) evaluated star / chain / tree / graph coordination and found graph best for research , and that adding agents beyond three lowered its overall score. AgentVerse (ICLR 2024) documents volunteer, conformity and destructive behaviors; conformity is both a feature (finding consensus) and, in debate, a risk (groupthink, Lesson 16.24 ). This lesson maps the topology space, builds each variant, and measures the coordination tax. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Self-consistency "Sample N times, vote" Wang 2022. Single model, N temperature>0 samples, majority vote on reasoning paths. Heterogeneity "Different models" Ensemble of different base models or prompt families. Breaks monoculture. MAD "Multi-agent debate" Generic term for agents exchanging critiques over rounds. See Du 2023. A-HMAD "Adversarial Heterogeneous MAD" MAD variant emphasizing different models + adversarial structure. Topology "Who talks to whom" Star, chain, tree, graph. Determines information flow. Coordination tax "Diminishing returns" Past a few agents, cost and coordination overhead grow faster than quality. Volunteer behavior "Unprompted help" AgentVerse emergent pattern: an agent offers to take a step. Conformity behavior "Agreement under pressure" AgentVerse emergent pattern: an agent corrects course after criticism; in debate, adopting a peer's answer. Jury "Small specialized panel" Sibyl-style debate jury: an Actor answers, a Critic hunts for errors. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.63 · Planning and reasoning patterns: ReAct, plan-and-execute, reflection and search Problem In plain words first The simplest way to combine agents is to ask several and take a vote. Self-consistency does this with one model sampled several times. Debate lets agents see each other's answers and revise. Topology is who sees whose answers: a star (everyone reports to a hub), a chain, a tree or a fully connected graph. Planning and reasoning patterns for a single agent are covered in Lesson 14.63 (linked above). This lesson measures what the lesson's simulator does and does not show, then compares one prompt sampled three times with three phrasings and a round of debate on a small real model. Debate can improve accuracy (Du et al., arXiv:2305.14325). It can also degrade it. Whether debate helps depends on four structural choices: Who talks to whom (topology). How many rounds (Du 2023: both rounds and agents matter independently). Whether agents are heterogeneous (different base models break monoculture). Whether an adversarial voice is present (steel-manning vs. straw-manning). Teams that bolt "run 5 agents and vote" onto a task often regress vs. a single agent. The failures are not random. They track topology and heterogeneity. This lesson is the topology map. Concept Self-consistency, the single-model baseline Wang et al. 2022 ("Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning") sampled the same model N times at temperature > 0 and majority-voted on reasoning-path answers. On GSM8K, 40 sampled paths raised PaLM 540B's accuracy by 17.9 points over a single greedy decode. Self-consistency is the single-agent precursor to multi-agent voting. Limit: self-consistency uses one base model. Errors are correlated by construction. If the model has a systematic bias, all N samples share it. Multi-agent vote, the heterogeneous extension Replace N samples with N different agents. Different base models (Claude, GPT, Llama), different prompts, different tool access. The benefit: uncorrelated errors. The cost: different agents cost different amounts; coordinating them adds overhead. This lesson calls heterogeneous debate with an adversarial voice A-HMAD (Adversarial Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Debate). There is no settled standard name; 2025–2026 papers describe similar designs as heterogeneous multi-agent debate, with different models debating to reduce errors they would share. The four topologies Copy Star: one hub, all others talk only to hub. Equivalent to supervisor-worker without back-channel. Chain: linear, each agent sees the prior one's output. Pipeline-like. Tree: hierarchical, used by hierarchical agent systems ( Lesson 16.6 ). Graph: any-to-any. Includes fully-connected clique and arbitrary DAGs. The coordination tax (MultiAgentBench) MultiAgentBench (MARBLE, ACL 2025, arXiv:2503.01935) compared star, chain, tree and graph coordination protocols in its research scenario, alongside coding, gaming and other tasks. What it reported: Graph did best on research tasks, with the best task score, planning efficiency and token use. Information flows any-to-any; agents can critique each other. Star scored about the same as graph on task score. Tree did worst: the highest token use and the lowest task and coordination scores. The paper does not single out chain. More agents, lower overall score. With 1, 3, 5 and 7 agents on research tasks, coordination improved sharply from 1 to 3 agents, task score rose only gradually, and the overall score fell as agents were added. This lesson calls that the coordination tax. The point where the tax bites is empirical, not fundamental. One reason is context capacity: each agent's context fills with peers' outputs, and the marginal value of agent N+1 drops once everyone can see everyone. Multi-Agent Debate Strategies ("Should we be going MAD?") arXiv:2311.17371 (Smit et al., ICML 2024) benchmarks MAD strategies. Its main finding: debate systems in their current form do not reliably outperform other prompting strategies such as self-consistency and ensembling, and they usually cost more calls. They are sensitive to hyperparameters: telling agents how often to agree with each other moved Multi-Persona from worst to best on MedQA. Disagreement helped on a counter-intuitive dataset (CIAR) and hurt on medical ones, so an adversarial voice is not a general win. AgentVerse emergent patterns AgentVerse (ICLR 2024, https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/578e65cdee35d00c708d4c64bce32971-Paper-Conference.pdf) documents three behaviors that emerge from multi-agent collaboration without explicit design (volunteer, conformity and destructive behaviors). Two matter most here: Volunteer. An agent offers help ("I can take the next step") unprompted. Useful: it allocates work to the most-capable agent for a subtask. Conformity. An agent that drifted from the shared goal corrects course after others criticise it. In AgentVerse this is useful. In debate, the same pull makes an agent adopt a peer's answer even when the peer is wrong, the debate form of sycophancy ( Lesson 16.14 ). Conformity is why debate-until-agreement rewards bullies. Bounded rounds with a separate judge mitigate. Heterogeneity: the actual knob that moves accuracy A common heuristic in practice: swapping one of your N agents for a different base model is worth more than adding one more copy of the same model. The intuition is monoculture: each new source of independent errors is worth more than another correlated sample. Measure it on your task; this lesson's small-model run below tests the prompt version of it. In the limit, heterogeneity can beat numerosity: if five copies of one model share most of their errors, three models with different errors can do better on tasks with clean ground truth. Jury methods Sibyl (Wang et al., arXiv:2407.10718), inspired by Minsky's Society of Mind, adds a "multi-agent debate-based jury" that refines the final answer. An Actor proposes an answer and explains its reasoning, and a Critic looks for logical errors in it; the Actor weighs the feedback. Jury methods are a midpoint between plain vote (cheap, monoculture-prone) and full MAD (expensive, conformity-prone). When vote-with-debate dominates The question has ground truth (fact, math, code behavior). Vote convergence is meaningful. Agents can access different sources or tools (heterogeneity is available). Rounds are bounded (2-3 typical) and there is a separate judge or verifier. Budget allows 3-5 agents. Beyond 5-7 on graph topology, coordination tax dominates. When vote-with-debate hurts The question is opinion-shaped. Agents converge to whichever answer looks most confident, not most correct. All agents share a base model. Monoculture makes consensus meaningless. Rounds are unbounded. Conformity wins every time. The task is simple. A single agent with self-consistency at N=5 is cheaper and as accurate. The same idea as a formula What a vote can reach. With independent voters each right with probability , majority accuracy is ​ ( k n ​ ) p k ( 1 − p ) n − k . With an even , ties need a rule; breaking them by "first answer" makes an even group no better than the odd group one smaller. Correlation. If two voters' errors coincide with probability when both are wrong, the vote can only outvote errors that do not coincide. Copies of one model have high ; different prompts or models lower it. Cost per correct answer. A topology that spends tokens per question and is right with probability costs tokens per correct answer. Doubling for a gain from 0.97 to 0.98 roughly doubles that cost. An agent only switches to the current majority, so every switch adds a vote to the majority and takes one from a minority. The majority can only grow. In the run, round 2 kept the round-1 majority in 2,000 of 2,000 trials. The second round costs a full set of calls and cannot change the result. Solution B1 · Copies, rounds and conformity What went wrong. Five copies of one model share most of their errors, so the vote adds little. Unbounded-looking debate with three rounds pulls every agent toward whoever spoke first, the conformity effect, so the final label is mostly the first agent's. The team paid for 15 calls to get roughly one agent's answer, and the drift sometimes overturned right answers. What to try instead: - Start with self-consistency: sample the model five times without debate and vote; measure the gain against one agent. - Lower correlation: vary prompts or use a second model family, and check how often wrong labels coincide. - If you keep debate, bound it: one round, answers shown without names or order effects, and a separate judge. - Report tokens per correct label next to accuracy, so a sixfold cost increase is visible. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Weigh a trade-off A team added an ensemble to a question-answering task: five agents on the same model debate until they agree, then answer. Accuracy fell below the single agent. They want to add more agents. What went wrong, and what would you change first? Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Whether debate helps depends on structure, not on the count: who talks to whom, how many rounds, whether the agents are different, and whether anyone argues against. Five copies of one model share their errors, so the vote is correlated, and debate until agreement rewards the most confident agent through conformity. Change the composition before the count: start from self-consistency with one strong model, then swap one agent for a different base model, bound the rounds at two or three, and add a judge that does not vote. The baseline they skipped. Self-consistency samples one model several times at a temperature above zero and takes the majority over the reasoning paths. On a grade-school math set it gave large gains with 40 samples over one greedy decode. Its limit is that one model's errors are correlated by construction. A systematic bias is in every sample. That is also the team's ensemble with extra coordination. Heterogeneity is the knob. Replacing one of the agents with a different base model gives a bigger gain than adding one more copy. Each independent source of error is worth more than another correlated sample. In the limit, three different models beat five copies of one on tasks with a clean ground truth. The literature's name for the design that leans on this is adversarial heterogeneous debate: different models, and one of them argues against. Rounds and conformity. Debate can also degrade accuracy. Agents adjust their stance to match a critic even when the critic is wrong, and debate until agreement rewards whoever pushes hardest. Bound the rounds, two to three is typical, and give the final call to a separate judge that scores the consensus and does not vote. A survey of debate strategies found that variants structurally like self-consistency often underperform it at the same budget, and that debate helps most when agents are heterogeneous and the structure is adversarial. Topology and the tax. Topology Best for Graph, any to any Research, where agents critique each other Star, one hub Fast factual consolidation Chain Stepwise refinement On a graph the coordination tax appears past about 4 agents: wall-clock and tokens grow faster than quality, because every window fills with every peer's output. The ceiling is empirical and tied to current context capacity, not fundamental. A sequence that measures each step. Self-consistency at five samples on one strong model. This is the cheap baseline. Heterogeneous voting at three agents if accuracy matters. Measure the delta. Debate only when the task has structure and bounded rounds are feasible. Log the minority cluster every time. A minority that is persistently right is a diversity signal. Report tokens and wall-clock next to accuracy, because better accuracy at ten times the cost is a business decision. Plausible wrong answers. "Add more agents until the vote stabilizes." A stable wrong vote is still wrong, and past a few agents the cost grows faster than the quality; MultiAgentBench's overall score fell as agents were added beyond three. "Let them debate until they agree, because agreement means confidence." Unbounded debate rewards conformity, and the agreed answer is the loudest one, not the right one. "Use the same model at different temperatures for diversity." That is self-consistency, and the systematic bias of the model survives every temperature. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does adding a sixth copy of the same model not help? Expected: it adds one more correlated sample, so the shared bias gets one more vote. (level 2) What does the judge do that the voters cannot? Expected: it scores the final consensus without having taken a position, so conformity pressure does not move it. (level 3) When is plain self-consistency the right final answer? Expected: a simple task with a clean ground truth, where five samples of one strong model are as accurate as any ensemble and far cheaper. (level 3) The task is opinion-shaped. What happens to the vote? Expected: agents converge on the most confident-looking answer rather than the most correct one, so a vote is an opinion poll and should be labeled as one. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Agents negotiate resources, prices, task allocations, and terms. The 2026 benchmark set is clear: NegotiationArena (arXiv:2402.05863) shows LLMs can improve payoffs ~20% via persona manipulation ("desperation"); "Measuring Bargaining Abilities" (arXiv:2402.15813) shows buyer is harder than seller and scale does not help — their OG-Narrator (deterministic offer generator + LLM narrator) pushed deal rate from 26.67% to 88.88%; the Large-Scale Autonomous Negotiation Competition (arXiv:2503.06416) ran about 183k negotiations and found warmth tied to better outcomes, while a top agent reasoned in hidden chain-of-thought its counterparts could not see; Bhattacharya et al. 2025 compared models' negotiation styles across bargaining games. This lesson implements Contract Net Protocol (the FIPA ancestor, Lesson 02), wires an LLM-style buyer/seller, runs an OG-Narrator-style decomposition, and measures how deal rate changes with each structural choice. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Contract Net "Task market" Smith 1980, FIPA 1996. cfp + propose + accept/reject. The canonical task-market. ZOPA "Zone of possible agreement" Overlap between buyer's max and seller's min. Offers outside it cannot close. BATNA "Best alternative to a negotiated agreement" Your fallback if this deal fails. Sets your reservation price. OG-Narrator "Offer generator + narrator" Decomposition: deterministic offer, LLM narration. Zeuthen strategy "Risk-minimizing concession" Classical offer-generator that concedes based on risk limits. Rubinstein bargaining "Alternating-offer equilibrium" Game-theoretic model for infinite-horizon bargaining with discounting. CoT concealment "Hide your reasoning" A top agent in arXiv:2503.06416 reasoned in tags its AI counterparts could not see; the public channel shows the offer only. Persona manipulation "Emotional posturing" arXiv:2402.05863: ~20% payoff gain from desperation/urgency personas. Problem In plain words first In a negotiation , two agents with private limits trade offers until they agree or give up. The buyer has a maximum it will pay, the seller a minimum it will accept, and any price between them is a possible deal. LLMs are good at the wording of offers and poor at choosing the numbers, so one fix is to compute the number with code and let the model write the message ( OG-Narrator ). Contract Net is the classic task market: a manager calls for bids and awards the work. There is no Zero to Agents chapter on this; it builds on Lesson 16.2 (FIPA messages and contract nets). This lesson checks what the lesson's simulator measures, then has a small model bargain and narrate. Two agents need to agree on a price. Left to themselves with pure language prompts, LLM buyers close deals at surprisingly low rates (26.67% for an unaligned model in arXiv:2402.15813). Scale does not fix the buyer's side: in that study, larger models of the same family did not bargain better as buyers, though larger sellers generally did. The root issue is that LLMs conflate two jobs — deciding the offer and narrating the offer. OG-Narrator separated these: a deterministic offer generator computes numeric moves; the LLM only narrates. The paper reports buyer deal rates rising from 26.67% to 88.88%, with about ten times the profit. This mirrors a classical multi-agent finding: decoupling the mechanism from the communication layer wins. Contract Net Protocol (FIPA, 1996; Smith, 1980) is the reference task-market mechanism. Plug an LLM into the narration slot and you get a modern LLM-powered task market. Concept Contract Net, in one paragraph Smith's 1980 Contract Net Protocol: a manager broadcasts a call for proposals (cfp) ; bidders respond with propose messages containing their offers; the manager picks a winner and sends accept-proposal to the winner and reject-proposal to the losers. The winner performs the work. Optional message: refuse (bidder declines to propose). FIPA codified this as fipa-contract-net interaction protocol. Why OG-Narrator wins "Measuring Bargaining Abilities of Language Models" (arXiv:2402.15813) observed that: LLMs often break the bargaining rules (offer at nonsensical prices, ignore the other side's ZOPA). They anchor poorly (accept bad first offers; counter-offer at symbolic rather than strategic amounts). Scale alone does not fix these. Larger models make more-plausible language with similar strategic error. The OG-Narrator decomposition: Copy The offer generator is a classical negotiation strategy: a Rubinstein bargaining model, a Zeuthen strategy, or a simple tit-for-tat over price. The LLM narrates. The message contains the deterministic price and the natural-language framing. Deal rate jumps because: - Prices stay in the bargaining zone. - Anchors are strategic, not emotional. - The LLM does what it is good at: writing. NegotiationArena findings arXiv:2402.05863 (Bianchi et al., ICML 2024) provides a widely used benchmark. Headline findings: LLMs can improve payoffs ~20% by adopting personas ("I am desperate to sell this by Friday") — persona manipulation is a real tactic. Weaker agents' mistakes can be exploited: the authors note that a less effective agent's erroneous behaviour could be used as a kind of adversarial attack. Turn order and role matter: the first player usually wins the ultimatum game, while the second tends to win in resource exchange. This is not "LLMs are bad negotiators." It is "LLMs negotiate too much like humans, including the exploitable parts." Chain-of-thought concealment The Large-Scale Autonomous Negotiation Competition (arXiv:2503.06416, Vaccaro et al., MIT) ran 182,812 negotiations between AI agents. Warm agents got better outcomes across its key metrics; dominant agents claimed more value but reached more impasses. Two AI-specific tactics stood out: one agent used prompt injection to make counterparts reveal their positions, and NegoMate, which earned the most individual points in integrative scenarios, wrote its chain-of-thought in tags its AI counterparts could not see. The paper credits its success to that preparation plus mutual-gains framing, not to concealment alone. What concealment protects: If an agent prints "I will only go to $75; my reservation price is $70" into a publicly visible scratchpad, the opponent reads it. Winners compute strategy privately; the output channel contains only the offer and minimum required narration. This is basic bargaining theory: revealing your reservation price lets the other side claim the whole surplus. LLMs do not intuit this and happily type their reservations in reasoning traces that become visible to the counterpart. Engineering takeaway: separate private-scratchpad context from public-message context. Not optional. Bhattacharya et al. 2025 — model styles Bhattacharya et al. (2025, "Evaluating Negotiation Capabilities of Large Language Models: From Ultimatum Games to Nash Bargaining") compare models across bargaining games. The lesson summarises their rankings as below; we could not check these against the paper's text, so treat them as a reported snapshot: Llama-3 was most-effective at striking bargains (deal rate + payoff). Claude-3 was the most-aggressive negotiator (high anchors, late concessions). GPT-4 was the fairest (smallest variance in payoff across pairings). This is a 2025 snapshot. The point is not which model wins in April 2026 — it is that different base models have persistent negotiation styles. Heterogeneous ensembles ( Lesson 16.15 ) include this as a diversity source. Task allocation via Contract Net + LLM The modern re-use of Contract Net for LLM multi-agent: Manager agent decomposes a task into units. Broadcasts cfp with task description to worker agents. Each worker returns an offer: (price, eta, confidence) where price could be tokens, compute units, or dollars. Manager picks winners (single or multiple, depending on task) and awards. Rejected workers are free to bid on other tasks. This scales well past 100 workers because coordination is broadcast-and-respond, not synchronous chat. Agent frameworks do not ship it as a built-in pattern (Microsoft Agent Framework's orchestrations are sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat and Magentic); you build it from their messaging primitives. LLM-Stakeholders Interactive Negotiation NeurIPS 2024 (https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/984dd3db213db2d1454a163b65b84d08-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf) introduces multi-party scorable games with secret scores and minimum-acceptance thresholds . Each stakeholder has private utilities; the LLM must infer them from messages. This is the generalization of two-party bargaining to N-party coalition formation. Relevant for production task markets with heterogeneous worker capabilities. The narration-vs-mechanism rule Across all 2024-2026 negotiation benchmarks, the consistent engineering rule is: Let the LLM narrate. Do not let the LLM compute the offer. The generator's opening uses the vendors' own price list as the "expected margin", so the vendors control where the agent opens, and a high opening closes deals quickly.
