Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Park et al. 2023 (UIST '23, arXiv:2304.03442) populated Smallville , a sandbox of 25 agents, with a three-part architecture: memory stream (natural-language log), reflection (higher-level syntheses the agent generates about its own stream), and plan (day-level behavior, then sub-plans). The landmark result was the Valentine's Day party emergence: one agent seeded with "wants to throw a Valentine's Day party," without further scripting, spread invitations through the population: 12 other agents heard about it, and 5 of the 12 who were invited showed up at Hobbs Cafe, though none of the 24 had been told about it at the start. Ablations show all three components are required for believability. The documented failures include spatial-norm errors (entering closed stores, sharing single-person bathrooms) and agents made overly polite and cooperative by instruction tuning. This is the reference architecture for agent simulations and multi-agent social evaluation in 2026. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Memory stream "The agent's diary" Append-only log of observations, actions, reflections, plans. Recency "How new is the memory" Exponential-decay score by age. Importance "How much does the agent care" Self-rated 1-10 at write time. Cached. Relevance "How related to the current query" Cosine similarity (embedding-based). Reflection "Higher-order belief" Synthesis generated from recent memories, re-ingested as a new memory. Plan "Day/hour/action decomposition" Top-down plan tree. Revisable when observations contradict. Smallville "Park 2023's sandbox" 25-agent simulation that produced the Valentine's Day emergence. Believability "The quality metric" Human-rater score for whether behavior seems like a plausible agent. Problem In plain words first A generative agent is an LLM character that keeps a diary of what it sees (the memory stream ), periodically writes down what it has concluded ( reflection ), and plans its day. Park et al. put 25 such agents in a small town called Smallville, told one of them to throw a party, and watched the invitation spread on its own. There is no Zero to Agents chapter on this; it builds on Lesson 16.13 (shared memory). This lesson tests which parts of the lesson's miniature are scripted, then hands two of its jobs, reflection and importance rating, to a small model. Most multi-agent systems are tightly-scripted teams: planner plans, coder codes, reviewer reviews. That works for well-defined tasks. It does not capture the emergent, unscripted behavior that arises when agents have memory, priorities, and an open world. Research, society simulation, and increasingly game AI need this second kind. The Smallville architecture is the benchmark for it. Until Park 2023, the best agent simulations were shallow script-followers; after it, the pattern is the default for generative agents in open worlds. If you build an agent simulation in 2026, you are either using Smallville's three components or explicitly justifying why you are not. Concept The three components Memory stream. An append-only log of observations, actions, reflections, and plans. Each entry has a timestamp, a type, a description (natural language), and derived metadata: recency , importance (self-rated 1-10 by the agent), and relevance (cosine similarity to current query). Copy Memory retrieval combines the three scores: score = w_recency * recency + w_importance * importance + w_relevance * cos_sim . In Park et al., recency decays by a factor of 0.995 per game hour since the memory was last retrieved, each score is min-max normalised to [0, 1] across the candidate memories, and all three weights are 1. Top-k entries enter the current prompt. Reflection. Periodically (every N memories or on important events), the agent generates higher-order syntheses from recent memories. Reflection entries go back into the stream and are retrievable like any other memory. This is how agents build "understandings" — the architecture's equivalent of long-term beliefs. Plan. Top-down decomposition. First, a day-level plan in broad strokes ("go to work, have dinner with Klaus"). Then hour-level plans. Then action-level plans. Plans are revisable: when an observation contradicts a plan, the agent replans the affected segment. Why all three matter (ablation) Park et al. ran nested ablations: no reflection; no reflection and no planning; and no memory, planning or reflection. Each removal hurts believability: Without observation the agent misses context and acts on stale beliefs. Without reflection the agent cannot form higher-order beliefs; interactions stay shallow. Without plan behavior becomes reactive noise; goals dissipate. Human evaluators (100 of them) ranked the full architecture highest, then no reflection, then no reflection or planning, then human crowdworkers role-playing the agents, then the fully ablated agent. The differences were significant except between the crowdworkers and the fully ablated agent. The Valentine's Day emergence One agent, Isabella Rodriguez, is seeded with the goal "wants to throw a Valentine's Day party at Hobbs Cafe on Feb 14 at 5pm." The 24 other agents receive no such seed. Over simulated days: Isabella's plan includes inviting people. Each invitation becomes an observation in a neighbor's memory stream. That neighbor's reflection generates beliefs: "Isabella is throwing a party." The neighbor's plan incorporates "attend party on Feb 14." Neighbors tell other neighbors. The invitation spreads without central coordination. At 5pm on Feb 14, five agents converge at Hobbs Cafe. Of the twelve invited, three cited conflicts and four said they were interested but made no plan to come. This is emergence in the technical sense: system-level behavior (a party) arose from local interactions (bilateral invitations + individual planning) without a central orchestrator. The documented failure modes Park et al. explicitly document: Spatial norm errors. Agents enter stores after they close around 5pm, and walk into a one-person dorm bathroom while someone is inside. The model does not infer social-physical norms from the environment alone; the authors suggest writing them into location descriptions. Worse choices as memory grows. As agents learn more places, retrieving the relevant memory gets harder, and some chose odd locations, such as lunch at a bar instead of the cafe. Practical remedy: periodic memory compaction (summarize-and-prune) and decay on low-importance entries. Embellishment. Agents sometimes add details that are not in their memory; Isabella described an announcement that never happened. Mitigation: include source memory ids in reflection prompts and verify at retrieval time. A related effect comes from instruction tuning: agents were overly polite and cooperative; Isabella rarely refused a suggestion, so others' interests gradually reshaped her own. The agents ran on gpt-3.5-turbo. These are production-relevant failure modes: any 2026 agent simulation inherits them. Three-component implementation rules Memory is append-only. Never mutate a memory entry. Corrections are new entries. Importance scores are cheap. Call the LLM to rate importance 1-10 at write time. Cache the score. Retrieval is ranked, not filtered. Top-k by combined score; do not use hard filters (which lose context). Reflection runs periodically. Trigger when the sum of importance of unprocessed memories exceeds a threshold (e.g., 150). Plans are revisable. When a new observation contradicts a plan, regenerate the affected segment only, not the whole plan. Generative agents beyond Smallville The 2024-2026 follow-up literature extends the architecture: Multi-agent social simulation for policy / market research. Smallville-like populations simulate user behavior in response to features. Faster than A/B tests; accuracy is contested. NPC AI for games. RPGs with Smallville agents produce emergent storylines instead of scripted quests. Generative-agent evaluation benchmarks. Rather than task accuracy, the metric becomes believability + coherence of behavior over long runs. The architecture is the reference. Extensions swap components (vector store for memory, retrieval-augmented reflection, neurosymbolic plan) but keep the three-part structure. Why this matters for multi-agent engineering Smallville is the proof of concept that multi-agent emergence is cheap when the components are right. Open-source re-implementations exist on smaller models; how much believability they keep is not well measured, and the small-model run below shows where a 0.5B model breaks. Any production system that needs emergent social behavior uses this shape. Any system that needs tight task execution uses the supervisor / roles / primitives patterns from earlier in this phase. The same idea as a formula Retrieval score. For memory at time , Park et al. score ( m ) + i ^ ( m ) + c ^ ( m ) , where for game hours since the memory was last retrieved, is the 1-to-10 importance, is the cosine similarity to the query, and each hat means min-max normalised over the candidates, so each term lies in . Without normalisation, whichever term has the widest range decides the ranking. Reflection trigger. Reflect when the importance of memories since the last reflection adds up past a threshold : , with in the paper. If the rater compresses every score into a narrow band, the trigger fires on volume, not on events that matter. Worked example Scoring the fire alarm against the party At tick 4 the query is "party cafe". Memory A: "I would enjoy a party at the cafe", tick 2, importance 6. Memory B: "the fire alarm went off in my building", tick 4, importance 10. The lesson's score is recency + importance/10 + a keyword bonus of 0.6 or 0.1. A: + 0.6 + 0.6 = 0.55 + 1.2 = 1.75 . B: + 1.0 + 0.1 = 2.10 . The unrelated alarm ranks first for a question about the party, because recency and importance together outweigh the keyword bonus. Using this lesson, what went wrong, and what would you change? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Simulated people for research. Park and colleagues' follow-up, generative agent simulations of 1,052 real people built from two-hour interviews, predicted their General Social Survey answers with 69.4% accuracy, against 79.5% for the participants' own answers two weeks apart. Games and companions. NPC systems in games and character apps use the same loop: memory, retrieval, reflection and plans, usually on a vector store with summarisation. Agent memory products. In-memory stdlib is for prototypes. Log the retrieval trace. For every action, log the top-k memories that drove it. This is your debug ability. Budget per-agent tokens. Each agent's retrieve + reflect + plan per tick is LLM calls. N agents × T ticks × calls-per-tick can dwarf your budget. Compact memory periodically. Summarize-and-prune low-importance entries. Retention policy is a design decision, not a detail. Detect spatial / social norm violations explicitly. The library and tick 2 in the invitation are never read. Nowhere, at importance 5. reflect skips memories below 6, so no belief forms and no plan is made. Solution B1 · A compressed rater driving reflection What went wrong. The small model's importance scores sit in a narrow 3-to-5 band, so the sum-over-150 trigger fires after enough ordinary memories, about every 40, and the town fills with reflections about breakfast. Those reflections are recent and often rated as high as anything else, so they crowd quest events out of retrieval. And with no memory rated as notable, the festival announcement never rises far enough to be retrieved and passed on. What to change: - Calibrate the rater: measure its scores on labelled examples and rescale them, or rank memories relative to each other instead of trusting absolute numbers. - Set the trigger from data: pick the threshold so reflections fire at the rate you want on real play logs. - Normalise retrieval terms and give event-type memories, such as announcements, a relevance boost. - Track spread as a metric: for each announced event, log how many NPCs know of it after a day, so a festival that reaches nobody shows up as a number. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Li et al. (arXiv:2310.10701) showed that LLM agents in a cooperative text game exhibit emergent high-order Theory of Mind (ToM) — reasoning about what another agent believes about a third agent's beliefs — but fail on long-horizon planning due to context management and hallucination. Riedl (arXiv:2510.05174, ICLR 2026) measured higher-order synergy in groups that cannot talk and found that personas produce identity-linked differentiation, and only adding a ToM prompt produces goal-directed alignment; a smaller model (Llama-3.1-8B) mostly failed the task and showed weak, mixed evidence. That is, coordination emergence is prompt-conditional and model-dependent, not free. This lesson implements a minimal ToM-aware agent, runs a cooperative task with and without its belief model, and checks where the measured coordination really comes from. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Theory of Mind "Understanding others' minds" The capacity to model another agent's beliefs. Graded by order (0, 1, 2+). Sally-Anne test "The false-belief test" 1985 developmental psychology; LLMs pass plain versions, fail complex ones. First-order ToM "A believes X" Modeling one other's beliefs about facts. Second-order ToM "A believes B believes X" Recursive modeling one level deeper. Identity-linked differentiation "Stable roles over time" Riedl's metric: roles persist, not random. Goal-directed complementarity "Disjoint actions" Agents target different subtasks, not the same one. Higher-order synergy "Group exceeds any subset" Riedl's information-theoretic measure: predictive information no subset of agents carries alone. Coordination illusion "It looks coordinated" Prompt-dressed appearance of coordination without measurable signal. Problem In plain words first Theory of mind (ToM) is the ability to model what someone else believes, including beliefs that are wrong. First-order ToM is "Alice believes the key is in the drawer"; second-order is "Alice believes Bob believes it". For agents, ToM is one way to coordinate without talking: predict what the others will do and pick something different. There is no Zero to Agents chapter on this; it builds on Lesson 16.7 (debate) and Lesson 16.17 (generative agents). This lesson checks where the lesson's coordination gain really comes from, then tests a small model on false-belief stories. Multi-agent coordination often looks magical: agents divide labor, anticipate each other, avoid redundancy. Usually this "emergence" is an artifact of prompt engineering — someone told the agents to "coordinate." Remove the prompt, remove the coordination. Riedl's 2025 finding is stricter. In his group game, every condition showed some temporal synergy, but agents aligned their behaviour toward the shared goal only when prompted to reason about other agents' minds (ToM), and success rates did not differ significantly between conditions. This matters for production: teams ship "multi-agent coordination" features that are prompt-dependent and brittle. This lesson treats ToM as a specific capability (reasoning about beliefs about beliefs), builds a minimal ToM-aware agent, and measures what real coordination looks like vs. what prompt dressing looks like. Concept What ToM means Developmental psychology: a 3-year-old thinks anyone's inner world matches theirs. A 5-year-old understands others have different beliefs. A 7-year-old reasons about beliefs about beliefs ("she thinks that I think the ball is under the cup"). These are zeroth, first, and second-order ToM. For LLM agents, ToM orders map to: Zeroth-order: no model of others. The agent acts on its own observations only. First-order: the agent has a model of each other agent's beliefs. "Alice believes X." Second-order: the agent models recursive beliefs. "Alice believes that Bob believes X." Li et al. 2023 found that high-order ToM emerges in LLM agents in a cooperative text game, but that planning suffers from failures in managing long-horizon context and from hallucination about the task state; giving agents an explicit belief state helped. The Sally-Anne test, in brief A 1985 false-belief test: Sally puts a marble in basket A, leaves. Anne moves it to basket B. Where will Sally look when she returns? A child with first-order ToM says basket A (Sally's belief differs from reality). A child without says basket B. GPT-4-era LLMs pass Sally-Anne-style tests when posed plainly. They fail when the narrative is long, the scene changes several times, or the question is phrased indirectly. That is the practical 2026 state of ToM in production LLMs. Riedl's coordination measurement Riedl (arXiv:2510.05174) built a population-scale test: groups of 10 agents that cannot communicate each guess a number, and the group gets only "too high" or "too low" feedback on the sum (a group binary search). Three prompt conditions: plain instructions, personas, and personas plus "think about what other agents might do". 200 groups per condition with GPT-4.1, plus other models. Measures: Identity-linked differentiation. Do agents develop stable role distinctions over time? Goal-directed complementarity. Do agents' actions complement each other (different subtasks) rather than duplicate? Higher-order synergy. A partial-information-decomposition measure of whether the group carries predictive information about its future that no single agent, pair or triad carries alone. Result: all three conditions showed temporal synergy. Personas added stable, identity-linked differentiation. Only the ToM condition raised the measures of alignment across agents, and even then the structure looked pairwise rather than irreducibly three-way. Success rates did not differ significantly, and ToM improved performance only indirectly, at marginal significance. Llama-3.1-8B mostly failed the game (5.5% to 14% success) with weak, mixed evidence of emergence. The coordination illusion Without statistical controls, "emergent coordination" in demos often reflects: Prompt engineering that bakes in coordination (system prompts that say "work together"). Observer bias (we see patterns we expect). Post-hoc selection of successful runs. Production systems that market "emergent coordination" without measurable signal should be treated as marketing. Measure before claiming. A minimal ToM-aware agent Structure: Copy The other_models attribute is the ToM state. First-order ToM keeps just one level. Second-order adds other_models[i][other_models_of_j] — what I think agent i thinks agent j believes. Why long-horizon hurts Li et al. document: context limits cause agents to forget which belief belongs to whom. Hallucination adds false beliefs to other-agent models. Both produce "I thought he thought X" errors that compound over time. Mitigations documented in the paper and in 2024-2026 follow-ups: Explicit ToM state in the prompt. Structured format: {agent_id: belief_list} . Forces retrieval to preserve identity-belief binding. Shorter reasoning chains. Fewer ToM updates per turn reduce compounding hallucination. External ToM store. Maintain the model outside the LLM context; inject only relevant parts per turn. Where ToM fails in production Adversarial settings. Agents with good ToM are easier to manipulate (you can model what they model of you, then exploit). Heterogeneous teams. When models are different, the ToM model that works for one opponent does not generalize. Ground-truth-dependent tasks. ToM is about beliefs; if correctness depends on facts, ToM can be a distraction. The coordination you can actually measure Three practical signals a team's coordination is real rather than prompt-dressed: Complementarity over time. Over a multi-turn task, do agents' actions cover disjoint sub-tasks? Anticipation. Does agent A's action at turn T+1 depend on a prediction about B's action at T+2 that turned out correct? Correction. When A misreads B's belief at turn T, does A correct by turn T+2? These are measurable in a logged multi-agent system. They are the substantive version of the "coordination" narrative. Riedl's information-theoretic tests (ICLR 2026) are one of the first ways to check whether a group's coordination is more than its prompts; the replication code is public. ToM benchmarks keep moving. Controls that would test the claim: - Same information, no model: give the baseline the assignment table too; if it also never collides, the table explains the result. - No table, with the model: remove the schedule and let robots infer intentions from each other's movement; measure collisions against random and against a fixed convention. - Perturbations: change assignments mid-shift without telling every robot, and see whether the model tracks who knows what. - Statistics: report collisions per hour with confidence intervals over many shifts, not one demo run. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Bio-inspired optimization is making an LLM comeback. LMPSO (arXiv:2504.09247) uses PSO where each particle's velocity is a prompt and the LLM generates the next candidate; works well on structured outputs (tours, math expressions, programs). Model Swarms (arXiv:2410.11163) treats each LLM expert as a PSO particle on a model-weight manifold and reports a 13.3% average gain over the strongest of 12 baselines on 9 datasets, with as few as 200 examples. SwarmPrompt (ICAART 2025) hybridizes PSO + Grey Wolf for prompt optimization. AMRO-S (arXiv:2603.12933) uses ACO-style pheromones for multi-agent LLM routing — interpretable routing evidence, a quality-gated asynchronous update that decouples inference from learning, and a 4.7x wall-clock speedup when concurrency rises from 20 to 1,000 processes. This lesson implements PSO on prompt parameter space and ACO on agent routing, measures why these classical algorithms fit the LLM era, and when they do not. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means PSO "Particle Swarm Optimization" Kennedy-Eberhart 1995. Population-based gradient-free optimizer. ACO "Ant Colony Optimization" Dorigo 1992. Path/route optimization via pheromone trails. LMPSO "PSO with LLM generation" arXiv:2504.09247. Velocity is a prompt; LLM produces candidates. Model Swarms "PSO on expert weights" arXiv:2410.11163. Gradient-free update on model parameter subspace. AMRO-S "ACO for agent routing" arXiv:2603.12933. Per-task-type pheromones over a layered graph of agents. This lesson's version is a task-type × agent matrix. p_best / g_best "Personal / global best" Per-particle and swarm-wide best solutions found so far. Pheromone "Routing memory" Strength on an edge; decays over time; deposits on quality. Quality-gated update "Only learn from good runs" Pheromone deposit conditioned on quality check. Catastrophic drift "Distribution shift" Fitness landscape changes; old p_best and pheromones become stale. Problem In plain words first Particle swarm optimisation (PSO) searches by moving a population of candidate solutions toward the best ones found so far, using only a score, no gradients. Ant colony optimisation (ACO) learns which routes work by leaving "pheromone" on good choices and letting it fade over time. Both suit LLM systems where you can score an output but cannot differentiate it. There is no Zero to Agents chapter on this; it builds on Lesson 16.9 (parallel swarms). This lesson compares the lesson's PSO and router with simple baselines, then runs PSO on a real model's sampling settings. You have a prompt that scores 62% on your task eval. You want to improve it. The naive move is gradient-free manual tweaking, which scales badly. Reinforcement learning needs reward signals and enough rollouts to train. Backprop through prompts is not really possible — the prompt is a discrete string, not a differentiable parameter. Classical bio-inspired optimization — PSO for continuous search spaces, ACO for path selection — was designed exactly for this regime: gradient-free, population-based, cheap per evaluation. Pair them with LLMs for the gradient-free search step, and you get a surprisingly practical optimizer. The same patterns apply to agent routing in multi-agent systems. An ACO-style pheromone trail records which agent worked best on which task-type, lets the router exploit the trail, and decays pheromones so routes can be rediscovered. Concept PSO refresher (Kennedy & Eberhart 1995) Particle Swarm Optimization: population of particles in a continuous search space. Each particle has position x_i and velocity v_i . Each iteration: Copy Where p_best is particle's own best, g_best is swarm's best, w, c1, c2 are inertia + cognitive + social weights, r1, r2 are random factors. PSO on LLM outputs — LMPSO arXiv:2504.09247 (Shinohara et al.) adapts PSO for LLM-generated structured outputs: travelling-salesman tours, Python heuristics and symbolic-regression expressions. Each particle is a candidate output. Velocity is a prompt that describes how to modify the current output toward the personal/global best. The LLM generates the new output from the velocity prompt. The "inertia" of the velocity is a prompt like "make small incremental changes." This works well when: - The output is structured (parseable, evaluable). - Fitness is automatic (test runs, arithmetic evaluation). - Population is small (~10-30 particles) so total LLM calls stay manageable. It does not work well when fitness needs human review — the per-iteration cost becomes prohibitive. Model Swarms arXiv:2410.11163 (Feng et al., ICML 2025) takes PSO off the output layer and into the model layer. Each "particle" is an expert LLM, located by its weights. The swarm moves the weights toward the collective best via a gradient-free update. Reported: 13.3% average gain over the second-strongest of 12 composition baselines on 9 datasets, working with as few as 200 examples. The key insight is that expert models fine-tuned from one base model sit near each other in weight space, so moving and combining them (the paper uses LoRA-adapted experts) stays cheap and effective. ACO refresher (Dorigo 1992) Ant Colony Optimization: ants traverse a graph; each path has a pheromone trail. Ant move probabilities weight by pheromone strength. Ants that complete the task deposit pheromone proportional to solution quality. Pheromone decays over time. AMRO-S — ACO for agent routing arXiv:2603.12933 uses ACO for multi-agent routing. It treats routing as choosing a path through a layered graph of agents; each task type keeps its own pheromone matrix over stage-to-stage transitions, and a query's task mixture blends the matrices. Pheromones strengthen paths that produce good outputs. Key contributions: Interpretable routing evidence. Pheromone strength is a human-readable signal. Quality-gated asynchronous update. A small sample of requests goes into a buffer off the serving path; an LLM judge gives each trajectory a pass or fail, and only passing ones reinforce pheromones, so learning never adds serving latency. Scales under load. The same workload ran 4.7x faster in wall-clock time at 1,000 concurrent processes than at 20, with GSM8K accuracy steady at about 96%; across five benchmarks it averaged 87.83 against 85.93 for the strongest routing baseline. The quality gate matters: without it, fast-but-wrong agents accrue pheromone, and the system locks in on bad routes. When to use PSO / ACO for LLMs Use PSO when: - Search space is continuous or maps to continuous parameters (prompt embeddings, LoRA weights, numeric generation parameters). - Fitness is cheap and automatic. - Population can be small (10-30). Use ACO when: - You have a routing or path-selection problem. - Decisions reinforce over time (the same task types come back). - You need interpretable evidence for routing decisions. Do not use either when: - Fitness requires human review (too expensive per iteration). - The search space is discrete and combinatorial in a way that PSO does not cover (use genetic algorithms instead). - Real-time decisions need strict latency (PSO/ACO converge slowly relative to single-pass heuristics). Why bio-inspired still wins Gradient-based methods need differentiable signals. LLM outputs and routing decisions are not trivially differentiable. Pseudo-gradient methods (reinforcement-learned routers, DPO-style prompt tuners) work but need expensive training. PSO and ACO need only an evaluator function. If you can score a candidate output or a routing decision, you can optimize over the space. That makes the bar for applicability much lower. Practical limits Population budget. N particles × T iterations × per-eval cost. For LLM evals at ~$0.02 / call, a 20-particle PSO running 50 iterations costs ~$20. Plan accordingly. Exploration vs exploitation. Pheromone decay rate and PSO inertia trade off; too fast decay → forget solutions; too slow → stuck on early local optima. Catastrophic drift. Both algorithms can converge and then diverge if fitness landscape shifts (new data distribution). Monitor best-fitness stability. The same idea as a formula PSO update. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, small NumPy-free implementations), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The reinforcement-learning heritage of multi-agent coordination, which still informs LLM-agent systems in 2026. MADDPG (Lowe et al., NeurIPS 2017, arXiv:1706.02275) introduced Centralized Training, Decentralized Execution (CTDE): each critic sees all agents' states and actions during training; at test time only local actors run. Works for cooperative, competitive, and mixed settings. QMIX (Rashid et al., ICML 2018, arXiv:1803.11485) is value-decomposition with a monotonic mixing network; per-agent Qs combine into joint Q so argmax distributes cleanly — dominant on StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC). MAPPO (Yu et al., NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2103.01955) is PPO with a centralized value function; "surprisingly effective" on particle-world, SMAC, Google Research Football, Hanabi with minimal tuning. These underpin training policies for agent teams that must act decentrally. MAPPO is a standard cooperative-MARL baseline . This lesson builds each from a small grid-world toy and lands the three ideas in muscle memory before touching LLM-agent training. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means MARL "Multi-Agent RL" Reinforcement learning for multi-agent systems. CTDE "Centralized Training, Decentralized Execution" Train with global info; deploy with local policies. MADDPG "Multi-Agent DDPG" CTDE with per-agent critic seeing all observations + actions. QMIX "Value decomposition" Monotonic mixing of per-agent Qs. Cooperative. MAPPO "Multi-Agent PPO" PPO with centralized value function. A standard cooperative-MARL baseline. Value decomposition "Sum of individual Qs" Joint Q represented as a monotone function of per-agent Qs. Non-stationarity "Moving targets" Each agent's env changes as others learn. The core MARL problem. On-policy / off-policy "Learn from current / replay" PPO is on-policy (MAPPO); DDPG and Q-learning are off-policy. SMAC "StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge" Cooperative micromanagement benchmark; QMIX's homegrown ground. Problem In plain words first Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) trains several agents that act together. The central trick is CTDE , centralized training with decentralized execution: during training you may use everything about everyone, but each agent must act at run time from what it alone can see. MADDPG gives each agent a critic that sees all agents; QMIX splits a team value into per-agent values; MAPPO is PPO with a value function that sees the whole state. There is no Zero to Agents chapter on this; it builds on Lesson 16.9 (parallel swarms) and Phase 9 (reinforcement learning). This lesson checks which side of CTDE the lesson's demos actually run, then tries a prompted small model as a decentralized policy. LLM-agent systems increasingly train policies for inter-agent coordination: when to defer, when to act, which peer to call. The literature that tells you how to train such policies is Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), which predates the LLM wave and has a small set of dominant algorithms. Reading MARL papers without the pattern vocabulary is painful. Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), value decomposition, and centralized critics are not buzzwords — they are specific answers to specific problems: Independent RL (each agent learns alone) is non-stationary from each agent's perspective. Bad. Centralized RL (one agent controls all) does not scale and violates execution constraints. CTDE gets the best of both: train with global information, deploy with local policies. Concept Three environments the papers use Particle World (multi-agent particle env). Simple 2D physics with cooperative/competitive tasks. MADDPG's original testbed. StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC). Cooperative micro-management, partial observation. QMIX's testbed. Discrete actions, continuous states. Google Research Football, Hanabi, MPE. MAPPO baselines. Different envs have different action/observation types. The algorithms pick accordingly. MADDPG (2017) — the CTDE pattern Each agent i has an actor mu_i(o_i) that maps its own observation to action. Each agent also has a critic Q_i(x, a_1, ..., a_n) that sees all observations and all actions during training. The actor is updated by policy gradient against the critic's evaluation. Copy Why CTDE: at training time, we know everyone's actions; we use that to reduce variance in each critic. At deploy time, each agent only sees o_i and calls mu_i(o_i) . Failure mode: each critic's input grows with the number of agents (it includes all actions), so the critics get harder to learn as teams grow, and large teams need approximations such as parameter sharing or attention over agents. QMIX (2018) — value decomposition Cooperative only. The joint action-value Q_tot is a monotone mixing function of per-agent Q-values: ​ ( τ , a ) = f ( Q 1 ​ ( τ 1 ​ , a 1 ​ ) , … , Q n ​ ( τ n ​ , a n ​ ) ) , ∂ Q i ​ ∂ f ​ ≥ 0 The monotonicity guarantees argmax_a Q_tot can be computed by each agent choosing argmax_{a_i} Q_i independently. That is exactly the decentralized execution property you need. At training time, a mixing network produces Q_tot from the per-agent Qs. Why QMIX wins on SMAC: cooperative StarCraft micro-management has homogeneous agents, local obs, global reward — perfect fit for value decomposition. Failure mode: the monotonicity constraint is restrictive; some tasks have reward structures that are not monotone decomposable (one agent sacrificing for the team). Extensions (QTRAN, QPLEX) relax this. MAPPO (2022) — the overlooked default Multi-Agent PPO: PPO with a centralized value function. Each agent has its own policy; all agents share (or have per-agent) value functions that see the full state. Yu et al. 2022 benchmarked MAPPO against MADDPG, QMIX, and their extensions on four testbeds and found: PPO-based methods were competitive with or better than off-policy MARL methods, in final returns and often in sample efficiency, on the particle-world environments (MPE), SMAC, Google Research Football and Hanabi. Minimal hyperparameter tuning required. Ablations identified the implementation details and hyperparameters that matter most, with practical advice for each. The community underrated on-policy MARL until this paper. Since then MAPPO has become a standard baseline for cooperative MARL that new methods are expected to beat. Why LLM-agent engineers should care Three direct uses: Router training. A meta-agent chooses which sub-agent handles a task. This is a MARL problem with N decentralized sub-agents and one centralized router. MAPPO fits. Role emergence. In generative-agent simulations, training agents to adopt complementary roles over time is a MARL problem in disguise. QMIX-style value decomposition forces complementarity by construction. Multi-agent tool use. When agents share tools and compete for budget, training them via CTDE produces deployable local policies that respect resource constraints. Practical caveat: in 2026, most production LLM-agent systems prompt their policies rather than train them. MARL comes in when you have (a) lots of interaction data, (b) a clear reward signal, and (c) willingness to invest in training infrastructure. CTDE as a design pattern beyond RL Even without training, CTDE is a useful architectural pattern: During design , assume full team visibility. At runtime , enforce decentralized execution: each agent sees only o_i . The pattern forces you to keep per-agent state explicit and to think about partial observability up front. Many production multi-agent systems silently assume shared state everywhere — CTDE discipline prevents that. The non-stationarity problem When multiple agents learn simultaneously, each agent's environment (which includes others' policies) is non-stationary. Classical single-agent RL proofs break. The MARL algorithms in this lesson all address this: MADDPG: global critic sees all actions, so its value estimate is stationary. QMIX: value decomposition moves learning to a joint-Q space where optimality is well-defined. MAPPO: the centralized value function dampens variance from others' policy changes. In LLM-agent systems, non-stationarity manifests as "my agent worked last month, now that other agent upstream changed, mine misbehaves." Training MARL with CTDE is the principled fix; prompt-level fixes are faster but less durable. What this lesson does NOT cover Training actual networks is a Phase 09 topic. This lesson builds scripted-policy versions that demonstrate the CTDE, value-decomposition, and centralized-value patterns without gradient updates. The goal is to internalize the patterns before you pick up a full MARL library (PyMARL, MARLlib, RLlib multi-agent). The same idea as a formula CTDE in one line. a1621: Course home / Phase 16 · Multi-Agent Systems and Swarms Reputation, Token Incentives and Agent Economies Lesson 16.21 75 min Learn Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 16 · 16 (Bargaining and Negotiation between Agents), Phase 16 · 09 (Parallel Swarm Networks) Type : Learn. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Long-horizon autonomous agents (METR now measures frontier agents' time horizons in hours) need economic agency. One proposed 5-layer stack (Xu, arXiv:2602.14219) is: DePIN (physical compute) → Identity (W3C DIDs + reputation capital) → Cognition (RAG + MCP) → Settlement (account abstraction) → Governance (Agentic DAOs). Production agent-incentive networks include Bittensor (TAO subnets reward task-specific models), Fetch.ai / ASI Alliance (ASI-1 Mini LLM + FET token), and Gonka (transformer-based PoW, with most network compute serving real AI inference). Academic work: an AAMAS 2025 Blue Sky paper on decentralized LaMAS proposes Shapley-value credit attribution to reward contributing agents fairly; Google Research's "Mechanism design for large language models" proposes token auctions in which agents bid to steer a jointly generated text, with second-price-style payments under monotone aggregation. This lesson builds a minimal agent marketplace, applies Shapley-value credit attribution to a multi-agent pipeline, and runs a plain second-price auction so the game-theory machinery lands concretely. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means DePIN "Decentralized physical infrastructure" Token-incentivized compute/storage/bandwidth. Bittensor, Akash, Render. DID "Decentralized identifier" W3C spec for portable IDs. Agent reputation binds to DID, not to a platform. ERC-4337 "Account abstraction" Contract accounts that can sponsor gas, enabling agent payments. Shapley value "Fair credit attribution" Unique allocation satisfying efficiency, symmetry, linearity, null. Second-price auction "Vickrey auction" Truthful mechanism: winner pays second-highest bid. The token auction generalises it to monotone aggregation. Reputation capital "Accumulated quality score" DID-bound score from confirmed contributions; decays over time. Agentic DAO "Agents + humans govern" DAO with agent voters as first-class, voting power tied to reputation. TAO / FET / GPU credits "Token denominations" Bittensor TAO, Fetch.ai FET, various DePIN tokens. Problem In plain words first When agents from different owners work together, someone has to decide who gets paid and how much. Shapley values split a team's result by each member's average extra contribution. A second-price auction gives a job to the highest bidder at the second-highest price, which makes bidding your true value the best strategy. Reputation is a running score that decides who gets the next job. There is no Zero to Agents chapter on this; it builds on Lesson 16.16 (negotiation). This lesson tests the lesson's auction and reputation code against tricks an open market invites, then asks a small model to bid. Multi-agent systems get complicated when agents produce value jointly but need to be rewarded individually. Classical mechanisms — equal split, last-contributor-takes-all — are unfair or gameable. Coalition-based rewarding via Shapley values is fair by construction but expensive to compute. The 2025-2026 literature pushes useful approximations: Shapley sampling, monotone aggregation auctions, and on-chain reputation that accrues from confirmed contributions. Beyond credit attribution, the field has turned to actual economic agents: Bittensor pays TAO to miners whose outputs validators rate highly on subnet-specific tasks, the ASI Alliance's Fetch.ai offers the ASI-1 Mini LLM and agent payments in FET, and Gonka points transformer proof-of-work at real AI inference. Agents that transact autonomously exist today; the question is how to align incentives. This lesson treats agent economies as a specific problem family — credit attribution, mechanism design, and reputation — and builds each with the minimal math so the ideas stick. Concept The 5-layer agent-economy stack DePIN (physical compute). Decentralized infrastructure that rents GPU, storage, bandwidth. Bittensor subnets, Render Network, Akash. Not agent-specific; agents use it. Identity. W3C Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) give each agent a durable ID independent of any platform. Reputation accrues to the DID. The Agent Network Protocol (ANP) uses DID as the discovery layer. Cognition. The agent's reasoning loop: LLM + RAG + MCP. This is what the other phases build. Settlement. Account abstraction (ERC-4337) lets agents pay gas from their own balances without holding ETH. Agents can pay for services, each other, or compute. Governance. Agentic DAOs: governance structures where humans and agents vote on protocol changes, with voting power tied to reputation. Not every production system uses all five. Bittensor uses 1, 2, partially 3, partially 4, none of 5. OpenAI agents use none except 3. The stack is a reference map, not a requirement. Bittensor, Fetch.ai, Gonka — what runs Bittensor (TAO). Subnets are specialized tasks (language modeling, image generation, forecasting). Miners submit model outputs. Validators rank them; stake-weighted scoring (Yuma Consensus) distributes the rewards. Second-price auction for aggregation Google Research (Dütting, Mirrokni, Paes Leme, Xu and Zuo; WWW 2024) proposes token auctions for jointly generated text, for example an ad summary several advertisers want to influence. Each agent is an LLM with its own next-token distribution and submits one bid; at every token an aggregation function combines the agents' distributions, weighted by their bids, into the distribution the text is sampled from. The aggregation is monotone if raising your bid never moves the output away from what you prefer. The paper shows that any monotone aggregation can be paired with a second-price-style payment, where an agent pays the critical bid at which its influence switches on, so that agents have no reason to misreport. The plain version of the same idea is the second-price (Vickrey) auction for a single slot, which this lesson's code implements: the highest bid wins and pays the second-highest bid, so bidding your true value is a dominant strategy. Why this matters for LLM systems: you can outsource tasks to agents with private costs or values, and the mechanism removes the incentive to misreport, as long as its assumptions hold. Solutions Solution P1 · Nothing, or 0.12 Second-price: nothing. agent-c still wins and still pays the second-highest bid, 0.82, so its gain stays . Lowering the bid below 0.82 would only risk losing. First-price: 0.12. It pays its own bid, so bidding 0.95 gains nothing, while bidding 0.83 still wins and gains . That is why first-price auctions invite shading and second-price auctions do not. Solution B1 · Shills and whitewashing What is happening. Operators run several identities from one account. Some bid just below the real winner as shills, raising what buyers pay. Others take jobs on their free top reputation, deliver poor work, and re-register when their score falls, which is whitewashing. The auction and the reputation rule both assume one identity per participant. What to change: - Start new identities low , and let them earn reputation on small or verified jobs first. - Tie identities to cost: stake, verified payment details or a deposit that is lost on bad behaviour. - Detect linked bidders: flag accounts that share payment sources, devices or timing, and drop their bids from price-setting. - Verify before paying , so poor work earns no reward or reputation, and watch price and quality per job type over time. In plain words first The idea in one line Scaling multi-agent systems to thousands of concurrent runs requires durable execution — work queues plus checkpoints, so any worker can resume any run after any crash, provided lease handling, idempotent side effects, and deterministic replay are in place. LangGraph's runtime is the reference example: it writes a checkpoint after each super-step keyed by thread_id (Postgres by default); worker crashes release a lease and another worker resumes. Agents can sleep indefinitely waiting for human input. MegaAgent (arXiv:2408.09955) ran a per-agent producer-consumer queue with three states (Idle / Processing / Response) and two-layer coordination (intra-group chat + inter-group admin chat). Fiber/async beats thread-per-job for LLM streaming: threads sit idle 99% of the time waiting for tokens, fibers cooperatively yield on I/O. Counterpoint: Ashpreet Bedi's "Scaling Agentic Software" argues for FastAPI + Postgres + nothing else until load proves otherwise — simple architectures go further than expected. This lesson builds a durable checkpoint log, a per-agent work queue with state transitions, an async-vs-thread demo, and lands the pragmatic "start simple" rule. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Durable execution "Persist the program state" Engine writes state after each super-step; crash recovery is deterministic. Super-step "Transactional boundary" Unit of work between checkpoints. LangGraph term. thread_id "Agent run identifier" Key that binds checkpoints and resume logic. Idempotency "Safe to retry" Repeating a side effect produces the same result as one attempt. Outbox pattern "Decouple side effects" Write intent to a table; a separate executor performs and marks done. At-least-once delivery "Possible duplicates" Message queue semantics; dedup key makes consumer effective-once. Rainbow deploy "Overlapping versions" Multiple runtime versions concurrent during long-running workloads. Async fiber "Cooperative yielding" User-mode concurrency; cheap compared to threads for I/O-bound loads. Checkpoint "State snapshot" Serialized state at a super-step boundary; key for resume. From Zero to Agents Already covered in your course These lessons teach the basics this one builds on. Read them first if the ideas are new; this lesson does not repeat them. Lesson 14.140 · Durable execution and deployment Lesson 14.141 · Scaling agents: capacity, quotas and tenants Lesson 14.149 · Platforms and multi-agent systems at scale Problem In plain words first In production, agent runs last minutes or hours, workers crash, and load spikes. Durable execution saves each run's state after every step (a checkpoint ), so any worker can pick the run up where it stopped. Two more things make that safe: side effects that can be repeated without harm ( idempotency ), and only one worker owning a run at a time (a lease ). Durable execution, scaling and multi-agent platforms are covered in Lessons 14.140, 14.141 and 14.149 (linked above). This lesson breaks the lesson's checkpoint store in the two ways production does, measures what threads cost, and checkpoints a small real agent. A prototype multi-agent system works on one laptop with three agents in an in-memory event loop. You move to production: Agents sometimes run for hours (long research, human-in-the-loop waits). Worker processes crash. Restarting loses state. Peak load is 10x average; you need horizontal scaling. Users pay per agent-run; you need exactly-once semantics for charging. The in-memory event loop does none of these. You need a durable execution layer underneath. The 2026 canonical options are: A workflow engine with checkpoints (Temporal, LangGraph runtime). A message queue with a state store (Postgres + SQS/RabbitMQ). Actor-model frameworks (MegaAgent's producer-consumer per agent). Hand-rolled FastAPI + Postgres (Bedi's argument). This lesson builds a miniature of each. Concept Durable execution, the pattern A durable-execution engine persists the full program state after each "step" (super-step, in LangGraph's language). On crash: Copy Requirements for this to work: Serializable state. All agent state has to be persistable. Function closures with live database connections do not survive. Deterministic resume. Given the same state and same inputs, the agent produces the same actions (or defers to an external deterministic oracle for LLM calls). Idempotent side effects. External calls (tool calls, payments) must be idempotent or use a deduplication key. LangGraph writes a checkpoint after each super-step; Temporal writes after each activity; Restate uses event-sourced journals. All three implement the same pattern. A checkpoint-per-step runtime LangGraph's runtime is the worked example: each agent has a thread_id ; state is a typed dict; each super-step writes a row to the checkpoints table. On resume, the runtime replays from the last checkpoint, not from scratch. Agents can interrupt() waiting for human input; the runtime persists and releases the worker. When input arrives, any worker can resume. This is a widely used production design in 2026. One cost to know: full snapshots of append-only state, such as a growing message list, make total checkpoint storage grow with the square of the number of steps; LangChain added delta channels in May 2026 that store per-step diffs with a full snapshot every K steps. MegaAgent's per-agent queue arXiv:2408.09955 describes MegaAgent, a system that organises LLM agents into groups without predefined procedures; its largest experiment, a national policy simulation, ran 590 agents. Architecture: Copy The two-layer coordination lets intra-group conversation happen densely while inter-group traffic stays sparse, because only admin agents talk across groups. In the Processing state an agent batches its queued messages into one model call, and in Response it checks its output before sending. Async vs thread-per-job LLM calls are I/O-bound. A thread waiting for the next token is idle almost all the time. Each OS thread reserves a stack (8 MB of virtual memory by default on Linux) and uses some tens of kilobytes of resident memory, plus scheduler overhead; at 10,000 concurrent calls that adds up. Fibers (Python asyncio , Go goroutines, Rust tokio ) cooperatively yield on I/O, and each costs only a few kilobytes. The same 10,000 calls fit comfortably in one process. At LLM-agent scale, async is not an optimization — it is the architecture. Exception: CPU-bound post-processing (embedding, tokenizer tricks) still wants threads or processes. Separate your I/O layer from your CPU layer. Bedi's counterpoint "Scaling Agentic Software" (Ashpreet Bedi of Agno, April 2026) argues that most teams over-engineer before they have measured load: "One FastAPI process. One Postgres database." may be enough for a multi-agent product with auth, persistence and observability, with queues, Redis or separate vector stores added only when load proves the need. The pragmatic default: FastAPI + Postgres. Each agent run is a row; state updated in-place with optimistic concurrency. Background jobs via pg_notify or a simple Celery worker. Retry policy in application code. Bedi leaves the breaking point to load tests rather than a number; measure your own. Upgrade when you see it failing. The rule: adopt durable-execution frameworks when you hit a concrete problem that simple architectures cannot solve. Premature adoption burns time on ceremonies that do not pay off. Exactly-once semantics For paid agent runs, you need "exactly-once effective" (at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumer). The engineering moves: Dedup key per run. Include it in every side-effect call. Outbox pattern. Side effects write to a table first, then a separate process executes them. Both steps idempotent. Compensating transactions. When a side effect succeeds but its tracking write fails, schedule a compensate. These are database-engineering patterns, not LLM-specific. The LLM tax is only that LLM calls are slow; everything else is standard distributed systems. Rainbow deployment Anthropic's multi-agent research system uses "rainbow deployments": multiple versions of the agent runtime run concurrently so long-running agents do not have to be killed on every code deploy. Canary new versions on a slice of traffic; retire old versions when their agents finish. This is standard for long-running stateful systems; the 2026 adaptation is that agents can live for hours, so deployment cycles must accommodate. The canonical production checklist Durable state (checkpoints, snapshots, or outbox + replayable log). Idempotent side effects. Async I/O layer for LLM calls. At-least-once delivery with dedup. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design Your multi-agent prototype runs in one process with an in-memory event loop. In production, runs last hours while they wait for human input, worker processes crash and lose everything, peak load is ten times the average, and users are charged per run so a retried side effect is a double charge. Design the layer that goes under the agents, and say what you would build first. Level 3 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Put a durable execution layer under the agents: persist the full run state after each step under a run id, so that when a worker crashes its lease expires and any other worker resumes from the last checkpoint. That needs serializable state, a deterministic resume, and idempotent side effects. For the charge, use a deduplication key per run and an outbox so that side effects are written as intent first and executed once, use asynchronous I/O for the model calls, and deploy new versions beside old ones so that in-flight runs are never killed. Build the simplest version first, a web service with a relational database, and adopt a workflow engine when a measured problem demands it. The resume path. Copy Three requirements make this work: Serializable state. Everything the agent holds must be persistable. A closure with a live database connection does not survive a crash. Deterministic resume. Given the same state and the same inputs, the agent takes the same actions, or defers to a recorded result for the model calls. Idempotent side effects. Every external call carries a key, or writes to a table first and is executed by a separate process. Graph runtimes write a checkpoint after each step under a thread id. Workflow engines write after each activity. Event-sourced runtimes keep a journal. The pattern is the same. The waiting run. A run that waits hours for a human must not hold a worker. The runtime persists the run, releases the worker, and any worker resumes when the input arrives. That is what makes the checkpoint the unit of the system rather than the process. Exactly once, effectively. At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer is the only kind of exactly-once you get. Move What it does Deduplication key per run Included in every side-effect call so a retry is recognized Outbox Intent is written to a table, and a separate executor performs it and marks it done Compensating transaction When the effect succeeded and the tracking write failed, schedule the reverse These are database patterns. The only agent-specific tax is that model calls are slow. Concurrency. Model calls are I/O bound, and a thread waiting for the next token is idle 99 percent of the time. At 10,000 concurrent calls, threads reserve about 80 GB of virtual address space for stacks and hundreds of megabytes of resident memory, plus scheduler overhead, while cooperative fibers fit easily in one process. Use asynchronous I/O for the model layer and threads or processes only for CPU-bound work such as embedding. Deploys. Long-running stateful agents cannot be hot-swapped. Run several versions of the runtime at once, send a slice of new runs to the new version, and retire the old version when its runs finish. What to build first. The lesson's counterpoint is that most teams over-engineer before they measure. A web service and a relational database, with each run as a row, optimistic concurrency on the state, a simple background worker and application-level retries, carries more load than most teams expect; measure where it breaks for your workload. Adopt a durable-execution engine when you hit a concrete problem the simple design cannot solve: hour-long waits at scale, cross-region coordination, or complex compensation policies. Plausible wrong answers. "Retry the whole run from the start when a worker dies." That repeats every side effect that already happened, which is the double charge in the prompt. "Use a thread per run; it is simpler." Threads idle while they wait for tokens, and at ten thousand concurrent calls the stacks alone exhaust memory. "Adopt a workflow engine on day one to be safe." The simple design carries about a hundred concurrent runs, and the engine's ceremony costs time until a measured problem pays for it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is the model call the hard part of deterministic resume? Expected: it is not deterministic, so the resume must replay the recorded result of the call rather than make it again. (level 3) What does the lease do? Expected: it marks a run as owned by one worker for a bounded time, so a crash frees the run for another worker without two workers running it at once. (level 4) How do you test the outbox? Expected: run the same side effect twice through the executor and assert one external call, then crash the executor between the effect and the mark and assert that the compensation or the idempotent redo leaves one effect. (level 4) Which feature of a workflow engine is hardest to replicate by hand, and is that a reason to adopt it? Expected: a reasoned pick such as durable timers for hour-long waits or compensation policies, with the rule that adoption follows a measured failure of the simple design. Where it is taught. Estimate it A swarm runtime uses one thread per in-flight model call. At peak it holds about 10,000 calls at once. Estimate the memory the threads take before any work is done, say what those threads are doing most of the time, and say what you would change. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Each thread reserves a stack (8 MB of virtual memory by default on Linux) and holds tens of kilobytes resident, so 10,000 threads reserve about 80 GB of address space and a few hundred megabytes of RAM before the first token arrives. Those threads are idle about 99 percent of the time, waiting for the next token from a model service. Move the model calls to cooperative fibers through asynchronous I/O, where the same 10,000 calls fit in one process, and keep threads or processes only for CPU-bound work such as embeddings. The estimate. Quantity Value Resident memory per waiting thread (measured in "Use it") about 16 KB, plus 8 MB of reserved virtual stack Concurrent calls 10,000 Resident memory for the threads about 160 MB, and about 80 GB of reserved address space That is the cost of holding the calls open, not of doing anything with them. A model call is I/O bound. The thread sends a request and then waits for tokens, and it is idle for about 99 percent of its life. What fibers change. Cooperative fibers yield on I/O instead of holding a stack while they wait. In the lesson's demo, 500 concurrent simulated 50 ms calls finish in about 0.055 s with asyncio and about 0.09 s with threads; the bigger difference is memory, about 16 KB resident and 8 MB of reserved stack per waiting thread against a few hundred bytes per asyncio task. At agent scale, asynchronous I/O is the architecture, not an optimization. The exception. CPU-bound post-processing wants threads or processes: embedding, tokenizer tricks, anything that computes rather than waits. Separate the I/O layer from the CPU layer and give each its own concurrency model. How this fits the rest of the runtime. The asynchronous layer handles the calls in flight. Durability is a separate concern: a checkpoint per step under a run id so that a crash of the process loses the in-flight calls and nothing else, and any worker resumes from the last checkpoint. Peak load at ten times the average is a reason for both: fibers to hold the calls cheaply, and queues with leases to spread them across workers. Plausible wrong answers. "Add memory until the threads fit." Memory for idle stacks is waste, and the next peak needs more, while fibers remove the cost. "Make the threads smaller with a reduced stack size." A smaller stack is still a stack per idle call, and the idle time stays at 99 percent. "Use fibers for everything, including embeddings." A CPU-bound step on the cooperative loop blocks every waiting call, so the CPU layer keeps threads or processes. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the thread count matter more than the request count? Expected: each thread holds a stack whether or not it is doing work, so memory scales with concurrency, not with throughput. (level 2) What breaks if you run the embedding step on the asynchronous loop? Expected: a CPU-bound task blocks the loop, so every waiting call stalls behind it, which is why CPU work goes to threads or processes. (level 3) The memory fits after the change. What is the next limit? Expected: the model service's rate limits and the queue depth, so the runtime needs back-pressure and a lease per run rather than more concurrency. (level 3) How do you prove the change before you ship it? Expected: run the lesson's comparison on your own call shape, measure wall-clock and peak memory for both versions at the same concurrency, and keep the numbers next to the decision. In plain words first The idea in one line The reference taxonomy for 2026 is MAST (Cemri et al., NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2503.13657), derived from 1642 execution traces across 7 state-of-the-art open-source MAS showing 41–86.7% failure rate . Three root categories, with 14 failure modes: system design issues — role ambiguity, unclear task definitions (41.77% in an earlier version of the paper); inter-agent misalignment — communication breakdowns, state desync (36.94%); task verification — missing validation, absent quality checks (21.30%). The Groupthink family, as this lesson calls it, comes from Gradient Institute's risk-analysis report (arXiv:2508.05687), which names six failure modes for governed multi-agent systems: monoculture collapse (same base model → correlated failures), conformity bias (agents reinforce each other's errors), deficient theory of mind, mixed-motive dynamics, cascading reliability failures and inter-agent communication failures. Cascading example: retry storms where a payment failure triggers order retries, which trigger inventory retries, which overwhelm inventory service (10x load in seconds — needs circuit breakers). Memory poisoning: one agent's hallucination enters shared memory, downstream agents treat it as fact; accuracy decays gradually, making root-cause diagnosis painful. STRATUS (NeurIPS 2025), a multi-agent system for cloud reliability engineering, beats earlier SRE agents by at least 1.5x on mitigation success using specialized detection, diagnosis and mitigation agents. This lesson treats failure modes as first-class engineering targets. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means MAST "The 2026 taxonomy" Cemri 2025; 3 root categories + 14 sub-types of failures. Specification Problem "Role ambiguity" Task or role under-defined; agents do not know what to do. Coordination Failure "State drift" Communication or sync breakdown between agents. Verification Gap "No one checked" Outputs accepted without independent validation. Groupthink family "Homogeneity failures" Monoculture, conformity, deficient ToM, mixed-motive, cascading (from Gradient Institute's six failure modes). Monoculture collapse "Same model, same hallucinations" Correlated errors from shared base model or training data. Retry storm "Cascading error amplification" One failure triggers retries which amplify load downstream. Circuit breaker "Fail fast on error rate" Open when error rate exceeds threshold; short-circuit with default. STRATUS "Incident response trio" Detection, diagnosis and mitigation agents for cloud SRE; at least 1.5x mitigation success over earlier SRE agents. Lesson 14.134 · Designing a production agent: specs, contracts and failure modes Problem In plain words first Multi-agent systems fail often, and in recognisable ways. MAST is a taxonomy of those failures from 1,642 real traces: badly specified tasks and roles, agents that misread or ignore each other, and results nobody checks. Other failures come from agents being too alike ( monoculture , conformity ) and from errors that spread from one service to the next ( cascades ), which circuit breakers contain. Specs, contracts and failure modes for a single production agent are covered in Lesson 14.134 (linked above). This lesson measures the lesson's retry-storm simulator and breaker, and tries a small model as a MAST annotator. Multi-agent systems fail 41-86.7% of the time on real tasks (Cemri et al. measured this across 7 open-source MAS, annotating 1,642 execution traces). That is not debuggable by "just add more agents." The failures have structural causes. The MAST taxonomy gives you the categories. This lesson maps each category to a concrete detection, diagnosis, and mitigation pattern so the numbers stop looking arbitrary. The 2026 production practice is to treat failure modes as design inputs. Your architecture is not "good enough" until you can point to each MAST category and name the mitigation you deployed. Concept MAST categories Specification Problems (system design issues in MAST; 41.77% of failures in an earlier version, about 44% when the latest version's per-mode rates are added up). The agent's task was not defined tightly enough. Examples: Role ambiguity: two agents both think they are the reviewer. Task underspecified: "summarize this" when the user wanted a specific angle. Success criteria implicit: the agent cannot tell if it succeeded. Mitigations: - Write explicit role contracts. Each agent's prompt states what it does and what it does not do . - Acceptance tests per task. Before the agent starts, define "done looks like X." - Pre-flight spec check: a separate agent reviews the task definition before dispatch. Coordination Failures (inter-agent misalignment; 36.94% earlier, about 32% in the latest version). Communication or state breakdowns. Examples: - Two agents update shared state without synchronization. - Message lost between agents (queue failure, timeout). - State drift: agent A thinks the task is done; agent B is still executing. Mitigations: - Versioned shared state with optimistic concurrency. - Explicit acknowledgment for critical messages (retry until acked). - Periodic state-sync checkpoints; detect drift early. Verification Gaps (task verification; 21.30% earlier, about 24% in the latest version). No independent check on outputs. Examples: - One agent claims success; no one verifies. - Chain of agents each trusts the prior's output. - Test coverage missing on the emergent composed behavior. Mitigations: - Independent verifier agent ( Lesson 16.13 ). Read-only, independent source access. - Explicit handoff contract: "A's output must pass checker C before B starts." - Outcome logging for post-hoc analysis. Groupthink family (Gradient Institute, arXiv:2508.05687) Gradient Institute's report on risk analysis for governed multi-agent systems lists six salient failure modes; this lesson groups five of them as the groupthink family (the sixth is inter-agent communication failure, close to MAST's misalignment category): Monoculture collapse. Same base model or training data → correlated errors. When three agents share an LLM, they share its hallucinations. Conformity bias. Agents adjust toward the loudest or most-confident peer, even when wrong. Deficient ToM. Agents fail to model each other's beliefs; coordination falls apart ( Lesson 16.18 ). Mixed-motive dynamics. Agents with partially-aligned incentives drift toward compromise-middle, which satisfies no one. Cascading reliability failures. One component's error pattern triggers error patterns in dependent components. Cascading example — the retry storm A classic 2026 incident pattern: Copy The fix is classical: circuit breakers . When downstream error rate exceeds threshold, short-circuit with cached or default results. Plus capped retry budgets per request. Circuit breakers are one of the few multi-agent failure mitigations you borrow directly from distributed systems without modification. Memory poisoning (revisited) From Lesson 16.13 : one agent's hallucination becomes shared-memory fact; downstream agents reason on the poisoned fact. In MAST terms, this is a verification gap at the shared-memory layer. Gradual accuracy decay is the symptom. You do not get a crash; you get slow drift that is hard to root-cause. Mitigation: append-only log, provenance, unwritable verifier. Already covered in Lesson 13. STRATUS — specialized agents for incident response STRATUS (NeurIPS 2025) is a multi-agent system for site reliability engineering of cloud services. On the AIOpsLab and ITBench benchmarks it beat earlier SRE agents by at least 1.5x on mitigation success, with separate agents for: Detection agent. Watches for symptom patterns (high disagreement, retry spikes, accuracy drift). Diagnosis agent. Given symptoms, infers likely root cause from the MAST taxonomy. Mitigation agent. Applies a fix, under a safety rule the paper calls transactional no-regression: changes that make things worse can be rolled back. Checking that symptoms clear afterwards plays the validation role. This is SRE-style incident response; the same roles transfer to agent systems. The three roles can all be LLM agents with specialized prompts. The failure-mode audit A 2026 best practice is a quarterly (and per-major-release) failure-mode audit: Trace sample. Collect ~1000 real execution traces. Categorize. For each trace's failures, map to MAST + Groupthink categories. Compute failure-by-category rate. Which categories dominate your system? Rank mitigations. Which fix would eliminate the most failures? Pick 2-3 mitigations. Implement; re-audit next quarter. The discipline is more important than the specific choices. Without audits, failures blend into noise and never get systematically addressed. When systems fail silently The most dangerous failure category is silent correctness failure. A system that fails loudly (crash, exception, alert) can be monitored. A system that produces plausible-but-wrong outputs cannot be detected by exception logs. This is why verification gaps are the most expensive category per failure, even though they are only about a fifth to a quarter of failures by count. Invest in: - Sample-based human review. - Golden-dataset regression tests. - Cross-agent cross-checking on important outputs. Failure vs slow failure Some failures are immediate; some are slow. Immediate failures (timeout, schema mismatch, auth error) are cheap to detect. Slow failures (memory poisoning, monoculture drift, role ambiguity) are expensive to detect and prevent. The 2026 engineering move: instrument slow-failure proxies so you can catch drift before it becomes a visible error. Agreement rate, retry rate, output-length distribution, and edit-distance between consecutive agent versions are all useful proxies. The same idea as a formula Retry amplification. If each call fails independently with probability and a request retries up to times, the expected calls per request are + ⋯ + p r = 1 − p 1 − p r + 1 ​ . For and that is 1.11. Storms come from feedback: if load raises , the sum grows toward calls per request, and every layer that retries multiplies it again. Circuit breaker. Open when the error rate over the last calls exceeds ; after a cooldown , let one probe through (half-open) and close on success. The cooldown must be measured on the same clock as the traffic. Category shares. If a trace can show several failure modes, shares computed per mode need not add up to 100% of traces, and a "per-category share" depends on how modes are counted. Worked example Reading the lesson's storm 200 requests made 328 calls, 1.64 per request, well below the 4 the retry cap allows. The service's failure rate is with load = total calls so far / 10, so it rises from 0.10 at the first request to 0.74 at the last, with or without retries. With the breaker, 87 requests were short-circuited and successes fell from 189 to 113. In this model the breaker protects a service that never recovers, so it trades 76 successes for 188 fewer calls.
